Our approach has been evaluated on common benchmarks, demonstrating improved performance and generalizability over the strong baseline NegBERT (Khandelwal and Sawant, 2020).

label: emnlp
text: Most language modeling methods rely on large-scale data to statistically learn the sequential patterns of words. In this paper, we argue that words are atomic language units but not necessarily atomic semantic units. Inspired by HowNet, we use sememes, the minimum semantic units in human languages, to represent the implicit semantics behind words for language modeling, named Sememe-Driven Language Model (SDLM). More specifically, to predict the next word, SDLM first estimates the sememe distribution given textual context. Afterwards, it regards each sememe as a distinct semantic expert, and these experts jointly identify the most probable senses and the corresponding word. In this way, SDLM enables language models to work beyond word-level manipulation to fine-grained sememe-level semantics, and offers us more powerful tools to fine-tune language models and improve the interpretability as well as the robustness of language models. Experiments on language modeling and the downstream application of headline generation demonstrate the significant effectiveness of SDLM.

label: emnlp
text: Most language modeling techniques depend on large datasets to learn the sequential patterns of words statistically. This paper argues that words are atomic language units, but not necessarily atomic semantic units. Inspired by HowNet, we propose the Sememe-Driven Language Model (SDLM), which uses sememes – the minimum semantic units in human languages – to represent the implicit semantics behind words. SDLM predicts the next word by first estimating the sememe distribution based on the textual context. Each sememe is then treated as a semantic expert, and these experts work together to identify the most probable senses and the corresponding word. This approach allows language models to work at a finer-grained sememe-level semantics, rather than just at the word-level. This results in more powerful tools for fine-tuning language models, and improves their interpretability and robustness. Our experiments on language modeling and headline generation demonstrate the significant effectiveness of SDLM.

label: acl
text: As language technologies become more ubiquitous, there are increasing efforts towards expanding the language diversity and coverage of natural language processing (NLP) systems. Arguably, the most important factor influencing the quality of modern NLP systems is data availability. In this work, we study the geographical representativeness of NLP datasets, aiming to quantify if and by how much do NLP datasets match the expected needs of the language speakers. In doing so, we use entity recognition and linking systems, also making important observations about their cross-lingual consistency and giving suggestions for more robust evaluation. Last, we explore some geographical and economic factors that may explain the observed dataset distributions.

label: acl
text: As language technologies become more widespread, there is a growing emphasis on expanding the diversity of languages and the coverage of natural language processing (NLP) systems. The quality of modern NLP systems is largely influenced by the availability of data. In our study, we examine the geographical representation of NLP datasets and aim to determine if they meet the needs of language speakers and to what extent. To do this, we use entity recognition and linking systems and make important observations about their cross-lingual consistency. We also provide suggestions for more robust evaluation. Finally, we investigate geographical and economic factors that may explain the distribution of datasets.

label: coling
text: Recently, Mixture-of-Experts (short as MoE) architecture has achieved remarkable success in increasing the model capacity of large-scale language models. However, MoE requires incorporating significantly more parameters than the base model being extended. In this paper, we propose building a parameter-efficient MoE architecture by sharing information across experts. We adopt matrix product operator (MPO, a tensor decomposition from quantum many-body physics) to reconstruct the parameter matrix in the expert layer and increase model capacity for pre-trained language models by sharing parameters of the central tensor (containing the core information) among different experts while enabling the specificity through the auxiliary tensors (complementing the central tensor) of different experts. To address the unbalanced optimization issue, we further design the gradient mask strategy for the MPO-based MoE architecture. Extensive experiments based on T5 and GPT-2 show improved performance and efficiency of the pre-trained language model (27.2x reduction in total parameters for the superior model performance, compared with the Switch Transformers). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/MPO/MPOE.

label: coling
text: Recently, the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has achieved remarkable success in increasing the capacity of large-scale language models. However, this approach requires incorporating significantly more parameters than the base model. In this paper, we propose a parameter-efficient MoE architecture by sharing information across experts. We use matrix product operator (MPO) decomposition to reconstruct the expert layer's parameter matrix and increase the model's capacity by sharing the central tensor's parameters among different experts while enabling specificity through the auxiliary tensors of each expert. To address unbalanced optimization, we design a gradient mask strategy for the MPO-based MoE architecture. Our experiments on T5 and GPT-2 show improved performance and efficiency, with a 27.2x reduction in total parameters compared to Switch Transformers. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/MPO/MPOE.

label: emnlp
text: A rich line of research attempts to make deep neural networks more transparent by generating human-interpretable `explanations' of their decision process, especially for interactive tasks like Visual Question Answering (VQA). In this work, we analyze if existing explanations indeed make a VQA model — its responses as well as failures — more predictable to a human. Surprisingly, we find that they do not. On the other hand, we find that human-in-the-loop approaches that treat the model as a black-box do.

label: emnlp
text: A wealth of research is devoted to improving the transparency of deep neural networks by producing human-understandable explanations of their decision-making processes, particularly in interactive tasks such as Visual Question Answering (VQA). Our study examines whether these existing explanations effectively make the responses and failures of a VQA model more predictable to humans. Surprisingly, we discovered that they do not. However, we found that human-in-the-loop methods that treat the model as a black box are effective.

label: naacl
text: In document-level event extraction (DEE) task, event arguments always scatter across sentences (across-sentence issue) and multipleevents may lie in one document (multi-event issue). In this paper, we argue that the relation information of event arguments is of greatsignificance for addressing the above two issues, and propose a new DEE framework which can model the relation dependencies, calledRelation-augmented Document-level Event Extraction (ReDEE). More specifically, this framework features a novel and tailored transformer,named as Relation-augmented Attention Transformer (RAAT). RAAT is scalable to capture multi-scale and multi-amount argument relations. To further leverage relation information, we introduce a separate event relation prediction task and adopt multi-task learning method to explicitly enhance event extraction performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which can achieve state-of-the-art performance on two public datasets.Our code is available at https://github.com/TencentYoutuResearch/RAAT.

label: naacl
text: In the task of document-level event extraction (DEE), event arguments are often dispersed across sentences and multiple events may occur in a single document. This paper presents a new DEE framework, Relation-augmented Document-level Event Extraction (ReDEE), which leverages the significance of relation information to address these issues. The framework features a novel transformer, the Relation-augmented Attention Transformer (RAAT), which is capable of capturing multi-scale and multi-amount argument relations. Additionally, the framework includes a separate event relation prediction task and employs multi-task learning to improve event extraction performance. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art results on two public datasets and our code is available on GitHub.

label: acl
text: Good quality monolingual word embeddings (MWEs) can be built for languages which have large amounts of unlabeled text. MWEs can be aligned to bilingual spaces using only a few thousand word translation pairs. For low resource languages training MWEs monolingually results in MWEs of poor quality, and thus poor bilingual word embeddings (BWEs) as well. This paper proposes a new approach for building BWEs in which the vector space of the high resource source language is used as a starting point for training an embedding space for the low resource target language. By using the source vectors as anchors the vector spaces are automatically aligned during training. We experiment on English-German, English-Hiligaynon and English-Macedonian. We show that our approach results not only in improved BWEs and bilingual lexicon induction performance, but also in improved target language MWE quality as measured using monolingual word similarity.

label: acl
text: Improved Quality Monolingual Word Embeddings (MWEs) can be created for languages that have large amounts of unlabeled text. Aligning MWEs to bilingual spaces is possible using only a few thousand word translation pairs. However, training MWEs monolingually for low resource languages results in poor quality MWEs and poor bilingual word embeddings (BWEs). This paper presents a new approach for building BWEs, which uses the vector space of a high resource source language as a starting point for training an embedding space for a low resource target language. During training, the source vectors serve as anchors, automatically aligning the vector spaces. Results from experiments on English-German, English-Hiligaynon, and English-Macedonian show that this approach leads to improved BWEs and bilingual lexicon induction performance, as well as improved target language MWE quality, as measured by monolingual word similarity.

label: emnlp
text: In this paper, we study how to learn a semantic parser of state-of-the-art accuracy with less supervised training data. We conduct our study on WikiSQL, the largest hand-annotated semantic parsing dataset to date. First, we demonstrate that question generation is an effective method that empowers us to learn a state-of-the-art neural network based semantic parser with thirty percent of the supervised training data. Second, we show that applying question generation to the full supervised training data further improves the state-of-the-art model. In addition, we observe that there is a logarithmic relationship between the accuracy of a semantic parser and the amount of training data.

label: emnlp
text: This paper explores the possibility of learning a state-of-the-art semantic parser with reduced supervised training data. Our study is based on WikiSQL, the largest hand-annotated semantic parsing dataset available. We show that question generation is an effective technique for learning a neural network-based semantic parser with only 30% of the supervised training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying question generation to the full supervised training data enhances the performance of the state-of-the-art model. Our findings also reveal a logarithmic relationship between the accuracy of a semantic parser and the amount of training data.

label: naacl
text: We present a reading comprehension challenge in which questions can only be answered by taking into account information from multiple sentences. We solicit and verify questions and answers for this challenge through a 4-step crowdsourcing experiment. Our challenge dataset contains 6,500+ questions for 1000+ paragraphs across 7 different domains (elementary school science, news, travel guides, fiction stories, etc) bringing in linguistic diversity to the texts and to the questions wordings. On a subset of our dataset, we found human solvers to achieve an F1-score of 88.1%. We analyze a range of baselines, including a recent state-of-art reading comprehension system, and demonstrate the difficulty of this challenge, despite a high human performance. The dataset is the first to study multi-sentence inference at scale, with an open-ended set of question types that requires reasoning skills.

label: naacl
text: We present a reading comprehension challenge in which questions can only be answered by taking into account information from multiple sentences. To create this challenge, we conducted a 4-step crowdsourcing experiment to solicit and verify questions and answers. Our challenge dataset contains 6,500+ questions for 1,000+ paragraphs across 7 different domains, including elementary school science, news, travel guides, fiction stories, and more, providing linguistic diversity in both the texts and question wordings. Our analysis of a subset of the dataset showed that human solvers achieved an F1-score of 88.1%. We evaluated a range of baselines, including a state-of-the-art reading comprehension system, and found that despite high human performance, the challenge remains difficult. This dataset represents the first study of multi-sentence inference at scale, featuring an open-ended set of question types that require reasoning skills.

label: emnlp
text: Sentiment expression in microblog posts can be affected by user's personal character, opinion bias, political stance and so on. Most of existing personalized microblog sentiment classification methods suffer from the insufficiency of discriminative tweets for personalization learning. We observed that microblog users have consistent individuality and opinion bias in different languages. Based on this observation, in this paper we propose a novel user-attention-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model with adversarial cross-lingual learning framework. The user attention mechanism is leveraged in CNN model to capture user's language-specific individuality from the posts. Then the attention-based CNN model is incorporated into a novel adversarial cross-lingual learning framework, in which with the help of user properties as bridge between languages, we can extract the language-specific features and language-independent features to enrich the user post representation so as to alleviate the data insufficiency problem. Results on English and Chinese microblog datasets confirm that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baseline algorithms with large margins.

label: emnlp
text: The sentiment expression in microblog posts can be influenced by various factors, including the user's personal character, opinion bias, political stance, etc. However, most existing personalized microblog sentiment classification methods struggle with the limited availability of discriminative tweets for personalization learning. Our study found that microblog users tend to exhibit consistent individuality and opinion bias across different languages. To address these challenges, we propose a novel user-attention-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model with an adversarial cross-lingual learning framework. The user attention mechanism in the CNN model captures the user's language-specific individuality from their posts. Our adversarial cross-lingual learning framework incorporates the attention-based CNN model and uses user properties as a bridge between languages to extract both language-specific and language-independent features to enhance the representation of the user's posts, effectively overcoming the data insufficiency problem. Our results, based on English and Chinese microblog datasets, show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baseline algorithms by a significant margin.

label: acl
text: A language-independent representation of meaning is one of the most coveted dreams in Natural Language Understanding. With this goal in mind, several formalisms have been proposed as frameworks for meaning representation in Semantic Parsing. And yet, the dependencies these formalisms share with respect to language-specific repositories of knowledge make the objective of closing the gap between high- and low-resourced languages hard to accomplish. In this paper, we present the BabelNet Meaning Representation (BMR), an interlingual formalism that abstracts away from language-specific constraints by taking advantage of the multilingual semantic resources of BabelNet and VerbAtlas. We describe the rationale behind the creation of BMR and put forward BMR 1.0, a dataset labeled entirely according to the new formalism. Moreover, we show how BMR is able to outperform previous formalisms thanks to its fully-semantic framing, which enables top-notch multilingual parsing and generation. We release the code at https://github.com/SapienzaNLP/bmr.

label: acl
text: The dream of having a language-independent representation of meaning is one of the most sought-after goals in the field of Natural Language Understanding. To achieve this objective, several formalisms have been proposed as frameworks for semantic parsing. However, the reliance of these formalisms on language-specific repositories of knowledge makes it challenging to bridge the gap between high- and low-resourced languages. This paper introduces the BabelNet Meaning Representation (BMR), an interlingual formalism that leverages the multilingual semantic resources of BabelNet and VerbAtlas to abstract away from language-specific constraints. The authors describe the motivation behind creating BMR and present BMR 1.0, a dataset labeled according to the new formalism. They also demonstrate how BMR outperforms previous formalisms thanks to its fully-semantic framing, which enables superior multilingual parsing and generation. The code for BMR is available at https://github.com/SapienzaNLP/bmr.

label: acl
text: Training semantic parsers from weak supervision (denotations) rather than strong supervision (programs) complicates training in two ways. First, a large search space of potential programs needs to be explored at training time to find a correct program. Second, spurious programs that accidentally lead to a correct denotation add noise to training. In this work we propose that in closed worlds with clear semantic types, one can substantially alleviate these problems by utilizing an abstract representation, where tokens in both the language utterance and program are lifted to an abstract form. We show that these abstractions can be defined with a handful of lexical rules and that they result in sharing between different examples that alleviates the difficulties in training. To test our approach, we develop the first semantic parser for CNLVR, a challenging visual reasoning dataset, where the search space is large and overcoming spuriousness is critical, because denotations are either TRUE or FALSE, and thus random programs are likely to lead to a correct denotation. Our method substantially improves performance, and reaches 82.5% accuracy, a 14.7% absolute accuracy improvement compared to the best reported accuracy so far.

label: acl
text: Training semantic parsers from weak supervision (denotations) instead of strong supervision (programs) is complicated by two factors. Firstly, a vast search space of potential programs must be explored during training to find the correct program. Secondly, the presence of spurious programs that produce correct denotations adds noise to the training process. To address these challenges, we propose utilizing an abstract representation in closed worlds with well-defined semantic types. This abstract representation lifts tokens in both the language utterance and program to a higher level, making it easier to find the correct program. Our approach is based on a few lexical rules and results in shared information between examples, which reduces the difficulties of training. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we develop the first semantic parser for CNLVR, a challenging visual reasoning dataset. Our parser achieves 82.5% accuracy, a 14.7% improvement over the previous best result.

label: coling
text: As political attitudes have diverged ideologically in the United States, political speech has diverged lingusitically. The ever-widening polarization between the US political parties is accelerated by an erosion of mutual understanding between them. We aim to make these communities more comprehensible to each other with a framework that probes community-specific responses to the same survey questions using community language models CommunityLM. In our framework we identify committed partisan members for each community on Twitter and fine-tune LMs on the tweets authored by them. We then assess the worldviews of the two groups using prompt-based probing of their corresponding LMs, with prompts that elicit opinions about public figures and groups surveyed by the American National Election Studies (ANES) 2020 Exploratory Testing Survey. We compare the responses generated by the LMs to the ANES survey results, and find a level of alignment that greatly exceeds several baseline methods. Our work aims to show that we can use community LMs to query the worldview of any group of people given a sufficiently large sample of their social media discussions or media diet.

label: coling
text: As political attitudes in the United States become increasingly divided along ideological lines, political speech has also become more linguistically diverse. The widening polarization between US political parties is exacerbated by a breakdown in mutual understanding. To address this, we have developed a framework, CommunityLM, that allows us to probe the community-specific responses to the same survey questions using community language models. Our framework identifies committed partisan members for each community on Twitter and fine-tunes language models on their tweets. We then use prompt-based probing to assess the worldviews of the two groups, using prompts that elicit opinions about public figures and groups surveyed by the American National Election Studies (ANES) 2020 Exploratory Testing Survey. Our results show that the responses generated by the language models align with the ANES survey results to a greater extent than several baseline methods. Our work demonstrates that community language models can be used to query the worldview of any group of people given a large enough sample of their social media discussions or media consumption.

label: naacl
text: Targeted Sentiment Analysis (TSA) is a central task for generating insights from consumer reviews. Such content is extremely diverse, with sites like Amazon or Yelp containing reviews on products and businesses from many different domains. A real-world TSA system should gracefully handle that diversity. This can be achieved by a multi-domain model – one that is robust to the domain of the analyzed texts, and performs well on various domains. To address this scenario, we present a multi-domain TSA system based on augmenting a given training set with diverse weak labels from assorted domains. These are obtained through self-training on the Yelp reviews corpus. Extensive experiments with our approach on three evaluation datasets across different domains demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution. We further analyze how restrictions imposed on the available labeled data affect the performance, and compare the proposed method to the costly alternative of manually gathering diverse TSA labeled data. Our results and analysis show that our approach is a promising step towards a practical domain-robust TSA system.

label: naacl
text: Targeted Sentiment Analysis (TSA) plays a crucial role in uncovering insights from consumer reviews. However, the content of these reviews can be highly diverse, ranging from products to businesses, and can be found on various websites such as Amazon and Yelp. To handle this diversity, a multi-domain model is necessary, one that can perform well across various domains and is robust to the domain of the analyzed text. To achieve this, we propose a multi-domain TSA system that augments a given training set with diverse weak labels from various domains. These labels are obtained through self-training on the Yelp reviews corpus. Our approach has been extensively evaluated on three evaluation datasets across different domains, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our results and analysis also show that our approach outperforms the costly alternative of manually gathering diverse TSA labeled data, and highlights the impact of restrictions imposed on available labeled data on performance. Our solution is a promising step towards a practical, domain-robust TSA system.

label: naacl
text: Understanding how social power structures affect the way we interact with one another is of great interest to social scientists who want to answer fundamental questions about human behavior, as well as to computer scientists who want to build automatic methods to infer the social contexts of interactions. In this paper, we employ advancements in extra-propositional semantics extraction within NLP to study how author commitment reflects the social context of an interactions. Specifically, we investigate whether the level of commitment expressed by individuals in an organizational interaction reflects the hierarchical power structures they are part of. We find that subordinates use significantly more instances of non-commitment than superiors. More importantly, we also find that subordinates attribute propositions to other agents more often than superiors do — an aspect that has not been studied before. Finally, we show that enriching lexical features with commitment labels captures important distinctions in social meanings.

label: naacl
text: Social scientists and computer scientists alike are intrigued by the impact of social power structures on human interaction. To further explore this topic, this paper utilizes advancements in NLP's extra-propositional semantics extraction to examine the relationship between author commitment and social context in organizational interactions. Our study focuses on whether the level of commitment expressed by individuals reflects the power dynamics within their hierarchy. The results indicate that subordinates use more instances of non-commitment and attribute propositions to other agents more frequently than superiors. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating commitment labels into lexical features enhances the capture of social meaning distinctions.

label: acl
text: Neural vector representations are ubiquitous throughout all subfields of NLP. While word vectors have been studied in much detail, thus far only little light has been shed on the properties of sentence embeddings. In this paper, we assess to what extent prominent sentence embedding methods exhibit select semantic properties. We propose a framework that generate triplets of sentences to explore how changes in the syntactic structure or semantics of a given sentence affect the similarities obtained between their sentence embeddings.

label: acl
text: The use of neural vector representations is widespread in all areas of NLP. Although much research has been conducted on word vectors, there has been limited study on the properties of sentence embeddings. In this paper, we evaluate the extent to which prominent sentence embedding methods possess specific semantic properties. We present a framework that creates triplets of sentences to investigate how changes in a sentence's syntax or meaning impact the similarity between their sentence embeddings.

label: naacl
text: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) are widely used structured models, both of which can be represented as factor graph grammars (FGGs), a powerful formalism capable of describing a wide range of models. Recent research found it beneficial to use large state spaces for HMMs and PCFGs. However, inference with large state spaces is computationally demanding, especially for PCFGs. To tackle this challenge, we leverage tensor rank decomposition (aka. CPD) to decrease inference computational complexities for a subset of FGGs subsuming HMMs and PCFGs. We apply CPD on the factors of an FGG and then construct a new FGG defined in the rank space. Inference with the new FGG produces the same result but has a lower time complexity when the rank size is smaller than the state size. We conduct experiments on HMM language modeling and unsupervised PCFG parsing, showing better performance than previous work. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/VPeterV/RankSpace-Models.

label: naacl
text: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) are two widely used structured models that can be represented as factor graph grammars (FGGs). Recent research has found that using large state spaces in these models can significantly improve performance. However, the computational demands of inference with large state spaces, especially in PCFGs, can be challenging. To address this challenge, we use tensor rank decomposition (CPD) to reduce the computational complexity of inference for a subset of FGGs that include HMMs and PCFGs. We apply CPD to the FGG factors and then construct a new FGG in the rank space, which produces the same results as the original FGG but with a lower time complexity if the rank size is smaller than the state size. Our experiments on HMM language modeling and unsupervised PCFG parsing show improved performance compared to previous work. Our code is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/VPeterV/RankSpace-Models.

label: naacl
text: Efficient word representations play an important role in solving various problems related to Natural Language Processing (NLP), data mining, text mining etc. The issue of data sparsity poses a great challenge in creating efficient word representation model for solving the underlying problem. The problem is more intensified in resource-poor scenario due to the absence of sufficient amount of corpus. In this work we propose to minimize the effect of data sparsity by leveraging bilingual word embeddings learned through a parallel corpus. We train and evaluate Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) based architecture for aspect level sentiment classification. The neural network architecture is further assisted by the hand-crafted features for the prediction. We show the efficacy of the proposed model against state-of-the-art methods in two experimental setups i.e. multi-lingual and cross-lingual.

label: naacl
text: Efficient word representations are crucial in addressing various Natural Language Processing (NLP), data mining, and text mining problems. However, the challenge of data sparsity poses a significant obstacle in creating an efficient word representation model. This issue is exacerbated in resource-limited scenarios due to the lack of sufficient corpus. To mitigate the effects of data sparsity, we propose using bilingual word embeddings learned from a parallel corpus. We train and evaluate a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for aspect-level sentiment classification, which is further enhanced by hand-crafted features for prediction. Our proposed model demonstrates its efficacy against state-of-the-art methods in both multi-lingual and cross-lingual experimental setups.

label: coling
text: Argumentation mining (AM) requires the identification of complex discourse structures and has lately been applied with success monolingually. In this work, we show that the existing resources are, however, not adequate for assessing cross-lingual AM, due to their heterogeneity or lack of complexity. We therefore create suitable parallel corpora by (human and machine) translating a popular AM dataset consisting of persuasive student essays into German, French, Spanish, and Chinese. We then compare (i) annotation projection and (ii) bilingual word embeddings based direct transfer strategies for cross-lingual AM, finding that the former performs considerably better and almost eliminates the loss from cross-lingual transfer. Moreover, we find that annotation projection works equally well when using either costly human or cheap machine translations. Our code and data are available at http://github.com/UKPLab/coling2018-xling_argument_mining.

label: coling
text: The field of Argumentation Mining (AM) involves identifying complex discourse structures and has seen recent success in monolingual applications. However, current resources are not suitable for cross-lingual AM due to their heterogeneity or lack of complexity. To address this issue, we have created parallel corpora by translating a popular AM dataset of persuasive student essays into German, French, Spanish, and Chinese through both human and machine translation methods. We then evaluated two cross-lingual AM transfer strategies: annotation projection and bilingual word embeddings-based direct transfer. Our results showed that annotation projection outperforms the latter, almost completely eliminating the loss from cross-lingual transfer. Furthermore, we found that annotation projection works equally well with both human and machine translations. The code and data for this study can be found at http://github.com/UKPLab/coling2018-xling_argument_mining.

label: coling
text: Learning the embeddings of knowledge graphs (KG) is vital in artificial intelligence, and can benefit various downstream applications, such as recommendation and question answering. In recent years, many research efforts have been proposed for knowledge graph embedding (KGE). However, most previous KGE methods ignore the semantic similarity between the related entities and entity-relation couples in different triples since they separately optimize each triple with the scoring function. To address this problem, we propose a simple yet efficient contrastive learning framework for tensor decomposition based (TDB) KGE, which can shorten the semantic distance of the related entities and entity-relation couples in different triples and thus improve the performance of KGE. We evaluate our proposed method on three standard KGE datasets: WN18RR, FB15k-237 and YAGO3-10. Our method can yield some new state-of-the-art results, achieving 51.2% MRR, 46.8% Hits@1 on the WN18RR dataset, 37.8% MRR, 28.6% Hits@1 on FB15k-237 dataset, and 59.1% MRR, 51.8% Hits@1 on the YAGO3-10 dataset.

label: coling
text: Embedding knowledge graphs (KG) is crucial in artificial intelligence and can enhance various downstream applications, such as recommendation and question answering. Despite numerous research efforts in knowledge graph embedding (KGE) in recent years, most methods overlook the semantic similarity between related entities and entity-relation couples in different triples, as they optimize each triple separately using a scoring function. To tackle this issue, we present a simple yet effective contrastive learning framework for tensor decomposition-based (TDB) KGE. This framework shortens the semantic distance between related entities and entity-relation couples in different triples, thereby improving the performance of KGE. Our proposed method was evaluated on three standard KGE datasets: WN18RR, FB15k-237, and YAGO3-10. Our results outperformed the state-of-the-art, achieving 51.2% MRR and 46.8% Hits@1 on the WN18RR dataset, 37.8% MRR and 28.6% Hits@1 on FB15k-237, and 59.1% MRR and 51.8% Hits@1 on YAGO3-10.

label: naacl
text: Deep learning (DL) is being used extensively for text classification. However, researchers have demonstrated the vulnerability of such classifiers to adversarial attacks. Attackers modify the text in a way which misleads the classifier while keeping the original meaning close to intact. State-of-the-art (SOTA) attack algorithms follow the general principle of making minimal changes to the text so as to not jeopardize semantics. Taking advantage of this we propose a novel and intuitive defense strategy called Sample Shielding.It is attacker and classifier agnostic, does not require any reconfiguration of the classifier or external resources and is simple to implement. Essentially, we sample subsets of the input text, classify them and summarize these into a final decision. We shield three popular DL text classifiers with Sample Shielding, test their resilience against four SOTA attackers across three datasets in a realistic threat setting. Even when given the advantage of knowing about our shielding strategy the adversary's attack success rate is =10% with only one exception and often  5%. Additionally, Sample Shielding maintains near original accuracy when applied to original texts. Crucially, we show that the `make minimal changes' approach of SOTA attackers leads to critical vulnerabilities that can be defended against with an intuitive sampling strategy.

label: naacl
text: The widespread use of Deep Learning (DL) for text classification has been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where attackers modify the text in a way that misleads the classifier while keeping the original meaning nearly intact. State-of-the-art (SOTA) attack algorithms aim to make minimal changes to the text to preserve semantics. To address this vulnerability, we propose a novel defense strategy called Sample Shielding. This attacker and classifier agnostic approach does not require any reconfiguration of the classifier or external resources and is easy to implement. The strategy involves sampling subsets of the input text, classifying them, and summarizing the results into a final decision. We test the resilience of three popular DL text classifiers against four SOTA attackers across three datasets in a realistic threat setting. Even when the adversary has knowledge of our shielding strategy, the attack success rate is reduced to 10% or less in most cases, with only one exception. Furthermore, Sample Shielding maintains near original accuracy when applied to unmodified text. Our results demonstrate that the minimal changes approach of SOTA attackers creates critical vulnerabilities that can be defended against with a simple sampling strategy.

label: emnlp
text: We present a simple and accurate span-based model for semantic role labeling (SRL). Our model directly takes into account all possible argument spans and scores them for each label. At decoding time, we greedily select higher scoring labeled spans. One advantage of our model is to allow us to design and use span-level features, that are difficult to use in token-based BIO tagging approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that our ensemble model achieves the state-of-the-art results, 87.4 F1 and 87.0 F1 on the CoNLL-2005 and 2012 datasets, respectively.

label: emnlp
text: We present a simple, yet accurate, span-based model for semantic role labeling (SRL). Our model takes into consideration all potential argument spans and assigns scores to each label. During the decoding process, we select the highest scoring labeled spans using a greedy approach. One of the key advantages of our model is that it enables us to incorporate span-level features, which are challenging to use in token-based BIO tagging methods. Our ensemble model has achieved state-of-the-art results, with an F1 score of 87.4 on the CoNLL-2005 dataset and 87.0 on the CoNLL-2012 dataset.

label: naacl
text: Neural information retrieval (IR) has greatly advanced search and other knowledge-intensive language tasks. While many neural IR methods encode queries and documents into single-vector representations, late interaction models produce multi-vector representations at the granularity of each token and decompose relevance modeling into scalable token-level computations. This decomposition has been shown to make late interaction more effective, but it inflates the space footprint of these models by an order of magnitude. In this work, we introduce ColBERTv2, a retriever that couples an aggressive residual compression mechanism with a denoised supervision strategy to simultaneously improve the quality and space footprint of late interaction. We evaluate ColBERTv2 across a wide range of benchmarks, establishing state-of-the-art quality within and outside the training domain while reducing the space footprint of late interaction models by 6–10x.

label: naacl
text: The neural information retrieval (IR) has significantly improved search and other language tasks that require knowledge. While many neural IR methods encode queries and documents into single-vector representations, late interaction models generate multi-vector representations at the token level and divide relevance modeling into scalable token-level computations. This division has been proven to make late interaction more effective, but it also increases the storage space of these models by a large margin. In this study, we present ColBERTv2, a retriever that combines a powerful residual compression mechanism with a denoised supervision strategy to enhance the quality and reduce the storage space of late interaction models. We evaluate ColBERTv2 on a wide range of benchmarks and find that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of quality both within and outside the training domain, while reducing the storage space of late interaction models by 6-10 times.

label: acl
text: Current Open-Domain Question Answering (ODQA) models typically include a retrieving module and a reading module, where the retriever selects potentially relevant passages from open-source documents for a given question, and the reader produces an answer based on the retrieved passages. The recently proposed Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) framework is a representative example, which is built on top of a dense passage retriever and a generative reader, achieving the state-of-the-art performance. In this paper we further improve the FiD approach by introducing a knowledge-enhanced version, namely KG-FiD. Our new model uses a knowledge graph to establish the structural relationship among the retrieved passages, and a graph neural network (GNN) to re-rank the passages and select only a top few for further processing. Our experiments on common ODQA benchmark datasets (Natural Questions and TriviaQA) demonstrate that KG-FiD can achieve comparable or better performance in answer prediction than FiD, with less than 40% of the computation cost.

text: In this paper we implement and compare 7 different data augmentation strategies for the task of automatic scoring of children's ability to understand others' thoughts, feelings, and desires (or “mindreading”). We recruit in-domain experts to re-annotate augmented samples and determine to what extent each strategy preserves the original rating. We also carry out multiple experiments to measure how much each augmentation strategy improves the performance of automatic scoring systems. To determine the capabilities of automatic systems to generalize to unseen data, we create UK-MIND-20 - a new corpus of children's performance on tests of mindreading, consisting of 10,320 question-answer pairs. We obtain a new state-of-the-art performance on the MIND-CA corpus, improving macro-F1-score by 6 points. Results indicate that both the number of training examples and the quality of the augmentation strategies affect the performance of the systems. The task-specific augmentations generally outperform task-agnostic augmentations. Automatic augmentations based on vectors (GloVe, FastText) perform the worst. We find that systems trained on MIND-CA generalize well to UK-MIND-20. We demonstrate that data augmentation strategies also improve the performance on unseen data.

text: In this paper, we compare and implement seven different data augmentation techniques for automatic scoring of children's ability to understand others' thoughts, feelings, and desires, also known as "mindreading." To assess the preservation of original ratings, we have in-domain experts re-annotate augmented samples. We conduct multiple experiments to evaluate the impact of each augmentation technique on the performance of automatic scoring systems. To assess the generalization capability of these systems, we create a new corpus of children's mindreading performance, UK-MIND-20, consisting of 10,320 question-answer pairs. Our results show a new state-of-the-art performance on the MIND-CA corpus, with a 6-point increase in macro-F1-score. Our findings indicate that both the number of training examples and the quality of the augmentation strategies significantly impact the performance of automatic systems. Task-specific augmentations perform better than task-agnostic ones, while automatic augmentations based on vectors (GloVe, FastText) yield the worst results. Our results also demonstrate that data augmentation strategies can improve the performance of automatic systems on unseen data, as systems trained on MIND-CA generalize well to UK-MIND-20.

label: naacl
text: Answering complex questions is a time-consuming activity for humans that requires reasoning and integration of information. Recent work on reading comprehension made headway in answering simple questions, but tackling complex questions is still an ongoing research challenge. Conversely, semantic parsers have been successful at handling compositionality, but only when the information resides in a target knowledge-base. In this paper, we present a novel framework for answering broad and complex questions, assuming answering simple questions is possible using a search engine and a reading comprehension model. We propose to decompose complex questions into a sequence of simple questions, and compute the final answer from the sequence of answers. To illustrate the viability of our approach, we create a new dataset of complex questions, ComplexWebQuestions, and present a model that decomposes questions and interacts with the web to compute an answer. We empirically demonstrate that question decomposition improves performance from 20.8 precision@1 to 27.5 precision@1 on this new dataset.

label: naacl
text: The process of answering complex questions can be time-consuming for humans as it entails reasoning and integrating information. Although recent advancements in reading comprehension have allowed for the answering of simple questions, tackling complex questions remains a challenge in ongoing research. On the other hand, semantic parsers have proven successful in handling compositionality, but only when the information is contained within a designated knowledge-base. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for answering broad and complex questions, which assumes that simple questions can be answered using a search engine and a reading comprehension model. Our approach involves decomposing complex questions into a series of simple questions, and then combining the answers to get the final answer. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, we present a new dataset, ComplexWebQuestions, and show how our model can decompose questions and interact with the web to obtain an answer. Our results show that question decomposition improves performance, with precision@1 increasing from 20.8 to 27.5 on this new dataset.

label: acl
text: This work addresses the question of the localization of syntactic information encoded in the transformers representations. We tackle this question from two perspectives, considering the object-past participle agreement in French, by identifying, first, in which part of the sentence and, second, in which part of the representation the syntactic information is encoded. The results of our experiments, using probing, causal analysis and feature selection method, show that syntactic information is encoded locally in a way consistent with the French grammar.

label: acl
text: This work explores the localization of syntactic information in the representations of transformers. We approach this question from two angles, focusing on the object-past participle agreement in French. Our aim is to determine the location of the syntactic information within the sentence and the representation. Our experiments, utilizing probing, causal analysis, and feature selection techniques, demonstrate that the syntactic information is locally encoded and aligns with French grammar.

label: coling
text: Neural topic models have been widely used in discovering the latent semantics from a corpus. Recently, there are several researches on hierarchical neural topic models since the relationships among topics are valuable for data analysis and exploration. However, the existing hierarchical neural topic models are limited to generate a single topic tree. In this study, we present a nonparametric forest-structured neural topic model by firstly applying the self-attention mechanism to capture parent-child topic relationships, and then build a sparse directed acyclic graph to form a topic forest. Experiments indicate that our model can automatically learn a forest-structured topic hierarchy with indefinite numbers of trees and leaves, and significantly outperforms the baseline models on topic hierarchical rationality and affinity.

label: coling
text: Neural topic models have been widely used to uncover latent semantics within a corpus. Recently, there has been a surge of research on hierarchical neural topic models, as the relationships between topics are crucial for data analysis and exploration. However, existing hierarchical neural topic models are limited to generating a single topic tree. In this study, we present a non-parametric forest-structured neural topic model that utilizes self-attention mechanisms to capture parent-child topic relationships and forms a sparse directed acyclic graph to create a topic forest. Our experiments show that our model can learn a forest-structured topic hierarchy with an indefinite number of trees and leaves, outperforming baseline models in terms of topic hierarchical rationality and affinity.

label: coling
text: This paper provides an evaluation of a wide range of advanced sentence-level Quality Estimation models, including Support Vector Regression, Ride Regression, Neural Networks, Gaussian Processes, Bayesian Neural Networks, Deep Kernel Learning and Deep Gaussian Processes. Beside the accurateness, our main concerns are also the robustness of Quality Estimation models. Our work raises the difficulty in building strong models. Specifically, we show that Quality Estimation models often behave differently in Quality Estimation feature space, depending on whether the scale of feature space is small, medium or large. We also show that Quality Estimation models often behave differently in evaluation settings, depending on whether test data come from the same domain as the training data or not. Our work suggests several strong candidates to use in different circumstances.

label: coling
text: This paper evaluates a variety of advanced sentence-level Quality Estimation models, including Support Vector Regression, Ridge Regression, Neural Networks, Gaussian Processes, Bayesian Neural Networks, Deep Kernel Learning, and Deep Gaussian Processes. Our focus is not only on the accuracy of these models, but also on their robustness. We highlight the challenges in developing robust models and demonstrate that the behavior of Quality Estimation models can vary depending on the size of the feature space and the domain of the test data. Our findings provide several strong candidates for use in different circumstances.

label: acl
text: Dependency trees have been intensively used with graph neural networks for aspect-based sentiment classification. Though being effective, such methods rely on external dependency parsers, which can be unavailable for low-resource languages or perform worse in low-resource domains. In addition, dependency trees are also not optimized for aspect-based sentiment classification. In this paper, we propose an aspect-specific and language-agnostic discrete latent opinion tree model as an alternative structure to explicit dependency trees. To ease the learning of complicated structured latent variables, we build a connection between aspect-to-context attention scores and syntactic distances, inducing trees from the attention scores. Results on six English benchmarks and one Chinese dataset show that our model can achieve competitive performance and interpretability.

label: acl
text: The use of dependency trees in conjunction with graph neural networks has been extensively explored for aspect-based sentiment classification. However, these methods are reliant on external dependency parsers, which may not be available for low-resource languages or may perform poorly in low-resource domains. Moreover, dependency trees are not optimized for aspect-based sentiment classification. To address these limitations, we propose a novel aspect-specific and language-agnostic discrete latent opinion tree model as an alternative to explicit dependency trees. To facilitate the learning of complex structured latent variables, we establish a link between aspect-to-context attention scores and syntactic distances, which allows us to derive trees from the attention scores. Our experiments on six English benchmarks and one Chinese dataset demonstrate that our model offers competitive performance and interpretability.

label: coling
text: With the rapid growth of scientific papers, understanding the changes and trends in a research area is rather time-consuming. The first challenge is to find related and comparable articles for the research. Comparative citations compare co-cited papers in a citation sentence and can serve as good guidance for researchers to track a research area. We thus go through comparative citations to find comparable objects and build a comparative scientific summarization corpus (CSSC). And then, we propose the comparative graph-based summarization (CGSUM) method to create comparative summaries using citations as guidance. The comparative graph is constructed using sentences as nodes and three different relationships of sentences as edges. The relationship that sentences occur in the same paper is used to calculate the salience of sentences, the relationship that sentences occur in two different papers is used to calculate the difference between sentences, and the relationship that sentences are related to citations is used to calculate the commonality of sentences. Experiments show that CGSUM outperforms comparative baselines on CSSC and performs well on DUC2006 and DUC2007.

label: coling
text: With the exponential increase in scientific papers, it can be challenging to stay up-to-date with changes and trends in a particular research area. One of the biggest obstacles is finding relevant and comparable articles for one's research. To aid researchers in this process, comparative citations - which compare co-cited papers in a citation sentence - can serve as a useful tool. To make use of this, we have created a comparative scientific summarization corpus (CSSC) by analyzing comparative citations. Our proposed method, the comparative graph-based summarization (CGSUM), uses citations as guidance to create comparative summaries. The comparative graph is constructed using sentences as nodes and three different types of relationships between sentences as edges. These relationships calculate the salience of sentences, the difference between sentences, and the commonality of sentences. Our experiments show that CGSUM outperforms comparative baselines on CSSC and performs well on DUC2006 and DUC2007.

label: acl
text: Dynamic oracles provide strong supervision for training constituency parsers with exploration, but must be custom defined for a given parser's transition system. We explore using a policy gradient method as a parser-agnostic alternative. In addition to directly optimizing for a tree-level metric such as F1, policy gradient has the potential to reduce exposure bias by allowing exploration during training; moreover, it does not require a dynamic oracle for supervision. On four constituency parsers in three languages, the method substantially outperforms static oracle likelihood training in almost all settings. For parsers where a dynamic oracle is available (including a novel oracle which we define for the transition system of Dyer et al., 2016), policy gradient typically recaptures a substantial fraction of the performance gain afforded by the dynamic oracle.

label: acl
text:
The method is also robust to different levels of supervision, as it can be trained with either gold or predicted trees, and can be fine-tuned with a small amount of additional supervision. The results suggest that policy gradient is a promising alternative to dynamic oracle supervision for constituency parsing.
Dynamic oracles provide effective guidance for training constituency parsers, but must be specifically designed for each parser's transition system. This study explores a parser-agnostic alternative, a policy gradient method. Unlike dynamic oracles, policy gradient allows for exploration during training, reduces exposure bias, and doesn't require a custom-defined oracle. The results show that policy gradient outperforms static oracle likelihood training in almost all settings, even recapturing a significant portion of the performance gain from dynamic oracles when they are available. Additionally, the method is flexible and can be trained with either gold or predicted trees, and can be fine-tuned with additional supervision. Overall, the results indicate that policy gradient is a viable alternative to dynamic oracle supervision for constituency parsing.

text: The paper introduces end-to-end neural network models that tokenize Sanskrit by jointly splitting compounds and resolving phonetic merges (Sandhi). Tokenization of Sanskrit depends on local phonetic and distant semantic features that are incorporated using convolutional and recurrent elements. Contrary to most previous systems, our models do not require feature engineering or extern linguistic resources, but operate solely on parallel versions of raw and segmented text. The models discussed in this paper clearly improve over previous approaches to Sanskrit word segmentation. As they are language agnostic, we will demonstrate that they also outperform the state of the art for the related task of German compound splitting.

label: emnlp
text: The paper presents end-to-end neural network models that tokenize Sanskrit by combining the processes of splitting compounds and resolving phonetic merges (Sandhi). These models utilize both local phonetic and distant semantic features, which are integrated through the use of convolutional and recurrent elements. Unlike previous systems, our models do not require any feature engineering or external linguistic resources and operate solely on parallel versions of raw and segmented text. The models discussed in the paper demonstrate a significant improvement over previous approaches to Sanskrit word segmentation, and their language-agnostic nature also allows them to outperform the state-of-the-art for the related task of German compound splitting.

label: acl
text: Behavior of deep neural networks can be inconsistent between different versions. Regressions during model update are a common cause of concern that often over-weigh the benefits in accuracy or efficiency gain. This work focuses on quantifying, reducing and analyzing regression errors in the NLP model updates. Using negative flip rate as regression measure, we show that regression has a prevalent presence across tasks in the GLUE benchmark. We formulate the regression-free model updates into a constrained optimization problem, and further reduce it into a relaxed form which can be approximately optimized through knowledge distillation training method. We empirically analyze how model ensemble reduces regression. Finally, we conduct CheckList behavioral testing to understand the distribution of regressions across linguistic phenomena, and the efficacy of ensemble and distillation methods.

label: acl
text: The behavior of deep neural networks can be inconsistent between different versions, and regressions during model updates are a common cause of concern. These regressions can often outweigh the benefits of increased accuracy or efficiency. This work focuses on quantifying, reducing, and analyzing these regression errors in NLP models. By using the negative flip rate as a measure of regression, we demonstrate that regressions are prevalent across tasks in the GLUE benchmark. We formulate the problem of regression-free model updates as a constrained optimization problem and reduce it to a relaxed form that can be approximately optimized through knowledge distillation training. We then analyze the effect of ensemble models on reducing regressions and conduct CheckList behavioral testing to understand the distribution of regressions across linguistic phenomena and evaluate the efficacy of ensemble and distillation methods.

label: acl
text: Recent work has shown pre-trained language models capture social biases from the large amounts of text they are trained on. This has attracted attention to developing techniques that mitigate such biases. In this work, we perform an empirical survey of five recently proposed bias mitigation techniques: Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), Dropout, Iterative Nullspace Projection, Self-Debias, and SentenceDebias. We quantify the effectiveness of each technique using three intrinsic bias benchmarks while also measuring the impact of these techniques on a model's language modeling ability, as well as its performance on downstream NLU tasks. We experimentally find that: (1) Self-Debias is the strongest debiasing technique, obtaining improved scores on all bias benchmarks; (2) Current debiasing techniques perform less consistently when mitigating non-gender biases; And (3) improvements on bias benchmarks such as StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs by using debiasing strategies are often accompanied by a decrease in language modeling ability, making it difficult to determine whether the bias mitigation was effective.

label: acl
text: Recently, studies have shown that pre-trained language models tend to capture social biases from the vast amounts of text they are trained on. As a result, researchers have started developing techniques to mitigate these biases. In this study, we conduct an empirical survey of five newly proposed bias mitigation techniques: Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), Dropout, Iterative Nullspace Projection, Self-Debias, and SentenceDebias. To evaluate their effectiveness, we use three intrinsic bias benchmarks and measure the impact of these techniques on the model's language modeling ability and performance on downstream Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks. Our findings reveal that: (1) the Self-Debias technique is the most robust in terms of debiasing, achieving improved scores on all bias benchmarks; (2) the current debiasing techniques are less effective in mitigating non-gender biases; and (3) improvements in bias benchmarks such as StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs using debiasing strategies often come at the cost of decreased language modeling ability, making it challenging to determine the effectiveness of the bias mitigation.

label: acl
text: Traditional word embedding approaches learn semantic information at word level while ignoring the meaningful internal structures of words like morphemes. Furthermore, existing morphology-based models directly incorporate morphemes to train word embeddings, but still neglect the latent meanings of morphemes. In this paper, we explore to employ the latent meanings of morphological compositions of words to train and enhance word embeddings. Based on this purpose, we propose three Latent Meaning Models (LMMs), named LMM-A, LMM-S and LMM-M respectively, which adopt different strategies to incorporate the latent meanings of morphemes during the training process. Experiments on word similarity, syntactic analogy and text classification are conducted to validate the feasibility of our models. The results demonstrate that our models outperform the baselines on five word similarity datasets. On Wordsim-353 and RG-65 datasets, our models nearly achieve 5% and 7% gains over the classic CBOW model, respectively. For the syntactic analogy and text classification tasks, our models also surpass all the baselines including a morphology-based model.

label: acl
text: Traditional word embedding methods learn semantic information at the word level, ignoring the meaningful internal structures of words such as morphemes. Despite the efforts of existing morphology-based models to incorporate morphemes in training word embeddings, they still overlook the latent meanings of these structures. In this paper, we aim to utilize the latent meanings of morphological compositions of words to train and improve word embeddings. To achieve this, we propose three Latent Meaning Models (LMMs), named LMM-A, LMM-S, and LMM-M, which adopt different strategies for incorporating the latent meanings of morphemes during training. We evaluate our models through experiments on word similarity, syntactic analogy, and text classification tasks, showing that our models outperform the baselines on five word similarity datasets. On the Wordsim-353 and RG-65 datasets, our models achieve nearly 5% and 7% gains over the classic CBOW model, respectively. Our models also surpass all the baselines, including a morphology-based model, on the syntactic analogy and text classification tasks.

label: acl
text: This work explores techniques to predict Part-of-Speech (PoS) tags from neural signals measured at millisecond resolution with electroencephalography (EEG) during text reading. We first show that information about word length, frequency and word class is encoded by the brain at different post-stimulus latencies. We then demonstrate that pre-training on averaged EEG data and data augmentation techniques boost PoS decoding accuracy for single EEG trials. Finally, applying optimised temporally-resolved decoding techniques we show that Transformers substantially outperform linear-SVMs on PoS tagging of unigram and bigram data.

label: acl
text: This study investigates methods for predicting Part-of-Speech (PoS) tags using millisecond-resolution electroencephalography (EEG) signals recorded during text reading. Our findings show that the brain encodes information about word length, frequency, and word class at various post-stimulus latencies. By using pre-training on averaged EEG data and data augmentation techniques, we were able to improve the accuracy of PoS decoding for individual EEG trials. Finally, by applying optimized, temporally-resolved decoding techniques, we found that Transformers outperformed linear-SVMs in PoS tagging of both unigram and bigram data.

label: coling
text: Aspect-term sentiment analysis (ATSA) is an important task that aims to infer the sentiment towards the given aspect-terms. It is often required in the industry that ATSA should be performed with interpretability, computational efficiency and high accuracy. However, such an ATSA method has not yet been developed. This study aims to develop an ATSA method that fulfills all these requirements. To achieve the goal, we propose a novel Sentiment Interpretable Logic Tensor Network (SILTN). SILTN is interpretable because it is a neurosymbolic formalism and a computational model that supports learning and reasoning about data with a differentiable first-order logic language (FOL). To realize SILTN with high inferring accuracy, we propose a novel learning strategy called the two-stage syntax knowledge distillation (TSynKD). Using widely used datasets, we experimentally demonstrate that the proposed TSynKD is effective for improving the accuracy of SILTN, and the SILTN has both high interpretability and computational efficiency.

label: coling
text: The task of Aspect-term Sentiment Analysis (ATSA) is crucial in inferring the sentiment towards specified aspect-terms. In the industry, ATSA must be performed with a combination of interpretability, computational efficiency, and high accuracy. However, a method that meets these requirements has yet to be developed. This study aims to create such a method by introducing the Sentiment Interpretable Logic Tensor Network (SILTN). SILTN is interpretable as it is a neurosymbolic formalism and computational model that uses a differentiable first-order logic language (FOL) for learning and reasoning about data. To enhance its accuracy, we propose the Two-stage Syntax Knowledge Distillation (TSynKD) learning strategy. Our experiments, using commonly used datasets, show that TSynKD effectively improves the accuracy of SILTN while maintaining its interpretability and computational efficiency.

label: naacl
text: The end-to-end nature of neural machine translation (NMT) removes many ways of manually guiding the translation process that were available in older paradigms. Recent work, however, has introduced a new capability: lexically constrained or guided decoding, a modification to beam search that forces the inclusion of pre-specified words and phrases in the output. However, while theoretically sound, existing approaches have computational complexities that are either linear (Hokamp and Liu, 2017) or exponential (Anderson et al., 2017) in the number of constraints. We present a algorithm for lexically constrained decoding with a complexity of O(1) in the number of constraints. We demonstrate the algorithm's remarkable ability to properly place these constraints, and use it to explore the shaky relationship between model and BLEU scores. Our implementation is available as part of Sockeye.

label: naacl
text: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has an end-to-end structure that eliminates many manual translation options available in older methods. However, recent advancements have introduced the concept of lexically constrained or guided decoding, which modifies the beam search process to include pre-determined words and phrases in the output. Although these approaches are theoretically sound, they have computational complexities that are either linear or exponential in the number of constraints. To address this issue, we present an algorithm for lexically constrained decoding with a complexity of O(1) in relation to the number of constraints. Our algorithm demonstrates exceptional capability in accurately placing these constraints and is used to examine the delicate relationship between model and BLEU scores. Our implementation can be found in Sockeye.

label: acl
text: A key challenge in attribute value extraction (AVE) from e-commerce sites is how to handle a large number of attributes for diverse products. Although this challenge is partially addressed by a question answering (QA) approach which finds a value in product data for a given query (attribute), it does not work effectively for rare and ambiguous queries. We thus propose simple knowledge-driven query expansion based on possible answers (values) of a query (attribute) for QA-based AVE. We retrieve values of a query (attribute) from the training data to expand the query. We train a model with two tricks, knowledge dropout and knowledge token mixing, which mimic the imperfection of the value knowledge in testing. Experimental results on our cleaned version of AliExpress dataset show that our method improves the performance of AVE (+6.08 macro F1), especially for rare and ambiguous attributes (+7.82 and +6.86 macro F1, respectively).

label: acl
text: The challenge of extracting attribute values (AVE) from e-commerce sites lies in handling the vast number of attributes for a diverse range of products. While a question answering (QA) approach partially addresses this challenge by finding values in product data for a given attribute query, it is ineffective for rare or ambiguous queries. To overcome this, we propose a knowledge-driven query expansion technique for QA-based AVE. Our method retrieves values from training data to expand the query and trains a model with two tricks - knowledge dropout and knowledge token mixing - to mimic the imperfection of value knowledge during testing. Our results, based on a cleaned version of the AliExpress dataset, show that our method significantly improves the performance of AVE by +6.08 in macro F1, especially for rare and ambiguous attributes, where it increases performance by +7.82 and +6.86 in macro F1, respectively.

text: Book recommender systems can help promote the practice of reading for pleasure, which has been declining in recent years. One factor that influences reading preferences is writing style. We propose a system that recommends books after learning their authors' style. To our knowledge, this is the first work that applies the information learned by an author-identification model to book recommendations. We evaluated the system according to a top-k recommendation scenario. Our system gives better accuracy when compared with many state-of-the-art methods. We also conducted a qualitative analysis by checking if similar books/authors were annotated similarly by experts.

label: coling

The results showed that our system performs well in terms of book recommendation.

Book recommendation systems can help revive the declining trend of reading for pleasure by considering writing styles as a factor in determining reading preferences. Our proposed system utilizes an author-identification model to recommend books, which is a novel approach in the field of book recommendations. Our evaluations, based on a top-k recommendation scenario, indicate that our system outperforms many state-of-the-art methods. A qualitative analysis, which involved comparing expert annotations of similar books and authors, further confirmed the effectiveness of our system in terms of book recommendations.

label: acl
text: Computer-aided translation (CAT), the use of software to assist a human translator in the translation process, has been proven to be useful in enhancing the productivity of human translators. Autocompletion, which suggests translation results according to the text pieces provided by human translators, is a core function of CAT. There are two limitations in previous research in this line. First, most research works on this topic focus on sentence-level autocompletion (i.e., generating the whole translation as a sentence based on human input), but word-level autocompletion is under-explored so far. Second, almost no public benchmarks are available for the autocompletion task of CAT. This might be among the reasons why research progress in CAT is much slower compared to automatic MT. In this paper, we propose the task of general word-level autocompletion (GWLAN) from a real-world CAT scenario, and construct the first public benchmark to facilitate research in this topic. In addition, we propose an effective method for GWLAN and compare it with several strong baselines. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed method can give significantly more accurate predictions than the baseline methods on our benchmark datasets.

label: acl
text: Computer-aided translation (CAT) involves the use of software to aid human translators in the translation process, which has been shown to increase their productivity. CAT's core function is autocompletion, which provides translation suggestions based on the text fragments inputted by human translators. However, previous research in this field has two limitations. Firstly, most studies have focused on sentence-level autocompletion, generating complete translations from human input, while word-level autocompletion has been under-researched. Secondly, there are few public benchmarks for the autocompletion aspect of CAT, which may be contributing to the slower progress of research in this area compared to automatic machine translation. In this study, we propose the general word-level autocompletion (GWLAN) task from a real-world CAT scenario and establish the first public benchmark to advance research in this field. Our proposed method for GWLAN proves to be effective and outperforms several strong baselines in accuracy.
