text: Most word representation learning methods are based on the distributional hypothesis in linguistics, according to which words that are used and occur in the same contexts tend to possess similar meanings. As a consequence, emotionally dissimilar words, such as “happy” and “sad” occurring in similar contexts would purport more similar meaning than emotionally similar words, such as “happy” and “joy”. This complication leads to rather undesirable outcome in predictive tasks that relate to affect (emotional state), such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. In order to address this limitation, we propose a novel method of obtaining emotion-enriched word representations, which projects emotionally similar words into neighboring spaces and emotionally dissimilar ones far apart. The proposed approach leverages distant supervision to automatically obtain a large training dataset of text documents and two recurrent neural network architectures for learning the emotion-enriched representations. Through extensive evaluation on two tasks, including emotion classification and emotion similarity, we demonstrate that the proposed representations outperform several competitive general-purpose and affective word representations.

text: The majority of word representation learning methods are built on the distributional hypothesis in linguistics, which states that words that are used and appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. This can lead to undesirable outcomes when dealing with affective tasks such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. For example, emotionally dissimilar words like "happy" and "sad" appearing in similar contexts may be perceived as having more similar meanings than emotionally similar words like "happy" and "joy." To address this limitation, we present a novel method for obtaining emotion-enriched word representations. This approach projects emotionally similar words into close proximity and emotionally dissimilar words far apart. We use distant supervision to automatically create a large training dataset of text documents and two recurrent neural network architectures to learn the emotion-enriched representations. Through thorough evaluations on two tasks, emotion classification and emotion similarity, we show that our proposed representations outperform several existing general-purpose and affective word representations.

text: In this paper, we describe an attempt towards the development of parallel corpora for English and Ethiopian Languages, such as Amharic, Tigrigna, Afan-Oromo, Wolaytta and Ge'ez. The corpora are used for conducting a bi-directional statistical machine translation experiments. The BLEU scores of the bi-directional Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems show a promising result. The morphological richness of the Ethiopian languages has a great impact on the performance of SMT specially when the targets are Ethiopian languages. Now we are working towards an optimal alignment for a bi-directional English-Ethiopian languages SMT.

text: This paper presents our efforts towards creating parallel corpora for English and Ethiopian languages, including Amharic, Tigrigna, Afan-Oromo, Wolaytta, and Ge'ez. text: The emotional state of a speaker can be influenced by many different factors in dialogues, such as dialogue scene, dialogue topic, and interlocutor stimulus. The currently available data resources to support such multimodal affective analysis in dialogues are however limited in scale and diversity. In this work, we propose a Multi-modal Multi-scene Multi-label Emotional Dialogue dataset, MC-C-CED, which contains 990 dyadic emotional dialogues from 56 different TV series, a total of 9,082 turns and 24,449 utterances. MD-D-DED is annotated with 7 emotion categories (happy, surprise, sad, disgust, anger, fear, and neutral) at utterance level, and encompasses acoustic, visual, and textual modalities. To the best of our knowledge, ME-E-EED is the first multimodal emotional dialogue dataset in Chinese.It is valuable for cross-culture emotion analysis and recognition. We apply several state-of-the-art methods on the MF-F-FED dataset to verify the validity and quality of the dataset. We also propose a general Multimodal Dialogue-aware Interaction framework, MDI, to model the dialogue context for emotion recognition, which achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods on the MG-G-GED. The full dataset and codes are available.

text: The emotional state of a speaker can be impacted by various factors in dialogues, such as the scene, topic, and interlocutor's stimulus. We evaluate the validity and quality of the dataset using state-of-the-art methods and propose a Multimodal Dialogue-aware Interaction framework, MDI, for emotion recognition that achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on the dataset. text: Large language models are shown to memorize privacy information such as social security numbers in training data. Given the sheer scale of the training corpus, it is challenging to screen and filter these privacy data, either manually or automatically. In this paper, we propose Confidentially Redacted Training (CRT), a method to train language generation models while protecting the confidential segments. We borrow ideas from differential privacy (which solves a related but distinct problem) and show that our method is able to provably prevent unintended memorization by randomizing parts of the training process. Moreover, we show that redaction with an approximately correct screening policy amplifies the confidentiality guarantee. We implement the method for both LSTM and GPT language models. Our experimental results show that the models trained by CRT obtain almost the same perplexity while preserving strong confidentiality.

label: naacl
text: Large language models have been found to memorize sensitive information, such as social security numbers, present in the training data. Given the vast size of the training corpus, it is difficult to screen and filter this confidential information, either manually or automatically. To address this issue, we present Confidentially Redacted Training (CRT), a method for training language generation models while protecting confidential segments. Our approach draws inspiration from differential privacy and ensures that unintended memorization is prevented by randomizing parts of the training process. Additionally, we demonstrate that redaction with an accurate screening policy enhances the confidentiality guarantee. We implement CRT for both LSTM and GPT language models and show that the models trained with CRT achieve similar perplexity while preserving strong confidentiality through our experimental results.

text: Transformer-based language models (LMs) pretrained on large text collections implicitly store a wealth of lexical semantic knowledge, but it is non-trivial to extract that knowledge effectively from their parameters. Inspired by prior work on semantic specialization of static word embedding (WE) models, we show that it is possible to expose and enrich lexical knowledge from the LMs, that is, to specialize them to serve as effective and universal “decontextualized” word encoders even when fed input words “in isolation” (i.e., without any context). Their transformation into such word encoders is achieved through a simple and efficient lexical fine-tuning procedure (termed LexFit) based on dual-encoder network structures. Further, we show that LexFit can yield effective word encoders even with limited lexical supervision and, via cross-lingual transfer, in different languages without any readily available external knowledge. Our evaluation over four established, structurally different lexical-level tasks in 8 languages indicates the superiority of LexFit-based WEs over standard static WEs (e.g., fastText) and WEs from vanilla LMs. Other extensive experiments and ablation studies further profile the LexFit framework, and indicate best practices and performance variations across LexFit variants, languages, and lexical tasks, also directly questioning the usefulness of traditional WE models in the era of large neural models.

text: Transformer-based language models (LMs) store a wealth of lexical semantic knowledge, but it is difficult to extract it effectively from their parameters. This is achieved through a simple and efficient fine-tuning procedure called LexFit, based on dual-encoder network structures. We show that LexFit can yield effective word encoders even with limited lexical supervision and can be transferred across languages without external knowledge. Our evaluation over four lexical-level tasks in 8 languages shows that LexFit-based WEs outperform standard static WEs (e.g., fastText) and WEs from vanilla LMs. Our experiments and ablation studies profile the LexFit framework and provide best practices and performance variations across LexFit variants, languages, and lexical tasks, raising questions about the usefulness of traditional WE models in the era of large neural models.

text: We present a neural transition-based model that uses a simple set of edit actions (copy, delete, insert) for morphological transduction tasks such as inflection generation, lemmatization, and reinflection. In a large-scale evaluation on four datasets and dozens of languages, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art systems on low and medium training-set sizes and is competitive in the high-resource setting. Learning to apply a generic copy action enables our approach to generalize quickly from a few data points. We successfully leverage minimum risk training to compensate for the weaknesses of MLE parameter learning and neutralize the negative effects of training a pipeline with a separate character aligner.

text: We present a neural transition-based model that utilizes a straightforward set of edit actions (copy, delete, insert) for handling morphological transduction tasks, including inflection generation, lemmatization, and reinflection. In a comprehensive evaluation on four datasets and numerous languages, our approach consistently outperforms the current state-of-the-art systems when training sets are of low to medium size and is competitive in high-resource settings. Our approach's ability to learn the generic copy action allows it to generalize quickly even with limited data points. Additionally, we effectively use minimum risk training to overcome the limitations of MLE parameter learning and counteract the negative impact of training a pipeline with a separate character aligner.

text: Fusion-in-decoder (Fid) (Izacard and Grave, 2020) is a generative question answering (QA) model that leverages passage retrieval with a pre-trained transformer and pushed the state of the art on single-hop QA. However, the complexity of multi-hop QA hinders the effectiveness of the generative QA approach. In this work, we propose a simple generative approach (PathFid) that extends the task beyond just answer generation by explicitly modeling the reasoning process to resolve the answer for multi-hop questions. By linearizing the hierarchical reasoning path of supporting passages, their key sentences, and finally the factoid answer, we cast the problem as a single sequence prediction task. To facilitate complex reasoning with multiple clues, we further extend the unified flat representation of multiple input documents by encoding cross-passage interactions. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that PathFid leads to strong performance gains on two multi-hop QA datasets: HotpotQA and IIRC. Besides the performance gains, PathFid is more interpretable, which in turn yields answers that are more faithfully grounded to the supporting passages and facts compared to the baseline Fid model.

text: The Fusion-in-Decoder (Fid) model by Izacard and Grave (2020) is a state-of-the-art generative question answering (QA) system that combines passage retrieval with a pre-trained transformer. To address this challenge, we introduce a simple generative approach called PathFid, which goes beyond just answer generation by explicitly modeling the reasoning process for multi-hop questions. PathFid linearizes the hierarchical reasoning path of supporting passages, key sentences, and factoid answers, casting the problem as a single sequence prediction task. To allow for complex reasoning with multiple clues, we also enhance the representation of multiple input documents by encoding cross-passage interactions. Our experiments show that PathFid outperforms the baseline Fid model on two multi-hop QA datasets: HotpotQA and IIRC. Furthermore, PathFid is more interpretable and generates answers that are more grounded in the supporting passages and facts.

text: Nominal metaphors are frequently used in human language and have been shown to be effective in persuading, expressing emotion, and stimulating interest. This paper tackles the problem of Chinese Nominal Metaphor (NM) generation. We introduce a novel multitask framework, which jointly optimizes three tasks: NM identification, NM component identification, and NM generation. The metaphor identification module is able to perform a self-training procedure, which discovers novel metaphors from a large-scale unlabeled corpus for NM generation. The NM component identification module emphasizes components during training and conditions the generation on these NM components for more coherent results. To train the NM identification and component identification modules, we construct an annotated corpus consisting of 6.3k sentences that contain diverse metaphorical patterns. Automatic metrics show that our method can produce diverse metaphors with good readability, where 92% of them are novel metaphorical comparisons. Human evaluation shows our model significantly outperforms baselines on consistency and creativity.

text: Nominal metaphors are widely used in human language and have been proven to be effective in persuasion, emotional expression, and arousing interest. A novel multitask framework is presented, which optimizes three tasks simultaneously: NM identification, NM component identification, and NM generation. The metaphor identification module has the ability to conduct a self-training procedure, which discovers new metaphors from a vast corpus for NM generation. The NM component identification module prioritizes components during training, ensuring the generated NMs are coherent. An annotated corpus of 6.3k sentences containing diverse metaphorical patterns was created to train the NM identification and component identification modules. The results of the automatic metrics show that our method can generate diverse, readable metaphors, with 92% of them being novel metaphorical comparisons. Human evaluation demonstrates that our model outperforms baselines in terms of consistency and creativity.

text: Research on Automatic Story Generation (ASG) relies heavily on human and automatic evaluation. However, there is no consensus on which human evaluation criteria to use, and no analysis of how well automatic criteria correlate with them. In this paper, we propose to re-evaluate ASG evaluation. We introduce a set of 6 orthogonal and comprehensive human criteria, carefully motivated by the social sciences literature. We also present HANNA, an annotated dataset of 1,056 stories produced by 10 different ASG systems. HANNA allows us to quantitatively evaluate the correlations of 72 automatic metrics with human criteria. Our analysis highlights the weaknesses of current metrics for ASG and allows us to formulate practical recommendations for ASG evaluation.

text: The research on Automatic Story Generation heavily depends on both human and automatic evaluations. text: Multi-choice reading comprehension is a challenging task, which involves the matching between a passage and a question-answer pair. This paper proposes a new co-matching approach to this problem, which jointly models whether a passage can match both a question and a candidate answer. Experimental results on the RACE dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

text: Multi-choice reading comprehension is a difficult challenge that requires matching between a passage and a question-answer pair. This paper presents a novel co-matching approach to tackle this challenge by jointly modeling the compatibility between a passage, a question, and a candidate answer. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experimental results on the RACE dataset, which show that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

label: coling
text: Most existing slot filling models tend to memorize inherent patterns of entities and corresponding contexts from training data. However, these models can lead to system failure or undesirable outputs when being exposed to spoken language perturbation or variation in practice. We propose a perturbed semantic structure awareness transferring method for training perturbation-robust slot filling models. Specifically, we introduce two MLM-based training strategies to respectively learn contextual semantic structure and word distribution from unsupervised language perturbation corpus. Then, we transfer semantic knowledge learned from upstream training procedure into the original samples and filter generated data by consistency processing. These procedures aims to enhance the robustness of slot filling models. Experimental results show that our method consistently outperforms the previous basic methods and gains strong generalization while preventing the model from memorizing inherent patterns of entities and contexts.

text: Most existing slot filling models tend to memorize inherent patterns of entities and their corresponding contexts from training data. However, this can result in system failure or undesirable outputs when exposed to spoken language perturbations or variations in practice. To address this issue, we propose a perturbed semantic structure awareness transferring method for training perturbation-robust slot filling models. Our method involves two MLM-based training strategies to learn contextual semantic structure and word distribution from an unsupervised language perturbation corpus. We then transfer the semantic knowledge learned from the upstream training process into the original samples and filter the generated data through consistency processing, which enhances the robustness of the slot filling models. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms previous basic methods, providing strong generalization while preventing the model from memorizing inherent patterns of entities and contexts.

text: We present a corrected version of a subset of the FactBank data set. Previously published results on FactBank are no longer valid. We perform experiments on FactBank using multiple training paradigms, data smoothing techniques, and polarity classifiers. We argue that f-measure is an important alternative evaluation metric for factuality. We provide new state-of-the-art results for four corpora including FactBank. We perform an error analysis on Factbank combined with two similar corpora.

label: coling
text: We present a refined version of a portion of the FactBank dataset. The previous results published on FactBank are now obsolete. Our experiments on FactBank involve utilizing various training methods, smoothing data techniques, and sentiment analysis algorithms. We assert that the f-measure is a crucial alternative evaluation metric for determining the accuracy of the data. Our findings result in new, leading-edge results for four corpora, including FactBank. Additionally, we conduct a thorough analysis of errors in FactBank, in conjunction with two similar datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Cross-lingual transfer of word embeddings aims to establish the semantic mappings among words in different languages by learning the transformation functions over the corresponding word embedding spaces. Successfully solving this problem would benefit many downstream tasks such as to translate text classification models from resource-rich languages (e.g. English) to low-resource languages. Supervised methods for this problem rely on the availability of cross-lingual supervision, either using parallel corpora or bilingual lexicons as the labeled data for training, which may not be available for many low resource languages. This paper proposes an unsupervised learning approach that does not require any cross-lingual labeled data. Given two monolingual word embedding spaces for any language pair, our algorithm optimizes the transformation functions in both directions simultaneously based on distributional matching as well as minimizing the back-translation losses. We use a neural network implementation to calculate the Sinkhorn distance, a well-defined distributional similarity measure, and optimize our objective through back-propagation. Our evaluation on benchmark datasets for bilingual lexicon induction and cross-lingual word similarity prediction shows stronger or competitive performance of the proposed method compared to other state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised baseline methods over many language pairs.

text: Cross-lingual transfer of word embeddings aims to create semantic connections between words in different languages by learning transformation functions in the corresponding word embedding spaces. This is beneficial for tasks such as translating text classification models from resource-rich languages (e.g. English) to low-resource languages. Typically, supervised methods for this problem require cross-lingual supervision, which is usually obtained from parallel corpora or bilingual lexicons. However, these resources may not be available for many low-resource languages. This paper presents an unsupervised learning approach that does not require any cross-lingual labeled data. Our algorithm optimizes transformation functions in both directions simultaneously, using distributional matching and minimizing back-translation losses. We use a neural network to calculate the Sinkhorn distance, a well-defined distributional similarity measure, and optimize our objective through back-propagation. Our evaluation on benchmark datasets for bilingual lexicon induction and cross-lingual word similarity prediction shows that our method outperforms or is comparable to state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised baseline methods for many language pairs.

label: acl
text: To quantify how well natural language understanding models can capture consistency in a general conversation, we introduce the DialoguE COntradiction DEtection task (DECODE) and a new conversational dataset containing both human-human and human-bot contradictory dialogues. We show that: (i) our newly collected dataset is notably more effective at providing supervision for the dialogue contradiction detection task than existing NLI data including those aimed to cover the dialogue domain; (ii) Transformer models that explicitly hinge on utterance structures for dialogue contradiction detection are more robust and generalize well on both analysis and out-of-distribution dialogues than standard (unstructured) Transformers. We also show that our best contradiction detection model correlates well with human judgments and further provide evidence for its usage in both automatically evaluating and improving the consistency of state-of-the-art generative chatbots.

label: acl
text: We introduce the DialoguE COntradiction DEtection task (DECODE) to quantify the ability of natural language understanding models to capture consistency in general conversations. Our new conversational dataset contains both human-human and human-bot contradictory dialogues and is more effective at providing supervision for the dialogue contradiction detection task than existing NLI data, even those specifically aimed at covering the dialogue domain. Our results show that Transformer models that explicitly take into account utterance structures for dialogue contradiction detection are more robust and generalize better on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution dialogues than standard (unstructured) Transformers. Our best contradiction detection model has a high correlation with human judgments and can be used to automatically evaluate and improve the consistency of state-of-the-art generative chatbots.

label: acl
text: This work investigates the use of interactively updated label suggestions to improve upon the efficiency of gathering annotations on the task of opinion mining in German Covid-19 social media data. We develop guidelines to conduct a controlled annotation study with social science students and find that suggestions from a model trained on a small, expert-annotated dataset already lead to a substantial improvement – in terms of inter-annotator agreement (+.14 Fleiss' κ) and annotation quality – compared to students that do not receive any label suggestions. We further find that label suggestions from interactively trained models do not lead to an improvement over suggestions from a static model. Nonetheless, our analysis of suggestion bias shows that annotators remain capable of reflecting upon the suggested label in general. Finally, we confirm the quality of the annotated data in transfer learning experiments between different annotator groups. To facilitate further research in opinion mining on social media data, we release our collected data consisting of 200 expert and 2,785 student annotations.

text: This work examines the impact of interactively updated label suggestions on the efficiency of gathering annotations for opinion mining in German Covid-19 social media data. We established guidelines for a controlled annotation study with social science students and found that suggestions from a model trained on a small, expert-annotated dataset significantly improved inter-annotator agreement (+.14 Fleiss' κ) and annotation quality compared to students who did not receive any suggestions. Although label suggestions from interactively trained models did not result in an improvement over suggestions from a static model, our analysis of suggestion bias showed that annotators were still able to reflect on the suggested label. Additionally, we validated the quality of the annotated data through transfer learning experiments between different annotator groups. To support further research in opinion mining on social media data, we have made our collected data, which includes 200 expert and 2,785 student annotations, available.

label: acl
text: The Out-of-Domain (OOD) intent classification is a basic and challenging task for dialogue systems. Previous methods commonly restrict the region (in feature space) of In-domain (IND) intent features to be compact or simply-connected implicitly, which assumes no OOD intents reside, to learn discriminative semantic features. Then the distribution of the IND intent features is often assumed to obey a hypothetical distribution (Gaussian mostly) and samples outside this distribution are regarded as OOD samples. In this paper, we start from the nature of OOD intent classification and explore its optimization objective. We further propose a simple yet effective method, named KNN-contrastive learning. Our approach utilizes k-nearest neighbors (KNN) of IND intents to learn discriminative semantic features that are more conducive to OOD detection.Notably, the density-based novelty detection algorithm is so well-grounded in the essence of our method that it is reasonable to use it as the OOD detection algorithm without making any requirements for the feature distribution.Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that our approach can not only enhance the OOD detection performance substantially but also improve the IND intent classification while requiring no restrictions on feature distribution.

label: acl
text: The Out-of-Domain (OOD) intent classification is a fundamental and demanding task for dialogue systems. Previous methods typically limit the region of In-domain (IND) intent features to be compact or simply-connected, implying that there are no OOD intents present, to learn discriminative semantic features. The distribution of IND intent features is often assumed to follow a hypothetical distribution (usually Gaussian), and samples outside this distribution are considered OOD samples. In this paper, we examine the nature of OOD intent classification and investigate its optimization objective. We introduce a new method, named KNN-contrastive learning, which is simple yet effective. Our approach leverages k-nearest neighbors (KNN) of IND intents to learn discriminative semantic features that are more conducive to OOD detection. Importantly, the density-based novelty detection algorithm is so intrinsic to our method that it can be used as the OOD detection algorithm without any requirements for the feature distribution. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves OOD detection performance, while also enhancing IND intent classification without any restrictions on feature distribution.

label: naacl
text: This work studies temporal reading comprehension (TRC), which reads a free-text passage and answers temporal ordering questions. Precise question understanding is critical for temporal reading comprehension. For example, the question “What happened before the victory” and “What happened after the victory” share almost all words except one, while their answers are totally different. Moreover, even if two questions query about similar temporal relations, different varieties might also lead to various answers. For example, although both the question “What usually happened during the press release?” and “What might happen during the press release” query events which happen after “the press release”, they convey divergent semantics.To this end, we propose a novel reading comprehension approach with precise question understanding. Specifically, a temporal ordering question is embedded into two vectors to capture the referred event and the temporal relation. Then we evaluate the temporal relation between candidate events and the referred event based on that. Such fine-grained representations offer two benefits. First, it enables a better understanding of the question by focusing on different elements of a question. Second, it provides good interpretability when evaluating temporal relations. Furthermore, we also harness an auxiliary contrastive loss for representation learning of temporal relations, which aims to distinguish relations with subtle but critical changes. The proposed approach outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the TORQUE dataset. It also increases the accuracy of four pre-trained language models (BERT base, BERT large, RoBERTa base, and RoBETRa large), demonstrating its generic effectiveness on divergent models.

label: naacl
text:
The present study focuses on Temporal Reading Comprehension (TRC), which involves reading a free-text passage and answering questions related to temporal ordering. Precise understanding of questions is crucial for TRC. For instance, the questions "What happened before the victory?" and "What happened after the victory?" share almost all words except one, yet their answers are significantly different. Additionally, even if two questions relate to similar temporal events, different variations may result in varying answers. For example, both questions "What usually happened during the press release?" and "What might happen during the press release?" relate to events that occur after "the press release," but they convey different semantics.

To address this issue, we propose a novel TRC approach that emphasizes precise question understanding. Our approach embeds a temporal ordering question into two vectors, capturing the referred event and the temporal relation. We then evaluate the temporal relationship between candidate events and the referred event based on these vectors. This fine-grained representation offers two benefits: it enables a better understanding of the question by focusing on its different elements, and it provides interpretability when evaluating temporal relations. Furthermore, we also employ an auxiliary contrastive loss for representation learning of temporal relations, which aims to distinguish subtle but critical changes in these relationships. Our approach outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the TORQUE dataset. Additionally, it increases the accuracy of four pre-trained language models (BERT base, BERT large, RoBERTa base, and RoBERTa large), demonstrating its generic effectiveness across diverse models.

label: acl
text: Research on overlapped and discontinuous named entity recognition (NER) has received increasing attention. The majority of previous work focuses on either overlapped or discontinuous entities. In this paper, we propose a novel span-based model that can recognize both overlapped and discontinuous entities jointly. The model includes two major steps. First, entity fragments are recognized by traversing over all possible text spans, thus, overlapped entities can be recognized. Second, we perform relation classification to judge whether a given pair of entity fragments to be overlapping or succession. In this way, we can recognize not only discontinuous entities, and meanwhile doubly check the overlapped entities. As a whole, our model can be regarded as a relation extraction paradigm essentially. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets (i.e., CLEF, GENIA and ACE05) show that our model is highly competitive for overlapped and discontinuous NER.

label: acl
text: Research on the recognition of both overlapped and discontinuous named entities (NER) has gained significant attention in recent years. Most previous studies have focused on either overlapped or discontinuous entities. This paper presents a novel span-based model that can recognize both types of entities jointly. The model consists of two main steps. First, entity fragments are identified by scanning all possible text spans, allowing for the recognition of overlapped entities. Second, relation classification is performed to determine whether a pair of entity fragments overlap or follow one another, enabling the recognition of discontinuous entities and the verification of overlapped entities. Our model can be considered a relation extraction paradigm. Results from experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including CLEF, GENIA, and ACE05, demonstrate that the model is highly effective for overlapped and discontinuous NER.

label: emnlp
text: Lexicon relation extraction given distributional representation of words is an important topic in NLP. We observe that the state-of-the-art projection-based methods cannot be generalized to handle unseen hypernyms. We propose to analyze it in the perspective of pollution and construct the corresponding indicator to measure it. We propose a word relation autoencoder (WRAE) model to address the challenge. Experiments on several hypernym-like lexicon datasets show that our model outperforms the competitors significantly.

label: emnlp
text: The extraction of lexical relationships based on the distributional representation of words is a crucial area of study in NLP. We have noted that current projection-based techniques are not capable of generalizing to handle previously unseen hypernyms. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that analyzes it from the perspective of pollution and develops an indicator to measure it. Our solution is a word relation autoencoder (WRAE) model, which has been shown to outperform other methods in experiments on multiple hypernym-like lexicon datasets.

label: coling
text: Incorporating syntactic information in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) can lead to better reorderings, particularly useful when the language pairs are syntactically highly divergent or when the training bitext is not large. Previous work on using syntactic information, provided by top-1 parse trees generated by (inevitably error-prone) parsers, has been promising. In this paper, we propose a forest-to-sequence NMT model to make use of exponentially many parse trees of the source sentence to compensate for the parser errors. Our method represents the collection of parse trees as a packed forest, and learns a neural transducer to translate from the input forest to the target sentence. Experiments on English to German, Chinese and Farsi translation tasks show the superiority of our approach over the sequence-to-sequence and tree-to-sequence neural translation models.

label: coling
text: Our proposed forest-to-sequence NMT model leverages the use of exponentially many parse trees of the source sentence to overcome the limitations of error-prone parsers. By representing the collection of parse trees as a packed forest, our model learns to translate from the input forest to the target sentence. Our experiments on English to German, Chinese, and Farsi translation tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional sequence-to-sequence and tree-to-sequence neural translation models.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we present a method which learns the word embedding for readability assessment. For the existing word embedding models, they typically focus on the syntactic or semantic relations of words, while ignoring the reading difficulty, thus they may not be suitable for readability assessment. Hence, we provide the knowledge-enriched word embedding (KEWE), which encodes the knowledge on reading difficulty into the representation of words. Specifically, we extract the knowledge on word-level difficulty from three perspectives to construct a knowledge graph, and develop two word embedding models to incorporate the difficulty context derived from the knowledge graph to define the loss functions. Experiments are designed to apply KEWE for readability assessment on both English and Chinese datasets, and the results demonstrate both effectiveness and potential of KEWE.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we propose a method for learning word embeddings for readability assessment. Existing word embedding models often focus on syntactic or semantic relations of words, neglecting the reading difficulty, making them unsuitable for readability assessment. To address this issue, we present the knowledge-enriched word embedding (KEWE), which incorporates knowledge of reading difficulty into the representation of words. To achieve this, we construct a knowledge graph by extracting word-level difficulty from three perspectives, and develop two word embedding models that incorporate the difficulty context from the knowledge graph into the loss functions. Our experiments, conducted on both English and Chinese datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of KEWE for readability assessment.

label: acl
text: The importance of parameter selection in supervised learning is well known. However, due to the many parameter combinations, an incomplete or an insufficient procedure is often applied. This situation may cause misleading or confusing conclusions. In this opinion paper, through an intriguing example we point out that the seriousness goes beyond what is generally recognized. In the topic of multilabel classification for medical code prediction, one influential paper conducted a proper parameter selection on a set, but when moving to a subset of frequently occurring labels, the authors used the same parameters without a separate tuning. The set of frequent labels became a popular benchmark in subsequent studies, which kept pushing the state of the art. However, we discovered that most of the results in these studies cannot surpass the approach in the original paper if a parameter tuning had been conducted at the time. Thus it is unclear how much progress the subsequent developments have actually brought. The lesson clearly indicates that without enough attention on parameter selection, the research progress in our field can be uncertain or even illusive.

label: acl
text: The significance of parameter selection in supervised learning is widely acknowledged. Unfortunately, due to the vast number of parameter combinations, researchers often adopt an incomplete or inadequate procedure, leading to misleading or confusing results. In this paper, we use an intriguing example to demonstrate that the impact of improper parameter selection is greater than what is commonly recognized. In the field of multilabel classification for medical code prediction, one influential study conducted a thorough parameter selection on a dataset, but when applied to a subset of frequently occurring labels, the authors used the same parameters without further tuning. This subset of frequent labels became a popular benchmark in subsequent studies, which were touted as advancing the state of the art. However, we have found that if proper parameter tuning had been conducted at the time, the majority of results from these subsequent studies would not have surpassed the original study. This highlights the importance of careful parameter selection and raises questions about the validity of research progress in our field.

label: naacl
text: The task of automatic text summarization is to generate a short text that summarizes the most important information in a given set of documents. Sentence regression is an emerging branch in automatic text summarizations. Its key idea is to estimate the importance of information via learned utility scores for individual sentences. These scores are then used for selecting sentences from the source documents, typically according to a greedy selection strategy. Recently proposed state-of-the-art models learn to predict ROUGE recall scores of individual sentences, which seems reasonable since the final summaries are evaluated according to ROUGE recall. In this paper, we show in extensive experiments that following this intuition leads to suboptimal results and that learning to predict ROUGE precision scores leads to better results. The crucial difference is to aim not at covering as much information as possible but at wasting as little space as possible in every greedy step.

label: naacl
text: The task of automatic text summarization is to generate a concise summary of the most vital information contained in a set of documents. The field of text summarization is seeing the emergence of sentence regression as a key concept. This approach focuses on estimating the significance of information through learned scores for individual sentences. The scores are then used to choose sentences from the source documents, typically through a greedy selection process. Currently, the state-of-the-art models predict ROUGE recall scores for individual sentences, as the final summaries are evaluated based on ROUGE recall. However, this paper presents extensive experiments that demonstrate that this approach leads to suboptimal results. Instead, we show that learning to predict ROUGE precision scores leads to better outcomes, as the aim is not to cover as much information as possible, but to minimize wasted space in every greedy step.

label: naacl
text: We introduce neural particle smoothing, a sequential Monte Carlo method for sampling annotations of an input string from a given probability model. In contrast to conventional particle filtering algorithms, we train a proposal distribution that looks ahead to the end of the input string by means of a right-to-left LSTM. We demonstrate that this innovation can improve the quality of the sample. To motivate our formal choices, we explain how neural transduction models and our sampler can be viewed as low-dimensional but nonlinear approximations to working with HMMs over very large state spaces.

label: naacl
text: We present Neural Particle Smoothing, a sequential Monte Carlo technique for obtaining annotations of an input string based on a given probability model. Unlike traditional particle filtering algorithms, we train a proposal distribution that considers the end of the input string through a right-to-left LSTM. Our approach demonstrates improved sample quality. We also explain how our method and neural transduction models can be seen as low-dimensional, nonlinear approximations of working with HMMs in large state spaces.

label: acl
text: Context-aware machine translation models are designed to leverage contextual information, but often fail to do so. As a result, they inaccurately disambiguate pronouns and polysemous words that require context for resolution. In this paper, we ask several questions: What contexts do human translators use to resolve ambiguous words? Are models paying large amounts of attention to the same context? What if we explicitly train them to do so? To answer these questions, we introduce SCAT (Supporting Context for Ambiguous Translations), a new English-French dataset comprising supporting context words for 14K translations that professional translators found useful for pronoun disambiguation. Using SCAT, we perform an in-depth analysis of the context used to disambiguate, examining positional and lexical characteristics of the supporting words. Furthermore, we measure the degree of alignment between the model's attention scores and the supporting context from SCAT, and apply a guided attention strategy to encourage agreement between the two.

label: acl
text: Our results show that the guided attention strategy significantly improves the performance of the model, demonstrating the importance of considering contextual information in machine translation. Context-aware machine translation models are designed to utilize contextual information, but often fall short in doing so. This leads to incorrect disambiguation of pronouns and polysemous words that require context for resolution. This paper poses several questions: What contextual information do human translators use to resolve ambiguous words? Are models paying significant attention to the same context? What happens if they are trained to do so explicitly? To answer these questions, the authors introduce SCAT (Supporting Context for Ambiguous Translations), a new English-French dataset that contains supporting context words for 14K translations that professional translators found useful for pronoun disambiguation. The authors use SCAT to perform a thorough analysis of the context used for disambiguation, examining the positional and lexical characteristics of the supporting words. Additionally, they measure the alignment between the model's attention scores and the supporting context from SCAT, and apply a guided attention strategy to increase agreement between the two. The results show that the guided attention strategy significantly improves the model's performance, highlighting the importance of considering contextual information in machine translation.

label: coling
text: Capturing interactions among multiple predicate-argument structures (PASs) is a crucial issue in the task of analyzing PAS in Japanese. In this paper, we propose new Japanese PAS analysis models that integrate the label prediction information of arguments in multiple PASs by extending the input and last layers of a standard deep bidirectional recurrent neural network (bi-RNN) model. In these models, using the mechanisms of pooling and attention, we aim to directly capture the potential interactions among multiple PASs, without being disturbed by the word order and distance. Our experiments show that the proposed models improve the prediction accuracy specifically for cases where the predicate and argument are in an indirect dependency relation and achieve a new state of the art in the overall C-C-C on a standard benchmark corpus.

label: coling
text: The task of analyzing predicate-argument structures (PASs) in Japanese requires capturing interactions among multiple PASs, which is a crucial issue. To address this, we propose new Japanese PAS analysis models that integrate label prediction information of arguments in multiple PASs. These models are based on a standard deep bidirectional recurrent neural network (bi-RNN) and extend the input and last layers. By using pooling and attention mechanisms, we aim to capture interactions among multiple PASs directly, without being affected by word order or distance. Our experiments show that the proposed models significantly improve prediction accuracy, especially for cases where the predicate and argument have an indirect dependency relation, resulting in a new state-of-the-art performance on a standard benchmark corpus.

label: acl
text: Languages are dynamic systems: word usage may change over time, reflecting various societal factors. However, all languages do not evolve identically: the impact of an event, the influence of a trend or thinking, can differ between communities. In this paper, we propose to track these divergences by comparing the evolution of a word and its translation across two languages. We investigate several methods of building time-varying and bilingual word embeddings, using contextualised and non-contextualised embeddings. We propose a set of scenarios to characterize semantic divergence across two languages, along with a setup to differentiate them in a bilingual corpus. We evaluate the different methods by generating a corpus of synthetic semantic change across two languages, English and French, before applying them to newspaper corpora to detect bilingual semantic divergence and provide qualitative insight for the task. We conclude that BERT embeddings coupled with a clustering step lead to the best performance on synthetic corpora; however, the performance of CBOW embeddings is very competitive and more adapted to an exploratory analysis on a large corpus.

label: acl
text: Languages are dynamic systems that change over time, reflecting various societal factors. However, not all languages evolve in the same way. The impact of an event or the influence of a trend or idea can vary between communities. In this paper, we aim to track these differences by comparing the evolution of a word and its translation across two languages. We explore several methods for building time-varying and bilingual word embeddings, including contextualised and non-contextualised embeddings. We propose a set of scenarios to characterize semantic divergence across two languages and a framework to differentiate them in a bilingual corpus. To evaluate our methods, we generate a corpus of synthetic semantic change in English and French, and then apply them to newspaper corpora to detect bilingual semantic divergence and provide qualitative insights. Our results show that BERT embeddings with a clustering step achieve the best performance on synthetic corpora, but CBOW embeddings are also competitive and well-suited for exploratory analysis on large corpora.

label: acl
text: In the field of dialogue summarization, due to the lack of training data, it is often difficult for supervised summary generation methods to learn vital information from dialogue context with limited data. Several attempts on unsupervised summarization for text by leveraging semantic information solely or auto-encoder strategy (i.e., sentence compression), it however cannot be adapted to the dialogue scene due to the limited words in utterances and huge gap between the dialogue and its summary. In this study, we propose a novel unsupervised strategy to address this challenge, which roots from the hypothetical foundation that a superior summary approximates a replacement of the original dialogue, and they are roughly equivalent for auxiliary (self-supervised) tasks, e.g., dialogue generation. The proposed strategy RepSum is applied to generate both extractive and abstractive summary with the guidance of the followed n\^th utterance generation and classification tasks. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model compared with the state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: Due to a lack of training data, it can be challenging for supervised dialogue summarization methods to learn vital information from limited context. Previous attempts to use unsupervised summarization with semantic information or auto-encoder strategies have not been successful in adapting to dialogue scenes because of the limited words in utterances and the large gap between dialogue and its summary. To address this challenge, we propose a novel unsupervised strategy, RepSum, based on the hypothesis that a superior summary is roughly equivalent to a replacement of the original dialogue and can be used for auxiliary (self-supervised) tasks such as dialogue generation. Our proposed strategy generates both extractive and abstractive summaries using n\^th utterance generation and classification tasks. Experiments on various datasets show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: Knowledge Graph (KG) embedding has emerged as an active area of research resulting in the development of several KG embedding methods. Relational facts in KG often show temporal dynamics, e.g., the fact (Cristiano_Ronaldo, playsFor, Manchester_United) is valid only from 2003 to 2009. Most of the existing KG embedding methods ignore this temporal dimension while learning embeddings of the KG elements. In this paper, we propose HyTE, a temporally aware KG embedding method which explicitly incorporates time in the entity-relation space by associating each timestamp with a corresponding hyperplane. HyTE not only performs KG inference using temporal guidance, but also predicts temporal scopes for relational facts with missing time annotations. Through extensive experimentation on temporal datasets extracted from real-world KGs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model over both traditional as well as temporal KG embedding methods.

label: emnlp
text: The field of Knowledge Graph (KG) embedding has seen a lot of activity in recent years, leading to the creation of various KG embedding methods. However, most of these methods ignore the temporal dynamics of relational facts in KGs, such as the fact that Cristiano Ronaldo played for Manchester United only from 2003 to 2009. To address this issue, we introduce HyTE, a temporally aware KG embedding method that explicitly incorporates time into the entity-relation space by connecting each timestamp to a corresponding hyperplane. HyTE not only performs KG inference with temporal guidance, but it also predicts temporal scopes for relational facts that lack time annotations. Through thorough experimentation on temporal datasets taken from real-world KGs, our model is shown to be more effective than traditional and temporal KG embedding methods.

label: naacl
text: Distillation efforts have led to language models that are more compact and efficient without serious drops in performance. The standard approach to distillation trains a student model against two objectives: a task-specific objective (e.g., language modeling) and an imitation objective that encourages the hidden states of the student model to be similar to those of the larger teacher model. In this paper, we show that it is beneficial to augment distillation with a third objective that encourages the student to imitate the causal dynamics of the teacher through a distillation interchange intervention training objective (DIITO). DIITO pushes the student model to become a causal abstraction of the teacher model – a faithful model with simpler causal structure. DIITO is fully differentiable, easily implemented, and combines flexibly with other objectives. Compared against standard distillation with the same setting, DIITO results in lower perplexity on the WikiText-103M corpus (masked language modeling) and marked improvements on the GLUE benchmark (natural language understanding), SQuAD (question answering), and CoNLL-2003 (named entity recognition).

label: naacl
text: Efforts in distillation have resulted in language models that are smaller and more efficient without sacrificing performance. The typical distillation process trains a student model using two objectives: a task-specific objective (e.g. language modeling) and an imitation objective that ensures the hidden states of the student model resemble those of the larger teacher model. In this study, we demonstrate the benefits of adding a third objective, the distillation interchange intervention training objective (DIITO), to the distillation process. DIITO encourages the student model to imitate the causal dynamics of the teacher model, resulting in a simpler, yet faithful, causal structure. DIITO is easy to implement, fully differentiable, and can be combined with other objectives. Compared to standard distillation, DIITO leads to lower perplexity on the WikiText-103M corpus and notable improvements on the GLUE benchmark, SQuAD, and CoNLL-2003.

label: emnlp
text: Multi-head attention is appealing for the ability to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. In this work, we introduce a disagreement regularization to explicitly encourage the diversity among multiple attention heads. Specifically, we propose three types of disagreement regularization, which respectively encourage the subspace, the attended positions, and the output representation associated with each attention head to be different from other heads. Experimental results on widely-used WMT14 English-German and WMT17 Chinese-English translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach.

label: emnlp
text: The appeal of multi-head attention lies in its ability to attend to information from different representation subspaces at various positions simultaneously. In this study, we introduce a disagreement regularization to promote diversity among multiple attention heads. Our approach involves three types of disagreement regularization, designed to encourage each attention head to have a different subspace, attended positions, and output representation from the others. Our experiments on the widely used WMT14 English-German and WMT17 Chinese-English translation tasks show the effectiveness and universality of our proposed method.

label: naacl
text: Conventionally, generation of natural language for dialogue agents may be viewed as a statistical learning problem: determine the patterns in human-provided data and generate appropriate responses with similar statistical properties. However, dialogue can also be regarded as a goal directed process, where speakers attempt to accomplish a specific task. Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are designed specifically for solving such goal-directed problems, but the most direct way to apply RL, through trial-and-error learning in human conversations, is costly. In this paper, we study how offline reinforcement learning can instead be used to train dialogue agents entirely using static datasets collected from human speakers. Our experiments show that recently developed offline RL methods can be combined with language models to yield realistic dialogue agents that better accomplish task goals.

label: naacl
text: Conventionally, the generation of natural language for dialogue agents is seen as a statistical learning problem, where the goal is to identify patterns in human-generated data and produce responses with similar statistical properties. However, dialogue can also be viewed as a goal-directed process, where speakers aim to achieve a specific outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are designed to solve such goal-directed problems, but the most straightforward application of RL through trial-and-error learning in human conversations is expensive. This paper explores the use of offline reinforcement learning to train dialogue agents using only static datasets collected from human speakers. Our findings demonstrate that recently developed offline RL methods can be combined with language models to create dialogue agents that are more effective in achieving task goals and produce more realistic responses.

label: coling
text: Most previous work in unsupervised semantic modeling in the presence of metadata has assumed that our goal is to make latent dimensions more correlated with metadata, but in practice the exact opposite is often true. Some users want topic models that highlight differences between, for example, authors, but others seek more subtle connections across authors. We introduce three metrics for identifying topics that are highly correlated with metadata, and demonstrate that this problem affects between 30 and 50% of the topics in models trained on two real-world collections, regardless of the size of the model. We find that we can predict which words cause this phenomenon and that by selectively subsampling these words we dramatically reduce topic-metadata correlation, improve topic stability, and maintain or even improve model quality.

label: coling
text: Previous studies in unsupervised semantic modeling with metadata have assumed that the goal is to align latent dimensions with metadata, but in reality, the opposite is often desired by users. To address this issue, we propose three metrics to identify topics that are strongly correlated with metadata, and show that this problem affects 30-50% of the topics in two real-world collections, regardless of the model size. Our findings indicate that specific words are responsible for this phenomenon, and by selectively excluding these words, we can significantly reduce topic-metadata correlation, enhance topic stability, and maintain or even improve model quality.

label: naacl
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) research has mostly focused on English. We show that it is possible to use AMR annotations for English as a semantic representation for sentences written in other languages. We exploit an AMR parser for English and parallel corpora to learn AMR parsers for Italian, Spanish, German and Chinese. Qualitative analysis show that the new parsers overcome structural differences between the languages. We further propose a method to evaluate the parsers that does not require gold standard data in the target languages. This method highly correlates with the gold standard evaluation, obtaining a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.95.

label: naacl
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) research has largely centered on English. We demonstrate that AMR annotations for English can be utilized as a semantic representation for sentences written in other languages. By utilizing an AMR parser for English and parallel corpora, we have learned AMR parsers for Italian, Spanish, German, and Chinese. Qualitative analysis indicates that these new parsers effectively overcome structural differences between the languages. Additionally, we propose an evaluation method for the parsers that does not require gold standard data in the target languages. This method demonstrates a high correlation with gold standard evaluation, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.95.

label: acl
text: The impression section of a radiology report summarizes the most prominent observation from the findings section and is the most important section for radiologists to communicate to physicians. Summarizing findings is time-consuming and can be prone to error for inexperienced radiologists, and thus automatic impression generation has attracted substantial attention. With the encoder-decoder framework, most previous studies explore incorporating extra knowledge (e.g., static pre-defined clinical ontologies or extra background information). Yet, they encode such knowledge by a separate encoder to treat it as an extra input to their models, which is limited in leveraging their relations with the original findings. To address the limitation, we propose a unified framework for exploiting both extra knowledge and the original findings in an integrated way so that the critical information (i.e., key words and their relations) can be extracted in an appropriate way to facilitate impression generation. In detail, for each input findings, it is encoded by a text encoder and a graph is constructed through its entities and dependency tree. Then, a graph encoder (e.g., graph neural networks (GNNs)) is adopted to model relation information in the constructed graph. Finally, to emphasize the key words in the findings, contrastive learning is introduced to map positive samples (constructed by masking non-key words) closer and push apart negative ones (constructed by masking key words). The experimental results on two datasets, OpenI and MIMIC-CXR, confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method, where the state-of-the-art results are achieved.

label: acl
text: The summary section of a radiology report, known as the impression, is crucial for radiologists to communicate their observations to physicians. However, summarizing findings can be time-consuming and prone to errors for inexperienced radiologists. To address this issue, automatic impression generation has gained significant attention. Most previous studies in this field use the encoder-decoder framework, incorporating extra knowledge (such as clinical ontologies or background information) using a separate encoder. However, this approach is limited in leveraging the relationship between the extra knowledge and the original findings. To overcome this limitation, we propose a unified framework that integrates both extra knowledge and original findings. Our framework encodes the input findings using a text encoder and constructs a graph with entities and dependency trees. The graph is then modeled using a graph encoder (such as graph neural networks) to capture relation information. Finally, contrastive learning is employed to emphasize key words in the findings. Our method has been tested on two datasets, OpenI and MIMIC-CXR, and achieved state-of-the-art results.

label: naacl
text: In modern interactive speech-based systems, speech is consumed and transcribed incrementally prior to having disfluencies removed. While this post-processing step is crucial for producing clean transcripts and high performance on downstream tasks (e.g. machine translation), most current state-of-the-art NLP models such as the Transformer operate non-incrementally, potentially causing unacceptable delays for the user. In this work we propose a streaming BERT-based sequence tagging model that, combined with a novel training objective, is capable of detecting disfluencies in real-time while balancing accuracy and latency. This is accomplished by training the model to decide whether to immediately output a prediction for the current input or to wait for further context, in essence learning to dynamically size the lookahead window. Our results demonstrate that our model produces comparably accurate predictions and does so sooner than our baselines, with lower flicker. Furthermore, the model attains state-of-the-art latency and stability scores when compared with recent work on incremental disfluency detection.

label: naacl
text: In modern interactive speech-based systems, speech is transcribed incrementally and disfluencies are removed post-processing. This step is crucial for producing clean transcripts and improving performance on downstream tasks, such as machine translation. However, most current NLP models, such as the Transformer, operate non-incrementally, which can result in unacceptable delays for users. To address this issue, we propose a streaming BERT-based sequence tagging model that can detect disfluencies in real-time, balancing accuracy and latency. The model is trained to dynamically size the lookahead window, deciding whether to immediately output a prediction or wait for further context. Our results show that our model produces accurate predictions faster than our baselines, with lower flicker. Additionally, our model achieves state-of-the-art latency and stability scores compared to recent work on incremental disfluency detection.

label: acl
text: Encoder pre-training is promising in end-to-end Speech Translation (ST), given the fact that speech-to-translation data is scarce. But ST encoders are not simple instances of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) or Machine Translation (MT) encoders. For example, we find that ASR encoders lack the global context representation, which is necessary for translation, whereas MT encoders are not designed to deal with long but locally attentive acoustic sequences. In this work, we propose a Stacked Acoustic-and-Textual Encoding (SATE) method for speech translation. Our encoder begins with processing the acoustic sequence as usual, but later behaves more like an MT encoder for a global representation of the input sequence. In this way, it is straightforward to incorporate the pre-trained models into the system. Also, we develop an adaptor module to alleviate the representation inconsistency between the pre-trained ASR encoder and MT encoder, and develop a multi-teacher knowledge distillation method to preserve the pre-training knowledge. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech En-Fr and MuST-C En-De ST tasks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art BLEU scores of 18.3 and 25.2. To our knowledge, we are the first to develop an end-to-end ST system that achieves comparable or even better BLEU performance than the cascaded ST counterpart when large-scale ASR and MT data is available.

label: acl
text: Encoder pre-training has shown promise in end-to-end Speech Translation (ST), given the scarcity of speech-to-translation data. However, ST encoders are not simply a combination of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) encoders. ASR encoders lack the necessary global context representation for translation, while MT encoders are not equipped to handle long, locally attentive acoustic sequences. To address this, we propose a Stacked Acoustic-and-Textual Encoding (SATE) method for speech translation. Our encoder starts with processing the acoustic sequence, but later behaves more like an MT encoder for global representation of the input. This makes it easy to incorporate pre-trained models into the system. Additionally, we have developed an adaptor module to resolve the representation inconsistency between the pre-trained ASR encoder and MT encoder, and a multi-teacher knowledge distillation method to retain the pre-training knowledge. Our results on the LibriSpeech En-Fr and MuST-C En-De ST tasks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art BLEU scores of 18.3 and 25.2, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to develop an end-to-end ST system that achieves comparable or even better BLEU performance than cascaded ST counterparts when large-scale ASR and MT data is available.

label: acl
text: Knowledge Graph (KG) embedding has emerged as a very active area of research over the last few years, resulting in the development of several embedding methods. These KG embedding methods represent KG entities and relations as vectors in a high-dimensional space. Despite this popularity and effectiveness of KG embeddings in various tasks (e.g., link prediction), geometric understanding of such embeddings (i.e., arrangement of entity and relation vectors in vector space) is unexplored – we fill this gap in the paper. We initiate a study to analyze the geometry of KG embeddings and correlate it with task performance and other hyperparameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of its kind. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, we discover several insights. For example, we find that there are sharp differences between the geometry of embeddings learnt by different classes of KG embeddings methods. We hope that this initial study will inspire other follow-up research on this important but unexplored problem.

label: acl
text: The field of Knowledge Graph (KG) embedding has experienced significant growth in recent years, resulting in the creation of various embedding methods. These methods represent KG entities and relationships as vectors in a high-dimensional space. Despite their popularity and success in various tasks, such as link prediction, the geometric arrangement of these embeddings remains unexplored. This paper aims to fill this gap by analyzing the geometry of KG embeddings and examining its correlation with task performance and hyperparameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of its kind. Through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, we uncover several important insights, including the significant differences in the geometry of embeddings produced by different KG embedding methods. We hope that this initial study will encourage further research in this important but under-explored area.

label: naacl
text: Emotion recognition in conversations is crucial for the development of empathetic machines. Present methods mostly ignore the role of inter-speaker dependency relations while classifying emotions in conversations. In this paper, we address recognizing utterance-level emotions in dyadic conversational videos. We propose a deep neural framework, termed Conversational Memory Network (CMN), which leverages contextual information from the conversation history. In particular, CMN uses multimodal approach comprising audio, visual and textual features with gated recurrent units to model past utterances of each speaker into memories. These memories are then merged using attention-based hops to capture inter-speaker dependencies. Experiments show a significant improvement of 3 − 4% in accuracy over the state of the art.

label: naacl
text: Emotion recognition in conversations is an important aspect in the development of empathetic machines. However, current methods often overlook the significance of inter-speaker dependency relations in classifying emotions. This paper presents a deep neural framework, called the Conversational Memory Network (CMN), for recognizing utterance-level emotions in dyadic conversational videos. The CMN leverages contextual information from the conversation history through a multimodal approach that combines audio, visual, and textual features. Gated recurrent units are used to model past utterances of each speaker into memories, which are then merged using attention-based hops to capture inter-speaker dependencies. The results of the experiments demonstrate a significant improvement of 3-4% in accuracy compared to the state of the art.

text: Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction (ASTE) is the most recent subtask of ABSA which outputs triplets of an aspect target, its associated sentiment, and the corresponding opinion term. Recent models perform the triplet extraction in an end-to-end manner but heavily rely on the interactions between each target word and opinion word. Thereby, they cannot perform well on targets and opinions which contain multiple words. Our proposed span-level approach explicitly considers the interaction between the whole spans of targets and opinions when predicting their sentiment relation. Thus, it can make predictions with the semantics of whole spans, ensuring better sentiment consistency. To ease the high computational cost caused by span enumeration, we propose a dual-channel span pruning strategy by incorporating supervision from the Aspect Term Extraction (ATE) and Opinion Term Extraction (OTE) tasks. This strategy not only improves computational efficiency but also distinguishes the opinion and target spans more properly. Our framework simultaneously achieves strong performance for the ASTE as well as ATE and OTE tasks. In particular, our analysis shows that our span-level approach achieves more significant improvements over the baselines on triplets with multi-word targets or opinions.

text: The most recent subtask of ABSA, Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction (ASTE), outputs triplets consisting of an aspect target, its sentiment, and the corresponding opinion term. text: Our goal is to study the novel task of distant supervision for multilingual relation extraction (Multi DS-RE). Research in Multi DS-RE has remained limited due to the absence of a reliable benchmarking dataset. The only available dataset for this task, RELX-Distant (Köksal and Özgür, 2020), displays several unrealistic characteristics, leading to a systematic overestimation of model performance. To alleviate these concerns, we release a new benchmark dataset for the task, named DiS-ReX. We also modify the widely-used bag attention models using an mBERT encoder and provide the first baseline results on the proposed task. We show that DiS-ReX serves as a more challenging dataset than RELX-Distant, leaving ample room for future research in this domain.

text: Our goal is to study the novel task of distant supervision for multilingual relation extraction (Multi DS-RE). Despite the limited research in this area, the only available dataset for this task, RELX-Distant (Köksal and Özgür, 2020), has several unrealistic characteristics, leading to systematic overestimation of model performance. To address these issues, we introduce a new benchmark dataset, DiS-ReX, and modify the widely-used bag attention models using an mBERT encoder. Our results demonstrate that DiS-ReX is a more challenging dataset than RELX-Distant and provides ample room for future research in this field.

text: In this paper we present the first model for directly synthesizing fluent, natural-sounding spoken audio captions for images that does not require natural language text as an intermediate representation or source of supervision. Instead, we connect the image captioning module and the speech synthesis module with a set of discrete, sub-word speech units that are discovered with a self-supervised visual grounding task. We conduct experiments on the Flickr8k spoken caption dataset in addition to a novel corpus of spoken audio captions collected for the popular MSCOCO dataset, demonstrating that our generated captions also capture diverse visual semantics of the images they describe. We investigate several different intermediate speech representations, and empirically find that the representation must satisfy several important properties to serve as drop-in replacements for text.

text: This paper introduces the first model that can directly synthesize fluent and natural-sounding spoken audio captions for images, without the need for natural language text as an intermediate representation or source of supervision. Our model connects the image captioning module and the speech synthesis module through a set of discrete sub-word speech units, which are discovered through a self-supervised visual grounding task. We evaluate our model on the Flickr8k spoken caption dataset and a novel corpus of spoken audio captions collected for the MSCOCO dataset, demonstrating that it captures diverse visual semantics of the images it describes. Our experiments also show that the intermediate speech representation must meet several important properties to effectively replace text.
