text: Weakly-supervised learning (WSL) has shown promising results in addressing label scarcity on many NLP tasks, but manually designing a comprehensive, high-quality labeling rule set is tedious and difficult. We study interactive weakly-supervised learning—the problem of iteratively and automatically discovering novel labeling rules from data to improve the WSL model. Our proposed model, named PRBoost, achieves this goal via iterative prompt-based rule discovery and model boosting. It uses boosting to identify large-error instances and discovers candidate rules from them by prompting pre-trained LMs with rule templates. The candidate rules are judged by human experts, and the accepted rules are used to generate complementary weak labels and strengthen the current model. Experiments on four tasks show PRBoost outperforms state-of-the-art WSL baselines up to 7.1%, and bridges the gaps with fully supervised models.

label: acl
text: Weakly-supervised learning (WSL) has shown promising results in addressing label scarcity in NLP tasks, but manual design of a comprehensive and high-quality labeling rule set is tedious and challenging. To address this issue, we propose a solution in the form of interactive weakly-supervised learning, which involves iteratively discovering novel labeling rules from data to improve the WSL model. Our proposed model, PRBoost, achieves this through a combination of iterative prompt-based rule discovery and model boosting. It uses boosting to identify instances with high errors, prompts pre-trained language models with rule templates to discover candidate rules, and then seeks judgment from human experts to determine which rules to accept. The accepted rules are then used to generate complementary weak labels and strengthen the current model. Our experiments on four tasks demonstrate that PRBoost outperforms state-of-the-art WSL baselines by up to 7.1%, and significantly reduces the gap with fully supervised models.

label: acl
text: Detecting Out-of-Domain (OOD) or unknown intents from user queries is essential in a task-oriented dialog system. A key challenge of OOD detection is to learn discriminative semantic features. Traditional cross-entropy loss only focuses on whether a sample is correctly classified, and does not explicitly distinguish the margins between categories. In this paper, we propose a supervised contrastive learning objective to minimize intra-class variance by pulling together in-domain intents belonging to the same class and maximize inter-class variance by pushing apart samples from different classes. Besides, we employ an adversarial augmentation mechanism to obtain pseudo diverse views of a sample in the latent space. Experiments on two public datasets prove the effectiveness of our method capturing discriminative representations for OOD detection.

text: Detecting Out-of-Domain (OOD) or unknown intents from user queries is crucial for a task-oriented dialog system. The challenge lies in learning discriminative semantic features. Traditional cross-entropy loss only focuses on whether a sample is correctly classified, and does not distinguish between categories. To address this, we propose a supervised contrastive learning objective that minimizes intra-class variance by bringing together in-domain intents of the same class and maximizes inter-class variance by separating samples from different classes. Additionally, we use an adversarial augmentation mechanism to generate diverse views of a sample in the latent space. Our experiments on two public datasets show the effectiveness of our method in capturing discriminative representations for OOD detection.

text: This paper examines the problem of generating natural language descriptions of chess games. We introduce a new large-scale chess commentary dataset and propose methods to generate commentary for individual moves in a chess game. The introduced dataset consists of more than 298K chess move-commentary pairs across 11K chess games. We highlight how this task poses unique research challenges in natural language generation: the data contain a large variety of styles of commentary and frequently depend on pragmatic context. We benchmark various baselines and propose an end-to-end trainable neural model which takes into account multiple pragmatic aspects of the game state that may be commented upon to describe a given chess move. Through a human study on predictions for a subset of the data which deals with direct move descriptions, we observe that outputs from our models are rated similar to ground truth commentary texts in terms of correctness and fluency.

label: acl
text: This paper explores the challenge of generating natural language descriptions for chess games. To tackle this challenge, we present a new large-scale chess commentary dataset, consisting of over 298,000 move-commentary pairs across 11,000 chess games. Our dataset highlights the unique research challenges in natural language generation, including the diverse styles of commentary and the dependency on the pragmatic context. We evaluate various baselines and propose an end-to-end trainable neural model that takes into account multiple pragmatic aspects of the game state to describe a chess move. Our human study on a subset of the data that focuses on direct move descriptions shows that our models are rated similarly to the ground truth commentary texts in terms of accuracy and fluency.

text: Recent work in multilingual machine translation (MMT) has focused on the potential of positive transfer between languages, particularly cases where higher-resourced languages can benefit lower-resourced ones. While training an MMT model, the supervision signals learned from one language pair can be transferred to the other via the tokens shared by multiple source languages. However, the transfer is inhibited when the token overlap among source languages is small, which manifests naturally when languages use different writing systems. In this paper, we tackle inhibited transfer by augmenting the training data with alternative signals that unify different writing systems, such as phonetic, romanized, and transliterated input. We test these signals on Indic and Turkic languages, two language families where the writing systems differ but languages still share common features. Our results indicate that a straightforward multi-source self-ensemble – training a model on a mixture of various signals and ensembling the outputs of the same model fed with different signals during inference, outperforms strong ensemble baselines by 1.3 BLEU points on both language families. Further, we find that incorporating alternative inputs via self-ensemble can be particularly effective when training set is small, leading to +5 BLEU when only 5% of the total training data is accessible. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that including alternative signals yields more consistency and translates named entities more accurately, which is crucial for increased factuality of automated systems.

text: Recently, research in multilingual machine translation (MMT) has focused on the potential for positive transfer between languages, particularly when higher-resourced languages can benefit lower-resourced ones. However, transfer is hindered when token overlap among source languages is limited, which often occurs when languages use different writing systems. To address this issue, we augment the training data with alternative signals, such as phonetic, romanized, and transliterated inputs, that unify different writing systems. We test these signals on Indic and Turkic languages, two language families that have different writing systems but share common features. Our results show that a multi-source self-ensemble, training a model on a combination of signals and ensembling the outputs of the same model fed with different signals during inference, outperforms strong ensemble baselines by 1.3 BLEU points in both language families. Furthermore, incorporating alternative inputs via self-ensemble can be especially effective when training data is limited, leading to a +5 BLEU improvement when only 5% of the total data is accessible. Our analysis also demonstrates that including alternative signals results in greater consistency and more accurate named entity translation, which is crucial for improving the factuality of automated systems.

text: Prior work has revealed that positive words occur more frequently than negative words in human expressions, which is typically attributed to positivity bias, a tendency for people to report positive views of reality. But what about the language used in negative reviews? Consistent with prior work, we show that English negative reviews tend to contain more positive words than negative words, using a variety of datasets. We reconcile this observation with prior findings on the pragmatics of negation, and show that negations are commonly associated with positive words in negative reviews. Furthermore, in negative reviews, the majority of sentences with positive words express negative opinions based on sentiment classifiers, indicating some form of negation.

label: acl
text: Prior research has shown that positive words are used more frequently in human expressions than negative words, which is usually attributed to a positivity bias, meaning people have a tendency to present positive views of reality. However, what about the language used in negative reviews? Our research confirms previous findings that negative reviews in English tend to contain more positive words than negative words, as seen in multiple datasets. We explain this phenomenon by linking it to the pragmatics of negation and demonstrate that negative words are often paired with positive words in negative reviews. Moreover, our analysis shows that the majority of sentences with positive words in negative reviews are actually expressing negative opinions, as determined by sentiment classifiers.

text: In dialogue state tracking, dialogue history is a crucial material, and its utilization varies between different models. However, no matter how the dialogue history is used, each existing model uses its own consistent dialogue history during the entire state tracking process, regardless of which slot is updated. Apparently, it requires different dialogue history to update different slots in different turns. Therefore, using consistent dialogue contents may lead to insufficient or redundant information for different slots, which affects the overall performance. To address this problem, we devise DiCoS-DST to dynamically select the relevant dialogue contents corresponding to each slot for state updating. Specifically, it first retrieves turn-level utterances of dialogue history and evaluates their relevance to the slot from a combination of three perspectives: (1) its explicit connection to the slot name; (2) its relevance to the current turn dialogue; (3) Implicit Mention Oriented Reasoning. Then these perspectives are combined to yield a decision, and only the selected dialogue contents are fed into State Generator, which explicitly minimizes the distracting information passed to the downstream state prediction. Experimental results show that our approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance on MultiWOZ 2.1 and MultiWOZ 2.2, and achieves superior performance on multiple mainstream benchmark datasets (including Sim-M, Sim-R, and DSTC2).

label: acl
text: In dialogue state tracking, the utilization of dialogue history varies between different models. However, each model consistently uses its own dialogue history throughout the tracking process, regardless of which slot is being updated. This can result in insufficient or redundant information for different slots, affecting the overall performance. To solve this problem, we propose DiCoS-DST, which dynamically selects relevant dialogue contents for each slot. This is achieved by evaluating the relevance of turn-level utterances from three perspectives: (1) explicit connection to the slot name, (2) relevance to the current turn, and (3) Implicit Mention Oriented Reasoning. The selected dialogue contents are then fed into the State Generator, reducing distracting information and improving performance. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on MultiWOZ 2.1 and MultiWOZ 2.2, and outperforms other benchmark datasets such as Sim-M, Sim-R, and DSTC2.

label: acl
text: Aspect based sentiment analysis (ABSA) can provide more detailed information than general sentiment analysis, because it aims to predict the sentiment polarities of the given aspects or entities in text. We summarize previous approaches into two subtasks: aspect-category sentiment analysis (ACSA) and aspect-term sentiment analysis (ATSA). Most previous approaches employ long short-term memory and attention mechanisms to predict the sentiment polarity of the concerned targets, which are often complicated and need more training time. We propose a model based on convolutional neural networks and gating mechanisms, which is more accurate and efficient. First, the novel Gated Tanh-ReLU Units can selectively output the sentiment features according to the given aspect or entity. The architecture is much simpler than attention layer used in the existing models. Second, the computations of our model could be easily parallelized during training, because convolutional layers do not have time dependency as in LSTM layers, and gating units also work independently. The experiments on SemEval datasets demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our models.

text: The Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) technique provides more in-depth information than general sentiment analysis as it aims to predict the sentiment polarity of specific aspects or entities in text. Previous approaches to ABSA can be grouped into two subtasks: Aspect-Category Sentiment Analysis (ACSA) and Aspect-Term Sentiment Analysis (ATSA). Most previous methods have relied on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and attention mechanisms to predict the sentiment polarity of the target, which can be complex and require more training time. To address these issues, we propose a model based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and gating mechanisms that is more accurate and efficient. Our novel Gated Tanh-ReLU Units selectively output sentiment features based on the aspect or entity, making the architecture simpler than the attention layers used in existing models. Additionally, the computations in our model can be easily parallelized during training as convolutional layers do not have time dependencies as in LSTM layers, and gating units also work independently. The results of our experiments on the SemEval datasets demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our model.

text: We consider negotiation settings in which two agents use natural language to bargain on goods. Agents need to decide on both high-level strategy (e.g., proposing $50) and the execution of that strategy (e.g., generating “The bike is brand new. Selling for just $50!”). Recent work on negotiation trains neural models, but their end-to-end nature makes it hard to control their strategy, and reinforcement learning tends to lead to degenerate solutions. In this paper, we propose a modular approach based on coarse dialogue acts (e.g., propose(price=50)) that decouples strategy and generation. We show that we can flexibly set the strategy using supervised learning, reinforcement learning, or domain-specific knowledge without degeneracy, while our retrieval-based generation can maintain context-awareness and produce diverse utterances. We test our approach on the recently proposed DEALORNODEAL game, and we also collect a richer dataset based on real items on Craigslist. Human evaluation shows that our systems achieve higher task success rate and more human-like negotiation behavior than previous approaches.

label: emnlp
text: We examine negotiation scenarios where two agents communicate using natural language to negotiate the exchange of goods. The agents must make decisions about both their overall strategy (e.g. proposing a price of $50) and the execution of that strategy (e.g. generating the statement "The bike is brand new. Selling for just $50!"). Previous work has utilized neural models in negotiation, but their end-to-end design makes it difficult to control their strategies and reinforcement learning often results in degenerate solutions. This paper introduces a modular approach that separates strategy and generation using coarse dialogue acts (e.g. propose(price=50)). Our approach allows for the flexible use of supervised learning, reinforcement learning, or domain-specific knowledge to set the strategy without degeneracy. Our retrieval-based generation system retains context-awareness and generates diverse utterances. We evaluate our approach using the DEALORNODEAL game and a richer dataset based on real items from Craigslist. Our results show that our system achieves a higher task success rate and more human-like negotiation behavior compared to previous methods, as confirmed by human evaluation.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a conditional non-autoregressive neural sequence model based on iterative refinement. The proposed model is designed based on the principles of latent variable models and denoising autoencoders, and is generally applicable to any sequence generation task. We extensively evaluate the proposed model on machine translation (En-De and En-Ro) and image caption generation, and observe that it significantly speeds up decoding while maintaining the generation quality comparable to the autoregressive counterpart.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a conditional non-autoregressive neural sequence model that is based on iterative refinement. This model is designed using the principles of latent variable models and denoising autoencoders, and can be applied to any sequence generation task. Our extensive evaluations of the proposed model on machine translation (En-De and En-Ro) and image caption generation show that it significantly accelerates decoding while maintaining comparable generation quality to its autoregressive counterpart.

text: Event Causality Identification (ECI) is the task of detecting causal relations between events mentioned in the text. Although this task has been extensively studied for English materials, it is under-explored for many other languages. A major reason for this issue is the lack of multilingual datasets that provide consistent annotations for event causality relations in multiple non-English languages. To address this issue, we introduce a new multilingual dataset for ECI, called MECI. The dataset employs consistent annotation guidelines for five typologically different languages, i.e., English, Danish, Spanish, Turkish, and Urdu. Our dataset thus enable a new research direction on cross-lingual transfer learning for ECI. Our extensive experiments demonstrate high quality for MECI that can provide ample research challenges and directions for future research. We will publicly release MECI to promote research on multilingual ECI.

text: Event Causality Identification (ECI) is the task of detecting causal relationships between events mentioned in text. Although this task has been studied extensively in English, it remains under-explored in many other languages. A major reason for this is the lack of multilingual datasets that provide consistent annotations for event causality relationships across non-English languages. To address this issue, we present a new multilingual dataset, called MECI. This dataset includes consistent annotation guidelines for five typologically diverse languages: English, Danish, Spanish, Turkish, and Urdu. Our dataset opens up new opportunities for cross-lingual transfer learning in ECI. Our experiments demonstrate the high quality of MECI and provide ample challenges and directions for future research. We aim to promote research in multilingual ECI by publicly releasing MECI.

text: Existing continual relation learning (CRL) methods rely on plenty of labeled training data for learning a new task, which can be hard to acquire in real scenario as getting large and representative labeled data is often expensive and time-consuming. It is therefore necessary for the model to learn novel relational patterns with very few labeled data while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of previous task knowledge. In this paper, we formulate this challenging yet practical problem as continual few-shot relation learning (CFRL). Based on the finding that learning for new emerging few-shot tasks often results in feature distributions that are incompatible with previous tasks' learned distributions, we propose a novel method based on embedding space regularization and data augmentation. Our method generalizes to new few-shot tasks and avoids catastrophic forgetting of previous tasks by enforcing extra constraints on the relational embeddings and by adding extra relevant data in a self-supervised manner. With extensive experiments we demonstrate that our method can significantly outperform previous state-of-the-art methods in CFRL task settings.

label: acl
text: Existing continual relation learning (CRL) methods are dependent on ample labeled training data for learning a new task. However, acquiring large and representative labeled data in real-world scenarios can be challenging, as it is often time-consuming and expensive. To overcome this challenge, it is crucial for the model to learn novel relational patterns with limited labeled data while retaining previous task knowledge. In this paper, we present a novel approach to this practical problem, referred to as continual few-shot relation learning (CFRL). Our method is based on the finding that learning for new few-shot tasks often results in incompatible feature distributions with previous tasks. To address this, we propose a novel approach that involves embedding space regularization and data augmentation. Our method generalizes to new tasks and prevents catastrophic forgetting of previous knowledge by imposing constraints on the relational embeddings and adding relevant data in a self-supervised manner. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in CFRL task settings.

label: acl
text: Today's text classifiers inevitably suffer from unintended dataset biases, especially the document-level label bias and word-level keyword bias, which may hurt models' generalization. Many previous studies employed data-level manipulations or model-level balancing mechanisms to recover unbiased distributions and thus prevent models from capturing the two types of biases. Unfortunately, they either suffer from the extra cost of data collection/selection/annotation or need an elaborate design of balancing strategies. Different from traditional factual inference in which debiasing occurs before or during training, counterfactual inference mitigates the influence brought by unintended confounders after training, which can make unbiased decisions with biased observations. Inspired by this, we propose a model-agnostic text classification debiasing framework – Corsair, which can effectively avoid employing data manipulations or designing balancing mechanisms. Concretely, Corsair first trains a base model on a training set directly, allowing the dataset biases `poison' the trained model. In inference, given a factual input document, Corsair imagines its two counterfactual counterparts to distill and mitigate the two biases captured by the poisonous model. Extensive experiments demonstrate Corsair's effectiveness, generalizability and fairness.

label: acl
text: Today's text classifiers often suffer from unintended biases, such as document-level label bias and word-level keyword bias, which can negatively impact models' generalization. Previous studies have attempted to mitigate these biases by either manipulating the data or implementing balancing mechanisms in the model. However, these solutions come with the cost of additional data collection, annotation, or complex balancing strategies. In contrast, our proposed framework, Corsair, uses a model-agnostic approach to debias text classification models. Unlike traditional debiasing methods that occur before or during training, Corsair debiases after training by imagining two counterfactual counterparts for each factual input document. This allows Corsair to effectively avoid the need for data manipulation or balancing mechanisms. Our experiments show that Corsair is effective, generalizable, and fair.

label: coling
text: One main challenge for incremental transition-based parsers, when future inputs are invisible, is to extract good features from a limited local context. In this work, we present a simple technique to maximally utilize the local features with an attention mechanism, which works as context- dependent dynamic feature selection. Our model learns, for example, which tokens should a parser focus on, to decide the next action. Our multilingual experiment shows its effectiveness across many languages. We also present an experiment with augmented test dataset and demon- strate it helps to understand the model's behavior on locally ambiguous points.

label: coling
text: The main challenge facing incremental transition-based parsers when future inputs are not visible is to extract meaningful features from a limited local context. To address this, we present a simple technique that leverages an attention mechanism to maximize the utilization of local features. This mechanism allows the parser to dynamically select features based on the context, learning which tokens to focus on when making its next action. Our multilingual experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach across several languages. Additionally, we conduct an experiment using an augmented test dataset to better understand the model's behavior in cases of local ambiguity.

label: acl
text: Cross-lingual named entity recognition task is one of the critical problems for evaluating the potential transfer learning techniques on low resource languages. Knowledge distillation using pre-trained multilingual language models between source and target languages have shown their superiority in transfer. However, existing cross-lingual distillation models merely consider the potential transferability between two identical single tasks across both domains. Other possible auxiliary tasks to improve the learning performance have not been fully investigated. In this study, based on the knowledge distillation framework and multi-task learning, we introduce the similarity metric model as an auxiliary task to improve the cross-lingual NER performance on the target domain. Specifically, an entity recognizer and a similarity evaluator are first trained in parallel as two teachers from the source domain. Then, two tasks in the student model are supervised by these teachers simultaneously. Empirical studies on the three datasets across 7 different languages confirm the effectiveness of the proposed model.

label: acl
text: Cross-lingual named entity recognition (NER) is a critical problem in evaluating the potential of transfer learning techniques for low-resource languages. Knowledge distillation using pre-trained multilingual language models has demonstrated superiority in transferring information between source and target languages. However, current cross-lingual distillation models only consider the transferability between two identical single tasks across both domains. The potential of other auxiliary tasks to improve learning performance has not been fully explored. In this study, we present a novel approach to improve cross-lingual NER performance through knowledge distillation and multi-task learning. Our model incorporates a similarity metric as an auxiliary task. An entity recognizer and a similarity evaluator are trained in parallel as two "teachers" from the source domain. These teachers then supervise the two tasks in the student model simultaneously. Empirical studies on three datasets across seven languages confirm the effectiveness of our proposed model.

label: acl
text: Embedding models for entities and relations are extremely useful for recovering missing facts in a knowledge base. Intuitively, a relation can be modeled by a matrix mapping entity vectors. However, relations reside on low dimension sub-manifolds in the parameter space of arbitrary matrices – for one reason, composition of two relations M1, M2 may match a third M3 (e.g. composition of relations currency_of_country and country_of_film usually matches currency_of_film_budget), which imposes compositional constraints to be satisfied by the parameters (i.e. M1*M2=M3). In this paper we investigate a dimension reduction technique by training relations jointly with an autoencoder, which is expected to better capture compositional constraints. We achieve state-of-the-art on Knowledge Base Completion tasks with strongly improved Mean Rank, and show that joint training with an autoencoder leads to interpretable sparse codings of relations, helps discovering compositional constraints and benefits from compositional training. Our source code is released at github.com/tianran/glimvec.

label: acl
text: Embedding models for entities and relations are highly valuable for filling in gaps in a knowledge base. Essentially, a relation can be represented by a matrix that maps entity vectors. However, relations exist on low-dimensional sub-manifolds within the parameter space of arbitrary matrices. This is due to the fact that the composition of two relations (M1 and M2) may match a third (M3, such as the composition of "currency_of_country" and "country_of_film" matching "currency_of_film_budget"). These compositional constraints must be satisfied by the parameters, meaning that M1*M2 must equal M3. In this study, we explore a dimension reduction technique by training relations in conjunction with an autoencoder, which is expected to better capture these compositional constraints. Our results show that joint training with an autoencoder leads to interpretable, sparse codings of relations, helps uncover compositional constraints, and benefits from compositional training. Our state-of-the-art performance on Knowledge Base Completion tasks is demonstrated by a strongly improved Mean Rank. Our source code is available on Github at github.com/tianran/glimvec.

label: acl
text: In neural machine translation, a source sequence of words is encoded into a vector from which a target sequence is generated in the decoding phase. Differently from statistical machine translation, the associations between source words and their possible target counterparts are not explicitly stored. Source and target words are at the two ends of a long information processing procedure, mediated by hidden states at both the source encoding and the target decoding phases. This makes it possible that a source word is incorrectly translated into a target word that is not any of its admissible equivalent counterparts in the target language. In this paper, we seek to somewhat shorten the distance between source and target words in that procedure, and thus strengthen their association, by means of a method we term bridging source and target word embeddings. We experiment with three strategies: (1) a source-side bridging model, where source word embeddings are moved one step closer to the output target sequence; (2) a target-side bridging model, which explores the more relevant source word embeddings for the prediction of the target sequence; and (3) a direct bridging model, which directly connects source and target word embeddings seeking to minimize errors in the translation of ones by the others. Experiments and analysis presented in this paper demonstrate that the proposed bridging models are able to significantly improve quality of both sentence translation, in general, and alignment and translation of individual source words with target words, in particular.

label: acl
text: In neural machine translation, the source sequence of words is transformed into a vector, which is then used to generate the target sequence during the decoding phase. Unlike statistical machine translation, the connections between source words and their potential target counterparts are not explicitly stored. The source and target words are at the two ends of a complex information processing procedure, which is mediated by hidden states during both the source encoding and target decoding phases. This can result in a source word being translated into a target word that is not its equivalent counterpart in the target language. To reduce the distance between source and target words in this procedure and strengthen their connection, we propose a method called "bridging source and target word embeddings." We experiment with three strategies: (1) a source-side bridging model, which moves source word embeddings closer to the target sequence; (2) a target-side bridging model, which identifies the most relevant source word embeddings for predicting the target sequence; and (3) a direct bridging model, which directly links source and target word embeddings to minimize translation errors. Our experiments and analysis show that these bridging models can significantly improve the quality of sentence translation and the alignment and translation of individual source words and target words.

label: coling
text: We formulate a generalization of Petrov et al. (2006)'s split/merge algorithm for interpreted regular tree grammars (Koller and Kuhlmann, 2011), which capture a large class of grammar formalisms. We evaluate its effectiveness empirically on the task of discontinuous constituent parsing with two mildly context-sensitive grammar formalisms: linear context-free rewriting systems (Vijay-Shanker et al., 1987) as well as hybrid grammars (Nederhof and Vogler, 2014).

label: coling
text: We present a generalization of Petrov et al.'s (2006) split/merge algorithm for interpreted regular tree grammars (as described by Koller and Kuhlmann, 2011), which encompasses a broad range of grammar formalisms. We empirically assess its efficacy on the task of discontinuous constituent parsing, using two mildly context-sensitive grammar formalisms: linear context-free rewriting systems (Vijay-Shanker et al., 1987) and hybrid grammars (Nederhof and Vogler, 2014).

label: acl
text: Transformers have advanced the field of natural language processing (NLP) on a variety of important tasks. At the cornerstone of the Transformer architecture is the multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism which models pairwise interactions between the elements of the sequence. Despite its massive success, the current framework ignores interactions among different heads, leading to the problem that many of the heads are redundant in practice, which greatly wastes the capacity of the model. To improve parameter efficiency, we re-formulate the MHA as a latent variable model from a probabilistic perspective. We present cascaded head-colliding attention (CODA) which explicitly models the interactions between attention heads through a hierarchical variational distribution. We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate that CODA outperforms the transformer baseline, by 0.6 perplexity on Wikitext-103 in language modeling, and by 0.6 BLEU on WMT14 EN-DE in machine translation, due to its improvements on the parameter efficiency.

label: acl
text: Transformers have revolutionized the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) by delivering impressive results on a wide range of tasks. The cornerstone of the Transformer architecture is the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mechanism, which models the interactions between elements in a sequence. Despite its success, the current framework has a drawback - it ignores interactions between different heads, which can lead to redundant heads and waste the model's capacity. To address this issue, we have re-formulated the MHA as a Latent Variable Model from a probabilistic perspective. We have introduced the Cascaded Head-Colliding Attention (CODA) mechanism, which explicitly models the interactions between attention heads through a hierarchical variational distribution. Our experiments show that CODA outperforms the Transformer baseline, with a 0.6 improvement in perplexity on Wikitext-103 for language modeling and a 0.6 improvement in BLEU on WMT14 EN-DE for machine translation, thanks to its improved parameter efficiency.

label: coling
text: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models, which eliminate the sequential dependencies within the target sentence, have achieved remarkable inference speed, but suffer from inferior translation quality. Towards exploring the underlying causes, we carry out a thorough preliminary study on the attention mechanism, which demonstrates the serious weakness in capturing localness compared with conventional autoregressive translation (AT). In response to this problem, we propose to improve the localness of NAT models by explicitly introducing the information about surrounding words. Specifically, temporal convolutions are incorporated into both encoder and decoder sides to obtain localness-aware representations. Extensive experiments on several typical translation datasets show that the proposed method can achieve consistent and significant improvements over strong NAT baselines. Further analyses on the WMT14 En-De translation task reveal that compared with baselines, our approach accelerates the convergence in training and can achieve equivalent performance with a reduction of 70% training steps.

label: coling
text: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models, which eliminate the sequential dependencies within target sentences, have achieved impressive inference speeds, but suffer from poor translation quality. To understand the underlying causes, we conducted a comprehensive preliminary study on the attention mechanism, which revealed its weakness in capturing localness compared to conventional autoregressive translation (AT) models. To address this issue, we propose to enhance the localness of NAT models by incorporating information about surrounding words. Specifically, we introduce temporal convolutions into both the encoder and decoder to obtain localness-aware representations. Our experiments on various translation datasets demonstrate that our proposed method consistently improves upon strong NAT baselines. Further analysis of the WMT14 En-De translation task shows that our approach accelerates convergence during training and achieves equivalent performance with a 70% reduction in training steps compared to baselines.

label: emnlp
text: Current state-of-the-art semantic role labeling (SRL) uses a deep neural network with no explicit linguistic features. However, prior work has shown that gold syntax trees can dramatically improve SRL decoding, suggesting the possibility of increased accuracy from explicit modeling of syntax. In this work, we present linguistically-informed self-attention (LISA): a neural network model that combines multi-head self-attention with multi-task learning across dependency parsing, part-of-speech tagging, predicate detection and SRL. Unlike previous models which require significant pre-processing to prepare linguistic features, LISA can incorporate syntax using merely raw tokens as input, encoding the sequence only once to simultaneously perform parsing, predicate detection and role labeling for all predicates. Syntax is incorporated by training one attention head to attend to syntactic parents for each token. Moreover, if a high-quality syntactic parse is already available, it can be beneficially injected at test time without re-training our SRL model. In experiments on CoNLL-2005 SRL, LISA achieves new state-of-the-art performance for a model using predicted predicates and standard word embeddings, attaining 2.5 F1 absolute higher than the previous state-of-the-art on newswire and more than 3.5 F1 on out-of-domain data, nearly 10% reduction in error. On ConLL-2012 English SRL we also show an improvement of more than 2.5 F1. LISA also out-performs the state-of-the-art with contextually-encoded (ELMo) word representations, by nearly 1.0 F1 on news and more than 2.0 F1 on out-of-domain text.

The proposed LISA model demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating syntax into SRL through multi-task learning and self-attention.

The current state-of-the-art in semantic role labeling (SRL) uses deep neural networks without explicit linguistic features. However, previous research has shown that incorporating gold syntax trees can significantly improve SRL decoding accuracy. To address this, we present Linguistically-Informed Self-Attention (LISA), a neural network model that combines multi-head self-attention with multi-task learning across dependency parsing, part-of-speech tagging, predicate detection, and SRL. Unlike previous models that require extensive pre-processing to prepare linguistic features, LISA can incorporate syntax using raw tokens as input, encoding the sequence only once to simultaneously perform parsing, predicate detection, and role labeling for all predicates. Syntax is incorporated by training an attention head to attend to syntactic parents for each token. If a high-quality syntactic parse is already available, it can be easily injected into the model at test time without re-training. In experiments on CoNLL-2005 SRL, LISA achieved new state-of-the-art performance, with a 2.5 F1 improvement over the previous state-of-the-art on newswire and more than 3.5 F1 on out-of-domain data, resulting in a nearly 10% reduction in error. On CoNLL-2012 English SRL, LISA also showed an improvement of more than 2.5 F1. Additionally, LISA outperformed the state-of-the-art with contextually-encoded (ELMo) word representations, with a nearly 1.0 F1 improvement on news and more than 2.0 F1 on out-of-domain text. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating syntax into SRL through multi-task learning and self-attention.

label: emnlp
text: Chinese pinyin input method engine (IME) converts pinyin into character so that Chinese characters can be conveniently inputted into computer through common keyboard. IMEs work relying on its core component, pinyin-to-character conversion (P2C). Usually Chinese IMEs simply predict a list of character sequences for user choice only according to user pinyin input at each turn. However, Chinese inputting is a multi-turn online procedure, which can be supposed to be exploited for further user experience promoting. This paper thus for the first time introduces a sequence-to-sequence model with gated-attention mechanism for the core task in IMEs. The proposed neural P2C model is learned by encoding previous input utterance as extra context to enable our IME capable of predicting character sequence with incomplete pinyin input. Our model is evaluated in different benchmark datasets showing great user experience improvement compared to traditional models, which demonstrates the first engineering practice of building Chinese aided IME.

label: emnlp
text: The Chinese Pinyin Input Method Engine (IME) converts Pinyin into characters, allowing for convenient inputting of Chinese characters into computers using a common keyboard. IMEs rely on the core component of Pinyin-to-Character Conversion (P2C). Typically, Chinese IMEs simply present a list of character sequences for the user to choose from based on their Pinyin input at each turn. However, this multi-turn online inputting process can be improved for a better user experience. This paper introduces, for the first time, a sequence-to-sequence model with a gated-attention mechanism for the core task in IMEs. The proposed neural P2C model learns to encode previous input utterances as extra context, enabling the IME to predict character sequences with incomplete Pinyin input. The model is evaluated on different benchmark datasets and shows significant improvement in user experience compared to traditional models, demonstrating the first successful implementation of a Chinese-aided IME.

label: naacl
text: The use of explicit object detectors as an intermediate step to image captioning – which used to constitute an essential stage in early work – is often bypassed in the currently dominant end-to-end approaches, where the language model is conditioned directly on a mid-level image embedding. We argue that explicit detections provide rich semantic information, and can thus be used as an interpretable representation to better understand why end-to-end image captioning systems work well. We provide an in-depth analysis of end-to-end image captioning by exploring a variety of cues that can be derived from such object detections. Our study reveals that end-to-end image captioning systems rely on matching image representations to generate captions, and that encoding the frequency, size and position of objects are complementary and all play a role in forming a good image representation. It also reveals that different object categories contribute in different ways towards image captioning.

label: naacl
text: The use of explicit object detectors as an intermediate step in image captioning, which was once considered essential in early work, is now often bypassed in current end-to-end approaches. In these approaches, the language model is directly conditioned on a mid-level image embedding, bypassing the use of explicit object detectors. However, we argue that these detectors provide rich semantic information and can serve as an interpretable representation to better understand the success of end-to-end image captioning systems. Our in-depth analysis of these systems explores the various cues that can be derived from explicit object detections, revealing that they rely on matching image representations to generate captions. Our study also shows that encoding the frequency, size, and position of objects all play a role in forming a good image representation, and that different object categories contribute differently towards image captioning.

label: acl
text: Linguistic alignment between dialogue partners has been claimed to be affected by their relative social power. A common finding has been that interlocutors of higher power tend to receive more alignment than those of lower power. However, these studies overlook some low-level linguistic features that can also affect alignment, which casts doubts on these findings. This work characterizes the effect of power on alignment with logistic regression models in two datasets, finding that the effect vanishes or is reversed after controlling for low-level features such as utterance length. Thus, linguistic alignment is explained better by low-level features than by social power. We argue that a wider range of factors, especially cognitive factors, need to be taken into account for future studies on observational data when social factors of language use are in question.

label: acl
text: The relationship between linguistic alignment and relative social power has been the subject of much research. It has been widely reported that individuals with higher power tend to receive more alignment from their dialogue partners. However, these findings have been called into question as they overlook low-level linguistic features that may also impact alignment. This study uses logistic regression models to examine the effect of power on alignment in two datasets. The results show that the impact of power on alignment disappears or is even reversed when considering low-level features such as utterance length. This suggests that low-level linguistic features play a more significant role in determining linguistic alignment than social power. Future studies on the social factors of language use should consider a wider range of factors, including cognitive factors, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon.

label: acl
text: Structured information is an important knowledge source for automatic verification of factual claims. Nevertheless, the majority of existing research into this task has focused on textual data, and the few recent inquiries into structured data have been for the closed-domain setting where appropriate evidence for each claim is assumed to have already been retrieved. In this paper, we investigate verification over structured data in the open-domain setting, introducing a joint reranking-and-verification model which fuses evidence documents in the verification component. Our open-domain model achieves performance comparable to the closed-domain state-of-the-art on the TabFact dataset, and demonstrates performance gains from the inclusion of multiple tables as well as a significant improvement over a heuristic retrieval baseline.

label: acl
text: The importance of structured information as a knowledge source for automatic verification of factual claims cannot be overstated. Despite this, most existing research in this area has focused on textual data, with only a few recent studies exploring structured data in a closed-domain setting where the appropriate evidence for each claim has already been retrieved. In this paper, we introduce a joint reranking-and-verification model that fuses evidence documents in the verification component and investigate verification over structured data in an open-domain setting. Our model performs comparably to the state-of-the-art in closed-domain settings on the TabFact dataset, and shows performance gains from incorporating multiple tables and significantly outperforms a heuristic retrieval baseline.

label: acl
text: Real-world natural language processing (NLP) models need to be continually updated to fix the prediction errors in out-of-distribution (OOD) data streams while overcoming catastrophic forgetting. However, existing continual learning (CL) problem setups cannot cover such a realistic and complex scenario. In response to this, we propose a new CL problem formulation dubbed continual model refinement (CMR). Compared to prior CL settings, CMR is more practical and introduces unique challenges (boundary-agnostic and non-stationary distribution shift, diverse mixtures of multiple OOD data clusters, error-centric streams, etc.). We extend several existing CL approaches to the CMR setting and evaluate them extensively. For benchmarking and analysis, we propose a general sampling algorithm to obtain dynamic OOD data streams with controllable non-stationarity, as well as a suite of metrics measuring various aspects of online performance. Our experiments and detailed analysis reveal the promise and challenges of the CMR problem, supporting that studying CMR in dynamic OOD streams can benefit the longevity of deployed NLP models in production.

label: acl
text: Real-world natural language processing (NLP) models require constant updates to correct prediction errors in out-of-distribution (OOD) data streams while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. However, existing continual learning (CL) setups do not adequately address this complex and realistic scenario. To address this, we introduce a new CL problem formulation called continual model refinement (CMR). CMR is more practical than prior CL settings and presents unique challenges, such as boundary-agnostic and non-stationary distribution shifts, diverse mixtures of multiple OOD data clusters, and error-centric streams. We extend several existing CL approaches to the CMR setting and evaluate them thoroughly. To benchmark and analyze performance, we develop a general sampling algorithm to obtain dynamic OOD data streams with controllable non-stationarity, and a suite of metrics to measure various aspects of online performance. Our experiments and analysis reveal the potential and challenges of the CMR problem, demonstrating that studying CMR in dynamic OOD streams can enhance the longevity of deployed NLP models in production.

label: emnlp
text: We introduce an automatic system that achieves state-of-the-art results on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), a common sense reasoning task that requires diverse, complex forms of inference and knowledge. Our method uses a knowledge hunting module to gather text from the web, which serves as evidence for candidate problem resolutions. Given an input problem, our system generates relevant queries to send to a search engine, then extracts and classifies knowledge from the returned results and weighs them to make a resolution. Our approach improves F1 performance on the full WSC by 0.21 over the previous best and represents the first system to exceed 0.5 F1. We further demonstrate that the approach is competitive on the Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) task, which suggests that it is generally applicable.

label: emnlp
text: We present an automatic system that achieves outstanding results on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), a test of common sense reasoning that demands diverse and complex forms of inference and knowledge. Our system employs a knowledge hunting module which gathers text from the web to serve as evidence for candidate problem resolutions. Our approach involves generating relevant queries, sending them to a search engine, extracting and classifying knowledge from the returned results, and weighing the information to make a resolution. Our approach outperforms the previous best by 0.21 in terms of F1 performance on the full WSC, and is the first system to exceed 0.5 F1. Our results also show that the approach is competitive on the Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) task, indicating its general applicability.

label: coling
text: Accurate fact verification depends on performing fine-grained reasoning over crucial entities by capturing their latent logical relations hidden in multiple evidence clues, which is generally lacking in existing fact verification models. In this work, we propose a novel Global-to-Local Aggregation and Fission network (GLAF) to fill this gap. Instead of treating entire sentences or all semantic elements within them as nodes to construct a coarse-grained or unstructured evidence graph as in previous methods, GLAF constructs a fine-grained and structured evidence graph by parsing the rambling sentences into structural triple-level reasoning clues and regarding them as graph nodes to achieve fine-grained and interpretable evidence graph reasoning. Specifically, to capture latent logical relations between the clues, GLAF first employs a local fission reasoning layer to conduct fine-grained multi-hop reasoning, and then uses a global evidence aggregation layer to achieve information sharing and the interchange of evidence clues for final claim label prediction. Experimental results on the FEVER dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of GLAF, showing that it achieves the state-of-the-art performance by obtaining a 77.62% FEVER score.

label: coling
text: The accuracy of fact verification relies on performing detailed reasoning over key entities by uncovering their hidden logical relationships within multiple pieces of evidence. This is often lacking in current fact verification models. To address this issue, we introduce a new Global-to-Local Aggregation and Fission Network (GLAF). Unlike previous methods that use entire sentences or all semantic elements within them to create a rough or unstructured evidence graph, GLAF creates a detailed and structured evidence graph by parsing sentences into structured triple-level reasoning clues and treating them as graph nodes. This results in a fine-grained, interpretable evidence graph. GLAF first uses a local fission reasoning layer to conduct detailed multi-hop reasoning, then employs a global evidence aggregation layer to share information and exchange evidence clues, ultimately leading to a prediction of the claim label. Our experiments on the FEVER dataset show that GLAF outperforms previous methods and achieves a 77.62% FEVER score, the current state-of-the-art performance.

label: acl
text: Wet laboratory protocols (WLPs) are critical for conveying reproducible procedures in biological research. They are composed of instructions written in natural language describing the step-wise processing of materials by specific actions. This process flow description for reagents and materials synthesis in WLPs can be captured by material state transfer graphs (MSTGs), which encode global temporal and causal relationships between actions. Here, we propose methods to automatically generate a MSTG for a given protocol by extracting all action relationships across multiple sentences. We also note that previous corpora and methods focused primarily on local intra-sentence relationships between actions and entities and did not address two critical issues: (i) resolution of implicit arguments and (ii) establishing long-range dependencies across sentences. We propose a new model that incrementally learns latent structures and is better suited to resolving inter-sentence relations and implicit arguments. This model draws upon a new corpus WLP-MSTG which was created by extending annotations in the WLP corpora for inter-sentence relations and implicit arguments. Our model achieves an F1 score of 54.53% for temporal and causal relations in protocols from our corpus, which is a significant improvement over previous models - DyGIE++:28.17%; spERT:27.81%. We make our annotated WLP-MSTG corpus available to the research community.

label: acl
text: Wet laboratory protocols (WLPs) are crucial for ensuring the reproducibility of procedures in biological research. They consist of instructions written in natural language that outline the step-by-step processing of materials through specific actions. To capture the process flow of reagents and materials synthesis in WLPs, material state transfer graphs (MSTGs) can be used, which encode the global temporal and causal relationships between actions. In this research, we propose methods for automatically generating an MSTG for a given protocol by extracting all action relationships across multiple sentences. Previous studies have primarily focused on local intra-sentence relationships between actions and entities, ignoring two crucial issues: (i) resolution of implicit arguments and (ii) establishing long-range dependencies across sentences. To address these issues, we present a new model that incrementally learns latent structures and is better equipped to resolve inter-sentence relations and implicit arguments. Our model is based on a new corpus, WLP-MSTG, which was created by extending annotations in the WLP corpora to include inter-sentence relations and implicit arguments. The model achieved an F1 score of 54.53% for temporal and causal relations in protocols from our corpus, outperforming previous models (DyGIE++: 28.17%; spERT: 27.81%). We make our annotated WLP-MSTG corpus available to the scientific community.

label: acl
text: As high-quality labeled data is scarce, unsupervised sentence representation learning has attracted much attention. In this paper, we propose a new framework with a two-branch Siamese Network which maximizes the similarity between two augmented views of each sentence. Specifically, given one augmented view of the input sentence, the online network branch is trained by predicting the representation yielded by the target network of the same sentence under another augmented view. Meanwhile, the target network branch is bootstrapped with a moving average of the online network. The proposed method significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on semantic textual similarity (STS) and classification tasks. It can be adopted as a post-training procedure to boost the performance of the supervised methods. We further extend our method for learning multilingual sentence representations and demonstrate its effectiveness on cross-lingual STS tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/yanzhangnlp/BSL.

label: acl
text: Due to the scarcity of high-quality labeled data, unsupervised sentence representation learning has gained significant attention. In this paper, we present a novel framework that utilizes a two-branch Siamese Network to maximize the similarity between two augmented views of each sentence. The online network branch predicts the representation of the same sentence under a different augmented view, while the target network branch is updated with a moving average of the online network. Our proposed method outperforms other state-of-the-art unsupervised methods in semantic textual similarity (STS) and classification tasks and can be used as a post-training procedure to enhance the performance of supervised methods. Additionally, we extend our method to learn multilingual sentence representations and demonstrate its effectiveness in cross-lingual STS tasks. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/yanzhangnlp/BSL.

label: coling
text: Current NLP techniques have been greatly applied in different domains. In this paper, we propose a human-in-the-loop framework for robotic grasping in cluttered scenes, investigating a language interface to the grasping process, which allows the user to intervene by natural language commands. This framework is constructed on a state-of-the-art grasping baseline, where we substitute a scene-graph representation with a text representation of the scene using BERT. Experiments on both simulation and physical robot show that the proposed method outperforms conventional object-agnostic and scene-graph based methods in the literature. In addition, we find that with human intervention, performance can be significantly improved. Our dataset and code are available on our project website https://sites.google.com/view/hitl-grasping-bert.

label: coling
text: Current NLP techniques have been widely utilized across various domains. In this study, we present a human-in-the-loop framework for robotic grasping in cluttered environments. Our framework features a language interface that allows the user to control the grasping process through natural language commands. We built this framework on top of a state-of-the-art grasping baseline, replacing the scene-graph representation with a text representation of the scene using BERT. Our experiments, conducted in both simulation and physical robot environments, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms previous object-agnostic and scene-graph-based methods in the literature. Furthermore, we found that human intervention can significantly improve performance. Our dataset and code can be accessed on our project website at https://sites.google.com/view/hitl-grasping-bert.

label: acl
text: We introduce Picturebook, a large-scale lookup operation to ground language via `snapshots' of our physical world accessed through image search. For each word in a vocabulary, we extract the top-C-C-C images from Google image search and feed the images through a convolutional network to extract a word embedding. We introduce a multimodal gating function to fuse our Picturebook embeddings with other word representations. We also introduce Inverse Picturebook, a mechanism to map a Picturebook embedding back into words. We experiment and report results across a wide range of tasks: word similarity, natural language inference, semantic relatedness, sentiment/topic classification, image-sentence ranking and machine translation. We also show that gate activations corresponding to Picturebook embeddings are highly correlated to human judgments of concreteness ratings.

label: acl
text: We present Picturebook, a large-scale lookup operation that grounds language by using `snapshots' of the physical world accessed through image search. For each word in a vocabulary, we extract the top C images from Google image search, and then feed these images through a convolutional network to obtain a word embedding. Our system also includes a multimodal gating function that fuses the Picturebook embeddings with other word representations. Additionally, we introduce Inverse Picturebook, a mechanism that maps Picturebook embeddings back into words. Our experiments and results cover a broad range of tasks, including word similarity, natural language inference, semantic relatedness, sentiment/topic classification, image-sentence ranking, and machine translation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the gate activations corresponding to Picturebook embeddings are strongly correlated with human judgments of concreteness ratings.

label: coling
text: Few-shot Question Generation (QG) is an important and challenging problem in the Natural Language Generation (NLG) domain. Multilingual BERT (mBERT) has been successfully used in various Natural Language Understanding (NLU) applications. However, the question of how to utilize mBERT for few-shot QG, possibly with cross-lingual transfer, remains. In this paper, we try to explore how mBERT performs in few-shot QG (cross-lingual transfer) and also whether applying meta-learning on mBERT further improves the results. In our setting, we consider mBERT as the base model and fine-tune it using a seq-to-seq language modeling framework in a cross-lingual setting. Further, we apply the model agnostic meta-learning approach to our base model. We evaluate our model for two low-resource Indian languages, Bengali and Telugu, using the TyDi QA dataset. The proposed approach consistently improves the performance of the base model in few-shot settings and even works better than some heavily parameterized models. Human evaluation also confirms the effectiveness of our approach.

label: coling
text: Few-shot Question Generation (QG) is a crucial and demanding task in the field of Natural Language Generation (NLG). Multilingual BERT (mBERT) has proven its effectiveness in various Natural Language Understanding (NLU) applications. However, the question of how to effectively apply mBERT in few-shot QG, with cross-lingual transfer, has yet to be answered. To address this, we explore the performance of mBERT in few-shot QG (with cross-lingual transfer) and the impact of meta-learning on mBERT's performance. Our approach involves fine-tuning mBERT using a seq-to-seq language modeling framework in a cross-lingual setting and applying model agnostic meta-learning to the base model. We evaluate our model on two low-resource Indian languages, Bengali and Telugu, using the TyDi QA dataset. Our results show that the proposed approach consistently improves the performance of the base model in few-shot settings and outperforms some heavily parameterized models. Our human evaluation confirms the effectiveness of our approach.

label: acl
text: Aiming for a better integration of data-driven and linguistically-inspired approaches, we explore whether RST Nuclearity, assigning a binary assessment of importance between text segments, can be replaced by automatically generated, real-valued scores, in what we call a Weighted-RST framework. In particular, we find that weighted discourse trees from auxiliary tasks can benefit key NLP downstream applications, compared to nuclearity-centered approaches. We further show that real-valued importance distributions partially and interestingly align with the assessment and uncertainty of human annotators.

label: acl
text: We aim to improve the integration of data-driven and linguistically-inspired approaches by exploring the possibility of replacing the binary assessment of importance in RST Nuclearity with automatically generated real-valued scores in a Weighted-RST framework. Our findings indicate that using weighted discourse trees from auxiliary tasks can lead to better results in key NLP downstream applications compared to traditional nuclearity-centered approaches. Additionally, we observe that the real-valued importance distributions align with the assessments and uncertainties of human annotators in a partially and intriguing manner.

label: emnlp
text: In this paper, we propose a novel deep attentive sentence ordering network (referred as ATTOrderNet) which integrates self-attention mechanism with LSTMs in the encoding of input sentences. It enables us to capture global dependencies among sentences regardless of their input order and obtains a reliable representation of the sentence set. With this representation, a pointer network is exploited to generate an ordered sequence. The proposed model is evaluated on Sentence Ordering and Order Discrimination tasks. The extensive experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness and superiority to the state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a new deep attentive sentence ordering network, referred to as ATTOrderNet, which combines self-attention mechanism and LSTMs to encode input sentences. This integration allows us to capture global dependencies between sentences, regardless of their input order, and to obtain a robust representation of the sentence set. The representation is then utilized by a pointer network to generate an ordered sequence. The proposed model has been evaluated on Sentence Ordering and Order Discrimination tasks, and the results of the experiments show its effectiveness and superiority over current state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: Emotions are expressed in nuanced ways, which varies by collective or individual experiences, knowledge, and beliefs. Therefore, to understand emotion, as conveyed through text, a robust mechanism capable of capturing and modeling different linguistic nuances and phenomena is needed. We propose a semi-supervised, graph-based algorithm to produce rich structural descriptors which serve as the building blocks for constructing contextualized affect representations from text. The pattern-based representations are further enriched with word embeddings and evaluated through several emotion recognition tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on emotion recognition tasks.

label: emnlp
text: Emotions are expressed in complex and varied ways, based on a person's collective or individual experiences, knowledge, and beliefs. To effectively understand emotions conveyed through text, a robust mechanism is needed to capture and model the linguistic nuances and phenomena involved. Our solution is a semi-supervised, graph-based algorithm that generates rich structural descriptors, serving as the foundation for contextualized affect representations from text. These pattern-based representations are further enhanced with word embeddings and evaluated through several emotion recognition tasks. Our results show that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in emotion recognition.

label: coling
text: Formulaic expressions (FEs) used in scholarly papers, such as `there has been little discussion about', are helpful for non-native English speakers. However, it is time-consuming for users to manually search for an appropriate expression every time they want to consult FE dictionaries. For this reason, we tackle the task of semantic searches of FE dictionaries. At the start of our research, we identified two salient difficulties in this task. First, the paucity of example sentences in existing FE dictionaries results in a shortage of context information, which is necessary for acquiring semantic representation of FEs. Second, while a semantic category label is assigned to each FE in many FE dictionaries, it is difficult to predict the labels from user input, forcing users to manually designate the semantic category when searching. To address these difficulties, we propose a new framework for semantic searches of FEs and propose a new method to leverage both existing dictionaries and domain sentence corpora. Further, we expand an existing FE dictionary to consider building a more comprehensive and domain-specific FE dictionary and to verify the effectiveness of our method.

text: Formulaic expressions (FEs) used in scholarly papers, such as `there has been little discussion about', are useful for non-native English speakers. Our research identified two main challenges in this task. Firstly, the lack of example sentences in existing FE dictionaries leads to a shortage of context information, which is crucial for understanding the semantic representation of FEs.
