text: This paper addresses a gap in existing cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) datasets and evaluates the disambiguation ability of CLIR systems. CLIR is typically tackled by combining translation and traditional information retrieval. However, the problem of ambiguity is exacerbated by translation ambiguity, making it more challenging than monolingual information retrieval. Existing auto-generated CLIR datasets are dominated by searches for named entity mentions, which does not accurately measure disambiguation performance as these mentions can often be transliterated across languages and tend to have a single translation. To address this inadequacy, we introduce a new evaluation dataset, MuSeCLIR, which focuses on polysemous common nouns with multiple possible translations. Constructed from multilingual Wikipedia, MuSeCLIR supports searches in European languages (French, German, Italian) and Asian languages (Chinese, Japanese). We provide baseline statistical and neural model results on MuSeCLIR, demonstrating its higher requirement for systems to disambiguate query terms.

label: naacl
text: We study few-shot learning in natural language domains. Compared to many existing works that apply either metric-based or optimization-based meta-learning to image domain with low inter-task variance, we consider a more realistic setting, where tasks are diverse. However, it imposes tremendous difficulties to existing state-of-the-art metric-based algorithms since a single metric is insufficient to capture complex task variations in natural language domain. To alleviate the problem, we propose an adaptive metric learning approach that automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task. Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy. We make our code and data available for further study.

label: naacl
text: We are investigating few-shot learning in the context of natural language domains. Unlike many existing works that focus on applying either metric-based or optimization-based meta-learning to image domains with low inter-task variance, we are exploring a more realistic setting where tasks are diverse and complex. This presents a significant challenge to traditional state-of-the-art metric-based algorithms, as a single metric is insufficient to capture the variations in natural language domains. To overcome this challenge, we have developed an adaptive metric learning approach that automatically selects the best combination of metrics from a set of meta-training tasks for a new few-shot task. Our extensive evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets have shown that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy. Our code and data are available for further study.

label: acl
text: We study the task of toxic spans detection, which concerns the detection of the spans that make a text toxic, when detecting such spans is possible. We introduce a dataset for this task, ToxicSpans, which we release publicly. By experimenting with several methods, we show that sequence labeling models perform best, but methods that add generic rationale extraction mechanisms on top of classifiers trained to predict if a post is toxic or not are also surprisingly promising. Finally, we use ToxicSpans and systems trained on it, to provide further analysis of state-of-the-art toxic to non-toxic transfer systems, as well as of human performance on that latter task. Our work highlights challenges in finer toxicity detection and mitigation.

label: acl
text: We investigate the task of detecting toxic spans in text, where such spans can be identified. To support our study, we introduce the ToxicSpans dataset, which we make publicly available. Our experiments reveal that sequence labeling models are the most effective, but adding generic rationale extraction mechanisms to classifiers that predict the toxicity of a text also shows promising results. Utilizing the ToxicSpans dataset and trained systems, we further analyze the performance of state-of-the-art toxic to non-toxic transfer systems and human performance in the same task. Our findings highlight the challenges in fine-tuning toxicity detection and mitigation.

label: coling
text: Fake news detection is a challenging problem due to its tremendous real-world political and social impacts. Recent fake news detection works focus on learning news features from News Propagation Graph (NPG). However, little attention is paid to the issues of both authenticity of the relationships and topology imbalance in the structure of NPG, which trick existing methods and thus lead to incorrect prediction results. To tackle these issues, in this paper, we propose a novel Topology imbalance and Relation inauthenticity aware Hierarchical Graph Attention Networks (TR-HGAN) to identify fake news on social media. Specifically, we design a new topology imbalance smoothing strategy to measure the topology weight of each node. Besides, we adopt a hierarchical-level attention mechanism for graph convolutional learning, which can adaptively identify the authenticity of relationships by assigning appropriate weights to each of them. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that TR-HGAN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

text: The detection of fake news is a complex problem due to its significant political and social impacts in the real world. Recent research in this field focuses on learning news features from News Propagation Graphs (NPGs), but there is a lack of attention paid to the authenticity of the relationships and the topology imbalance in the NPG structure. This can lead to incorrect prediction results and trick existing methods. To address these issues, we propose a novel Topology Imbalance and Relation Inauthenticity Aware Hierarchical Graph Attention Network (TR-HGAN) to identify fake news on social media. Our approach includes a new topology imbalance smoothing strategy to measure the weight of each node and a hierarchical-level attention mechanism for graph convolutional learning. This mechanism can identify the authenticity of relationships and assign appropriate weights to each of them. Our experiments on real-world datasets show that TR-HGAN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

label: coling
text: Sentiment composition is a fundamental sentiment analysis problem. Previous work relied on manual rules and manually-created lexical resources such as negator lists, or learned a composition function from sentiment-annotated phrases or sentences. We propose a new approach for learning sentiment composition from a large, unlabeled corpus, which only requires a word-level sentiment lexicon for supervision. We automatically generate large sentiment lexicons of bigrams and unigrams, from which we induce a set of lexicons for a variety of sentiment composition processes. The effectiveness of our approach is confirmed through manual annotation, as well as sentiment classification experiments with both phrase-level and sentence-level benchmarks.

text: The fundamental problem of sentiment composition is addressed in sentiment analysis. In the past, sentiment analysis relied on manual rules and lexical resources such as negator lists that were created manually. However, we are introducing a new approach to sentiment composition that is learned from a large, unlabeled corpus. This approach only requires a word-level sentiment lexicon for supervision, and it automatically generates large sentiment lexicons of bigrams and unigrams. These lexicons are then used to induce a set of lexicons for various sentiment composition processes. The effectiveness of our approach has been confirmed through both manual annotation and sentiment classification experiments that use both phrase-level and sentence-level benchmarks.

label: acl
text: Current methods for few-shot fine-tuning of pretrained masked language models (PLMs) require carefully engineered prompts and verbalizers for each new task to convert examples into a cloze-format that the PLM can score. In this work, we propose Perfect, a simple and efficient method for few-shot fine-tuning of PLMs without relying on any such handcrafting, which is highly effective given as few as 32 data points. Perfect makes two key design choices: First, we show that manually engineered task prompts can be replaced with task-specific adapters that enable sample-efficient fine-tuning and reduce memory and storage costs by roughly factors of 5 and 100, respectively. Second, instead of using handcrafted verbalizers, we learn new multi-token label embeddings during fine-tuning, which are not tied to the model vocabulary and which allow us to avoid complex auto-regressive decoding. These embeddings are not only learnable from limited data but also enable nearly 100x faster training and inference. Experiments on a wide range of few shot NLP tasks demonstrate that Perfect, while being simple and efficient, also outperforms existing state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rabeehk/perfect.

text: Current methods for fine-tuning pretrained masked language models (PLMs) using few-shot learning require carefully crafted prompts and verbalizers to convert examples into a cloze-format that the PLM can score. In this work, we present Perfect, a more efficient method that does not rely on any handcrafting and is effective with as few as 32 data points. Perfect has two key design choices: First, we demonstrate that task-specific adapters can replace manually crafted prompts, leading to more sample-efficient fine-tuning and reducing memory and storage costs by about 5 and 100 times, respectively. Second, instead of handcrafted verbalizers, we learn new multi-token label embeddings during fine-tuning, which are not tied to the model vocabulary and eliminate the need for complex auto-regressive decoding. These embeddings are not only learnable from limited data but also allow for nearly 100 times faster training and inference. Experiments on various NLP tasks show that Perfect, while simple and efficient, outperforms existing state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/rabeehk/perfect.

text: Pretrained Language Models (PLMs), though popular, have been diagnosed to encode bias against protected groups in the representations they learn, which may harm the prediction fairness of downstream models. Given that such bias is believed to be related to the amount of demographic information carried in the learned representations, this study aimed to quantify the awareness that a PLM (i.e., BERT) has regarding people's protected attributes and augment BERT to improve prediction fairness of downstream models by inhibiting this awareness. Specifically, we developed a method to dynamically sample data to continue the pretraining of BERT and enable it to generate representations carrying minimal demographic information, which can be directly used as input to downstream models for fairer predictions. By experimenting on the task of classifying educational forum posts and measuring fairness between students of different gender or first-language backgrounds, we showed that, compared to a baseline without any additional pretraining, our method improved not only fairness (with a maximum improvement of 52.33%) but also accuracy (with a maximum improvement of 2.53%). Our method can be generalized to any PLM and demographic attributes. All the codes used in this study can be accessed via https://github.com/lsha49/FairBERT_deploy.

text: Pretrained Language Models (PLMs), despite their popularity, are known to encode biases against protected groups in their learned representations, which can negatively impact the fairness of downstream predictions. This study aims to quantify the extent to which a PLM (BERT) is aware of people's protected attributes and improve the fairness of downstream predictions by reducing this awareness. To achieve this, we developed a method to dynamically sample data during the pretraining of BERT, allowing it to generate representations that carry minimal demographic information. This leads to fairer predictions from downstream models. Our experiments on classifying educational forum posts and measuring fairness between students of different gender or first-language backgrounds showed that our method improved both fairness (with a maximum improvement of 52.33%) and accuracy (with a maximum improvement of 2.53%) compared to a baseline without additional pretraining. Our method can be applied to any PLM and demographic attribute, and all the codes used in this study are available at https://github.com/lsha49/FairBERT_deploy.

text: Lexicon based methods for sentiment analysis rely on high quality polarity lexicons. In recent years, automatic methods for inducing lexicons have increased the viability of lexicon based methods for polarity classification. SentProp is a framework for inducing domain-specific polarities from word embeddings. We elaborate on SentProp by evaluating its use for enhancing DuOMan, a general-purpose lexicon, for use in the political domain. By adding only top sentiment bearing words from the vocabulary and applying small polarity shifts in the general-purpose lexicon, we increase accuracy in an in-domain classification task. The enhanced lexicon performs worse than the original lexicon in an out-domain task, showing that the words we added and the polarity shifts we applied are domain-specific and do not translate well to an out-domain setting.

text: Lexicon-based methods for sentiment analysis depend on high-quality polarity lexicons. SentProp is a framework for creating domain-specific polarities from word embeddings. We examine the effectiveness of SentProp by evaluating its use in enhancing DuOMan, a general-purpose lexicon, for use in the political domain. By incorporating only the top sentiment-bearing words from the vocabulary and applying small polarity shifts in the general-purpose lexicon, we observe an improvement in accuracy in a classification task within the domain. However, the enhanced lexicon performs worse than the original lexicon in an out-of-domain task, demonstrating that the added words and polarity shifts are specific to the domain and do not translate well to other contexts.

label: acl
text: Item Response Theory (IRT) has been extensively used to numerically characterize question difficulty and discrimination for human subjects in domains including cognitive psychology and education (Primi et al., 2014; Downing, 2003). More recently, IRT has been used to similarly characterize item difficulty and discrimination for natural language models across various datasets (Lalor et al., 2019; Vania et al., 2021; Rodriguez et al., 2021). In this work, we explore predictive models for directly estimating and explaining these traits for natural language questions in a question-answering context. We use HotpotQA for illustration. Our experiments show that it is possible to predict both difficulty and discrimination parameters for new questions, and these traits are correlated with features of questions, answers, and associated contexts. Our findings can have significant implications for the creation of new datasets and tests on the one hand and strategies such as active learning and curriculum learning on the other.

text: Item Response Theory (IRT) has been widely applied to assess the difficulty and discrimination of questions for human subjects in cognitive psychology and education (Primi et al., 2014; Downing, 2003). Recently, IRT has also been used to evaluate the difficulty and discrimination of natural language questions in various datasets (Lalor et al., 2019; Vania et al., 2021; Rodriguez et al., 2021). In this study, we investigate the potential of predictive models to directly estimate and explain these traits in the context of question-answering using HotpotQA as an example. Our experiments demonstrate that it is possible to predict both difficulty and discrimination parameters for new questions and that these traits are correlated with features of questions, answers, and their related contexts. Our results have significant implications for the creation of new datasets and tests, as well as for strategies such as active learning and curriculum learning.

label: acl
text: To understand a story with multiple events, it is important to capture the proper relations across these events. However, existing event relation extraction (ERE) framework regards it as a multi-class classification task and do not guarantee any coherence between different relation types, such as anti-symmetry. If a phone line “died” after “storm”, then it is obvious that the “storm” happened before the “died”. Current framework of event relation extraction do not guarantee this coherence and thus enforces it via constraint loss function (Wang et al., 2020). In this work, we propose to modify the underlying ERE model to guarantee coherence by representing each event as a box representation (BERE) without applying explicit constraints. From our experiments, BERE also shows stronger conjunctive constraint satisfaction while performing on par or better in F1 compared to previous models with constraint injection.

text: To comprehend a story with multiple events, it is crucial to accurately capture the relationships between these events. For example, if a phone line "dies" after a "storm," it is clear that the "storm" occurred before the "died." The current ERE framework does not guarantee this consistency and enforces it through a constraint loss function (Wang et al., 2020). In this study, we propose modifying the ERE model to ensure consistency by representing each event as a box representation (BERE) without using explicit constraints. Our experiments show that BERE also demonstrates stronger conjunctive constraint satisfaction while achieving comparable or better F1 scores compared to previous models that use constraint injection.

text: Vulgarity is a common linguistic expression and is used to perform several linguistic functions. Understanding their usage can aid both linguistic and psychological phenomena as well as benefit downstream natural language processing applications such as sentiment analysis. This study performs a large-scale, data-driven empirical analysis of vulgar words using social media data. We analyze the socio-cultural and pragmatic aspects of vulgarity using tweets from users with known demographics. Further, we collect sentiment ratings for vulgar tweets to study the relationship between the use of vulgar words and perceived sentiment and show that explicitly modeling vulgar words can boost sentiment analysis performance.

label: coling
text: Vulgar language is a common form of expression that serves various linguistic purposes. By comprehending its usage, we can gain insights into both linguistic and psychological phenomena, as well as enhance the accuracy of downstream natural language processing applications, such as sentiment analysis. This study conducts a comprehensive, data-driven analysis of vulgar language using social media data. Our analysis focuses on the socio-cultural and pragmatic aspects of vulgarity and uses tweets from users with known demographics. Additionally, we gather sentiment ratings for vulgar tweets to examine the correlation between the use of vulgar language and perceived sentiment. Our findings demonstrate that explicitly considering vulgar language in sentiment analysis can significantly improve its performance.

label: naacl
text: Users write to-dos as personal notes to themselves, about things they need to complete, remember or organize. To-do texts are usually short and under-specified, which poses a challenge for current text representation models. Yet, understanding and representing their meaning is the first step towards providing intelligent assistance for to-do management. We address this problem by proposing a neural multi-task learning framework, LITE, which extracts representations of English to-do tasks with a multi-head attention mechanism on top of a pre-trained text encoder. To adapt representation models to to-do texts, we collect weak-supervision labels from semantically rich external resources (e.g., dynamic commonsense knowledge bases), following the principle that to-do tasks with similar intents have similar labels. We then train the model on multiple generative/predictive training objectives jointly. We evaluate our representation model on four downstream tasks and show that our approach consistently improves performance over baseline models, achieving error reduction of up to 38.7%.

text: Users create personal notes in the form of to-dos, which encompass tasks they need to complete, remember, or organize. However, due to their short and under-specified nature, to-do texts pose a challenge for existing text representation models. To overcome this, we introduce LITE, a neural multi-task learning framework that extracts representations of English to-do tasks using a multi-head attention mechanism on top of a pre-trained text encoder. To tailor the representation models to to-do texts, we gather weak-supervision labels from semantically rich external resources such as dynamic commonsense knowledge bases. Our approach is based on the principle that to-dos with similar intents have similar labels. By training the model on multiple generative/predictive objectives simultaneously, we achieve improved performance on four downstream tasks, reducing errors by up to 38.7%.

label: acl
text: Recently, the retrieval models based on dense representations have been gradually applied in the first stage of the document retrieval tasks, showing better performance than traditional sparse vector space models. To obtain high efficiency, the basic structure of these models is Bi-encoder in most cases. However, this simple structure may cause serious information loss during the encoding of documents since the queries are agnostic. To address this problem, we design a method to mimic the queries to each of the documents by an iterative clustering process and represent the documents by multiple pseudo queries (i.e., the cluster centroids). To boost the retrieval process using approximate nearest neighbor search library, we also optimize the matching function with a two-step score calculation procedure. Experimental results on several popular ranking and QA datasets show that our model can achieve state-of-the-art results while still remaining high efficiency.

label: acl
text: Recently, dense representation-based retrieval models have been increasingly used in the first stage of document retrieval tasks, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional sparse vector space models. Typically, these models have a bi-encoder structure for high efficiency. However, this simple structure can result in significant information loss when encoding documents since queries are agnostic. To address this issue, we propose a method that mimics queries to each document through an iterative clustering process and represents documents using multiple pseudo queries (i.e., cluster centroids). To enhance the retrieval process using an approximate nearest neighbor search library, we optimize the matching function with a two-step score calculation procedure. Our model has been tested on several popular ranking and QA datasets, yielding state-of-the-art results while maintaining high efficiency.

label: naacl
text: Labelled data is the foundation of most natural language processing tasks. However, labelling data is difficult and there often are diverse valid beliefs about what the correct data labels should be. So far, dataset creators have acknowledged annotator subjectivity, but rarely actively managed it in the annotation process. This has led to partly-subjective datasets that fail to serve a clear downstream use. To address this issue, we propose two contrasting paradigms for data annotation. The descriptive paradigm encourages annotator subjectivity, whereas the prescriptive paradigm discourages it. Descriptive annotation allows for the surveying and modelling of different beliefs, whereas prescriptive annotation enables the training of models that consistently apply one belief. We discuss benefits and challenges in implementing both paradigms, and argue that dataset creators should explicitly aim for one or the other to facilitate the intended use of their dataset. Lastly, we conduct an annotation experiment using hate speech data that illustrates the contrast between the two paradigms.

text: Labelled data is the foundation of most natural language processing tasks, but labelling can be difficult due to diverse valid beliefs about what the correct data labels should be. Although dataset creators have acknowledged annotator subjectivity, they rarely manage it in the annotation process, resulting in partly-subjective datasets that fail to serve a clear purpose. To address this, we propose two contrasting paradigms for data annotation: the descriptive paradigm, which encourages annotator subjectivity, and the prescriptive paradigm, which discourages it. The descriptive paradigm allows for the surveying and modelling of different beliefs, while the prescriptive paradigm enables the training of models that consistently apply one belief. We discuss the benefits and challenges of implementing both paradigms, arguing that dataset creators should explicitly aim for one or the other to facilitate the intended use of their dataset. To illustrate the contrast between the two paradigms, we conduct an annotation experiment using hate speech data.

label: coling
text: Unsupervised pre-trained word embeddings are used effectively for many tasks in natural language processing to leverage unlabeled textual data. Often these embeddings are either used as initializations or as fixed word representations for task-specific classification models. In this work, we extend our classification model's task loss with an unsupervised auxiliary loss on the word-embedding level of the model. This is to ensure that the learned word representations contain both task-specific features, learned from the supervised loss component, and more general features learned from the unsupervised loss component. We evaluate our approach on the task of temporal relation extraction, in particular, narrative containment relation extraction from clinical records, and show that continued training of the embeddings on the unsupervised objective together with the task objective gives better task-specific embeddings, and results in an improvement over the state of the art on the THYME dataset, using only a general-domain part-of-speech tagger as linguistic resource.

label: coling
text: Unsupervised pre-trained word embeddings are widely used in natural language processing to effectively leverage unlabeled textual data. These embeddings are either utilized as initializations or fixed representations for task-specific classification models. In this study, we enhance our classification model by incorporating an unsupervised auxiliary loss at the word-embedding level. This ensures that the learned word representations contain both task-specific features learned from the supervised loss and general features learned from the unsupervised loss. Our approach is evaluated on the task of temporal relation extraction, specifically narrative containment relation extraction from clinical records, and demonstrates that continuing to train the embeddings on the unsupervised objective in conjunction with the task objective results in improved task-specific embeddings and surpasses the state of the art on the THYME dataset, using only a general-domain part-of-speech tagger as a linguistic resource.

label: coling
text: Knowledge representation learning is a key step required for link prediction tasks with knowledge graphs (KGs). During the learning process, the semantics of each entity are embedded by a vector or a point in a feature space. The distance between these points is a measure of semantic similarity. However, in a KG, while two entities may have similar semantics in some relations, they have different semantics in others. It is ambiguous to assign a fixed distance to depict the variant semantic similarity of entities. To alleviate the semantic ambiguity in KGs, we design a new embedding approach named OpticE, which is derived from the well-known physical phenomenon of optical interference. It is a lightweight and relation-adaptive model based on coherence theory, in which each entity's semantics vary automatically regarding different relations. In addition, a unique negative sampling method is proposed to combine the multimapping properties and self-adversarial learning during the training process. The experimental results obtained on practical KG benchmarks show that the OpticE model, with elegant structures, can compete with existing link prediction methods.

label: coling
text: The process of learning knowledge representation is crucial in link prediction tasks with knowledge graphs (KGs). During this process, the semantic meaning of each entity is embedded as a vector or point in a feature space, where the distance between these points represents semantic similarity. However, in KGs, two entities may have similar semantics in some relations, but different semantics in others, making it challenging to assign a fixed distance to depict their semantic similarity. To address this issue, we introduce OpticE, a new embedding approach based on coherence theory, which is derived from the physical phenomenon of optical interference. OpticE is a lightweight, relation-adaptive model that automatically adjusts entity semantics based on different relations. Additionally, we propose a unique negative sampling method that combines multimapping properties and self-adversarial learning during the training process. Our experiments on practical KG benchmarks demonstrate that OpticE, with its elegant structure, can perform competitively with existing link prediction methods.

label: emnlp
text: We address the problem of detecting duplicate questions in forums, which is an important step towards automating the process of answering new questions. As finding and annotating such potential duplicates manually is very tedious and costly, automatic methods based on machine learning are a viable alternative. However, many forums do not have annotated data, i.e., questions labeled by experts as duplicates, and thus a promising solution is to use domain adaptation from another forum that has such annotations. Here we focus on adversarial domain adaptation, deriving important findings about when it performs well and what properties of the domains are important in this regard. Our experiments with StackExchange data show an average improvement of 5.6% over the best baseline across multiple pairs of domains.

label: emnlp
text: We tackle the issue of identifying duplicate questions in online forums, which is a crucial step in automating the answer generation process. Manually finding and marking these duplicates is time-consuming and costly, making machine learning-based automatic methods a practical alternative. However, many forums lack annotated data, meaning questions labeled as duplicates by experts. To overcome this challenge, we propose using domain adaptation from a forum that has annotated data. Our focus is on adversarial domain adaptation, and we have discovered key findings regarding its performance and the significance of domain properties. Our experiments using StackExchange data demonstrate an average improvement of 5.6% compared to the best baseline across multiple domain pairs.

label: naacl
text: This paper explores the time course of lexical memory retrieval by modeling fluent language production. The duration of retrievals is predicted using the ACT-R cognitive architecture. In a large-scale observational study of a spoken corpus, we find that language production at a time point preceding a word is sped up or slowed down depending on activation of that word. This computational analysis has consequences for the theoretical model of language production. The results point to interference between lexical and phonological stages as well as a quantifiable buffer for lexical information that opens up the possibility of non-sequential retrievals.

label: naacl
text: This paper investigates the temporal dynamics of lexical memory retrieval in fluent language production. The time course of these retrievals is predicted using the ACT-R cognitive architecture. Through a comprehensive observational study of a spoken corpus, we discovered that the speed of language production preceding a word is influenced by the activation of that word. Our computational analysis has significant implications for the theoretical model of language production, highlighting the interference between lexical and phonological stages and the existence of a quantifiable buffer for lexical information, allowing for non-sequential retrievals.

label: naacl
text: We present IBR, an Iterative Backward Reasoning model to solve the proof generation tasks on rule-based Question Answering (QA), where models are required to reason over a series of textual rules and facts to find out the related proof path and derive the final answer. We handle the limitations of existed works in two folds: 1) enhance the interpretability of reasoning procedures with detailed tracking, by predicting nodes and edges in the proof path iteratively backward from the question; 2) promote the efficiency and accuracy via reasoning on the elaborate representations of nodes and history paths, without any intermediate texts that may introduce external noise during proof generation. There are three main modules in IBR, QA and proof strategy prediction to obtain the answer and offer guidance for the following procedure; parent node prediction to determine a node in the existing proof that a new child node will link to; child node prediction to find out which new node will be added to the proof. Experiments on both synthetic and paraphrased datasets demonstrate that IBR has better in-domain performance as well as cross-domain transferability than several strong baselines. Our code and models are available at https://github. com/find-knowledge/IBR.

label: naacl
text: We present IBR, a novel Iterative Backward Reasoning model designed to solve proof generation tasks in rule-based Question Answering (QA). The model reasons over a series of textual rules and facts to find the relevant proof path and derive the final answer. IBR addresses the limitations of existing works in two ways: first, it enhances the interpretability of reasoning procedures with detailed tracking by predicting nodes and edges in the proof path iteratively from the question; second, it improves efficiency and accuracy by reasoning on elaborate representations of nodes and history paths, without any intermediate texts that may introduce external noise during proof generation. The IBR model consists of three main modules: QA and proof strategy prediction to obtain the answer and provide guidance for the following procedure; parent node prediction to determine the node in the existing proof that a new child node will link to; and child node prediction to find the new node that will be added to the proof. Experiments on synthetic and paraphrased datasets show that IBR outperforms several strong baselines in both in-domain performance and cross-domain transferability. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/find-knowledge/IBR.

label: acl
text: Recent years have seen numerous NLP datasets introduced to evaluate the performance of fine-tuned models on natural language understanding tasks. Recent results from large pretrained models, though, show that many of these datasets are largely saturated and unlikely to be able to detect further progress. What kind of datasets are still effective at discriminating among strong models, and what kind of datasets should we expect to be able to detect future improvements? To measure this uniformly across datasets, we draw on Item Response Theory and evaluate 29 datasets using predictions from 18 pretrained Transformer models on individual test examples. We find that Quoref, HellaSwag, and MC-TACO are best suited for distinguishing among state-of-the-art models, while SNLI, MNLI, and CommitmentBank seem to be saturated for current strong models. We also observe span selection task format, which is used for QA datasets like QAMR or SQuAD2.0, is effective in differentiating between strong and weak models.

label: acl
text:
In conclusion, as NLP researchers continue to develop new models, it is important to use datasets that are still effective in detecting progress and can help to distinguish between state-of-the-art models.

Recently, numerous NLP datasets have been introduced to evaluate the performance of fine-tuned models on natural language understanding tasks. However, recent results from large pre-trained models indicate that many of these datasets are largely saturated and unlikely to detect further progress. To determine which datasets are still effective in discriminating among strong models and which ones are suitable for detecting future improvements, we used Item Response Theory to evaluate 29 datasets using predictions from 18 pre-trained Transformer models on individual test examples. Our findings reveal that Quoref, HellaSwag, and MC-TACO are the most effective datasets for differentiating between state-of-the-art models, while SNLI, MNLI, and CommitmentBank seem to be saturated for current strong models. Additionally, the span selection task format used in QA datasets like QAMR or SQuAD2.0 was found to be effective in differentiating between strong and weak models. In conclusion, it is crucial for NLP researchers to use datasets that are still effective in detecting progress and can help distinguish between state-of-the-art models.

label: acl
text: Aligning with ACL 2022 special Theme on “Language Diversity: from Low Resource to Endangered Languages”, we discuss the major linguistic and sociopolitical challenges facing development of NLP technologies for African languages. Situating African languages in a typological framework, we discuss how the particulars of these languages can be harnessed. To facilitate future research, we also highlight current efforts, communities, venues, datasets, and tools. Our main objective is to motivate and advocate for an Afrocentric approach to technology development. With this in mind, we recommend what technologies to build and how to build, evaluate, and deploy them based on the needs of local African communities.

label: acl
text: Aligned with the special theme of ACL 2022 on "Language Diversity: from Low Resource to Endangered Languages," we explore the significant linguistic and sociopolitical challenges in the development of NLP technologies for African languages. By positioning African languages within a typological framework, we examine how their unique characteristics can be leveraged. Additionally, we highlight the current initiatives, communities, venues, datasets, and tools to support future research. Our primary goal is to promote and advocate for an Afrocentric approach to technology development. To achieve this, we suggest the technologies that should be developed and provide guidance on how to build, evaluate, and deploy them in response to the needs of African communities.

label: naacl
text: The present work investigates whether different quantification mechanisms (set comparison, vague quantification, and proportional estimation) can be jointly learned from visual scenes by a multi-task computational model. The motivation is that, in humans, these processes underlie the same cognitive, non-symbolic ability, which allows an automatic estimation and comparison of set magnitudes. We show that when information about lower-complexity tasks is available, the higher-level proportional task becomes more accurate than when performed in isolation. Moreover, the multi-task model is able to generalize to unseen combinations of target/non-target objects. Consistently with behavioral evidence showing the interference of absolute number in the proportional task, the multi-task model no longer works when asked to provide the number of target objects in the scene.

label: naacl
text: The present study examines whether a multi-task computational model can learn different quantification mechanisms (set comparison, vague quantification, and proportional estimation) from visual scenes simultaneously. The reason behind this is that these processes are based on the same cognitive, non-symbolic ability in humans, which enables automatic estimation and comparison of set magnitudes. The results show that when lower-complexity task information is available, the accuracy of the higher-level proportional task improves. Furthermore, the multi-task model is able to generalize to new combinations of target/non-target objects. However, when asked to provide the number of target objects in the scene, the multi-task model fails, which is consistent with behavioral evidence indicating the interference of absolute number in the proportional task.

label: acl
text: The goal of dialogue state tracking (DST) is to predict the current dialogue state given all previous dialogue contexts. Existing approaches generally predict the dialogue state at every turn from scratch. However, the overwhelming majority of the slots in each turn should simply inherit the slot values from the previous turn. Therefore, the mechanism of treating slots equally in each turn not only is inefficient but also may lead to additional errors because of the redundant slot value generation. To address this problem, we devise the two-stage DSS-DST which consists of the Dual Slot Selector based on the current turn dialogue, and the Slot Value Generator based on the dialogue history. The Dual Slot Selector determines each slot whether to update slot value or to inherit the slot value from the previous turn from two aspects: (1) if there is a strong relationship between it and the current turn dialogue utterances; (2) if a slot value with high reliability can be obtained for it through the current turn dialogue. The slots selected to be updated are permitted to enter the Slot Value Generator to update values by a hybrid method, while the other slots directly inherit the values from the previous turn. Empirical results show that our method achieves 56.93%, 60.73%, and 58.04% joint accuracy on MultiWOZ 2.0, MultiWOZ 2.1, and MultiWOZ 2.2 datasets respectively and achieves a new state-of-the-art performance with significant improvements.

label: acl
text: The objective of Dialogue State Tracking (DST) is to predict the current state of a dialogue based on all previous dialogue contexts. Most existing approaches predict the dialogue state at each turn from scratch. However, this method is inefficient and can lead to errors as it overlooks the fact that most slots should simply retain their values from the previous turn. To overcome this, we propose a two-stage DSS-DST system that consists of a Dual Slot Selector and a Slot Value Generator. The Dual Slot Selector determines whether a slot should be updated or inherit its value based on its relationship with the current turn dialogue and the reliability of its value obtained from the current turn. The slots selected for updating are processed by the Slot Value Generator using a hybrid method, while the others retain their values from the previous turn. Our approach achieved a joint accuracy of 56.93%, 60.73%, and 58.04% on the MultiWOZ 2.0, MultiWOZ 2.1, and MultiWOZ 2.2 datasets respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art performance with significant improvements.

label: emnlp
text: We present QuAC, a dataset for Question Answering in Context that contains 14K information-seeking QA dialogs (100K questions in total). The dialogs involve two crowd workers: (1) a student who poses a sequence of freeform questions to learn as much as possible about a hidden Wikipedia text, and (2) a teacher who answers the questions by providing short excerpts from the text. QuAC introduces challenges not found in existing machine comprehension datasets: its questions are often more open-ended, unanswerable, or only meaningful within the dialog context, as we show in a detailed qualitative evaluation. We also report results for a number of reference models, including a recently state-of-the-art reading comprehension architecture extended to model dialog context. Our best model underperforms humans by 20 F1, suggesting that there is significant room for future work on this data. Dataset, baseline, and leaderboard available at http://quac.ai.

label: emnlp
text: The QuAC dataset presents 14,000 information-seeking Question and Answer dialogs, with a total of 100,000 questions, that challenge existing machine comprehension models. The dialogs consist of two crowd workers: a student who asks a series of open-ended questions to gain as much knowledge as possible about a hidden Wikipedia text, and a teacher who provides short text excerpts in response. QuAC's questions are often more complex, unanswerable, or only meaningful within the context of the dialog, as demonstrated in a thorough qualitative evaluation. Results from a number of reference models, including a state-of-the-art reading comprehension architecture, are reported. The best model underperforms human performance by 20 F1, highlighting the need for further work in this area. The dataset, baseline models, and leaderboard can be accessed at http://quac.ai.

label: acl
text: Measuring similarity between texts is an important task for several applications. Available approaches to measure document similarity are inadequate for document pairs that have non-comparable lengths, such as a long document and its summary. This is because of the lexical, contextual and the abstraction gaps between a long document of rich details and its concise summary of abstract information. In this paper, we present a document matching approach to bridge this gap, by comparing the texts in a common space of hidden topics. We evaluate the matching algorithm on two matching tasks and find that it consistently and widely outperforms strong baselines. We also highlight the benefits of the incorporation of domain knowledge to text matching.

label: acl
text: Measuring the similarity between texts is crucial for various applications. However, existing methods for measuring document similarity are insufficient for comparing document pairs of unequal lengths, such as a lengthy document and its concise summary. This is due to the differences in lexical, contextual, and abstraction levels between the detailed information in the long document and the abstract information in the summary. To address this issue, we propose a document matching approach that aligns the texts in a shared space of hidden topics. Our evaluation of the matching algorithm on two matching tasks shows that it outperforms strong baselines consistently and significantly. Additionally, we demonstrate the advantages of incorporating domain knowledge into text matching.

label: acl
text: Medical imaging is widely used in clinical practice for diagnosis and treatment. Report-writing can be error-prone for unexperienced physicians, and time-consuming and tedious for experienced physicians. To address these issues, we study the automatic generation of medical imaging reports. This task presents several challenges. First, a complete report contains multiple heterogeneous forms of information, including findings and tags. Second, abnormal regions in medical images are difficult to identify. Third, the reports are typically long, containing multiple sentences. To cope with these challenges, we (1) build a multi-task learning framework which jointly performs the prediction of tags and the generation of paragraphs, (2) propose a co-attention mechanism to localize regions containing abnormalities and generate narrations for them, (3) develop a hierarchical LSTM model to generate long paragraphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods on two publicly available dataset.

label: acl
text: Medical imaging is commonly utilized in clinical settings for both diagnosis and treatment. Writing reports can prove challenging for inexperienced physicians and time-consuming for experienced ones. To overcome these obstacles, our research focuses on the automated generation of medical imaging reports. This task presents several difficulties, including the need to incorporate multiple forms of information, such as findings and tags, the difficulty in identifying abnormal regions within medical images, and the length of the reports, which often contain multiple sentences. To tackle these challenges, we have developed a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously predicts tags and generates paragraphs. Our co-attention mechanism is designed to locate abnormal regions and generate corresponding narrations. Additionally, we have implemented a hierarchical LSTM model to generate lengthy paragraphs. Our methods have been tested and proven effective on two publicly available datasets.

label: naacl
text: Pretrained language models (PLMs) have made remarkable progress in text generation tasks via fine-tuning. While, it is challenging to fine-tune PLMs in a data-scarce situation. Therefore, it is non-trivial to develop a general and lightweight model that can adapt to various text generation tasks based on PLMs. To fulfill this purpose, the recent prompt-based learning offers a potential solution. In this paper, we improve this technique and propose a novel prompt-based method (PTG) for text generation in a transferable setting. First, PTG learns a set of source prompts for various source generation tasks and then transfers these prompts as target prompts to perform target generation tasks. To consider both task- and instance-level information, we design an adaptive attention mechanism to derive the target prompts. For each data instance, PTG learns a specific target prompt by attending to highly relevant source prompts. In extensive experiments, PTG yields competitive or better results than fine-tuning methods. We release our source prompts as an open resource, where users can add or reuse them to improve new text generation tasks for future research. Code and data can be available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Transfer-Prompts-for-Text-Generation.

label: naacl
text: Pretrained language models have made great strides in text generation through fine-tuning. However, fine-tuning these models in a data-scarce environment is challenging. As a result, it is difficult to create a general, lightweight model that can be adapted to various text generation tasks based on these models. The recent prompt-based learning approach offers a potential solution to this problem. In this paper, we enhance this technique and propose a new prompt-based method (PTG) for transferable text generation. PTG starts by learning source prompts for various source generation tasks and then transfers these prompts as target prompts for performing target generation tasks. To take into account both task-level and instance-level information, we use an adaptive attention mechanism to determine the target prompts. PTG learns a specific target prompt for each data instance by focusing on the most relevant source prompts. Our experiments show that PTG outperforms or is competitive with fine-tuning methods. We have made our source prompts available as an open resource, allowing users to add or reuse them for future research on new text generation tasks. The code and data can be found at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Transfer-Prompts-for-Text-Generation.

label: naacl
text: We propose syntactically controlled paraphrase networks (SCPNs) and use them to generate adversarial examples. Given a sentence and a target syntactic form (e.g., a constituency parse), SCPNs are trained to produce a paraphrase of the sentence with the desired syntax. We show it is possible to create training data for this task by first doing backtranslation at a very large scale, and then using a parser to label the syntactic transformations that naturally occur during this process. Such data allows us to train a neural encoder-decoder model with extra inputs to specify the target syntax. A combination of automated and human evaluations show that SCPNs generate paraphrases that follow their target specifications without decreasing paraphrase quality when compared to baseline (uncontrolled) paraphrase systems. Furthermore, they are more capable of generating syntactically adversarial examples that both (1) “fool” pretrained models and (2) improve the robustness of these models to syntactic variation when used to augment their training data.

label: naacl
text: We propose Syntactically Controlled Paraphrase Networks (SCPNs) to generate adversarial examples. Given a sentence and a target syntactic form, such as a constituency parse, SCPNs are trained to produce a paraphrase of the sentence with the desired syntax. We demonstrate that it is possible to create training data for this task by using backtranslation on a large scale, followed by labeling the syntactic transformations that occur naturally during the process. This data enables us to train a neural encoder-decoder model with extra inputs to specify the target syntax. Automated and human evaluations show that SCPNs generate paraphrases that follow their target specifications while maintaining high paraphrase quality compared to baseline paraphrase systems. Additionally, they are more effective in generating syntactically adversarial examples that can "fool" pretrained models and improve their robustness to syntactic variation when used to augment their training data.

label: acl
text: Translate-train is a general training approach to multilingual tasks. The key idea is to use the translator of the target language to generate training data to mitigate the gap between the source and target languages. However, its performance is often hampered by the artifacts in the translated texts (translationese). We discover that such artifacts have common patterns in different languages and can be modeled by deep learning, and subsequently propose an approach to conduct translate-train using Translationese Embracing the effect of Artifacts (TEA). TEA learns to mitigate such effect on the training data of a source language (whose original and translationese are both available), and applies the learned module to facilitate the inference on the target language. Extensive experiments on the multilingual QA dataset TyDiQA demonstrate that TEA outperforms strong baselines.

label: acl
text: The Translate-train approach is a general method for training multilingual tasks, where the goal is to use the target language's translator to generate training data to reduce the gap between the source and target languages. However, this approach is often hindered by the presence of artifacts in translated texts, known as "translationese." Our research has revealed that these artifacts have common patterns across different languages, and can be modeled using deep learning. To address this, we propose the Translationese Embracing the effect of Artifacts (TEA) approach, which learns to mitigate the impact of translationese on the source language's training data. This learned module can then be applied to improve performance on the target language. Our experiments on the TyDiQA multilingual QA dataset show that TEA outperforms existing strong baselines.

label: acl
text: Despite recent progress of pre-trained language models on generating fluent text, existing methods still suffer from incoherence problems in long-form text generation tasks that require proper content control and planning to form a coherent high-level logical flow. In this work, we propose PLANET, a novel generation framework leveraging autoregressive self-attention mechanism to conduct content planning and surface realization dynamically. To guide the generation of output sentences, our framework enriches the Transformer decoder with latent representations to maintain sentence-level semantic plans grounded by bag-of-words. Moreover, we introduce a new coherence-based contrastive learning objective to further improve the coherence of output. Extensive experiments are conducted on two challenging long-form text generation tasks including counterargument generation and opinion article generation. Both automatic and human evaluations show that our method significantly outperforms strong baselines and generates more coherent texts with richer contents.

label: acl
text: Despite recent advancements in pre-trained language models for generating fluent text, there are still issues with coherence in long-form text generation tasks. These tasks require proper content control and planning to form a logical flow. To address this, we introduce PLANET, a novel generation framework that leverages an autoregressive self-attention mechanism for dynamic content planning and surface realization. Our framework enriches the Transformer decoder with latent representations to maintain sentence-level semantic plans, and uses a coherence-based contrastive learning objective to improve output coherence. We conduct extensive experiments on two challenging long-form text generation tasks, counterargument generation and opinion article generation, and find that our method outperforms strong baselines, producing more coherent and content-rich texts, as demonstrated by both automatic and human evaluations.

label: emnlp
text: An established method for Word Sense Induction (WSI) uses a language model to predict probable substitutes for target words, and induces senses by clustering these resulting substitute vectors. We replace the ngram-based language model (LM) with a recurrent one. Beyond being more accurate, the use of the recurrent LM allows us to effectively query it in a creative way, using what we call dynamic symmetric patterns. The combination of the RNN-LM and the dynamic symmetric patterns results in strong substitute vectors for WSI, allowing to surpass the current state-of-the-art on the SemEval 2013 WSI shared task by a large margin.

label: emnlp
text: An established technique for Word Sense Induction (WSI) involves utilizing a language model to predict potential substitutes for target words and inducing senses by grouping these resulting substitute vectors. We have replaced the traditional n-gram based language model (LM) with a recurrent neural network (RNN) model. The use of the RNN model not only increases accuracy, but also enables us to creatively query it using dynamic symmetric patterns. The combination of the RNN-LM and dynamic symmetric patterns results in powerful substitute vectors for WSI, enabling us to outperform the current state-of-the-art in the SemEval 2013 WSI shared task by a significant margin.

label: acl
text: Most of the current abstractive text summarization models are based on the sequence-to-sequence model (Seq2Seq). The source content of social media is long and noisy, so it is difficult for Seq2Seq to learn an accurate semantic representation. Compared with the source content, the annotated summary is short and well written. Moreover, it shares the same meaning as the source content. In this work, we supervise the learning of the representation of the source content with that of the summary. In implementation, we regard a summary autoencoder as an assistant supervisor of Seq2Seq. Following previous work, we evaluate our model on a popular Chinese social media dataset. Experimental results show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art performances on the benchmark dataset.

label: acl
text: Most current abstractive text summarization models are based on the sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model. However, the source content of social media is often long and noisy, making it difficult for Seq2Se to accurately learn a semantic representation. In contrast, the annotated summaries are short and well-written, sharing the same meaning as the source content. To address this issue, we supervise Seq2Seq's learning of the source content representation with that of the summary. This is achieved by using a summary autoencoder as an assistant supervisor. Our model was evaluated on a popular Chinese social media dataset and achieved state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark.

label: coling
text: Distributed word embeddings have shown superior performances in numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. However, their performances vary significantly across different tasks, implying that the word embeddings learnt by those methods capture complementary aspects of lexical semantics. Therefore, we believe that it is important to combine the existing word embeddings to produce more accurate and complete meta-embeddings of words. We model the meta-embedding learning problem as an autoencoding problem, where we would like to learn a meta-embedding space that can accurately reconstruct all source embeddings simultaneously. Thereby, the meta-embedding space is enforced to capture complementary information in different source embeddings via a coherent common embedding space. We propose three flavours of autoencoded meta-embeddings motivated by different requirements that must be satisfied by a meta-embedding. Our experimental results on a series of benchmark evaluations show that the proposed autoencoded meta-embeddings outperform the existing state-of-the-art meta-embeddings in multiple tasks.

label: coling
text: Distributed word embeddings have demonstrated outstanding results in various NLP tasks. However, their performance varies greatly among different tasks, indicating that these embeddings capture different aspects of lexical semantics. As a result, it is crucial to combine existing word embeddings to create more accurate and comprehensive meta-embeddings. We approach the meta-embedding learning problem as an autoencoding task, where we aim to learn a meta-embedding space that can accurately reconstruct all source embeddings. This ensures that the meta-embedding space captures complementary information from different source embeddings by forming a coherent common embedding space. We introduce three variations of autoencoded meta-embeddings, each motivated by different requirements that must be met by a meta-embedding. Our experiments on a range of benchmark evaluations show that our proposed autoencoded meta-embeddings outperform current state-of-the-art meta-embeddings in multiple tasks.

label: naacl
text: Global models are typically trained to be as generalizable as possible. Invariance to the specific user is considered desirable since models are shared across multitudes of users. However, these models are often unable to produce personalized responses for individual users, based on their data. Contrary to widely-used personalization techniques based on few-shot and meta-learning, we propose UserIdentifier, a novel scheme for training a single shared model for all users. Our approach produces personalized responses by prepending a fixed, user-specific non-trainable string (called “user identifier”) to each user's input text. Unlike prior work, this method doesn't need any additional model parameters, any extra rounds of personal few-shot learning or any change made to the vocabulary. We empirically study different types of user identifiers (numeric, alphanumeric, and also randomly generated) and demonstrate that, surprisingly, randomly generated user identifiers outperform the prefix-tuning based state-of-the-art approach by up to 13, on a suite of sentiment analysis datasets.

label: naacl
text: Typically, global models are trained to be as generalizable as possible, with invariance to specific users being considered desirable since these models are shared across many users. However, these models often fail to produce personalized responses for individual users based on their data. To address this issue, we introduce UserIdentifier, a novel approach for training a single shared model for all users that produces personalized responses by prepending a fixed, non-trainable user-specific string (known as the "user identifier") to each user's input text. Unlike prior work, this method does not require any additional model parameters, extra rounds of personal few-shot learning, or changes to the vocabulary. Our empirical study of different types of user identifiers (numeric, alphanumeric, and random) reveals that, surprisingly, randomly generated user identifiers outperform the state-of-the-art prefix-tuning approach by up to 13% on a suite of sentiment analysis datasets.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a method to perform automatic document summarisation without using reference summaries. Instead, our method interactively learns from users' preferences. The merit of preference-based interactive summarisation is that preferences are easier for users to provide than reference summaries. Existing preference-based interactive learning methods suffer from high sample complexity, i.e. they need to interact with the oracle for many rounds in order to converge. In this work, we propose a new objective function, which enables us to leverage active learning, preference learning and reinforcement learning techniques in order to reduce the sample complexity. Both simulation and real-user experiments suggest that our method significantly advances the state of the art. Our source code is freely available at https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2018-april.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a novel method for automatic document summarization that does not rely on reference summaries. Instead, our method utilizes user preferences to interactively learn and improve. The advantage of this preference-based approach is that it is easier for users to provide preferences than complete reference summaries. However, previous preference-based interactive learning methods have a high sample complexity, meaning they require many interactions with the oracle to converge. To address this issue, we have developed a new objective function that incorporates active learning, preference learning, and reinforcement learning techniques, thereby reducing the sample complexity. Our results from simulations and real-user experiments demonstrate that our method significantly advances the state of the art in this field. Our source code is available for free at https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2018-april.

label: emnlp
text: Sememes are defined as the minimum semantic units of human languages. As important knowledge sources, sememe-based linguistic knowledge bases have been widely used in many NLP tasks. However, most languages still do not have sememe-based linguistic knowledge bases. Thus we present a task of cross-lingual lexical sememe prediction, aiming to automatically predict sememes for words in other languages. We propose a novel framework to model correlations between sememes and multi-lingual words in low-dimensional semantic space for sememe prediction. Experimental results on real-world datasets show that our proposed model achieves consistent and significant improvements as compared to baseline methods in cross-lingual sememe prediction. The codes and data of this paper are available at https://github.com/thunlp/CL-SP.

label: emnlp
text: Sememes are considered the smallest semantic units in human languages and are widely used as important sources of knowledge in various NLP tasks. However, many languages still lack sememe-based linguistic knowledge bases. To address this issue, we present a cross-lingual lexical sememe prediction task aimed at automatically predicting sememes for words in different languages. Our proposed framework models the correlations between sememes and multilingual words in a low-dimensional semantic space for improved sememe prediction. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms baseline methods, delivering consistent and significant improvements in cross-lingual sememe prediction. The code and data used in this study are available at https://github.com/thunlp/CL-SP.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we present AnlamVer, which is a semantic model evaluation dataset for Turkish designed to evaluate word similarity and word relatedness tasks while discriminating those two relations from each other. Our dataset consists of 500 word-pairs annotated by 12 human subjects, and each pair has two distinct scores for similarity and relatedness. Word-pairs are selected to enable the evaluation of distributional semantic models by multiple attributes of words and word-pair relations such as frequency, morphology, concreteness and relation types (e.g., synonymy, antonymy). Our aim is to provide insights to semantic model researchers by evaluating models in multiple attributes. We balance dataset word-pairs by their frequencies to evaluate the robustness of semantic models concerning out-of-vocabulary and rare words problems, which are caused by the rich derivational and inflectional morphology of the Turkish language.

label: coling
text: This paper presents AnlamVer, a semantic model evaluation dataset for Turkish. label: emnlp
text: We propose to decompose instruction execution to goal prediction and action generation. We design a model that maps raw visual observations to goals using LINGUNET, a language-conditioned image generation network, and then generates the actions required to complete them. Our model is trained from demonstration only without external resources. To evaluate our approach, we introduce two benchmarks for instruction following: LANI, a navigation task; and CHAI, where an agent executes household instructions. Our evaluation demonstrates the advantages of our model decomposition, and illustrates the challenges posed by our new benchmarks.

label: emnlp
text: We suggest breaking down the process of instruction execution into two parts: goal prediction and action generation. We have designed a model that uses LINGUNET, a language-conditioned image generation network, to translate raw visual observations into goals. The model then generates the necessary actions to achieve those goals, all while being trained solely from demonstrations and without the use of external resources. To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we have created two benchmark tasks for instruction following: LANI, a navigation challenge, and CHAI, which involves the execution of household instructions. Our evaluation results highlight the benefits of our model's decomposition and showcase the difficulties posed by these new benchmarks.

label: acl
text: Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems learn harmful societal biases that cause them to amplify inequality as they are deployed in more and more situations. To guide efforts at debiasing these systems, the NLP community relies on a variety of metrics that quantify bias in models. Some of these metrics are intrinsic, measuring bias in word embedding spaces, and some are extrinsic, measuring bias in downstream tasks that the word embeddings enable. Do these intrinsic and extrinsic metrics correlate with each other? We compare intrinsic and extrinsic metrics across hundreds of trained models covering different tasks and experimental conditions. Our results show no reliable correlation between these metrics that holds in all scenarios across tasks and languages. We urge researchers working on debiasing to focus on extrinsic measures of bias, and to make using these measures more feasible via creation of new challenge sets and annotated test data. To aid this effort, we release code, a new intrinsic metric, and an annotated test set focused on gender bias in hate speech.

label: acl
text: The NLP systems often learn harmful biases from society, leading to unequal amplification of these biases as they are utilized in a wider range of situations. To tackle this issue, the NLP community relies on a range of metrics to quantify bias in these models. These metrics can be divided into two categories: intrinsic metrics, which measure bias in word embedding spaces, and extrinsic metrics, which measure bias in downstream tasks that the word embeddings enable. However, our research has found that there is no consistent correlation between these two types of metrics across different tasks and languages. As a result, we recommend that researchers focus on extrinsic measures of bias and work towards making these measures more accessible through the creation of new challenge sets and annotated test data. To support this goal, we have made available code, a new intrinsic metric, and an annotated test set focused on gender bias in hate speech.

label: acl
text: We present ReadOnce Transformers, an approach to convert a transformer-based model into one that can build an information-capturing, task-independent, and compressed representation of text. The resulting representation is reusable across different examples and tasks, thereby requiring a document shared across many examples or tasks to only be read once. This leads to faster training and evaluation of models. Additionally, we extend standard text-to-text transformer models to Representation+Text-to-text models, and evaluate on multiple downstream tasks: multi-hop QA, abstractive QA, and long-document summarization. Our one-time computed representation results in a 2x-5x speedup compared to standard text-to-text models, while the compression also allows existing language models to handle longer documents without the need for designing new pre-trained models.

text: We present the ReadOnce Transformers, a solution that converts a transformer-based model into one that can generate an information-rich, task-independent, and compact representation of text. This representation is reusable across various examples and tasks, so a document that is shared across multiple examples or tasks only needs to be read once, resulting in faster training and evaluation. Furthermore, we extend the standard text-to-text transformer models to Representation+Text-to-text models and evaluate them on multiple downstream tasks such as multi-hop QA, abstractive QA, and long-document summarization. Our one-time computed representation leads to a speedup of 2x to 5x compared to the standard text-to-text models, and the compression enables existing language models to process longer documents without the need for designing new pre-trained models.
