text: Automatic Essay Scoring (AES) is the task of using the computer to evaluate the quality of essays automatically. Current research on AES focuses on scoring the overall quality or single trait of prompt-specific essays. However, the users not only expect to obtain the overall score but also the instant feedback from different traits to help their writing in the real world. Therefore, we first annotate a mutli-trait dataset ACEA including 1220 argumentative essays from four traits, i.e., essay organization, topic, logic, and language. And then we design a hierarchical multi-task trait scorer HMTS to evaluate the quality of writing by modeling these four traits. Moreover, we propose an inter-sequence attention mechanism to enhance information interaction between different tasks and design the trait-specific features for various tasks in AES. The experimental results on ACEA show that our HMTS can effectively score essays from multiple traits, outperforming several strong models.

text: Automatic Essay Scoring (AES) is the process of using computer technology to evaluate the quality of essays automatically. The current focus of AES research is on scoring the overall quality or single trait of essays written in response to specific prompts. However, users expect not only an overall score but also instant feedback on various traits to help improve their writing in the real world. To address this need, we have annotated a multi-trait dataset called ACEA, which includes 1220 argumentative essays and four traits: essay organization, topic, logic, and language. We then designed a hierarchical multi-task trait scorer (HMTS) to evaluate writing quality by modeling these four traits. Additionally, we introduced an inter-sequence attention mechanism to enhance information interaction between different tasks and designed trait-specific features for various tasks in AES. Our experiments on the ACEA dataset show that our HMTS is effective in scoring essays from multiple traits and outperforms several strong models.

text: We consider few-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) intent detection, a practical and important problem for the development of task-oriented dialogue systems. Despite its importance, this problem is seldom studied in the literature, let alone examined in a systematic way. In this work, we take a closer look at this problem and identify key issues for research. In our pilot study, we reveal the reason why existing OOD intent detection methods are not adequate in dealing with this problem. Based on the observation, we propose a promising approach to tackle this problem based on latent representation generation and self-supervision. Comprehensive experiments on three real-world intent detection benchmark datasets demonstrate the high effectiveness of our proposed approach and its great potential in improving state-of-the-art methods for few-shot OOD intent detection.

text: We examine the problem of few-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) intent detection, a crucial aspect in the development of task-oriented dialogue systems. Despite its significance, this issue has received limited attention in the literature. In this study, we delve into this problem and identify the key challenges for research. Our pilot study reveals the limitations of existing OOD intent detection methods in addressing this issue. Based on our findings, we propose a novel approach that leverages latent representation generation and self-supervision to tackle this problem. Our comprehensive experiments on three real-world intent detection benchmark datasets demonstrate the exceptional performance of our proposed approach and its potential to enhance state-of-the-art methods for few-shot OOD intent detection.

text: In this paper we show that a simple beam approximation of the joint distribution between attention and output is an easy, accurate, and efficient attention mechanism for sequence to sequence learning. The method combines the advantage of sharp focus in hard attention and the implementation ease of soft attention. On five translation tasks we show effortless and consistent gains in BLEU compared to existing attention mechanisms.

text: In this paper, we demonstrate that using a simple beam approximation of the joint distribution between attention and output is an effective, accurate, and efficient attention mechanism for sequence-to-sequence learning. Our method combines the benefits of sharp focus in hard attention with the ease of implementation of soft attention. Through experiments on five translation tasks, we consistently achieve improved BLEU scores with minimal effort compared to existing attention mechanisms.

text: Span-based methods with the neural networks backbone have great potential for the nested named entity recognition (NER) problem. However, they face problems such as degenerating when positive instances and negative instances largely overlap. Besides, the generalization ability matters a lot in nested NER, as a large proportion of entities in the test set hardly appear in the training set. In this work, we try to improve the span representation by utilizing retrieval-based span-level graphs, connecting spans and entities in the training data based on C-C-C-gram features. Specifically, we build the entity-entity graph and span-entity graph globally based on D-D-D-gram similarity to integrate the information of similar neighbor entities into the span representation. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments on three common nested NER datasets, ACE2004, ACE2005, and GENIA datasets. Experimental results show that our method achieves general improvements on all three benchmarks (+E-E-E micro-F1), and obtains special superiority on low frequency entities (+F-F-F recall).

text: Span-based methods that utilize a neural network backbone have great potential for solving the nested named entity recognition (NER) problem. However, they may experience issues such as degradation when positive and negative instances overlap significantly. Additionally, the ability to generalize is crucial in nested NER, as a large portion of entities in the test set may not have appeared in the training set. To address these challenges, we propose to improve the span representation by using retrieval-based span-level graphs that connect spans and entities in the training data based on C-C-C-gram features. Our approach involves building both an entity-entity graph and a span-entity graph globally using D-D-D-gram similarity, which integrates information from similar neighboring entities into the span representation. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments on three common nested NER datasets: ACE2004, ACE2005, and GENIA. Results show that our method leads to general improvements in all three benchmarks (+E-E-E micro-F1), and particularly excels in low-frequency entity recognition (+F-F-F recall).

text: When processing a text, humans and machines must disambiguate between different uses of the pronoun it, including non-referential, nominal anaphoric or clause anaphoric ones. In this paper we use eye-tracking data to learn how humans perform this disambiguation and use this knowledge to improve the automatic classification of it. We show that by using gaze data and a POS-tagger we are able to significantly outperform a common baseline and classify between three categories of it with an accuracy comparable to that of linguistic-based approaches. In addition, the discriminatory power of specific gaze features informs the way humans process the pronoun, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not been explored using data from a natural reading task.

text: When processing text, humans and machines must differentiate between various uses of the pronoun "it", including non-referential, nominal anaphoric, and clause anaphoric uses. This paper uses eye-tracking data to study how humans perform this differentiation, and applies this knowledge to improve the automatic classification of "it". Our results demonstrate that by incorporating gaze data and a Part-of-Speech (POS) tagger, we can outperform a common baseline and classify "it" into three categories with accuracy comparable to that of linguistic-based methods. Furthermore, the discriminatory power of certain gaze features sheds light on the way humans process the pronoun, an aspect that has not been previously explored through the analysis of data from natural reading tasks.

text: Modern and post-modern free verse poems feature a large and complex variety in their poetic prosodies that falls along a continuum from a more fluent to a more disfluent and choppy style. As the poets of modernism overcame rhyme and meter, they oriented themselves in these two opposing directions, creating a free verse spectrum that calls for new analyses of prosodic forms. We present a method, grounded in philological analysis and current research on cognitive (dis)fluency, for automatically analyzing this spectrum. We define and relate six classes of poetic styles (ranging from parlando to lettristic decomposition) by their gradual differentiation. Based on this discussion, we present a model for automatic prosodic classification of spoken free verse poetry that uses deep hierarchical attention networks to integrate the source text and audio and predict the assigned class. We evaluate our model on a large corpus of German author-read post-modern poetry and find that classes can reliably be differentiated, reaching a weighted f-measure of 0.73, when combining textual and phonetic evidence. In our further analyses, we validate the model's decision-making process, the philologically hypothesized continuum of fluency and investigate the relative importance of various features.

text: The modern and post-modern free verse poems exhibit a wide range of prosodic complexities that fall along a spectrum from fluent to disfluent and choppy styles. As modernist poets moved away from rhyme and meter, they created this spectrum of free verse styles, which requires new approaches to prosodic analysis. This paper proposes a method for automatically analyzing this spectrum, based on philological analysis and research on cognitive fluency. Six classes of poetic styles are defined and differentiated, ranging from parlando to lettristic decomposition. A model is presented for automatic prosodic classification of spoken free verse poetry, using deep hierarchical attention networks to integrate text and audio and predict the assigned class. The model is evaluated on a large corpus of German author-read post-modern poetry and achieves a weighted f-measure of 0.73 when combining textual and phonetic evidence. Further analyses validate the model's decision-making process, the hypothesized continuum of fluency, and the relative importance of various features.

text: Large-scale pretrained language models have led to significant improvements in Natural Language Processing. Unfortunately, they come at the cost of high computational and storage requirements that complicate their deployment on low-resource devices. This issue can be addressed by distilling knowledge from larger models to smaller ones through pseudo-labels on task-specific datasets. However, this can be difficult for tasks with very limited data. To overcome this challenge, we present a novel approach where knowledge can be distilled from a teacher model to a student model through the generation of synthetic data. For this to be done, we first fine-tune the teacher and student models, as well as a Natural Language Generation (NLG) model, on the target task dataset. We then let both student and teacher work together to condition the NLG model to generate examples that can enhance the performance of the student. We tested our approach on two data generation methods: a) Targeted generation using the Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm, and b) A Non-Targeted Text Generation (NTTG) method. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approaches against a baseline that uses the BERT model for data augmentation through random word replacement. By testing this approach on the SST-2, MRPC, YELP-2, DBpedia, and TREC-6 datasets, we consistently witnessed considerable improvements over the word-replacement baseline.

text: Large-scale pre-trained language models have significantly improved Natural Language Processing, but they come with high computational and storage demands that make their deployment on low-resource devices challenging. Our approach involves fine-tuning the teacher and student models, as well as a Natural Language Generation (NLG) model, on the target task dataset. The student and teacher then work together to condition the NLG model to generate examples that can improve the student's performance. We tested two data generation methods: (a) targeted generation using the Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm and (b) a Non-Targeted Text Generation (NTTG) method. Our approach was evaluated against a baseline that uses the BERT model for data augmentation through random word replacement. Our results on the SST-2, MRPC, YELP-2, DBpedia, and TREC-6 datasets consistently showed significant improvements over the word-replacement baseline.

text: Most of the recent work on personality detection from online posts adopts multifarious deep neural networks to represent the posts and builds predictive models in a data-driven manner, without the exploitation of psycholinguistic knowledge that may unveil the connections between one's language use and his psychological traits. In this paper, we propose a psycholinguistic knowledge-based tripartite graph network, TrigNet, which consists of a tripartite graph network and a BERT-based graph initializer. The graph network injects structural psycholinguistic knowledge in LIWC, a computerized instrument for psycholinguistic analysis, by constructing a heterogeneous tripartite graph. The initializer is employed to provide initial embeddings for the graph nodes. To reduce the computational cost in graph learning, we further propose a novel flow graph attention network (GAT) that only transmits messages between neighboring parties in the tripartite graph. Benefiting from the tripartite graph, TrigNet can aggregate post information from a psychological perspective, which is a novel way of exploiting domain knowledge. Extensive experiments on two datasets show that TrigNet outperforms the existing state-of-art model by 3.47 and 2.10 points in average F1. Moreover, the flow GAT reduces the FLOPS and Memory measures by 38% and 32%, respectively, in comparison to the original GAT in our setting.

The tripartite graph network incorporates structural psycholinguistic knowledge from LIWC, a computerized instrument for psycholinguistic analysis, by constructing a heterogeneous tripartite graph. The initializer is used to provide initial node embeddings for the graph. To reduce computational costs in graph learning, we further propose a novel flow graph attention network (GAT) that only transmits messages between neighboring nodes in the tripartite graph. TrigNet leverages the tripartite graph to aggregate post information from a psychological perspective, a novel approach to exploiting domain knowledge. Our experiments on two datasets show that TrigNet outperforms the current state-of-the-art model by 3.47 and 2.10 points on average F1. text: Semantic role labeling (SRL) is a fundamental yet challenging task in the NLP community. Recent works of SRL mainly fall into two lines: 1) BIO-based; 2) span-based. Despite ubiquity, they share some intrinsic drawbacks of not considering internal argument structures, potentially hindering the model's expressiveness. The key challenge is arguments are flat structures, and there are no determined subtree realizations for words inside arguments. To remedy this, in this paper, we propose to regard flat argument spans as latent subtrees, accordingly reducing SRL to a tree parsing task. In particular, we equip our formulation with a novel span-constrained TreeCRF to make tree structures span-aware and further extend it to the second-order case. We conduct extensive experiments on CoNLL05 and CoNLL12 benchmarks. Results reveal that our methods perform favorably better than all previous syntax-agnostic works, achieving new state-of-the-art under both end-to-end and w/ gold predicates settings.

text: The task of semantic role labeling (SRL) is a fundamental yet challenging area in the field of NLP. The two main approaches to SRL are BIO-based and span-based, but both have limitations. These approaches don't consider internal argument structures, which can limit the model's expressiveness. The main challenge is that arguments are flat structures, and there are no determined subtree realizations for words inside arguments. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that regards flat argument spans as latent subtrees and reduces SRL to a tree parsing task. Our formulation includes a novel span-constrained TreeCRF, which makes tree structures span-aware and can be extended to the second-order case. We conducted experiments on the CoNLL05 and CoNLL12 benchmarks and found that our methods perform better than previous syntax-agnostic works, achieving new state-of-the-art results under both end-to-end and w/gold predicates settings.

text: Pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives have shown remarkable success in dialog understanding tasks. However, current contrastive learning solely considers the self-augmented dialog samples as positive samples and treats all other dialog samples as negative ones, which enforces dissimilar representations even for dialogs that are semantically related. In this paper, we propose SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained conversation model, which learns dialog representations from limited labeled dialogs and large-scale unlabeled dialog corpora via semi-supervised contrastive pre-training. Concretely, we first define a general semantic tree structure (STS) to unify the inconsistent annotation schema across different dialog datasets, so that the rich structural information stored in all labeled data can be exploited. Then we propose a novel multi-view score function to increase the relevance of all possible dialogs that share similar STSs and only push away other completely different dialogs during supervised contrastive pre-training. To fully exploit unlabeled dialogs, a basic self-supervised contrastive loss is also added to refine the learned representations. Experiments show that our method can achieve new state-of-the-art results on the DialoGLUE benchmark consisting of seven datasets and four popular dialog understanding tasks.

text: Pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives have achieved remarkable success in dialog understanding tasks. However, current contrastive learning methods only consider self-augmented dialog samples as positive samples and treat all other dialog samples as negative ones, leading to dissimilar representations even for semantically related dialogs. This paper introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained conversation model that learns dialog representations from limited labeled dialogs and large-scale unlabeled dialog corpora through semi-supervised contrastive pre-training. To exploit the rich structural information stored in all labeled data, the paper defines a general semantic tree structure (STS) to unify inconsistent annotation schemas across different dialog datasets. A novel multi-view score function is also proposed to increase the relevance of dialogs with similar STSs and reduce the impact of completely different dialogs during supervised contrastive pre-training. The method is further refined with a basic self-supervised contrastive loss to fully exploit unlabeled dialogs. Experiments show that SPACE-2 achieves new state-of-the-art results on the DialoGLUE benchmark, which consists of seven datasets and four popular dialog understanding tasks.

text: Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) has been recently extended to multiple knowledge graph (KG) structures, initiating new research directions, e.g. static KGC, temporal KGC and few-shot KGC. Previous works often design KGC models closely coupled with specific graph structures, which inevitably results in two drawbacks: 1) structure-specific KGC models are mutually incompatible; 2) existing KGC methods are not adaptable to emerging KGs. In this paper, we propose KG-S2S, a Seq2Seq generative framework that could tackle different verbalizable graph structures by unifying the representation of KG facts into “flat” text, regardless of their original form. To remedy the KG structure information loss from the “flat” text, we further improve the input representations of entities and relations, and the inference algorithm in KG-S2S. Experiments on five benchmarks show that KG-S2S outperforms many competitive baselines, setting new state-of-the-art performance. Finally, we analyze KG-S2S's ability on the different relations and the Non-entity Generations.

text: The field of Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) has been expanded to include multiple knowledge graph structures, leading to new research directions such as static KGC, temporal KGC, and few-shot KGC. However, previous KGC models have been closely tied to specific graph structures, resulting in two major drawbacks: 1) these models are not compatible with each other, and 2) they cannot be adapted to new knowledge graphs. To address these issues, we propose KG-S2S, a Seq2Seq generative framework that can handle various verbalizable graph structures by converting KG facts into a "flat" text representation, regardless of their original form. To mitigate the loss of KG structure information from the "flat" text, we enhance the input representations of entities and relations and improve the inference algorithm in KG-S2S. Our experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that KG-S2S outperforms many competitive baselines and sets new state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, we analyze KG-S2S's performance on different relations and non-entity generations.

label: acl
text: Comprehending a dialogue requires a model to capture diverse kinds of key information in the utterances, which are either scattered around or implicitly implied in different turns of conversations. Therefore, dialogue comprehension requires diverse capabilities such as paraphrasing, summarizing, and commonsense reasoning. Towards the objective of pre-training a zero-shot dialogue comprehension model, we develop a novel narrative-guided pre-training strategy that learns by narrating the key information from a dialogue input. However, the dialogue-narrative parallel corpus for such a pre-training strategy is currently unavailable. For this reason, we first construct a dialogue-narrative parallel corpus by automatically aligning movie subtitles and their synopses. We then pre-train a BART model on the data and evaluate its performance on four dialogue-based tasks that require comprehension. Experimental results show that our model not only achieves superior zero-shot performance but also exhibits stronger fine-grained dialogue comprehension capabilities. The data and code are available at https://github.com/zhaochaocs/Diana.

label: acl
text: To understand a dialogue, a model must be able to capture various types of crucial information that may be scattered or implicitly hinted at in different conversation turns. This requires the model to have diverse abilities such as summarizing, paraphrasing, and reasoning with common sense. To pre-train a model for zero-shot dialogue comprehension, we propose a novel narrative-guided pre-training approach that trains the model to narrate the key information from a dialogue. However, the required dialogue-narrative parallel corpus is currently unavailable. To address this, we construct a parallel corpus by aligning movie subtitles with their synopses. We then pre-train a BART model on the data and evaluate its performance on four dialogue-based tasks that test comprehension. Our results show that our model outperforms other models in zero-shot performance and has stronger fine-grained dialogue comprehension abilities. The data and code can be found at https://github.com/zhaochaocs/Diana.

label: naacl
text: The recent transition to the online educational domain has increased the need for Automatic Short Answer Grading (ASAG). ASAG automatically evaluates a student's response against a (given) correct response and thus has been a prevalent semantic matching task. Most existing methods utilize sequential context to compare two sentences and ignore the structural context of the sentence; therefore, these methods may not result in the desired performance. In this paper, we overcome this problem by proposing a Multi-Relational Graph Transformer, MitiGaTe, to prepare token representations considering the structural context. Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) graph is created by parsing the text response and then segregated into multiple subgraphs, each corresponding to a particular relationship in AMR. A Graph Transformer is used to prepare relation-specific token embeddings within each subgraph, then aggregated to obtain a subgraph representation. Finally, we compare the correct answer and the student response subgraph representations to yield a final score. Experimental results on Mohler's dataset show that our system outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods. We have released our implementation https://github.com/kvarun07/asag-gt, as we believe that our model can be useful for many future applications.

label: naacl
text: The recent shift to online education has heightened the demand for Automatic Short Answer Grading (ASAG). ASAG evaluates a student's response against a correct answer using semantic matching, a commonly used task in this field. However, existing methods often rely solely on sequential context, ignoring the structural context of sentences, which can negatively impact performance. To address this issue, we introduce the Multi-Relational Graph Transformer, MitiGaTe, which prepares token representations while considering the structural context of sentences. Our approach involves creating an Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) graph from the text response, dividing it into subgraphs that correspond to specific relationships in AMR, and using a Graph Transformer to prepare relation-specific token embeddings within each subgraph. These subgraph representations are then aggregated to obtain a final score by comparing the correct answer and the student response subgraph representations. Our experiments on Mohler's dataset demonstrate that MitiGaTe outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. We have made our implementation publicly available at https://github.com/kvarun07/asag-gt, as we believe it will be useful for future applications.

label: acl
text: Weakly supervised question answering usually has only the final answers as supervision signals while the correct solutions to derive the answers are not provided. This setting gives rise to the spurious solution problem: there may exist many spurious solutions that coincidentally derive the correct answer, but training on such solutions can hurt model performance (e.g., producing wrong solutions or answers). For example, for discrete reasoning tasks as on DROP, there may exist many equations to derive a numeric answer, and typically only one of them is correct. Previous learning methods mostly filter out spurious solutions with heuristics or using model confidence, but do not explicitly exploit the semantic correlations between a question and its solution. In this paper, to alleviate the spurious solution problem, we propose to explicitly exploit such semantic correlations by maximizing the mutual information between question-answer pairs and predicted solutions. Extensive experiments on four question answering datasets show that our method significantly outperforms previous learning methods in terms of task performance and is more effective in training models to produce correct solutions.

label: acl
text: The problem of weakly supervised question answering is that it only provides the final answers as supervision signals, but not the correct solutions to derive the answers. This leads to the issue of spurious solutions, where many incorrect solutions coincidentally derive the correct answer. For instance, in discrete reasoning tasks like DROP, there may be many equations to derive a numeric answer, but only one of them is correct. Previous methods have attempted to address this issue by using heuristics or model confidence to filter out spurious solutions, but they do not exploit the semantic correlations between questions and their solutions. To tackle this problem, we propose a method that maximizes the mutual information between question-answer pairs and predicted solutions, thereby exploiting semantic correlations. Our method outperforms previous methods in terms of task performance, as demonstrated by experiments on four question answering datasets.

text: Framing is a political strategy in which journalists and politicians emphasize certain aspects of a societal issue in order to influence and sway public opinion. Frameworks for detecting framing in news articles or social media posts are critical in understanding the spread of biased information in our society. In this paper, we propose CLoSE, a multi-task BERT-based model which uses contrastive learning to embed indicators of frames from news articles in order to predict political bias. We evaluate the performance of our proposed model on subframes and political bias classification tasks. We also demonstrate the model's classification accuracy on zero-shot and few-shot learning tasks, providing a promising avenue for framing detection in unlabeled data.

text: Framing is a political tactic where journalists and politicians highlight specific aspects of a social issue to influence public opinion. The ability to detect framing in news articles or social media posts is crucial for understanding the spread of biased information in society. This paper introduces CLoSE, a multi-task BERT-based model that uses contrastive learning to embed indicators of frames from news articles. The model is evaluated on subframe and political bias classification tasks and demonstrates high accuracy in zero-shot and few-shot learning, offering a promising solution for detecting framing in unlabeled data.

text: Mental Health Disorders continue plaguing humans worldwide. Aggravating this situation is the severe shortage of qualified and competent mental health professionals (MHPs), which underlines the need for developing Virtual Assistants (VAs) that can assist MHPs. The data+ML for automation can come from platforms that allow visiting and posting messages in peer-to-peer anonymous manner for sharing their experiences (frequently stigmatized) and seeking support. In this paper, we propose a VA that can act as the first point of contact and comfort for mental health patients. We curate a dataset, Motivational VA: MotiVAte comprising of 7k dyadic conversations collected from a peer-to-peer support platform. The system employs two mechanisms: (i) Mental Illness Classification: an attention based BERT classifier that outputs the mental disorder category out of the 4 categories, viz., Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Anxiety, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) and Post-traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), based on the input ongoing dialog between the support seeker and the VA; and (ii) Mental Illness Conditioned Motivational Dialogue Generation (MI-MDG): a sentiment driven Reinforcement Learning (RL) based motivational response generator. The empirical evaluation demonstrates the system capability by way of outperforming several baselines.

label: naacl
text: Mental health disorders continue to affect people globally, and the shortage of competent mental health professionals exacerbates this issue. To address this, we propose the development of virtual assistants (VAs) that can assist mental health professionals. To train these VAs, we gather data from peer-to-peer support platforms where users can share their experiences anonymously and seek support. Our VA, called Motivational VA: MotiVAte, serves as the first point of contact and comfort for mental health patients. We have curated a dataset of 7k dyadic conversations collected from a peer-to-peer support platform. The VA employs two mechanisms: mental illness classification using an attention-based BERT classifier, and mental illness-conditioned motivational dialogue generation using a sentiment-driven reinforcement learning approach. The results of our empirical evaluation show that our system outperforms several baselines.

label: emnlp
text: Extractive summarization models need sentence level labels, which are usually created with rule-based methods since most summarization datasets only have document summary pairs. These labels might be suboptimal. We propose a latent variable extractive model, where sentences are viewed as latent variables and sentences with activated variables are used to infer gold summaries. During training, the loss can come directly from gold summaries. Experiments on CNN/Dailymail dataset show our latent extractive model outperforms a strong extractive baseline trained on rule-based labels and also performs competitively with several recent models.

label: emnlp
text: The requirement for sentence-level labels in extractive summarization models is typically met through rule-based methods, as most summarization datasets only contain document-summary pairs. However, these labels may not be optimal. To overcome this issue, we propose a latent variable extractive model, where sentences are treated as latent variables. The model uses activated variables to infer the gold summaries. During training, the loss is calculated directly from the gold summaries. Our experiments on the CNN/Dailymail dataset demonstrate that our latent extractive model outperforms a strong extractive baseline that was trained on rule-based labels, and it also performs comparably with several recent models.

label: acl
text: In the era of big data, focused analysis for diverse topics with a short response time becomes an urgent demand. As a fundamental task, information filtering therefore becomes a critical necessity. In this paper, we propose a novel deep relevance model for zero-shot document filtering, named DAZER. DAZER estimates the relevance between a document and a category by taking a small set of seed words relevant to the category. With pre-trained word embeddings from a large external corpus, DAZER is devised to extract the relevance signals by modeling the hidden feature interactions in the word embedding space. The relevance signals are extracted through a gated convolutional process. The gate mechanism controls which convolution filters output the relevance signals in a category dependent manner. Experiments on two document collections of two different tasks (i.e., topic categorization and sentiment analysis) demonstrate that DAZER significantly outperforms the existing alternative solutions, including the state-of-the-art deep relevance ranking models.

text: In the era of big data, there is an urgent demand for focused analysis of diverse topics with a quick response time. As a result, information filtering has become a critical necessity. To address this need, we introduce a novel deep relevance model for zero-shot document filtering, called DAZER. This model calculates the relevance between a document and a category by using a small set of seed words relevant to the category. DAZER uses pre-trained word embeddings from a large external corpus to extract relevance signals by modeling the hidden interactions between features in the word embedding space. This is achieved through a gated convolutional process, where the gate mechanism controls the relevance signals output in a category-dependent manner. Our experiments on two document collections for two different tasks (topic categorization and sentiment analysis) show that DAZER outperforms existing solutions, including state-of-the-art deep relevance ranking models.

text: This paper presents a simple recipe to trainstate-of-the-art multilingual Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) models. We achieve this by first proposing a language-agnostic method to generate a large number of synthetic examples. The second ingredient is to use large-scale multilingual language models (up to 11B parameters). Once fine-tuned on language-specific supervised sets we surpass the previous state-of-the-art results on GEC benchmarks in four languages: English, Czech, German and Russian. Having established a new set of baselines for GEC, we make our results easily reproducible and accessible by releasing a CLANG-8 dataset. It is produced by using our best model, which we call gT5, to clean the targets of a widely used yet noisy Lang-8 dataset. cLang-8 greatly simplifies typical GEC training pipelines composed of multiple fine-tuning stages – we demonstrate that performing a single fine-tuning stepon cLang-8 with the off-the-shelf language models yields further accuracy improvements over an already top-performing gT5 model for English.

text: This paper presents a simple recipe for training state-of-the-art multilingual Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) models. The recipe includes two key ingredients: a language-agnostic method for generating a large number of synthetic examples and the use of large-scale multilingual language models with up to 11B parameters. After fine-tuning on language-specific supervised sets, the proposed method surpasses previous state-of-the-art results for GEC in four languages: English, Czech, German, and Russian. To make the results accessible and easily reproducible, the authors have released the cLang-8 dataset, produced by using the best model (gT5) to clean the targets of the widely used but noisy Lang-8 dataset. The cLang-8 greatly simplifies typical GEC training pipelines, which typically involve multiple fine-tuning stages. The authors demonstrate that a single fine-tuning step on cLang-8 with off-the-shelf language models yields further accuracy improvements over the already top-performing gT5 model for English.

text: This paper proposes to cast end-to-end span-based SRL as a word-based graph parsing task. The major challenge is how to represent spans at the word level. Borrowing ideas from research on Chinese word segmentation and named entity recognition, we propose and compare four different schemata of graph representation, i.e., BES, BE, BIES, and BII, among which we find that the BES schema performs the best. We further gain interesting insights through detailed analysis. Moreover, we propose a simple constrained Viterbi procedure to ensure the legality of the output graph according to the constraints of the SRL structure. We conduct experiments on two widely used benchmark datasets, i.e., CoNLL05 and CoNLL12. Results show that our word-based graph parsing approach achieves consistently better performance than previous results, under all settings of end-to-end and predicate-given, without and with pre-trained language models (PLMs). More importantly, our model can parse 669/252 sentences per second, without and with PLMs respectively.

text: This paper presents a novel approach to cast end-to-end span-based semantic role labeling (SRL) as a word-based graph parsing task. The main challenge is to represent spans at the word level. To address this, we borrow ideas from research in Chinese word segmentation and named entity recognition and propose four different graph representation schemata (BES, BE, BIES, and BII). Our experiments show that the BES schema performs the best. Additionally, we introduce a simple constrained Viterbi procedure to ensure the legality of the output graph according to the constraints of the SRL structure. Our approach was evaluated on two widely used benchmark datasets (CoNLL05 and CoNLL12) and showed consistently better performance compared to previous results, for both end-to-end and predicate-given settings, with and without pre-trained language models. Furthermore, our model can parse 669/252 sentences per second with and without pre-trained language models, respectively.

text: We propose a novel recurrent neural network-based approach to simultaneously handle nested named entity recognition and nested entity mention detection. The model learns a hypergraph representation for nested entities using features extracted from a recurrent neural network. In evaluations on three standard data sets, we show that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, which are feature-based. The approach is also efficient: it operates linearly in the number of tokens and the number of possible output labels at any token. Finally, we present an extension of our model that jointly learns the head of each entity mention.

label: naacl
text: We propose a new approach based on recurrent neural networks for simultaneous nested named entity recognition and nested entity mention detection. Our model utilizes a hypergraph representation of nested entities, which is learned through the extraction of features from a recurrent neural network. Our approach has been evaluated on three standard data sets and has been shown to significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art methods, which are based on features. Additionally, our approach is highly efficient, operating linearly in the number of tokens and possible output labels at any given token. Finally, we have also developed an extension to our model that allows for the joint learning of the head of each entity mention.

text: Logical approaches to representing language have developed and evaluated computational models of quantifier words since the 19th century, but today's NLU models still struggle to capture their semantics. We rely on Generalized Quantifier Theory for language-independent representations of the semantics of quantifier words, to quantify their contribution to the errors of NLU models. We find that quantifiers are pervasive in NLU benchmarks, and their occurrence at test time is associated with performance drops. Multilingual models also exhibit unsatisfying quantifier reasoning abilities, but not necessarily worse for non-English languages. To facilitate directly-targeted probing, we present an adversarial generalized quantifier NLI task (GQNLI) and show that pre-trained language models have a clear lack of robustness in generalized quantifier reasoning.

label: naacl
text: For over a century, researchers have been developing and evaluating computational models for representing the semantics of quantifier words in language. Despite these efforts, current Natural Language Understanding (NLU) models still struggle to capture their meaning accurately. To address this issue, we utilize the Generalized Quantifier Theory to create language-independent representations of quantifier words. Our findings indicate that quantifiers are prevalent in NLU benchmarks and their presence is a significant factor in performance drops. Although multilingual models show poor quantifier reasoning abilities, this is not necessarily worse for non-English languages. To better understand this challenge, we introduce an adversarial Generalized Quantifier Natural Language Inference (GQNLI) task. Our results show that pre-trained language models lack robustness in generalized quantifier reasoning.

text: While modern machine translation has relied on large parallel corpora, a recent line of work has managed to train Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems from monolingual corpora only (Artetxe et al., 2018c; Lample et al., 2018). Despite the potential of this approach for low-resource settings, existing systems are far behind their supervised counterparts, limiting their practical interest. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach based on phrase-based Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) that significantly closes the gap with supervised systems. Our method profits from the modular architecture of SMT: we first induce a phrase table from monolingual corpora through cross-lingual embedding mappings, combine it with an n-gram language model, and fine-tune hyperparameters through an unsupervised MERT variant. In addition, iterative backtranslation improves results further, yielding, for instance, 14.08 and 26.22 BLEU points in WMT 2014 English-German and English-French, respectively, an improvement of more than 7-10 BLEU points over previous unsupervised systems, and closing the gap with supervised SMT (Moses trained on Europarl) down to 2-5 BLEU points. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/artetxem/monoses.

text: Modern machine translation has traditionally relied on large parallel corpora. However, recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have allowed for training systems from monolingual corpora only (Artetxe et al., 2018c; Lample et al., 2018). While this approach has potential for low-resource settings, current systems are far from being as effective as supervised systems, limiting their practical applications. In this paper, we present an alternative approach based on phrase-based Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) that significantly narrows the gap with supervised systems. Our method leverages the modular architecture of SMT by inducing a phrase table from monolingual corpora through cross-lingual embedding mappings, combining it with an n-gram language model, and fine-tuning hyperparameters using an unsupervised MERT variant. Additionally, iterative backtranslation further improves results, resulting in a 14.08 BLEU score in WMT 2014 English-German and 26.22 BLEU score in English-French, an improvement of over 7-10 BLEU points compared to previous unsupervised systems, and reducing the gap with supervised SMT (Moses trained on Europarl) to 2-5 BLEU points. The implementation of our method is available at https://github.com/artetxem/monoses.

text: Knowledge of the creation date of documents facilitates several tasks such as summarization, event extraction, temporally focused information extraction etc. Unfortunately, for most of the documents on the Web, the time-stamp metadata is either missing or can't be trusted. Thus, predicting creation time from document content itself is an important task. In this paper, we propose Attentive Deep Document Dater (AD3), an attention-based neural document dating system which utilizes both context and temporal information in documents in a flexible and principled manner. We perform extensive experimentation on multiple real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of AD3 over neural and non-neural baselines.

text:
The results show that AD3 outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

The knowledge of the creation date of documents can simplify several tasks such as summarization, event extraction, and focused information extraction. Unfortunately, the time-stamp metadata for most documents found on the web is either missing or unreliable. To address this issue, we propose Attentive Deep Document Dater (AD3), a neural document dating system that uses both context and temporal information in documents in a flexible and systematic manner. Our extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of AD3 over existing neural and non-neural methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

text: Entity typing aims to classify semantic types of an entity mention in a specific context. Most existing models obtain training data using distant supervision, and inevitably suffer from the problem of noisy labels. To address this issue, we propose entity typing with language model enhancement. It utilizes a language model to measure the compatibility between context sentences and labels, and thereby automatically focuses more on context-dependent labels. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method is capable of enhancing the entity typing model with information from the language model, and significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline. Code and data for this paper can be found from https://github.com/thunlp/LME.

text: The aim of entity typing is to classify the semantic types of an entity mention within a specific context. Most current models are trained using distant supervision, which results in noisy labels. To overcome this challenge, we introduce entity typing with language model enhancement. Our approach leverages a language model to assess the compatibility between context sentences and labels, thereby automatically focusing on context-dependent labels. Our experiments on benchmark datasets show that our method enhances the entity typing model with information from the language model and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code and data for this paper can be found on https://github.com/thunlp/LME.

text: Recurrent models have been dominating the field of neural machine translation (NMT) for the past few years. Transformers have radically changed it by proposing a novel architecture that relies on a feed-forward backbone and self-attention mechanism. Although Transformers are powerful, they could fail to properly encode sequential/positional information due to their non-recurrent nature. To solve this problem, position embeddings are defined exclusively for each time step to enrich word information. However, such embeddings are fixed after training regardless of the task and word ordering system of the source and target languages. In this paper, we address this shortcoming by proposing a novel architecture with new position embeddings that take the order of the target words into consideration. Instead of using predefined position embeddings, our solution generates new embeddings to refine each word's position information. Since we do not dictate the position of the source tokens and we learn them in an end-to-end fashion, we refer to our method as dynamic position encoding (DPE). We evaluated the impact of our model on multiple datasets to translate from English to German, French, and Italian and observed meaningful improvements in comparison to the original Transformer.

text: Over the past few years, recurrent models have dominated the field of neural machine translation (NMT). The introduction of Transformers, however, has revolutionized the field with its novel architecture that utilizes a feed-forward backbone and self-attention mechanism. Despite the power of Transformers, they can struggle to encode sequential/positional information due to their non-recurrent nature. To overcome this issue, position embeddings are defined for each time step to enhance word information. However, these embeddings are fixed after training, regardless of the task and word ordering system of the source and target languages. This paper presents a new architecture with dynamic position encoding (DPE), which generates new position embeddings to refine each word's positional information. Unlike traditional position embeddings which are predefined, DPE learns the position of source tokens in an end-to-end fashion. Our evaluation of multiple datasets for English to German, French, and Italian translations showed meaningful improvements compared to the original Transformer.

text: In Sanskrit, small words (morphemes) are combined to form compound words through a process known as Sandhi. Sandhi splitting is the process of splitting a given compound word into its constituent morphemes. Although rules governing word splitting exists in the language, it is highly challenging to identify the location of the splits in a compound word. Though existing Sandhi splitting systems incorporate these pre-defined splitting rules, they have a low accuracy as the same compound word might be broken down in multiple ways to provide syntactically correct splits. In this research, we propose a novel deep learning architecture called Double Decoder RNN (DD-RNN), which (i) predicts the location of the split(s) with 95% accuracy, and (ii) predicts the constituent words (learning the Sandhi splitting rules) with 79.5% accuracy, outperforming the state-of-art by 20%. Additionally, we show the generalization capability of our deep learning model, by showing competitive results in the problem of Chinese word segmentation, as well.

text: In Sanskrit, the formation of compound words is achieved by combining small words (morphemes) through a process known as Sandhi. The process of splitting a compound word into its constituent morphemes is referred to as Sandhi splitting. Although there are rules governing word splitting in the language, it can be challenging to identify the split points in a compound word. Existing Sandhi splitting systems apply pre-defined splitting rules but have limited accuracy as the same compound word may be divided in multiple ways that are syntactically correct. We propose a novel deep learning architecture called Double Decoder RNN (DD-RNN) that predicts the split points with 95% accuracy and the constituent words with 79.5% accuracy, outperforming the state-of-the-art by 20%. Our model also demonstrates its generalization capability by achieving competitive results in Chinese word segmentation.

text: With the recent advance in neural machine translation demonstrating its importance, research on quality estimation (QE) has been steadily progressing. QE aims to automatically predict the quality of machine translation (MT) output without reference sentences. Despite its high utility in the real world, there remain several limitations concerning manual QE data creation: inevitably incurred non-trivial costs due to the need for translation experts, and issues with data scaling and language expansion. To tackle these limitations, we present QUAK, a Korean-English synthetic QE dataset generated in a fully automatic manner. This consists of three sub-QUAK datasets QUAK-M, QUAK-P, and QUAK-H, produced through three strategies that are relatively free from language constraints. Since each strategy requires no human effort, which facilitates scalability, we scale our data up to 1.58M for QUAK-P, H and 6.58M for QUAK-M. As an experiment, we quantitatively analyze word-level QE results in various ways while performing statistical analysis. Moreover, we show that datasets scaled in an efficient way also contribute to performance improvements by observing meaningful performance gains in QUAK-M, P when adding data up to 1.58M.

text: With the recent advances in neural machine translation, research on quality estimation (QE) has gained momentum. QE aims to predict the quality of machine translation (MT) output without reference sentences. However, manual QE data creation is limited by the need for translation experts and the associated non-trivial costs, as well as issues with data scaling and language expansion. To overcome these limitations, we introduce QUAK, a Korean-English synthetic QE dataset generated in a fully automatic manner, consisting of three sub-datasets: QUAK-M, QUAK-P, and QUAK-H. These datasets are produced through three strategies that are relatively free from language constraints, and they require no human effort, making them scalable. We have scaled our data up to 1.58 million for QUAK-P and QUAK-H and 6.58 million for QUAK-M. In our experiments, we analyze word-level QE results and perform statistical analysis. Additionally, we demonstrate that the efficient scaling of our datasets contributes to performance improvements, as evidenced by the meaningful performance gains observed in QUAK-M and QUAK-P when adding data up to 1.58 million.

text: We explore deception detection in interview dialogues. We analyze a set of linguistic features in both truthful and deceptive responses to interview questions. We also study the perception of deception, identifying characteristics of statements that are perceived as truthful or deceptive by interviewers. Our analysis show significant differences between truthful and deceptive question responses, as well as variations in deception patterns across gender and native language. This analysis motivated our selection of features for machine learning experiments aimed at classifying globally deceptive speech. Our best classification performance is 72.74% F1-Score (about 17% better than human performance), which is achieved using a combination of linguistic features and individual traits.

label: naacl
text: We investigate deception detection in interview dialogues by analyzing a set of linguistic features in both truthful and deceptive responses to interview questions. Our study also examines the perception of deception, identifying the characteristics of statements that are perceived as truthful or deceptive by interviewers. Our analysis reveals significant differences between truthful and deceptive responses, as well as variations in deception patterns across gender and native language. This led us to select specific features for our machine learning experiments aimed at classifying globally deceptive speech. Our best classification performance, with an F1-Score of 72.74%, is 17% better than human performance and achieved through a combination of linguistic features and individual traits.

label: acl
text: Token-level adaptive training approaches can alleviate the token imbalance problem and thus improve neural machine translation, through re-weighting the losses of different target tokens based on specific statistical metrics (e.g., token frequency or mutual information). Given that standard translation models make predictions on the condition of previous target contexts, we argue that the above statistical metrics ignore target context information and may assign inappropriate weights to target tokens. While one possible solution is to directly take target contexts into these statistical metrics, the target-context-aware statistical computing is extremely expensive, and the corresponding storage overhead is unrealistic. To solve the above issues, we propose a target-context-aware metric, named conditional bilingual mutual information (CBMI), which makes it feasible to supplement target context information for statistical metrics. Particularly, our CBMI can be formalized as the log quotient of the translation model probability and language model probability by decomposing the conditional joint distribution. Thus CBMI can be efficiently calculated during model training without any pre-specific statistical calculations and large storage overhead. Furthermore, we propose an effective adaptive training approach based on both the token- and sentence-level CBMI. Experimental results on WMT14 English-German and WMT19 Chinese-English tasks show our approach can significantly outperform the Transformer baseline and other related methods.

label: acl
text: Token-level adaptive training can improve neural machine translation by re-weighting the losses of different target tokens based on statistical metrics such as token frequency or mutual information. However, standard translation models make predictions based on previous target contexts, so these metrics ignore target context information and may assign incorrect weights to tokens. A solution to this problem would be to incorporate target context into the metrics, but this is expensive and requires too much storage. To overcome this, we propose a target-context-aware metric called conditional bilingual mutual information (CBMI), which incorporates target context and can be calculated efficiently during model training without the need for pre-calculations or large storage. Our approach, which is based on both token- and sentence-level CBMI, outperforms the Transformer baseline and other related methods on the WMT14 English-German and WMT19 Chinese-English tasks, as shown by our experimental results.

label: naacl
text: Many text classification tasks are known to be highly domain-dependent. Unfortunately, the availability of training data can vary drastically across domains. Worse still, for some domains there may not be any annotated data at all. In this work, we propose a multinomial adversarial network (MAN) to tackle this real-world problem of multi-domain text classification (MDTC) in which labeled data may exist for multiple domains, but in insufficient amounts to train effective classifiers for one or more of the domains. We provide theoretical justifications for the MAN framework, proving that different instances of MANs are essentially minimizers of various f-divergence metrics (Ali and Silvey, 1966) among multiple probability distributions. MANs are thus a theoretically sound generalization of traditional adversarial networks that discriminate over two distributions. More specifically, for the MDTC task, MAN learns features that are invariant across multiple domains by resorting to its ability to reduce the divergence among the feature distributions of each domain. We present experimental results showing that MANs significantly outperform the prior art on the MDTC task. We also show that MANs achieve state-of-the-art performance for domains with no labeled data.

label: naacl
text: Many text classification tasks are known to be highly dependent on the domain. Unfortunately, the availability of training data can vary greatly across domains, and for some domains, there may not be any annotated data at all. To address this real-world issue of multi-domain text classification (MDTC), we propose a multinomial adversarial network (MAN). The MAN framework is a theoretically sound solution for MDTC, as it minimizes various f-divergence metrics among multiple probability distributions. This makes it a generalization of traditional adversarial networks that discriminate between two distributions. In the MDTC task, MAN learns features that are invariant across multiple domains by reducing the divergence among the feature distributions of each domain. Our experimental results show that MANs outperform prior art and achieve state-of-the-art performance for domains with no labeled data.

label: coling
text: Document-level Event Factuality Identification (DEFI) predicts the factuality of a specific event based on a document from which the event can be derived, which is a fundamental and crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, most previous studies only considered sentence-level task and did not adopt document-level knowledge. Moreover, they modelled DEFI as a typical text classification task depending on annotated information heavily, and limited to the task-specific corpus only, which resulted in data scarcity. To tackle these issues, we propose a new framework formulating DEFI as Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) tasks considering both Span-Extraction (Ext) and Multiple-Choice (Mch). Our model does not employ any other explicit annotated information, and utilizes Transfer Learning (TL) to extract knowledge from universal large-scale MRC corpora for cross-domain data augmentation. The empirical results on DLEFM corpus demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms several state-of-the-arts.

label: coling
text: The Document-level Event Factuality Identification (DEFI) is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that predicts the factuality of a specific event based on a document. However, most previous studies only considered sentence-level tasks and lacked document-level knowledge. These studies also heavily relied on annotated information and were limited to task-specific corpora, leading to a scarcity of data. To address these limitations, we propose a new framework that formulates DEFI as a Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) task and considers both Span-Extraction and Multiple-Choice. Our model does not require any explicit annotated information and leverages Transfer Learning to extract knowledge from large-scale MRC corpora for cross-domain data augmentation. The results on the DLEFM corpus show that our proposed model outperforms several state-of-the-art models.

label: naacl
text: In neural machine translation, an attention model is used to identify the aligned source words for a target word (target foresight word) in order to select translation context, but it does not make use of any information of this target foresight word at all. Previous work proposed an approach to improve the attention model by explicitly accessing this target foresight word and demonstrated the substantial gains in alignment task. However, this approach is useless in machine translation task on which the target foresight word is unavailable. In this paper, we propose a new attention model enhanced by the implicit information of target foresight word oriented to both alignment and translation tasks. Empirical experiments on Chinese-to-English and Japanese-to-English datasets show that the proposed attention model delivers significant improvements in terms of both alignment error rate and BLEU.

label: naacl
text: The neural machine translation process uses an attention model to identify the relevant source words for a target word in order to select the appropriate translation context. However, this model does not utilize any information about the target word itself. Previous research has proposed an approach that improves the attention model by incorporating information about the target word, resulting in substantial gains in alignment accuracy. However, this approach is not useful in machine translation tasks where the target word is not available. In this paper, we present a new attention model that leverages implicit information about the target word, aimed at improving both alignment and translation tasks. Our experiments on Chinese-to-English and Japanese-to-English datasets demonstrate that the proposed attention model significantly improves alignment error rate and BLEU scores.

label: coling
text: This paper presents novel methods to automatically convert posts and their comments from discussion forums such as Reddit into multi-turn dialogues. Our methods are generalizable to any forums; thus, they allow us to generate a massive amount of dialogues for diverse topics that can be used to pretrain language models. Four methods are introduced, Greedy_Baseline, Greedy_Advanced, Beam Search and Threading, which are applied to posts from 10 subreddits and assessed. Each method makes a noticeable improvement over its predecessor such that the best method shows an improvement of 36.3% over the baseline for appropriateness. Our best method is applied to posts from those 10 subreddits for the creation of a corpus comprising 10,098 dialogues (3.3M tokens), 570 of which are compared against dialogues in three other datasets, Blended Skill Talk, Daily Dialogue, and Topical Chat. Our dialogues are found to be more engaging but slightly less natural than the ones in the other datasets, while it costs a fraction of human labor and money to generate our corpus compared to the others. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first work to create a large multi-turn dialogue corpus from Reddit that can advance neural dialogue systems.

label: coling
text: This paper introduces novel methods for automatically converting posts and comments from discussion forums, such as Reddit, into multi-turn dialogues. Our methods are generalizable to any forum, enabling us to generate a vast amount of dialogues on diverse topics for pretraining language models. Four methods are introduced: Greedy_Baseline, Greedy_Advanced, Beam Search, and Threading, which are applied to posts from ten subreddits and evaluated. Each method shows a noticeable improvement over its predecessor, with the best method demonstrating a 36.3% improvement in appropriateness over the baseline. Our best method is used to create a corpus of 10,098 dialogues (3.3M tokens) from ten subreddits, 570 of which are compared to dialogues from three other datasets: Blended Skill Talk, Daily Dialogue, and Topical Chat. Our dialogues are found to be more engaging, but slightly less natural than the dialogues in the other datasets, while costing a fraction of the human labor and money required to generate the other datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to create a large multi-turn dialogue corpus from Reddit, which has the potential to advance neural dialogue systems.

text: Neural machine translation has achieved great success in bilingual settings, as well as in multilingual settings. With the increase of the number of languages, multilingual systems tend to underperform their bilingual counterparts. Model capacity has been found crucial for massively multilingual NMT to support language pairs with varying typological characteristics. Previous work increases the modeling capacity by deepening or widening the Transformer. However, modeling cardinality based on aggregating a set of transformations with the same topology has been proven more effective than going deeper or wider when increasing capacity. In this paper, we propose to efficiently increase the capacity for multilingual NMT by increasing the cardinality. Unlike previous work which feeds the same input to several transformations and merges their outputs into one, we present a Multi-Input-Multi-Output (MIMO) architecture that allows each transformation of the block to have its own input. We also present a task-aware attention mechanism to learn to selectively utilize individual transformations from a set of transformations for different translation directions. Our model surpasses previous work and establishes a new state-of-the-art on the large scale OPUS-100 corpus while being 1.31 times as fast.

label: acl
text: Neural machine translation (NMT) has been highly successful in both bilingual and multilingual settings. However, as the number of languages increases, multilingual NMT systems tend to underperform compared to bilingual systems. Model capacity is crucial for massively multilingual NMT to support language pairs with varying typological characteristics. Previous work has attempted to increase capacity by either deepening or widening the Transformer model. However, it has been found that increasing the cardinality (i.e., aggregating a set of transformations with the same topology) is more effective than going deeper or wider. In this paper, we propose an efficient way to increase the capacity of multilingual NMT by increasing the cardinality. Our Multi-Input-Multi-Output (MIMO) architecture allows each transformation of the block to have its own input, unlike previous work that feeds the same input to multiple transformations and merges their outputs. Additionally, we present a task-aware attention mechanism to selectively utilize individual transformations for different translation directions. Our model outperforms previous work and sets a new state-of-the-art on the large-scale OPUS-100 corpus while being 1.31 times faster.

label: acl
text: Small perturbations in the input can severely distort intermediate representations and thus impact translation quality of neural machine translation (NMT) models. In this paper, we propose to improve the robustness of NMT models with adversarial stability training. The basic idea is to make both the encoder and decoder in NMT models robust against input perturbations by enabling them to behave similarly for the original input and its perturbed counterpart. Experimental results on Chinese-English, English-German and English-French translation tasks show that our approaches can not only achieve significant improvements over strong NMT systems but also improve the robustness of NMT models.

label: acl
text: Small disruptions in the input can drastically affect the quality of intermediate representations in neural machine translation (NMT) models, leading to a decline in translation quality. To enhance the robustness of NMT models, we present a novel approach of adversarial stability training. Our method aims to make both the encoder and decoder in NMT models resilient against input disruptions by ensuring that they respond similarly to both the original input and its perturbed counterpart. Our experiments on Chinese-English, English-German, and English-French translation tasks demonstrate that our approach not only outperforms strong NMT systems but also enhances the robustness of NMT models.

label: coling
text: Large scale knowledge graphs (KGs) such as Freebase are generally incomplete. Reasoning over multi-hop (mh) KG paths is thus an important capability that is needed for question answering or other NLP tasks that require knowledge about the world. mh-KG reasoning includes diverse scenarios, e.g., given a head entity and a relation path, predict the tail entity; or given two entities connected by some relation paths, predict the unknown relation between them. We present ROPs, recurrent one-hop predictors, that predict entities at each step of mh-KB paths by using recurrent neural networks and vector representations of entities and relations, with two benefits: (i) modeling mh-paths of arbitrary lengths while updating the entity and relation representations by the training signal at each step; (ii) handling different types of mh-KG reasoning in a unified framework. Our models show state-of-the-art for two important multi-hop KG reasoning tasks: Knowledge Base Completion and Path Query Answering.

text: Large-scale knowledge graphs (KGs) such as Freebase are often incomplete. As a result, reasoning over multi-hop (mh) KG paths is a crucial capability that is necessary for question answering or other NLP tasks that require knowledge about the world. mh-KG reasoning encompasses a wide range of scenarios, including predicting the tail entity given a head entity and a relation path, or predicting the unknown relation between two entities connected by some relation paths. We introduce ROPs, or recurrent one-hop predictors, which predict entities at each step of mh-KB paths by using recurrent neural networks and vector representations of entities and relations. This approach has two key benefits: (i) it allows for modeling mh-paths of varying lengths while updating the entity and relation representations with each step, and (ii) it provides a unified framework for handling different types of mh-KG reasoning. Our models demonstrate state-of-the-art performance for two important multi-hop KG reasoning tasks: Knowledge Base Completion and Path Query Answering.

text: This work deals with SciTail, a natural entailment challenge derived from a multi-choice question answering problem. The premises and hypotheses in SciTail were generated with no awareness of each other, and did not specifically aim at the entailment task. This makes it more challenging than other entailment data sets and more directly useful to the end-task – question answering. We propose DEISTE (deep explorations of inter-sentence interactions for textual entailment) for this entailment task. Given word-to-word interactions between the premise-hypothesis pair (P, H), DEISTE consists of: (i) a parameter-dynamic convolution to make important words in P and H play a dominant role in learnt representations; and (ii) a position-aware attentive convolution to encode the representation and position information of the aligned word pairs. Experiments show that DEISTE gets C-C-C5% improvement over prior state of the art and that the pretrained DEISTE on SciTail generalizes well on RTE-5.
