text: We propose a sketch-based two-step neural model for generating structured queries (SQL) based on a user's request in natural language. The sketch is obtained by using placeholders for specific entities in the SQL query, such as column names, table names, aliases and variables, in a process similar to semantic parsing. The first step is to apply a sequence-to-sequence (SEQ2SEQ) model to determine the most probable SQL sketch based on the request in natural language. Then, a second network designed as a dual-encoder SEQ2SEQ model using both the text query and the previously obtained sketch is employed to generate the final SQL query. Our approach shows improvements over previous approaches on two recent large datasets (WikiSQL and SENLIDB) suitable for data-driven solutions for natural language interfaces for databases.

label: coling
text: We present a two-step neural model for generating structured queries (SQL) based on a user's request in natural language. The model starts by using placeholders to obtain a sketch of the SQL query, which includes specific entities such as column names, table names, aliases, and variables. This process is similar to semantic parsing. The first step uses a sequence-to-sequence (SEQ2SEQ) model to determine the most probable SQL sketch based on the natural language request. In the second step, a dual-encoder SEQ2SEQ model, which utilizes both the text query and the obtained sketch, is employed to generate the final SQL query. Our approach demonstrates improved performance on two large datasets (WikiSQL and SENLIDB) suitable for natural language interfaces for databases.

label: acl
text: Class-based language models (LMs) have been long devised to address context sparsity in C-C-C-gram LMs. In this study, we revisit this approach in the context of neural LMs. We hypothesize that class-based prediction leads to an implicit context aggregation for similar words and thus can improve generalization for rare words. We map words that have a common WordNet hypernym to the same class and train large neural LMs by gradually annealing from predicting the class to token prediction during training. Empirically, this curriculum learning strategy consistently improves perplexity over various large, highly-performant state-of-the-art Transformer-based models on two datasets, WikiText-103 and ARXIV. Our analysis shows that the performance improvement is achieved without sacrificing performance on rare words. Finally, we document other attempts that failed to yield empirical gains, and discuss future directions for the adoption of class-based LMs on a larger scale.

label: acl
text: Class-based language models (LMs) have been used for a long time to address the issue of context sparsity in N-gram LMs. In this study, we re-examine this approach in the context of neural LMs. Our hypothesis is that class-based prediction leads to implicit context aggregation for similar words, thus improving generalization for rare words. We map words with common WordNet hypernyms to the same class and train large neural LMs by gradually transitioning from class prediction to token prediction during training. Our results show that this curriculum learning strategy consistently improves perplexity on two datasets, WikiText-103 and ARXIV, when compared to various state-of-the-art Transformer-based models. Our analysis indicates that the improvement in performance is achieved without sacrificing performance on rare words. We also discuss other attempts that failed to produce empirical gains and outline potential future directions for the widespread adoption of class-based LMs.

label: naacl
text: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a well-known and challenging task that requires systems to jointly reason about natural language and vision. Deep learning models in various forms have been the standard for solving VQA. However, some of these VQA models are better at certain types of image-question pairs than other models. Ensembling VQA models intelligently to leverage their diverse expertise is, therefore, advantageous. Stacking With Auxiliary Features (SWAF) is an intelligent ensembling technique which learns to combine the results of multiple models using features of the current problem as context. We propose four categories of auxiliary features for ensembling for VQA. Three out of the four categories of features can be inferred from an image-question pair and do not require querying the component models. The fourth category of auxiliary features uses model-specific explanations. In this paper, we describe how we use these various categories of auxiliary features to improve performance for VQA. Using SWAF to effectively ensemble three recent systems, we obtain a new state-of-the-art. Our work also highlights the advantages of explainable AI models.

label: naacl
text: The task of Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a well-known and challenging one that requires systems to effectively reason about natural language and vision. Deep learning models have become the standard for solving VQA, but some models are better suited for certain image-question pairs than others. To leverage the strengths of these models, ensembling them intelligently is advantageous. The Stacking With Auxiliary Features (SWAF) technique is an intelligent ensembling approach that combines the results of multiple models using context-based features. In this paper, we propose four categories of auxiliary features for ensembling in VQA, three of which can be inferred from the image-question pair without querying the component models. The fourth category uses model-specific explanations. We show how these various categories of auxiliary features can be used to improve performance in VQA and demonstrate how SWAF can effectively ensemble three recent systems, resulting in a new state-of-the-art. Our work also highlights the benefits of explainable AI models.

label: acl
text: Getting manually labeled data in each domain is always an expensive and a time consuming task. Cross-domain sentiment analysis has emerged as a demanding concept where a labeled source domain facilitates a sentiment classifier for an unlabeled target domain. However, polarity orientation (positive or negative) and the significance of a word to express an opinion often differ from one domain to another domain. Owing to these differences, cross-domain sentiment classification is still a challenging task. In this paper, we propose that words that do not change their polarity and significance represent the transferable (usable) information across domains for cross-domain sentiment classification. We present a novel approach based on χ2 test and cosine-similarity between context vector of words to identify polarity preserving significant words across domains. Furthermore, we show that a weighted ensemble of the classifiers enhances the cross-domain classification performance.

label: acl
text: Getting labeled data in each domain is a costly and time-consuming process. Cross-domain sentiment analysis is a growing field that utilizes a labeled source domain to train a sentiment classifier for an unlabeled target domain. However, the polarity orientation (positive or negative) and the significance of words in expressing opinions can vary greatly between domains. This makes cross-domain sentiment classification a difficult task. Our proposed solution is based on identifying words that maintain their polarity and significance across domains as transferable information. We use a novel approach using the χ2 test and cosine-similarity between context vectors of words to identify these words. Additionally, we demonstrate that using a weighted ensemble of classifiers can improve cross-domain classification performance.

label: coling
text: In this article, we discuss which text, speech, and image technologies have been developed, and would be feasible to develop, for the approximately 60 Indigenous languages spoken in Canada. In particular, we concentrate on technologies that may be feasible to develop for most or all of these languages, not just those that may be feasible for the few most-resourced of these. We assess past achievements and consider future horizons for Indigenous language transliteration, text prediction, spell-checking, approximate search, machine translation, speech recognition, speaker diarization, speech synthesis, optical character recognition, and computer-aided language learning.

label: coling
text: In this article, we examine the advancements in text, speech, and image technologies that have been developed and could be feasible to create for the 60 Indigenous languages spoken in Canada. Our focus is on technologies that could be feasible for most or all of these languages, not just those that are feasible for the few most-resourced languages. We will review past successes and look towards future possibilities in areas such as Indigenous language transliteration, text prediction, spell-checking, approximate search, machine translation, speech recognition, speaker diarization, speech synthesis, optical character recognition, and computer-assisted language learning.

label: acl
text: A current open question in natural language processing is to what extent language models, which are trained with access only to the form of language, are able to capture the meaning of language. This question is challenging to answer in general, as there is no clear line between meaning and form, but rather meaning constrains form in consistent ways. The goal of this study is to offer insights into a narrower but critical subquestion: Under what conditions should we expect that meaning and form covary sufficiently, such that a language model with access only to form might nonetheless succeed in emulating meaning? Focusing on several formal languages (propositional logic and a set of programming languages), we generate training corpora using a variety of motivated constraints, and measure a distributional language model's ability to differentiate logical symbols (AND, OR, and NOT). Our findings are largely negative: none of our simulated training corpora result in models which definitively differentiate meaningfully different symbols (e.g., AND vs. OR), suggesting a limitation to the types of semantic signals that current models are able to exploit.

label: acl
text: A current open question in NLP is to what extent language models that are trained only with the form of language can capture its meaning. This is a challenging question as there is no clear distinction between meaning and form, as meaning influences form in consistent ways. This study focuses on a critical subquestion: under what conditions should we expect meaning and form to be correlated enough for a language model trained only with form to successfully emulate meaning? The study examines several formal languages (propositional logic and programming languages) by generating training corpora with motivated constraints and measuring the ability of a distributional language model to differentiate between logical symbols (AND, OR, and NOT). Unfortunately, the findings are mostly negative, as none of the simulated training corpora result in models that can differentiate meaningfully different symbols, indicating a limitation in the types of semantic signals that current models can exploit.

label: emnlp
text: Many important entity types in web documents, such as dates, times, email addresses, and course numbers, follow or closely resemble patterns that can be described by Regular Expressions (REs). Due to a vast diversity of web documents and ways in which they are being generated, even seemingly straightforward tasks such as identifying mentions of date in a document become very challenging. It is reasonable to claim that it is impossible to create a RE that is capable of identifying such entities from web documents with perfect precision and recall. Rather than abandoning REs as a go-to approach for entity detection, this paper explores ways to combine the expressive power of REs, ability of deep learning to learn from large data, and human-in-the loop approach into a new integrated framework for entity identification from web data. The framework starts by creating or collecting the existing REs for a particular type of an entity. Those REs are then used over a large document corpus to collect weak labels for the entity mentions and a neural network is trained to predict those RE-generated weak labels. Finally, a human expert is asked to label a small set of documents and the neural network is fine tuned on those documents. The experimental evaluation on several entity identification problems shows that the proposed framework achieves impressive accuracy, while requiring very modest human effort.

label: emnlp
text: Many important entity types in web documents, such as dates, times, email addresses, and course numbers, are structured in ways that can be described using Regular Expressions (REs). However, the diversity of web documents and the various methods used to generate them make identifying entities like dates a challenging task. It is unrealistic to expect that a single RE could accurately identify all entity mentions in web documents with perfect precision and recall. This paper presents a new framework for entity identification from web data that combines the power of REs, the learning capabilities of deep learning, and a human-in-the-loop approach. The framework starts by collecting existing REs for a specific entity type or creating new ones. These REs are then applied to a large document corpus to generate weak labels for entity mentions, which are used to train a neural network. Finally, a human expert labels a small set of documents, which are used to fine-tune the network. The results of several entity identification experiments show that this framework provides impressive accuracy with minimal human effort.

label: acl
text: Recent studies on neural networks with pre-trained weights (i.e., BERT) have mainly focused on a low-dimensional subspace, where the embedding vectors computed from input words (or their contexts) are located. In this work, we propose a new approach, called OoMMix, to finding and regularizing the remainder of the space, referred to as out-of-manifold, which cannot be accessed through the words. Specifically, we synthesize the out-of-manifold embeddings based on two embeddings obtained from actually-observed words, to utilize them for fine-tuning the network. A discriminator is trained to detect whether an input embedding is located inside the manifold or not, and simultaneously, a generator is optimized to produce new embeddings that can be easily identified as out-of-manifold by the discriminator. These two modules successfully collaborate in a unified and end-to-end manner for regularizing the out-of-manifold. Our extensive evaluation on various text classification benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, as well as its good compatibility with existing data augmentation techniques which aim to enhance the manifold.

label: acl
text: Recent studies on neural networks with pre-trained weights, such as BERT, have mainly focused on the low-dimensional subspace where the input word embeddings are located. In this work, we propose a new approach, called OoMMix, to finding and regularizing the out-of-manifold, the remaining space that cannot be accessed through the words. Our approach synthesizes the out-of-manifold embeddings by combining two embeddings obtained from actual words, and uses them for fine-tuning the network. A discriminator is trained to differentiate between embeddings in the manifold and those that are out-of-manifold, while a generator produces new embeddings that are easily identified as out-of-manifold by the discriminator. These two modules work together in a unified and end-to-end manner to regularize the out-of-manifold. Our results from various text classification benchmarks show the effectiveness of our approach and its compatibility with existing data augmentation techniques that enhance the manifold.

label: emnlp
text: Extracting typed entity mentions from text is a fundamental component to language understanding and reasoning. While there exist substantial labeled text datasets for multiple subsets of biomedical entity types—such as genes and proteins, or chemicals and diseases—it is rare to find large labeled datasets containing labels for all desired entity types together. This paper presents a method for training a single CRF extractor from multiple datasets with disjoint or partially overlapping sets of entity types. Our approach employs marginal likelihood training to insist on labels that are present in the data, while filling in “missing labels”. This allows us to leverage all the available data within a single model. In experimental results on the Biocreative V CDR (chemicals/diseases), Biocreative VI ChemProt (chemicals/proteins) and MedMentions (19 entity types) datasets, we show that joint training on multiple datasets improves NER F1 over training in isolation, and our methods achieve state-of-the-art results.

label: emnlp
text: Extracting typed entity mentions from text is a critical aspect of language comprehension and reasoning. While there are numerous labeled text datasets for specific biomedical entity types, such as genes, proteins, chemicals, and diseases, finding large datasets with labels for all desired entity types is rare. This paper presents a novel approach for training a single CRF extractor from multiple datasets with disjoint or partially overlapping entity types. Our method uses marginal likelihood training to prioritize existing labels and fill in "missing labels." This allows us to utilize all available data within a single model. Our experimental results on the Biocreative V CDR, Biocreative VI ChemProt, and MedMentions datasets show that joint training on multiple datasets leads to improved NER F1 compared to training in isolation and achieves state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: We propose a novel data-augmentation technique for neural machine translation based on ROT-C-C-C ciphertexts. ROT-D-D-D is a simple letter substitution cipher that replaces a letter in the plaintext with the E-E-Eth letter after it in the alphabet. We first generate multiple ROT-F-F-F ciphertexts using different values of G-G-G for the plaintext which is the source side of the parallel data. We then leverage this enciphered training data along with the original parallel data via multi-source training to improve neural machine translation. Our method, CipherDAug, uses a co-regularization-inspired training procedure, requires no external data sources other than the original training data, and uses a standard Transformer to outperform strong data augmentation techniques on several datasets by a significant margin. This technique combines easily with existing approaches to data augmentation, and yields particularly strong results in low-resource settings.

label: acl
text: We propose a novel data augmentation technique for neural machine translation based on the ROT-C-C-C ciphertext. The ROT-D-D-D cipher is a simple letter substitution method that replaces a letter in the plaintext with the next letter in the alphabet. To generate multiple ROT-F-F-F ciphertexts, we use different values of G-G-G for the plaintext, which is the source side of the parallel data. By combining this encrypted training data with the original parallel data, we improve neural machine translation through multi-source training. Our technique, CipherDAug, uses a co-regularization-inspired training procedure and requires no external data sources other than the original training data. It outperforms strong data augmentation techniques on several datasets by a significant margin, using a standard Transformer. This technique can easily be combined with existing data augmentation approaches and yields particularly strong results in low-resource settings.

label: coling
text: Fine-grained entity typing (FET) aims to deduce specific semantic types of the entity mentions in the text. Modern methods for FET mainly focus on learning what a certain type looks like. And few works directly model the type differences, that is, let models know the extent that which one type is different from others. To alleviate this problem, we propose a type-enriched hierarchical contrastive strategy for FET. Our method can directly model the differences between hierarchical types and improve the ability to distinguish multi-grained similar types. On the one hand, we embed type into entity contexts to make type information directly perceptible. On the other hand, we design a constrained contrastive strategy on the hierarchical structure to directly model the type differences, which can simultaneously perceive the distinguishability between types at different granularity. Experimental results on three benchmarks, BBN, OntoNotes, and FIGER show that our method achieves significant performance on FET by effectively modeling type differences.

label: coling
text: Fine-grained entity typing (FET) aims to deduce the specific semantic types of entity mentions in text. Modern methods for FET mainly focus on learning what a certain type looks like, with few works directly modeling the differences between types. To address this issue, we propose a type-enriched hierarchical contrastive strategy for FET. This method can directly model the differences between hierarchical types, improving the ability to distinguish multi-grained, similar types. We embed type information directly into entity contexts and design a constrained contrastive strategy on the hierarchical structure to directly model type differences, enhancing the ability to perceive the distinguishability between types at different granularities. Our method achieves significant performance on FET, as demonstrated by experimental results on three benchmarks: BBN, OntoNotes, and FIGER.

label: naacl
text: NLP models that process multiple texts often struggle in recognizing corresponding and salient information that is often differently phrased, and consolidating the redundancies across texts. To facilitate research of such challenges, the sentence fusion task was proposed, yet previous datasets for this task were very limited in their size and scope. In this paper, we revisit and substantially extend previous dataset creation efforts. With careful modifications, relabeling, and employing complementing data sources, we were able to more than triple the size of a notable earlier dataset.Moreover, we show that our extended version uses more representative texts for multi-document tasks and provides a more diverse training set, which substantially improves model performance.

label: naacl
text: NLP models that process multiple texts often face difficulties in recognizing relevant information that is phrased differently across texts and consolidating redundant information. To address these challenges, the sentence fusion task was introduced, but previous datasets for this task were limited in size and scope. In this paper, we revisit and significantly expand previous dataset creation efforts. By making careful modifications, relabeling, and incorporating complementary data sources, we were able to increase the size of a notable earlier dataset by more than three times. Furthermore, our extended version features more representative texts for multi-document tasks and provides a more diverse training set, resulting in substantial improvements in model performance.

label: acl
text: In this work, we demonstrate that the contextualized word vectors derived from pretrained masked language model-based encoders share a common, perhaps undesirable pattern across layers. Namely, we find cases of persistent outlier neurons within BERT and RoBERTa's hidden state vectors that consistently bear the smallest or largest values in said vectors. In an attempt to investigate the source of this information, we introduce a neuron-level analysis method, which reveals that the outliers are closely related to information captured by positional embeddings. We also pre-train the RoBERTa-base models from scratch and find that the outliers disappear without using positional embeddings. These outliers, we find, are the major cause of anisotropy of encoders' raw vector spaces, and clipping them leads to increased similarity across vectors. We demonstrate this in practice by showing that clipped vectors can more accurately distinguish word senses, as well as lead to better sentence embeddings when mean pooling. In three supervised tasks, we find that clipping does not affect the performance.

label: acl
text: The present study reveals that the contextualized word vectors generated from pre-trained masked language model-based encoders exhibit a common pattern across layers. This pattern is characterized by the presence of persistent outlier neurons in the hidden state vectors of BERT and RoBERTa, which consistently exhibit the smallest or largest values. To understand the source of this information, we propose a neuron-level analysis method that shows that these outliers are closely related to the information captured by positional embeddings. Our findings indicate that pre-training RoBERTa-base models from scratch eliminates the outliers, which are the primary cause of anisotropy in the raw vector spaces of the encoders. Clipping these outliers leads to increased similarity across vectors, which can improve the accuracy of word sense differentiation and sentence embeddings obtained through mean pooling. Our results also demonstrate that clipping does not negatively impact the performance of the encoders in three supervised tasks.

label: naacl
text: Pretrained language models have significantly improved the performance of downstream language understanding tasks, including extractive question answering, by providing high-quality contextualized word embeddings. However, training question answering models still requires large amounts of annotated data for specific domains. In this work, we propose a cooperative self-training framework, RGX, for automatically generating more non-trivial question-answer pairs to improve model performance. RGX is built upon a masked answer extraction task with an interactive learning environment containing an answer entity Recognizer, a question Generator, and an answer eXtractor. Given a passage with a masked entity, the generator generates a question around the entity, and the extractor is trained to extract the masked entity with the generated question and raw texts. The framework allows the training of question generation and answering models on any text corpora without annotation. We further leverage a self-training technique to improve the performance of both question generation and answer extraction models. Experiment results show that RGX outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) pretrained language models and transfer learning approaches on standard question-answering benchmarks, and yields the new SOTA performance under given model size and transfer learning settings.

label: naacl
text: Pretrained language models have significantly improved the performance of downstream language understanding tasks, such as extractive question answering, by providing high-quality contextualized word embeddings. However, training question answering models still requires large amounts of annotated data for specific domains. To address this challenge, we propose RGX, a cooperative self-training framework for automatically generating more non-trivial question-answer pairs to enhance model performance. RGX is comprised of an answer entity Recognizer, a question Generator, and an answer eXtractor. It operates within an interactive learning environment, where a masked answer extraction task is performed. Given a passage with a masked entity, the generator creates a question around the entity, and the extractor is trained to extract the masked entity using the generated question and raw texts. This framework enables the training of question generation and answering models on any text corpus without the need for annotation. Additionally, we leverage a self-training technique to further improve the performance of both question generation and answer extraction models. Our experiments demonstrate that RGX outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) pretrained language models and transfer learning approaches on standard question-answering benchmarks, achieving new SOTA performance under given model size and transfer learning settings.

label: acl
text: Entity Matching (EM) aims at recognizing entity records that denote the same real-world object. Neural EM models learn vector representation of entity descriptions and match entities end-to-end. Though robust, these methods require many annotated resources for training, and lack of interpretability. In this paper, we propose a novel EM framework that consists of Heterogeneous Information Fusion (HIF) and Key Attribute Tree (KAT) Induction to decouple feature representation from matching decision. Using self-supervised learning and mask mechanism in pre-trained language modeling, HIF learns the embeddings of noisy attribute values by inter-attribute attention with unlabeled data. Using a set of comparison features and a limited amount of annotated data, KAT Induction learns an efficient decision tree that can be interpreted by generating entity matching rules whose structure is advocated by domain experts. Experiments on 6 public datasets and 3 industrial datasets show that our method is highly efficient and outperforms SOTA EM models in most cases. We will release the codes upon acceptance.

label: acl
text: Entity Matching (EM) is a process that aims to identify records that represent the same real-world object. Neural EM models learn to match entities end-to-end by creating vector representations of entity descriptions. However, these methods can be robust, but they require a large amount of annotated data for training and lack interpretability. In this paper, we present a novel EM framework that combines Heterogeneous Information Fusion (HIF) and Key Attribute Tree (KAT) Induction. This framework separates feature representation from matching decisions, making it more interpretable. The HIF component self-supervises the learning of embeddings for noisy attribute values using inter-attribute attention and unlabeled data. The KAT Induction component uses a limited amount of annotated data and a set of comparison features to learn an efficient decision tree that can be interpreted through the generation of entity matching rules. Our experiments on 6 public datasets and 3 industrial datasets show that our method is highly efficient and outperforms state-of-the-art EM models in most cases. The code will be released upon acceptance.

label: acl
text: Increasing the input length has been a driver of progress in language modeling with transformers. We identify conditions where shorter inputs are not harmful, and achieve perplexity and efficiency improvements through two new methods that decrease input length. First, we show that initially training a model on short subsequences before moving on to longer ones both reduces overall training time and, surprisingly, substantially improves perplexity. Second, we show how to improve the efficiency of recurrence methods in transformers, which let models condition on previously processed tokens when generating sequences that exceed the maximal length the transformer can handle at once. Existing methods require computationally expensive relative position embeddings; we introduce a simple alternative of adding absolute position embeddings to queries and keys instead of to word embeddings, which efficiently produces superior results. We show that these recurrent models also benefit from short input lengths. Combining these techniques speeds up training by a factor of 1.65, reduces memory usage, and substantially improves perplexity on WikiText-103, without adding any parameters.

label: acl
text: The progress in language modeling with transformers has been driven by increasing the input length. However, we have identified conditions where shorter inputs do not harm the model and can even improve its performance. To achieve this, we have developed two new methods that decrease input length. Firstly, we have found that training the model on short subsequences before moving on to longer ones not only reduces the overall training time but also improves the perplexity. Secondly, we have improved the efficiency of recurrence methods in transformers by introducing a simple alternative of adding absolute position embeddings to queries and keys instead of to word embeddings. This efficient method has produced superior results compared to existing methods that require computationally expensive relative position embeddings. Additionally, we have found that these recurrent models also benefit from shorter input lengths. By combining these techniques, we have been able to speed up the training process by a factor of 1.65, reduce memory usage, and significantly improve perplexity on WikiText-103, without adding any parameters.

label: acl
text: We explore story generation: creative systems that can build coherent and fluent passages of text about a topic. We collect a large dataset of 300K human-written stories paired with writing prompts from an online forum. Our dataset enables hierarchical story generation, where the model first generates a premise, and then transforms it into a passage of text. We gain further improvements with a novel form of model fusion that improves the relevance of the story to the prompt, and adding a new gated multi-scale self-attention mechanism to model long-range context. Experiments show large improvements over strong baselines on both automated and human evaluations. Human judges prefer stories generated by our approach to those from a strong non-hierarchical model by a factor of two to one.

label: acl
text: We investigate the field of story generation by examining creative systems that produce coherent and articulate passages of text about a given topic. To support this research, we have compiled a large database of 300,000 human-written stories, each paired with a writing prompt from an online forum. Our database enables the development of a hierarchical story generation model that first generates a premise and then transforms it into a written passage. We further enhance the model's performance by incorporating a novel form of model fusion that enhances the relevance of the story to the prompt, as well as a new gated multi-scale self-attention mechanism that better models long-range context. Our experiments demonstrate significant improvements over established baselines, as determined by both automated and human evaluations. In fact, human judges prefer the stories generated by our approach to those generated by a strong non-hierarchical model by a margin of two to one.

label: acl
text: In data-to-text (D2T) generation, training on in-domain data leads to overfitting to the data representation and repeating training data noise. We examine how to avoid finetuning pretrained language models (PLMs) on D2T generation datasets while still taking advantage of surface realization capabilities of PLMs. Inspired by pipeline approaches, we propose to generate text by transforming single-item descriptions with a sequence of modules trained on general-domain text-based operations: ordering, aggregation, and paragraph compression. We train PLMs for performing these operations on a synthetic corpus WikiFluent which we build from English Wikipedia. Our experiments on two major triple-to-text datasets—WebNLG and E2E—show that our approach enables D2T generation from RDF triples in zero-shot settings.

label: acl
text: In data-to-text generation, training on in-domain data can result in overfitting to the data representation and repeating training data noise. To avoid this, we explore how to use pretrained language models (PLMs) without finetuning them on data-to-text generation datasets while still leveraging their surface realization capabilities. Our approach, inspired by pipeline methods, involves transforming single-item descriptions through a series of modules trained on general-domain text-based operations, such as ordering, aggregation, and paragraph compression. We train PLMs on a synthetic corpus, WikiFluent, which we created from English Wikipedia, to perform these operations. Our experiments on two major triple-to-text datasets, WebNLG and E2E, demonstrate that our approach enables data-to-text generation from RDF triples in zero-shot settings.

label: naacl
text: One of the difficulties of neural machine translation (NMT) is the recall and appropriate translation of low-frequency words or phrases. In this paper, we propose a simple, fast, and effective method for recalling previously seen translation examples and incorporating them into the NMT decoding process. Specifically, for an input sentence, we use a search engine to retrieve sentence pairs whose source sides are similar with the input sentence, and then collect n-grams that are both in the retrieved target sentences and aligned with words that match in the source sentences, which we call “translation pieces”. We compute pseudo-probabilities for each retrieved sentence based on similarities between the input sentence and the retrieved source sentences, and use these to weight the retrieved translation pieces. Finally, an existing NMT model is used to translate the input sentence, with an additional bonus given to outputs that contain the collected translation pieces. We show our method improves NMT translation results up to 6 BLEU points on three narrow domain translation tasks where repetitiveness of the target sentences is particularly salient. It also causes little increase in the translation time, and compares favorably to another alternative retrieval-based method with respect to accuracy, speed, and simplicity of implementation.

label: naacl
text: One of the challenges in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is the recall and proper translation of low-frequency words or phrases. To address this, we propose a fast and effective method for recalling previously seen translations and incorporating them into the NMT decoding process. Our method uses a search engine to retrieve sentence pairs with similar source sides to the input sentence. We then collect n-grams that are both in the retrieved target sentences and aligned with matching words in the source sentences, which we refer to as "translation pieces." We compute pseudo-probabilities for each retrieved sentence based on the similarities between the input sentence and the retrieved source sentences, and use these to weight the retrieved translation pieces. The existing NMT model is then used to translate the input sentence, with an additional bonus given to outputs that contain the collected translation pieces. Our method improves NMT translation results by up to 6 BLEU points on three narrow domain translation tasks where repetitiveness of the target sentences is particularly pronounced. It also results in little increase in translation time, and compares favorably to an alternative retrieval-based method in terms of accuracy, speed, and ease of implementation.

label: naacl
text: Visual Question Answering (VQA) has benefited from increasingly sophisticated models, but has not enjoyed the same level of engagement in terms of data creation. In this paper, we propose a method that automatically derives VQA examples at volume, by leveraging the abundance of existing image-caption annotations combined with neural models for textual question generation. We show that the resulting data is of high-quality. VQA models trained on our data improve state-of-the-art zero-shot accuracy by double digits and achieve a level of robustness that lacks in the same model trained on human-annotated VQA data.

label: naacl
text: Visual Question Answering (VQA) has seen advancements in model sophistication, however, data creation has not received the same level of attention. To address this issue, we present a method that generates VQA examples in large quantities by utilizing the abundance of image-caption annotations and neural models for textual question generation. Our results demonstrate that the generated data is of high quality, leading to improved zero-shot accuracy by double digits and robustness compared to models trained on human-annotated VQA data.

label: naacl
text: Deep learning for Information Retrieval (IR) requires a large amount of high-quality query-document relevance labels, but such labels are inherently sparse. Label smoothing redistributes some observed probability mass over unobserved instances, often uniformly, uninformed of the true distribution. In contrast, we propose knowledge distillation for informed labeling, without incurring high computation overheads at evaluation time. Our contribution is designing a simple but efficient teacher model which utilizes collective knowledge, to outperform state-of-the-arts distilled from a more complex teacher model. Specifically, we train up to C-C-C faster than the state-of-the-art teacher, while distilling the rankings better. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jihyukkim-nlp/CollectiveKD.

label: naacl
text: Deep learning for Information Retrieval (IR) requires a significant amount of high-quality query-document relevance labels, however, these labels are naturally scarce. Label smoothing redistributes some of the observed probability mass over unseen instances, often evenly, without considering the true distribution. In contrast, we propose a knowledge distillation approach for informed labeling that does not result in high computational overhead during evaluation. Our innovation involves the design of a simple yet effective teacher model that leverages collective knowledge, outperforming state-of-the-art models distilled from more complex teacher models. Specifically, we train up to three times faster than the state-of-the-art teacher, while still achieving better rankings. Our code is freely accessible at https://github.com/jihyukkim-nlp/CollectiveKD.

label: acl
text: We present a human-and-model-in-the-loop process for dynamically generating datasets and training better performing and more robust hate detection models. We provide a new dataset of 40,000 entries, generated and labelled by trained annotators over four rounds of dynamic data creation. It includes 15,000 challenging perturbations and each hateful entry has fine-grained labels for the type and target of hate. Hateful entries make up 54% of the dataset, which is substantially higher than comparable datasets. We show that model performance is substantially improved using this approach. Models trained on later rounds of data collection perform better on test sets and are harder for annotators to trick. They also have better performance on HateCheck, a suite of functional tests for online hate detection. We provide the code, dataset and annotation guidelines for other researchers to use.

label: acl
text: We present a human-and-model-in-the-loop process for dynamically generating datasets and training more robust and better-performing hate detection models. Our process involves the creation of a new dataset of 40,000 entries, which was generated and labeled by trained annotators over four rounds of dynamic data creation. The dataset includes 15,000 challenging perturbations and fine-grained labels for the type and target of hate. With hateful entries making up 54% of the dataset, which is significantly higher than comparable datasets, our approach demonstrates substantial improvement in model performance. Models trained on later rounds of data collection perform better on test sets and are harder for annotators to trick, and they also exhibit better performance on HateCheck, a suite of functional tests for online hate detection. We provide the code, dataset, and annotation guidelines for other researchers to use.

label: acl
text: Unsupervised machine translation - i.e., not assuming any cross-lingual supervision signal, whether a dictionary, translations, or comparable corpora - seems impossible, but nevertheless, Lample et al. (2017) recently proposed a fully unsupervised machine translation (MT) model. The model relies heavily on an adversarial, unsupervised cross-lingual word embedding technique for bilingual dictionary induction (Conneau et al., 2017), which we examine here. Our results identify the limitations of current unsupervised MT: unsupervised bilingual dictionary induction performs much worse on morphologically rich languages that are not dependent marking, when monolingual corpora from different domains or different embedding algorithms are used. We show that a simple trick, exploiting a weak supervision signal from identical words, enables more robust induction and establish a near-perfect correlation between unsupervised bilingual dictionary induction performance and a previously unexplored graph similarity metric.

label: acl
text: Unsupervised machine translation, which does not rely on any cross-lingual supervision signal such as dictionaries, translations, or comparable corpora, is considered to be an impossible task. However, Lample et al. (2017) proposed a fully unsupervised machine translation (MT) model that heavily relies on adversarial unsupervised cross-lingual word embedding technique for bilingual dictionary induction (Conneau et al., 2017). In this study, we examine the limitations of the current unsupervised MT model. Our findings reveal that unsupervised bilingual dictionary induction performs poorly on morphologically rich languages that are not dependent marking, particularly when monolingual corpora from different domains or different embedding algorithms are used. However, we also show that a simple trick that exploits a weak supervision signal from identical words can lead to more robust induction. Furthermore, we establish a near-perfect correlation between unsupervised bilingual dictionary induction performance and a previously unexplored graph similarity metric.

label: acl
text: Language exhibits hierarchical structure, but recent work using a subject-verb agreement diagnostic argued that state-of-the-art language models, LSTMs, fail to learn long-range syntax sensitive dependencies. Using the same diagnostic, we show that, in fact, LSTMs do succeed in learning such dependencies—provided they have enough capacity. We then explore whether models that have access to explicit syntactic information learn agreement more effectively, and how the way in which this structural information is incorporated into the model impacts performance. We find that the mere presence of syntactic information does not improve accuracy, but when model architecture is determined by syntax, number agreement is improved. Further, we find that the choice of how syntactic structure is built affects how well number agreement is learned: top-down construction outperforms left-corner and bottom-up variants in capturing non-local structural dependencies.

label: acl
text: Language has a hierarchical structure, but recent research using a subject-verb agreement diagnostic suggests that state-of-the-art language models, LSTMs, struggle to learn long-range syntax-sensitive dependencies. However, our results using the same diagnostic show that LSTMs can learn such dependencies if they have enough capacity. We then examine whether models with access to explicit syntactic information learn agreement better and how the incorporation of this information affects performance. Our findings indicate that the mere presence of syntactic information does not improve accuracy, but when the model architecture is based on syntax, number agreement performance improves. Additionally, we discovered that the way in which syntactic structure is built affects the learning of number agreement, with top-down construction outperforming left-corner and bottom-up variants in capturing non-local structural dependencies.

text: This paper is an initial study on multi-task and multi-lingual joint learning for lexical utterance classification. A major problem in constructing lexical utterance classification modules for spoken dialogue systems is that individual data resources are often limited or unbalanced among tasks and/or languages. Various studies have examined joint learning using neural-network based shared modeling; however, previous joint learning studies focused on either cross-task or cross-lingual knowledge transfer. In order to simultaneously support both multi-task and multi-lingual joint learning, our idea is to explicitly divide state-of-the-art neural lexical utterance classification into language-specific components that can be shared between different tasks and task-specific components that can be shared between different languages. In addition, in order to effectively transfer knowledge between different task data sets and different language data sets, this paper proposes a partially-shared modeling method that possesses both shared components and components specific to individual data sets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed method using Japanese and English data sets with three different lexical utterance classification tasks.

label: coling
text: This paper presents an initial study on multi-task and multi-lingual joint learning for lexical utterance classification. One of the major challenges in constructing lexical utterance classification modules for spoken dialogue systems is the limited or unbalanced data resources among tasks and languages. Previous studies have explored joint learning using neural-network-based shared modeling, but they have only focused on either cross-task or cross-lingual knowledge transfer. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a partially-shared modeling method that divides state-of-the-art neural lexical utterance classification into language-specific and task-specific components, allowing for simultaneous multi-task and multi-lingual joint learning. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated using Japanese and English data sets with three different lexical utterance classification tasks.

label: coling
text: Question-Answer (QA) matching is a fundamental task in the Natural Language Processing community. In this paper, we first build a novel QA matching corpus with informal text which is collected from a product reviewing website. Then, we propose a novel QA matching approach, namely One vs. Many Matching, which aims to address the novel scenario where one question sentence often has an answer with multiple sentences. Furthermore, we improve our matching approach by employing both word-level and sentence-level attentions for solving the noisy problem in the informal text. Empirical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach to question-answer matching.

label: coling
text: Question-Answer matching is a crucial task in the field of Natural Language Processing. In this study, we introduce a new QA matching corpus that consists of informal text collected from a product review website. Our proposed approach, called One vs. Many Matching, addresses the unique challenge of matching a single question with multiple answer sentences. To improve accuracy, our approach incorporates both word-level and sentence-level attention mechanisms to address the issue of noise in informal text. Our results show that the proposed approach is highly effective in QA matching.

label: emnlp
text: Answering complex questions that involve multiple entities and multiple relations using a standard knowledge base is an open and challenging task. Most existing KBQA approaches focus on simpler questions and do not work very well on complex questions because they were not able to simultaneously represent the question and the corresponding complex query structure. In this work, we encode such complex query structure into a uniform vector representation, and thus successfully capture the interactions between individual semantic components within a complex question. This approach consistently outperforms existing methods on complex questions while staying competitive on simple questions.

label: emnlp
text: Answering complex questions that involve multiple entities and multiple relationships can be a difficult and unresolved task using a standard knowledge base. Most current KBQA methods concentrate on simpler questions and are not effective in handling complex questions as they are unable to represent both the question and the complicated query structure simultaneously. In this research, we transform the complex query structure into a uniform vector representation, enabling us to capture the interactions between the semantic components within the complex question. Our approach outperforms existing methods in handling complex questions while maintaining competitiveness in answering simple questions.

label: coling
text: Target-oriented multimodal sentiment classification (TMSC) is a new subtask of aspect-based sentiment analysis, which aims to determine the sentiment polarity of the opinion target mentioned in a (sentence, image) pair. Recently, dominant works employ the attention mechanism to capture the corresponding visual representations of the opinion target, and then aggregate them as evidence to make sentiment predictions. However, they still suffer from two problems: (1) The granularity of the opinion target in two modalities is inconsistent, which causes visual attention sometimes fail to capture the corresponding visual representations of the target; (2) Even though it is captured, there are still significant differences between the visual representations expressing the same mood, which brings great difficulty to sentiment prediction. To this end, we propose a novel Knowledge-enhanced Framework (KEF) in this paper, which can successfully exploit adjective-noun pairs extracted from the image to improve the visual attention capability and sentiment prediction capability of the TMSC task. Extensive experimental results show that our framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art works on two public datasets.

label: coling
text: The Target-oriented Multimodal Sentiment Classification (TMSC) task is a new aspect-based sentiment analysis subtask that aims to determine the sentiment polarity of the opinion target mentioned in a (sentence, image) pair. The dominant works in this area use attention mechanisms to capture the visual representations of the target and aggregate them as evidence for sentiment predictions. However, these works still face two challenges: (1) the granularity of the opinion target in the two modalities is inconsistent, which can cause the visual attention to fail to capture the target's visual representations; and (2) even if the representation is captured, there can still be significant differences between the visual representations expressing the same mood, making sentiment prediction difficult. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Knowledge-enhanced Framework (KEF) that leverages adjective-noun pairs extracted from the image to improve the TMSC task's visual attention and sentiment prediction capabilities. Our extensive experimental results show that our framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art works on two public datasets.

label: acl
text: Datasets with induced emotion labels are scarce but of utmost importance for many NLP tasks. We present a new, automated method for collecting texts along with their induced reaction labels. The method exploits the online use of reaction GIFs, which capture complex affective states. We show how to augment the data with induced emotion and induced sentiment labels. We use our method to create and publish ReactionGIF, a first-of-its-kind affective dataset of 30K tweets. We provide baselines for three new tasks, including induced sentiment prediction and multilabel classification of induced emotions. Our method and dataset open new research opportunities in emotion detection and affective computing.

label: acl
text: Datasets with emotion labels that have been induced are rare, but they are of critical importance for many NLP applications. We introduce a new, automated approach for collecting texts and their corresponding induced reaction labels. This method leverages the online use of reaction GIFs, which effectively capture complex emotional states. Our approach also involves augmenting the data with induced emotion and sentiment labels. As a result, we have created and published ReactionGIF, a groundbreaking affective dataset of 30,000 tweets, which is the first of its kind. Our study provides baseline results for three novel tasks, including induced sentiment prediction and multi-label classification of induced emotions. Our method and dataset provide new opportunities for research in the field of emotion detection and affective computing.

label: emnlp
text: Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging for Twitter has received considerable attention in recent years. Because most POS tagging methods are based on supervised models, they usually require a large amount of labeled data for training. However, the existing labeled datasets for Twitter are much smaller than those for newswire text. Hence, to help POS tagging for Twitter, most domain adaptation methods try to leverage newswire datasets by learning the shared features between the two domains. However, from a linguistic perspective, Twitter users not only tend to mimic the formal expressions of traditional media, like news, but they also appear to be developing linguistically informal styles. Therefore, POS tagging for the formal Twitter context can be learned together with the newswire dataset, while POS tagging for the informal Twitter context should be learned separately. To achieve this task, in this work, we propose a hypernetwork-based method to generate different parameters to separately model contexts with different expression styles. Experimental results on three different datasets show that our approach achieves better performance than state-of-the-art methods in most cases.

label: emnlp
text: The attention given to Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging for Twitter has increased in recent years. This is due to the fact that most POS tagging methods are based on supervised models, which require a large amount of labeled data for training. However, the available labeled datasets for Twitter are smaller compared to those for newswire text. To overcome this challenge, most domain adaptation methods attempt to leverage newswire datasets by identifying shared features between the two domains. However, from a linguistic perspective, Twitter users often mimic formal expressions from traditional media, but also develop their own informal linguistic styles. Thus, it is important to separately model the formal and informal styles of Twitter context for effective POS tagging. To achieve this, we propose a hypernetwork-based method to generate different parameters for each style, resulting in improved performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Our approach is validated through experiments on three different datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Pseudo relevance feedback (PRF) is commonly used to boost the performance of traditional information retrieval (IR) models by using top-ranked documents to identify and weight new query terms, thereby reducing the effect of query-document vocabulary mismatches. While neural retrieval models have recently demonstrated strong results for ad-hoc retrieval, combining them with PRF is not straightforward due to incompatibilities between existing PRF approaches and neural architectures. To bridge this gap, we propose an end-to-end neural PRF framework that can be used with existing neural IR models by embedding different neural models as building blocks. Extensive experiments on two standard test collections confirm the effectiveness of the proposed NPRF framework in improving the performance of two state-of-the-art neural IR models.

label: emnlp
text: Pseudo relevance feedback (PRF) is a commonly used technique to enhance the performance of traditional information retrieval (IR) models. It does so by using the top-ranked documents to identify and weight new query terms, reducing the impact of vocabulary mismatches between queries and documents. However, incorporating PRF into neural retrieval models is challenging due to incompatibilities between existing PRF approaches and neural architectures. To overcome this challenge, we present an end-to-end neural PRF framework that can be integrated with existing neural IR models by embedding different neural models as building blocks. Our experiments on two standard test collections show the effectiveness of the proposed NPRF framework in improving the performance of two state-of-the-art neural IR models.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we empirically investigate adversarial attack on NMT from two aspects: languages (the source vs. the target language) and positions (front vs. rear). For autoregressive NMT models that generate target words from left to right, we observe that adversarial attack on the source language is more effective than on the target language, and that attacking front positions of target sentences or positions of source sentences aligned to the front positions of corresponding target sentences is more effective than attacking other positions. We further exploit the attention distribution of the victim model to attack source sentences at positions that have a strong association with front target words. Experiment results demonstrate that our attention-based adversarial attack is more effective than adversarial attacks by sampling positions randomly or according to gradients.

label: acl
text: This paper investigates the impact of adversarial attacks on NMT models by considering two factors: language (the source vs. the target language) and position (front vs. rear). Our study focuses on autoregressive NMT models that generate target words in a left-to-right order. Our results show that adversarial attacks on the source language are more effective than those on the target language. Additionally, attacking the front positions of target sentences or the positions of source sentences aligned with the front positions of corresponding target sentences is more effective than attacking other positions. To further enhance the effectiveness of adversarial attacks, we leverage the attention distribution of the victim model to target source sentences at positions with a strong association with front target words. Our experiments demonstrate that our attention-based adversarial attack is more effective than random sampling or gradient-based attacks.

label: emnlp
text: Many existing systems for analyzing and summarizing customer reviews about products or service are based on a number of prominent review aspects. Conventionally, the prominent review aspects of a product type are determined manually. This costly approach cannot scale to large and cross-domain services such as Amazon.com, Taobao.com or Yelp.com where there are a large number of product types and new products emerge almost every day. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, for extracting the most prominent aspects of a given product type from textual reviews. The proposed framework, ExtRA, extracts K most prominent aspect terms or phrases which do not overlap semantically automatically without supervision. Extensive experiments show that ExtRA is effective and achieves the state-of-the-art performance on a dataset consisting of different product types.

label: emnlp
text: Many systems for analyzing and summarizing customer reviews about products or services are based on prominent review aspects. Typically, these aspects are determined manually, but this approach is costly and cannot be scaled to large, cross-domain services like Amazon, Taobao, or Yelp, where there are numerous product types and new products are constantly emerging. In this paper, we present a novel framework, ExtRA, for automatically extracting the most prominent aspects of a given product type from textual reviews. ExtRA extracts the K most prominent aspect terms or phrases without overlap and without supervision. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that ExtRA is effective and achieves state-of-the-art performance on a diverse dataset of product types.

label: coling
text: The 2017 Fake News Challenge Stage 1 (FNC-1) shared task addressed a stance classification task as a crucial first step towards detecting fake news. To date, there is no in-depth analysis paper to critically discuss FNC-1's experimental setup, reproduce the results, and draw conclusions for next-generation stance classification methods. In this paper, we provide such an in-depth analysis for the three top-performing systems. We first find that FNC-1's proposed evaluation metric favors the majority class, which can be easily classified, and thus overestimates the true discriminative power of the methods. Therefore, we propose a new F1-based metric yielding a changed system ranking. Next, we compare the features and architectures used, which leads to a novel feature-rich stacked LSTM model that performs on par with the best systems, but is superior in predicting minority classes. To understand the methods' ability to generalize, we derive a new dataset and perform both in-domain and cross-domain experiments. Our qualitative and quantitative study helps interpreting the original FNC-1 scores and understand which features help improving performance and why. Our new dataset and all source code used during the reproduction study are publicly available for future research.

label: coling
text: The 2017 Fake News Challenge Stage 1 (FNC-1) aimed to tackle the issue of fake news by addressing a stance classification task. Despite its importance, there has been no comprehensive analysis of the results and the methods used. In this paper, we provide an in-depth investigation of the three top-performing systems in the FNC-1 challenge. Our analysis reveals that the evaluation metric used in the challenge overestimates the true discriminative power of the methods. To address this, we propose a new F1-based metric that changes the system ranking. We also compare the features and architectures used by the top-performing systems, leading to the development of a novel feature-rich stacked LSTM model that outperforms the others, particularly in predicting minority classes. Our study also includes a cross-domain and in-domain evaluation of the methods' ability to generalize. Our findings provide valuable insights into the performance of the original FNC-1 systems and help to understand which features are crucial for improving stance classification. All source code and a new dataset derived from our study are publicly available for future research.

label: emnlp
text: Text might express or evoke multiple emotions with varying intensities. As such, it is crucial to predict and rank multiple relevant emotions by their intensities. Moreover, as emotions might be evoked by hidden topics, it is important to unveil and incorporate such topical information to understand how the emotions are evoked. We proposed a novel interpretable neural network approach for relevant emotion ranking. Specifically, motivated by transfer learning, the neural network is initialized to make the hidden layer approximate the behavior of topic models. Moreover, a novel error function is defined to optimize the whole neural network for relevant emotion ranking. Experimental results on three real-world corpora show that the proposed approach performs remarkably better than the state-of-the-art emotion detection approaches and multi-label learning methods. Moreover, the extracted emotion-associated topic words indeed represent emotion-evoking events and are in line with our common-sense knowledge.

label: emnlp
text: The text may evoke multiple emotions with varying intensities, making it crucial to predict and rank them based on their intensities. Additionally, emotions may be triggered by hidden topics, making it important to uncover and incorporate this information to understand the emotions being evoked. We have proposed a novel, interpretable neural network approach for relevant emotion ranking that is based on transfer learning. The neural network is initialized to resemble the behavior of topic models and a novel error function is defined to optimize the entire network for relevant emotion ranking. The results of our experiments on three real-world corpora show that our approach outperforms existing emotion detection and multi-label learning methods. The extracted emotion-related topic words accurately represent the events that evoke emotions and align with our common-sense understanding.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we analyze several neural network designs (and their variations) for sentence pair modeling and compare their performance extensively across eight datasets, including paraphrase identification, semantic textual similarity, natural language inference, and question answering tasks. Although most of these models have claimed state-of-the-art performance, the original papers often reported on only one or two selected datasets. We provide a systematic study and show that (i) encoding contextual information by LSTM and inter-sentence interactions are critical, (ii) Tree-LSTM does not help as much as previously claimed but surprisingly improves performance on Twitter datasets, (iii) the Enhanced Sequential Inference Model is the best so far for larger datasets, while the Pairwise Word Interaction Model achieves the best performance when less data is available. We release our implementations as an open-source toolkit.

label: coling
text: In this study, we comprehensively analyze various neural network designs for sentence pair modeling and evaluate their performance across eight datasets, including tasks such as paraphrase identification, semantic textual similarity, natural language inference, and question answering. Despite previous claims of state-of-the-art performance, these models were often only tested on one or two datasets. Our systematic evaluation reveals that (i) encoding contextual information through LSTMs and inter-sentence interactions is crucial, (ii) Tree-LSTMs do not perform as well as previously reported, but surprisingly improve results on Twitter datasets, (iii) the Enhanced Sequential Inference Model is the best option for larger datasets, while the Pairwise Word Interaction Model excels when less data is available. Our implementations are available as an open-source toolkit.

label: coling
text: Spam detection has long been a research topic in both academic and industry due to its wide applications. Previous studies are mainly focused on extracting linguistic or behavior features to distinguish the spam and legitimate reviews. Such features are either ineffective or take long time to collect and thus are hard to be applied to cold-start spam review detection tasks. Recent advance leveraged the neural network to encode the textual and behavior features for the cold-start problem. However, the abundant attribute information are largely neglected by the existing framework. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning architecture for incorporating entities and their inherent attributes from various domains into a unified framework. Specifically, our model not only encodes the entities of reviewer, item, and review, but also their attributes such as location, date, price ranges. Furthermore, we present a domain classifier to adapt the knowledge from one domain to the other. With the abundant attributes in existing entities and knowledge in other domains, we successfully solve the problem of data scarcity in the cold-start settings. Experimental results on two Yelp datasets prove that our proposed framework significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
