text: There is a growing interest in the combined use of NLP and machine learning techniques for predicting gaze patterns during naturalistic reading. Promising results have been achieved through the application of transformer-based language models, but little work has been done to investigate the relationship between these models' performance and general text characteristics. This paper presents the results of experiments conducted on two eye-tracking corpora of naturalistic reading, using two language models (BERT and GPT-2). The experiments aimed to test the impact of a wide range of features, divided into five categories (syntactic complexity, lexical richness, register-based multiword combinations, readability, and psycholinguistic word properties), on predicting human reading behavior. Our results indicate that both the features used and the architecture of the transformer-based language models play a significant role in predicting multiple eye-tracking measures during naturalistic reading. Additionally, the experiments using SP-LIME were conducted to determine the relative importance of features from different groups.

label: emnlp
text: Prepositions are highly polysemous, and their variegated senses encode significant semantic information. In this paper we match each preposition's left- and right context, and their interplay to the geometry of the word vectors to the left and right of the preposition. Extracting these features from a large corpus and using them with machine learning models makes for an efficient preposition sense disambiguation (PSD) algorithm, which is comparable to and better than state-of-the-art on two benchmark datasets. Our reliance on no linguistic tool allows us to scale the PSD algorithm to a large corpus and learn sense-specific preposition representations. The crucial abstraction of preposition senses as word representations permits their use in downstream applications–phrasal verb paraphrasing and preposition selection–with new state-of-the-art results.

label: emnlp
text: The use of prepositions is highly polysemous and their different senses carry significant semantic information. In this study, we match each preposition's left and right context, as well as their interplay with the geometry of the word vectors to the left and right of the preposition, to develop an efficient preposition sense disambiguation (PSD) algorithm. By extracting these features from a large corpus and using machine learning models, our PSD algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark datasets. Our approach does not rely on any linguistic tools, allowing us to scale the algorithm to a large corpus and learn sense-specific preposition representations. The abstraction of preposition senses as word representations enables their use in downstream applications such as phrasal verb paraphrasing and preposition selection with improved results compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

label: naacl
text: We show that the choice of pretraining languages affects downstream cross-lingual transfer for BERT-based models. We inspect zero-shot performance in balanced data conditions to mitigate data size confounds, classifying pretraining languages that improve downstream performance as donors, and languages that are improved in zero-shot performance as recipients. We develop a method of quadratic time complexity in the number of languages to estimate these relations, instead of an exponential exhaustive computation of all possible combinations. We find that our method is effective on a diverse set of languages spanning different linguistic features and two downstream tasks.Our findings can inform developers of large-scale multilingual language models in choosing better pretraining configurations.

label: naacl
text: The choice of pretraining languages has a significant impact on the downstream cross-lingual transfer performance of BERT-based models. To mitigate the impact of data size, we evaluate the zero-shot performance in balanced data conditions. We classify languages that improve the downstream performance as "donors" and those that are improved in zero-shot performance as "recipients". To avoid an exhaustive computation of all possible combinations, we adopt a quadratic time complexity method in the number of languages to estimate these relationships. Our method proves to be effective on a diverse set of languages and two downstream tasks. Our findings can provide valuable guidance to developers of large-scale multilingual language models in making informed decisions on pretraining configurations.

label: acl
text: Sememes are minimum semantic units of concepts in human languages, such that each word sense is composed of one or multiple sememes. Words are usually manually annotated with their sememes by linguists, and form linguistic common-sense knowledge bases widely used in various NLP tasks. Recently, the lexical sememe prediction task has been introduced. It consists of automatically recommending sememes for words, which is expected to improve annotation efficiency and consistency. However, existing methods of lexical sememe prediction typically rely on the external context of words to represent the meaning, which usually fails to deal with low-frequency and out-of-vocabulary words. To address this issue for Chinese, we propose a novel framework to take advantage of both internal character information and external context information of words. We experiment on HowNet, a Chinese sememe knowledge base, and demonstrate that our framework outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a large margin, and maintains a robust performance even for low-frequency words.

label: acl
text: Sememes are the smallest semantic units of concepts in human language, and each word sense is made up of one or more sememes. Linguists typically annotate words with their sememes manually, creating linguistic common-sense knowledge bases that are widely used in various NLP tasks. Recently, the lexical sememe prediction task has been introduced, which involves automatically recommending sememes for words with the goal of improving annotation efficiency and consistency. However, current methods for lexical sememe prediction often rely solely on external context to represent the meaning of words, which can be problematic for low-frequency and out-of-vocabulary words. To address this issue for the Chinese language, we present a novel framework that takes into account both internal character information and external context information of words. Our experiments on the Chinese sememe knowledge base, HowNet, show that our framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin and maintains strong performance even for low-frequency words.

label: coling
text: Deploying large-scale pre-trained models in the prompt-tuning paradigm has demonstrated promising performance in few-shot learning. Particularly, vision-language pre-training models (VL-PTMs) have been intensively explored in various few-shot downstream tasks. However, most existing works only apply VL-PTMs to visual tasks like image classification, with few attempts being made on language tasks like text classification. In few-shot text classification, a feasible paradigm for deploying VL-PTMs is to align the input samples and their category names via the text encoders. However, it leads to the waste of visual information learned by the image encoders of VL-PTMs. To overcome this drawback, we propose a novel method named Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT). To our best knowledge, this method is the first attempt to deploy VL-PTM in few-shot text classification task. The main idea is to generate the image embeddings w.r.t. category names as visual prompt and then add them to the aligning process. Extensive experiments show that our VPT can achieve significant improvements under both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Importantly, our VPT even outperforms the most recent prompt-tuning methods on five public text classification datasets.

label: coling
text: Deploying large-scale pre-trained models in the prompt-tuning paradigm has shown promising results in few-shot learning. Specifically, vision-language pre-training models (VL-PTMs) have been widely explored in various few-shot downstream tasks, particularly in visual tasks such as image classification. However, few attempts have been made to apply VL-PTMs to language tasks, such as text classification. In few-shot text classification, a common approach is to align the input samples and category names using text encoders. However, this approach results in the waste of visual information learned by the image encoders of VL-PTMs. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to deploy VL-PTMs in the few-shot text classification task. Our method involves generating image embeddings based on category names as visual prompts, and incorporating them into the alignment process. Our experiments show that VPT outperforms recent prompt-tuning methods on five public text classification datasets, achieving significant improvements in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.

label: coling
text: This paper empirically studies the effects of representation choices on neural sentiment analysis for Modern Hebrew, a morphologically rich language (MRL) for which no sentiment analyzer currently exists. We study two dimensions of representational choices: (i) the granularity of the input signal (token-based vs. morpheme-based), and (ii) the level of encoding of vocabulary items (string-based vs. character-based). We hypothesise that for MRLs, languages where multiple meaning-bearing elements may be carried by a single space-delimited token, these choices will have measurable effects on task perfromance, and that these effects may vary for different architectural designs — fully-connected, convolutional or recurrent. Specifically, we hypothesize that morpheme-based representations will have advantages in terms of their generalization capacity and task accuracy, due to their better OOV coverage. To empirically study these effects, we develop a new sentiment analysis benchmark for Hebrew, based on 12K social media comments, and provide two instances of these data: in token-based and morpheme-based settings. Our experiments show that representation choices empirical effects vary with architecture type. While fully-connected and convolutional networks slightly prefer token-based settings, RNNs benefit from a morpheme-based representation, in accord with the hypothesis that explicit morphological information may help generalize. Our endeavour also delivers the first state-of-the-art broad-coverage sentiment analyzer for Hebrew, with over 89% accuracy, alongside an established benchmark to further study the effects of linguistic representation choices on neural networks' task performance.

label: coling
text: This paper investigates the impact of representation choices on neural sentiment analysis for Modern Hebrew, a morphologically rich language which currently lacks a sentiment analyzer. The study focuses on two dimensions of representation: (i) input signal granularity (token-based vs. morpheme-based) and (ii) vocabulary item encoding level (string-based vs. character-based). The hypothesis is that for morphologically rich languages, where a single token may carry multiple meaning-bearing elements, these representation choices will have a significant effect on task performance and that these effects may vary based on the architectural design of the network (fully-connected, convolutional, or recurrent). It is believed that morpheme-based representations will provide better generalization capacity and task accuracy due to improved out-of-vocabulary coverage. To test these hypotheses, a new sentiment analysis benchmark for Hebrew is developed based on 12K social media comments, which are provided in both token-based and morpheme-based settings. The results show that the impact of representation choices varies depending on the network architecture. While fully-connected and convolutional networks perform better with token-based representations, RNNs benefit from morpheme-based representations, supporting the hypothesis that explicit morphological information can help with generalization. The study delivers the first state-of-the-art sentiment analyzer for Hebrew with over 89% accuracy and provides an established benchmark for further studies on the impact of linguistic representation choices on neural network performance.

label: acl
text: In this work, we provide a systematic and comprehensive empirical comparison of pretrained multilingual language models versus their monolingual counterparts with regard to their monolingual task performance. We study a set of nine typologically diverse languages with readily available pretrained monolingual models on a set of five diverse monolingual downstream tasks. We first aim to establish, via fair and controlled comparisons, if a gap between the multilingual and the corresponding monolingual representation of that language exists, and subsequently investigate the reason for any performance difference. To disentangle conflating factors, we train new monolingual models on the same data, with monolingually and multilingually trained tokenizers. We find that while the pretraining data size is an important factor, a designated monolingual tokenizer plays an equally important role in the downstream performance. Our results show that languages that are adequately represented in the multilingual model's vocabulary exhibit negligible performance decreases over their monolingual counterparts. We further find that replacing the original multilingual tokenizer with the specialized monolingual tokenizer improves the downstream performance of the multilingual model for almost every task and language.

label: acl
text: In this study, we conduct a systematic and comprehensive comparison of the performance of pretrained multilingual language models with their monolingual counterparts on monolingual tasks. We examine nine typologically diverse languages and five diverse monolingual tasks, using readily available pretrained monolingual models. Our goal is to determine, through fair and controlled comparisons, if there is a gap in performance between the multilingual and monolingual representations of each language, and to investigate the reasons for any differences. To isolate confounding factors, we train new monolingual models using both monolingual and multilingual tokenizers on the same data. Our findings indicate that the size of the pretraining data is an important factor, but the use of a designated monolingual tokenizer is equally crucial for downstream performance. We observe that languages with adequate representation in the multilingual model's vocabulary experience minimal decreases in performance compared to their monolingual counterparts. Additionally, we find that replacing the original multilingual tokenizer with a specialized monolingual tokenizer significantly improves the performance of the multilingual model for almost all tasks and languages.

label: emnlp
text: Amidst growing concern over media manipulation, NLP attention has focused on overt strategies like censorship and “fake news”. Here, we draw on two concepts from political science literature to explore subtler strategies for government media manipulation: agenda-setting (selecting what topics to cover) and framing (deciding how topics are covered). We analyze 13 years (100K articles) of the Russian newspaper Izvestia and identify a strategy of distraction: articles mention the U.S. more frequently in the month directly following an economic downturn in Russia. We introduce embedding-based methods for cross-lingually projecting English frames to Russian, and discover that these articles emphasize U.S. moral failings and threats to the U.S. Our work offers new ways to identify subtle media manipulation strategies at the intersection of agenda-setting and framing.

label: emnlp
text: Amidst growing concerns about media manipulation, NLP research has shifted its focus to overt strategies such as censorship and "fake news." However, in this study, we delve into subtler strategies used by governments for media manipulation. We draw upon two concepts from political science literature: agenda-setting and framing. Our analysis of 13 years' worth of articles (100,000 pieces) from the Russian newspaper Izvestia reveals a strategy of distraction. During months following an economic downturn in Russia, the number of articles mentioning the U.S. increases. We also introduce embedding-based methods for projecting English frames into Russian and find that these articles tend to highlight the moral shortcomings and threats posed by the U.S. Our research provides new ways of identifying subtle media manipulation strategies that lie at the intersection of agenda-setting and framing.

label: emnlp
text: Multimodal learning has shown promising performance in content-based recommendation due to the auxiliary user and item information of multiple modalities such as text and images. However, the problem of incomplete and missing modality is rarely explored and most existing methods fail in learning a recommendation model with missing or corrupted modalities. In this paper, we propose LRMM, a novel framework that mitigates not only the problem of missing modalities but also more generally the cold-start problem of recommender systems. We propose modality dropout (m-drop) and a multimodal sequential autoencoder (m-auto) to learn multimodal representations for complementing and imputing missing modalities. Extensive experiments on real-world Amazon data show that LRMM achieves state-of-the-art performance on rating prediction tasks. More importantly, LRMM is more robust to previous methods in alleviating data-sparsity and the cold-start problem.

label: emnlp
text: Multimodal learning has demonstrated promising results in content-based recommendation due to the integration of auxiliary user and item information from multiple modalities such as text and images. However, the issue of incomplete or missing modalities has been largely neglected and most existing methods struggle to learn a recommendation model with missing or corrupted information. In this paper, we present LRMM, a novel framework that not only addresses the problem of missing modalities but also more broadly, the cold-start problem of recommender systems. We introduce the concept of modality dropout (m-drop) and a multimodal sequential autoencoder (m-auto) to learn multimodal representations that can complement and impute missing modalities. Our extensive experiments on real-world Amazon data demonstrate that LRMM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in rating prediction tasks. Furthermore, LRMM is more effective in alleviating data-sparsity and the cold-start problem compared to previous methods.

label: coling
text: Cross-lingual word embeddings (CLWE) have been proven useful in many cross-lingual tasks. However, most existing approaches to learn CLWE including the ones with contextual embeddings are sense agnostic. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align contextual embeddings at the sense level by leveraging cross-lingual signal from bilingual dictionaries only. We operationalize our framework by first proposing a novel sense-aware cross entropy loss to model word senses explicitly. The monolingual ELMo and BERT models pretrained with our sense-aware cross entropy loss demonstrate significant performance improvement for word sense disambiguation tasks. We then propose a sense alignment objective on top of the sense-aware cross entropy loss for cross-lingual model pretraining, and pretrain cross-lingual models for several language pairs (English to German/Spanish/Japanese/Chinese). Compared with the best baseline results, our cross-lingual models achieve 0.52%, 2.09% and 1.29% average performance improvements on zero-shot cross-lingual NER, sentiment classification and XNLI tasks, respectively.

label: coling
text: Cross-lingual word embeddings (CLWEs) have demonstrated their usefulness in various cross-lingual tasks. However, existing CLWE learning approaches, including those using contextual embeddings, are sense-agnostic. In this study, we present a novel framework that aligns contextual embeddings at the sense level by utilizing cross-lingual signals from bilingual dictionaries alone. Our framework involves the creation of a sense-aware cross-entropy loss to model word senses explicitly. The monolingual ELMo and BERT models pretrained with this loss show significant improvements in word sense disambiguation tasks. Additionally, we propose a sense alignment objective for cross-lingual model pretraining, which we apply to several language pairs (English to German, Spanish, Japanese, and Chinese). Our cross-lingual models outperform the best baseline results by 0.52%, 2.09%, and 1.29% on average for zero-shot cross-lingual NER, sentiment classification, and XNLI tasks, respectively.

label: acl
text: It is generally believed that a translation memory (TM) should be beneficial for machine translation tasks. Unfortunately, existing wisdom demonstrates the superiority of TM-based neural machine translation (NMT) only on the TM-specialized translation tasks rather than general tasks, with a non-negligible computational overhead. In this paper, we propose a fast and accurate approach to TM-based NMT within the Transformer framework: the model architecture is simple and employs a single bilingual sentence as its TM, leading to efficient training and inference; and its parameters are effectively optimized through a novel training criterion. Extensive experiments on six TM-specialized tasks show that the proposed approach substantially surpasses several strong baselines that use multiple TMs, in terms of BLEU and running time. In particular, the proposed approach also advances the strong baselines on two general tasks (WMT news Zh-En and En-De).

label: acl
text: It is widely accepted that a Translation Memory (TM) can be beneficial for Machine Translation (MT) tasks. However, current research has shown that TM-based Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is only superior for TM-specific tasks, with a significant computational overhead. In this paper, we present a fast and accurate TM-based NMT approach within the Transformer framework. Our model architecture is straightforward and utilizes a single bilingual sentence as its TM, resulting in efficient training and inference. Additionally, our parameters are optimized using a novel training criterion. Our experiments on six TM-specific tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms several strong baselines that use multiple TMs in terms of BLEU scores and running time. Notably, our approach also surpasses the strong baselines on two general tasks (WMT news Zh-En and En-De).

label: acl
text: The relational facts in sentences are often complicated. Different relational triplets may have overlaps in a sentence. We divided the sentences into three types according to triplet overlap degree, including Normal, EntityPairOverlap and SingleEntiyOverlap. Existing methods mainly focus on Normal class and fail to extract relational triplets precisely. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end model based on sequence-to-sequence learning with copy mechanism, which can jointly extract relational facts from sentences of any of these classes. We adopt two different strategies in decoding process: employing only one united decoder or applying multiple separated decoders. We test our models in two public datasets and our model outperform the baseline method significantly.

label: acl
text: The relational facts in sentences can be complex and challenging to extract. In some cases, different relational triplets may overlap within a single sentence. To address this, we categorize sentences into three types based on the degree of triplet overlap: Normal, EntityPairOverlap, and SingleEntityOverlap. Current methods primarily focus on the Normal class and are limited in their ability to accurately extract relational triplets. To overcome this challenge, we present an end-to-end model that leverages sequence-to-sequence learning with a copy mechanism to extract relational facts from sentences of any of these three classes. Our model offers two decoding strategies: using a single, unified decoder or multiple, separate decoders. Our results, obtained from testing on two public datasets, demonstrate that our model outperforms the baseline method by a significant margin.

label: acl
text: We present a novel end-to-end reinforcement learning approach to automatic taxonomy induction from a set of terms. While prior methods treat the problem as a two-phase task (i.e.,, detecting hypernymy pairs followed by organizing these pairs into a tree-structured hierarchy), we argue that such two-phase methods may suffer from error propagation, and cannot effectively optimize metrics that capture the holistic structure of a taxonomy. In our approach, the representations of term pairs are learned using multiple sources of information and used to determine which term to select and where to place it on the taxonomy via a policy network. All components are trained in an end-to-end manner with cumulative rewards, measured by a holistic tree metric over the training taxonomies. Experiments on two public datasets of different domains show that our approach outperforms prior state-of-the-art taxonomy induction methods up to 19.6% on ancestor F1.

label: acl
text: We introduce a new, end-to-end reinforcement learning approach for automatic taxonomy induction from a set of terms. Unlike previous methods that tackle the problem as a two-step process (i.e., detecting hypernymy pairs and organizing these pairs into a tree-structured hierarchy), we believe that such methods may be prone to error propagation and may not effectively optimize metrics that consider the overall structure of a taxonomy. Our approach involves learning representations of term pairs using multiple sources of information, which are then used to determine the selection and placement of terms in the taxonomy through a policy network. All components are trained in an end-to-end manner, with cumulative rewards measured by a holistic tree metric across the training taxonomies. Our experiments on two publicly available datasets from different domains demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art taxonomy induction methods by up to 19.6% on the ancestor F1 metric.

label: naacl
text: Trojan attacks raise serious security concerns. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of Trojaned BERT models. We observe the attention focus drifting behavior of Trojaned models, i.e., when encountering an poisoned input, the trigger token hijacks the attention focus regardless of the context. We provide a thorough qualitative and quantitative analysis of this phenomenon, revealing insights into the Trojan mechanism. Based on the observation, we propose an attention-based Trojan detector to distinguish Trojaned models from clean ones. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to analyze the Trojan mechanism and develop a Trojan detector based on the transformer's attention.

label: naacl
text: The Trojan attacks pose a significant threat to security. This study delves into the inner workings of Trojaned BERT models and uncovers their attention focus drift behavior. When faced with a poisoned input, the trigger token manipulates the model's attention, regardless of the context. Our detailed qualitative and quantitative analysis sheds light on the underlying Trojan mechanism and enables us to develop an attention-based detector to identify Trojaned models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time the Trojan mechanism has been analyzed and a detector has been created based on the attention mechanism of transformers.

label: acl
text: This paper introduces QAConv, a new question answering (QA) dataset that uses conversations as a knowledge source. We focus on informative conversations, including business emails, panel discussions, and work channels. Unlike open-domain and task-oriented dialogues, these conversations are usually long, complex, asynchronous, and involve strong domain knowledge. In total, we collect 34,608 QA pairs from 10,259 selected conversations with both human-written and machine-generated questions. We use a question generator and a dialogue summarizer as auxiliary tools to collect and recommend questions. The dataset has two testing scenarios: chunk mode and full mode, depending on whether the grounded partial conversation is provided or retrieved. Experimental results show that state-of-the-art pretrained QA systems have limited zero-shot performance and tend to predict our questions as unanswerable. Our dataset provides a new training and evaluation testbed to facilitate QA on conversations research.

label: acl
text: This paper presents QAConv, a novel question answering (QA) dataset that utilizes conversations as a source of knowledge. Our focus is on informative conversations, including business emails, panel discussions, and work channels, which tend to be long, complex, asynchronous, and require strong domain knowledge. We have collected 34,608 QA pairs from 10,259 selected conversations, comprising both human-written and machine-generated questions. To gather and recommend questions, we utilized a question generator and a dialogue summarizer. The dataset offers two testing scenarios: chunk mode and full mode, depending on whether the grounded partial conversation is provided or needs to be retrieved. Our experiments reveal that state-of-the-art pretrained QA systems have limited zero-shot performance and often predict our questions as unanswerable. QAConv provides a new training and evaluation platform for QA research on conversations.

label: acl
text: Word translation or bilingual lexicon induction (BLI) is a key cross-lingual task, aiming to bridge the lexical gap between different languages. In this work, we propose a robust and effective two-stage contrastive learning framework for the BLI task. At Stage C1, we propose to refine standard cross-lingual linear maps between static word embeddings (WEs) via a contrastive learning objective; we also show how to integrate it into the self-learning procedure for even more refined cross-lingual maps. In Stage C2, we conduct BLI-oriented contrastive fine-tuning of mBERT, unlocking its word translation capability. We also show that static WEs induced from the `C2-tuned' mBERT complement static WEs from Stage C1. Comprehensive experiments on standard BLI datasets for diverse languages and different experimental setups demonstrate substantial gains achieved by our framework. While the BLI method from Stage C1 already yields substantial gains over all state-of-the-art BLI methods in our comparison, even stronger improvements are met with the full two-stage framework: e.g., we report gains for 112/112 BLI setups, spanning 28 language pairs.

label: acl
text: Bridging the lexical gap between different languages, Word Translation or Bilingual Lexicon Induction (BLI) is a crucial cross-lingual task. To address this challenge, we present a robust and effective two-stage framework for BLI. In the first stage (C1), we refine standard cross-lingual linear maps between static word embeddings (WEs) using a contrastive learning objective. We also incorporate self-learning into the process to further refine the cross-lingual maps. In the second stage (C2), we perform BLI-focused fine-tuning of mBERT, unlocking its word translation capabilities. The static WEs induced from the C2-tuned mBERT complement the WEs from stage C1. Our experiments on standard BLI datasets for various languages and experimental setups demonstrate the superiority of our framework, with substantial gains over state-of-the-art methods. Our full two-stage framework outperforms all other methods, with gains reported in 112 out of 112 BLI setups across 28 language pairs.

label: acl
text: Question Answering (QA), as a research field, has primarily focused on either knowledge bases (KBs) or free text as a source of knowledge. These two sources have historically shaped the kinds of questions that are asked over these sources, and the methods developed to answer them. In this work, we look towards a practical use-case of QA over user-instructed knowledge that uniquely combines elements of both structured QA over knowledge bases, and unstructured QA over narrative, introducing the task of multi-relational QA over personal narrative. As a first step towards this goal, we make three key contributions: (i) we generate and release TextWorldsQA, a set of five diverse datasets, where each dataset contains dynamic narrative that describes entities and relations in a simulated world, paired with variably compositional questions over that knowledge, (ii) we perform a thorough evaluation and analysis of several state-of-the-art QA models and their variants at this task, and (iii) we release a lightweight Python-based framework we call TextWorlds for easily generating arbitrary additional worlds and narrative, with the goal of allowing the community to create and share a growing collection of diverse worlds as a test-bed for this task.

label: acl
text: The research field of Question Answering (QA) has primarily focused on either knowledge bases (KBs) or free text as sources of knowledge. These sources have influenced the types of questions asked and the methods used to answer them. In this study, we explore a practical use-case of QA that combines elements of structured QA over KBs and unstructured QA over narrative. This is known as multi-relational QA over personal narrative. To achieve this, we make three important contributions: (i) we generate and release TextWorldsQA, a collection of five datasets that contain dynamic narratives describing entities and relationships in simulated worlds, along with questions that vary in composition, (ii) we evaluate and analyze several state-of-the-art QA models and their variations for this task, and (iii) we release a Python-based framework called TextWorlds that allows for the generation of additional worlds and narratives. This will enable the community to create and share a growing collection of diverse worlds for testing purposes.

label: acl
text: Recurrent neural network (RNN) has achieved remarkable performance in text categorization. RNN can model the entire sequence and capture long-term dependencies, but it does not do well in extracting key patterns. In contrast, convolutional neural network (CNN) is good at extracting local and position-invariant features. In this paper, we present a novel model named disconnected recurrent neural network (DRNN), which incorporates position-invariance into RNN. By limiting the distance of information flow in RNN, the hidden state at each time step is restricted to represent words near the current position. The proposed model makes great improvements over RNN and CNN models and achieves the best performance on several benchmark datasets for text categorization.

label: acl
text: The Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) has demonstrated exceptional results in text categorization. While RNN is capable of modeling the entire sequence and capturing long-term dependencies, it struggles to extract key patterns. On the other hand, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) excels in extracting local and position-invariant features. This paper introduces a novel model, the Disconnected Recurrent Neural Network (DRNN), which combines the strengths of both RNN and CNN by incorporating position-invariance into RNN. The proposed model restricts the distance of information flow in RNN, ensuring that the hidden state at each time step only represents words close to the current position. As a result, the DRNN model outperforms both RNN and CNN models and achieves the best results on several benchmark datasets for text categorization.

label: acl
text: Generating long and coherent text is an important but challenging task, particularly for open-ended language generation tasks such as story generation. Despite the success in modeling intra-sentence coherence, existing generation models (e.g., BART) still struggle to maintain a coherent event sequence throughout the generated text. We conjecture that this is because of the difficulty for the decoder to capture the high-level semantics and discourse structures in the context beyond token-level co-occurrence. In this paper, we propose a long text generation model, which can represent the prefix sentences at sentence level and discourse level in the decoding process. To this end, we propose two pretraining objectives to learn the representations by predicting inter-sentence semantic similarity and distinguishing between normal and shuffled sentence orders. Extensive experiments show that our model can generate more coherent texts than state-of-the-art baselines.

label: acl
text: Generating long, coherent text is a crucial but challenging task, especially for open-ended language generation tasks such as story generation. Although there has been success in modeling intra-sentence coherence, existing generation models, such as BART, still struggle to maintain a coherent event sequence throughout the generated text. This is likely due to the difficulty of capturing high-level semantics and discourse structures beyond token-level co-occurrence. To address this issue, we propose a long text generation model that incorporates sentence-level and discourse-level representations in the decoding process. To achieve this, we introduce two pretraining objectives: predicting inter-sentence semantic similarity and distinguishing between normal and shuffled sentence orders. Our experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of generating more coherent text.

label: coling
text: Temporal sentence grounding (TSG) is crucial and fundamental for video understanding. Previous works typically model the target activity referred to the sentence query in a video by extracting the appearance information from each whole frame. However, these methods fail to distinguish visually similar background noise and capture subtle details of small objects. Although a few recent works additionally adopt a detection model to filter out the background contents and capture local appearances of foreground objects, they rely on the quality of the detection model and suffer from the time-consuming detection process. To this end, we propose a novel detection-free framework for TSG—Grounding with Learnable Foreground (GLF), which efficiently learns to locate the foreground regions related to the query in consecutive frames for better modelling the target activity. Specifically, we first split each video frame into multiple patch candidates of equal size, and reformulate the foreground detection problem as a patch localization task. Then, we develop a self-supervised coarse-to-fine paradigm to learn to locate the most query-relevant patch in each frame and aggregate them among the video for final grounding. Further, we employ a multi-scale patch reasoning strategy to capture more fine-grained foreground information. Extensive experiments on three challenging datasets (Charades-STA, TACoS, ActivityNet) show that the proposed GLF outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

label: coling
text: Temporal sentence grounding (TSG) is essential for video understanding. Previous works have attempted to model the target activity in a video referred to by a sentence query by extracting appearance information from each frame. However, these methods struggle to differentiate visually similar background noise and capture subtle details of small objects. While some recent works have adopted a detection model to filter out background content and capture local appearances of foreground objects, they are dependent on the quality of the detection model and suffer from a time-consuming detection process. To address these issues, we present a novel detection-free framework for TSG called Grounding with Learnable Foreground (GLF). Our method efficiently learns to locate the foreground regions related to the query in consecutive frames, improving the modeling of the target activity. We achieve this by splitting each video frame into multiple patch candidates of equal size, reformulating the foreground detection problem as a patch localization task, and using a self-supervised coarse-to-fine approach to learn the most query-relevant patch in each frame. We also employ a multi-scale patch reasoning strategy to capture fine-grained foreground information. Our experiments on three challenging datasets (Charades-STA, TACoS, ActivityNet) show that GLF outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: Dependency trees help relation extraction models capture long-range relations between words. However, existing dependency-based models either neglect crucial information (e.g., negation) by pruning the dependency trees too aggressively, or are computationally inefficient because it is difficult to parallelize over different tree structures. We propose an extension of graph convolutional networks that is tailored for relation extraction, which pools information over arbitrary dependency structures efficiently in parallel. To incorporate relevant information while maximally removing irrelevant content, we further apply a novel pruning strategy to the input trees by keeping words immediately around the shortest path between the two entities among which a relation might hold. The resulting model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the large-scale TACRED dataset, outperforming existing sequence and dependency-based neural models. We also show through detailed analysis that this model has complementary strengths to sequence models, and combining them further improves the state of the art.

label: emnlp
text: Dependency trees play a crucial role in helping relation extraction models capture long-range relationships between words. However, current dependency-based models either ignore important information (such as negation) by over-pruning the trees, or are computationally inefficient due to the difficulty in parallelizing different tree structures. To address these issues, we propose an extension of graph convolutional networks specifically designed for relation extraction. This model pools information efficiently over arbitrary dependency structures in parallel, while incorporating relevant information and removing irrelevant content through a novel pruning strategy. The strategy involves keeping only the words immediately surrounding the shortest path between the two entities that might have a relation. Our model outperforms existing sequence and dependency-based neural models, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the TACRED dataset. Our detailed analysis also shows that this model has complementary strengths to sequence models, and combining them further improves the state of the art.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a novel strategy to encode the syntax parse tree of sentence into a learnable distributed representation. The proposed syntax encoding scheme is provably information-lossless. In specific, an embedding vector is constructed for each word in the sentence, encoding the path in the syntax tree corresponding to the word. The one-to-one correspondence between these “syntax-embedding” vectors and the words (hence their embedding vectors) in the sentence makes it easy to integrate such a representation with all word-level NLP models. We empirically show the benefits of the syntax embeddings on the Authorship Attribution domain, where our approach improves upon the prior art and achieves new performance records on five benchmarking data sets.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a new approach to encoding the syntax parse tree of a sentence into a learnable, distributed representation. Our syntax encoding scheme is information-lossless and provides an embedding vector for each word in the sentence, which encodes the path in the syntax tree corresponding to that word. The one-to-one correspondence between these "syntax-embedding" vectors and the words in the sentence makes it easy to integrate this representation into various NLP models. Our empirical results demonstrate the benefits of the syntax embeddings, as our approach outperforms previous methods in the Authorship Attribution domain and sets new performance records on five benchmarking datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Previous work on question-answering systems mainly focuses on answering individual questions, assuming they are independent and devoid of context. Instead, we investigate sequential question answering, asking multiple related questions. We present QBLink, a new dataset of fully human-authored questions. We extend existing strong question answering frameworks to include previous questions to improve the overall question-answering accuracy in open-domain question answering. The dataset is publicly available at http://sequential.qanta.org.

label: emnlp
text: Previous work on question-answering systems has primarily concentrated on answering individual questions, assuming they are isolated and lack context. In contrast, our research explores sequential question answering, which involves asking a series of interrelated questions. We introduce QBLink, a novel dataset of questions that have been entirely written by humans. To enhance the accuracy of open-domain question answering, we expand existing robust question-answering frameworks to incorporate prior questions. The QBLink dataset can be accessed at http://sequential.qanta.org.

label: naacl
text: How can we learn unified representations for spoken utterances and their written text? Learning similar representations for semantically similar speech and text is important for speech translation. To this end, we propose ConST, a cross-modal contrastive learning method for end-to-end speech-to-text translation. We evaluate ConST and a variety of previous baselines on a popular benchmark MuST-C. Experiments show that the proposed ConST consistently outperforms the previous methods, and achieves an average BLEU of 29.4. The analysis further verifies that ConST indeed closes the representation gap of different modalities — its learned representation improves the accuracy of cross-modal speech-text retrieval from 4% to 88%. Code and models are available at https://github.com/ReneeYe/ConST.

label: naacl
text: How can we achieve a unified representation for both spoken utterances and their corresponding written text? It is crucial to have similar representations for speech and text that are semantically equivalent, particularly for speech-to-text translation. To address this issue, we present ConST, a cross-modal contrastive learning technique for end-to-end speech-to-text translation. We evaluate ConST and various previous methods using the popular benchmark MuST-C. Our experiments demonstrate that ConST outperforms previous methods, with an average BLEU score of 29.4. Our analysis also confirms that ConST effectively closes the representation gap between different modalities, as it increases cross-modal speech-text retrieval accuracy from 4% to 88%. The code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/ReneeYe/ConST.

label: emnlp
text: In models to generate program source code from natural language, representing this code in a tree structure has been a common approach. However, existing methods often fail to generate complex code correctly due to a lack of ability to memorize large and complex structures. We introduce RECODE, a method based on subtree retrieval that makes it possible to explicitly reference existing code examples within a neural code generation model. First, we retrieve sentences that are similar to input sentences using a dynamic-programming-based sentence similarity scoring method. Next, we extract n-grams of action sequences that build the associated abstract syntax tree. Finally, we increase the probability of actions that cause the retrieved n-gram action subtree to be in the predicted code. We show that our approach improves the performance on two code generation tasks by up to +2.6 BLEU.

label: emnlp
text: In the generation of program source code from natural language, representing the code in a tree structure is a common approach. However, existing methods often struggle to generate complex code accurately due to their limited ability to retain large and complex structures. To address this issue, we present RECODE, a subtree retrieval-based method that enables explicit referencing of existing code examples within a neural code generation model. Our method first retrieves sentences similar to the input sentence using a dynamic-programming-based sentence similarity scoring mechanism. Then, we extract n-grams of action sequences that construct the associated abstract syntax tree. Finally, we enhance the probability of actions that result in the predicted code containing the retrieved n-gram action subtree. Our approach significantly improves the performance on two code generation tasks by up to +2.6 BLEU.

label: naacl
text: Existing Math Word Problem (MWP) solvers have achieved high accuracy on benchmark datasets. However, prior works have shown that such solvers do not generalize well and rely on superficial cues to achieve high performance. In this paper, we first conduct experiments to showcase that this behaviour is mainly associated with the limited size and diversity present in existing MWP datasets. Next, we propose several data augmentation techniques broadly categorized into Substitution and Paraphrasing based methods. By deploying these methods we increase the size of existing datasets by five folds. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets across three state-of-the-art MWP solvers shows that proposed methods increase the generalization and robustness of existing solvers. On average, proposed methods significantly increase the state-of-the-art results by over five percentage points on benchmark datasets. Further, the solvers trained on the augmented dataset performs comparatively better on the challenge test set. We also show the effectiveness of proposed techniques through ablation studies and verify the quality of augmented samples through human evaluation.

label: naacl
text: Existing Math Word Problem (MWP) solvers have achieved high accuracy on benchmark datasets, but prior research has shown that these solvers struggle to generalize and rely on superficial cues to achieve their results. In this paper, we demonstrate that this behavior is largely due to the limited size and diversity of existing MWP datasets. To address this issue, we propose several data augmentation techniques, categorized into Substitution and Paraphrasing methods, which increase the size of existing datasets by five times. Our experiments on two benchmark datasets and three state-of-the-art MWP solvers show that our methods significantly improve the generalization and robustness of existing solvers, with an average increase of over five percentage points on benchmark datasets. Additionally, the solvers trained on our augmented dataset perform better on challenging test sets. We also validate the effectiveness of our techniques through ablation studies and human evaluations of the quality of the augmented samples.

label: acl
text: Neural lexicalized PCFGs (L-PCFGs) have been shown effective in grammar induction. However, to reduce computational complexity, they make a strong independence assumption on the generation of the child word and thus bilexical dependencies are ignored. In this paper, we propose an approach to parameterize L-PCFGs without making implausible independence assumptions. Our approach directly models bilexical dependencies and meanwhile reduces both learning and representation complexities of L-PCFGs. Experimental results on the English WSJ dataset confirm the effectiveness of our approach in improving both running speed and unsupervised parsing performance.

label: acl
text: Neural Lexicalized PCFGs (L-PCFGs) have been demonstrated to be effective in grammar induction. However, to reduce computational complexity, they make a strong assumption of independence in the generation of child words, leading to the ignoring of bilexical dependencies. In this paper, we present a novel approach to parameterize L-PCFGs without making unrealistic independence assumptions. Our approach models bilexical dependencies directly and reduces both the learning and representation complexities of L-PCFGs. The results of our experiments on the English WSJ dataset confirm the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing both performance and speed in unsupervised parsing.

label: coling
text: In this work, we focus on improving the captions generated by image-caption generation systems. We propose a novel re-ranking approach that leverages visual-semantic measures to identify the ideal caption that maximally captures the visual information in the image. Our re-ranker utilizes the Belief Revision framework (Blok et al., 2003) to calibrate the original likelihood of the top-n captions by explicitly exploiting semantic relatedness between the depicted caption and the visual context. Our experiments demonstrate the utility of our approach, where we observe that our re-ranker can enhance the performance of a typical image-captioning system without necessity of any additional training or fine-tuning.

label: coling
text: In this study, we aim to enhance the captions produced by image-caption generation systems. To achieve this, we introduce a new re-ranking technique that uses visual-semantic measures to select the most appropriate caption that accurately represents the visual content of the image. Our re-ranker employs the Belief Revision framework (Blok et al., 2003) to adjust the original probability of the top-n captions by considering the semantic relationship between the caption and the visual context. Our results show that our approach can effectively improve the performance of a standard image-caption generation system without requiring any additional training or fine-tuning.

label: coling
text: Most previous work on temporal relation extraction only focused on extracting the temporal relations among events or suffered from the issue of different expressions of events, timexes and Document Creation Time (DCT). Moreover, DCT can act as a hub to semantically connect the other events and timexes in a document. Unfortunately, previous work cannot benefit from such critical information. To address the above issues, we propose a unified DCT-centered Temporal Relation Extraction model DTRE to identify the relations among events, timexes and DCT. Specifically, sentence-style DCT representation is introduced to address the first issue and unify event expressions, timexes and DCT. Then, a DCT-aware graph is applied to obtain their contextual structural representations. Furthermore, a DCT-anchoring multi-task learning framework is proposed to jointly predict three types of temporal relations in a batch. Finally, we apply a DCT-guided global inference to further enhance the global consistency among different relations. Experimental results on three datasets show that our DTRE outperforms several SOTA baselines on E-E, E-T and E-D significantly.

label: coling
text: Previous work on temporal relation extraction has mainly focused on extracting the relationships between events or has faced the challenge of different expressions of events, timexes, and Document Creation Time (DCT). The DCT can serve as a central point for connecting the other events and timexes in a document, but previous work has been unable to take advantage of this critical information. To address these issues, we introduce the DCT-Centered Temporal Relation Extraction (DTRE) model, which identifies relationships among events, timexes, and DCT. The DTRE model features a sentence-style DCT representation, a DCT-aware graph for contextual structural representations, a DCT-anchored multi-task learning framework for predicting three types of temporal relations, and a DCT-guided global inference for enhancing the consistency of relationships. Our experiments on three datasets show that the DTRE model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in extracting Event-Event (E-E), Event-Timex (E-T), and Event-DCT (E-D) relationships.

label: emnlp
text: Distributional semantic models (DSMs) generally require sufficient examples for a word to learn a high quality representation. This is in stark contrast with human who can guess the meaning of a word from one or a few referents only. In this paper, we propose Mem2Vec, a memory based embedding learning method capable of acquiring high quality word representations from fairly limited context. Our method directly adapts the representations produced by a DSM with a longterm memory to guide its guess of a novel word. Based on a pre-trained embedding space, the proposed method delivers impressive performance on two challenging few-shot word similarity tasks. Embeddings learned with our method also lead to considerable improvements over strong baselines on NER and sentiment classification.

label: emnlp
text: In this paper, we present Mem2Vec, a memory-based embedding learning method designed to acquire high-quality word representations from limited context. Unlike distributional semantic models (DSMs), which typically require a large number of examples to generate accurate representations, Mem2Vec leverages a long-term memory to guide its guess of a novel word. Our method is based on a pre-trained embedding space and has been demonstrated to deliver superior results on two challenging few-shot word similarity tasks. Additionally, our embeddings lead to significant improvements over strong baselines in NER and sentiment classification.

label: coling
text: Previous studies have shown that linguistic features of a word such as possession, genitive or other grammatical cases can be employed in word representations of a named entity recognition (NER) tagger to improve the performance for morphologically rich languages. However, these taggers require external morphological disambiguation (MD) tools to function which are hard to obtain or non-existent for many languages. In this work, we propose a model which alleviates the need for such disambiguators by jointly learning NER and MD taggers in languages for which one can provide a list of candidate morphological analyses. We show that this can be done independent of the morphological annotation schemes, which differ among languages. Our experiments employing three different model architectures that join these two tasks show that joint learning improves NER performance. Furthermore, the morphological disambiguator's performance is shown to be competitive.

label: coling
text: Previous studies have shown that linguistic features, such as possession and genitive, can be used to improve the performance of a named entity recognition (NER) tagger in morphologically rich languages. However, these taggers require external morphological disambiguation (MD) tools, which are often difficult to obtain or unavailable for many languages. To address this issue, we propose a model that eliminates the need for these disambiguators by jointly learning NER and MD taggers for languages where a list of candidate morphological analyses is available. This model is independent of the morphological annotation schemes, which vary among languages. Our experiments, using three different architectures, demonstrate that joint learning improves NER performance and that the morphological disambiguator's performance is competitive.

label: coling
text: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence neural network models learn to jointly align and translate. The quadratic-time attention mechanism is powerful as it is capable of handling arbitrary long-distance reordering, but computationally expensive. In this paper, towards making neural translation both accurate and efficient, we follow the traditional pre-reordering approach to decouple reordering from translation. We add a reordering RNN that shares the input encoder with the decoder. The RNNs are trained jointly with a multi-task loss function and applied sequentially at inference time. The task of the reordering model is to predict the permutation of the input words following the target language word order. After reordering, the attention in the decoder becomes more peaked and monotonic. For reordering, we adopt the Inversion Transduction Grammars (ITG) and propose a transition system to parse input to trees for reordering. We harness the ITG transition system with RNN. With the modeling power of RNN, we achieve superior reordering accuracy without any feature engineering. In experiments, we apply the model to the task of text normalization. Compared to a strong baseline of attention-based RNN, our ITG RNN re-ordering model can reach the same reordering accuracy with only 1/10 of the training data and is 2.5x faster in decoding.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a solution to make neural translation both accurate and efficient. We propose a reordering RNN that shares the input encoder with the decoder and is trained with a multi-task loss function. The reordering RNN predicts the permutation of the input words following the target language word order, making the attention in the decoder more peaked and monotonic. We adopt the Inversion Transduction Grammars (ITG) and propose a transition system to parse input to trees for reordering. The ITG transition system is harnessed with RNN, achieving superior reordering accuracy without any feature engineering. In experiments, our ITG RNN reordering model reaches the same reordering accuracy as a strong baseline with only 1/10 of the training data and is 2.5x faster in decoding. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed solution in improving the accuracy and efficiency of neural translation.

label: acl
text: The open-ended nature of visual captioning makes it a challenging area for evaluation. The majority of proposed models rely on specialized training to improve human-correlation, resulting in limited adoption, generalizability, and explainabilty. We introduce “typicality”, a new formulation of evaluation rooted in information theory, which is uniquely suited for problems lacking a definite ground truth. Typicality serves as our framework to develop a novel semantic comparison, SPARCS, as well as referenceless fluency evaluation metrics. Over the course of our analysis, two separate dimensions of fluency naturally emerge: style, captured by metric SPURTS, and grammar, captured in the form of grammatical outlier penalties. Through extensive experiments and ablation studies on benchmark datasets, we show how these decomposed dimensions of semantics and fluency provide greater system-level insight into captioner differences. Our proposed metrics along with their combination, SMURF, achieve state-of-the-art correlation with human judgment when compared with other rule-based evaluation metrics.

label: acl
text: The open-ended nature of visual captioning presents a challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce "typicality," a new evaluation framework rooted in information theory, which is well-suited for problems lacking a definite ground truth. Our framework includes a novel semantic comparison, SPARCS, and referenceless fluency evaluation metrics. Our analysis reveals two separate dimensions of fluency: style, captured by the SPURTS metric, and grammar, captured in the form of grammatical outlier penalties. Through experiments and ablation studies on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate how these dimensions of semantics and fluency provide a deeper understanding of captioner differences. Our proposed metrics, including the combination of SMURF, achieve state-of-the-art correlation with human judgment when compared to other rule-based evaluation metrics.

label: acl
text: Conversational semantic parsers map user utterances to executable programs given dialogue histories composed of previous utterances, programs, and system responses. Existing parsers typically condition on rich representations of history that include the complete set of values and computations previously discussed. We propose a model that abstracts over values to focus prediction on type- and function-level context. This approach provides a compact encoding of dialogue histories and predicted programs, improving generalization and computational efficiency. Our model incorporates several other components, including an atomic span copy operation and structural enforcement of well-formedness constraints on predicted programs, that are particularly advantageous in the low-data regime. Trained on the SMCalFlow and TreeDST datasets, our model outperforms prior work by 7.3% and 10.6% respectively in terms of absolute accuracy. Trained on only a thousand examples from each dataset, it outperforms strong baselines by 12.4% and 6.4%. These results indicate that simple representations are key to effective generalization in conversational semantic parsing.

label: acl
text: The conversational semantic parser maps user utterances to executable programs by using dialogue histories, which consist of previous utterances, programs, and system responses. Existing parsers typically rely on a rich representation of history that includes all values and computations discussed so far. Our proposed model, however, abstracts over values to focus on type- and function-level context, resulting in a more compact encoding of dialogue histories and predicted programs. This approach improves generalization and computational efficiency. Additionally, our model includes several other components, such as an atomic span copy operation and structural enforcement of well-formedness constraints on predicted programs, which are particularly beneficial in low-data regimes. Our model was trained on the SMCalFlow and TreeDST datasets and outperformed prior work by 7.3% and 10.6% in terms of accuracy. With only a thousand examples from each dataset, our model still outperformed strong baselines by 12.4% and 6.4%. These results demonstrate that simple representations are crucial for effective generalization in conversational semantic parsing.

label: acl
text: Informal social interaction is the primordial home of human language. Linguistically diverse conversational corpora are an important and largely untapped resource for computational linguistics and language technology. Through the efforts of a worldwide language documentation movement, such corpora are increasingly becoming available. We show how interactional data from 63 languages (26 families) harbours insights about turn-taking, timing, sequential structure and social action, with implications for language technology, natural language understanding, and the design of conversational interfaces. Harnessing linguistically diverse conversational corpora will provide the empirical foundations for flexible, localizable, humane language technologies of the future.

label: acl
text: Informal social interaction is the birthplace of human language. Linguistically diverse conversational data, which is a largely untapped resource for computational linguistics and language technology, is becoming increasingly accessible through the efforts of the worldwide language documentation movement. Our research demonstrates that interactional data from 63 languages, representing 26 language families, holds valuable insights into turn-taking, timing, sequential structure, and social action. These findings have significant implications for language technology, natural language understanding, and the design of conversational interfaces. By utilizing linguistically diverse conversational data, we can lay the empirical foundation for future language technologies that are flexible, culturally sensitive, and human-centered.

label: acl
text: Everyday billions of multimodal posts containing both images and text are shared in social media sites such as Snapchat, Twitter or Instagram. This combination of image and text in a single message allows for more creative and expressive forms of communication, and has become increasingly common in such sites. This new paradigm brings new challenges for natural language understanding, as the textual component tends to be shorter, more informal, and often is only understood if combined with the visual context. In this paper, we explore the task of name tagging in multimodal social media posts. We start by creating two new multimodal datasets: the first based on Twitter posts and the second based on Snapchat captions (exclusively submitted to public and crowd-sourced stories). We then propose a novel model architecture based on Visual Attention that not only provides deeper visual understanding on the decisions of the model, but also significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art baseline methods for this task.

label: acl
text: Every day, billions of social media posts containing both images and text are shared on sites such as Snapchat, Twitter, and Instagram. The combination of image and text in a single message allows for more creative and expressive forms of communication and has become increasingly popular on these sites. However, this new paradigm presents new challenges for natural language understanding, as the text component tends to be shorter, more informal, and often only comprehensible when combined with the visual context. This paper explores the task of name tagging in multimodal social media posts by creating two new multimodal datasets based on Twitter posts and Snapchat captions. We propose a novel model architecture that utilizes Visual Attention and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods for this task. Additionally, our model provides deeper visual understanding of the model's decisions.

label: acl
text: Pretrained language models (PLMs) have achieved superhuman performance on many benchmarks, creating a need for harder tasks. We introduce CoDA21 (Context Definition Alignment), a challenging benchmark that measures natural language understanding (NLU) capabilities of PLMs: Given a definition and a context each for k words, but not the words themselves, the task is to align the k definitions with the k contexts. CoDA21 requires a deep understanding of contexts and definitions, including complex inference and world knowledge. We find that there is a large gap between human and PLM performance, suggesting that CoDA21 measures an aspect of NLU that is not sufficiently covered in existing benchmarks.

label: acl
text: Pretrained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on numerous benchmarks, resulting in the need for more challenging tasks. To address this, we present CoDA21 (Context Definition Alignment), a new benchmark designed to evaluate the natural language understanding (NLU) capabilities of PLMs. CoDA21 requires the alignment of k definitions with k contexts, where the words themselves are not provided. The task demands a deep understanding of both the context and definition, including the ability to perform complex inferences and utilize world knowledge. Our results indicate a significant gap between human and PLM performance, highlighting that CoDA21 assesses a crucial aspect of NLU that has not been adequately covered in existing benchmarks.

label: coling
text: Despite the revolutionary advances made by Transformer in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), inference efficiency remains an obstacle due to the heavy use of attention operations in auto-regressive decoding. We thereby propose a lightweight attention structure called Attention Refinement Network (ARN) for speeding up Transformer. Specifically, we design a weighted residual network, which reconstructs the attention by reusing the features across layers. To further improve the Transformer efficiency, we merge the self-attention and cross-attention components for parallel computing. Extensive experiments on ten WMT machine translation tasks show that the proposed model yields an average of 1.35x faster (with almost no decrease in BLEU) over the state-of-the-art inference implementation. Results on widely used WMT14 En-De machine translation tasks demonstrate that our model achieves a higher speed-up, giving highly competitive performance compared to AAN and SAN models with fewer parameter numbers.

label: coling
text: Despite the significant progress made in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) with the Transformer model, inference efficiency remains a challenge due to the extensive use of attention operations in auto-regressive decoding. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight attention structure called the Attention Refinement Network (ARN). Our ARN design consists of a weighted residual network that reconstructs attention by reusing features across layers. Additionally, we merge the self-attention and cross-attention components for improved parallel computing. Our experiments on ten WMT machine translation tasks show that the ARN model provides an average speed-up of 1.35x with minimal impact on BLEU scores compared to the state-of-the-art inference implementation. Results on the widely used WMT14 En-De machine translation task demonstrate that our model outperforms AAN and SAN models with fewer parameters, providing highly competitive performance.

label: coling
text: Datasets with significant proportions of bias present threats for training a trustworthy model on NLU tasks. Despite yielding great progress, current debiasing methods impose excessive reliance on the knowledge of bias attributes. Definition of the attributes, however, is elusive and varies across different datasets. In addition, leveraging these attributes at input level to bias mitigation may leave a gap between intrinsic properties and the underlying decision rule. To narrow down this gap and liberate the supervision on bias, we suggest extending bias mitigation into feature space. Therefore, a novel model, Recovering Intended-Feature Subspace with Knowledge-Free (RISK) is developed. Assuming that shortcut features caused by various biases are unintended for prediction, RISK views them as redundant features. When delving into a lower manifold to remove redundancies, RISK reveals that an extremely low-dimensional subspace with intended features can robustly represent the highly biased dataset. Empirical results demonstrate our model can consistently improve model generalization to out-of-distribution set, and achieves a new state-of-the-art performance.

label: coling
text: Datasets with a high proportion of bias pose a threat to training a trustworthy model for natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. Despite the progress made by current debiasing methods, they rely heavily on the knowledge of the attributes that cause the bias. However, defining these attributes is challenging and varies across datasets. Additionally, addressing the bias at the input level may result in a disconnect between the intrinsic properties of the dataset and the decision rule used by the model. To overcome these limitations and reduce the dependence on bias knowledge, we propose extending the debiasing process into the feature space. Our novel model, the Recovering Intended-Feature Subspace with Knowledge-Free (RISK) approach, assumes that features caused by biases are unintended and redundant. By removing these redundancies, RISK reveals a low-dimensional subspace of intended features that robustly represents the highly biased dataset. Empirical results show that our model consistently improves model generalization to out-of-distribution sets and achieves a new state-of-the-art performance.

label: coling
text: We present a new dataset comprising tweets for the novel task of detecting biographically relevant utterances. Biographically relevant utterances are all those utterances that reveal some persistent and non-trivial information about the author of a tweet, e.g. habits, (dis)likes, family status, physical appearance, employment information, health issues etc. Unlike previous research we do not restrict biographical relevance to a small fixed set of pre-defined relations. Next to classification experiments employing state-of-the-art classifiers to establish strong baselines for future work, we carry out a linguistic analysis that compares the predictiveness of various high-level features. We also show that the task is different from established tasks, such as aspectual classification or sentiment analysis.

label: coling
text: We present a new dataset of tweets for the purpose of detecting biographically relevant utterances. These utterances are those that reveal persistent and non-trivial information about the author of the tweet, such as habits, likes and dislikes, family status, physical appearance, employment information, and health issues. Unlike previous research, we do not limit biographical relevance to a fixed set of pre-defined relations. In addition to conducting classification experiments using state-of-the-art classifiers to establish strong baselines for future work, we also perform a linguistic analysis to compare the predictiveness of various high-level features. Our results demonstrate that this task is distinct from established tasks, such as aspectual classification and sentiment analysis.

label: coling
text: As AI is more and more pervasive in everyday life, humans have an increasing demand to understand its behavior and decisions. Most research on explainable AI builds on the premise that there is one ideal explanation to be found. In fact, however, everyday explanations are co-constructed in a dialogue between the person explaining (the explainer) and the specific person being explained to (the explainee). In this paper, we introduce a first corpus of dialogical explanations to enable NLP research on how humans explain as well as on how AI can learn to imitate this process. The corpus consists of 65 transcribed English dialogues from the Wired video series 5 Levels, explaining 13 topics to five explainees of different proficiency. All 1550 dialogue turns have been manually labeled by five independent professionals for the topic discussed as well as for the dialogue act and the explanation move performed. We analyze linguistic patterns of explainers and explainees, and we explore differences across proficiency levels. BERT-based baseline results indicate that sequence information helps predicting topics, acts, and moves effectively.
