text: Chit-chat models are known to have several problems: they lack specificity, do not display a consistent personality and are often not very captivating. In this work we present the task of making chit-chat more engaging by conditioning on profile information. We collect data and train models to (i)condition on their given profile information; and (ii) information about the person they are talking to, resulting in improved dialogues, as measured by next utterance prediction. Since (ii) is initially unknown our model is trained to engage its partner with personal topics, and we show the resulting dialogue can be used to predict profile information about the interlocutors.

label: acl
text: Chit-chat models are plagued by several issues, including a lack of specificity, inconsistent personalities, and unengaging conversations. To overcome these challenges, our work focuses on enhancing chit-chat by incorporating profile information. We gather data and train models to take into account both their own profile information and information about the person they are communicating with. This results in more engaging dialogues, as demonstrated by improved next utterance prediction. Initially, the information about the interlocutor (ii) is unknown, so our model is trained to initiate conversations with personal topics. Our findings show that such dialogues can be used to accurately predict profile information about the individuals involved.

label: acl
text: Procedural text understanding aims at tracking the states (e.g., create, move, destroy) and locations of the entities mentioned in a given paragraph. To effectively track the states and locations, it is essential to capture the rich semantic relations between entities, actions, and locations in the paragraph. Although recent works have achieved substantial progress, most of them focus on leveraging the inherent constraints or incorporating external knowledge for state prediction. The rich semantic relations in the given paragraph are largely overlooked. In this paper, we propose a novel approach (REAL) to procedural text understanding, where we build a general framework to systematically model the entity-entity, entity-action, and entity-location relations using a graph neural network. We further develop algorithms for graph construction, representation learning, and state and location tracking. We evaluate the proposed approach on two benchmark datasets, ProPara, and Recipes. The experimental results show that our method outperforms strong baselines by a large margin, i.e., 5.0% on ProPara and 3.2% on Recipes, illustrating the utility of semantic relations and the effectiveness of the graph-based reasoning model.

label: acl
text: The aim of procedural text understanding is to monitor the changes in states (such as creation, movement, and destruction) and locations of entities within a given paragraph. To achieve this, it is crucial to identify the complex semantic relationships between entities, actions, and locations in the text. Although recent advancements have been made in this field, most of the existing methods concentrate on predicting states through inherent constraints or external knowledge. The rich semantic relationships within the paragraph are often disregarded. In this study, we introduce a new approach, REAL, to tackle this issue. Our approach involves constructing a graph neural network to model entity-entity, entity-action, and entity-location relationships. We have developed algorithms for graph construction, representation learning, and state and location tracking. Our method was tested on two benchmark datasets, ProPara, and Recipes, and it outperformed strong baselines by a large margin of 5.0% on ProPara and 3.2% on Recipes. This demonstrates the importance of semantic relationships and the effectiveness of our graph-based reasoning model.

label: acl
text: Embedding knowledge graphs (KGs) into continuous vector spaces is a focus of current research. Early works performed this task via simple models developed over KG triples. Recent attempts focused on either designing more complicated triple scoring models, or incorporating extra information beyond triples. This paper, by contrast, investigates the potential of using very simple constraints to improve KG embedding. We examine non-negativity constraints on entity representations and approximate entailment constraints on relation representations. The former help to learn compact and interpretable representations for entities. The latter further encode regularities of logical entailment between relations into their distributed representations. These constraints impose prior beliefs upon the structure of the embedding space, without negative impacts on efficiency or scalability. Evaluation on WordNet, Freebase, and DBpedia shows that our approach is simple yet surprisingly effective, significantly and consistently outperforming competitive baselines. The constraints imposed indeed improve model interpretability, leading to a substantially increased structuring of the embedding space. Code and data are available at https://github.com/iieir-km/ComplEx-NNE_AER.

label: acl
text: The focus of current research is embedding knowledge graphs (KGs) into continuous vector spaces. Early works attempted this task using simple models based on KG triples. However, recent efforts have shifted towards more complex triple scoring models or incorporating additional information beyond triples. This paper explores the impact of using simple constraints to enhance KG embedding, examining non-negativity constraints on entity representations and approximate entailment constraints on relation representations. These constraints provide prior beliefs about the structure of the embedding space, without sacrificing efficiency or scalability. Our approach, which is simple yet effective, outperforms competitive baselines on WordNet, Freebase, and DBpedia. The constraints imposed lead to a more interpretable and structured embedding space. The code and data can be found at https://github.com/iieir-km/ComplEx-NNE_AER.

label: naacl
text: Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) aims to predict the sentiment polarity towards a particular aspect in a sentence. Recently, graph neural networks based on dependency tree convey rich structural information which is proven to be utility for ABSA. However, how to effectively harness the semantic and syntactic structure information from the dependency tree remains a challenging research question. In this paper, we propose a novel Syntactic and Semantic Enhanced Graph Convolutional Network (SSEGCN) model for ABSA task. Specifically, we propose an aspect-aware attention mechanism combined with self-attention to obtain attention score matrices of a sentence, which can not only learn the aspect-related semantic correlations, but also learn the global semantics of the sentence. In order to obtain comprehensive syntactic structure information, we construct syntactic mask matrices of the sentence according to the different syntactic distances between words. Furthermore, to combine syntactic structure and semantic information, we equip the attention score matrices by syntactic mask matrices. Finally, we enhance the node representations with graph convolutional network over attention score matrices for ABSA. Experimental results on benchmark datasets illustrate that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

label: naacl
text: The Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) aims to predict the sentiment polarity towards a specific aspect in a sentence. Recently, graph neural networks based on dependency trees have been found to be useful in ABSA due to their ability to convey rich structural information. However, effectively utilizing the semantic and syntactic information from the dependency tree remains a challenging research question. To address this issue, we propose a novel Syntactic and Semantic Enhanced Graph Convolutional Network (SSEGCN) model for ABSA. Our model incorporates an aspect-aware attention mechanism combined with self-attention to obtain attention score matrices for a sentence, which can learn both the aspect-related semantic correlations and the global semantics of the sentence. Additionally, we construct syntactic mask matrices to obtain comprehensive syntactic structure information and enhance node representations with graph convolutional networks over attention score matrices. Our experiments on benchmark datasets show that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: The SimpleQuestions dataset is one of the most commonly used benchmarks for studying single-relation factoid questions. In this paper, we present new evidence that this benchmark can be nearly solved by standard methods. First, we show that ambiguity in the data bounds performance at 83.4%; many questions have more than one equally plausible interpretation. Second, we introduce a baseline that sets a new state-of-the-art performance level at 78.1% accuracy, despite using standard methods. Finally, we report an empirical analysis showing that the upperbound is loose; roughly a quarter of the remaining errors are also not resolvable from the linguistic signal. Together, these results suggest that the SimpleQuestions dataset is nearly solved.

label: emnlp
text: The SimpleQuestions dataset is a widely used benchmark for evaluating single-relation factoid question-answering systems. In this paper, we provide new evidence that standard methods can nearly solve this benchmark. We demonstrate that ambiguity in the data limits performance to 83.4% accuracy, as many questions have multiple plausible interpretations. We also establish a new state-of-the-art performance level at 78.1% accuracy using standard methods. Our empirical analysis reveals that the upper bound is not strict, with roughly 25% of remaining errors being unresolvable from the linguistic signal. These findings indicate that the SimpleQuestions dataset is close to being fully solved.

label: acl
text: Neural models for distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) encode each sentence in an entity-pair bag separately. These are then aggregated for bag-level relation prediction. Since, at encoding time, these approaches do not allow information to flow from other sentences in the bag, we believe that they do not utilize the available bag data to the fullest. In response, we explore a simple baseline approach (PARE) in which all sentences of a bag are concatenated into a passage of sentences, and encoded jointly using BERT. The contextual embeddings of tokens are aggregated using attention with the candidate relation as query – this summary of whole passage predicts the candidate relation. We find that our simple baseline solution outperforms existing state-of-the-art DS-RE models in both monolingual and multilingual DS-RE datasets.

label: acl
text: Neural models for Distantly Supervised Relation Extraction (DS-RE) encode each sentence in an entity-pair bag separately, which are then aggregated for bag-level relation prediction. However, this approach does not allow information to flow from other sentences in the bag, leading to a suboptimal utilization of the available bag data. To address this, we propose a simple baseline solution, PARE, in which all sentences of a bag are concatenated into a single passage, and jointly encoded using BERT. The contextual embeddings of tokens are aggregated using attention with the candidate relation as the query, resulting in a summary of the entire passage that predicts the candidate relation. Our results show that this simple baseline outperforms existing state-of-the-art DS-RE models on both monolingual and multilingual DS-RE datasets.

label: acl
text: As a fine-grained task, the annotation cost of aspect term extraction is extremely high. Recent attempts alleviate this issue using domain adaptation that transfers common knowledge across domains. Since most aspect terms are domain-specific, they cannot be transferred directly. Existing methods solve this problem by associating aspect terms with pivot words (we call this passive domain adaptation because the transfer of aspect terms relies on the links to pivots). However, all these methods need either manually labeled pivot words or expensive computing resources to build associations. In this paper, we propose a novel active domain adaptation method. Our goal is to transfer aspect terms by actively supplementing transferable knowledge. To this end, we construct syntactic bridges by recognizing syntactic roles as pivots instead of as links to pivots. We also build semantic bridges by retrieving transferable semantic prototypes. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches.

label: acl
text: The cost of annotating aspect term extraction is very high due to its fine-grained nature. Recent efforts have attempted to reduce this cost by using domain adaptation, which transfers common knowledge across domains. However, most aspect terms are specific to a particular domain and cannot be transferred directly. Existing methods address this issue by linking aspect terms with pivot words, which we refer to as passive domain adaptation. However, these methods require either manual labeling of pivot words or significant computational resources to establish the links. In this paper, we present a novel active domain adaptation method that transfers aspect terms by actively supplementing transferable knowledge. Our approach involves constructing syntactic bridges by recognizing syntactic roles as pivots, and semantic bridges by retrieving transferable semantic prototypes. Our experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches.

label: naacl
text: Virtual agents are becoming a prominent channel of interaction in customer service. Not all customer interactions are smooth, however, and some can become almost comically bad. In such instances, a human agent might need to step in and salvage the conversation. Detecting bad conversations is important since disappointing customer service may threaten customer loyalty and impact revenue. In this paper, we outline an approach to detecting such egregious conversations, using behavioral cues from the user, patterns in agent responses, and user-agent interaction. Using logs of two commercial systems, we show that using these features improves the detection F1-score by around 20% over using textual features alone. In addition, we show that those features are common across two quite different domains and, arguably, universal.

label: naacl
text: Virtual agents are becoming a widely-used channel for customer service interactions. However, not all interactions are seamless and some can become incredibly problematic. In such cases, a human agent may be required to intervene and resolve the situation. Detecting these problematic interactions is crucial as poor customer service can negatively affect customer loyalty and result in revenue loss. This paper outlines an approach to identify these problematic interactions by analyzing behavioral cues from the customer, patterns in the agent's responses, and the overall interaction between the customer and agent. Using data from two commercial systems, we demonstrate that incorporating these features into the detection process results in a 20% improvement in the F1-score compared to using textual features alone. Furthermore, we show that these features are universal across different domains.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based pre-trained language models like BERT, though powerful in many tasks, are expensive in both memory and computation, due to their large number of parameters. Previous works show that some parameters in these models can be pruned away without severe accuracy drop. However, these redundant features contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the training data and removing them weakens the model's representation ability. In this paper, we propose GhostBERT, which generates more features with very cheap operations from the remaining features. In this way, GhostBERT has similar memory and computational cost as the pruned model, but enjoys much larger representation power. The proposed ghost module can also be applied to unpruned BERT models to enhance their performance with negligible additional parameters and computation. Empirical results on the GLUE benchmark on three backbone models (i.e., BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA) verify the efficacy of our proposed method.

label: acl
text: The Transformer-based pre-trained language models such as BERT are highly effective in many tasks, but they are costly in terms of both memory and computation due to the large number of parameters they possess. Previous studies have shown that some of these parameters can be removed without causing a significant drop in accuracy. However, these redundant features play a crucial role in providing a comprehensive understanding of the training data, and their removal weakens the representation ability of the model. To address this issue, we introduce GhostBERT, a model that generates additional features from the remaining ones using cheap operations. This results in a model that has a similar memory and computational cost to the pruned model, but with a much larger representation power. Additionally, the proposed ghost module can be applied to unpruned BERT models to improve performance with minimal additional parameters and computation. Our empirical results on the GLUE benchmark using three backbone models (BERT, RoBERTa, and ELECTRA) demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

label: acl
text: Natural language inference (NLI) has been widely used as a task to train and evaluate models for language understanding. However, the ability of NLI models to perform inferences requiring understanding of figurative language such as idioms and metaphors remains understudied. We introduce the IMPLI (Idiomatic and Metaphoric Paired Language Inference) dataset, an English dataset consisting of paired sentences spanning idioms and metaphors. We develop novel methods to generate 24k semiautomatic pairs as well as manually creating 1.8k gold pairs. We use IMPLI to evaluate NLI models based on RoBERTa fine-tuned on the widely used MNLI dataset. We then show that while they can reliably detect entailment relationship between figurative phrases with their literal counterparts, they perform poorly on similarly structured examples where pairs are designed to be non-entailing. This suggests the limits of current NLI models with regard to understanding figurative language and this dataset serves as a benchmark for future improvements in this direction.

label: acl
text: Natural language inference (NLI) is a widely used task to train and evaluate models for language understanding. However, the understanding of figurative language like idioms and metaphors in NLI models is understudied. To address this, we introduce the IMPLI (Idiomatic and Metaphoric Paired Language Inference) dataset, a collection of 24k semiautomatic and 1.8k manually created English paired sentences that span idioms and metaphors. We evaluate the performance of RoBERTa fine-tuned on the MNLI dataset using IMPLI, and find that while these models can accurately detect entailment relationships between figurative phrases and their literal counterparts, they struggle with non-entailing pairs. This highlights the limitations of current NLI models in understanding figurative language and IMPLI serves as a benchmark for future advancements in this area.

label: naacl
text: Understanding longer narratives or participating in conversations requires tracking of discourse entities that have been mentioned. Indefinite noun phrases (NPs), such as `a dog', frequently introduce discourse entities but this behavior is modulated by sentential operators such as negation. For example, `a dog' in `Arthur doesn't own a dog' does not introduce a discourse entity due to the presence of negation. In this work, we adapt the psycholinguistic assessment of language models paradigm to higher-level linguistic phenomena and introduce an English evaluation suite that targets the knowledge of the interactions between sentential operators and indefinite NPs. We use this evaluation suite for a fine-grained investigation of the entity tracking abilities of the Transformer-based models GPT-2 and GPT-3. We find that while the models are to a certain extent sensitive to the interactions we investigate, they are all challenged by the presence of multiple NPs and their behavior is not systematic, which suggests that even models at the scale of GPT-3 do not fully acquire basic entity tracking abilities.

label: naacl
text: To understand longer narratives or participate in conversations, it is important to track the discourse entities that have been mentioned. Indefinite noun phrases (NPs), such as "a dog," often introduce discourse entities. However, this behavior can be affected by sentential operators, such as negation. For instance, the NP "a dog" in "Arthur doesn't own a dog" does not introduce a discourse entity due to the presence of negation. In this study, we adapt the psycholinguistic assessment of language models paradigm to higher-level linguistic phenomena and introduce an English evaluation suite that focuses on the relationship between sentential operators and indefinite NPs. We use this evaluation suite to examine the entity tracking abilities of GPT-2 and GPT-3, two Transformer-based models. Our findings reveal that while these models are somewhat sensitive to the interactions we investigate, they struggle with multiple NPs and their behavior is inconsistent, which suggests that even large models like GPT-3 do not fully possess basic entity tracking abilities.

label: coling
text: Supervised open relation extraction aims to discover novel relations by leveraging supervised data of pre-defined relations. However, most existing methods do not achieve effective knowledge transfer from pre-defined relations to novel relations, they have difficulties generating high-quality pseudo-labels for unsupervised data of novel relations and usually suffer from the error propagation issue. In this paper, we propose a Cluster-aware Pseudo-Labeling (CaPL) method to improve the pseudo-labels quality and transfer more knowledge for discovering novel relations. Specifically, the model is firstly pre-trained with the pre-defined relations to learn the relation representations. To improve the pseudo-labels quality, the distances between each instance and all cluster centers are used to generate the cluster-aware soft pseudo-labels for novel relations. To mitigate the catastrophic forgetting issue, we design the consistency regularization loss to make better use of the pseudo-labels and jointly train the model with both unsupervised and supervised data. Experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate that our proposed method achieves new state-of-the-arts performance.

label: coling
text: The aim of supervised open relation extraction is to uncover new relations by utilizing supervised data of predefined relations. However, most existing methods struggle to effectively transfer knowledge from predefined relations to new relations, and they often face challenges in generating high-quality pseudo-labels for unsupervised data of new relations, as well as suffer from error propagation. In this paper, we present a Cluster-aware Pseudo-Labeling (CaPL) method to enhance the quality of pseudo-labels and better transfer knowledge for discovering new relations. Our method begins by pre-training the model with predefined relations to learn the relation representations. To improve pseudo-label quality, we use the distances between each instance and all cluster centers to generate cluster-aware soft pseudo-labels for new relations. To address the issue of catastrophic forgetting, we introduce a consistency regularization loss to make better use of the pseudo-labels and train the model with both unsupervised and supervised data. Our experiments on two public datasets show that our proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

label: naacl
text: Vocabulary selection, or lexical shortlisting, is a well-known technique to improve latency of Neural Machine Translation models by constraining the set of allowed output words during inference. The chosen set is typically determined by separately trained alignment model parameters, independent of the source-sentence context at inference time. While vocabulary selection appears competitive with respect to automatic quality metrics in prior work, we show that it can fail to select the right set of output words, particularly for semantically non-compositional linguistic phenomena such as idiomatic expressions, leading to reduced translation quality as perceived by humans. Trading off latency for quality by increasing the size of the allowed set is often not an option in real-world scenarios. We propose a model of vocabulary selection, integrated into the neural translation model, that predicts the set of allowed output words from contextualized encoder representations. This restores translation quality of an unconstrained system, as measured by human evaluations on WMT newstest2020 and idiomatic expressions, at an inference latency competitive with alignment-based selection using aggressive thresholds, thereby removing the dependency on separately trained alignment models.

label: naacl
text: The technique of vocabulary selection, also known as lexical shortlisting, is used to improve the speed of Neural Machine Translation models by limiting the set of words that can be used in the output during inference. This set is usually determined by a separate alignment model that is not influenced by the source-sentence context during inference. Although vocabulary selection has been shown to be effective in prior work, it can be problematic for semantically non-compositional linguistic phenomena such as idiomatic expressions, leading to lower quality translations as perceived by humans. In real-world scenarios, increasing the size of the allowed set to improve quality is not always possible due to the trade-off with latency. We propose a new model of vocabulary selection that integrates into the neural translation model and predicts the set of allowed output words based on the encoder's contextualized representations. This approach restores translation quality to the level of an unconstrained system, as demonstrated by human evaluations on WMT newstest2020 and idiomatic expressions. The latency of this method is competitive with alignment-based selection using aggressive thresholds, and it eliminates the need for a separate alignment model.

label: naacl
text: Although transfer learning has been shown to be successful for tasks like object and speech recognition, its applicability to question answering (QA) has yet to be well-studied. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments to investigate the transferability of knowledge learned from a source QA dataset to a target dataset using two QA models. The performance of both models on a TOEFL listening comprehension test (Tseng et al., 2016) and MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013) is significantly improved via a simple transfer learning technique from MovieQA (Tapaswi et al., 2016). In particular, one of the models achieves the state-of-the-art on all target datasets; for the TOEFL listening comprehension test, it outperforms the previous best model by 7%. Finally, we show that transfer learning is helpful even in unsupervised scenarios when correct answers for target QA dataset examples are not available.

label: naacl
text: Although transfer learning has been shown to be effective for tasks such as object and speech recognition, its applicability to question answering (QA) has not been thoroughly explored. This paper presents the results of extensive experiments that investigate the transfer of knowledge from a source QA dataset to a target dataset using two QA models. The results showed that the performance of both models on the TOEFL listening comprehension test (Tseng et al., 2016) and MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013) was significantly improved through the application of a simple transfer learning technique from MovieQA (Tapaswi et al., 2016). In particular, one of the models achieved the state-of-the-art results on all target datasets and outperformed the previous best model by 7% on the TOEFL listening comprehension test. The findings also demonstrate that transfer learning can be beneficial even in unsupervised scenarios where the correct answers for the target QA dataset examples are not available.

label: acl
text: Relation linking is a crucial component of Knowledge Base Question Answering systems. Existing systems use a wide variety of heuristics, or ensembles of multiple systems, heavily relying on the surface question text. However, the explicit semantic parse of the question is a rich source of relation information that is not taken advantage of. We propose a simple transformer-based neural model for relation linking that leverages the AMR semantic parse of a sentence. Our system significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on 4 popular benchmark datasets. These are based on either DBpedia or Wikidata, demonstrating that our approach is effective across KGs.

label: acl
text: Relation linking is a vital aspect of Knowledge Base Question Answering systems. Despite the use of various heuristics or combinations of multiple systems, current systems heavily rely on the text of the surface question. However, the explicit semantic parse of the question provides a wealth of relation information that goes unused. Our proposed solution is a straightforward transformer-based neural model that utilizes the AMR semantic parse of the sentence. Our system surpasses the state-of-the-art performance on four popular benchmark datasets based on DBpedia or Wikidata, showing that our approach is effective across different knowledge graphs.

label: coling
text: Developing conversational systems that can converse in many languages is an interesting challenge for natural language processing. In this paper, we introduce multilingual addressee and response selection. In this task, a conversational system predicts an appropriate addressee and response for an input message in multiple languages. A key to developing such multilingual responding systems is how to utilize high-resource language data to compensate for low-resource language data. We present several knowledge transfer methods for conversational systems. To evaluate our methods, we create a new multilingual conversation dataset. Experiments on the dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods.

label: coling
text: The development of conversational systems capable of communicating in multiple languages presents a fascinating challenge for natural language processing. This paper introduces a multilingual addressee and response selection system, which predicts the appropriate addressee and response for an incoming message in multiple languages. A crucial aspect of creating such multilingual conversational systems is the utilization of high-resource language data to overcome limitations in low-resource language data. We propose several knowledge transfer methods for conversational systems and evaluate them using a newly created multilingual conversation dataset. The results of our experiments show the efficacy of our methods.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we propose a generalizable dialog generation approach that adapts multi-turn reasoning, one recent advancement in the field of document comprehension, to generate responses (“answers”) by taking current conversation session context as a “document” and current query as a “question”. The major idea is to represent a conversation session into memories upon which attention-based memory reading mechanism can be performed multiple times, so that (1) user's query is properly extended by contextual clues and (2) optimal responses are step-by-step generated. Considering that the speakers of one conversation are not limited to be one, we separate the single memory used for document comprehension into different groups for speaker-specific topic and opinion embedding. Namely, we utilize the queries' memory, the responses' memory, and their unified memory, following the time sequence of the conversation session. Experiments on Japanese 10-sentence (5-round) conversation modeling show impressive results on how multi-turn reasoning can produce more diverse and acceptable responses than state-of-the-art single-turn and non-reasoning baselines.

label: naacl
text: We present a novel approach to dialog generation that incorporates multi-turn reasoning, a recent advancement in document comprehension, to generate responses by treating the current conversation session as a "document" and the current query as a "question." Our approach involves representing the conversation session as memories, which are then processed multiple times using an attention-based memory reading mechanism to extend the user's query with contextual clues and generate optimal responses step-by-step. To accommodate for the possibility of multiple speakers in a conversation, we divide the memory used for document comprehension into separate groups for speaker-specific topic and opinion embedding, using the queries' memory, the responses' memory, and their unified memory in sequence. Our experiments on a 10-sentence (5-round) conversation modeling task in Japanese demonstrate that multi-turn reasoning can produce more diverse and acceptable responses than single-turn and non-reasoning baselines.

label: emnlp
text: We carry out a syntactic analysis of two state-of-the-art sentiment analyzers, Google Cloud Natural Language and Stanford CoreNLP, to assess their classification accuracy on sentences with negative polarity items. We were motivated by the absence of studies investigating sentiment analyzer performance on sentences with polarity items, a common construct in human language. Our analysis focuses on two sentential structures: downward entailment and non-monotone quantifiers; and demonstrates weaknesses of Google Natural Language and CoreNLP in capturing polarity item information. We describe the particular syntactic phenomenon that these analyzers fail to understand that any ideal sentiment analyzer must. We also provide a set of 150 test sentences that any ideal sentiment analyzer must be able to understand.

label: emnlp
text: We conducted a syntactic analysis of two state-of-the-art sentiment analyzers, Google Cloud Natural Language and Stanford CoreNLP, to evaluate their classification accuracy on sentences with negative polarity items. The motivation for this study stems from the lack of research on the performance of sentiment analyzers on sentences with polarity items, a common feature in human language. Our analysis focused on two types of sentential structures: downward entailment and non-monotone quantifiers, and revealed weaknesses in the ability of Google Natural Language and CoreNLP to capture polarity item information. We identified the specific syntactic phenomenon that these analyzers fail to comprehend, which is essential for any ideal sentiment analyzer. Additionally, we have provided a set of 150 test sentences that should be understood by any ideal sentiment analyzer.

label: acl
text: We present a direct speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) model that translates speech from one language to speech in another language without relying on intermediate text generation. We tackle the problem by first applying a self-supervised discrete speech encoder on the target speech and then training a sequence-to-sequence speech-to-unit translation (S2UT) model to predict the discrete representations of the target speech. When target text transcripts are available, we design a joint speech and text training framework that enables the model to generate dual modality output (speech and text) simultaneously in the same inference pass. Experiments on the Fisher Spanish-English dataset show that the proposed framework yields improvement of 6.7 BLEU compared with a baseline direct S2ST model that predicts spectrogram features. When trained without any text transcripts, our model performance is comparable to models that predict spectrograms and are trained with text supervision, showing the potential of our system for translation between unwritten languages.

label: acl
text: We present a direct speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) model that translates speech from one language to speech in another language without relying on intermediate text generation. Our approach involves applying a self-supervised discrete speech encoder on the target speech and training a sequence-to-sequence speech-to-unit translation (S2UT) model to predict the discrete representations of the target speech. When text transcripts are available, we have designed a joint speech and text training framework that allows the model to generate both speech and text outputs simultaneously during the same inference process. Our experiments on the Fisher Spanish-English dataset demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms a baseline direct S2ST model that predicts spectrogram features by 6.7 BLEU. Furthermore, when trained without any text transcripts, our model performance is comparable to models that predict spectrograms and are trained with text supervision, highlighting the potential of our system for translation between unwritten languages.

label: coling
text: Often questions provided to open-domain question answering systems are ambiguous. Traditional QA systems that provide a single answer are incapable of answering ambiguous questions since the question may be interpreted in several ways and may have multiple distinct answers. In this paper, we address multi-answer retrieval which entails retrieving passages that can capture majority of the diverse answers to the question. We propose a re-ranking based approach using Determinantal point processes utilizing BERT as kernels. Our method jointly considers query-passage relevance and passage-passage correlation to retrieve passages that are both query-relevant and diverse. Results demonstrate that our re-ranking technique outperforms state-of-the-art method on the AmbigQA dataset.

label: coling
text: Open-domain question answering systems are frequently presented with ambiguous questions, which pose a challenge for traditional QA systems that only provide a single answer. These systems are not equipped to handle ambiguous questions as the same question may have multiple interpretations and answers. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a multi-answer retrieval approach that retrieves passages that capture the majority of diverse answers to the question. Our re-ranking-based approach uses Determinantal Point Processes with BERT as kernels and considers both query-passage relevance and passage-passage correlation to retrieve passages that are both relevant to the query and diverse in their answers. Our results show that our re-ranking technique outperforms the state-of-the-art method on the AmbigQA dataset.

label: coling
text: Multi-label Text Classification (MLTC) is the task of categorizing documents into one or more topics. Considering the large volumes of data and varying domains of such tasks, fully supervised learning requires manually fully annotated datasets which is costly and time-consuming. In this paper, we propose BERT-Flow-VAE (BFV), a Weakly-Supervised Multi-Label Text Classification (WSMLTC) model that reduces the need for full supervision. This new model (1) produces BERT sentence embeddings and calibrates them using a flow model, (2) generates an initial topic-document matrix by averaging results of a seeded sparse topic model and a textual entailment model which only require surface name of topics and 4-6 seed words per topic, and (3) adopts a VAE framework to reconstruct the embeddings under the guidance of the topic-document matrix. Finally, (4) it uses the means produced by the encoder model in the VAE architecture as predictions for MLTC. Experimental results on 6 multi-label datasets show that BFV can substantially outperform other baseline WSMLTC models in key metrics and achieve approximately 84% performance of a fully-supervised model.

label: coling
text: Multi-label Text Classification (MLTC) involves categorizing documents into one or more topics. The large volume of data and diverse domains of these tasks make fully supervised learning challenging, as it requires manually annotated datasets, which are costly and time-consuming. To address this issue, we present BERT-Flow-VAE (BFV), a Weakly-Supervised Multi-Label Text Classification (WSMLTC) model that reduces the need for full supervision. BFV (1) creates BERT sentence embeddings and calibrates them using a flow model, (2) generates an initial topic-document matrix by combining the results of a seeded sparse topic model and a textual entailment model, which only require surface names of topics and 4-6 seed words per topic, (3) employs a VAE framework to reconstruct the embeddings guided by the topic-document matrix, and (4) uses the means produced by the encoder model in the VAE architecture as MLTC predictions. Our experiments on six multi-label datasets demonstrate that BFV outperforms other baseline WSMLTC models in key metrics, reaching approximately 84% performance of a fully-supervised model.

text: Automated radiology report generation aims to generate paragraphs that describe fine-grained visual differences among cases, especially those between the normal and the diseased. Existing methods seldom consider the cross-modal alignment between textual and visual features and tend to ignore disease tags as an auxiliary for report generation. To bridge the gap between textual and visual information, in this study, we propose a “Jointly learning framework for automated disease Prediction and radiology report Generation (JPG)” to improve the quality of reports through the interaction between the main task (report generation) and two auxiliary tasks (feature alignment and disease prediction). The feature alignment and disease prediction help the model learn text-correlated visual features and record diseases as keywords so that it can output high-quality reports. Besides, the improved reports in turn provide additional harder samples for feature alignment and disease prediction to learn more precise visual and textual representations and improve prediction accuracy. All components are jointly trained in a manner that helps improve them iteratively and progressively. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of JPG on the most commonly used IU X-RAY dataset, showing its superior performance over multiple state-of-the-art image captioning and medical report generation methods with regard to BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE metrics.

label: coling
text: The goal of automated radiology report generation is to produce descriptions of subtle visual differences between cases, particularly those that distinguish between normal and diseased images. However, current methods often neglect the connection between textual and visual features and overlook the use of disease tags as a tool for report generation. To address this gap, we introduce the Jointly learning framework for automated disease Prediction and radiology report Generation (JPG). This framework enhances report quality by integrating the main task of report generation with two auxiliary tasks: feature alignment and disease prediction. The feature alignment and disease prediction help the model to learn text-correlated visual features and identify disease-related keywords, resulting in high-quality reports. Additionally, the improved reports provide more challenging samples for the feature alignment and disease prediction tasks, leading to improved visual and textual representations and improved prediction accuracy. All components are trained together, allowing for iterative and progressive improvement. Our experiments on the widely used IU X-RAY dataset demonstrate the superiority of JPG compared to state-of-the-art image captioning and medical report generation methods, as measured by BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE metrics.

label: naacl
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental and important task in NLP, aiming at identifying named entities (NEs) from free text. Recently, since the multi-head attention mechanism applied in the Transformer model can effectively capture longer contextual information, Transformer-based models have become the mainstream methods and have achieved significant performance in this task. Unfortunately, although these models can capture effective global context information, they are still limited in the local feature and position information extraction, which is critical in NER. In this paper, to address this limitation, we propose a novel Hero-Gang Neural structure (HGN), including the Hero and Gang module, to leverage both global and local information to promote NER. Specifically, the Hero module is composed of a Transformer-based encoder to maintain the advantage of the self-attention mechanism, and the Gang module utilizes a multi-window recurrent module to extract local features and position information under the guidance of the Hero module. Afterward, the proposed multi-window attention effectively combines global information and multiple local features for predicting entity labels. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

label: naacl
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP) that involves identifying named entities (NEs) from free text. Recently, the application of the multi-head attention mechanism in the Transformer model has made it the dominant method for NER, as it effectively captures longer contextual information. However, these models are still limited in their ability to extract local features and position information, which is critical for NER. To address this limitation, we present a novel Hero-Gang Neural structure (HGN) that leverages both global and local information to enhance NER. The Hero module is a Transformer-based encoder that leverages the self-attention mechanism, while the Gang module uses a multi-window recurrent module to extract local features and position information, guided by the Hero module. Our proposed multi-window attention then effectively combines global information and multiple local features to predict entity labels. Our experiments on various benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of our proposed model.

label: acl
text: It is a common practice for recent works in vision language cross-modal reasoning to adopt a binary or multi-choice classification formulation taking as input a set of source image(s) and textual query. In this work, we take a sober look at such an “unconditional” formulation in the sense that no prior knowledge is specified with respect to the source image(s). Inspired by the designs of both visual commonsense reasoning and natural language inference tasks, we propose a new task termed “Premise-based Multi-modal Reasoning” (PMR) where a textual premise is the background presumption on each source image.The PMR dataset contains 15,360 manually annotated samples which are created by a multi-phase crowd-sourcing process. With selected high-quality movie screenshots and human-curated premise templates from 6 pre-defined categories, we ask crowd-source workers to write one true hypothesis and three distractors (4 choices) given the premise and image through a cross-check procedure.

text:
The proposed PMR task and dataset present a new challenge for the research community in the field of cross-modal reasoning and vision-language integration.

It is common for recent works in cross-modal reasoning between vision and language to adopt a binary or multi-choice classification format, using a set of source images and a textual query as input. However, in this work, we critically examine this "unconditional" format, which does not specify any prior knowledge with regards to the source images. We introduce a new task, "Premise-based Multi-modal Reasoning" (PMR), that draws inspiration from both visual commonsense reasoning and natural language inference tasks. PMR is based on a textual premise that serves as a background assumption for each source image. The PMR dataset consists of 15,360 samples, created through a multi-phase crowd-sourcing process. High-quality movie screenshots and human-curated premise templates from six pre-defined categories were selected, and crowd-source workers were asked to write one true hypothesis and three distractors (four choices in total) based on the premise and image, following a cross-check procedure. The PMR task and dataset present a new challenge for research in cross-modal reasoning and vision-language integration.

text: Acronym extraction is the task of identifying acronyms and their expanded forms in texts that is necessary for various NLP applications. Despite major progress for this task in recent years, one limitation of existing AE research is that they are limited to the English language and certain domains (i.e., scientific and biomedical). Challenges of AE in other languages and domains are mainly unexplored. As such, lacking annotated datasets in multiple languages and domains has been a major issue to prevent research in this direction. To address this limitation, we propose a new dataset for multilingual and multi-domain AE. Specifically, 27,200 sentences in 6 different languages and 2 new domains, i.e., legal and scientific, are manually annotated for AE. Our experiments on the dataset show that AE in different languages and learning settings has unique challenges, emphasizing the necessity of further research on multilingual and multi-domain AE.

text: Acronym extraction, the task of identifying acronyms and their expanded forms in texts, is crucial for various NLP applications. However, despite recent advancements in this field, existing research is limited to the English language and specific domains, such as scientific and biomedical. The challenges of acronym extraction in other languages and domains remain largely unexplored. The lack of annotated datasets in multiple languages and domains is a major hindrance to further research in this area. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new dataset for multilingual and multi-domain acronym extraction. This dataset includes 27,200 sentences in six languages and two new domains, legal and scientific, which have been manually annotated for acronym extraction. Our experiments on the dataset reveal the unique challenges of acronym extraction in different languages and learning settings, highlighting the need for further research in multilingual and multi-domain acronym extraction.

text: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been recently applied in natural language processing. Various GNN research studies are proposed to learn node interactions within the local graph of each document that contains words, sentences, or topics for inductive text classification. However, most inductive GNNs that are built on a word graph generally take global word embeddings as node features, without referring to document-wise contextual information. Consequently, we find that BERT models can perform better than inductive GNNs. An intuitive follow-up approach is used to enrich GNNs with contextual embeddings from BERT, yet there is a lack of related research. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective unified model, coined ConTextING, with a joint training mechanism to learn from both document embeddings and contextual word interactions simultaneously. Our experiments show that ConTextING outperforms pure inductive GNNs and BERT-style models. The analyses also highlight the benefits of the sub-word graph and joint training with separated classifiers.

text: Recently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to natural language processing. There have been various studies proposing GNNs to learn the interactions between nodes within the local graph of each document. This graph contains words, sentences, or topics for inductive text classification. However, most inductive GNNs that are built on a word graph typically only use global word embeddings as node features and do not consider document-wise contextual information. As a result, we have found that BERT models perform better than inductive GNNs. To address this, we have proposed a simple yet effective solution, ConTextING, which enriches GNNs with contextual embeddings from BERT. Our experiments have shown that ConTextING outperforms both pure inductive GNNs and BERT-style models. The analyses also highlight the benefits of the sub-word graph and joint training with separated classifiers.

label: acl
text: Recent research in multilingual language models (LM) has demonstrated their ability to effectively handle multiple languages in a single model. This holds promise for low web-resource languages (LRL) as multilingual models can enable transfer of supervision from high resource languages to LRLs. However, incorporating a new language in an LM still remains a challenge, particularly for languages with limited corpora and in unseen scripts. In this paper we argue that relatedness among languages in a language family may be exploited to overcome some of the corpora limitations of LRLs, and propose RelateLM. We focus on Indian languages, and exploit relatedness along two dimensions: (1) script (since many Indic scripts originated from the Brahmic script), and (2) sentence structure. RelateLM uses transliteration to convert the unseen script of limited LRL text into the script of a Related Prominent Language (RPL) (Hindi in our case). While exploiting similar sentence structures, RelateLM utilizes readily available bilingual dictionaries to pseudo translate RPL text into LRL corpora. Experiments on multiple real-world benchmark datasets provide validation to our hypothesis that using a related language as pivot, along with transliteration and pseudo translation based data augmentation, can be an effective way to adapt LMs for LRLs, rather than direct training or pivoting through English.

text: Recently, studies on multilingual language models (LMs) have shown their ability to effectively handle multiple languages in a single model. This offers hope for low web-resource languages (LRLs) as multilingual models can transfer supervision from high resource languages to these LRLs. However, adding a new language to an LM remains a challenge, especially for languages with limited corpora and unseen scripts. In this paper, we propose RelateLM, which leverages the relatedness among languages in a language family to overcome some of the limitations of LRLs. We focus on Indian languages and exploit relatedness along two dimensions: script (since many Indic scripts have roots in the Brahmic script) and sentence structure. RelateLM uses transliteration to convert the script of limited LRL text into the script of a related prominent language (RPL) (in our case, Hindi), and uses readily available bilingual dictionaries to pseudo-translate RPL text into LRL corpora. Our experiments on multiple real-world benchmark datasets support our hypothesis that using a related language as a pivot, combined with transliteration and pseudo-translation-based data augmentation, is an effective way to adapt LMs for LRLs, instead of direct training or pivoting through English.

label: coling
text: Humans use different wordings depending on the context to facilitate efficient communication. For example, instead of completely new information, information related to the preceding context is typically placed at the sentence-initial position. In this study, we analyze whether neural language models (LMs) can capture such discourse-level preferences in text generation. Specifically, we focus on a particular aspect of discourse, namely the topic-comment structure. To analyze the linguistic knowledge of LMs separately, we chose the Japanese language, a topic-prominent language, for designing probing tasks, and we created human topicalization judgment data by crowdsourcing. Our experimental results suggest that LMs have different generalizations from humans; LMs exhibited less context-dependent behaviors toward topicalization judgment. These results highlight the need for the additional inductive biases to guide LMs to achieve successful discourse-level generalization.

label: coling
text: Humans use varying wordings in different contexts to communicate effectively. For instance, information related to the previous context is often placed at the beginning of a sentence instead of presenting completely new information. This study examines whether neural language models (LMs) can understand such discourse-level preferences in text generation. Our focus is on the topic-comment structure, a specific aspect of discourse. To assess the linguistic knowledge of LMs, we chose Japanese, a topic-prominent language, for our probing tasks and generated human topicalization judgment data through crowdsourcing. Our results show that LMs have different generalizations from humans, as they exhibit less context-dependent behavior in topicalization judgment. These findings emphasize the need for additional inductive biases to guide LMs in achieving successful discourse-level generalization.

label: emnlp
text: Attention-based neural models have achieved great success in natural language inference (NLI). In this paper, we propose the Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), a general model to capture the interaction between two sentences, which can be an alternative to the attention mechanism for NLI. Specifically, CIN encodes one sentence with the filters dynamically generated based on another sentence. Since the filters may be designed to have various numbers and sizes, CIN can capture more complicated interaction patterns. Experiments on three large datasets demonstrate CIN's efficacy.

label: emnlp
text: In this paper, we present the Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), a novel model for capturing the interaction between two sentences in natural language inference (NLI). CIN offers an alternative to the traditional attention mechanism by encoding one sentence with filters dynamically generated based on the second sentence. This allows for the capture of more complex interaction patterns, as the filters can be designed with varying numbers and sizes. Our experiments on three large datasets demonstrate the efficacy of CIN.

label: coling
text: Applying Reinforcement learning (RL) following maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) pre-training is a versatile method for enhancing neural machine translation (NMT) performance. However, recent work has argued that the gains produced by RL for NMT are mostly due to promoting tokens that have already received a fairly high probability in pre-training. We hypothesize that the large action space is a main obstacle to RL's effectiveness in MT, and conduct two sets of experiments that lend support to our hypothesis. First, we find that reducing the size of the vocabulary improves RL's effectiveness. Second, we find that effectively reducing the dimension of the action space without changing the vocabulary also yields notable improvement as evaluated by BLEU, semantic similarity, and human evaluation. Indeed, by initializing the network's final fully connected layer (that maps the network's internal dimension to the vocabulary dimension), with a layer that generalizes over similar actions, we obtain a substantial improvement in RL performance: 1.5 BLEU points on average.

text: The application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) after Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a useful technique for enhancing Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. However, recent studies have suggested that the improvement in NMT performance achieved through RL is mostly due to the promotion of tokens that already have a high probability from pre-training. Our hypothesis is that the large action space is a major hindrance to the effectiveness of RL in MT. To test this hypothesis, we conducted two sets of experiments. Our findings indicate that reducing the size of the vocabulary improves RL's effectiveness. Additionally, we discovered that reducing the dimension of the action space without changing the vocabulary also results in notable improvement as measured by BLEU, semantic similarity, and human evaluation. Finally, by initializing the final fully connected layer of the network with a layer that generalizes over similar actions, we observed a substantial improvement in RL performance, with an average increase of 1.5 BLEU points.

label: acl
text: Automatic rumor detection is technically very challenging. In this work, we try to learn discriminative features from tweets content by following their non-sequential propagation structure and generate more powerful representations for identifying different type of rumors. We propose two recursive neural models based on a bottom-up and a top-down tree-structured neural networks for rumor representation learning and classification, which naturally conform to the propagation layout of tweets. Results on two public Twitter datasets demonstrate that our recursive neural models 1) achieve much better performance than state-of-the-art approaches; 2) demonstrate superior capacity on detecting rumors at very early stage.

label: acl
text: Automated rumor detection is a technically challenging task. To overcome this challenge, we aim to learn discriminative features from tweet content by considering the non-sequential structure of rumor propagation. Our proposed recursive neural models, based on bottom-up and top-down tree-structured neural networks, generate more powerful representations for identifying different types of rumors. The results of our models on two public Twitter datasets show that they outperform state-of-the-art approaches and have a superior capacity for detecting rumors at an early stage.

text: In this reproduction paper, we replicate and extend several past studies on transfer learning for entity recognition. In particular, we are interested in entity recognition problems where the class labels in the source and target domains are different. Our work is the first direct comparison of these previously published approaches in this problem setting. In addition, we perform experiments on seven new source/target corpus pairs, nearly doubling the total number of corpus pairs that have been studied in all past work combined. Our results empirically demonstrate when each of the published approaches tends to do well. In particular, simpler approaches often work best when there is very little labeled target data, while neural transfer approaches tend to do better when there is more labeled target data.

text: In this paper, we replicate and extend several previous studies on transfer learning for entity recognition. Our focus is on entity recognition problems where the class labels in the source and target domains differ. Our work represents the first direct comparison of these previously published approaches in this specific setting. Additionally, we conduct experiments on seven new source/target corpus pairs, nearly doubling the total number of corpus pairs studied in all previous works combined. Our results provide empirical evidence of when each of the published approaches performs optimally. It is observed that simpler approaches tend to be more effective when there is limited labeled target data, while neural transfer approaches tend to perform better when there is a larger amount of labeled target data.

text: Is bias amplified when neural machine translation (NMT) models are optimized for speed and evaluated on generic test sets using BLEU? We investigate architectures and techniques commonly used to speed up decoding in Transformer-based models, such as greedy search, quantization, average attention networks (AANs) and shallow decoder models and show their effect on gendered noun translation. We construct a new gender bias test set, SimpleGEN, based on gendered noun phrases in which there is a single, unambiguous, correct answer. While we find minimal overall BLEU degradation as we apply speed optimizations, we observe that gendered noun translation performance degrades at a much faster rate.

label: acl
text:
Our results suggest that speed optimizations can amplify gender bias in NMT models.

The amplification of bias in neural machine translation (NMT) models when optimized for speed and evaluated on generic test sets using BLEU is investigated in this study. The impact of commonly used techniques, such as greedy search, quantization, average attention networks (AANs), and shallow decoder models, on gendered noun translation is examined. A new gender bias test set, SimpleGEN, is created based on gendered noun phrases that have a clear and unambiguous correct answer. The results show that while applying speed optimizations results in minimal overall BLEU degradation, gendered noun translation performance deteriorates much faster. Our findings indicate that speed optimizations can increase gender bias in NMT models.

label: acl
text: Entity linking involves aligning textual mentions of named entities to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base. Entity linking systems often exploit relations between textual mentions in a document (e.g., coreference) to decide if the linking decisions are compatible. Unlike previous approaches, which relied on supervised systems or heuristics to predict these relations, we treat relations as latent variables in our neural entity-linking model. We induce the relations without any supervision while optimizing the entity-linking system in an end-to-end fashion. Our multi-relational model achieves the best reported scores on the standard benchmark (AIDA-CoNLL) and substantially outperforms its relation-agnostic version. Its training also converges much faster, suggesting that the injected structural bias helps to explain regularities in the training data.

label: acl
text: Entity linking involves connecting textual mentions of named entities to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base. This process is often facilitated by exploiting the relationships between mentions in a document (such as coreference) to determine the compatibility of linking decisions. Our approach to entity linking is unique in that we treat these relationships as latent variables in our neural entity-linking model. This allows us to induce the relationships without any supervision, optimizing the entity-linking system in an end-to-end manner. Our multi-relational model outperforms previous approaches, achieving the highest scores on the standard benchmark (AIDA-CoNLL) and outperforming its relation-agnostic version. Additionally, its faster convergence during training suggests that the structural bias injected into the model helps to explain the regularities in the training data.

label: acl
text: Cross-domain sentiment analysis has achieved promising results with the help of pre-trained language models. As GPT-3 appears, prompt tuning has been widely explored to enable better semantic modeling in many natural language processing tasks. However, directly using a fixed predefined template for cross-domain research cannot model different distributions of the C-C-C token in different domains, thus making underuse of the prompt tuning technique. In this paper, we propose a novel Adversarial Soft Prompt Tuning method (AdSPT) to better model cross-domain sentiment analysis. On the one hand, AdSPT adopts separate soft prompts instead of hard templates to learn different vectors for different domains, thus alleviating the domain discrepancy of the D-D-D token in the masked language modeling task. On the other hand, AdSPT uses a novel domain adversarial training strategy to learn domain-invariant representations between each source domain and the target domain. Experiments on a publicly available sentiment analysis dataset show that our model achieves the new state-of-the-art results for both single-source domain adaptation and multi-source domain adaptation.

label: acl
text: Cross-domain sentiment analysis has promising results, thanks to pre-trained language models. The advent of GPT-3 has led to widespread exploration of prompt tuning to enhance semantic modeling in NLP tasks. However, using a fixed template for cross-domain research is limited as it cannot model the varying distributions of the C-C-C token across domains, thus not fully utilizing the potential of prompt tuning. To address this issue, we propose Adversarial Soft Prompt Tuning (AdSPT), a novel method for cross-domain sentiment analysis. AdSPT uses separate soft prompts, instead of hard templates, to learn domain-specific vectors for the D-D-D token in masked language modeling, thus reducing domain discrepancy. Additionally, AdSPT employs a domain adversarial training strategy to achieve domain-invariant representations between source and target domains. Our experiments on a publicly available sentiment analysis dataset demonstrate that AdSPT outperforms existing methods and achieves new state-of-the-art results for both single-source and multi-source domain adaptation.

label: emnlp
text: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

text: Despite significant advancements in current reading comprehension systems, their promising results often come at the cost of using an ensemble of multiple models. Additionally, these systems are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper addresses these issues by utilizing knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. Our approach first shows that knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then introduce two novel techniques that not only penalize predictions made on confusing answers but also guide training using alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Our experiments demonstrate that our best student model has only a slight 0.4% decrease in F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12 times faster during inference. Additionally, it outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and the NarrativeQA benchmark.

text: Having an entity annotated corpus of the clinical domain is one of the basic requirements for detection of clinical entities using machine learning (ML) approaches. Past researches have shown the superiority of statistical/ML approaches over the rule based approaches. But in order to take full advantage of the ML approaches, an accurately annotated corpus becomes an essential requirement. Though there are a few annotated corpora available either on a small data set, or covering a narrower domain (like cancer patients records, lab reports), annotation of a large data set representing the entire clinical domain has not been created yet. In this paper, we have described in detail the annotation guidelines, annotation process and our approaches in creating a CER (clinical entity recognition) corpus of 5,160 clinical documents from forty different clinical specialities. The clinical entities range across various types such as diseases, procedures, medications, medical devices and so on. We have classified them into eleven categories for annotation. Our annotation also reflects the relations among the group of entities that constitute larger concepts altogether.

text: Having a corpus of clinical entities annotated in the clinical domain is crucial for detecting clinical entities using machine learning (ML) techniques. Past research has demonstrated that statistical/ML approaches outperform rule-based methods. However, to fully leverage the benefits of ML, an accurately annotated corpus is necessary. Although there are some annotated corpora available that cover smaller data sets or narrower domains (such as cancer patients' records or lab reports), a large data set representing the entire clinical domain has not been created yet. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of the annotation guidelines, process, and our efforts to create a Clinical Entity Recognition (CER) corpus of 5,160 clinical documents from 40 different specialties. The clinical entities covered range from diseases and procedures to medications and medical devices, and are classified into 11 categories for annotation. Our annotation also includes the relationships among entities that make up larger concepts.

text: This paper demonstrates that multilingual pretraining and multilingual fine-tuning are both critical for facilitating cross-lingual transfer in zero-shot translation, where the neural machine translation (NMT) model is tested on source languages unseen during supervised training. Following this idea, we present SixT+, a strong many-to-English NMT model that supports 100 source languages but is trained with a parallel dataset in only six source languages. SixT+ initializes the decoder embedding and the full encoder with XLM-R large and then trains the encoder and decoder layers with a simple two-stage training strategy. SixT+ achieves impressive performance on many-to-English translation. It significantly outperforms CRISS and m2m-100, two strong multilingual NMT systems, with an average gain of 7.2 and 5.0 BLEU respectively. Additionally, SixT+ offers a set of model parameters that can be further fine-tuned to other unsupervised tasks. We demonstrate that adding SixT+ initialization outperforms state-of-the-art explicitly designed unsupervised NMT models on Si-En and Ne-En by over 1.2 average BLEU. When applied to zero-shot cross-lingual abstractive summarization, it produces an average performance gain of 12.3 ROUGE-L over mBART-ft. We conduct detailed analyses to understand the key ingredients of SixT+, including multilinguality of the auxiliary parallel data, positional disentangled encoder, and the cross-lingual transferability of its encoder.

text: This paper shows the importance of multilingual pretraining and fine-tuning in facilitating cross-lingual transfer in zero-shot translation. We present SixT+, a powerful many-to-English NMT model that supports 100 source languages, but is only trained with parallel data in six source languages. The model is initialized with XLM-R large and then trained using a two-stage strategy. SixT+ outperforms CRISS and m2m-100 by an average of 7.2 and 5.0 BLEU, respectively. It also offers parameters that can be fine-tuned for other unsupervised tasks. The results demonstrate that SixT+ initialization outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised NMT models on Si-En and Ne-En by over 1.2 average BLEU. When applied to zero-shot cross-lingual abstractive summarization, it produces a 12.3 ROUGE-L performance gain over mBART-ft. The key ingredients of SixT+ include multilinguality, positional disentangled encoder, and cross-lingual transferability of the encoder.
