text: This paper studies the relative importance of attention heads in Transformer-based models to aid their interpretability in cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks. Prior research has found that only a few attention heads are important in each mono-lingual Natural Language Processing (NLP) task and pruning the remaining heads leads to comparable or improved performance of the model. However, the impact of pruning attention heads is not yet clear in cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks. Through extensive experiments, we show that (1) pruning a number of attention heads in a multi-lingual Transformer-based model has, in general, positive effects on its performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks and (2) the attention heads to be pruned can be ranked using gradients and identified with a few trial experiments. Our experiments focus on sequence labeling tasks, with potential applicability on other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks. For comprehensiveness, we examine two pre-trained multi-lingual models, namely multi-lingual BERT (mBERT) and XLM-R, on three tasks across 9 languages each. We also discuss the validity of our findings and their extensibility to truly resource-scarce languages and other task settings.

label: acl
text: This paper investigates the significance of attention heads in Transformer-based models for enhancing their interpretability in cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks. Previous studies have revealed that only a limited number of attention heads are crucial in each mono-lingual Natural Language Processing (NLP) task, and pruning the remaining heads can result in comparable or improved performance of the model. However, the effect of pruning attention heads in cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks is yet to be determined. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that (1) pruning a specific number of attention heads in a multi-lingual Transformer-based model can have a positive impact on its performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and (2) the attention heads to be pruned can be ranked based on gradients and determined through a few trial experiments. Our focus is on sequence labeling tasks, but our findings may have potential applications in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks. To provide a comprehensive analysis, we evaluate two pre-trained multi-lingual models, namely multi-lingual BERT (mBERT) and XLM-R, on three tasks across 9 languages each. We also examine the validity of our results and their applicability to resource-scarce languages and other task settings.

text: Continuity of care is crucial to ensuring positive health outcomes for patients discharged from an inpatient hospital setting, and improved information sharing can help. To share information, caregivers write discharge notes containing action items to share with patients and their future caregivers, but these action items are easily lost due to the lengthiness of the documents. In this work, we describe our creation of a dataset of clinical action items annotated over MIMIC-III, the largest publicly available dataset of real clinical notes. This dataset, which we call CLIP, is annotated by physicians and covers 718 documents representing 100K sentences. We describe the task of extracting the action items from these documents as multi-aspect extractive summarization, with each aspect representing a type of action to be taken. We evaluate several machine learning models on this task, and show that the best models exploit in-domain language model pre-training on 59K unannotated documents, and incorporate context from neighboring sentences. We also propose an approach to pre-training data selection that allows us to explore the trade-off between size and domain-specificity of pre-training datasets for this task.

text: Continuity of care is vital to ensuring positive health outcomes for patients who have been discharged from an inpatient hospital setting. Improved information sharing can help achieve this goal. Caregivers write discharge notes that include action items to be shared with patients and future caregivers, but these items can be easily overlooked due to the length of the documents. To address this issue, we have created a dataset of clinical action items annotated over MIMIC-III, the largest publicly available dataset of real clinical notes. This dataset, referred to as CLIP, has been annotated by physicians and includes 718 documents, representing 100K sentences. We consider the task of extracting action items from these documents as multi-aspect extractive summarization, with each aspect representing a specific type of action. We evaluate several machine learning models on this task and demonstrate that the best models leverage in-domain language model pre-training on 59K unannotated documents and incorporate context from neighboring sentences. Additionally, we propose an approach to pre-training data selection that allows us to assess the trade-off between the size and domain-specificity of pre-training datasets for this task.

text: We introduce a method of adapting neural paragraph-level question answering models to the case where entire documents are given as input. Most current question answering models cannot scale to document or multi-document input, and naively applying these models to each paragraph independently often results in them being distracted by irrelevant text. We show that it is possible to significantly improve performance by using a modified training scheme that teaches the model to ignore non-answer containing paragraphs. Our method involves sampling multiple paragraphs from each document, and using an objective function that requires the model to produce globally correct output. We additionally identify and improve upon a number of other design decisions that arise when working with document-level data. Experiments on TriviaQA and SQuAD shows our method advances the state of the art, including a 10 point gain on TriviaQA.

label: acl
text: We present a novel approach to adapting neural paragraph-level question answering models to handle entire document inputs. Unlike current models that can't scale to document or multi-document inputs and tend to be misled by irrelevant text when applied to each paragraph independently, our method leverages a modified training scheme to help the model ignore non-answer-containing paragraphs. This is achieved by sampling multiple paragraphs from each document and using an objective function that requires the model to produce globally correct outputs. Furthermore, we optimize several design decisions that arise when working with document-level data, leading to improved performance. Our experiments on TriviaQA and SQuAD demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, as it surpasses the state of the art with a 10-point gain on TriviaQA.

text: Dense passage retrieval has been shown to be an effective approach for information retrieval tasks such as open domain question answering. Under this paradigm, a dual-encoder model is learned to encode questions and passages separately into vector representations, and all the passage vectors are then pre-computed and indexed, which can be efficiently retrieved by vector space search during inference time. In this paper, we propose a new contrastive learning method called Cross Momentum Contrastive learning (xMoCo), for learning a dual-encoder model for question-passage matching. Our method efficiently maintains a large pool of negative samples like the original MoCo, and by jointly optimizing question-to-passage and passage-to-question matching tasks, enables using separate encoders for questions and passages. We evaluate our method on various open-domain question answering dataset, and the experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

label: acl
text: The dense passage retrieval approach has proven to be effective in information retrieval tasks, such as open-domain question answering. This approach uses a dual-encoder model to encode questions and passages into vector representations, which are then pre-computed and indexed for efficient retrieval during inference time. In this paper, we introduce Cross Momentum Contrastive learning (xMoCo), a new contrastive learning method for learning a dual-encoder model for question-passage matching. Our method maintains a large pool of negative samples like the original MoCo, and by optimizing both question-to-passage and passage-to-question matching tasks, it enables the use of separate encoders for questions and passages. We evaluate xMoCo on various open-domain question answering datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.

text: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have shown great potentials in natural language processing (NLP) including rhetorical structure theory (RST) discourse parsing.Current PLMs are obtained by sentence-level pre-training, which is different from the basic processing unit, i.e. element discourse unit (EDU).To this end, we propose a second-stage EDU-level pre-training approach in this work, which presents two novel tasks to learn effective EDU representations continually based on well pre-trained language models.Concretely, the two tasks are (1) next EDU prediction (NEP) and (2) discourse marker prediction (DMP).We take a state-of-the-art transition-based neural parser as baseline, and adopt it with a light bi-gram EDU modification to effectively explore the EDU-level pre-trained EDU representation.Experimental results on a benckmark dataset show that our method is highly effective,leading a 2.1-point improvement in F1-score.All codes and pre-trained models will be released publicly to facilitate future studies.

text: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have shown tremendous potential in natural language processing (NLP), particularly in the area of rhetorical structure theory (RST) discourse parsing. However, current PLMs are trained at the sentence-level, which is different from the basic processing unit, i.e. element discourse unit (EDU). To address this issue, we propose a second-stage EDU-level pre-training approach in this work. This approach involves two novel tasks, Next EDU Prediction (NEP) and Discourse Marker Prediction (DMP), which aim to learn effective EDU representations based on pre-trained language models. We use a state-of-the-art transition-based neural parser as a baseline and modify it with a light bi-gram EDU approach to effectively explore the EDU-level pre-trained EDU representation. Our results on a benchmark dataset show that our method is highly effective, leading to a 2.1-point improvement in F1-score. All codes and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate further research.

label: emnlp
text: Recently, non-recurrent architectures (convolutional, self-attentional) have outperformed RNNs in neural machine translation. CNNs and self-attentional networks can connect distant words via shorter network paths than RNNs, and it has been speculated that this improves their ability to model long-range dependencies. However, this theoretical argument has not been tested empirically, nor have alternative explanations for their strong performance been explored in-depth. We hypothesize that the strong performance of CNNs and self-attentional networks could also be due to their ability to extract semantic features from the source text, and we evaluate RNNs, CNNs and self-attention networks on two tasks: subject-verb agreement (where capturing long-range dependencies is required) and word sense disambiguation (where semantic feature extraction is required). Our experimental results show that: 1) self-attentional networks and CNNs do not outperform RNNs in modeling subject-verb agreement over long distances; 2) self-attentional networks perform distinctly better than RNNs and CNNs on word sense disambiguation.

label: emnlp
text:
These findings suggest that the strong performance of self-attentional networks may be due to their ability to extract semantic features, rather than their ability to model long-range dependencies.

Recently, non-recurrent architectures (convolutional and self-attentional) have outperformed RNNs in neural machine translation. The reason behind this is that CNNs and self-attentional networks can connect distant words via shorter network paths than RNNs, which is speculated to improve their ability to model long-range dependencies. However, this theory has not been tested empirically, and alternative explanations for their strong performance have not been thoroughly explored. Our hypothesis is that the strong performance of CNNs and self-attentional networks could also be due to their ability to extract semantic features from the source text. To test this, we evaluated RNNs, CNNs, and self-attention networks on two tasks: subject-verb agreement (which requires capturing long-range dependencies) and word sense disambiguation (which requires semantic feature extraction). Our results showed that self-attentional networks and CNNs did not outperform RNNs in modeling subject-verb agreement over long distances. However, self-attentional networks performed distinctly better than RNNs and CNNs on word sense disambiguation, suggesting that their strong performance may be due to their ability to extract semantic features, rather than their ability to model long-range dependencies.

text: BERT has been shown to be extremely effective on a wide variety of natural language processing tasks, including sentiment analysis and emotion detection. However, the proposed pretraining objectives of BERT do not induce any sentiment or emotion-specific biases into the model. In this paper, we present Emotion Masked Language Modelling, a variation of Masked Language Modelling aimed at improving the BERT language representation model for emotion detection and sentiment analysis tasks. Using the same pre-training corpora as the original model, Wikipedia and BookCorpus, our BERT variation manages to improve the downstream performance on 4 tasks from emotion detection and sentiment analysis by an average of 1.2% F-1. Moreover, our approach shows an increased performance in our task-specific robustness tests.

text: BERT has proven to be highly effective in a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including sentiment analysis and emotion detection. However, its proposed pre-training objectives do not introduce any biases related to sentiment or emotion. In this paper, we introduce Emotion Masked Language Modelling, a variation of Masked Language Modelling that enhances BERT's language representation model for sentiment analysis and emotion detection tasks. Using the same pre-training corpora as the original BERT model, Wikipedia and BookCorpus, our variation improves the downstream performance on 4 emotion detection and sentiment analysis tasks by an average of 1.2% F-1. Additionally, our approach demonstrates improved performance in task-specific robustness tests.

label: emnlp
text: Identifying optimistic and pessimistic viewpoints and users from Twitter is useful for providing better social support to those who need such support, and for minimizing the negative influence among users and maximizing the spread of positive attitudes and ideas. In this paper, we explore a range of deep learning models to predict optimism and pessimism in Twitter at both tweet and user level and show that these models substantially outperform traditional machine learning classifiers used in prior work. In addition, we show evidence that a sentiment classifier would not be sufficient for accurately predicting optimism and pessimism in Twitter. Last, we study the verb tense usage as well as the presence of polarity words in optimistic and pessimistic tweets.

label: emnlp
text: In this paper, we investigate the use of deep learning models to predict optimism and pessimism in Twitter at both the tweet and user level. Our goal is to provide better social support to those in need and reduce the spread of negative attitudes and ideas. Our findings demonstrate that these deep learning models surpass traditional machine learning classifiers used in previous studies. Furthermore, we also demonstrate that relying solely on sentiment analysis is insufficient for accurately predicting optimism and pessimism in Twitter. Lastly, we examine the role of verb tense and the presence of polarity words in shaping optimistic and pessimistic tweets.

label: naacl
text: The Word-in-Context (WiC) task has attracted considerable attention in the NLP community, as demonstrated by the popularity of the recent MCL-WiC SemEval shared task. Systems and lexical resources from word sense disambiguation (WSD) are often used for the WiC task and WiC dataset construction. In this paper, we establish the exact relationship between WiC and WSD, as well as the related task of target sense verification (TSV). Building upon a novel hypothesis on the equivalence of sense and meaning distinctions, we demonstrate through the application of tools from theoretical computer science that these three semantic classification problems can be pairwise reduced to each other, and therefore are equivalent. The results of experiments that involve systems and datasets for both WiC and WSD provide strong empirical evidence that our problem reductions work in practice.

label: naacl
text:
The findings of our research have important implications for the development of NLP systems, as well as for the design of future WiC and WSD shared tasks.

The WiC task has garnered significant attention from the NLP community, as evidenced by the popularity of the recent MCL-WiC SemEval shared task. Systems and resources from WSD are frequently utilized in WiC task and dataset construction. This paper explores the relationship between WiC, WSD, and the related task of target sense verification (TSV). Based on a novel hypothesis on the equivalence of sense and meaning distinction, we use tools from theoretical computer science to demonstrate that these three semantic classification problems are equivalent and can be reduced to each other. Our experiments, involving systems and datasets for both WiC and WSD, provide strong evidence that the problem reductions are effective. Our findings have significant implications for NLP system development and the design of future WiC and WSD shared tasks.

label: acl
text: Solving crossword puzzles requires diverse reasoning capabilities, access to a vast amount of knowledge about language and the world, and the ability to satisfy the constraints imposed by the structure of the puzzle. In this work, we introduce solving crossword puzzles as a new natural language understanding task. We release a corpus of crossword puzzles collected from the New York Times daily crossword spanning 25 years and comprised of a total of around nine thousand puzzles. These puzzles include a diverse set of clues: historic, factual, word meaning, synonyms/antonyms, fill-in-the-blank, abbreviations, prefixes/suffixes, wordplay, and cross-lingual, as well as clues that depend on the answers to other clues. We separately release the clue-answer pairs from these puzzles as an open-domain question answering dataset containing over half a million unique clue-answer pairs. For the question answering task, our baselines include several sequence-to-sequence and retrieval-based generative models. We also introduce a non-parametric constraint satisfaction baseline for solving the entire crossword puzzle. Finally, we propose an evaluation framework which consists of several complementary performance metrics.

label: acl
text: Solving crossword puzzles requires a combination of diverse reasoning skills, extensive knowledge of language and the world, and the ability to adhere to the puzzle's structural constraints. In this study, we present crossword puzzle solving as a new challenge in natural language understanding. Our corpus consists of approximately 9,000 crossword puzzles collected from the New York Times daily crossword over 25 years. These puzzles feature a wide range of clues, including historical, factual, word meaning, synonyms/antonyms, fill-in-the-blank, abbreviations, prefixes/suffixes, wordplay, cross-lingual, and clues that rely on other answers. We also provide the clue-answer pairs as an open-domain question-answering dataset, containing over 500,000 unique pairs. Our evaluation framework includes several state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence and retrieval-based generative models as well as a non-parametric constraint satisfaction baseline for solving the entire puzzle. Our evaluation framework consists of several complementary performance metrics.

label: naacl
text: Emotions are an inherent part of human interactions, and consequently, it is imperative to develop AI systems that understand and recognize human emotions. During a conversation involving various people, a person's emotions are influenced by the other speaker's utterances and their own emotional state over the utterances. In this paper, we propose COntextualized Graph Neural Network based Multi- modal Emotion recognitioN (COGMEN) system that leverages local information (i.e., inter/intra dependency between speakers) and global information (context). The proposed model uses Graph Neural Network (GNN) based architecture to model the complex dependencies (local and global information) in a conversation. Our model gives state-of-the- art (SOTA) results on IEMOCAP and MOSEI datasets, and detailed ablation experiments show the importance of modeling information at both levels.

label: naacl
text: Human interactions are inherently emotional, making it crucial to develop AI systems that can understand and recognize human emotions. During conversations, a person's emotions are shaped by the emotions of the other speaker and their own emotional state. To address this challenge, we propose the COntextualized Graph Neural Network based Multi-modal Emotion recognitioN (COGMEN) system. This system leverages both local information, such as the inter/intra dependencies between speakers, and global information, such as the context, to model emotional interactions. Our COGMEN system uses a Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture to capture the complex dependencies in a conversation. Our results show that COGMEN outperforms state-of-the-art models on the IEMOCAP and MOSEI datasets. Ablation experiments also demonstrate the importance of considering both local and global information in the recognition of human emotions.

label: emnlp
text: Distantly supervised relation extraction employs existing knowledge graphs to automatically collect training data. While distant supervision is effective to scale relation extraction up to large-scale corpora, it inevitably suffers from the wrong labeling problem. Many efforts have been devoted to identifying valid instances from noisy data. However, most existing methods handle each relation in isolation, regardless of rich semantic correlations located in relation hierarchies. In this paper, we aim to incorporate the hierarchical information of relations for distantly supervised relation extraction and propose a novel hierarchical attention scheme. The multiple layers of our hierarchical attention scheme provide coarse-to-fine granularity to better identify valid instances, which is especially effective for extracting those long-tail relations. The experimental results on a large-scale benchmark dataset demonstrate that our models are capable of modeling the hierarchical information of relations and significantly outperform other baselines. The source code of this paper can be obtained from https://github.com/thunlp/HNRE.

label: emnlp
text: The process of Distantly Supervised Relation Extraction uses existing knowledge graphs to gather training data automatically. Although this method is effective in scaling up relation extraction to large corpora, it is prone to the problem of incorrect labeling. Many attempts have been made to identify valid instances from noisy data, but most existing methods do not take into account the rich semantic correlations present in relation hierarchies. In this paper, we propose a novel Hierarchical Attention Scheme to incorporate the hierarchical information of relations in distantly supervised relation extraction. Our scheme provides a coarse-to-fine granularity, allowing for better identification of valid instances, particularly for extracting long-tail relations. The results of our experiments on a large-scale benchmark dataset show that our models are effective in modeling the hierarchical information of relations and outperform other baselines. The source code for this paper is available at https://github.com/thunlp/HNRE.

label: coling
text: Emotion cause pair extraction (ECPE), as one of the derived subtasks of emotion cause analysis (ECA), shares rich inter-related features with emotion extraction (EE) and cause extraction (CE). Therefore EE and CE are frequently utilized as auxiliary tasks for better feature learning, modeled via multi-task learning (MTL) framework by prior works to achieve state-of-the-art (SoTA) ECPE results. However, existing MTL-based methods either fail to simultaneously model the specific features and the interactive feature in between, or suffer from the inconsistency of label prediction. In this work, we consider addressing the above challenges for improving ECPE by performing two alignment mechanisms with a novel A\^2Net model. We first propose a feature-task alignment to explicitly model the specific emotion-&cause-specific features and the shared interactive feature. Besides, an inter-task alignment is implemented, in which the label distance between the ECPE and the combinations of EE&CE are learned to be narrowed for better label consistency. Evaluations of benchmarks show that our methods outperform current best-performing systems on all ECA subtasks. Further analysis proves the importance of our proposed alignment mechanisms for the task.

label: coling
text: The Emotion Cause Pair Extraction (ECPE) task is a subtask of Emotion Cause Analysis (ECA) and shares features with Emotion Extraction (EE) and Cause Extraction (CE). Prior research has utilized EE and CE as auxiliary tasks in a Multi-Task Learning (MTL) framework to achieve state-of-the-art results. However, existing MTL-based methods either fail to model specific and interactive features simultaneously or suffer from inconsistent label prediction. To address these challenges, we propose a novel A\^2Net model that performs two alignment mechanisms. The first mechanism, feature-task alignment, explicitly models specific emotion and cause features, as well as shared interactive features. The second mechanism, inter-task alignment, narrows the label distance between ECPE and the combination of EE and CE to improve label consistency. Our methods outperform current best-performing systems on all ECA subtasks and our analysis highlights the importance of our proposed alignment mechanisms.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we propose a new strategy, called Text Deconvolution Saliency (TDS), to visualize linguistic information detected by a CNN for text classification. We extend Deconvolution Networks to text in order to present a new perspective on text analysis to the linguistic community. We empirically demonstrated the efficiency of our Text Deconvolution Saliency on corpora from three different languages: English, French, and Latin. For every tested dataset, our Text Deconvolution Saliency automatically encodes complex linguistic patterns based on co-occurrences and possibly on grammatical and syntax analysis.

label: acl
text: We present a novel strategy, Text Deconvolution Saliency (TDS), to visualize the linguistic information detected by a CNN in text classification. Our approach extends Deconvolution Networks to text, offering a new perspective on text analysis for the linguistic community. Our empirical results demonstrate the efficiency of TDS on corpora from English, French, and Latin, and show that it automatically encodes complex linguistic patterns based on co-occurrences and possibly grammatical and syntax analysis.

label: acl
text: The few-shot natural language understanding (NLU) task has attracted much recent attention. However, prior methods have been evaluated under a disparate set of protocols, which hinders fair comparison and measuring the progress of the field. To address this issue, we introduce an evaluation framework that improves previous evaluation procedures in three key aspects, i.e., test performance, dev-test correlation, and stability. Under this new evaluation framework, we re-evaluate several state-of-the-art few-shot methods for NLU tasks. Our framework reveals new insights: (1) both the absolute performance and relative gap of the methods were not accurately estimated in prior literature; (2) no single method dominates most tasks with consistent performance; (3) improvements of some methods diminish with a larger pretrained model; and (4) gains from different methods are often complementary and the best combined model performs close to a strong fully-supervised baseline. We open-source our toolkit, FewNLU, that implements our evaluation framework along with a number of state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: The recent interest in few-shot natural language understanding (NLU) tasks has resulted in a multitude of methods being proposed. However, the evaluation of these methods has been done using disparate protocols, making it difficult to compare their performance and assess the progress of the field. To address this issue, we present a new evaluation framework that improves upon previous evaluation procedures in three key areas: test performance, dev-test correlation, and stability. Using this framework, we re-evaluate several state-of-the-art few-shot NLU methods. Our evaluation reveals new insights, including that: (1) previous evaluations have not accurately estimated the absolute performance and relative gap between methods; (2) no single method consistently outperforms others across all tasks; (3) some methods' improvements may diminish when using a larger pretrained model, and (4) combining the best methods results in performance close to a strong fully-supervised baseline. Our toolkit, FewNLU, which implements our evaluation framework along with several state-of-the-art methods, is open-sourced for the community.

label: coling
text: In this paper we present FeatureBART, a linguistically motivated sequence-to-sequence monolingual pre-training strategy in which syntactic features such as lemma, part-of-speech and dependency labels are incorporated into the span prediction based pre-training framework (BART). These automatically extracted features are incorporated via approaches such as concatenation and relevance mechanisms, among which the latter is known to be better than the former. When used for low-resource NMT as a downstream task, we show that these feature based models give large improvements in bilingual settings and modest ones in multilingual settings over their counterparts that do not use features.

label: coling
text: This paper presents FeatureBART, a linguistically motivated sequence-to-sequence monolingual pre-training strategy that incorporates syntactic features, such as lemma, part-of-speech, and dependency labels, into the span prediction-based pre-training framework (BART). The extracted features are integrated using concatenation and relevance mechanisms, with the latter approach being more effective than the former. Our results show that when used for low-resource NMT as a downstream task, the feature-based models provide substantial improvements in bilingual settings and moderate improvements in multilingual settings compared to models that do not incorporate features.

label: acl
text: Recent works on Lottery Ticket Hypothesis have shown that pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain smaller matching subnetworks(winning tickets) which are capable of reaching accuracy comparable to the original models. However, these tickets are proved to be notrobust to adversarial examples, and even worse than their PLM counterparts. To address this problem, we propose a novel method based on learning binary weight masks to identify robust tickets hidden in the original PLMs. Since the loss is not differentiable for the binary mask, we assign the hard concrete distribution to the masks and encourage their sparsity using a smoothing approximation of L0 regularization.Furthermore, we design an adversarial loss objective to guide the search for robust tickets and ensure that the tickets perform well bothin accuracy and robustness. Experimental results show the significant improvement of the proposed method over previous work on adversarial robustness evaluation.

label: acl
text: Recent works on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis have demonstrated that pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain smaller subnetworks (winning tickets) that can achieve accuracy comparable to the original models. However, these tickets have been shown to be not robust to adversarial examples and even worse than their PLM counterparts. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel method that uses learning binary weight masks to identify robust tickets within the original PLMs. Since the loss is not differentiable for the binary mask, we assign the hard concrete distribution to the masks and use a smoothed approximation of L0 regularization to encourage their sparsity. Additionally, we design an adversarial loss objective to guide the search for robust tickets and ensure that the tickets perform well in both accuracy and robustness. Experimental results demonstrate the significant improvement of our proposed method over previous works in terms of adversarial robustness evaluation.

label: emnlp
text: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject. The open book that comes with our questions is a set of 1326 elementary level science facts. Roughly 6000 questions probe an understanding of these facts and their application to novel situations. This requires combining an open book fact (e.g., metals conduct electricity) with broad common knowledge (e.g., a suit of armor is made of metal) obtained from other sources. While existing QA datasets over documents or knowledge bases, being generally self-contained, focus on linguistic understanding, OpenBookQA probes a deeper understanding of both the topic—in the context of common knowledge—and the language it is expressed in. Human performance on OpenBookQA is close to 92%, but many state-of-the-art pre-trained QA methods perform surprisingly poorly, worse than several simple neural baselines we develop. Our oracle experiments designed to circumvent the knowledge retrieval bottleneck demonstrate the value of both the open book and additional facts. We leave it as a challenge to solve the retrieval problem in this multi-hop setting and to close the large gap to human performance.

label: emnlp
text: We introduce OpenBookQA, a new type of question-answering dataset modeled after open-book exams. This dataset aims to evaluate human understanding of a subject by providing a set of 1326 elementary-level science facts as an "open book." Approximately 6000 questions are designed to test understanding of these facts and their application to novel situations. This requires combining the open book facts (e.g., metals conduct electricity) with general knowledge (e.g., a suit of armor is made of metal) obtained from other sources. Unlike existing QA datasets that focus on linguistic understanding and are self-contained, OpenBookQA assesses a deeper understanding of the topic, in the context of general knowledge, and the language in which it is expressed. Although human performance on OpenBookQA is close to 92%, many state-of-the-art pre-trained QA methods perform poorly, worse than several simple neural baselines we developed. Our oracle experiments, designed to address the knowledge retrieval bottleneck, demonstrate the value of both the open book and additional facts. The challenge remains to solve the retrieval problem in this multi-hop setting and close the gap to human performance.

label: coling
text: Hierarchical Multiscale LSTM (Chung et. al., 2016) is a state-of-the-art language model that learns interpretable structure from character-level input. Such models can provide fertile ground for (cognitive) computational linguistics studies. However, the high complexity of the architecture, training and implementations might hinder its applicability. We provide a detailed reproduction and ablation study of the architecture, shedding light on some of the potential caveats of re-purposing complex deep-learning architectures. We further show that simplifying certain aspects of the architecture can in fact improve its performance. We also investigate the linguistic units (segments) learned by various levels of the model, and argue that their quality does not correlate with the overall performance of the model on language modeling.

label: coling
text: The Hierarchical Multiscale LSTM (Chung et al., 2016) is a cutting-edge language model that extracts interpretable structure from character-level input. This model presents a valuable opportunity for cognitive computational linguistics studies. However, its complex architecture, training, and implementation may limit its practicality. Our study provides a comprehensive reproduction and ablation analysis of the architecture, illuminating some of the potential drawbacks of using complex deep-learning models. Our results demonstrate that simplifying certain aspects of the architecture can actually enhance its performance. Additionally, we examine the linguistic units (segments) learned by the model at different levels and find that their quality does not necessarily correspond with the model's overall language modeling performance.

label: coling
text: Human communication includes information, opinions and reactions. Reactions are often captured by the affective-messages in written as well as verbal communications. While there has been work in affect modeling and to some extent affective content generation, the area of affective word distributions is not well studied. Synsets and lexica capture semantic relationships across words. These models, however, lack in encoding affective or emotional word interpretations. Our proposed model, Aff2Vec, provides a method for enriched word embeddings that are representative of affective interpretations of words. Aff2Vec outperforms the state-of-the-art in intrinsic word-similarity tasks. Further, the use of Aff2Vec representations outperforms baseline embeddings in downstream natural language understanding tasks including sentiment analysis, personality detection, and frustration prediction.

label: coling
text: Human communication encompasses the exchange of information, opinions, and reactions. Reactions are often expressed through affective messages in both written and verbal forms. Although there has been research in affect modeling and affective content generation, the area of affective word distributions remains largely unexplored. While synset and lexica models capture semantic relationships among words, they lack the ability to encode affective or emotional word interpretations. Our proposed model, Aff2Vec, offers a method for creating enriched word embeddings that accurately reflect affective interpretations. Aff2Vec outperforms existing models in intrinsic word-similarity tasks and delivers superior results in downstream natural language understanding tasks, including sentiment analysis, personality detection, and frustration prediction.

label: acl
text: The state-of-the-art model for structured sentiment analysis casts the task as a dependency parsing problem, which has some limitations: (1) The label proportions for span prediction and span relation prediction are imbalanced. (2) The span lengths of sentiment tuple components may be very large in this task, which will further exacerbates the imbalance problem. (3) Two nodes in a dependency graph cannot have multiple arcs, therefore some overlapped sentiment tuples cannot be recognized. In this work, we propose nichetargeting solutions for these issues. First, we introduce a novel labeling strategy, which contains two sets of token pair labels, namely essential label set and whole label set. The essential label set consists of the basic labels for this task, which are relatively balanced and applied in the prediction layer. The whole label set includes rich labels to help our model capture various token relations, which are applied in the hidden layer to softly influence our model. Moreover, we also propose an effective model to well collaborate with our labeling strategy, which is equipped with the graph attention networks to iteratively refine token representations, and the adaptive multi-label classifier to dynamically predict multiple relations between token pairs. We perform extensive experiments on 5 benchmark datasets in four languages. Experimental results show that our model outperforms previous SOTA models by a large margin.

label: acl
text: The state-of-the-art model for structured sentiment analysis has limitations, including an imbalance in label proportions for span prediction and span relation prediction, large span lengths of sentiment tuple components, and an inability to recognize overlapped sentiment tuples due to restrictions on multiple arcs in a dependency graph. To address these issues, we propose innovative solutions, including a novel labeling strategy with two sets of token pair labels (essential and whole) and an effective model equipped with graph attention networks and an adaptive multi-label classifier. Our model is tested on five benchmark datasets in four languages and shows significant improvement over previous state-of-the-art models.

label: acl
text: Although BERT and its variants have reshaped the NLP landscape, it still remains unclear how best to derive sentence embeddings from such pre-trained Transformers. In this work, we propose a contrastive learning method that utilizes self-guidance for improving the quality of BERT sentence representations. Our method fine-tunes BERT in a self-supervised fashion, does not rely on data augmentation, and enables the usual [CLS] token embeddings to function as sentence vectors. Moreover, we redesign the contrastive learning objective (NT-Xent) and apply it to sentence representation learning. We demonstrate with extensive experiments that our approach is more effective than competitive baselines on diverse sentence-related tasks. We also show it is efficient at inference and robust to domain shifts.

label: acl
text: The NLP landscape has been reshaped by BERT and its variants, but it is still not clear how to obtain the best sentence embeddings from these pre-trained Transformers. To address this issue, we propose a contrastive learning method that leverages self-guidance to improve the quality of BERT sentence representations. Our method fine-tunes BERT in a self-supervised manner, without relying on data augmentation. It allows the standard [CLS] token embeddings to serve as sentence vectors. Additionally, we have redesigned the contrastive learning objective (NT-Xent) to apply it to sentence representation learning. Our approach has been proven to be more effective than other competitive baselines on various sentence-related tasks through extensive experiments. Furthermore, it is efficient during inference and robust to domain shifts.

label: emnlp
text: Existing neural semantic parsers mainly utilize a sequence encoder, i.e., a sequential LSTM, to extract word order features while neglecting other valuable syntactic information such as dependency or constituent trees. In this paper, we first propose to use the syntactic graph to represent three types of syntactic information, i.e., word order, dependency and constituency features; then employ a graph-to-sequence model to encode the syntactic graph and decode a logical form. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that our model is comparable to the state-of-the-art on Jobs640, ATIS, and Geo880. Experimental results on adversarial examples demonstrate the robustness of the model is also improved by encoding more syntactic information.

label: emnlp
text: Current neural semantic parsers mainly rely on a sequential LSTM to capture word order features, ignoring other valuable syntactic information such as dependency or constituent trees. In this study, we propose using a syntactic graph to incorporate three types of syntactic information: word order, dependency, and constituency features. We then use a graph-to-sequence model to encode the syntactic graph and produce a logical form. Our experiments on benchmark datasets, including Jobs640, ATIS, and Geo880, show that our model is on par with the state-of-the-art. Additionally, our results on adversarial examples highlight the improved robustness of our model due to the incorporation of more syntactic information.

label: naacl
text: We focus on creating agents that act in alignment with socially beneficial norms and values in interactive narratives or text-based games—environments wherein an agent perceives and interacts with a world through natural language. Such interactive agents are often trained via reinforcement learning to optimize task performance, even when such rewards may lead to agent behaviors that violate societal norms—causing harm either to the agent itself or other entities in the environment. Social value alignment refers to creating agents whose behaviors conform to expected moral and social norms for a given context and group of people—in our case, it means agents that behave in a manner that is less harmful and more beneficial for themselves and others.We build on the Jiminy Cricket benchmark (Hendrycks et al. 2021), a set of 25 annotated interactive narratives containing thousands of morally salient scenarios covering everything from theft and bodily harm to altruism. We introduce the GALAD (Game-value ALignment through Action Distillation) agent that uses the social commonsense knowledge present in specially trained language models to contextually restrict its action space to only those actions that are aligned with socially beneficial values. An experimental study shows that the GALAD agent makes decisions efficiently enough to improve state-of-the-art task performance by 4% while reducing the frequency of socially harmful behaviors by 25% compared to strong contemporary value alignment approaches.

label: naacl
text: We concentrate on developing agents that align with socially beneficial norms and values in interactive narratives and text-based games. These agents perceive and interact with the world through natural language. Despite being trained through reinforcement learning to optimize task performance, their behavior may violate societal norms and cause harm, either to the agent itself or to other entities in the environment. To address this issue, we aim to create agents whose behaviors conform to expected moral and social norms - a concept known as social value alignment. Our approach builds on the Jiminy Cricket benchmark, a set of 25 annotated interactive narratives covering various scenarios from theft to altruism. We present the GALAD (Game-value ALignment through Action Distillation) agent, which uses the social commonsense knowledge in specially trained language models to restrict its actions to those that are aligned with socially beneficial values. Our experimental results show that the GALAD agent outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by 4% in task performance and reduces the frequency of harmful behaviors by 25%.

label: coling
text: Multi-relation Question Answering is a challenging task, due to the requirement of elaborated analysis on questions and reasoning over multiple fact triples in knowledge base. In this paper, we present a novel model called Interpretable Reasoning Network that employs an interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning process for question answering. The model dynamically decides which part of an input question should be analyzed at each hop; predicts a relation that corresponds to the current parsed results; utilizes the predicted relation to update the question representation and the state of the reasoning process; and then drives the next-hop reasoning. Experiments show that our model yields state-of-the-art results on two datasets. More interestingly, the model can offer traceable and observable intermediate predictions for reasoning analysis and failure diagnosis, thereby allowing manual manipulation in predicting the final answer.

label: coling
text: Multi-relation Question Answering is a challenging task due to the need for detailed analysis of questions and reasoning over multiple fact triples in a knowledge base. To address this challenge, we present a novel model called the Interpretable Reasoning Network. This model employs an interpretable, step-by-step reasoning process for question answering. It dynamically decides which part of the input question should be analyzed at each step, predicts the relation that corresponds to the current parsed results, updates the question representation and the state of the reasoning process using the predicted relation, and then drives the next step of reasoning. Our experiments show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art results on two datasets. Additionally, the model offers traceable and observable intermediate predictions for reasoning analysis and failure diagnosis, allowing for manual manipulation in predicting the final answer.

label: acl
text: We consider the problem of generating natural language given a communicative goal and a world description. We ask the question: is it possible to combine complementary meaning representations to scale a goal-directed NLG system without losing expressiveness? In particular, we consider using two meaning representations, one based on logical semantics and the other based on distributional semantics. We build upon an existing goal-directed generation system, S-STRUCT, which models sentence generation as planning in a Markov decision process. We develop a hybrid approach, which uses distributional semantics to quickly and imprecisely add the main elements of the sentence and then uses first-order logic based semantics to more slowly add the precise details. We find that our hybrid method allows S-STRUCT's generation to scale significantly better in early phases of generation and that the hybrid can often generate sentences with the same quality as S-STRUCT in substantially less time. However, we also observe and give insight into cases where the imprecision in distributional semantics leads to generation that is not as good as using pure logical semantics.

label: acl
text: We investigate the challenge of generating natural language that fulfills a communicative goal and reflects a world description. Our question is whether it is possible to enhance the scalability of a goal-directed NLG system by combining complementary meaning representations, without sacrificing expressiveness. To this end, we consider two meaning representations: one based on logical semantics and the other on distributional semantics. We build upon a pre-existing goal-directed generation system, S-STRUCT, which models sentence generation as a Markov decision process. Our hybrid approach leverages distributional semantics to quickly and roughly add the sentence's main elements, and then employs logical semantics to add the precise details more slowly. Our results show that the hybrid method enables S-STRUCT to scale significantly better in the early stages of generation, and it can often produce sentences with the same quality as S-STRUCT in a much shorter time. However, we also identify cases where the imprecision in distributional semantics results in lower quality generation compared to using pure logical semantics.

label: acl
text: Tables store rich numerical data, but numerical reasoning over tables is still a challenge. In this paper, we find that the spreadsheet formula, a commonly used language to perform computations on numerical values in spreadsheets, is a valuable supervision for numerical reasoning in tables. Considering large amounts of spreadsheets available on the web, we propose FORTAP, the first exploration to leverage spreadsheet formulas for table pretraining. Two novel self-supervised pretraining objectives are derived from formulas, numerical reference prediction (NRP) and numerical calculation prediction (NCP). While our proposed objectives are generic for encoders, to better capture spreadsheet table layouts and structures, FORTAP is built upon TUTA, the first transformer-based method for spreadsheet table pretraining with tree attention. FORTAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods by large margins on three representative datasets of formula prediction, question answering, and cell type classification, showing the great potential of leveraging formulas for table pretraining.

label: acl
text: Tables contain a wealth of numerical data, but numerical reasoning over these tables remains a challenge. This paper explores the use of spreadsheet formulas, a commonly used language for computing numerical values in spreadsheets, as a supervision mechanism for numerical reasoning in tables. Given the abundance of spreadsheets available on the web, we introduce FORTAP, the first attempt to leverage spreadsheet formulas for table pre-training. We develop two novel self-supervised pre-training objectives, numerical reference prediction (NRP) and numerical calculation prediction (NCP), derived from formulas. Although these objectives are generic for encoders, FORTAP is built on TUTA, a transformer-based method for spreadsheet table pre-training with tree attention, to better capture spreadsheet table layouts and structures. Our results show that FORTAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins on three datasets for formula prediction, question answering, and cell type classification, demonstrating the tremendous potential of leveraging formulas for table pre-training.

label: coling
text: Due to the increasing use of service chatbots in E-commerce platforms in recent years, customer satisfaction prediction (CSP) is gaining more and more attention. CSP is dedicated to evaluating subjective customer satisfaction in conversational service and thus helps improve customer service experience. However, previous methods focus on modeling customer-chatbot interaction across different turns, which are hard to represent the important dynamic satisfaction states throughout the customer journey. In this work, we investigate the problem of satisfaction states tracking and its effects on CSP in E-commerce service chatbots. To this end, we propose a dialogue-level classification model named DialogueCSP to track satisfaction states for CSP. In particular, we explore a novel two-step interaction module to represent the dynamic satisfaction states at each turn. In order to capture dialogue-level satisfaction states for CSP, we further introduce dialogue-aware attentions to integrate historical informative cues into the interaction module. To evaluate the proposed approach, we also build a Chinese E-commerce dataset for CSP. Experiment results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms multiple baselines, illustrating the benefits of satisfaction states tracking on CSP.

label: coling
text: Due to the growing use of service chatbots in E-commerce platforms, customer satisfaction prediction (CSP) has become a topic of increasing interest. CSP aims to evaluate customer satisfaction in conversational service and improve the customer experience. However, previous methods have focused on modeling customer-chatbot interactions across multiple turns, which can be challenging to represent the dynamic satisfaction states throughout the customer journey. In this study, we investigate the impact of satisfaction state tracking on CSP in E-commerce service chatbots. To this end, we propose the DialogueCSP, a dialogue-level classification model that tracks satisfaction states for CSP. Our model includes a novel two-step interaction module that represents dynamic satisfaction states at each turn and dialogue-aware attention to integrate historical information into the interaction module. We also build a Chinese E-commerce dataset for CSP to evaluate our approach. Our results show that our model outperforms multiple baselines, highlighting the benefits of satisfaction state tracking on CSP.

label: naacl
text: The named concepts and compositional operators present in natural language provide a rich source of information about the abstractions humans use to navigate the world. Can this linguistic background knowledge improve the generality and efficiency of learned classifiers and control policies? This paper aims to show that using the space of natural language strings as a parameter space is an effective way to capture natural task structure. In a pretraining phase, we learn a language interpretation model that transforms inputs (e.g. images) into outputs (e.g. labels) given natural language descriptions. To learn a new concept (e.g. a classifier), we search directly in the space of descriptions to minimize the interpreter's loss on training examples. Crucially, our models do not require language data to learn these concepts: language is used only in pretraining to impose structure on subsequent learning. Results on image classification, text editing, and reinforcement learning show that, in all settings, models with a linguistic parameterization outperform those without.

label: naacl
text: The concepts and compositional operators found in natural languages provide a wealth of information about the abstractions that humans use to understand the world. This paper explores whether this linguistic knowledge can improve the generality and efficiency of learned classifiers and control policies. Our research shows that using the space of natural language strings as a parameter space is an effective way to capture the natural structure of tasks. In a preliminary training phase, we develop a language interpretation model that transforms inputs (e.g. images) into outputs (e.g. labels) based on natural language descriptions. To learn a new concept (e.g. a classifier), we perform a direct search in the space of descriptions to minimize the loss of the interpreter on training examples. Importantly, our models do not require language data to learn these concepts. Instead, language is used only in the preliminary training phase to impose structure on subsequent learning. Our results on image classification, text editing, and reinforcement learning demonstrate that, in all settings, models with a linguistic parameterization perform better than those without.

label: coling
text: Recently, many task-oriented dialogue systems need to serve users in different languages. However, it is time-consuming to collect enough data of each language for training. Thus, zero-shot adaptation of cross-lingual task-oriented dialog systems has been studied. Most of existing methods consider the word-level alignments to conduct two main tasks for task-oriented dialogue system, i.e., intent detection and slot filling, and they rarely explore the dependency relations among these two tasks. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical framework to classify the pre-defined intents in the high-level and fulfill slot filling under the guidance of intent in the low-level. Particularly, we incorporate sentence-level alignment among different languages to enhance the performance of intent detection. The extensive experiments report that our proposed method achieves the SOTA performance on a public task-oriented dialog dataset.

label: coling
text: Recently, many task-oriented dialogue systems are required to serve users in different languages. However, collecting enough data for each language to train these systems is time-consuming. To address this challenge, zero-shot adaptation of cross-lingual task-oriented dialogue systems has been studied. Most existing methods focus on word-level alignments to perform two main tasks in task-oriented dialogue systems: intent detection and slot filling. However, they rarely consider the dependency relations between these tasks. In this paper, we present a hierarchical framework that classifies pre-defined intents at a high level and performs slot filling at a low level, guided by the intent. We also incorporate sentence-level alignments between different languages to improve the performance of intent detection. Our experiments show that our proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art on a public task-oriented dialogue dataset.

label: acl
text: NLP is currently dominated by language models like RoBERTa which are pretrained on billions of words. But what exact knowledge or skills do Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pretraining that they cannot learn from less data? To explore this question, we adopt five styles of evaluation: classifier probing, information-theoretic probing, unsupervised relative acceptability judgments, unsupervised language model knowledge probing, and fine-tuning on NLU tasks. We then draw learning curves that track the growth of these different measures of model ability with respect to pretraining data volume using the MiniBERTas, a group of RoBERTa models pretrained on 1M, 10M, 100M and 1B words. We find that these LMs require only about 10M to 100M words to learn to reliably encode most syntactic and semantic features we test. They need a much larger quantity of data in order to acquire enough commonsense knowledge and other skills required to master typical downstream NLU tasks. The results suggest that, while the ability to encode linguistic features is almost certainly necessary for language understanding, it is likely that other, unidentified, forms of knowledge are the major drivers of recent improvements in language understanding among large pretrained models.

label: acl
text: The field of NLP is currently dominated by language models such as RoBERTa, which are pre-trained on billions of words. However, the exact knowledge or skills that these Transformer LMs learn from large-scale pre-training that they cannot learn from less data is unclear. To address this question, we evaluate five styles of learning: classifier probing, information-theoretic probing, unsupervised relative acceptability judgments, unsupervised language model knowledge probing, and fine-tuning on NLU tasks. Using MiniBERTas, a group of RoBERTa models pre-trained on 1M, 10M, 100M, and 1B words, we track the growth of these different measures of model ability with respect to pre-training data volume. Our results suggest that these LMs require only 10M to 100M words to learn to encode most syntactic and semantic features. However, they need a larger quantity of data to acquire enough commonsense knowledge and other skills required to master typical downstream NLU tasks. Our findings indicate that while the ability to encode linguistic features is essential for language understanding, other forms of knowledge, yet to be identified, may be the major drivers of recent improvements in language understanding among large pre-trained models.

label: emnlp
text: In natural language processing, a lot of the tasks are successfully solved with recurrent neural networks, but such models have a huge number of parameters. The majority of these parameters are often concentrated in the embedding layer, which size grows proportionally to the vocabulary length. We propose a Bayesian sparsification technique for RNNs which allows compressing the RNN dozens or hundreds of times without time-consuming hyperparameters tuning. We also generalize the model for vocabulary sparsification to filter out unnecessary words and compress the RNN even further. We show that the choice of the kept words is interpretable.

label: emnlp
text: Natural language processing often relies on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to solve tasks, but these models can have a large number of parameters, many of which are concentrated in the embedding layer. To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian sparsification technique for RNNs, which significantly reduces the number of parameters without requiring time-consuming hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, we extend the model to include vocabulary sparsification, which filters out unnecessary words and further compresses the RNN. Our results demonstrate that the choice of words to keep is interpretable.

label: acl
text: We introduce the novel task of predicting adverbial presupposition triggers, which is useful for natural language generation tasks such as summarization and dialogue systems. We introduce two new corpora, derived from the Penn Treebank and the Annotated English Gigaword dataset and investigate the use of a novel attention mechanism tailored to this task. Our attention mechanism augments a baseline recurrent neural network without the need for additional trainable parameters, minimizing the added computational cost of our mechanism. We demonstrate that this model statistically outperforms our baselines.

label: acl
text: We present a novel task of predicting adverbial presupposition triggers for natural language generation tasks, such as summarization and dialogue systems. To support this task, we have created two new corpora from the Penn Treebank and the Annotated English Gigaword dataset. Our research also includes the implementation of a novel attention mechanism, specifically designed for this task. This mechanism enhances a baseline recurrent neural network without adding any extra trainable parameters, thus keeping computational cost to a minimum. Our results show that this model outperforms our baselines statistically.

label: acl
text: Dense retrieval models, which aim at retrieving the most relevant document for an input query on a dense representation space, have gained considerable attention for their remarkable success. Yet, dense models require a vast amount of labeled training data for notable performance, whereas it is often challenging to acquire query-document pairs annotated by humans. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple but effective Document Augmentation for dense Retrieval (DAR) framework, which augments the representations of documents with their interpolation and perturbation. We validate the performance of DAR on retrieval tasks with two benchmark datasets, showing that the proposed DAR significantly outperforms relevant baselines on the dense retrieval of both the labeled and unlabeled documents.

label: acl
text: Dense retrieval models, which aim to find the most relevant document for a given query on a dense representation space, have received significant attention for their impressive results. However, these models require a considerable amount of labeled training data, which can be difficult to obtain due to the need for human annotation of query-document pairs. To address this challenge, we present a straightforward but effective Document Augmentation for Dense Retrieval (DAR) framework. This framework enhances document representations through interpolation and perturbation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DAR through experiments on two benchmark datasets, showing that it outperforms relevant baselines in the dense retrieval of both labeled and unlabeled documents.

label: coling
text: With the development of pre-trained models (PTMs), the performance of text classification has been continuously improved by directly employing the features generated by PTMs. However such way might not fully explore the knowledge in PTMs as it is constrained by the difficulty of the task. Compared to difficult task, the learning algorithms tend to saturate early on the simple task. Moreover, the native sentence representations derived from BERT are prone to be collapsed and directly employing such representation for text classification might fail to fully capture discriminative features. In order to address these issues, in this paper we propose a novel framework for text classification which implements a two-stage training strategy. In the pre-training stage, auxiliary labels are introduced to increase the task difficulties and to fully exploit the knowledge in the pre-trained model. In the fine-tuning stage, the textual representation learned in the pre-training stage is employed and the classifier is fine-tuned to obtain better classification performance. Experiments were conducted on six text classification corpora and the results showed that the proposed framework outperformed several state-of-the-art baselines.

label: coling
text: With the advancement of pre-trained models (PTMs), the performance of text classification has been continuously improved. However, this method may not fully utilize the knowledge contained in PTMs, as it is limited by the difficulty of the task. Simple tasks are more likely to saturate early on, compared to more challenging tasks. Furthermore, the sentence representations generated by BERT are prone to collapse, and using them directly for text classification may not capture the discriminative features effectively. To address these issues, this paper presents a novel framework for text classification that implements a two-stage training strategy. In the pre-training stage, auxiliary labels are introduced to increase the task difficulty and to fully exploit the knowledge in the PTM. In the fine-tuning stage, the textual representation learned during pre-training is employed and the classifier is fine-tuned to enhance the classification performance. Experiments were conducted on six text classification corpora, and the results showed that the proposed framework outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines.

label: acl
text: Recent work in cross-lingual semantic parsing has successfully applied machine translation to localize parsers to new languages. However, these advances assume access to high-quality machine translation systems and word alignment tools. We remove these assumptions and study cross-lingual semantic parsing as a zero-shot problem, without parallel data (i.e., utterance-logical form pairs) for new languages. We propose a multi-task encoder-decoder model to transfer parsing knowledge to additional languages using only English-logical form paired data and in-domain natural language corpora in each new language. Our model encourages language-agnostic encodings by jointly optimizing for logical-form generation with auxiliary objectives designed for cross-lingual latent representation alignment. Our parser performs significantly above translation-based baselines and, in some cases, competes with the supervised upper-bound.

label: acl
text: Recent advancements in cross-lingual semantic parsing have utilized machine translation to localize parsers to new languages. However, these methods require access to high-quality machine translation systems and word alignment tools. Our study aims to remove these assumptions and address cross-lingual semantic parsing as a zero-shot problem without parallel data (i.e., utterance-logical form pairs) for new languages. Our solution is a multi-task encoder-decoder model that transfers parsing knowledge to additional languages using only English-logical form paired data and in-domain natural language corpora in each new language. This model promotes language-agnostic encodings by optimizing for logical-form generation and cross-lingual latent representation alignment through auxiliary objectives. Our parser outperforms translation-based baselines and, in some cases, even rivals the supervised upper-bound.

label: emnlp
text: We present disambiguated skip-gram: a neural-probabilistic model for learning multi-sense distributed representations of words. Disambiguated skip-gram jointly estimates a skip-gram-like context word prediction model and a word sense disambiguation model. Unlike previous probabilistic models for learning multi-sense word embeddings, disambiguated skip-gram is end-to-end differentiable and can be interpreted as a simple feed-forward neural network. We also introduce an effective pruning strategy for the embeddings learned by disambiguated skip-gram. This allows us to control the granularity of representations learned by our model. In experimental evaluation disambiguated skip-gram improves state-of-the are results in several word sense induction benchmarks.

label: emnlp
text: We present the Disambiguated Skip-Gram model, a neural-probabilistic approach for learning multi-sense distributed representations of words. This model jointly estimates a context word prediction model, similar to Skip-Gram, and a word sense disambiguation model. Unlike previous probabilistic models for multi-sense word embeddings, Disambiguated Skip-Gram is end-to-end differentiable and can be interpreted as a simple feed-forward neural network. We also introduce an effective pruning strategy for the learned embeddings, allowing us to control the granularity of the representations. Our experimental evaluation shows that Disambiguated Skip-Gram outperforms current state-of-the-art results in several word sense induction benchmarks.

label: coling
text: We propose a new approach, Knowledge Distillation using Optimal Transport (KNOT), to distill the natural language semantic knowledge from multiple teacher networks to a student network. KNOT aims to train a (global) student model by learning to minimize the optimal transport cost of its assigned probability distribution over the labels to the weighted sum of probabilities predicted by the (local) teacher models, under the constraints that the student model does not have access to teacher models' parameters or training data. To evaluate the quality of knowledge transfer, we introduce a new metric, Semantic Distance (SD), that measures semantic closeness between the predicted and ground truth label distributions. The proposed method shows improvements in the global model's SD performance over the baseline across three NLP tasks while performing on par with Entropy-based distillation on standard accuracy and F1 metrics. The implementation pertaining to this work is publicly available at https://github.com/declare-lab/KNOT.

label: coling
text: We propose a novel method, called Knowledge Distillation using Optimal Transport (KNOT), for distilling semantic knowledge from multiple teacher networks into a student network. The goal of KNOT is to train the student model by minimizing the optimal transport cost between its predicted label distribution and the weighted sum of the teacher models' predicted distributions, while ensuring that the student model does not have access to the teacher models' parameters or training data. To assess the quality of knowledge transfer, we introduce a new metric, Semantic Distance (SD), which measures the semantic similarity between the predicted and ground truth label distributions. Our results demonstrate that KNOT outperforms the baseline in terms of SD across three NLP tasks and performs similarly to Entropy-based distillation in terms of accuracy and F1 metrics. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/declare-lab/KNOT.

label: emnlp
text: Consider two competitive machine learning models, one of which was considered state-of-the art, and the other a competitive baseline. Suppose that by just permuting the examples of the training set, say by reversing the original order, by shuffling, or by mini-batching, you could report substantially better/worst performance for the system of your choice, by multiple percentage points. In this paper, we illustrate this scenario for a trending NLP task: Natural Language Inference (NLI). We show that for the two central NLI corpora today, the learning process of neural systems is far too sensitive to permutations of the data. In doing so we reopen the question of how to judge a good neural architecture for NLI, given the available dataset and perhaps, further, the soundness of the NLI task itself in its current state.

label: emnlp
text: Consider two competitive machine learning models, one of which is considered state-of-the-art and the other a competitive baseline. By simply rearranging the examples in the training set, such as reversing the order, shuffling, or mini-batching, it is possible to report a substantial improvement or decline in performance for the model of choice by multiple percentage points. This paper illustrates this scenario for a popular NLP task, Natural Language Inference (NLI). We demonstrate that the learning process of neural systems for the two central NLI corpora is highly sensitive to permutations of the data, raising questions about the validity of evaluating a good neural architecture for the NLI task based on the available dataset and the soundness of the task itself in its current state.

label: acl
text: Despite pre-trained language models have proven useful for learning high-quality semantic representations, these models are still vulnerable to simple perturbations. Recent works aimed to improve the robustness of pre-trained models mainly focus on adversarial training from perturbed examples with similar semantics, neglecting the utilization of different or even opposite semantics. Different from the image processing field, the text is discrete and few word substitutions can cause significant semantic changes. To study the impact of semantics caused by small perturbations, we conduct a series of pilot experiments and surprisingly find that adversarial training is useless or even harmful for the model to detect these semantic changes. To address this problem, we propose Contrastive Learning with semantIc Negative Examples (CLINE), which constructs semantic negative examples unsupervised to improve the robustness under semantically adversarial attacking. By comparing with similar and opposite semantic examples, the model can effectively perceive the semantic changes caused by small perturbations. Empirical results show that our approach yields substantial improvements on a range of sentiment analysis, reasoning, and reading comprehension tasks. And CLINE also ensures the compactness within the same semantics and separability across different semantics in sentence-level.

label: acl
text: Despite pre-trained language models having proven useful for learning high-quality semantic representations, they are still vulnerable to simple perturbations. Recent efforts to improve the robustness of these models have mainly focused on adversarial training from perturbed examples with similar semantics, neglecting the utilization of different or even opposite semantics. Unlike image processing, text is discrete and small word substitutions can cause significant semantic changes. To understand the impact of these semantic changes, we conducted a series of pilot experiments and surprisingly found that adversarial training is either useless or even harmful for detecting these changes. To address this issue, we propose Contrastive Learning with Semantic Negative Examples (CLINE), which unsupervisedly constructs semantic negative examples to improve robustness against semantically adversarial attacks. By comparing similar and opposite semantic examples, the model can effectively detect semantic changes caused by small perturbations.
