Our results show substantial improvements on a range of sentiment analysis, reasoning, and reading comprehension tasks. CLINE also ensures compactness within the same semantics and separability across different semantics at the sentence level.

label: coling
text: A critical component of competence in language is being able to identify relevant components of an utterance and reply appropriately. In this paper we examine the extent of such dialogue response sensitivity in pre-trained language models, conducting a series of experiments with a particular focus on sensitivity to dynamics involving phenomena of at-issueness and ellipsis. We find that models show clear sensitivity to a distinctive role of embedded clauses, and a general preference for responses that target main clause content of prior utterances. However, the results indicate mixed and generally weak trends with respect to capturing the full range of dynamics involved in targeting at-issue versus not-at-issue content. Additionally, models show fundamental limitations in grasp of the dynamics governing ellipsis, and response selections show clear interference from superficial factors that outweigh the influence of principled discourse constraints.

label: coling
text: The critical aspect of language competence is being able to identify the crucial elements of an utterance and reply to them appropriately. In this paper, we investigate the level of sensitivity to dialogue response in pre-trained language models by conducting a series of experiments. Our focus is on the sensitivity to dynamics related to at-issueness and ellipsis. Our findings suggest that the models exhibit sensitivity to the unique role of embedded clauses and tend to respond to the main clause content of prior utterances. However, the results are mixed and generally weak regarding capturing the full range of dynamics related to targeting at-issue versus not-at-issue content. The models also show fundamental limitations in understanding the dynamics of ellipsis, and the response selections are influenced by superficial factors that override the impact of discourse constraints.

label: acl
text: A dialogue is essentially a multi-turn interaction among interlocutors. Effective evaluation metrics should reflect the dynamics of such interaction. Existing automatic metrics are focused very much on the turn-level quality, while ignoring such dynamics. To this end, we propose DynaEval, a unified automatic evaluation framework which is not only capable of performing turn-level evaluation, but also holistically considers the quality of the entire dialogue. In DynaEval, the graph convolutional network (GCN) is adopted to model a dialogue in totality, where the graph nodes denote each individual utterance and the edges represent the dependency between pairs of utterances. A contrastive loss is then applied to distinguish well-formed dialogues from carefully constructed negative samples. Experiments show that DynaEval significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art dialogue coherence model, and correlates strongly with human judgements across multiple dialogue evaluation aspects at both turn and dialogue level.

label: acl
text: A dialogue is a multi-turn interaction among interlocutors. Effective evaluation metrics should reflect the dynamics of this interaction. Currently, automatic metrics focus solely on turn-level quality and ignore these dynamics. To address this, we propose DynaEval, an automatic evaluation framework that not only assesses turn-level quality but also considers the overall quality of the dialogue. DynaEval uses a graph convolutional network (GCN) to model the entire dialogue, with each utterance represented as a graph node and the dependencies between utterances represented as edges. A contrastive loss is applied to distinguish well-formed dialogues from negative samples. Experiments show that DynaEval outperforms the state-of-the-art dialogue coherence model and strongly correlates with human judgments across multiple dialogue evaluation aspects at both the turn and dialogue level.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we focus on the problem of building assistive systems that can help users to write reviews. We cast this problem using an encoder-decoder framework that generates personalized reviews by expanding short phrases (e.g. review summaries, product titles) provided as input to the system. We incorporate aspect-level information via an aspect encoder that learns aspect-aware user and item representations. An attention fusion layer is applied to control generation by attending on the outputs of multiple encoders. Experimental results show that our model successfully learns representations capable of generating coherent and diverse reviews. In addition, the learned aspect-aware representations discover those aspects that users are more inclined to discuss and bias the generated text toward their personalized aspect preferences.

label: acl
text: In this research, we concentrate on developing assistive systems that aid users in writing reviews. We address this challenge by utilizing an encoder-decoder framework that generates personalized reviews by expanding short input phrases, such as product titles or review summaries. Our model incorporates aspect-level information through an aspect encoder that learns aspect-sensitive user and item representations. An attention fusion layer is used to control the generation process by focusing on the outputs from multiple encoders. Our experiments demonstrate that our model effectively learns representations that generate coherent and diverse reviews. Furthermore, the aspect-sensitive representations discovered by our model reveal the aspects that users are more likely to discuss, thereby biasing the generated text towards their personalized aspect preferences.

label: naacl
text: Recent works have empirically shown the effectiveness of data augmentation (DA) in NLP tasks, especially for those suffering from data scarcity. Intuitively, given the size of generated data, their diversity and quality are crucial to the performance of targeted tasks. However, to the best of our knowledge, most existing methods consider only either the diversity or the quality of augmented data, thus cannot fully mine the potential of DA for NLP. In this paper, we present an easy and plug-in data augmentation framework EPiDA to support effective text classification. EPiDA employs two mechanisms: relative entropy maximization (REM) and conditional entropy minimization (CEM) to control data generation, where REM is designed to enhance the diversity of augmented data while CEM is exploited to ensure their semantic consistency. EPiDA can support efficient and continuous data generation for effective classifier training. Extensive experiments show that EPiDA outperforms existing SOTA methods in most cases, though not using any agent networks or pre-trained generation networks, and it works well with various DA algorithms and classification models.

label: naacl
text: Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of data augmentation (DA) in NLP tasks, particularly for those that are limited by a lack of data. The diversity and quality of the generated data are key factors in determining the performance of the target task. However, most existing methods only focus on either the diversity or quality of the augmented data, leaving the full potential of DA untapped. To address this issue, we introduce EPiDA, a simple and versatile data augmentation framework for effective text classification. EPiDA employs two mechanisms, relative entropy maximization (REM) and conditional entropy minimization (CEM), to control the generation of data. REM is used to increase the diversity of the augmented data, while CEM ensures their semantic consistency. EPiDA enables efficient and continuous data generation, which results in improved classifier training. Our experiments show that EPiDA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most cases, despite not relying on agent networks or pre-trained generation networks. Additionally, EPiDA is compatible with various DA algorithms and classification models.

label: coling
text: Table-based fact verification aims to verify whether a statement sentence is trusted or fake. Most existing methods rely on graph feature or data augmentation but fail to investigate evidence correlation between the statement and table effectively. In this paper, we propose a self-Labeled Keypoint Alignment model, named LKA, to explore the correlation between the two. Specifically, a dual-view alignment module based on the statement and table views is designed to discriminate the salient words through multiple interactions, where one regular and one adversarial alignment network cooperatively character the alignment discrepancy. Considering the interaction characteristic inherent in the alignment module, we introduce a novel mixture-of experts block to elaborately integrate the interacted information for supporting the alignment and final classification. Furthermore, a contrastive learning loss is utilized to learn the precise representation of the structure-involved words, encouraging the words closer to words with the same table attribute and farther from the words with the unrelated attribute. Experimental results on three widely-studied datasets show that our model can outperform the state-of-the-art baselines and capture interpretable evidence words.

label: coling
text: Table-based fact verification aims to determine the credibility of a statement sentence. Existing methods often use graph features or data augmentation, but they are not effective in investigating the correlation between the statement and the table. To address this issue, we present a self-Labeled Keypoint Alignment (LKA) model. This model explores the correlation between the statement and table by using a dual-view alignment module that discriminates salient words through multiple interactions. The module is composed of one regular and one adversarial alignment network, which work together to characterize the alignment discrepancy. We also introduce a novel mixture-of-experts block to integrate the interacted information for final classification. Additionally, a contrastive learning loss is used to learn the precise representation of structure-involved words, promoting words that have similar table attributes to be closer and words that are unrelated to be farther apart. Our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three widely-studied datasets and provides interpretable evidence words.

label: acl
text: Retrieval-based methods have been shown to be effective in NLP tasks via introducing external knowledge. However, the indexing and retrieving of large-scale corpora bring considerable computational cost. Surprisingly, we found that REtrieving from the traINing datA (REINA) only can lead to significant gains on multiple NLG and NLU tasks. We retrieve the labeled training instances most similar to the input text and then concatenate them with the input to feed into the model to generate the output. Experimental results show that this simple method can achieve significantly better performance on a variety of NLU and NLG tasks, including summarization, machine translation, language modeling, and question answering tasks. For instance, our proposed method achieved state-of-the-art results on XSum, BigPatent, and CommonsenseQA. Our code is released, https://github.com/microsoft/REINA .

label: acl
text: Retrieval-based techniques have been demonstrated to be effective in NLP tasks, thanks to the integration of external knowledge. However, the indexing and retrieval of large-scale corpora can be computationally expensive. To our surprise, we discovered that retrieving from the training data (REINA) alone can result in significant improvements on multiple NLG and NLU tasks. Our approach involves retrieving the most similar labeled training instances to the input text and then concatenating them with the input to feed into the model for generating the output. Our experiments show that this simple method can deliver significantly better performance on a range of NLU and NLG tasks, including summarization, machine translation, language modeling, and question answering. For example, our proposed method achieved state-of-the-art results on XSum, BigPatent, and CommonsenseQA. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/REINA.

label: coling
text: Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been used for dialogue policy optimization. However, many DRL-based policies are not sample-efficient. Most recent advances focus on improving DRL optimization algorithms to address this issue. Here, we take an alternative route of designing neural network structure that is better suited for DRL-based dialogue management. The proposed structured deep reinforcement learning is based on graph neural networks (GNN), which consists of some sub-networks, each one for a node on a directed graph. The graph is defined according to the domain ontology and each node can be considered as a sub-agent. During decision making, these sub-agents have internal message exchange between neighbors on the graph. We also propose an approach to jointly optimize the graph structure as well as the parameters of GNN. Experiments show that structured DRL significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches in almost all of the 18 tasks of the PyDial benchmark.

label: coling
text: Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have been utilized for optimizing dialogue policies. However, many of these policies are not sample-efficient. Efforts have been made to improve DRL optimization algorithms to address this issue. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach by designing a neural network structure that is better suited for DRL-based dialogue management. Our structured deep reinforcement learning is based on graph neural networks (GNN) and consists of multiple sub-networks, each representing a node on a directed graph. The graph is defined based on the domain ontology and each node can be considered as a sub-agent. During decision-making, these sub-agents communicate with each other through internal messaging on the graph. Additionally, we present a method for jointly optimizing the graph structure and the parameters of the GNN. Our experiments demonstrate that structured DRL outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches in almost all 18 tasks of the PyDial benchmark.

label: acl
text: Recurrent and convolutional neural networks comprise two distinct families of models that have proven to be useful for encoding natural language utterances. In this paper we present SoPa, a new model that aims to bridge these two approaches. SoPa combines neural representation learning with weighted finite-state automata (WFSAs) to learn a soft version of traditional surface patterns. We show that SoPa is an extension of a one-layer CNN, and that such CNNs are equivalent to a restricted version of SoPa, and accordingly, to a restricted form of WFSA. Empirically, on three text classification tasks, SoPa is comparable or better than both a BiLSTM (RNN) baseline and a CNN baseline, and is particularly useful in small data settings.

label: acl
text: The Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) are two different families of models that have been successful in encoding natural language utterances. In this paper, we introduce SoPa, a new model that aims to merge these two approaches. SoPa combines neural representation learning with weighted finite-state automata (WFSAs) to create a soft version of traditional surface patterns. Our research shows that SoPa is an extension of a one-layer CNN, and that such CNNs are equivalent to a restricted form of SoPa and WFSA. Empirically, SoPa outperforms both a BiLSTM (RNN) baseline and a CNN baseline in three text classification tasks, especially in small data settings.

label: naacl
text: When people answer questions about a specific situation, e.g., “I cheated on my mid-term exam last week. Was that wrong?”, cognitive science suggests that they form a mental picture of that situation before answering. While we do not know how language models (LMs) answer such questions, we conjecture that they may answer more accurately if they are also provided with additional details about the question situation, elaborating the “scene”. To test this conjecture, we train a new model, DREAM, to answer questions that elaborate the scenes that situated questions are about, and then provide those elaborations as additional context to a question-answering (QA) model. We find that DREAM is able to create better scene elaborations (more accurate, useful, and consistent) than a representative state-of-the-art, zero-shot model (Macaw). We also find that using the scene elaborations as additional context improves the answer accuracy of a downstream QA system, including beyond that obtainable by simply further fine-tuning the QA system on DREAM's training data. These results suggest that adding focused elaborations about a situation can improve a system's reasoning about it, and may serve as an effective way of injecting new scenario-based knowledge into QA models. Finally, our approach is dataset-neutral; we observe improved QA performance across different models, with even bigger gains on models with fewer parameters.

label: naacl
text: According to cognitive science, when people are asked questions about a specific situation, they form a mental picture of that scenario before answering. The way language models (LMs) answer such questions is not yet clear, but it is believed that they may provide more accurate answers if they are given additional details about the situation in question. To test this hypothesis, a new model called DREAM was trained to answer questions that elaborate on the scenes depicted in the questions. The elaborations were then used as additional context for a question-answering (QA) model. The results showed that DREAM was able to create more accurate, useful, and consistent scene elaborations than a state-of-the-art, zero-shot model (Macaw). Additionally, using the scene elaborations as additional context improved the accuracy of the downstream QA system, even beyond what could be achieved by simply fine-tuning the QA system on DREAM's training data. These findings suggest that adding focused elaborations about a situation can enhance a system's reasoning and may provide a way to inject new scenario-based knowledge into QA models. Importantly, the approach is dataset-neutral and showed improved QA performance across different models, with even greater gains in models with fewer parameters.

label: acl
text: Generating some appealing questions in open-domain conversations is an effective way to improve human-machine interactions and lead the topic to a broader or deeper direction. To avoid dull or deviated questions, some researchers tried to utilize answer, the “future” information, to guide question generation. However, they separate a post-question-answer (PQA) triple into two parts: post-question (PQ) and question-answer (QA) pairs, which may hurt the overall coherence. Besides, the QA relationship is modeled as a one-to-one mapping that is not reasonable in open-domain conversations. To tackle these problems, we propose a generative triple-wise model with hierarchical variations for open-domain conversational question generation (CQG). Latent variables in three hierarchies are used to represent the shared background of a triple and one-to-many semantic mappings in both PQ and QA pairs. Experimental results on a large-scale CQG dataset show that our method significantly improves the quality of questions in terms of fluency, coherence and diversity over competitive baselines.

label: acl
text: Generating appealing questions in open-domain conversations is an effective way to enhance human-machine interactions and steer the conversation in a broader or deeper direction. To avoid dull or deviated questions, some researchers have attempted to utilize answer information to guide question generation. However, this approach separates a post-question-answer (PQA) triple into two parts: post-question (PQ) and question-answer (QA) pairs, which can negatively impact the overall coherence. Additionally, the QA relationship is modeled as a one-to-one mapping, which is not feasible in open-domain conversations. To address these issues, we propose a generative triple-wise model with hierarchical variations for open-domain conversational question generation (CQG). The model uses latent variables in three hierarchies to represent the shared background of a triple and enables one-to-many semantic mappings in both PQ and QA pairs. Our experiments on a large-scale CQG dataset show that our method significantly improves the quality of questions in terms of fluency, coherence, and diversity compared to competitive baselines.

label: acl
text: There is content such as hate speech, offensive, toxic or aggressive documents, which are perceived differently by their consumers. They are commonly identified using classifiers solely based on textual content that generalize pre-agreed meanings of difficult problems. Such models provide the same results for each user, which leads to high misclassification rate observable especially for contentious, aggressive documents. Both document controversy and user nonconformity require new solutions. Therefore, we propose novel personalized approaches that respect individual beliefs expressed by either user conformity-based measures or various embeddings of their previous text annotations. We found that only a few annotations of most controversial documents are enough for all our personalization methods to significantly outperform classic, generalized solutions. The more controversial the content, the greater the gain. The personalized solutions may be used to efficiently filter unwanted aggressive content in the way adjusted to a given person.

label: acl
text: There is content, such as hate speech, offensive, toxic, or aggressive documents, which is perceived differently by different consumers. These documents are commonly identified using classifiers based solely on their textual content, which generalizes pre-agreed meanings of difficult problems. However, this leads to a high misclassification rate, particularly for contentious and aggressive documents. To address this issue, we propose novel personalized approaches that respect individual beliefs expressed through user conformity-based measures or through various embeddings of their previous text annotations. Our findings show that only a few annotations of the most controversial documents are enough for our personalization methods to significantly outperform traditional, generalized solutions. The more controversial the content, the greater the improvement. These personalized solutions can be used to efficiently filter unwanted aggressive content, tailored to the individual's preferences.

label: acl
text: While there is an abundance of advice to podcast creators on how to speak in ways that engage their listeners, there has been little data-driven analysis of podcasts that relates linguistic style with engagement. In this paper, we investigate how various factors – vocabulary diversity, distinctiveness, emotion, and syntax, among others – correlate with engagement, based on analysis of the creators' written descriptions and transcripts of the audio. We build models with different textual representations, and show that the identified features are highly predictive of engagement. Our analysis tests popular wisdom about stylistic elements in high-engagement podcasts, corroborating some pieces of advice and adding new perspectives on others.

label: acl
text: While there is a wealth of advice for podcast creators on how to engage their listeners through their speech, there has been limited data-driven analysis of the relationship between linguistic style and engagement in podcasts. In this study, we examine the correlation between engagement and various factors such as vocabulary diversity, distinctiveness, emotion, and syntax, among others, using analysis of the written descriptions and audio transcripts of the podcasts. Our models, which employ various textual representations, reveal that the identified features are highly indicative of engagement. Our findings validate some of the conventional wisdom about the stylistic elements of highly engaging podcasts, while also offering new insights into others.

label: emnlp
text: A challenge in creating a dataset for machine reading comprehension (MRC) is to collect questions that require a sophisticated understanding of language to answer beyond using superficial cues. In this work, we investigate what makes questions easier across recent 12 MRC datasets with three question styles (answer extraction, description, and multiple choice). We propose to employ simple heuristics to split each dataset into easy and hard subsets and examine the performance of two baseline models for each of the subsets. We then manually annotate questions sampled from each subset with both validity and requisite reasoning skills to investigate which skills explain the difference between easy and hard questions. From this study, we observed that (i) the baseline performances for the hard subsets remarkably degrade compared to those of entire datasets, (ii) hard questions require knowledge inference and multiple-sentence reasoning in comparison with easy questions, and (iii) multiple-choice questions tend to require a broader range of reasoning skills than answer extraction and description questions. These results suggest that one might overestimate recent advances in MRC.

label: emnlp
text: The creation of a dataset for machine reading comprehension (MRC) poses a challenge as it requires the collection of questions that require a sophisticated understanding of language, beyond relying on superficial cues. In this study, we analyzed the ease of questions across 12 recent MRC datasets, focusing on three question styles: answer extraction, description, and multiple choice. We divided each dataset into easy and hard subsets using simple heuristics and evaluated the performance of two baseline models on each subset. Additionally, we manually annotated questions from each subset to determine the reasoning skills required to answer them. Our results showed that the baseline performance on the hard subsets was significantly lower compared to that of the entire datasets. We also found that hard questions required knowledge inference and multi-sentence reasoning, whereas easy questions did not. Furthermore, we discovered that multiple-choice questions tended to require a broader range of reasoning skills compared to answer extraction and description questions. These findings suggest that recent advances in MRC may be overestimated.

label: acl
text: Although teacher forcing has become the main training paradigm for neural machine translation, it usually makes predictions only conditioned on past information, and hence lacks global planning for the future. To address this problem, we introduce another decoder, called seer decoder, into the encoder-decoder framework during training, which involves future information in target predictions. Meanwhile, we force the conventional decoder to simulate the behaviors of the seer decoder via knowledge distillation. In this way, at test the conventional decoder can perform like the seer decoder without the attendance of it. Experiment results on the Chinese-English, English-German and English-Romanian translation tasks show our method can outperform competitive baselines significantly and achieves greater improvements on the bigger data sets. Besides, the experiments also prove knowledge distillation the best way to transfer knowledge from the seer decoder to the conventional decoder compared to adversarial learning and L2 regularization.

label: acl
text: The main training paradigm for neural machine translation is teacher forcing, but it has a limitation in that it only makes predictions based on past information and lacks global planning for the future. To overcome this, we introduce the seer decoder into the encoder-decoder framework during training. This decoder involves future information in target predictions and is used to train the conventional decoder through knowledge distillation. This allows the conventional decoder to perform like the seer decoder without its presence during testing. Our method outperforms competitive baselines on Chinese-English, English-German, and English-Romanian translation tasks, especially on larger data sets. Experiments also show that knowledge distillation is the most effective way to transfer knowledge from the seer decoder to the conventional decoder, compared to adversarial learning and L2 regularization.

label: coling
text: Semantically meaningful sentence embeddings are important for numerous tasks in natural language processing. To obtain such embeddings, recent studies explored the idea of utilizing synthetically generated data from pretrained language models(PLMs) as a training corpus. However, PLMs often generate sentences different from the ones written by human. We hypothesize that treating all these synthetic examples equally for training can have an adverse effect on learning semantically meaningful embeddings. To analyze this, we first train a classifier that identifies machine-written sentences and observe that the linguistic features of the sentences identified as written by a machine are significantly different from those of human-written sentences. Based on this, we propose a novel approach that first trains the classifier to measure the importance of each sentence. The distilled information from the classifier is then used to train a reliable sentence embedding model. Through extensive evaluation on four real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our model trained on synthetic data generalizes well and outperforms the baselines.

label: coling
text: Meaningful sentence embeddings are crucial for various natural language processing tasks. To achieve such embeddings, recent studies have explored using synthetically generated data from pretrained language models (PLMs) as a training corpus. However, PLMs often generate sentences that differ from those written by humans. We hypothesize that treating all synthetic examples equally during training can negatively impact the learning of semantically meaningful embeddings. To test this, we train a classifier to identify machine-written sentences and find that the linguistic features of sentences identified as machine-written are significantly different from those written by humans. Based on these findings, we present a novel approach that trains the classifier to assess the importance of each sentence before training a reliable sentence embedding model. Through extensive evaluation on four real-world datasets, we show that our model, trained on synthetic data, generalizes well and outperforms existing methods.

label: acl
text: Backdoor attacks are a kind of insidious security threat against machine learning models. After being injected with a backdoor in training, the victim model will produce adversary-specified outputs on the inputs embedded with predesigned triggers but behave properly on normal inputs during inference. As a sort of emergent attack, backdoor attacks in natural language processing (NLP) are investigated insufficiently. As far as we know, almost all existing textual backdoor attack methods insert additional contents into normal samples as triggers, which causes the trigger-embedded samples to be detected and the backdoor attacks to be blocked without much effort. In this paper, we propose to use the syntactic structure as the trigger in textual backdoor attacks. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that the syntactic trigger-based attack method can achieve comparable attack performance (almost 100% success rate) to the insertion-based methods but possesses much higher invisibility and stronger resistance to defenses. These results also reveal the significant insidiousness and harmfulness of textual backdoor attacks. All the code and data of this paper can be obtained at https://github.com/thunlp/HiddenKiller.

label: acl
text: Backdoor attacks pose a serious security threat to machine learning models. Once the model is infected during training, it will produce adversary-specified outputs when triggered by predesigned inputs, while still appearing to function normally on normal inputs during inference. Despite the growing importance of natural language processing (NLP) in machine learning, backdoor attacks in this area have not been thoroughly investigated. Existing textual backdoor attack methods primarily rely on inserting additional content into normal samples as triggers, which can easily be detected and prevented. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to textual backdoor attacks, using the syntactic structure as the trigger. Our extensive experiments show that this syntactic trigger-based method can achieve comparable attack performance (nearly 100% success rate) to insertion-based methods, while being much more invisible and resistant to defenses. These results highlight the insidious nature and potential harm of textual backdoor attacks in NLP. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thunlp/HiddenKiller.

label: acl
text: Human activities can be seen as sequences of events, which are crucial to understanding societies. Disproportional event distribution for different demographic groups can manifest and amplify social stereotypes, and potentially jeopardize the ability of members in some groups to pursue certain goals. In this paper, we present the first event-centric study of gender biases in a Wikipedia corpus. To facilitate the study, we curate a corpus of career and personal life descriptions with demographic information consisting of 7,854 fragments from 10,412 celebrities. Then we detect events with a state-of-the-art event detection model, calibrate the results using strategically generated templates, and extract events that have asymmetric associations with genders. Our study discovers that the Wikipedia pages tend to intermingle personal life events with professional events for females but not for males, which calls for the awareness of the Wikipedia community to formalize guidelines and train the editors to mind the implicit biases that contributors carry. Our work also lays the foundation for future works on quantifying and discovering event biases at the corpus level.

label: acl
text: Human activities can be viewed as a series of events, which are essential for comprehending societies. Disproportionate event distribution among different demographic groups can lead to the manifestation and amplification of social stereotypes, thereby hindering the ability of some group members to achieve their goals. This paper presents the first event-focused study of gender biases in a Wikipedia corpus, using a curated corpus of 7,854 career and personal life descriptions of 10,412 celebrities, with demographic information. Our study employs state-of-the-art event detection models, calibrated using strategically generated templates, to identify events with asymmetric associations with gender. Our findings indicate that Wikipedia pages tend to mix personal life events with professional events for females, but not for males, highlighting the need for the Wikipedia community to address implicit biases and provide training for editors. This work lays the foundation for future research on quantifying and identifying event biases at the corpus level.

label: acl
text: Fine-tuning the entire set of parameters of a large pretrained model has become the mainstream approach for transfer learning. To increase its efficiency and prevent catastrophic forgetting and interference, techniques like adapters and sparse fine-tuning have been developed. Adapters are modular, as they can be combined to adapt a model towards different facets of knowledge (e.g., dedicated language and/or task adapters). Sparse fine-tuning is expressive, as it controls the behavior of all model components. In this work, we introduce a new fine-tuning method with both these desirable properties. In particular, we learn sparse, real-valued masks based on a simple variant of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis. Task-specific masks are obtained from annotated data in a source language, and language-specific masks from masked language modeling in a target language. Both these masks can then be composed with the pretrained model. Unlike adapter-based fine-tuning, this method neither increases the number of parameters at inference time nor alters the original model architecture. Most importantly, it outperforms adapters in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer by a large margin in a series of multilingual benchmarks, including Universal Dependencies, MasakhaNER, and AmericasNLI. Based on an in-depth analysis, we additionally find that sparsity is crucial to prevent both 1) interference between the fine-tunings to be composed and 2) overfitting. We release the code and models at https://github.com/cambridgeltl/composable-sft.

label: acl
text: The mainstream approach for transfer learning is fine-tuning the entire set of parameters of a large pre-trained model. To improve its efficiency and avoid catastrophic forgetting and interference, techniques such as adapters and sparse fine-tuning have been developed. Adapters are modular and can be combined to adapt the model to different knowledge facets (e.g. language and task adapters). Sparse fine-tuning is expressive and allows for control over all model components. In this study, we present a new fine-tuning method that combines these desirable properties. The method involves learning sparse, real-valued masks based on a variant of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis. Task-specific masks are obtained from annotated data in the source language, and language-specific masks from masked language modeling in the target language. Both masks can then be combined with the pre-trained model. Unlike adapter-based fine-tuning, this approach does not increase the number of parameters at inference time or alter the original model architecture. Furthermore, it outperforms adapters in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer by a significant margin in various multilingual benchmarks, including Universal Dependencies, MasakhaNER, and AmericasNLI. An in-depth analysis reveals that sparsity is critical in preventing both 1) interference between the fine-tunings and 2) overfitting. The code and models are available at https://github.com/cambridgeltl/composable-sft.

label: naacl
text: We propose novel AI-empowered chat bots for learning as conversation where a user does not read a passage but gains information and knowledge through conversation with a teacher bot. Our information acquisition-oriented dialogue system employs a novel adaptation of reinforced self-play so that the system can be transferred to various domains without in-domain dialogue data, and can carry out conversations both informative and attentive to users.

label: naacl
text: We propose a new AI-powered chatbot for learning through conversation, where the user can gain knowledge and information without having to read a passage. Our information-acquisition-focused dialogue system uses a unique adaptation of reinforced self-play, allowing the system to be transferred to different domains without the need for in-domain dialogue data. Additionally, the chatbot is designed to engage in both informative and attentive conversations with the user.

label: coling
text: The state-of-the-art methods for relation classification are primarily based on deep neural net- works. This kind of supervised learning method suffers from not only limited training data, but also the large number of low-frequency relations in specific domains. In this paper, we propose the task of exploratory relation classification for domain knowledge harvesting. The goal is to learn a classifier on pre-defined relations and discover new relations expressed in texts. A dynamically structured neural network is introduced to classify entity pairs to a continuously expanded relation set. We further propose the similarity sensitive Chinese restaurant process to discover new relations. Experiments conducted on a large corpus show the effectiveness of our neural network, while new relations are discovered with high precision and recall.

label: coling
text: The state-of-the-art methods for relation classification are primarily based on deep neural networks. These supervised learning methods suffer from limited training data and a large number of low-frequency relations in specific domains. To address this issue, we propose a task of exploratory relation classification for harvesting domain knowledge. Our goal is to learn a classifier for pre-defined relations and uncover new relations expressed in text. To achieve this, we introduce a dynamically structured neural network that classifies entity pairs into a continuously expanding relation set. Additionally, we propose a similarity-sensitive Chinese restaurant process to discover new relations. Our experiments on a large corpus demonstrate the effectiveness of our neural network, with high precision and recall in uncovering new relations.

label: coling
text: Prior studies addressing target-oriented conversational tasks lack a crucial notion that has been intensively studied in the context of goal-oriented artificial intelligence agents, namely, planning. In this study, we propose the task of Target-Guided Open-Domain Conversation Planning (TGCP) task to evaluate whether neural conversational agents have goal-oriented conversation planning abilities. Using the TGCP task, we investigate the conversation planning abilities of existing retrieval models and recent strong generative models. The experimental results reveal the challenges facing current technology.

label: coling
text: Prior research on target-oriented conversational tasks has overlooked an important aspect that has received significant attention in the field of goal-oriented artificial intelligence agents: planning. To address this gap, we introduce the Target-Guided Open-Domain Conversation Planning (TGCP) task to assess the ability of neural conversational agents to engage in goal-oriented conversations. Our experiments using the TGCP task compare the conversation planning abilities of existing retrieval models and recent state-of-the-art generative models. The results highlight the challenges faced by current technology.

label: coling
text: Multilingual topic models enable crosslingual tasks by extracting consistent topics from multilingual corpora. Most models require parallel or comparable training corpora, which limits their ability to generalize. In this paper, we first demystify the knowledge transfer mechanism behind multilingual topic models by defining an alternative but equivalent formulation. Based on this analysis, we then relax the assumption of training data required by most existing models, creating a model that only requires a dictionary for training. Experiments show that our new method effectively learns coherent multilingual topics from partially and fully incomparable corpora with limited amounts of dictionary resources.

label: coling
text: Multilingual topic models can perform crosslingual tasks by identifying consistent topics from multilingual corpora. However, most models need parallel or comparable training corpora, which restricts their generalization capabilities. In this paper, we clarify the knowledge transfer mechanism behind multilingual topic models by introducing an equivalent alternative formulation. With this understanding, we develop a model that only requires a dictionary for training, without relying on parallel or comparable training data. Our experiments demonstrate that our new method can effectively learn coherent multilingual topics from partially and fully incomparable corpora with limited dictionary resources.

label: emnlp
text: Cross-lingual word embeddings are becoming increasingly important in multilingual NLP. Recently, it has been shown that these embeddings can be effectively learned by aligning two disjoint monolingual vector spaces through linear transformations, using no more than a small bilingual dictionary as supervision. In this work, we propose to apply an additional transformation after the initial alignment step, which moves cross-lingual synonyms towards a middle point between them. By applying this transformation our aim is to obtain a better cross-lingual integration of the vector spaces. In addition, and perhaps surprisingly, the monolingual spaces also improve by this transformation. This is in contrast to the original alignment, which is typically learned such that the structure of the monolingual spaces is preserved. Our experiments confirm that the resulting cross-lingual embeddings outperform state-of-the-art models in both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation tasks.

label: emnlp
text: Cross-lingual word embeddings are becoming increasingly crucial in multilingual NLP. Researchers have shown that these embeddings can be effectively learned through aligning two disjoint monolingual vector spaces by linear transformations with the use of a small bilingual dictionary. In this study, we propose to apply an additional transformation after the initial alignment step, which brings cross-lingual synonyms closer to a common point between them. This transformation aims to improve the cross-lingual integration of the vector spaces and surprisingly, it also enhances the monolingual spaces. In contrast, the original alignment is usually learned to preserve the structure of the monolingual spaces. Our experiments confirm that the resulting cross-lingual embeddings are superior to state-of-the-art models in both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation tasks.

label: acl
text: Does the effectiveness of neural language models derive entirely from accurate modeling of surface word co-occurrence statistics, or do these models represent and reason about the world they describe? In BART and T5 transformer language models, we identify contextual word representations that function as *models of entities and situations* as they evolve throughout a discourse. These neural representations have functional similarities to linguistic models of dynamic semantics: they support a linear readout of each entity's current properties and relations, and can be manipulated with predictable effects on language generation. Our results indicate that prediction in pretrained neural language models is supported, at least in part, by dynamic representations of meaning and implicit simulation of entity state, and that this behavior can be learned with only text as training data.

label: acl
text: The effectiveness of neural language models is not solely dependent on accurate modeling of surface word co-occurrence statistics. These models also represent and reason about the world they describe. Our research has found that in BART and T5 transformer language models, there are contextual word representations that serve as models of entities and situations, which evolve throughout a discourse. These neural representations have functional similarities to linguistic models of dynamic semantics, as they allow for a linear readout of each entity's current properties and relations, and can be manipulated to produce predictable effects on language generation. Our findings suggest that the prediction capabilities of pretrained neural language models are partially supported by dynamic representations of meaning and implicit simulation of entity state, which can be learned using only text as training data.

label: acl
text: Semantic parsing is challenging due to the structure gap and the semantic gap between utterances and logical forms. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised semantic parsing method - Synchronous Semantic Decoding (SSD), which can simultaneously resolve the semantic gap and the structure gap by jointly leveraging paraphrasing and grammar-constrained decoding. Specifically, we reformulate semantic parsing as a constrained paraphrasing problem: given an utterance, our model synchronously generates its canonical utterancel and meaning representation. During synchronously decoding: the utterance paraphrasing is constrained by the structure of the logical form, therefore the canonical utterance can be paraphrased controlledly; the semantic decoding is guided by the semantics of the canonical utterance, therefore its logical form can be generated unsupervisedly. Experimental results show that SSD is a promising approach and can achieve state-of-the-art unsupervised semantic parsing performance on multiple datasets.

label: acl
text: Semantic parsing is a challenging task due to the existing structure gap and semantic gap between utterances and logical forms. To resolve these gaps, we propose an unsupervised method called Synchronous Semantic Decoding (SSD). This method leverages both paraphrasing and grammar-constrained decoding to simultaneously resolve the semantic and structure gaps. Our method reformulates semantic parsing as a constrained paraphrasing problem, where the model generates a canonical utterance and its meaning representation, synchronously. The utterance paraphrasing is controlled by the logical form's structure, while the semantic decoding is guided by the canonical utterance's semantics. Our experiments show that SSD is a promising approach and outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised semantic parsing methods on multiple datasets.

label: coling
text: Aspect-level sentiment analysis aims to distinguish the sentiment polarity of each specific aspect term in a given sentence. Both industry and academia have realized the importance of the relationship between aspect term and sentence, and made attempts to model the relationship by designing a series of attention models. However, most existing methods usually neglect the fact that the position information is also crucial for identifying the sentiment polarity of the aspect term. When an aspect term occurs in a sentence, its neighboring words should be given more attention than other words with long distance. Therefore, we propose a position-aware bidirectional attention network (PBAN) based on bidirectional GRU. PBAN not only concentrates on the position information of aspect terms, but also mutually models the relation between aspect term and sentence by employing bidirectional attention mechanism. The experimental results on SemEval 2014 Datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed PBAN model.

label: coling
text: The aim of aspect-level sentiment analysis is to identify the sentiment polarity of specific aspect terms within a sentence. Both industry and academia have recognized the significance of the relationship between aspect terms and sentences and attempted to model this relationship through the design of various attention models. However, most current methods overlook the importance of the position information in determining the sentiment polarity of aspect terms. When an aspect term appears in a sentence, its proximity to neighboring words should be given more weight than words that are further away. To address this, we propose a position-aware bidirectional attention network (PBAN), which utilizes a bidirectional GRU. PBAN not only takes into account the position information of aspect terms but also models the relationship between aspect terms and sentences through bidirectional attention mechanisms. Our experiments on the SemEval 2014 dataset show the effectiveness of the PBAN model.

label: naacl
text: Machine reading comprehension (MRC) that requires discrete reasoning involving symbolic operations, e.g., addition, sorting, and counting, is a challenging task. According to this nature, semantic parsing-based methods predict interpretable but complex logical forms. However, logical form generation is nontrivial and even a little perturbation in a logical form will lead to wrong answers. To alleviate this issue, multi-predictor -based methods are proposed to directly predict different types of answers and achieve improvements. However, they ignore the utilization of symbolic operations and encounter a lack of reasoning ability and interpretability. To inherit the advantages of these two types of methods, we propose OPERA, an operation-pivoted discrete reasoning framework, where lightweight symbolic operations (compared with logical forms) as neural modules are utilized to facilitate the reasoning ability and interpretability. Specifically, operations are first selected and then softly executed to simulate the answer reasoning procedure. Extensive experiments on both DROP and RACENum datasets show the reasoning ability of OPERA. Moreover, further analysis verifies its interpretability.

label: naacl
text: The task of machine reading comprehension (MRC) that requires discrete reasoning involving symbolic operations, such as addition, sorting, and counting, is challenging. Semantic parsing-based methods predict interpretable but complex logical forms, but generating logical forms is nontrivial and even small perturbations can result in incorrect answers. To address this issue, multi-predictor methods have been proposed to directly predict different types of answers, improving performance. However, these methods ignore the use of symbolic operations and lack reasoning ability and interpretability. To overcome these limitations, we propose OPERA, an operation-pivoted discrete reasoning framework that utilizes lightweight symbolic operations as neural modules to enhance reasoning ability and interpretability. Operations are selected and softly executed to simulate the answer reasoning process. Our experiments on the DROP and RACENum datasets demonstrate OPERA's reasoning ability and further analysis confirms its interpretability.

label: acl
text: Tree-based neural machine translation (NMT) approaches, although achieved impressive performance, suffer from a major drawback: they only use the 1-best parse tree to direct the translation, which potentially introduces translation mistakes due to parsing errors. For statistical machine translation (SMT), forest-based methods have been proven to be effective for solving this problem, while for NMT this kind of approach has not been attempted. This paper proposes a forest-based NMT method that translates a linearized packed forest under a simple sequence-to-sequence framework (i.e., a forest-to-sequence NMT model). The BLEU score of the proposed method is higher than that of the sequence-to-sequence NMT, tree-based NMT, and forest-based SMT systems.

label: acl
text: Tree-based Neural Machine Translation (NMT) approaches have achieved impressive results, but suffer from a significant drawback - they only use the 1-best parse tree to direct the translation. This can result in translation mistakes due to parsing errors. For Statistical Machine Translation (SMT), forest-based methods have been proven to be effective in addressing this issue. However, this has not yet been attempted for NMT. This paper proposes a forest-based NMT method that translates a linearized packed forest using a simple sequence-to-sequence framework, resulting in a higher BLEU score compared to sequence-to-sequence NMT, tree-based NMT, and forest-based SMT systems.

label: naacl
text: A document can be summarized in a number of ways. Reference-based evaluation of summarization has been criticized for its inflexibility. The more sufficient the number of abstracts, the more accurate the evaluation results. However, it is difficult to collect sufficient reference summaries. In this paper, we propose a new automatic reference-free evaluation metric that compares semantic distribution between source document and summary by pretrained language models and considers summary compression ratio. The experiments show that this metric is more consistent with human evaluation in terms of coherence, consistency, relevance and fluency.

label: naacl
text: A document can be summarized in various ways. The traditional reference-based evaluation of summarization has been criticized for its lack of flexibility. The accuracy of the evaluation results improves with the availability of more reference summaries. However, collecting a sufficient number of reference summaries can be challenging. To address this issue, we propose a new automatic reference-free evaluation metric. This metric compares the semantic distribution of the source document and summary using pretrained language models and takes into account the summary compression ratio. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this metric is more aligned with human evaluation in terms of coherence, consistency, relevance, and fluency.

label: coling
text: We use a broad coverage, linguistically precise English Resource Grammar (ERG) to detect negation scope in sentences taken from pathology reports. We show that incorporating this information in feature extraction has a positive effect on classification of the reports with respect to cancer laterality compared with NegEx, a commonly used tool for negation detection. We analyze the differences between NegEx and ERG results on our dataset and how these differences indicate some directions for future work.

label: coling
text: We utilize a comprehensive and linguistically accurate English Resource Grammar (ERG) to identify the scope of negation in pathology reports. Our results demonstrate that incorporating this information into feature extraction enhances the accuracy of classifying the reports regarding cancer laterality, compared to NegEx, a widely utilized tool for negation detection. We examine the disparities between the results obtained from NegEx and ERG on our dataset, and how these disparities suggest avenues for future research.

label: acl
text: To date, most of recent work under the retrieval-reader framework for open-domain QA focuses on either extractive or generative reader exclusively. In this paper, we study a hybrid approach for leveraging the strengths of both models. We apply novel techniques to enhance both extractive and generative readers built upon recent pretrained neural language models, and find that proper training methods can provide large improvement over previous state-of-the-art models. We demonstrate that a simple hybrid approach by combining answers from both readers can efficiently take advantages of extractive and generative answer inference strategies and outperforms single models as well as homogeneous ensembles. Our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art models by 3.3 and 2.7 points in exact match on NaturalQuestions and TriviaQA respectively.

label: acl
text: So far, most recent work in open-domain QA under the retrieval-reader framework has focused on either extractive or generative readers. In this paper, we explore a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both models. We use novel techniques to enhance extractive and generative readers built on recent pretrained neural language models. Our results show that proper training methods can significantly improve upon previous state-of-the-art models. Our hybrid approach combines answers from both readers to take advantage of the strengths of both extractive and generative answer inference strategies, outperforming single models and homogeneous ensembles. We achieve a 3.3 point improvement in exact match on NaturalQuestions and a 2.7 point improvement on TriviaQA compared to previous state-of-the-art models.

label: coling
text: Entity Linking aims to link entity mentions in texts to knowledge bases, and neural models have achieved recent success in this task. However, most existing methods rely on local contexts to resolve entities independently, which may usually fail due to the data sparsity of local information. To address this issue, we propose a novel neural model for collective entity linking, named as NCEL. NCEL apply Graph Convolutional Network to integrate both local contextual features and global coherence information for entity linking. To improve the computation efficiency, we approximately perform graph convolution on a subgraph of adjacent entity mentions instead of those in the entire text. We further introduce an attention scheme to improve the robustness of NCEL to data noise and train the model on Wikipedia hyperlinks to avoid overfitting and domain bias. In experiments, we evaluate NCEL on five publicly available datasets to verify the linking performance as well as generalization ability. We also conduct an extensive analysis of time complexity, the impact of key modules, and qualitative results, which demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method.

label: coling
text: Entity Linking is the process of linking entity mentions in texts to knowledge bases. Neural models have recently seen success in this task, but most existing methods rely on local contexts to resolve entities independently, which can lead to failure due to the sparsity of local information. To overcome this, we propose a novel neural model, NCEL, which integrates both local contextual features and global coherence information for entity linking using Graph Convolutional Networks. For improved computation efficiency, NCEL performs graph convolution on a subgraph of adjacent entity mentions instead of the entire text. Additionally, an attention scheme is introduced to increase the robustness of NCEL to data noise, and the model is trained on Wikipedia hyperlinks to prevent overfitting and domain bias. Our experiments on five publicly available datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of NCEL, and we conduct an extensive analysis of time complexity, the impact of key modules, and qualitative results.

label: acl
text: Higher-order methods for dependency parsing can partially but not fully address the issue that edges in dependency trees should be constructed at the text span/subtree level rather than word level. In this paper, we propose a new method for dependency parsing to address this issue. The proposed method constructs dependency trees by directly modeling span-span (in other words, subtree-subtree) relations. It consists of two modules: the text span proposal module which proposes candidate text spans, each of which represents a subtree in the dependency tree denoted by (root, start, end); and the span linking module, which constructs links between proposed spans. We use the machine reading comprehension (MRC) framework as the backbone to formalize the span linking module, where one span is used as query to extract the text span/subtree it should be linked to. The proposed method has the following merits: (1) it addresses the fundamental problem that edges in a dependency tree should be constructed between subtrees; (2) the MRC framework allows the method to retrieve missing spans in the span proposal stage, which leads to higher recall for eligible spans. Extensive experiments on the PTB, CTB and Universal Dependencies (UD) benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code is available at https://github.com/ShannonAI/mrc-for-dependency-parsing.

label: acl
text: Higher-order methods for dependency parsing can only partially resolve the challenge of constructing edges in dependency trees at the text span/subtree level instead of the word level. To fully address this issue, we present a new method for dependency parsing that directly models span-span (i.e., subtree-subtree) relationships. Our method consists of two modules: the text span proposal module, which generates candidate text spans representing subtrees in the dependency tree, and the span linking module, which creates links between the proposed spans. The span linking module is formalized using the machine reading comprehension framework, where one span acts as a query to identify the text span/subtree it should be linked to. The proposed method offers several benefits, including addressing the fundamental problem of constructing edges between subtrees and utilizing the MRC framework to retrieve missing spans, resulting in higher recall for eligible spans. Our experiments on the PTB, CTB, and Universal Dependencies benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code is available at https://github.com/ShannonAI/mrc-for-dependency-parsing.

label: naacl
text: The creation of a quality summarization dataset is an expensive, time-consuming effort, requiring the production and evaluation of summaries by both trained humans and machines. The returns to such an effort would increase significantly if the dataset could be used in additional languages without repeating human annotations. To investigate how much we can trust machine translation of summarization datasets, we translate the English SummEval dataset to seven languages and compare performances across automatic evaluation measures. We explore equivalence testing as the appropriate statistical paradigm for evaluating correlations between human and automated scoring of summaries. We also consider the effect of translation on the relative performance between measures. We find some potential for dataset reuse in languages similar to the source and along particular dimensions of summary quality. Our code and data can be found at https://github.com/PrimerAI/primer-research/.

label: naacl
text: The creation of a high-quality summarization dataset is a costly and time-consuming task that requires the production and evaluation of summaries by both trained humans and machines. To maximize the returns of this effort, it is important to determine if the dataset can be used in multiple languages without needing to repeat the human annotations. To investigate this, we have translated the English SummEval dataset into seven languages and compared the performance of the automatic evaluation measures across these languages. We have used equivalence testing as the statistical paradigm to evaluate the correlation between human and automated scoring of summaries. Additionally, we have considered the impact of translation on the relative performance between different measures. Our findings suggest that there is potential to reuse the dataset in languages that are similar to the source language and for specific dimensions of summary quality. The code and data for this research can be found at https://github.com/PrimerAI/primer-research/.

label: acl
text: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at https://github.com/longyuewangdcu/RLFW-NAT.

label: acl
text: The use of knowledge distillation (KD) to create synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models is a common practice. However, there is a discrepancy between the distilled and original data when it comes to low-frequency words, leading to a higher error rate in predicting these words. To address this issue, we propose a new training strategy that leverages pretraining and directly exposes the raw data to the NAT model. Our analysis of directed alignments reveals that while KD makes low-frequency source words more deterministically aligned with targets, it fails to align enough low-frequency words from the target to the source. To remedy this, we introduce reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. By combining these complementary approaches, our new training strategy significantly and universally improves NAT performance. Our experiments on five translation benchmarks and two advanced architectures demonstrate this, with a 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU point improvement on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models can be found at https://github.com/longyuewangdcu/RLFW-NAT.

label: naacl
text: This work exploits translation data as a source of semantically relevant learning signal for models of word representation. In particular, we exploit equivalence through translation as a form of distributional context and jointly learn how to embed and align with a deep generative model. Our EmbedAlign model embeds words in their complete observed context and learns by marginalisation of latent lexical alignments. Besides, it embeds words as posterior probability densities, rather than point estimates, which allows us to compare words in context using a measure of overlap between distributions (e.g. KL divergence). We investigate our model's performance on a range of lexical semantics tasks achieving competitive results on several standard benchmarks including natural language inference, paraphrasing, and text similarity.

label: naacl
text: This work leverages translation data as a source of semantically meaningful learning signals for word representation models. We utilize the equivalence of words through translation as a form of distributional context and jointly learn word embeddings and alignments using a deep generative model. The EmbedAlign model embeds words in their full observed context and learns through marginalizing latent lexical alignments. Additionally, it embeds words as posterior probability densities, rather than point estimates, allowing for comparison of words in context using measures of distributional overlap, such as KL divergence. Our model demonstrates competitive performance on a variety of lexical semantics tasks, including natural language inference, paraphrasing, and text similarity, as shown by its results on several standard benchmarks.

label: naacl
text: Learning high-quality dialogue representations is essential for solving a variety of dialogue-oriented tasks, especially considering that dialogue systems often suffer from data scarcity. In this paper, we introduce Dialogue Sentence Embedding (DSE), a self-supervised contrastive learning method that learns effective dialogue representations suitable for a wide range of dialogue tasks. DSE learns from dialogues by taking consecutive utterances of the same dialogue as positive pairs for contrastive learning. Despite its simplicity, DSE achieves significantly better representation capability than other dialogue representation and universal sentence representation models. We evaluate DSE on five downstream dialogue tasks that examine dialogue representation at different semantic granularities. Experiments in few-shot and zero-shot settings show that DSE outperforms baselines by a large margin, for example, it achieves 13% average performance improvement over the strongest unsupervised baseline in 1-shot intent classification on 6 datasets. We also provide analyses on the benefits and limitations of our model.

label: naacl
text: The acquisition of high-quality dialogue representations is crucial for the successful completion of various dialogue-oriented tasks, particularly given the scarcity of data that dialogue systems often face. This paper introduces Dialogue Sentence Embedding (DSE), a self-supervised contrastive learning method that generates effective dialogue representations that are suitable for a broad range of dialogue tasks. DSE trains on dialogues by using consecutive utterances within the same dialogue as positive pairs for contrastive learning. Despite its simplicity, DSE demonstrates a significantly improved representation capability compared to other dialogue representation and universal sentence representation models. The effectiveness of DSE is evaluated on five downstream dialogue tasks that assess dialogue representation at varying semantic levels. Results from experiments in both few-shot and zero-shot settings reveal that DSE outperforms baseline models by a substantial margin, with an average performance improvement of 13% over the strongest unsupervised baseline in 1-shot intent classification on 6 datasets. The benefits and limitations of the model are also analyzed.

label: emnlp
text: Monolingual dictionaries are widespread and semantically rich resources. This paper presents a simple model that learns to compute word embeddings by processing dictionary definitions and trying to reconstruct them. It exploits the inherent recursivity of dictionaries by encouraging consistency between the representations it uses as inputs and the representations it produces as outputs. The resulting embeddings are shown to capture semantic similarity better than regular distributional methods and other dictionary-based methods. In addition, our method shows strong performance when trained exclusively on dictionary data and generalizes in one shot.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a simple model that computes word embeddings by processing dictionary definitions and attempting to reconstruct them. Our model leverages the richness of monolingual dictionaries, which are widely available resources, and exploits the recursive nature of dictionaries by promoting consistency between input and output representations. The resulting embeddings are demonstrated to be more effective in capturing semantic similarity compared to traditional distributional methods and other dictionary-based approaches. Furthermore, our method has strong performance when trained solely on dictionary data and generalizes well in a single step.

label: emnlp
text: In this study, we explore capsule networks with dynamic routing for text classification. We propose three strategies to stabilize the dynamic routing process to alleviate the disturbance of some noise capsules which may contain “background” information or have not been successfully trained. A series of experiments are conducted with capsule networks on six text classification benchmarks. Capsule networks achieve state of the art on 4 out of 6 datasets, which shows the effectiveness of capsule networks for text classification. We additionally show that capsule networks exhibit significant improvement when transfer single-label to multi-label text classification over strong baseline methods. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that capsule networks have been empirically investigated for text modeling.

label: emnlp
text: In this study, we examine the use of capsule networks with dynamic routing for text classification. We introduce three strategies to stabilize the dynamic routing process and mitigate the impact of noise capsules that may contain irrelevant information or have not been adequately trained. Our experiments on six text classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of capsule networks, as they achieve state-of-the-art results on four out of six datasets. Furthermore, we show that capsule networks outperform strong baseline methods when transferring from single-label to multi-label text classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the application of capsule networks to text modeling has been explored.

label: acl
text: Prompt tuning has recently emerged as an effective method for adapting pre-trained language models to a number of language understanding and generation tasks. In this paper, we investigate prompt tuning for semantic parsing—the task of mapping natural language utterances onto formal meaning representations. On the low-resource splits of Overnight and TOPv2, we find that a prompt tuned T5-xl significantly outperforms its fine-tuned counterpart, as well as strong GPT-3 and BART baselines. We also conduct ablation studies across different model scales and target representations, finding that, with increasing model scale, prompt tuned T5 models improve at generating target representations that are far from the pre-training distribution.

label: acl
text: Prompt tuning has recently become a popular method for adapting pre-trained language models to various language understanding and generation tasks. This study focuses on its application to semantic parsing, which involves mapping natural language utterances to formal meaning representations. Our results on the low-resource splits of Overnight and TOPv2 datasets show that prompt tuning a T5-xl model significantly outperforms fine-tuning and strong GPT-3 and BART baselines. Through ablation studies across various model scales and target representations, we observe that prompt tuned T5 models improve in generating target representations that are far from the pre-training distribution, especially with increasing model scale.

label: naacl
text: Standard automatic metrics, e.g. BLEU, are not reliable for document-level MT evaluation. They can neither distinguish document-level improvements in translation quality from sentence-level ones, nor identify the discourse phenomena that cause context-agnostic translations. This paper introduces a novel automatic metric BlonDe to widen the scope of automatic MT evaluation from sentence to document level. BlonDe takes discourse coherence into consideration by categorizing discourse-related spans and calculating the similarity-based F1 measure of categorized spans. We conduct extensive comparisons on a newly constructed dataset BWB. The experimental results show that BlonDe possesses better selectivity and interpretability at the document-level, and is more sensitive to document-level nuances. In a large-scale human study, BlonDe also achieves significantly higher Pearson's r correlation with human judgments compared to previous metrics.

label: naacl
text: Standard automatic metrics, such as BLEU, are not adequate for evaluating document-level machine translation (MT). These metrics are unable to distinguish between improvements in translation quality at the document level and those at the sentence level, nor can they identify the discourse phenomena that lead to context-agnostic translations. This paper presents a novel automatic metric, BlonDe, which expands the scope of MT evaluation from sentence to document level by taking discourse coherence into account. BlonDe categorizes discourse-related spans and calculates a similarity-based F1 measure for these spans. Through extensive comparisons on the newly constructed BWB dataset, the results demonstrate that BlonDe has greater selectivity and interpretability at the document level and is more sensitive to document-level nuances.
