text: Even though machine learning has become the major scene in dialogue research community, the real breakthrough has been blocked by the scale of data available.To address this fundamental obstacle, we introduce the Multi-Domain Wizard-of-Oz dataset (MultiWOZ), a fully-labeled collection of human-human written conversations spanning over multiple domains and topics.At a size of 10k dialogues, it is at least one order of magnitude larger than all previous annotated task-oriented corpora.The contribution of this work apart from the open-sourced dataset is two-fold:firstly, a detailed description of the data collection procedure along with a summary of data structure and analysis is provided. The proposed data-collection pipeline is entirely based on crowd-sourcing without the need of hiring professional annotators;secondly, a set of benchmark results of belief tracking, dialogue act and response generation is reported, which shows the usability of the data and sets a baseline for future studies.

label: emnlp
text: Although machine learning is the dominant trend in the dialogue research community, the real breakthrough has been hindered by the limited data available. To overcome this challenge, we present the Multi-Domain Wizard-of-Oz dataset (MultiWOZ), a fully-labeled collection of human-human written conversations covering various domains and topics. With a size of 10,000 dialogues, it is at least ten times larger than any previous annotated task-oriented corpus. This work not only includes the open-sourced dataset but also offers two key contributions: first, a comprehensive description of the data collection process, including a summary of the data structure and analysis, is provided. Our data collection pipeline is based on crowd-sourcing, eliminating the need for professional annotators. Secondly, we present benchmark results for belief tracking, dialogue act, and response generation, demonstrating the usefulness of the data and setting a baseline for future studies.

label: naacl
text: When learning POS taggers and syntactic chunkers for low-resource languages, different resources may be available, and often all we have is a small tag dictionary, motivating type-constrained unsupervised induction. Even small dictionaries can improve the performance of unsupervised induction algorithms. This paper shows that performance can be further improved by including data that is readily available or can be easily obtained for most languages, i.e., eye-tracking, speech, or keystroke logs (or any combination thereof). We project information from all these data sources into shared spaces, in which the union of words is represented. For English unsupervised POS induction, the additional information, which is not required at test time, leads to an average error reduction on Ontonotes domains of 1.5% over systems augmented with state-of-the-art word embeddings. On Penn Treebank the best model achieves 5.4% error reduction over a word embeddings baseline. We also achieve significant improvements for syntactic chunk induction. Our analysis shows that improvements are even bigger when the available tag dictionaries are smaller.

label: naacl
text: When learning POS taggers and syntactic chunkers for low-resource languages, different resources may be available, but often, all we have is a small tag dictionary. This motivates the use of type-constrained unsupervised induction. Despite its limitations, a small tag dictionary can still improve the performance of unsupervised induction algorithms. This paper demonstrates that performance can be further enhanced by including readily available or easily obtainable data sources such as eye-tracking, speech, or keystroke logs, or any combination thereof. We project this information into a shared space where the union of words is represented. For English unsupervised POS induction, the additional information, which is not required at test time, results in an average error reduction of 1.5% on Ontonotes domains compared to systems augmented with state-of-the-art word embeddings. On Penn Treebank, the best model achieves a 5.4% error reduction over a word embeddings baseline. We also observe significant improvements for syntactic chunk induction. Our analysis indicates that the improvements are even greater when the available tag dictionaries are smaller.

label: naacl
text: It has been proven that automatic conversational agents can be built up using the Endto-End Neural Response Generation (NRG) framework, and such a data-driven methodology requires a large number of dialog pairs for model training and reasonable evaluation metrics for testing. This paper proposes a Large Scale Domain-Specific Conversational Corpus (LSDSCC) composed of high-quality queryresponse pairs extracted from the domainspecific online forum, with thorough preprocessing and cleansing procedures. Also, a testing set, including multiple diverse responses annotated for each query, is constructed, and on this basis, the metrics for measuring the diversity of generated results are further presented. We evaluate the performances of neural dialog models with the widely applied diversity boosting strategies on the proposed dataset. The experimental results have shown that our proposed corpus can be taken as a new benchmark dataset for the NRG task, and the presented metrics are promising to guide the optimization of NRG models by quantifying the diversity of the generated responses reasonably.

label: naacl
text: The proof exists that automatic conversational agents can be created using the End-to-End Neural Response Generation (NRG) framework. This data-driven approach requires a large number of dialogue pairs for model training and appropriate evaluation metrics for testing. This paper presents a Large Scale Domain-Specific Conversational Corpus (LSDSCC) consisting of high-quality query-response pairs extracted from a domain-specific online forum, with extensive preprocessing and cleansing procedures. Additionally, a testing set with diverse annotated responses for each query has been created, and metrics for measuring the diversity of generated results have been proposed. The performance of neural dialogue models with commonly used diversity boosting strategies is evaluated on the proposed dataset. The results demonstrate that the proposed corpus can serve as a new benchmark for the NRG task, and the presented metrics are an effective means of guiding the optimization of NRG models by quantifying the diversity of generated responses.

label: emnlp
text: Recent progress in dialogue generation has inspired a number of studies on dialogue systems that are capable of accomplishing tasks through natural language interactions. A promising direction among these studies is the use of reinforcement learning techniques, such as self-play, for training dialogue agents. However, current datasets are limited in size, and the environment for training agents and evaluating progress is relatively unsophisticated. We present AirDialogue, a large dataset that contains 301,427 goal-oriented conversations. To collect this dataset, we create a context-generator which provides travel and flight restrictions. We then ask human annotators to play the role of a customer or an agent and interact with the goal of successfully booking a trip given the restrictions. Key to our environment is the ease of evaluating the success of the dialogue, which is achieved by using ground-truth states (e.g., the flight being booked) generated by the restrictions. Any dialogue agent that does not generate the correct states is considered to fail. Our experimental results indicate that state-of-the-art dialogue models can only achieve a score of 0.17 while humans can reach a score of 0.91, which suggests significant opportunities for future improvement.

label: emnlp
text: Recent advancements in dialogue generation have inspired numerous studies on natural language interaction-based dialogue systems. One promising avenue in these studies is the application of reinforcement learning techniques, such as self-play, for training dialogue agents. However, existing datasets are limited in size, and the training and evaluation environments for the agents are relatively rudimentary. To address these limitations, we introduce AirDialogue, a large dataset containing 301,427 goal-oriented conversations. We generated this dataset by creating a context-generator that imposes travel and flight restrictions, and then asked human annotators to play the role of either a customer or an agent and interact with the goal of successfully booking a trip within the given restrictions. The key feature of our environment is the ease of evaluating the success of the dialogue, which is achieved by using ground-truth states (e.g., booked flight) generated by the restrictions. Any dialogue agent that fails to produce the correct states is considered unsuccessful. Our results show that state-of-the-art dialogue models only achieve a score of 0.17, while humans reach a score of 0.91, highlighting significant opportunities for future improvement.

label: acl
text: Code completion, which aims to predict the following code token(s) according to the code context, can improve the productivity of software development. Recent work has proved that statistical language modeling with transformers can greatly improve the performance in the code completion task via learning from large-scale source code datasets. However, current approaches focus only on code context within the file or project, i.e. internal context. Our distinction is utilizing ”external” context, inspired by human behaviors of copying from the related code snippets when writing code. Specifically, we propose a retrieval-augmented code completion framework, leveraging both lexical copying and referring to code with similar semantics by retrieval. We adopt a stage-wise training approach that combines a source code retriever and an auto-regressive language model for programming language. We evaluate our approach in the code completion task in Python and Java programming languages, achieving a state-of-the-art performance on CodeXGLUE benchmark.

label: acl
text: The aim of code completion is to predict the next code token(s) based on the code context, which can enhance the efficiency of software development. Recent studies have demonstrated that statistical language modeling with transformers can significantly improve code completion performance by learning from large-scale source code datasets. However, these approaches only consider the internal context within a file or project. Our approach is unique in that it utilizes external context, mimicking human behavior of copying related code snippets when writing code. To this end, we propose a retrieval-augmented code completion framework that leverages both lexical copying and code retrieval with similar semantics. Our framework incorporates a stage-wise training approach, combining a source code retriever and an auto-regressive language model for programming languages. Our results, evaluated on the CodeXGLUE benchmark, demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in code completion for Python and Java programming languages.

label: emnlp
text: How to generate relevant and informative responses is one of the core topics in response generation area. Following the task formulation of machine translation, previous works mainly consider response generation task as a mapping from a source sentence to a target sentence. To realize this mapping, existing works tend to design intuitive but complex models. However, the relevant information existed in large dialogue corpus is mainly overlooked. In this paper, we propose Sequence to Sequence with Prototype Memory Network (S2SPMN) to exploit the relevant information provided by the large dialogue corpus to enhance response generation. Specifically, we devise two simple approaches in S2SPMN to select the relevant information (named prototypes) from the dialogue corpus. These prototypes are then saved into prototype memory network (PMN). Furthermore, a hierarchical attention mechanism is devised to extract the semantic information from the PMN to assist the response generation process. Empirical studies reveal the advantage of our model over several classical and strong baselines.

label: emnlp
text: One of the central topics in response generation is how to produce relevant and informative responses. Previous works have approached the task as a mapping from a source sentence to a target sentence, based on the task formulation of machine translation. However, these existing models tend to be complex and overlook the relevant information present in large dialogue corpora. In this paper, we propose the Sequence to Sequence with Prototype Memory Network (S2SPMN) to exploit this information and improve response generation. Our model selects relevant information (prototypes) from the dialogue corpus and saves them in the prototype memory network (PMN). Then, a hierarchical attention mechanism is used to extract semantic information from the PMN to assist in the response generation process. Our results show that S2SPMN outperforms several classical and strong baselines.

label: acl
text: Nowadays, fake news detection, which aims to verify whether a news document is trusted or fake, has become urgent and important. Most existing methods rely heavily on linguistic and semantic features from the news content, and fail to effectively exploit external knowledge which could help determine whether the news document is trusted. In this paper, we propose a novel end-to-end graph neural model called CompareNet, which compares the news to the knowledge base (KB) through entities for fake news detection. Considering that fake news detection is correlated with topics, we also incorporate topics to enrich the news representation. Specifically, we first construct a directed heterogeneous document graph for each news incorporating topics and entities. Based on the graph, we develop a heterogeneous graph attention network for learning the topic-enriched news representation as well as the contextual entity representations that encode the semantics of the news content. The contextual entity representations are then compared to the corresponding KB-based entity representations through a carefully designed entity comparison network, to capture the consistency between the news content and KB. Finally, the topic-enriched news representation combining the entity comparison features is fed into a fake news classifier. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that CompareNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

text: The detection of fake news has become a pressing issue, as it is crucial to determine the credibility of news documents. Currently, most methods for fake news detection rely heavily on linguistic and semantic features from the content, neglecting external knowledge that could aid in determining the trustworthiness of the news. To address this issue, we present a novel end-to-end graph neural model called CompareNet. This model verifies the authenticity of news by comparing it to a knowledge base (KB) through entities. To further enhance the representation of the news, we incorporate topics into the model. We construct a directed heterogeneous document graph that incorporates both topics and entities. Then, we use a heterogeneous graph attention network to learn the topic-enriched news representation and the contextual entity representations, which encode the semantics of the news content. The consistency between the news content and KB is captured by comparing the contextual entity representations to the corresponding KB-based entity representations through a carefully designed entity comparison network. Finally, the topic-enriched news representation, combined with the entity comparison features, is fed into a fake news classifier. Our experiments on two benchmark datasets show that CompareNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods significantly.

label: naacl
text: A core step in statistical data-to-text generation concerns learning correspondences between structured data representations (e.g., facts in a database) and associated texts. In this paper we aim to bootstrap generators from large scale datasets where the data (e.g., DBPedia facts) and related texts (e.g., Wikipedia abstracts) are loosely aligned. We tackle this challenging task by introducing a special-purpose content selection mechanism. We use multi-instance learning to automatically discover correspondences between data and text pairs and show how these can be used to enhance the content signal while training an encoder-decoder architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained with content-specific objectives improve upon a vanilla encoder-decoder which solely relies on soft attention.

label: naacl
text: The key step in statistical data-to-text generation is learning the connections between structured data representations (such as facts in a database) and the accompanying texts. This paper aims to create generators using large-scale datasets where the data (such as DBPedia facts) and related texts (such as Wikipedia abstracts) are not closely aligned. To address this difficult task, we introduce a specialized content selection mechanism. We utilize multi-instance learning to identify connections between data and text pairs, and demonstrate how these connections can improve the content signal when training an encoder-decoder architecture. Our experimental results show that models trained with content-specific objectives outperform a standard encoder-decoder that only uses soft attention.

label: naacl
text: In this work, we focus on Cross-Lingual Event Detection where a model is trained on data from a C-C-C language but its performance is evaluated on data from a second, D-D-D, language. Most recent works in this area have harnessed the language-invariant qualities displayed by pre-trained Multi-lingual Language Models. Their performance, however, reveals there is room for improvement as the cross-lingual setting entails particular challenges. We employ Adversarial Language Adaptation to train a Language Discriminator to discern between the source and target languages using unlabeled data. The discriminator is trained in an adversarial manner so that the encoder learns to produce refined, language-invariant representations that lead to improved performance. More importantly, we optimize the adversarial training process by only presenting the discriminator with the most informative samples. We base our intuition about what makes a sample informative on two disparate metrics: sample similarity and event presence. Thus, we propose leveraging Optimal Transport as a solution to naturally combine these two distinct information sources into the selection process. Extensive experiments on 8 different language pairs, using 4 languages from unrelated families, show the flexibility and effectiveness of our model that achieves state-of-the-art results.

label: naacl
text: This work focuses on Cross-Lingual Event Detection, where a model trained on data in one language (C-C-C) is evaluated on data in another language (D-D-D). Most recent studies in this area have utilized pre-trained Multi-lingual Language Models, but their performance suggests that there is room for improvement due to the unique challenges of cross-lingual settings. To address these challenges, we use Adversarial Language Adaptation to train a Language Discriminator to distinguish between the source and target languages using unlabeled data. The encoder learns to produce refined, language-invariant representations through adversarial training, which leads to improved performance. To optimize the adversarial training process, we only present the discriminator with the most informative samples, which are selected based on two metrics: sample similarity and event presence. To combine these metrics, we propose using Optimal Transport. Our experiments on eight different language pairs, including four languages from unrelated families, demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our model, which achieves state-of-the-art results.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we study how we can improve a deep learning approach to textual entailment by incorporating lexical entailment relations from WordNet. Our idea is to embed the lexical entailment knowledge contained in WordNet in specially-learned word vectors, which we call “entailment vectors.” We present a standard neural network model and a novel set-theoretic model to learn these entailment vectors from word pairs with known lexical entailment relations derived from WordNet. We further incorporate these entailment vectors into a decomposable attention model for textual entailment and evaluate the model on the SICK and the SNLI dataset. We find that using these special entailment word vectors, we can significantly improve the performance of textual entailment compared with a baseline that uses only standard word2vec vectors. The final performance of our model is close to or above the state of the art, but our method does not rely on any manually-crafted rules or extensive syntactic features.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a study on how to enhance a deep learning approach for textual entailment by incorporating lexical entailment relations from WordNet. Our approach involves embedding the lexical entailment knowledge from WordNet in specialized word vectors, known as "entailment vectors." We introduce two models, a standard neural network model and a novel set-theoretic model, to learn these entailment vectors from word pairs with known lexical entailment relations from WordNet. These entailment vectors are then integrated into a decomposable attention model for textual entailment and evaluated on the SICK and SNLI datasets. The results show that the use of these specialized entailment word vectors significantly improves the performance of textual entailment compared to a baseline using only standard word2vec vectors. Our method outperforms or is close to the state of the art, without relying on manually-crafted rules or extensive syntactic features.

label: emnlp
text: Due to the benefits of model compactness, multilingual translation (including many-to-one, many-to-many and one-to-many) based on a universal encoder-decoder architecture attracts more and more attention. However, previous studies show that one-to-many translation based on this framework cannot perform on par with the individually trained models. In this work, we introduce three strategies to improve one-to-many multilingual translation by balancing the shared and unique features. Within the architecture of one decoder for all target languages, we first exploit the use of unique initial states for different target languages. Then, we employ language-dependent positional embeddings. Finally and especially, we propose to divide the hidden cells of the decoder into shared and language-dependent ones. The extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed methods can obtain remarkable improvements over the strong baselines. Moreover, our strategies can achieve comparable or even better performance than the individually trained translation models.

label: emnlp
text: The compactness of the model has made multilingual translation (including many-to-one, many-to-many, and one-to-many) based on a universal encoder-decoder architecture increasingly popular. However, previous studies have shown that one-to-many translation using this framework falls short of the performance of individually trained models. To address this issue, we introduce three strategies to improve one-to-many multilingual translation by balancing shared and unique features within the architecture of a single decoder for all target languages. Our strategies include the use of unique initial states for different target languages, language-dependent positional embeddings, and dividing the decoder's hidden cells into shared and language-dependent ones. Our extensive experiments show that these methods lead to significant improvements over strong baselines, and in some cases, even surpass the performance of individually trained translation models.

label: emnlp
text: This paper tackles automation of the pyramid method, a reliable manual evaluation framework. To construct a pyramid, we transform human-made reference summaries into extractive reference summaries that consist of Elementary Discourse Units (EDUs) obtained from source documents and then weight every EDU by counting the number of extractive reference summaries that contain the EDU. A summary is scored by the correspondences between EDUs in the summary and those in the pyramid. Experiments on DUC and TAC data sets show that our methods strongly correlate with various manual evaluations.

label: emnlp
text: This paper aims to automate the Pyramid Method, a trusted manual evaluation framework. The process of constructing a pyramid involves transforming human-created reference summaries into extractive reference summaries, which consist of Elementary Discourse Units (EDUs) obtained from source documents. The weight of each EDU is determined by counting the number of extractive reference summaries that contain it. The score of a summary is determined by the match between EDUs in the summary and those in the pyramid. Our methods have been proven to be highly correlated with various manual evaluations through experiments on DUC and TAC data sets.

label: coling
text: The state of bridging resolution research is rather unsatisfactory: not only are state-of-the-art resolvers evaluated in unrealistic settings, but the neural models underlying these resolvers are weaker than those used for entity coreference resolution. In light of these problems, we evaluate bridging resolvers in an end-to-end setting, strengthen them with better encoders, and attempt to gain a better understanding of them via perturbation experiments and a manual analysis of their outputs.

label: coling
text: The current state of bridging resolution research is unsatisfactory, as state-of-the-art resolvers are evaluated in unrealistic settings, and their underlying neural models are weaker than those used for entity coreference resolution. To address these issues, we evaluate bridging resolvers in a more realistic end-to-end setting, enhance them with stronger encoders, and gain deeper insights into their workings through perturbation experiments and manual analysis of their outputs.

label: emnlp
text: In this paper, we present a crowdsourcing-based approach to model the human perception of sentence complexity. We collect a large corpus of sentences rated with judgments of complexity for two typologically-different languages, Italian and English. We test our approach in two experimental scenarios aimed to investigate the contribution of a wide set of lexical, morpho-syntactic and syntactic phenomena in predicting i) the degree of agreement among annotators independently from the assigned judgment and ii) the perception of sentence complexity.

label: emnlp
text: We present a crowdsourcing-based approach to model human perceptions of sentence complexity in this paper. We have collected a large corpus of sentences rated for complexity in two typologically different languages, Italian and English. Our approach is tested in two experimental scenarios to determine the impact of various lexical, morpho-syntactic, and syntactic phenomena on both the degree of agreement among annotators and the perception of sentence complexity.

label: coling
text: Large pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated superior performance in industrial applications. Recent studies have explored parameter-efficient PLM tuning, which only updates a small amount of task-specific parameters while achieving both high efficiency and comparable performance against standard fine-tuning. However, all these methods ignore the inefficiency problem caused by the task-specific output layers, which is inflexible for us to re-use PLMs and introduces non-negligible parameters. In this work, we focus on the text classification task and propose plugin-tuning, a framework that further improves the efficiency of existing parameter-efficient methods with a unified classifier. Specifically, we re-formulate both token and sentence classification tasks into a unified language modeling task, and map label spaces of different tasks into the same vocabulary space. In this way, we can directly re-use the language modeling heads of PLMs, avoiding introducing extra parameters for different tasks. We conduct experiments on six classification benchmarks. The experimental results show that plugin-tuning can achieve comparable performance against fine-tuned PLMs, while further saving around 50% parameters on top of other parameter-efficient methods.

label: coling
text: Large pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in industrial applications. Recent studies have explored parameter-efficient tuning methods for PLMs, which update only a small number of task-specific parameters while achieving both high efficiency and comparable performance compared to standard fine-tuning. However, these methods overlook the inefficiency problem caused by inflexible task-specific output layers, which introduce non-negligible parameters and prevent the re-use of PLMs. To address this issue, we propose a framework called plugin-tuning for text classification tasks that further improves the efficiency of existing parameter-efficient methods. Our framework unifies the classifier by re-formulating both token and sentence classification tasks into a single language modeling task and mapping the label spaces of different tasks into the same vocabulary space. This allows us to directly re-use the language modeling heads of PLMs, eliminating the need for extra parameters for different tasks. We conduct experiments on six classification benchmarks and the results show that plugin-tuning achieves comparable performance to fine-tuned PLMs while saving around 50% of the parameters compared to other parameter-efficient methods.

label: acl
text: Argument pair extraction (APE) aims to automatically mine argument pairs from two interrelated argumentative documents. Existing studies typically identify argument pairs indirectly by predicting sentence-level relations between two documents, neglecting the modeling of the holistic argument-level interactions. Towards this issue, we propose to address APE via a machine reading comprehension (MRC) framework with two phases. The first phase employs an argument mining (AM) query to identify all arguments in two documents. The second phase considers each identified argument as an APE query to extract its paired arguments from another document, allowing to better capture the argument-level interactions. Also, this framework enables these two phases to be jointly trained in a single MRC model, thereby maximizing the mutual benefits of them. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves the best performance, outperforming the state-of-the-art method by 7.11% in F1 score.

text: The aim of Argument Pair Extraction (APE) is to automatically find argument pairs from two interrelated argumentative documents. Previous studies usually identify argument pairs by predicting sentence-level relations between two documents, ignoring the holistic argument-level interactions. To address this issue, we propose a two-phase machine reading comprehension (MRC) framework. The first phase uses an argument mining (AM) query to identify all the arguments in both documents. The second phase considers each identified argument as an APE query to extract its paired argument from the other document, allowing for better capture of argument-level interactions. Our framework enables these two phases to be jointly trained in a single MRC model, maximizing the benefits of both. The results show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art method by 7.11% in F1 score.

text: With the growing popularity of deep-learning models, model understanding becomes more important. Much effort has been devoted to demystify deep neural networks for better explainability. Some feature attribution methods have shown promising results in computer vision, especially the gradient-based methods where effectively smoothing the gradients with reference data is the key to a robust and faithful result. However, direct application of these gradient-based methods to NLP tasks is not trivial due to the fact that the input consists of discrete tokens and the “reference” tokens are not explicitly defined. In this work, we propose Locally Aggregated Feature Attribution (LAFA), a novel gradient-based feature attribution method for NLP models. Instead of relying on obscure reference tokens, it smooths gradients by aggregating similar reference texts derived from language model embeddings. For evaluation purpose, we also design experiments on different NLP tasks including Entity Recognition and Sentiment Analysis on public datasets and key words detection on constructed Amazon catalogue dataset. The superior performance of the proposed method is demonstrated through experiments.

text: With the increasing popularity of deep-learning models, understanding these models has become crucial. Much effort has been put into demystifying deep neural networks for better explainability. Our experiments demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method.

text: In conversational question answering (CQA), the task of question rewriting (QR) in context aims to rewrite a context-dependent question into an equivalent self-contained question that gives the same answer. In this paper, we are interested in the robustness of a QR system to questions varying in rewriting hardness or difficulty. Since there is a lack of questions classified based on their rewriting hardness, we first propose a heuristic method to automatically classify questions into subsets of varying hardness, by measuring the discrepancy between a question and its rewrite. To find out what makes questions hard or easy for rewriting, we then conduct a human evaluation to annotate the rewriting hardness of questions. Finally, to enhance the robustness of QR systems to questions of varying hardness, we propose a novel learning framework for QR that first trains a QR model independently on each subset of questions of a certain level of hardness, then combines these QR models as one joint model for inference. Experimental results on two datasets show that our framework improves the overall performance compared to the baselines.

label: acl
text: The task of question rewriting (QR) in conversational question answering (CQA) is to transform a context-dependent question into a self-sufficient equivalent question that provides the same answer. In this study, we examine the robustness of QR systems to questions of varying levels of difficulty. As there is a scarcity of questions classified by their rewriting difficulty, we introduce a heuristic method to categorize questions into subsets of varying difficulty by determining the difference between a question and its rewrite. To identify the factors that make questions challenging or straightforward to rewrite, we perform a human evaluation to annotate the rewriting difficulty of questions. Finally, to enhance the robustness of QR systems to questions of varying difficulty, we present a novel learning framework for QR that trains a QR model independently on each subset of questions of a specific level of difficulty, and then integrates these QR models into a single joint model for inference. Our experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that our framework outperforms the baselines.

label: naacl
text: We show that Transformer encoder architectures can be sped up, with limited accuracy costs, by replacing the self-attention sublayers with simple linear transformations that “mix” input tokens. Most surprisingly, we find that replacing the self-attention sublayer in a Transformer encoder with a standard, unparameterized Fourier Transform achieves 92-97% of the accuracy of BERT counterparts on the GLUE benchmark, but trains 80% faster on GPUs and 70% faster on TPUs at standard 512 input lengths. At longer input lengths, our FNet model is significantly faster: when compared to the “efficient Transformers” on the Long Range Arena benchmark, FNet matches the accuracy of the most accurate models, while outpacing the fastest models across all sequence lengths on GPUs (and across relatively shorter lengths on TPUs). Finally, FNet has a light memory footprint and is particularly efficient at smaller model sizes; for a fixed speed and accuracy budget, small FNet models outperform Transformer counterparts.

text: We demonstrate that the Transformer encoder architecture can be made faster with limited accuracy loss by replacing the self-attention sublayers with linear transformations that mix input tokens. Additionally, FNet has a small memory footprint and is highly efficient at smaller model sizes, making it the best choice for a fixed speed and accuracy budget.

text: Speakers often have more than one way to express the same meaning. What general principles govern speaker choice in the face of optionality when near semantically invariant alternation exists? Studies have shown that optional reduction in language is sensitive to contextual predictability, such that more predictable a linguistic unit is, the more likely it is to get reduced. Yet it is unclear whether these cases of speaker choice are driven by audience design versus toward facilitating production. Here we argue that for a different optionality phenomenon, namely classifier choice in Mandarin Chinese, Uniform Information Density and at least one plausible variant of availability-based production make opposite predictions regarding the relationship between the predictability of the upcoming material and speaker choices. In a corpus analysis of Mandarin Chinese, we show that the distribution of speaker choices supports the availability-based production account and not the Uniform Information Density.

label: naacl
text: Speakers often have multiple ways to convey the same meaning. What are the general principles that govern their choice when there is near semantically invariant alternation? Studies have shown that the reduction of language in optional contexts is influenced by contextual predictability, meaning that the more predictable a linguistic unit is, the more likely it is to be reduced. However, it is not clear whether these choices are driven by audience design or to simplify production. In this study, we examine classifier choice in Mandarin Chinese and argue that Uniform Information Density and availability-based production make opposing predictions about the relationship between predictability and speaker choices. Our corpus analysis of Mandarin Chinese supports the availability-based production account and refutes the Uniform Information Density.

text: We present a novel deep learning architecture to address the natural language inference (NLI) task. Existing approaches mostly rely on simple reading mechanisms for independent encoding of the premise and hypothesis. Instead, we propose a novel dependent reading bidirectional LSTM network (DR-BiLSTM) to efficiently model the relationship between a premise and a hypothesis during encoding and inference. We also introduce a sophisticated ensemble strategy to combine our proposed models, which noticeably improves final predictions. Finally, we demonstrate how the results can be improved further with an additional preprocessing step. Our evaluation shows that DR-BiLSTM obtains the best single model and ensemble model results achieving the new state-of-the-art scores on the Stanford NLI dataset.

label: naacl
text: We introduce a new deep learning architecture for the Natural Language Inference (NLI) task. Unlike existing solutions that mostly utilize simple reading mechanisms for individual encoding of the premise and hypothesis, our proposed architecture, the Dependent Reading Bidirectional LSTM Network (DR-BiLSTM), efficiently models the relationship between the premise and hypothesis during encoding and inference. Additionally, we implement a sophisticated ensemble strategy to further enhance the predictions. Our results indicate that DR-BiLSTM outperforms existing solutions, achieving the new state-of-the-art scores on the Stanford NLI dataset, both as a single model and as an ensemble. Finally, we demonstrate that these results can be improved even further through a preprocessing step.

text: Attempts to find a single technique for general-purpose intrinsic evaluation of word embeddings have so far not been successful. We present a new approach based on scaled-up qualitative analysis of word vector neighborhoods that quantifies interpretable characteristics of a given model (e.g. its preference for synonyms or shared morphological forms as nearest neighbors). We analyze 21 such factors and show how they correlate with performance on 14 extrinsic and intrinsic task datasets (and also explain the lack of correlation between some of them). Our approach enables multi-faceted evaluation, parameter search, and generally – a more principled, hypothesis-driven approach to development of distributional semantic representations.

label: coling
text: Efforts to develop a unified method for evaluating word embeddings have been unsuccessful thus far. We introduce a new method that involves a scaled-up qualitative analysis of word vector neighborhoods. This approach quantifies interpretable characteristics of a given model, such as its preference for synonyms or shared morphological forms as nearest neighbors. We examine 21 such factors and demonstrate their correlation with performance on 14 extrinsic and intrinsic task datasets. Our method enables multi-faceted evaluation, parameter optimization, and a more systematic, hypothesis-driven approach to creating distributional semantic representations.

text: Several semi-supervised representation learning methods have been proposed recently that mitigate the drawbacks of traditional bootstrapping: they reduce the amount of semantic drift introduced by iterative approaches through one-shot learning; others address the sparsity of data through the learning of custom, dense representation for the information modeled. In this work, we are the first to adapt three of these methods, most of which have been originally proposed for image processing, to an information extraction task, specifically, named entity classification. Further, we perform a rigorous comparative analysis on two distinct datasets. Our analysis yields several important observations. First, all representation learning methods outperform state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods that do not rely on representation learning. To the best of our knowledge, we report the latest state-of-the-art results on the semi-supervised named entity classification task. Second, one-shot learning methods clearly outperform iterative representation learning approaches. Lastly, one of the best performers relies on the mean teacher framework (Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017), a simple teacher/student approach that is independent of the underlying task-specific model.

text: Recently, several semi-supervised representation learning methods have been developed to overcome the limitations of traditional bootstrapping. These methods reduce semantic drift through one-shot learning and address data sparsity by learning custom dense representations. In this study, we adapt three of these methods, which were originally designed for image processing, to the task of named entity classification in information extraction. We conduct a comprehensive comparison of these methods on two different datasets and make several key observations. Firstly, all representation learning methods outperform existing semi-supervised methods that don't use representation learning. We report the latest state-of-the-art results in semi-supervised named entity classification. Secondly, one-shot learning methods outperform iterative representation learning approaches. Lastly, the best performing method is based on the mean teacher framework (Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017), a simple teacher/student approach that is independent of the task-specific model.

text: We propose the task of Open-Domain Information Narration (OIN) as the reverse task of Open Information Extraction (OIE), to implement the dual structure between language and knowledge in the open domain. Then, we develop an agent, called Orator, to accomplish the OIN task, and assemble the Orator and the recently proposed OIE agent — Logician into a dual system to utilize the duality structure with a reinforcement learning paradigm. Experimental results reveal the dual structure between OIE and OIN tasks helps to build better both OIE agents and OIN agents.

label: emnlp
text: We propose the task of Open-Domain Information Narration (OIN) as the reverse of Open Information Extraction (OIE) in order to implement the dual relationship between language and knowledge in an open domain. We have developed an agent named Orator to perform the OIN task and combined it with Logician, a recently proposed OIE agent, in a dual system. This system uses a reinforcement learning paradigm to leverage the dual relationship between OIE and OIN tasks. Our experiments show that the dual relationship between these tasks leads to improved performance for both OIE and OIN agents.

text: Long short-term memory (LSTM) language model (LM) has been widely investigated for automatic speech recognition (ASR) and natural language processing (NLP). Although excellent performance is obtained for large vocabulary tasks, tremendous memory consumption prohibits the use of LSTM LM in low-resource devices. The memory consumption mainly comes from the word embedding layer. In this paper, a novel binarized LSTM LM is proposed to address the problem. Words are encoded into binary vectors and other LSTM parameters are further binarized to achieve high memory compression. This is the first effort to investigate binary LSTM for large vocabulary LM. Experiments on both English and Chinese LM and ASR tasks showed that can achieve a compression ratio of 11.3 without any loss of LM and ASR performances and a compression ratio of 31.6 with acceptable minor performance degradation.

The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) language model has been extensively studied for use in automatic speech recognition and natural language processing. Despite its excellent performance for large vocabulary tasks, its high memory consumption makes it unsuitable for use in low-resource devices. This is mainly due to the memory consumption of the word embedding layer. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel binarized LSTM language model. Words are encoded into binary vectors, and other LSTM parameters are further binarized to achieve high memory compression. This is the first study to investigate binary LSTM for large vocabulary language models. Experiments on both English and Chinese language models and automatic speech recognition tasks showed that the proposed method can achieve a compression ratio of 11.3 without any loss of language model and automatic speech recognition performance, and a compression ratio of 31.6 with only minor performance degradation. This method has significant potential for use in low-resource devices.

label: emnlp
text: Although end-to-end neural machine translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in the recent years, the idea of adopting multi-pass decoding mechanism into conventional NMT is not well explored. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture called adaptive multi-pass decoder, which introduces a flexible multi-pass polishing mechanism to extend the capacity of NMT via reinforcement learning. More specifically, we adopt an extra policy network to automatically choose a suitable and effective number of decoding passes, according to the complexity of source sentences and the quality of the generated translations. Extensive experiments on Chinese-English translation demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed adaptive multi-pass decoder upon the conventional NMT with a significant improvement about 1.55 BLEU.

label: emnlp
text: The recent years have seen remarkable progress in end-to-end neural machine translation (NMT), but the idea of incorporating a multi-pass decoding mechanism into conventional NMT has not been fully explored. In this paper, we introduce a novel architecture called the adaptive multi-pass decoder, which uses a flexible multi-pass polishing mechanism to enhance the capacity of NMT through reinforcement learning. Our approach involves the use of a policy network to determine the optimal number of decoding passes, based on the complexity of the source sentences and the quality of the generated translations. Our experiments on Chinese-English translation show that our proposed adaptive multi-pass decoder outperforms conventional NMT, with a significant improvement of 1.55 BLEU.

label: acl
text: Pre-trained language models derive substantial linguistic and factual knowledge from the massive corpora on which they are trained, and prompt engineering seeks to align these models to specific tasks. Unfortunately, existing prompt engineering methods require significant amounts of labeled data, access to model parameters, or both. We introduce a new method for selecting prompt templates without labeled examples and without direct access to the model. Specifically, over a set of candidate templates, we choose the template that maximizes the mutual information between the input and the corresponding model output. Across 8 datasets representing 7 distinct NLP tasks, we show that when a template has high mutual information, it also has high accuracy on the task. On the largest model, selecting prompts with our method gets 90% of the way from the average prompt accuracy to the best prompt accuracy and requires no ground truth labels.

label: acl
text: Our new method for selecting prompt templates without labeled examples and without direct access to the model involves choosing the candidate template that maximizes the mutual information between the input and the corresponding model output. However, traditional prompt engineering methods require significant amounts of labeled data or access to model parameters. Our method shows promising results across eight datasets representing seven different NLP tasks, with 90% of the best prompt accuracy being achieved without the need for ground truth labels.

text: This work connects language model adaptation with concepts of machine learning theory. We consider a training setup with a large out-of-domain set and a small in-domain set. We derive how the benefit of training a model on either set depends on the size of the sets and the distance between their underlying distributions. We analyze how out-of-domain pre-training before in-domain fine-tuning achieves better generalization than either solution independently. Finally, we present how adaptation techniques based on data selection, such as importance sampling, intelligent data selection and influence functions, can be presented in a common framework which highlights their similarity and also their subtle differences.

label: acl
text: This work explores the connection between language model adaptation and machine learning theory. We examine a training scenario that involves a large out-of-domain set and a small in-domain set. We analyze the impact of the size of these sets and the difference between their underlying distributions on the benefits of training the model on either set. Our findings show that pre-training the model on the out-of-domain set before fine-tuning it on the in-domain set leads to better generalization than using either solution independently. Additionally, we present a unified framework for adaptation techniques, including importance sampling, intelligent data selection, and influence functions, highlighting their similarities and differences.

text: The rapid growth of social media in recent years has fed into some highly undesirable phenomena such as proliferation of hateful and offensive language on the Internet. Previous research suggests that such abusive content tends to come from users who share a set of common stereotypes and form communities around them. The current state-of-the-art approaches to abuse detection are oblivious to user and community information and rely entirely on textual (i.e., lexical and semantic) cues. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to this problem that incorporates community-based profiling features of Twitter users. Experimenting with a dataset of 16k tweets, we show that our methods significantly outperform the current state of the art in abuse detection. Further, we conduct a qualitative analysis of model characteristics. We release our code, pre-trained models and all the resources used in the public domain.

text: The recent growth of social media has led to the proliferation of hateful and offensive language on the Internet. text: In view of the differences between the annotations of micro and macro discourse rela-tionships, this paper describes the relevant experiments on the construction of the Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB), a higher-level Chinese discourse corpus. Fol-lowing RST (Rhetorical Structure Theory), we annotate the macro discourse information, including discourse structure, nuclearity and relationship, and the additional discourse information, including topic sentences, lead and abstract, to make the macro discourse annotation more objective and accurate. Finally, we annotated 720 articles with a Kappa value greater than 0.6. Preliminary experiments on this corpus verify the computability of MCDTB.

label: coling
text: Considering the disparities between the annotations of micro and macro discourse relationships, this paper outlines the experiments carried out in the development of the Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB), a high-level Chinese discourse corpus. Based on Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST), the macro discourse information, including discourse structure, nuclearity, and relationship, was annotated, as well as additional discourse information like topic sentences, lead, and abstract, to enhance the objectivity and accuracy of the macro discourse annotations. The corpus was annotated by 720 articles, achieving a Kappa value of over 0.6. The preliminary experiments on the corpus confirmed its computational viability.

label: acl
text: Dense video event captioning aims to generate a sequence of descriptive captions for each event in a long untrimmed video. Video-level context provides important information and facilities the model to generate consistent and less redundant captions between events. In this paper, we introduce a novel Hierarchical Context-aware Network for dense video event captioning (HCN) to capture context from various aspects. In detail, the model leverages local and global context with different mechanisms to jointly learn to generate coherent captions. The local context module performs full interaction between neighbor frames and the global context module selectively attends to previous or future events. According to our extensive experiment on both Youcook2 and Activitynet Captioning datasets, the video-level HCN model outperforms the event-level context-agnostic model by a large margin. The code is available at https://github.com/KirkGuo/HCN.

label: acl
text: The aim of dense video event captioning is to generate descriptive captions for each event in long, untrimmed videos. Video-level context is crucial in facilitating consistent and non-redundant captions between events. This paper introduces a novel Hierarchical Context-aware Network (HCN) to capture context from various aspects for dense video event captioning. The HCN model jointly learns to generate coherent captions by leveraging local and global context with different mechanisms. The local context module interacts fully with neighboring frames, while the global context module selectively attends to previous or future events. The results of our extensive experiments on the Youcook2 and Activitynet Captioning datasets show that the video-level HCN model significantly outperforms the event-level, context-agnostic model. The code for the HCN model is available at https://github.com/KirkGuo/HCN.

label: coling
text: Natural language inference (NLI) is the task of determining if a natural language hypothesis can be inferred from a given premise in a justifiable manner. NLI was proposed as a benchmark task for natural language understanding. Existing models perform well at standard datasets for NLI, achieving impressive results across different genres of text. However, the extent to which these models understand the semantic content of sentences is unclear. In this work, we propose an evaluation methodology consisting of automatically constructed “stress tests” that allow us to examine whether systems have the ability to make real inferential decisions. Our evaluation of six sentence-encoder models on these stress tests reveals strengths and weaknesses of these models with respect to challenging linguistic phenomena, and suggests important directions for future work in this area.

label: coling
text: The task of Natural Language Inference (NLI) involves determining if a hypothesis expressed in natural language can be inferred from a given premise in a justifiable manner. NLI was established as a benchmark for evaluating natural language understanding in machine learning models. Despite the impressive results achieved by existing models on standard datasets for NLI, the level of semantic understanding of these models remains unclear. To address this issue, we propose an evaluation methodology that uses automatically constructed "stress tests" to assess the models' ability to make real inferential decisions. Our evaluation of six sentence-encoder models on these stress tests highlights the strengths and weaknesses of these models with respect to challenging linguistic phenomena and provides insights into future directions for improvement in this field.

label: acl
text: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (Temporal KGs) extend regular Knowledge Graphs by providing temporal scopes (start and end times) on each edge in the KG. While Question Answering over KG (KGQA) has received some attention from the research community, QA over Temporal KGs (Temporal KGQA) is a relatively unexplored area. Lack of broad coverage datasets has been another factor limiting progress in this area. We address this challenge by presenting CRONQUESTIONS, the largest known Temporal KGQA dataset, clearly stratified into buckets of structural complexity. CRONQUESTIONS expands the only known previous dataset by a factor of 340x. We find that various state-of-the-art KGQA methods fall far short of the desired performance on this new dataset. In response, we also propose CRONKGQA, a transformer-based solution that exploits recent advances in Temporal KG embeddings, and achieves performance superior to all baselines, with an increase of 120% in accuracy over the next best performing method. Through extensive experiments, we give detailed insights into the workings of CRONKGQA, as well as situations where significant further improvements appear possible. In addition to the dataset, we have released our code as well.

label: acl
text: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (Temporal KGs) enhance traditional Knowledge Graphs by including temporal scopes (start and end times) on each edge. Although Question Answering over Knowledge Graphs (KGQA) has gained some attention from the research community, Question Answering over Temporal Knowledge Graphs (Temporal KGQA) remains an under-explored area. One of the reasons for this is the lack of comprehensive datasets. To address this challenge, we present CRONQUESTIONS, the largest known Temporal KGQA dataset that is clearly categorized into structural complexity buckets. CRONQUESTIONS expands the previous dataset by 340 times. Our findings show that existing KGQA methods fall short of the desired performance on the new dataset. To overcome this, we introduce CRONKGQA, a transformer-based solution that leverages recent advancements in Temporal KG embeddings and outperforms all baselines, with a 120% increase in accuracy compared to the next best performing method. Through thorough experimentation, we provide in-depth insights into the functioning of CRONKGQA and highlight areas where further improvements are possible. Additionally, we have made our code available to the public.

label: naacl
text: Adversarial training (AT) is a powerful regularization method for neural networks, aiming to achieve robustness to input perturbations. Yet, the specific effects of the robustness obtained from AT are still unclear in the context of natural language processing. In this paper, we propose and analyze a neural POS tagging model that exploits AT. In our experiments on the Penn Treebank WSJ corpus and the Universal Dependencies (UD) dataset (27 languages), we find that AT not only improves the overall tagging accuracy, but also 1) prevents over-fitting well in low resource languages and 2) boosts tagging accuracy for rare / unseen words. We also demonstrate that 3) the improved tagging performance by AT contributes to the downstream task of dependency parsing, and that 4) AT helps the model to learn cleaner word representations. 5) The proposed AT model is generally effective in different sequence labeling tasks. These positive results motivate further use of AT for natural language tasks.

naacl
text: The emergence of language between artificial agents is a recent focus of computational linguistics, as it offers a synthetic substrate for reasoning about human language evolution. From the perspective of cognitive science, sophisticated categorization in humans is thought to enable reasoning about novel observations, and thus compose old information to describe new phenomena. Unfortunately, the literature to date has not managed to isolate the effect of categorization power in artificial agents on their inter-communication ability, particularly on novel, unseen objects. In this work, we propose the use of disentangled representations from representation learning to quantify the categorization power of agents, enabling a differential analysis between combinations of heterogeneous systems, e.g., pairs of agents which learn to communicate despite mismatched concept realization. Through this approach, we observe that agent heterogeneity can cut signaling accuracy by up to 40%, despite encouraging compositionality in the artificial language. We conclude that the reasoning process of agents plays a key role in their communication, with unexpected benefits arising from their mixing, such as better language compositionality.

label: naacl
text: The study of language emergence between artificial agents is a recent area of interest in computational linguistics. This is because it provides a synthetic platform for exploring the evolution of human language. In cognitive science, it is believed that advanced categorization in humans allows for reasoning about new experiences and combining existing information to describe new phenomena. However, the current literature has not yet been able to determine the impact of categorization power on the communication ability of artificial agents, particularly when it comes to novel, unseen objects. This study proposes using disentangled representations from representation learning to measure the categorization power of agents. This will allow for a comparison of different combinations of heterogeneous systems, such as pairs of agents that learn to communicate despite having different concepts. The results show that agent heterogeneity can reduce signaling accuracy by up to 40%, even though it promotes compositionality in the artificial language. The conclusion is that the reasoning process of the agents plays a crucial role in their ability to communicate, and that the mixing of agents can lead to unexpected benefits, such as improved language compositionality.

label: coling
text: We develop CALM, a coordination analyzer that improves upon the conjuncts identified from dependency parses. It uses a language model based scoring and several linguistic constraints to search over hierarchical conjunct boundaries (for nested coordination). By splitting a conjunctive sentence around these conjuncts, CALM outputs several simple sentences. We demonstrate the value of our coordination analyzer in the end task of Open Information Extraction (Open IE). State-of-the-art Open IE systems lose substantial yield due to ineffective processing of conjunctive sentences. Our Open IE system, CALMIE, performs extraction over the simple sentences identified by CALM to obtain up to 1.8x yield with a moderate increase in precision compared to extractions from original sentences.

label: coling
text: We have developed CALM, a coordination analyzer that improves upon the identification of conjuncts from dependency parses. With the use of a language model-based scoring system and various linguistic constraints, CALM searches for hierarchical conjunct boundaries, including those within nested coordination. As a result, CALM outputs several simple sentences by splitting the conjunctive sentence at these conjuncts. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of CALM in the Open Information Extraction (Open IE) task. Current state-of-the-art Open IE systems suffer from a significant loss of yield due to their ineffective processing of conjunctive sentences. Our Open IE system, CALMIE, leverages the simple sentences generated by CALM to achieve up to 1.8 times the yield with a moderate increase in precision compared to extractions from the original sentences.

label: acl
text: A good translation should not only translate the original content semantically, but also incarnate personal traits of the original text. For a real-world neural machine translation (NMT) system, these user traits (e.g., topic preference, stylistic characteristics and expression habits) can be preserved in user behavior (e.g., historical inputs). However, current NMT systems marginally consider the user behavior due to: 1) the difficulty of modeling user portraits in zero-shot scenarios, and 2) the lack of user-behavior annotated parallel dataset. To fill this gap, we introduce a novel framework called user-driven NMT. Specifically, a cache-based module and a user-driven contrastive learning method are proposed to offer NMT the ability to capture potential user traits from their historical inputs under a zero-shot learning fashion. Furthermore, we contribute the first Chinese-English parallel corpus annotated with user behavior called UDT-Corpus. Experimental results confirm that the proposed user-driven NMT can generate user-specific translations.

label: acl
text: A good translation should not only convey the meaning of the original text, but also embody the personal traits of the original text. For a real-world neural machine translation (NMT) system, these user traits, such as topic preference, stylistic characteristics, and expression habits, can be preserved in the user's behavior, such as historical inputs. However, current NMT systems do not adequately consider user behavior due to two challenges: the difficulty of modeling user portraits in zero-shot scenarios and the lack of user behavior annotated parallel datasets. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework called user-driven NMT. Our framework includes a cache-based module and a user-driven contrastive learning method, which enable NMT to capture potential user traits from historical inputs in a zero-shot learning fashion. Additionally, we contribute the first Chinese-English parallel corpus annotated with user behavior, called UDT-Corpus. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed user-driven NMT can generate user-specific translations.

label: naacl
text: Efficient machine translation models are commercially important as they can increase inference speeds, and reduce costs and carbon emissions. Recently, there has been much interest in non-autoregressive (NAR) models, which promise faster translation. In parallel to the research on NAR models, there have been successful attempts to create optimized autoregressive models as part of the WMT shared task on efficient translation. In this paper, we point out flaws in the evaluation methodology present in the literature on NAR models and we provide a fair comparison between a state-of-the-art NAR model and the autoregressive submissions to the shared task. We make the case for consistent evaluation of NAR models, and also for the importance of comparing NAR models with other widely used methods for improving efficiency. We run experiments with a connectionist-temporal-classification-based (CTC) NAR model implemented in C++ and compare it with AR models using wall clock times. Our results show that, although NAR models are faster on GPUs, with small batch sizes, they are almost always slower under more realistic usage conditions. We call for more realistic and extensive evaluation of NAR models in future work.

label: naacl
text: Efficient machine translation is commercially vital as it can enhance inference speeds and decrease costs and carbon emissions. There has been growing interest in non-autoregressive (NAR) models, which offer the potential for faster translation. However, there have also been successful efforts to optimize autoregressive models as part of the WMT shared task on efficient translation. This paper highlights flaws in the evaluation methodology used in NAR model research and provides a fair comparison between a state-of-the-art NAR model and autoregressive submissions to the shared task. We emphasize the importance of consistent evaluation of NAR models and comparison with other methods of improving efficiency. Our experiments, using a CTC-based NAR model implemented in C++ and comparing it to AR models, show that while NAR models are faster on GPUs with small batch sizes, they are often slower under more realistic conditions. We advocate for more comprehensive and realistic evaluations of NAR models in future research.

text: Lifelong event detection aims to incrementally update a model with new event types and data while retaining the capability on previously learned old types. One critical challenge is that the model would catastrophically forget old types when continually trained on new data. In this paper, we introduce Episodic Memory Prompts (EMP) to explicitly retain the learned task-specific knowledge. Our method adopts continuous prompt for each task and they are optimized to instruct the model prediction and learn event-specific representation. The EMPs learned in previous tasks are carried along with the model in subsequent tasks, and can serve as a memory module that keeps the old knowledge and transferring to new tasks. Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Furthermore, we also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the new and old event types in lifelong learning.

label: coling
text: The goal of lifelong event detection is to incrementally update a model with new event types and data while preserving its ability to recognize previously learned old types. A major challenge in this process is that the model may forget old types when continually trained on new data. To address this issue, we propose the use of Episodic Memory Prompts (EMP) to explicitly retain task-specific knowledge. Our method employs continuous prompts for each task, which are optimized to guide the model's predictions and facilitate event-specific representation learning. The EMPs learned in previous tasks are carried over to subsequent tasks, serving as a memory module that retains old knowledge and transfers it to new tasks. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and we also perform a comprehensive analysis of new and old event types in lifelong learning.

text: This paper introduces our Diversity Advanced Actor-Critic reinforcement learning (A2C) framework (DAAC) to improve the generalization and accuracy of Natural Language Processing (NLP). We show that the diversification of training samples alleviates overfitting and improves model generalization and accuracy. We quantify diversity on a set of samples using the max dispersion, convex hull volume, and graph entropy based on sentence embeddings in high-dimensional metric space. We also introduce A2C to select such a diversified training subset efficiently. Our experiments achieve up to +23.8 accuracy increase (38.0% relatively) in sentiment analysis, -44.7 perplexity decrease (37.9% relatively) in language modeling, and consistent improvements in named entity recognition over various domains. In particular, our method outperforms both domain adaptation and generalization baselines without using any target domain knowledge.

text: This paper presents the Diversity Advanced Actor-Critic reinforcement learning framework (DAAC) aimed at enhancing the generalization and accuracy of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Our approach demonstrates that diversifying the training samples reduces overfitting and improves both generalization and accuracy. We quantify diversity using three metrics: max dispersion, convex hull volume, and graph entropy, which are based on sentence embeddings in high-dimensional metric space. The A2C algorithm is used to efficiently select a diversified training subset. Our experiments show significant improvements in sentiment analysis, language modeling, and named entity recognition across various domains, with up to a 23.8% accuracy increase in sentiment analysis, a 44.7% decrease in perplexity in language modeling, and consistent improvements in named entity recognition. Our method outperforms both domain adaptation and generalization baselines, and does not require any target domain knowledge.

label: acl
text: Several studies have reported the inability of Transformer models to generalize compositionally, a key type of generalization in many NLP tasks such as semantic parsing. In this paper we explore the design space of Transformer models showing that the inductive biases given to the model by several design decisions significantly impact compositional generalization. We identified Transformer configurations that generalize compositionally significantly better than previously reported in the literature in many compositional tasks. We achieve state-of-the-art results in a semantic parsing compositional generalization benchmark (COGS), and a string edit operation composition benchmark (PCFG).

label: acl
text: Several studies have indicated that Transformer models struggle with compositional generalization, a crucial aspect of NLP tasks such as semantic parsing. In this study, we examine the design space of Transformer models and demonstrate that the inductive biases imposed by design choices significantly affect compositional generalization. We have identified Transformer configurations that outperform previous literature in compositional tasks and achieved state-of-the-art results in the COGS semantic parsing benchmark and the PCFG string edit operation benchmark.

label: acl
text: Despite recent advances in natural language generation, it remains challenging to control attributes of generated text. We propose DExperts: Decoding-time Experts, a decoding-time method for controlled text generation that combines a pretrained language model with “expert” LMs and/or “anti-expert” LMs in a product of experts. Intuitively, under the ensemble, tokens only get high probability if they are considered likely by the experts, and unlikely by the anti-experts. We apply DExperts to language detoxification and sentiment-controlled generation, where we outperform existing controllable generation methods on both automatic and human evaluations. Moreover, because DExperts operates only on the output of the pretrained LM, it is effective with (anti-)experts of smaller size, including when operating on GPT-3. Our work highlights the promise of tuning small LMs on text with (un)desirable attributes for efficient decoding-time steering.

label: acl
text: Despite recent advancements in natural language generation, controlling the attributes of generated text remains a challenge. To address this, we introduce DExperts: Decoding-time Experts, a method for controlled text generation that leverages a combination of a pretrained language model with "expert" LMs and/or "anti-expert" LMs during the decoding process. The ensemble approach ensures that only tokens with high probabilities, as determined by the experts and unlikely by the anti-experts, are generated. We apply DExperts to language detoxification and sentiment-controlled generation and achieve superior results compared to existing controllable generation methods, as demonstrated by both automatic and human evaluations. Additionally, because DExperts operates only on the output of the pretrained LM, it is effective even with smaller-sized experts and anti-experts, including when using GPT-3. Our findings highlight the potential of fine-tuning small LMs on text with desired or undesired attributes for efficient control during the decoding process.

label: coling
text: User demographic inference from social media text has the potential to improve a range of downstream applications, including real-time passive polling or quantifying demographic bias. This study focuses on developing models for user-level race and ethnicity prediction. We introduce a data set of users who self-report their race/ethnicity through a survey, in contrast to previous approaches that use distantly supervised data or perceived labels. We develop predictive models from text which accurately predict the membership of a user to the four largest racial and ethnic groups with up to .884 AUC and make these available to the research community.

label: coling
text: This study aims to enhance the accuracy of user demographic inference from social media text by developing models for user-level race and ethnicity prediction. To achieve this, we introduce a novel data set that consists of users who self-report their race/ethnicity through a survey, as opposed to previous methods that use distantly supervised data or perceived labels. Our predictive models, which are based on text analysis, can accurately predict the membership of a user to the four largest racial and ethnic groups with an AUC of up to .884. These models are made available to the research community for further study and application.
