In this paper, we propose CINO (Chinese Minority Pre-trained Language Model), a multilingual pre-trained language model for Chinese minority languages. It covers Standard Chinese, Yue Chinese, and six other ethnic minority languages. To evaluate the cross-lingual ability of the multilingual model on ethnic minority languages, we collect documents from Wikipedia and news websites, and construct two text classification datasets, WCM (Wiki-Chinese-Minority) and CMNews (Chinese-Minority-News). We show that CINO notably outperforms the baselines on various classification tasks. The CINO model and the datasets are publicly available at http://cino.hfl-rc.com.

label: coling
text: Multilingual pre-trained language models have demonstrated exceptional performance on cross-lingual tasks, enabling the application of natural language processing to low-resource languages. However, there are still some languages that are not well-supported by current models. To address this issue, we present CINO (Chinese Minority Pre-trained Language Model), a multilingual pre-trained model that covers Standard Chinese, Yue Chinese, and six other Chinese minority languages. To evaluate the cross-lingual ability of the model on these minority languages, we have created two text classification datasets, WCM (Wiki-Chinese-Minority) and CMNews (Chinese-Minority-News), using documents from Wikipedia and news websites. The results demonstrate that CINO outperforms the baselines on various classification tasks. The CINO model and datasets are publicly accessible at http://cino.hfl-rc.com.

label: acl
text: Generalization is an important ability that helps to ensure that a machine learning model can perform well on unseen data. In this paper, we study the effect of data bias on model generalization, using Chinese Named Entity Recognition (NER) as a case study. Specifically, we analyzed five benchmarking datasets for Chinese NER, and observed the following two types of data bias that can compromise model generalization ability. Firstly, the test sets of all the five datasets contain a significant proportion of entities that have been seen in the training sets. Such test data would therefore not be able to reflect the true generalization ability of a model. Secondly, all datasets are dominated by a few fat-head entities, i.e., entities appearing with particularly high frequency. As a result, a model might be able to produce high prediction accuracy simply by keyword memorization without leveraging context knowledge. To address these data biases, we first refine each test set by excluding seen entities from it, so as to better evaluate a model's generalization ability. Then, we propose a simple yet effective entity resampling method to make entities within the same category distributed equally, encouraging a model to leverage both name and context knowledge in the training process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed entity resampling method significantly improves a model's ability in detecting unseen entities, especially for company, organization and position categories.

label: acl
text: Generalization is a crucial ability that helps ensure that a machine learning model performs well on unseen data. This paper examines the impact of data bias on model generalization using Chinese Named Entity Recognition (NER) as a case study. We analyzed five benchmarking datasets for Chinese NER and found two types of data bias that can compromise model generalization. Firstly, the test sets of all five datasets contain a significant proportion of entities that have been seen in the training sets, making it difficult to evaluate a model's true generalization ability. Secondly, all datasets are dominated by a few entities that appear with high frequency, leading to a model relying on keyword memorization rather than context knowledge. To address these data biases, we refined each test set by excluding seen entities and proposed a simple but effective entity resampling method to make entities within the same category equally distributed, encouraging the model to use both name and context knowledge in the training process. Our experimental results show that the proposed entity resampling method significantly improves the model's ability to detect unseen entities, especially for company, organization, and position categories.

label: acl
text: Continual learning is essential for real-world deployment when there is a need to quickly adapt the model to new tasks without forgetting knowledge of old tasks. Existing work on continual sequence generation either always reuses existing parameters to learn new tasks, which is vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting on dissimilar tasks, or blindly adds new parameters for every new task, which could prevent knowledge sharing between similar tasks. To get the best of both worlds, in this work, we propose continual sequence generation with adaptive compositional modules to adaptively add modules in transformer architectures and compose both old and new modules for new tasks. We also incorporate pseudo experience replay to facilitate knowledge transfer in those shared modules. Experiment results on various sequences of generation tasks show that our framework can adaptively add modules or reuse modules based on task similarity, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in terms of both performance and parameter efficiency. We make our code public at https://github.com/GT-SALT/Adaptive-Compositional-Modules.

label: acl
text: Continuous learning is crucial for real-world deployment, especially when it is necessary to adapt the model quickly to new tasks while retaining knowledge of old tasks. Existing research on continual sequence generation either relies on reusing existing parameters, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting in dissimilar tasks, or blindly adds new parameters for each new task, hindering knowledge sharing between similar tasks. To overcome these limitations, we propose a method for continual sequence generation with adaptive compositional modules. Our approach adaptively adds modules to transformer architectures and combines both old and new modules for new tasks. Additionally, we use pseudo experience replay to facilitate knowledge transfer in shared modules. Our experiments on various sequence generation tasks show that our framework outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of performance and parameter efficiency. The code for our work is available at https://github.com/GT-SALT/Adaptive-Compositional-Modules.

label: acl
text: Fine-tuning pre-trained cross-lingual language models can transfer task-specific supervision from one language to the others. In this work, we propose to improve cross-lingual fine-tuning with consistency regularization. Specifically, we use example consistency regularization to penalize the prediction sensitivity to four types of data augmentations, i.e., subword sampling, Gaussian noise, code-switch substitution, and machine translation. In addition, we employ model consistency to regularize the models trained with two augmented versions of the same training set. Experimental results on the XTREME benchmark show that our method significantly improves cross-lingual fine-tuning across various tasks, including text classification, question answering, and sequence labeling.

label: acl
text: Fine-tuning pre-trained cross-lingual language models can transfer task-specific supervision from one language to others. In this work, we propose to enhance cross-lingual fine-tuning with consistency regularization. Our approach uses example consistency regularization to penalize the prediction sensitivity to four types of data augmentations: subword sampling, Gaussian noise, code-switch substitution, and machine translation. We also incorporate model consistency to regulate the models trained with two augmented versions of the same training set. Our experimentation on the XTREME benchmark demonstrates that our method significantly improves cross-lingual fine-tuning performance across various tasks, including text classification, question answering, and sequence labeling.

label: acl
text: Role-oriented dialogue summarization is to generate summaries for different roles in the dialogue, e.g., merchants and consumers. Existing methods handle this task by summarizing each role's content separately and thus are prone to ignore the information from other roles. However, we believe that other roles' content could benefit the quality of summaries, such as the omitted information mentioned by other roles. Therefore, we propose a novel role interaction enhanced method for role-oriented dialogue summarization. It adopts cross attention and decoder self-attention interactions to interactively acquire other roles' critical information. The cross attention interaction aims to select other roles' critical dialogue utterances, while the decoder self-attention interaction aims to obtain key information from other roles' summaries. Experimental results have shown that our proposed method significantly outperforms strong baselines on two public role-oriented dialogue summarization datasets. Extensive analyses have demonstrated that other roles' content could help generate summaries with more complete semantics and correct topic structures.

label: acl
text: The task of role-oriented dialogue summarization involves generating summaries for different roles in a dialogue, such as merchants and consumers. Existing methods for this task summarize each role's content separately, which can result in the omission of important information from other roles. To address this issue, we propose a novel role interaction enhanced method for role-oriented dialogue summarization. This method uses cross attention and decoder self-attention interactions to acquire information from other roles in the dialogue, improving the quality of the generated summaries. Our approach was shown to significantly outperform strong baselines on two public role-oriented dialogue summarization datasets. Analysis revealed that incorporating information from other roles in the summaries results in more complete semantics and accurate topic structures.

label: naacl
text: The remarkable success of large language models has been driven by dense models trained on massive unlabeled, unstructured corpora. These corpora typically contain text from diverse, heterogeneous sources, but information about the source of the text is rarely used during training. Transferring their knowledge to a target domain is typically done by continuing training in-domain. In this paper, we introduce a method to permit domain adaptation to many diverse domains using a computationally efficient adapter approach. Our method is based on the observation that textual domains are partially overlapping, and we represent domains as a hierarchical tree structure where each node in the tree is associated with a set of adapter weights. When combined with a frozen pretrained language model, this approach enables parameter sharing among related domains, while avoiding negative interference between unrelated ones. Experimental results with GPT-2 and a large fraction of the 100 most represented websites in C4 show across-the-board improvements in-domain. We additionally provide an inference time algorithm for a held-out domain and show that averaging over multiple paths through the tree enables further gains in generalization, while adding only a marginal cost to inference.

label: naacl
text: The success of large language models can be attributed to dense models trained on vast amounts of unstructured, unlabeled text from diverse and heterogeneous sources. However, the source information of the text is rarely used during the training process. Transferring the knowledge to a target domain is usually achieved through continued in-domain training. This paper introduces a more efficient method for domain adaptation to multiple diverse domains using an adapter approach. Our method is based on the partial overlap of textual domains and represents them as a hierarchical tree structure, where each node is linked to a set of adapter weights. By combining this approach with a frozen pre-trained language model, we can share parameters among related domains while avoiding negative interference between unrelated ones. Our experiments with GPT-2 and a significant portion of the 100 most represented websites in C4 show improved in-domain performance. We also provide an algorithm for inference time in a held-out domain and demonstrate that averaging multiple paths through the tree leads to further generalization gains with only a minimal cost to inference.

label: emnlp
text: Many efforts have been made to facilitate natural language processing tasks with pre-trained language models (LMs), and brought significant improvements to various applications. To fully leverage the nearly unlimited corpora and capture linguistic information of multifarious levels, large-size LMs are required; but for a specific task, only parts of these information are useful. Such large-sized LMs, even in the inference stage, may cause heavy computation workloads, making them too time-consuming for large-scale applications. Here we propose to compress bulky LMs while preserving useful information with regard to a specific task. As different layers of the model keep different information, we develop a layer selection method for model pruning using sparsity-inducing regularization. By introducing the dense connectivity, we can detach any layer without affecting others, and stretch shallow and wide LMs to be deep and narrow. In model training, LMs are learned with layer-wise dropouts for better robustness. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

label: emnlp
text: Efforts have been made to improve natural language processing tasks through the use of pre-trained language models (LMs), resulting in significant advancements in various applications. Large-sized LMs are necessary to capture the vast amount of linguistic information, but only a portion of this information is useful for a specific task. However, these large-sized LMs can be time-consuming due to heavy computation workloads, making them unsuitable for large-scale applications. To address this issue, we propose a method to compress bulky LMs while preserving useful information for a specific task. Our method uses sparsity-inducing regularization to select specific layers of the model for pruning, and dense connectivity to allow for the detachment of any layer without affecting others. The LMs are also trained with layer-wise dropouts for improved robustness. Our method has been tested on two benchmark datasets and has proven to be effective.

label: acl
text: Neural methods have been shown to achieve high performance in Named Entity Recognition (NER), but rely on costly high-quality labeled data for training, which is not always available across languages. While previous works have shown that unlabeled data in a target language can be used to improve cross-lingual model performance, we propose a novel adversarial approach (AdvPicker) to better leverage such data and further improve results. We design an adversarial learning framework in which an encoder learns entity domain knowledge from labeled source-language data and better shared features are captured via adversarial training - where a discriminator selects less language-dependent target-language data via similarity to the source language. Experimental results on standard benchmark datasets well demonstrate that the proposed method benefits strongly from this data selection process and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods; without requiring any additional external resources (e.g., gazetteers or via machine translation).

label: acl
text: The proposed novel adversarial approach, AdvPicker, leverages unlabeled data in the target language to improve cross-lingual Named Entity Recognition (NER) performance. The approach utilizes an adversarial learning framework where an encoder learns entity domain knowledge from labeled source-language data and captures better shared features via adversarial training. A discriminator selects less language-dependent target-language data based on similarity to the source language. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods and does not require any external resources such as gazetteers or machine translation. The experimental results demonstrate the strong benefits of the data selection process in the proposed method.

label: acl
text: Nowadays, open-domain dialogue models can generate acceptable responses according to the historical context based on the large-scale pre-trained language models. However, they generally concatenate the dialogue history directly as the model input to predict the response, which we named as the flat pattern and ignores the dynamic information flow across dialogue utterances. In this work, we propose the DialoFlow model, in which we introduce a dynamic flow mechanism to model the context flow, and design three training objectives to capture the information dynamics across dialogue utterances by addressing the semantic influence brought about by each utterance in large-scale pre-training. Experiments on the multi-reference Reddit Dataset and DailyDialog Dataset demonstrate that our DialoFlow significantly outperforms the DialoGPT on the dialogue generation task. Besides, we propose the Flow score, an effective automatic metric for evaluating interactive human-bot conversation quality based on the pre-trained DialoFlow, which presents high chatbot-level correlation (C-C-C) with human ratings among 11 chatbots. Code and pre-trained models will be public.

label: acl
text: Nowadays, open-domain dialogue models are capable of generating acceptable responses based on historical context using large-scale pre-trained language models. However, these models often rely on a flat pattern, where the dialogue history is simply concatenated as input to predict the response, ignoring the dynamic flow of information across dialogue utterances. To address this issue, we present the DialoFlow model, which incorporates a dynamic flow mechanism to model context flow and three training objectives to capture the information dynamics across dialogue utterances. Our experiments on the multi-reference Reddit Dataset and DailyDialog Dataset show that DialoFlow outperforms DialoGPT in dialogue generation. Additionally, we propose the Flow score, an effective automatic metric for evaluating the quality of human-bot conversation based on pre-trained DialoFlow, which demonstrates high correlation with human ratings among 11 chatbots. The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

label: coling
text: Commonsense, real-world knowledge about the events that entities or “things in the world” are typically involved in, as well as part-whole relationships, is valuable for allowing computational systems to draw everyday inferences about the world. Here, we focus on automatically extracting information about (1) the events that typically bring about certain entities (origins), (2) the events that are the typical functions of entities, and (3) part-whole relationships in entities. These correspond to the agentive, telic and constitutive qualia central to the Generative Lexicon. We describe our motivations and methods for extracting these qualia relations from the Suggested Upper Merged Ontology (SUMO) and show that human annotators overwhelmingly find the information extracted to be reasonable. Because ontologies provide a way of structuring this information and making it accessible to agents and computational systems generally, efforts are underway to incorporate the extracted information to an ontology hub of Natural Language Processing semantic role labeling resources, the Rich Event Ontology.

label: coling
text: Commonsense knowledge about the events that entities or "things in the world" participate in, as well as their part-whole relationships, is crucial for enabling computational systems to make everyday inferences about the world. Our focus is on automatically extracting information about (1) the events that typically result in certain entities (origins), (2) the typical functions of entities, and (3) the part-whole relationships in entities. These correspond to the agentive, telic, and constitutive qualia central to the Generative Lexicon. We outline our motivations and methods for extracting these qualia relations from the Suggested Upper Merged Ontology (SUMO) and demonstrate that human annotators overwhelmingly consider the information to be reasonable. To make this information accessible to agents and computational systems, we are working to incorporate it into the Rich Event Ontology, a hub of Natural Language Processing semantic role labeling resources.

label: acl
text: Car-focused navigation services are based on turns and distances of named streets, whereas navigation instructions naturally used by humans are centered around physical objects called landmarks. We present a neural model that takes OpenStreetMap representations as input and learns to generate navigation instructions that contain visible and salient landmarks from human natural language instructions. Routes on the map are encoded in a location- and rotation-invariant graph representation that is decoded into natural language instructions. Our work is based on a novel dataset of 7,672 crowd-sourced instances that have been verified by human navigation in Street View. Our evaluation shows that the navigation instructions generated by our system have similar properties as human-generated instructions, and lead to successful human navigation in Street View.

label: acl
text: Car-based navigation services rely on turns and distances between named streets, while human-centered navigation instructions are based on physical landmarks. We introduce a neural model that uses OpenStreetMap representations as input and learns to generate human-like navigation instructions that highlight visible and prominent landmarks. The routes on the map are encoded in a graph representation that is invariant to location and rotation, and decoded into natural language instructions. Our work is supported by a novel dataset of 7,672 crowd-sourced instances that have been verified through human navigation in Street View. Our evaluation results show that the navigation instructions generated by our system have similar characteristics to human-generated instructions and result in successful human navigation in Street View.

label: coling
text: We address contextualized code retrieval, the search for code snippets helpful to fill gaps in a partial input program. Our approach facilitates a large-scale self-supervised contrastive training by splitting source code randomly into contexts and targets. To combat leakage between the two, we suggest a novel approach based on mutual identifier masking, dedentation, and the selection of syntax-aligned targets. Our second contribution is a new dataset for direct evaluation of contextualized code retrieval, based on a dataset of manually aligned subpassages of code clones. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach improves retrieval substantially, and yields new state-of-the-art results for code clone and defect detection.

label: coling
text: We focus on contextualized code retrieval, which involves finding code snippets that can be used to complete a partially written program. Our approach involves self-supervised contrastive training of large-scale source code, by dividing it randomly into contexts and targets. To prevent any leakage between the two, we introduce a novel technique based on mutual identifier masking, dedentation, and the selection of syntax-aligned targets. Additionally, we present a new dataset for the direct evaluation of contextualized code retrieval, which is based on a dataset of manually aligned subpassages of code clones. Our experiments show that our approach significantly improves retrieval and achieves new state-of-the-art results for code clone and defect detection.

label: naacl
text: Recently, Multi-modal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) has attracted a lot of attention. Most of the work utilizes image information through region-level visual representations obtained from a pretrained object detector and relies on an attention mechanism to model the interactions between image and text representations. However, it is difficult to model such interactions as image and text representations are trained separately on the data of their respective modality and are not aligned in the same space. As text representations take the most important role in MNER, in this paper, we propose Image-text Alignments (ITA) to align image features into the textual space, so that the attention mechanism in transformer-based pretrained textual embeddings can be better utilized. ITA first aligns the image into regional object tags, image-level captions and optical characters as visual contexts, concatenates them with the input texts as a new cross-modal input, and then feeds it into a pretrained textual embedding model. This makes it easier for the attention module of a pretrained textual embedding model to model the interaction between the two modalities since they are both represented in the textual space. ITA further aligns the output distributions predicted from the cross-modal input and textual input views so that the MNER model can be more practical in dealing with text-only inputs and robust to noises from images. In our experiments, we show that ITA models can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on multi-modal Named Entity Recognition datasets, even without image information.

label: naacl
text: Recently, Multi-modal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) has received a lot of attention and most of the work focuses on utilizing image information through region-level visual representations obtained from a pre-trained object detector, relying on an attention mechanism to model the interaction between image and text representations. However, this interaction is difficult to model because the image and text representations are trained separately on data from their respective modalities, and they are not aligned in the same space. To address this issue, we propose Image-text Alignments (ITA) to align the image features into the textual space. This allows the attention mechanism in the transformer-based pre-trained textual embeddings to be better utilized. ITA aligns the image into regional object tags, image-level captions, and optical characters as visual contexts, concatenates them with the input text, and then feeds it into a pre-trained textual embedding model. This makes it easier for the attention module of the pre-trained textual embedding model to model the interaction between the two modalities since they are both represented in the textual space. ITA further aligns the output distributions predicted from the cross-modal input and textual input views, making the MNER model more practical for dealing with text-only inputs and more robust to noise from images. Our experiments show that ITA models can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on multi-modal Named Entity Recognition datasets, even without image information.

label: acl
text: The connection between the maximum spanning tree in a directed graph and the best dependency tree of a sentence has been exploited by the NLP community. However, for many dependency parsing schemes, an important detail of this approach is that the spanning tree must have exactly one edge emanating from the root. While work has been done to efficiently solve this problem for finding the one-best dependency tree, no research has attempted to extend this solution to finding the K-best dependency trees. This is arguably a more important extension as a larger proportion of decoded trees will not be subject to the root constraint of dependency trees. Indeed, we show that the rate of root constraint violations increases by an average of 13 times when decoding with K=50 as opposed to K=1. In this paper, we provide a simplification of the K-best spanning tree algorithm of Camerini et al. (1980). Our simplification allows us to obtain a constant time speed-up over the original algorithm. Furthermore, we present a novel extension of the algorithm for decoding the K-best dependency trees of a graph which are subject to a root constraint.

label: acl
text: The NLP community has leveraged the connection between the maximum spanning tree in a directed graph and the best dependency tree of a sentence. However, many dependency parsing schemes require that the spanning tree must have exactly one edge emanating from the root. Although research has been conducted to efficiently find the one-best dependency tree, there is a lack of studies on finding the K-best dependency trees, which is a more significant extension as it eliminates the root constraint of dependency trees. Our research shows that the rate of root constraint violations increases by an average of 13 times when decoding with K=50 compared to K=1. This paper presents a simplified version of the K-best spanning tree algorithm of Camerini et al. (1980), which results in a constant time speed-up. Additionally, we introduce a novel extension of the algorithm to decode the K-best dependency trees subject to a root constraint.

label: acl
text: Discourse relations among arguments reveal logical structures of a debate conversation. However, no prior work has explicitly studied how the sequence of discourse relations influence a claim's impact. This paper empirically shows that the discourse relations between two arguments along the context path are essential factors for identifying the persuasive power of an argument. We further propose DisCOC to inject and fuse the sentence-level structural discourse information with contextualized features derived from large-scale language models. Experimental results and extensive analysis show that the attention and gate mechanisms that explicitly model contexts and texts can indeed help the argument impact classification task defined by Durmus et al. (2019), and discourse structures among the context path of the claim to be classified can further boost the performance.

label: acl
text: The discourse relations between arguments reveal the logical structures of a debate conversation. However, no previous work has explicitly examined the impact of the sequence of these relations. This paper provides empirical evidence that the discourse relations between two arguments along the context path are crucial in determining the persuasive power of an argument. We introduce DisCOC, which combines sentence-level structural discourse information with context-based features derived from large language models. Our experiments and analysis demonstrate that the attention and gate mechanisms, which model both context and text, can improve the argument impact classification task defined by Durmus et al. (2019). Additionally, incorporating discourse structures along the context path of the claim being classified can further enhance performance.

label: naacl
text: We investigate the computational complexity of various problems for simple recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as formal models for recognizing weighted languages. We focus on the single-layer, ReLU-activation, rational-weight RNNs with softmax, which are commonly used in natural language processing applications. We show that most problems for such RNNs are undecidable, including consistency, equivalence, minimization, and the determination of the highest-weighted string. However, for consistent RNNs the last problem becomes decidable, although the solution length can surpass all computable bounds. If additionally the string is limited to polynomial length, the problem becomes NP-complete. In summary, this shows that approximations and heuristic algorithms are necessary in practical applications of those RNNs.

label: naacl
text: We examine the computational complexity of various problems for simple recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as a means of recognizing weighted languages. Our focus is on the single-layer, ReLU-activation, rational-weight RNNs with a softmax activation function, which are commonly utilized in natural language processing. Our findings reveal that most problems for these RNNs are undecidable, including consistency, equivalence, minimization, and the determination of the highest-weighted string. However, for consistent RNNs, the latter problem becomes decidable, though the solution length may exceed all computable bounds. If the string length is limited to a polynomial, the problem becomes NP-complete. In conclusion, this highlights the need for approximations and heuristic algorithms in practical applications of these RNNs.

label: emnlp
text: Representing entities and relations in an embedding space is a well-studied approach for machine learning on relational data. Existing approaches, however, primarily focus on simple link structure between a finite set of entities, ignoring the variety of data types that are often used in knowledge bases, such as text, images, and numerical values. In this paper, we propose multimodal knowledge base embeddings (MKBE) that use different neural encoders for this variety of observed data, and combine them with existing relational models to learn embeddings of the entities and multimodal data. Further, using these learned embedings and different neural decoders, we introduce a novel multimodal imputation model to generate missing multimodal values, like text and images, from information in the knowledge base. We enrich existing relational datasets to create two novel benchmarks that contain additional information such as textual descriptions and images of the original entities. We demonstrate that our models utilize this additional information effectively to provide more accurate link prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results with a considerable gap of 5-7% over existing methods. Further, we evaluate the quality of our generated multimodal values via a user study.

label: emnlp
text: Representing entities and their relationships in an embedding space is a well-established approach for machine learning on relational data. However, existing methods primarily focus on simple link structures between a finite set of entities, ignoring the variety of data types often used in knowledge bases, such as text, images, and numerical values. This paper introduces multimodal knowledge base embeddings (MKBE), which use different neural encoders to handle this variety of observed data and combine them with existing relational models to learn embeddings of entities and multimodal data. Additionally, we present a novel multimodal imputation model that generates missing multimodal values, such as text and images, from information in the knowledge base, using these learned embeddings and different neural decoders. To evaluate our approach, we enrich existing relational datasets to create two new benchmarks that include textual descriptions and images of entities. Our models effectively utilize this additional information, leading to more accurate link prediction and state-of-the-art results with a significant improvement of 5-7% over existing methods. We also evaluate the quality of our generated multimodal values through a user study.

label: acl
text: Complex machine learning models for NLP are often brittle, making different predictions for input instances that are extremely similar semantically. To automatically detect this behavior for individual instances, we present semantically equivalent adversaries (SEAs) – semantic-preserving perturbations that induce changes in the model's predictions. We generalize these adversaries into semantically equivalent adversarial rules (SEARs) – simple, universal replacement rules that induce adversaries on many instances. We demonstrate the usefulness and flexibility of SEAs and SEARs by detecting bugs in black-box state-of-the-art models for three domains: machine comprehension, visual question-answering, and sentiment analysis. Via user studies, we demonstrate that we generate high-quality local adversaries for more instances than humans, and that SEARs induce four times as many mistakes as the bugs discovered by human experts. SEARs are also actionable: retraining models using data augmentation significantly reduces bugs, while maintaining accuracy.

label: acl
text: The use of complex machine learning models for NLP can result in brittleness, leading to different predictions for input instances that are semantically similar. To address this issue, we introduce semantically equivalent adversaries (SEAs) - semantic-preserving perturbations that alter the model's predictions. Furthermore, we generalize these adversaries into semantically equivalent adversarial rules (SEARs), which are simple and universal replacement rules that can induce adversaries on many instances. Our method has been tested on black-box state-of-the-art models in three domains: machine comprehension, visual question-answering, and sentiment analysis. The results of our user studies show that our method generates high-quality local adversaries for more instances than humans, resulting in four times as many mistakes as those discovered by human experts. Additionally, retraining models using data augmentation significantly reduces bugs while maintaining accuracy, proving the actionability of SEARs.

label: naacl
text: Different from previous fact extraction and verification tasks that only consider evidence of a single format, FEVEROUS brings further challenges by extending the evidence format to both plain text and tables. Existing works convert all candidate evidence into either sentences or tables, thus often failing to fully capture the rich context in their original format from the converted evidence, let alone the context information lost during conversion. In this paper, we propose a Dual Channel Unified Format fact verification model (DCUF), which unifies various evidence into parallel streams, i.e., natural language sentences and a global evidence table, simultaneously. With carefully-designed evidence conversion and organization methods, DCUF makes the most of pre-trained table/language models to encourage each evidence piece to perform early and thorough interactions with other pieces in its original format. Experiments show that our model can make better use of existing pre-trained models to absorb evidence of two formats, thus outperforming previous works by a large margin. Our code and models are publicly available.

label: naacl
text: The FEVEROUS task brings new challenges to fact extraction and verification by considering evidence in both plain text and table formats. Previous works have failed to fully capture the rich context in the original format due to the conversion of evidence into either sentences or tables, resulting in the loss of context information. To address this issue, we propose the Dual Channel Unified Format (DCUF) fact verification model, which unifies various evidence into parallel streams - natural language sentences and a global evidence table. By utilizing carefully-designed evidence conversion and organization methods, DCUF leverages pre-trained table/language models to encourage each piece of evidence to interact with other pieces in its original format. Our experiments demonstrate that DCUF outperforms previous works by effectively utilizing pre-trained models to absorb evidence from both formats. Our code and models are publicly available.

label: coling
text: Driven by recent advances in neural networks, various Deep Embedding Clustering (DEC) based short text clustering models are being developed. In these works, latent representation learning and text clustering are performed simultaneously. Although these methods are becoming increasingly popular, they use pure cluster-oriented objectives, which can produce meaningless representations. To alleviate this problem, several improvements have been developed to introduce additional learning objectives in the clustering process, such as models based on contrastive learning. However, existing efforts rely heavily on learning meaningful representations at the instance level. They have limited focus on learning global representations, which are necessary to capture the overall data structure at the cluster level. In this paper, we propose a novel DEC model, which we named the deep embedded clustering model with cluster-level representation learning (DECCRL) to jointly learn cluster and instance level representations. Here, we extend the embedded topic modelling approach to introduce reconstruction constraints to help learn cluster-level representations. Experimental results on real-world short text datasets demonstrate that our model produces meaningful clusters.

label: coling
text: Advances in neural networks have led to the development of various Deep Embedding Clustering (DEC) models for short text clustering. These models perform latent representation learning and text clustering simultaneously, but they often rely on cluster-oriented objectives, which can result in meaningless representations. To address this issue, some models have been improved with additional learning objectives, such as contrastive learning. However, these efforts primarily focus on learning meaningful representations at the instance level, neglecting the importance of learning global representations, which are crucial for capturing the overall data structure at the cluster level. To address this gap, we propose a novel DEC model, the Deep Embedded Clustering Model with Cluster-Level Representation Learning (DECCRL), which jointly learns cluster- and instance-level representations. Our model extends the embedded topic modelling approach by introducing reconstruction constraints to help learn cluster-level representations. Our experiments on real-world short text datasets show that our model produces meaningful clusters.

label: acl
text: Natural language processing for sign language video—including tasks like recognition, translation, and search—is crucial for making artificial intelligence technologies accessible to deaf individuals, and is gaining research interest in recent years. In this paper, we address the problem of searching for fingerspelled keywords or key phrases in raw sign language videos. This is an important task since significant content in sign language is often conveyed via fingerspelling, and to our knowledge the task has not been studied before. We propose an end-to-end model for this task, FSS-Net, that jointly detects fingerspelling and matches it to a text sequence. Our experiments, done on a large public dataset of ASL fingerspelling in the wild, show the importance of fingerspelling detection as a component of a search and retrieval model. Our model significantly outperforms baseline methods adapted from prior work on related tasks.

label: acl
text: Natural language processing for sign language video, including recognition, translation, and search, is crucial for making artificial intelligence technologies accessible to the deaf community and has garnered increasing research interest in recent years. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of searching for fingerspelled keywords or phrases in raw sign language videos. This is a significant task as a significant portion of sign language content is often conveyed through fingerspelling and to the best of our knowledge, this task has not been explored previously. We present an end-to-end model, FSS-Net, that detects fingerspelling and matches it to a text sequence. Our experiments, conducted on a large public dataset of American Sign Language fingerspelling in real-world scenarios, highlight the importance of fingerspelling detection in a search and retrieval model. Our model outperforms baseline methods adapted from prior work on related tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness.

label: acl
text: Neural machine translation models are often biased toward the limited translation references seen during training. To amend this form of overfitting, in this paper we propose fine-tuning the models with a novel training objective based on the recently-proposed BERTScore evaluation metric. BERTScore is a scoring function based on contextual embeddings that overcomes the typical limitations of n-gram-based metrics (e.g. synonyms, paraphrases), allowing translations that are different from the references, yet close in the contextual embedding space, to be treated as substantially correct. To be able to use BERTScore as a training objective, we propose three approaches for generating soft predictions, allowing the network to remain completely differentiable end-to-end. Experiments carried out over four, diverse language pairs show improvements of up to 0.58 pp (3.28%) in BLEU score and up to 0.76 pp (0.98%) in BERTScore (F_BERT) when fine-tuning a strong baseline.

label: acl
text: Neural machine translation models tend to be biased towards the limited translation references seen during training, leading to overfitting. To address this issue, we propose a novel training objective in this paper, based on the recently proposed BERTScore evaluation metric. BERTScore is a scoring function that utilizes contextual embeddings, overcoming the limitations of n-gram-based metrics, such as synonyms and paraphrases. As a result, it allows for translations that are different from the references but close in the contextual embedding space to be considered substantially correct. To use BERTScore as a training objective, we propose three approaches for generating soft predictions, ensuring that the network remains completely differentiable end-to-end. Our experiments, conducted on four diverse language pairs, demonstrate improvements of up to 0.58 pp (3.28%) in BLEU score and up to 0.76 pp (0.98%) in BERTScore (F_BERT) when fine-tuning a strong baseline.

label: acl
text: We introduce a neural reading comprehension model that integrates external commonsense knowledge, encoded as a key-value memory, in a cloze-style setting. Instead of relying only on document-to-question interaction or discrete features as in prior work, our model attends to relevant external knowledge and combines this knowledge with the context representation before inferring the answer. This allows the model to attract and imply knowledge from an external knowledge source that is not explicitly stated in the text, but that is relevant for inferring the answer. Our model improves results over a very strong baseline on a hard Common Nouns dataset, making it a strong competitor of much more complex models. By including knowledge explicitly, our model can also provide evidence about the background knowledge used in the RC process.

label: acl
text: We present a neural reading comprehension model that integrates external commonsense knowledge as a key-value memory in a cloze-style setting. Unlike prior models that only relied on document-to-question interaction or discrete features, our model combines relevant external knowledge with the context representation to infer the answer. This enables the model to draw upon external knowledge that is not explicitly stated in the text but is still relevant for answering the question. Our model outperforms a strong baseline on a challenging Common Nouns dataset, making it a strong contender against more complex models. Additionally, by incorporating knowledge explicitly, our model provides insights into the background knowledge used in the RC process.

label: naacl
text: In this work, we present a hybrid learning method for training task-oriented dialogue systems through online user interactions. Popular methods for learning task-oriented dialogues include applying reinforcement learning with user feedback on supervised pre-training models. Efficiency of such learning method may suffer from the mismatch of dialogue state distribution between offline training and online interactive learning stages. To address this challenge, we propose a hybrid imitation and reinforcement learning method, with which a dialogue agent can effectively learn from its interaction with users by learning from human teaching and feedback. We design a neural network based task-oriented dialogue agent that can be optimized end-to-end with the proposed learning method. Experimental results show that our end-to-end dialogue agent can learn effectively from the mistake it makes via imitation learning from user teaching. Applying reinforcement learning with user feedback after the imitation learning stage further improves the agent's capability in successfully completing a task.

label: naacl
text: In this work, we introduce a hybrid learning method for training task-oriented dialogue systems through online user interactions. The common approach to learning task-oriented dialogues is to use reinforcement learning with user feedback on pre-trained supervised models. However, this method can be less effective due to the mismatch of dialogue state distribution between offline training and online interactive learning. To overcome this challenge, we propose a hybrid imitation and reinforcement learning method that allows the dialogue agent to effectively learn from user interactions by combining human teaching and feedback. Our neural network-based task-oriented dialogue agent can be optimized end-to-end using this method. Our results demonstrate that the end-to-end dialogue agent can effectively learn from its mistakes through imitation learning from user teaching. Additionally, reinforcement learning with user feedback after the imitation learning stage further improves the agent's ability to successfully complete a task.

label: acl
text: The process of translation is ambiguous, in that there are typically many valid translations for a given sentence. This gives rise to significant variation in parallel corpora, however, most current models of machine translation do not account for this variation, instead treating the problem as a deterministic process. To this end, we present a deep generative model of machine translation which incorporates a chain of latent variables, in order to account for local lexical and syntactic variation in parallel corpora. We provide an in-depth analysis of the pitfalls encountered in variational inference for training deep generative models. Experiments on several different language pairs demonstrate that the model consistently improves over strong baselines.

label: acl
text: The translation process is inherently ambiguous, as there are often multiple valid translations for a single sentence. This leads to significant disparities in parallel corpora. Despite this, most existing machine translation models do not consider this variation, instead treating the task as a deterministic process. To address this, we introduce a deep generative model that incorporates a series of latent variables to account for local lexical and syntactic variations in parallel corpora. We also examine the challenges faced during variational inference when training deep generative models. Our experiments on multiple language pairs show that the model consistently outperforms existing models.

label: acl
text: The cross-database context-dependent Text-to-SQL (XDTS) problem has attracted considerable attention in recent years due to its wide range of potential applications. However, we identify two biases in existing datasets for XDTS: (1) a high proportion of context-independent questions and (2) a high proportion of easy SQL queries. These biases conceal the major challenges in XDTS to some extent. In this work, we present Chase, a large-scale and pragmatic Chinese dataset for XDTS. It consists of 5,459 coherent question sequences (17,940 questions with their SQL queries annotated) over 280 databases, in which only 35% of questions are context-independent, and 28% of SQL queries are easy. We experiment on Chase with three state-of-the-art XDTS approaches. The best approach only achieves an exact match accuracy of 40% over all questions and 16% over all question sequences, indicating that Chase highlights the challenging problems of XDTS. We believe that XDTS can provide fertile soil for addressing the problems.

label: acl
text: The cross-database context-dependent Text-to-SQL (XDTS) problem has gained significant attention in recent years due to its broad range of potential applications. However, we have identified two biases in existing XDTS datasets: (1) a high proportion of context-independent questions and (2) a high proportion of simple SQL queries. These biases obscure the major challenges in the XDTS problem. To address this, we present Chase, a large-scale and practical Chinese dataset for XDTS. It includes 5,459 coherent question sequences (17,940 questions with annotated SQL queries) across 280 databases, with only 35% of questions being context-independent and 28% of SQL queries being simple. We tested three state-of-the-art XDTS approaches on Chase and found that the best approach only achieved an exact match accuracy of 40% for all questions and 16% for all question sequences, highlighting the challenging nature of XDTS. We believe that XDTS has the potential to provide a fertile ground for addressing these challenges.

label: naacl
text: Multi-triple extraction is a challenging task due to the existence of informative inter-triple correlations, and consequently rich interactions across the constituent entities and relations.While existing works only explore entity representations, we propose to explicitly introduce relation representation, jointly represent it with entities, and novelly align them to identify valid triples.We perform comprehensive experiments on document-level relation extraction and joint entity and relation extraction along with ablations to demonstrate the advantage of the proposed method.

label: naacl
text: The task of multi-triple extraction is challenging due to the presence of informative correlations between triples and complex interactions between entities and relations. Current approaches only focus on entity representation, but we introduce a novel method that incorporates relation representation and aligns entities and relations to identify accurate triples. Through extensive experiments on document-level relation extraction and joint entity and relation extraction, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method.

label: emnlp
text: We introduce a novel multi-source technique for incorporating source syntax into neural machine translation using linearized parses. This is achieved by employing separate encoders for the sequential and parsed versions of the same source sentence; the resulting representations are then combined using a hierarchical attention mechanism. The proposed model improves over both seq2seq and parsed baselines by over 1 BLEU on the WMT17 English-German task. Further analysis shows that our multi-source syntactic model is able to translate successfully without any parsed input, unlike standard parsed methods. In addition, performance does not deteriorate as much on long sentences as for the baselines.

label: emnlp
text: We present a new approach for incorporating source syntax into neural machine translation by using linearized parses. This is accomplished by utilizing separate encoders for the sequential and parsed versions of the source sentence, and then combining the representations through a hierarchical attention mechanism. Our proposed model outperforms both seq2seq and parsed baselines by more than 1 BLEU on the WMT17 English-German task. Further examination reveals that our multi-source syntactic model can translate effectively even without parsed input, in contrast to traditional parsed methods. Additionally, the performance of our model does not decline as significantly on long sentences compared to the baselines.

label: acl
text: Atomic clauses are fundamental text units for understanding complex sentences. Identifying the atomic sentences within complex sentences is important for applications such as summarization, argument mining, discourse analysis, discourse parsing, and question answering. Previous work mainly relies on rule-based methods dependent on parsing. We propose a new task to decompose each complex sentence into simple sentences derived from the tensed clauses in the source, and a novel problem formulation as a graph edit task. Our neural model learns to Accept, Break, Copy or Drop elements of a graph that combines word adjacency and grammatical dependencies. The full processing pipeline includes modules for graph construction, graph editing, and sentence generation from the output graph. We introduce DeSSE, a new dataset designed to train and evaluate complex sentence decomposition, and MinWiki, a subset of MinWikiSplit. ABCD achieves comparable performance as two parsing baselines on MinWiki. On DeSSE, which has a more even balance of complex sentence types, our model achieves higher accuracy on the number of atomic sentences than an encoder-decoder baseline. Results include a detailed error analysis.

label: acl
text: Atomic clauses are the fundamental building blocks for comprehending complex sentences. Identifying these atomic sentences within complex sentences is crucial for various applications, such as summarization, argument mining, discourse analysis, discourse parsing, and question answering. Most previous work has relied on rule-based methods that depend on parsing. This study proposes a new task of decomposing complex sentences into simple sentences derived from tense clauses in the source, using a novel problem formulation as a graph edit task. Our neural model is capable of accepting, breaking, copying, or dropping elements of a graph that combines word adjacency and grammatical dependencies. The full processing pipeline includes modules for graph construction, graph editing, and sentence generation from the output graph. We also introduce DeSSE, a new dataset designed for training and evaluating complex sentence decomposition, and MinWiki, a subset of MinWikiSplit. Our model, ABCD, performs comparably to two parsing baselines on MinWiki, and outperforms an encoder-decoder baseline on DeSSE, which has a more balanced distribution of complex sentence types. The results are accompanied by a comprehensive error analysis.

label: acl
text: While syntactic dependency annotations concentrate on the surface or functional structure of a sentence, semantic dependency annotations aim to capture between-word relationships that are more closely related to the meaning of a sentence, using graph-structured representations. We extend the LSTM-based syntactic parser of Dozat and Manning (2017) to train on and generate these graph structures. The resulting system on its own achieves state-of-the-art performance, beating the previous, substantially more complex state-of-the-art system by 0.6% labeled F1. Adding linguistically richer input representations pushes the margin even higher, allowing us to beat it by 1.9% labeled F1.

label: acl
text: The syntactic dependency annotations focus on the surface or functional structure of sentences, while semantic dependency annotations concentrate on capturing the relationships between words that are more closely related to the meaning of a sentence. To accomplish this, graph-structured representations are utilized. The LSTM-based syntactic parser of Dozat and Manning (2017) has been extended to train and generate these graph structures, resulting in a system that outperforms the previous state-of-the-art system by 0.6% labeled F1. By incorporating linguistically richer input representations, the system's performance is further improved, resulting in a 1.9% increase in labeled F1 over the previous state-of-the-art system.

label: coling
text: In aspect level sentiment classification, there are two common tasks: to identify the sentiment of an aspect (category) or a term. As specific instances of aspects, terms explicitly occur in sentences. It is beneficial for models to focus on nearby context words. In contrast, as high level semantic concepts of terms, aspects usually have more generalizable representations. However, conventional methods cannot utilize the information of aspects and terms at the same time, because few datasets are annotated with both aspects and terms. In this paper, we propose a novel deep memory network with auxiliary memory to address this problem. In our model, a main memory is used to capture the important context words for sentiment classification. In addition, we build an auxiliary memory to implicitly convert aspects and terms to each other, and feed both of them to the main memory. With the interaction between two memories, the features of aspects and terms can be learnt simultaneously. We compare our model with the state-of-the-art methods on four datasets from different domains. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

label: coling
text: In the field of aspect-level sentiment classification, there are two common tasks: identifying the sentiment of an aspect or term. Aspects are high-level semantic concepts that have generalizable representations, while terms are specific instances that explicitly occur in sentences. To focus on nearby context words, it is beneficial for models to consider both aspects and terms. However, conventional methods struggle to utilize both aspects and terms, as few datasets are annotated with both. To address this issue, we propose a novel deep memory network with an auxiliary memory. Our model uses a main memory to capture important context words for sentiment classification and an auxiliary memory to convert aspects and terms to each other. The interaction between the two memories allows for simultaneous learning of aspect and term features. Our model is compared to state-of-the-art methods on four datasets from different domains, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.

label: acl
text: Attention mechanisms have achieved substantial improvements in neural machine translation by dynamically selecting relevant inputs for different predictions. However, recent studies have questioned the attention mechanisms' capability for discovering decisive inputs. In this paper, we propose to calibrate the attention weights by introducing a mask perturbation model that automatically evaluates each input's contribution to the model outputs. We increase the attention weights assigned to the indispensable tokens, whose removal leads to a dramatic performance decrease. The extensive experiments on the Transformer-based translation have demonstrated the effectiveness of our model. We further find that the calibrated attention weights are more uniform at lower layers to collect multiple information while more concentrated on the specific inputs at higher layers. Detailed analyses also show a great need for calibration in the attention weights with high entropy where the model is unconfident about its decision.

label: acl

The proposed approach not only improves the model's performance but also provides a better interpretation of the attention mechanism.

Attention mechanisms have significantly improved neural machine translation by selecting relevant inputs for predictions. However, recent studies have questioned the ability of attention mechanisms to identify crucial inputs. In this paper, we propose a mask perturbation model to calibrate attention weights. This model automatically evaluates each input's contribution to the model outputs and increases the attention weights assigned to essential tokens, the removal of which leads to a significant decrease in performance. Our experiments on Transformer-based translation demonstrate the effectiveness of our model. We also found that the calibrated attention weights are more uniform at lower layers to gather multiple information, and more focused on specific inputs at higher layers. Analyses reveal a clear need for calibration in attention weights with high entropy, where the model is uncertain about its decision. Our proposed approach improves the model's performance and provides a better understanding of the attention mechanism.

label: coling
text: Supervised methods have achieved remarkable results in disfluency detection. However, in real-world scenarios, human-annotated data is difficult to obtain. Recent works try to handle disfluency detection with unsupervised self-training, which can exploit existing large-scale unlabeled data efficiently. However, their self-training-based methods suffer from the problems of selection bias and error accumulation. To tackle these problems, we propose an adaptive unsupervised self-training method for disfluency detection. Specifically, we re-weight the importance of each training example according to its grammatical feature and prediction confidence. Experiments on the Switchboard dataset show that our method improves 2.3 points over the current SOTA unsupervised method. Moreover, our method is competitive with the SOTA supervised method.

label: coling
text: Supervised methods have achieved considerable success in detecting disfluencies, but obtaining human-annotated data can be challenging in real-world scenarios. Recent studies have attempted to address this issue by using unsupervised self-training, which can effectively utilize large-scale unlabeled data. However, these methods face the challenges of selection bias and error accumulation. To overcome these limitations, we present an adaptive unsupervised self-training approach for disfluency detection. Our method re-weights the significance of each training example based on its grammatical features and prediction accuracy. Our experiments on the Switchboard dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art unsupervised method by 2.3 points and is comparable to the state-of-the-art supervised method.

label: acl
text: Dialogue State Tracking (DST) is primarily evaluated using Joint Goal Accuracy (JGA) defined as the fraction of turns where the ground-truth dialogue state exactly matches the prediction. Generally in DST, the dialogue state or belief state for a given turn contain all the intents shown by the user till that turn. Due to this cumulative nature of the belief state, it is difficult to get a correct prediction once a misprediction has occurred. Thus, although being a useful metric, it can be harsh at times and underestimate the true potential of a DST model. Moreover, an improvement in JGA can sometimes decrease the performance of turn-level or non-cumulative belief state prediction due to inconsistency in annotations. So, using JGA as the only metric for model selection may not be ideal for all scenarios. In this work, we discuss various evaluation metrics used for DST along with their shortcomings. To address the existing issues, we propose a new evaluation metric named Flexible Goal Accuracy (FGA). FGA is a generalized version of JGA. But unlike JGA, it tries to give penalized rewards to mispredictions that are locally correct i.e. the root cause of the error is an earlier turn. By doing so, FGA considers the performance of both cumulative and turn-level prediction flexibly and provides a better insight than the existing metrics. We also show that FGA is a better discriminator of DST model performance.

label: acl
text: Dialogue State Tracking (DST) is typically evaluated using Joint Goal Accuracy (JGA), which is defined as the fraction of turns where the ground-truth dialogue state exactly matches the prediction. However, this can be a harsh metric since the dialogue state or belief state for a given turn contains all the intents shown by the user up to that point. This cumulative nature of the belief state makes it challenging to get a correct prediction once a misprediction has occurred. As a result, JGA can sometimes underestimate the true potential of a DST model. Additionally, an improvement in JGA may not always lead to better performance in turn-level or non-cumulative belief state prediction because of inconsistencies in annotations. Therefore, relying solely on JGA for model selection may not be appropriate in all cases. In this work, we examine various evaluation metrics used for DST and their limitations. To address these issues, we propose a new evaluation metric called Flexible Goal Accuracy (FGA). FGA is a generalized version of JGA, but it provides penalized rewards for mispredictions that are locally correct, meaning the error is rooted in an earlier turn. This approach allows FGA to consider both cumulative and turn-level prediction performance more flexibly and provides a more comprehensive insight compared to existing metrics. We also demonstrate that FGA is a better discriminator of DST model performance.

label: coling
text: The difficulty of generating coherent long texts lies in the fact that existing models overwhelmingly focus on the tasks of local word prediction, and cannot make high level plans on what to generate or capture the high-level discourse dependencies between chunks of texts. Inspired by how humans write, where a list of bullet points or a catalog is first outlined, and then each bullet point is expanded to form the whole article, we propose SOE, a pipelined system that involves of summarizing, outlining and elaborating for long text generation: the model first outlines the summaries for different segments of long texts, and then elaborates on each bullet point to generate the corresponding segment. To avoid the labor-intensive process of summary soliciting, we propose the reconstruction strategy, which extracts segment summaries in an unsupervised manner by selecting its most informative part to reconstruct the segment. The proposed generation system comes with the following merits: (1) the summary provides high-level guidance for text generation and avoids the local minimum of individual word predictions; (2) the high-level discourse dependencies are captured in the conditional dependencies between summaries and are preserved during the summary expansion process and (3) additionally, we are able to consider significantly more contexts by representing contexts as concise summaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SOE produces long texts with significantly better quality, along with faster convergence speed.

label: coling
text: The challenge of producing coherent long texts lies in the fact that current models primarily focus on local word prediction, making it difficult to create high-level plans or capture the high-level discourse dependencies between text chunks. To address this issue, we propose SOE (Summarizing, Outlining, and Elaborating), a pipelined system that emulates the way humans write by first outlining bullet points or a catalog and then expanding each point to form the article. To avoid the time-consuming process of soliciting summaries, we introduce the reconstruction strategy, which extracts summaries in an unsupervised manner by selecting the most informative parts to reconstruct the segment. Our proposed system offers several advantages: (1) the summary provides high-level guidance for text generation, reducing the risk of local minimums; (2) high-level discourse dependencies are captured in the conditional dependencies between summaries and are maintained during the expansion process; and (3) by representing contexts as concise summaries, we can consider more contexts. Extensive experiments show that SOE produces high-quality long texts with faster convergence speeds.

label: coling
text: Social media based micro-blogging sites like Twitter have become a common source of real-time information (impacting organizations and their strategies, and are used for expressing emotions and opinions. Automated analysis of such content therefore rises in importance. To this end, we explore the viability of using deep neural networks on the specific task of emotion intensity prediction in tweets. We propose a neural architecture combining convolutional and fully connected layers in a non-sequential manner - done for the first time in context of natural language based tasks. Combined with lexicon-based features along with transfer learning, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the previous system by 0.044 or 4.4% Pearson correlation on the WASSA'17 EmoInt shared task dataset. We investigate the performance of deep multi-task learning models trained for all emotions at once in a unified architecture and get encouraging results. Experiments performed on evaluating correlation between emotion pairs offer interesting insights into the relationship between them.

As a result, the importance of automated analysis of such content is increasing. To this end, we have explored the feasibility of using deep neural networks for the task of predicting emotion intensity in tweets. Our proposed neural architecture, which combines convolutional and fully connected layers in a non-sequential manner, is a novel approach for natural language-based tasks. By incorporating lexicon-based features and transfer learning, our model achieved state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the previous system by 4.4% Pearson correlation on the WASSA'17 EmoInt shared task dataset. Our investigation of deep multi-task learning models trained for all emotions simultaneously in a unified architecture has produced encouraging results. Our experiments evaluating the correlation between emotion pairs provide insightful observations into the relationship between them.
