label: emnlp
text: Automated Post-Editing (PE) is the task of automatically correct common and repetitive errors found in machine translation (MT) output. In this paper, we present a neural programmer-interpreter approach to this task, resembling the way that human perform post-editing using discrete edit operations, wich we refer to as programs. Our model outperforms previous neural models for inducing PE programs on the WMT17 APE task for German-English up to +1 BLEU score and -0.7 TER scores.

label: emnlp
text: Automated Post-Editing (PE) involves automatically correcting common and repetitive errors in machine translation (MT) outputs. This paper presents a novel neural programmer-interpreter approach to PE that mimics the way humans perform post-editing by using discrete edit operations, referred to as programs. Our model outperforms previous neural models for inducing PE programs in the WMT17 APE task for German-English, yielding an improvement of up to +1 BLEU score and a reduction of -0.7 TER scores.

label: acl
text: Generating metaphors is a difficult task as it requires understanding nuanced relationships between abstract concepts. In this paper, we aim to generate a metaphoric sentence given a literal expression by replacing relevant verbs. Guided by conceptual metaphor theory, we propose to control the generation process by encoding conceptual mappings between cognitive domains to generate meaningful metaphoric expressions. To achieve this, we develop two methods: 1) using FrameNet-based embeddings to learn mappings between domains and applying them at the lexical level (CM-Lex), and 2) deriving source/target pairs to train a controlled seq-to-seq generation model (CM-BART). We assess our methods through automatic and human evaluation for basic metaphoricity and conceptual metaphor presence. We show that the unsupervised CM-Lex model is competitive with recent deep learning metaphor generation systems, and CM-BART outperforms all other models both in automatic and human evaluations.

label: acl
text: Generating metaphors can be a challenging task as it demands a deep understanding of the nuanced relationships between abstract concepts. This paper endeavors to create a metaphoric sentence from a literal expression by replacing relevant verbs. Our approach is guided by the conceptual metaphor theory, and we aim to control the generation process by encoding the conceptual mappings between cognitive domains. To achieve this goal, we have developed two methods - 1) using FrameNet-based embeddings to learn the mappings between domains and apply them at the lexical level (CM-Lex), and 2) deriving source/target pairs to train a controlled seq-to-seq generation model (CM-BART). The effectiveness of our methods was evaluated through automatic and human evaluations, assessing basic metaphoricity and the presence of conceptual metaphors. Our results indicate that the unsupervised CM-Lex model is comparable to recent deep learning metaphor generation systems, while CM-BART outperforms all other models in both automatic and human evaluations.

label: acl
text: We pioneer the first extractive summarization-based collaborative filtering model called ESCOFILT. Our proposed model specifically produces extractive summaries for each item and user. Unlike other types of explanations, summary-level explanations closely resemble real-life explanations. The strength of ESCOFILT lies in the fact that it unifies representation and explanation. In other words, extractive summaries both represent and explain the items and users. Our model uniquely integrates BERT, K-Means embedding clustering, and multilayer perceptron to learn sentence embeddings, representation-explanations, and user-item interactions, respectively. We argue that our approach enhances both rating prediction accuracy and user/item explainability. Our experiments illustrate that ESCOFILT's prediction accuracy is better than the other state-of-the-art recommender models. Furthermore, we propose a comprehensive set of criteria that assesses the real-life explainability of explanations. Our explainability study demonstrates the superiority of and preference for summary-level explanations over other explanation types.

label: acl
text: We have introduced the first extractive summarization-based collaborative filtering model, called ESCOFILT, which produces extractive summaries for each item and user. Unlike other explanation types, these summary-level explanations closely resemble real-life explanations. The strength of ESCOFILT lies in its ability to unify representation and explanation, as the extractive summaries both represent and explain the items and users. The model integrates BERT, K-Means embedding clustering, and multilayer perceptron to learn sentence embeddings, representation-explanations, and user-item interactions, respectively. Our experiments show that ESCOFILT outperforms state-of-the-art recommender models in terms of rating prediction accuracy and user/item explainability. We have also proposed a comprehensive set of criteria for assessing the real-life explainability of explanations, and our study demonstrates the superiority and preference for summary-level explanations over other explanation types.

label: acl
text: Misinformation has recently become a well-documented matter of public concern. Existing studies on this topic have hitherto adopted a coarse concept of misinformation, which incorporates a broad spectrum of story types ranging from political conspiracies to misinterpreted pranks. This paper aims to structurize these misinformation stories by leveraging fact-check articles. Our intuition is that key phrases in a fact-check article that identify the misinformation type(s) (e.g., doctored images, urban legends) also act as rationales that determine the verdict of the fact-check (e.g., false). We experiment on rationalized models with domain knowledge as weak supervision to extract these phrases as rationales, and then cluster semantically similar rationales to summarize prevalent misinformation types. Using archived fact-checks from Snopes.com, we identify ten types of misinformation stories. We discuss how these types have evolved over the last ten years and compare their prevalence between the 2016/2020 US presidential elections and the H1N1/COVID-19 pandemics.

label: acl
text: Recently, misinformation has become a widely recognized issue of public concern. Previous studies on this topic have used a broad definition of misinformation, which encompasses a range of story types, including political conspiracies and misinterpreted pranks. This paper seeks to categorize these misinformation stories by utilizing fact-check articles. Our hypothesis is that key phrases in these articles that identify the type of misinformation (such as doctored images or urban legends) also serve as the basis for the fact-check verdict (e.g., false). We test this hypothesis by using domain knowledge as weak supervision to extract these key phrases and then clustering similar phrases to summarize the prevalent types of misinformation. Our analysis of archived fact-checks from Snopes.com identifies ten types of misinformation stories. We examine how these types have evolved over the past ten years and compare their prevalence during the 2016/2020 US presidential elections and the H1N1/COVID-19 pandemics.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based models are widely used in natural language understanding (NLU) tasks, and multimodal transformers have been effective in visual-language tasks. This study explores distilling visual information from pretrained multimodal transformers to pretrained language encoders. Our framework is inspired by cross-modal encoders' success in visual-language tasks while we alter the learning objective to cater to the language-heavy characteristics of NLU. After training with a small number of extra adapting steps and finetuned, the proposed XDBERT (cross-modal distilled BERT) outperforms pretrained-BERT in general language understanding evaluation (GLUE), situations with adversarial generations (SWAG) benchmarks, and readability benchmarks. We analyze the performance of XDBERT on GLUE to show that the improvement is likely visually grounded.

label: acl
text: Transformers-based models are widely utilized in natural language understanding (NLU) tasks and have proven to be effective in visual-language tasks, particularly with the use of multimodal transformers. In this study, we investigate the potential of distilling visual information from pre-trained multimodal transformers to pre-trained language encoders. Our framework is inspired by the success of cross-modal encoders in visual-language tasks, but with a modified learning objective to align with the language-heavy characteristics of NLU. Upon training with a small number of additional adaptation steps and fine-tuning, our proposed XDBERT (cross-modal distilled BERT) outperforms pre-trained BERT in various language understanding evaluations, including the GLUE, SWAG, and readability benchmarks. Our analysis of XDBERT's performance on GLUE suggests that the improvement is likely due to its visually grounded nature.

label: acl
text: We propose to measure fine-grained domain relevance– the degree that a term is relevant to a broad (e.g., computer science) or narrow (e.g., deep learning) domain. Such measurement is crucial for many downstream tasks in natural language processing. To handle long-tail terms, we build a core-anchored semantic graph, which uses core terms with rich description information to bridge the vast remaining fringe terms semantically. To support a fine-grained domain without relying on a matching corpus for supervision, we develop hierarchical core-fringe learning, which learns core and fringe terms jointly in a semi-supervised manner contextualized in the hierarchy of the domain. To reduce expensive human efforts, we employ automatic annotation and hierarchical positive-unlabeled learning. Our approach applies to big or small domains, covers head or tail terms, and requires little human effort. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods outperform strong baselines and even surpass professional human performance.

label: acl
text: We propose to measure fine-grained domain relevance, which refers to the extent to which a term is relevant to a broad (e.g. computer science) or narrow (e.g. deep learning) domain. This measurement is crucial for various natural language processing tasks. To tackle the issue of long-tail terms, we construct a core-anchored semantic graph that utilizes core terms with comprehensive descriptions to semantically link the vast array of fringe terms. To achieve fine-grained domain relevance without relying on a matching corpus for supervision, we introduce hierarchical core-fringe learning. This method allows for the joint learning of core and fringe terms in a semi-supervised manner, contextualized within the hierarchy of the domain. To minimize the need for manual annotation, we implement automatic annotation and hierarchical positive-unlabeled learning. Our approach is applicable to both big and small domains, covers head and tail terms, and requires minimal human effort. Experiments show that our methods outperform strong baselines and even surpass professional human performance.

text: Event extraction (EE) is one of the fundamental tasks for information extraction whose goal is to identify mentions of events and their participants in text. Due to its importance, different methods and datasets have been introduced for EE. However, existing EE datasets are limited to formally written documents such as news articles or scientific papers. As such, the challenges of EE in informal and noisy texts are not adequately studied. In particular, video transcripts constitute an important domain that can benefit tremendously from EE systems (e.g., video retrieval), but has not been studied in EE literature due to the lack of necessary datasets. To address this limitation, we propose the first large-scale EE dataset obtained for transcripts of streamed videos on the video hosting platform Behance to promote future research in this area. In addition, we extensively evaluate existing state-of-the-art EE methods on our new dataset. We demonstrate that such systems cannot achieve adequate performance on the proposed dataset, revealing challenges and opportunities for further research effort.

label: coling
text: Event extraction (EE) is a crucial task in information extraction that aims to identify mentions of events and their participants in text. Despite the numerous methods and datasets introduced for EE, existing datasets are limited to formally written documents such as news articles or scientific papers. This means that the challenges of EE in informal and noisy texts, such as video transcripts, have not been adequately studied. To address this gap, we introduce the first large-scale EE dataset for video transcripts from the video hosting platform Behance. Our dataset will enable future research in this area and we extensively evaluate existing state-of-the-art EE methods to demonstrate the challenges and opportunities for further research.

text: The billions, and sometimes even trillions, of parameters involved in pre-trained language models significantly hamper their deployment in resource-constrained devices and real-time applications. Knowledge distillation (KD) can transfer knowledge from the original model (i.e., teacher) into a compact model (i.e., student) to achieve model compression. However, previous KD methods have usually frozen the teacher and applied its immutable output feature maps as soft labels to guide the student's training. Moreover, the goal of the teacher is to achieve the best performance on downstream tasks rather than knowledge transfer. Such a fixed architecture may limit the teacher's teaching and student's learning abilities. Herein, a knowledge distillation method with reptile meta-learning is proposed to facilitate the transfer of knowledge from the teacher to the student. The teacher can continuously meta-learn the student's learning objective to adjust its parameters for maximizing the student's performance throughout the distillation process. In this way, the teacher learns to teach, produces more suitable soft labels, and transfers more appropriate knowledge to the student, resulting in improved performance. Unlike previous KD using meta-learning, the proposed method only needs to calculate the first-order derivatives to update the teacher, leading to lower computational cost but better convergence. Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark show the competitive performance achieved by the proposed method. For reproducibility, the code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/maxinge8698/ReptileDistil.

label: coling
text: The vast number of parameters in pre-trained language models often hinders their use in resource-limited devices and real-time applications. To address this issue, a technique called Knowledge Distillation (KD) is used to transfer knowledge from the original model (teacher) to a smaller model (student). However, conventional KD methods have a fixed architecture, which limits the teacher's ability to teach and the student's ability to learn. A new KD method that incorporates Reptile meta-learning has been proposed to improve the transfer of knowledge from the teacher to the student. The teacher continuously updates its parameters to maximize the student's performance, resulting in improved performance and more appropriate knowledge transfer. The proposed method is computationally more efficient and has better convergence compared to previous KD methods using meta-learning. The results of experiments on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate the competitiveness of the proposed method. The code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/maxinge8698/ReptileDistil.

label: acl
text: Training language models for Code-mixed (CM) language is known to be a difficult problem because of lack of data compounded by the increased confusability due to the presence of more than one language. We present a computational technique for creation of grammatically valid artificial CM data based on the Equivalence Constraint Theory. We show that when training examples are sampled appropriately from this synthetic data and presented in certain order (aka training curriculum) along with monolingual and real CM data, it can significantly reduce the perplexity of an RNN-based language model. We also show that randomly generated CM data does not help in decreasing the perplexity of the LMs.

text: Training language models for code-mixed languages is a challenging task due to the scarcity of data and the increased confusion caused by the presence of multiple languages. To address this issue, we propose a computational approach for generating grammatically valid artificial code-mixed data based on the Equivalence Constraint Theory. Our results demonstrate that when the synthetic data is combined with monolingual and real code-mixed data in a specific training curriculum, it can significantly reduce the perplexity of an RNN-based language model. However, randomly generated code-mixed data does not have the same impact on reducing perplexity.

label: coling
text: Incorporating information from other languages can improve the results of tasks in low-resource languages. A powerful method of building functional natural language processing systems for low-resource languages is to combine multilingual pre-trained representations with cross-lingual transfer learning. In general, however, shared representations are learned separately, either across tasks or across languages. This paper proposes a meta-learning approach for inferring natural language in Persian. Alternately, meta-learning uses different task information (such as QA in Persian) or other language information (such as natural language inference in English). Also, we investigate the role of task augmentation strategy for forming additional high-quality tasks. We evaluate the proposed method using four languages and an auxiliary task. Compared to the baseline approach, the proposed model consistently outperforms it, improving accuracy by roughly six percent. We also examine the effect of finding appropriate initial parameters using zero-shot evaluation and CCA similarity.

text: In computational psycholinguistics, various language models have been evaluated against human reading behavior (e.g., eye movement) to build human-like computational models. However, most previous efforts have focused almost exclusively on English, despite the recent trend towards linguistic universal within the general community. In order to fill the gap, this paper investigates whether the established results in computational psycholinguistics can be generalized across languages. Specifically, we re-examine an established generalization —the lower perplexity a language model has, the more human-like the language model is— in Japanese with typologically different structures from English. Our experiments demonstrate that this established generalization exhibits a surprising lack of universality; namely, lower perplexity is not always human-like. Moreover, this discrepancy between English and Japanese is further explored from the perspective of (non-)uniform information density. Overall, our results suggest that a cross-lingual evaluation will be necessary to construct human-like computational models.

text: In computational psycholinguistics, researchers have evaluated various language models against human reading behavior, such as eye movements, to develop human-like computational models. However, most previous studies have focused almost solely on English, despite the increasing trend towards linguistic universality in the field. To address this gap, this paper investigates the generalizability of established results in computational psycholinguistics across languages. Specifically, we re-examine the established notion that a lower perplexity in a language model leads to a more human-like model in Japanese, which has typologically different structures from English. Our experiments reveal that this established generalization lacks universality, as lower perplexity does not always result in a human-like language model. Furthermore, we explore the discrepancy between English and Japanese from the perspective of non-uniform information density. In conclusion, our results highlight the need for cross-lingual evaluations to construct human-like computational models.

text: Automatic medical question summarization can significantly help the system to understand consumer health questions and retrieve correct answers. The Seq2Seq model based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) has been applied in this task, which faces two general problems: the model can not capture well question focus and and the traditional MLE strategy lacks the ability to understand sentence-level semantics. To alleviate these problems, we propose a novel question focus-driven contrastive learning framework (QFCL). Specially, we propose an easy and effective approach to generate hard negative samples based on the question focus, and exploit contrastive learning at both encoder and decoder to obtain better sentence level representations. On three medical benchmark datasets, our proposed model achieves new state-of-the-art results, and obtains a performance gain of 5.33, 12.85 and 3.81 points over the baseline BART model on three datasets respectively. Further human judgement and detailed analysis prove that our QFCL model learns better sentence representations with the ability to distinguish different sentence meanings, and generates high-quality summaries by capturing question focus.

label: coling
text: The proposed QFCL framework can significantly improve the automatic medical question summarization system by helping it to understand consumer health questions and retrieve accurate answers. The Seq2Seq model, which is based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), has been applied to this task, but it faces two main challenges: the model struggles to capture the question focus and the traditional MLE strategy lacks the ability to understand sentence-level semantics. To address these issues, we introduce a novel question focus-driven contrastive learning framework. Our approach involves generating hard negative samples based on the question focus and utilizing contrastive learning at both the encoder and decoder levels to enhance sentence-level representations. Our model outperforms the baseline BART model on three medical benchmark datasets, achieving a performance increase of 5.33, 12.85, and 3.81 points, respectively. Further evaluation and analysis reveal that our QFCL model effectively learns sentence representations that can distinguish between different meanings and generates high-quality summaries by capturing the question focus.

label: emnlp
text: Abstractive text summarization aims to shorten long text documents into a human readable form that contains the most important facts from the original document. However, the level of actual abstraction as measured by novel phrases that do not appear in the source document remains low in existing approaches. We propose two techniques to improve the level of abstraction of generated summaries. First, we decompose the decoder into a contextual network that retrieves relevant parts of the source document, and a pretrained language model that incorporates prior knowledge about language generation. Second, we propose a novelty metric that is optimized directly through policy learning to encourage the generation of novel phrases. Our model achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art models, as determined by ROUGE scores and human evaluations, while achieving a significantly higher level of abstraction as measured by n-gram overlap with the source document.

label: emnlp
text: The aim of abstractive text summarization is to condense long text documents into a concise and readable form that highlights the most important information. However, existing approaches have a low level of abstraction, as evidenced by the limited use of novel phrases not found in the source document. To improve the level of abstraction, we introduce two techniques. Firstly, we divide the decoder into a contextual network that identifies relevant parts of the source document and a pre-trained language model that leverages prior knowledge of language generation. Secondly, we develop a novelty metric that is optimized through policy learning to encourage the creation of novel phrases. Our model performs similarly to state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated by ROUGE scores and human evaluations, while also achieving a significantly higher level of abstraction, as indicated by a reduced n-gram overlap with the source document.

label: acl
text: Recent studies have determined that the learned token embeddings of large-scale neural language models are degenerated to be anisotropic with a narrow-cone shape. This phenomenon, called the representation degeneration problem, facilitates an increase in the overall similarity between token embeddings that negatively affect the performance of the models. Although the existing methods that address the degeneration problem based on observations of the phenomenon triggered by the problem improves the performance of the text generation, the training dynamics of token embeddings behind the degeneration problem are still not explored. In this study, we analyze the training dynamics of the token embeddings focusing on rare token embedding. We demonstrate that the specific part of the gradient for rare token embeddings is the key cause of the degeneration problem for all tokens during training stage. Based on the analysis, we propose a novel method called, adaptive gradient gating(AGG). AGG addresses the degeneration problem by gating the specific part of the gradient for rare token embeddings. Experimental results from language modeling, word similarity, and machine translation tasks quantitatively and qualitatively verify the effectiveness of AGG.

label: acl
text: Recent studies have found that the token embeddings learned by large-scale neural language models tend to be anisotropic with a narrow-cone shape, a phenomenon known as the representation degeneration problem. This problem leads to increased similarity between token embeddings, hindering the performance of the models. Although current methods that address the degeneration problem improve text generation performance, the underlying training dynamics of token embeddings have not been fully explored. In this study, we focus on the training dynamics of rare token embeddings and find that a specific part of the gradient is the key cause of the degeneration problem for all tokens. To address this, we propose a new method called adaptive gradient gating (AGG), which gates the specific part of the gradient for rare token embeddings. Our experiments in language modeling, word similarity, and machine translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of AGG, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

label: emnlp
text: Generating the English transliteration of a name written in a foreign script is an important and challenging step in multilingual knowledge acquisition and information extraction. Existing approaches to transliteration generation require a large (5000) number of training examples. This difficulty contrasts with transliteration discovery, a somewhat easier task that involves picking a plausible transliteration from a given list. In this work, we present a bootstrapping algorithm that uses constrained discovery to improve generation, and can be used with as few as 500 training examples, which we show can be sourced from annotators in a matter of hours. This opens the task to languages for which large number of training examples are unavailable. We evaluate transliteration generation performance itself, as well the improvement it brings to cross-lingual candidate generation for entity linking, a typical downstream task. We present a comprehensive evaluation of our approach on nine languages, each written in a unique script.

label: emnlp
text: Generating the English transliteration of a foreign script name is a crucial and challenging aspect of multilingual knowledge acquisition and information extraction. The existing transliteration generation methods require a large number of training examples, typically 5000. This is in contrast to the easier task of transliteration discovery, which involves selecting a plausible transliteration from a given list. This study presents a bootstrapping algorithm that leverages constrained discovery to improve generation and can be used with as few as 500 training examples, which can be quickly obtained from annotators. This makes it possible to apply the method to languages for which large training examples are not available. The evaluation of the transliteration generation performance, as well as the improvement it brings to cross-lingual candidate generation for entity linking, a common downstream task, is presented for nine languages written in unique scripts.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based pre-trained models, such as BERT, have shown extraordinary success in achieving state-of-the-art results in many natural language processing applications. However, deploying these models can be prohibitively costly, as the standard self-attention mechanism of the Transformer suffers from quadratic computational cost in the input sequence length. To confront this, we propose FCA, a fine- and coarse-granularity hybrid self-attention that reduces the computation cost through progressively shortening the computational sequence length in self-attention. Specifically, FCA conducts an attention-based scoring strategy to determine the informativeness of tokens at each layer. Then, the informative tokens serve as the fine-granularity computing units in self-attention and the uninformative tokens are replaced with one or several clusters as the coarse-granularity computing units in self-attention. Experiments on the standard GLUE benchmark show that BERT with FCA achieves 2x reduction in FLOPs over original BERT with 1% loss in accuracy. We show that FCA offers a significantly better trade-off between accuracy and FLOPs compared to prior methods.

text: Transformer-based pre-trained models, such as BERT, have demonstrated exceptional success in various natural language processing applications, with state-of-the-art results. However, deploying these models can be challenging as the standard self-attention mechanism of the Transformer incurs quadratic computational cost, proportional to the input sequence length. To address this issue, we introduce FCA, a hybrid self-attention mechanism that combines fine- and coarse-granularity attention, reducing computation cost by shortening the sequence length in self-attention. FCA employs an attention-based scoring strategy to evaluate the informativeness of tokens at each layer, using the most informative tokens for fine-granularity computing and replacing less informative tokens with one or several clusters for coarse-granularity computing. Our experiments on the GLUE benchmark show that BERT with FCA reduces FLOPs by 2x compared to the original BERT, with a mere 1% drop in accuracy. FCA provides a superior trade-off between accuracy and FLOPs compared to existing methods.

label: acl
text: Most studies on word-level Quality Estimation (QE) of machine translation focus on language-specific models. The obvious disadvantages of these approaches are the need for labelled data for each language pair and the high cost required to maintain several language-specific models. To overcome these problems, we explore different approaches to multilingual, word-level QE. We show that multilingual QE models perform on par with the current language-specific models. In the cases of zero-shot and few-shot QE, we demonstrate that it is possible to accurately predict word-level quality for any given new language pair from models trained on other language pairs. Our findings suggest that the word-level QE models based on powerful pre-trained transformers that we propose in this paper generalise well across languages, making them more useful in real-world scenarios.

text: Most studies in the field of word-level Quality Estimation (QE) for machine translation concentrate on language-specific models. To address these issues, we investigate alternative approaches to multilingual, word-level QE. Our results reveal that multilingual QE models perform similarly to current language-specific models. Additionally, in cases of zero-shot and few-shot QE, we prove that it is possible to predict word-level quality for new language pairs accurately using models trained on other language pairs. Our findings indicate that the word-level QE models based on pre-trained transformers that we propose in this paper generalize well across languages, making them more practical for real-world applications.

text: We study German affixoids, a type of morpheme in between affixes and free stems. Several properties have been associated with them – increased productivity; a bleached semantics, which is often evaluative and/or intensifying and thus of relevance to sentiment analysis; and the existence of a free morpheme counterpart – but not been validated empirically. In experiments on a new data set that we make available, we put these key assumptions from the morphological literature to the test and show that despite the fact that affixoids generate many low-frequency formations, we can classify these as affixoid or non-affixoid instances with a best F1-score of 74%.

label: coling
text: We investigate German affixoids, which are morphemes that occupy a position between affixes and free stems. These affixoids have been attributed various properties, such as increased productivity, a bleached semantics that often has evaluative and intensifying qualities relevant to sentiment analysis, and the presence of a free morpheme counterpart. However, these properties have yet to be empirically validated. Through experiments on a newly created data set, we test these central assumptions from the morphological literature and demonstrate that despite the prevalence of low-frequency formations generated by affixoids, we can accurately classify them as affixoid or non-affixoid instances with a maximum F1-score of 74%.

text: Identifying emergent research trends is a key issue for both primary researchers as well as secondary research managers. Such processes can uncover the historical development of an area, and yield insight on developing topics. We propose an embedded trend detection framework for this task which incorporates our bijunctive hypothesis that important phrases are written by important authors within a field and vice versa. By ranking both author and phrase information in a multigraph, our method jointly determines key phrases and authoritative authors. We represent this intermediate output as phrasal embeddings, and feed this to a recurrent neural network (RNN) to compute trend scores that identify research trends. Over two large datasets of scientific articles, we demonstrate that our approach successfully detects past trends from the field, outperforming baselines based solely on text centrality or citation.

text: To effectively identify emerging research trends, it is crucial for both primary researchers and secondary research managers. This process enables the examination of an area's historical development and provides insight into developing topics. We have developed an innovative framework for trend detection that incorporates our bijunctive hypothesis that important phrases are written by important authors within a field and vice versa. Our method ranks both author and phrase information in a multigraph, jointly determining key phrases and authoritative authors. The intermediate output is represented as phrasal embeddings and fed into a recurrent neural network (RNN) to compute trend scores, thereby identifying research trends. Through testing on two large datasets of scientific articles, our approach was proven to be successful in detecting past trends from the field, outperforming baselines that rely solely on text centrality or citation.

label: acl
text: Crowdsourcing is widely used to create data for common natural language understanding tasks. Despite the importance of these datasets for measuring and refining model understanding of language, there has been little focus on the crowdsourcing methods used for collecting the datasets. In this paper, we compare the efficacy of interventions that have been proposed in prior work as ways of improving data quality. We use multiple-choice question answering as a testbed and run a randomized trial by assigning crowdworkers to write questions under one of four different data collection protocols. We find that asking workers to write explanations for their examples is an ineffective stand-alone strategy for boosting NLU example difficulty. However, we find that training crowdworkers, and then using an iterative process of collecting data, sending feedback, and qualifying workers based on expert judgments is an effective means of collecting challenging data. But using crowdsourced, instead of expert judgments, to qualify workers and send feedback does not prove to be effective. We observe that the data from the iterative protocol with expert assessments is more challenging by several measures. Notably, the human–model gap on the unanimous agreement portion of this data is, on average, twice as large as the gap for the baseline protocol data.

label: acl
text: Crowdsourcing is a widely used method for creating data for natural language understanding tasks. However, there has been a lack of focus on the crowdsourcing methods used to collect these datasets, which are crucial for measuring and refining model understanding of language. This paper compares the efficacy of various interventions aimed at improving data quality. We test these interventions by assigning crowdworkers to write questions under one of four different data collection protocols, using multiple-choice question answering as a testbed. Our results show that asking workers to write explanations for their examples is not an effective way to increase the difficulty of natural language understanding examples. However, we find that training crowdworkers and using an iterative process of data collection, feedback, and worker qualification based on expert judgments is an effective method of collecting challenging data. On the other hand, using crowdsourced assessments instead of expert judgments to qualify workers and provide feedback does not prove to be effective. Our findings indicate that the data collected through the iterative protocol with expert assessments is more challenging, with the human-model gap on the unanimous agreement portion of this data being, on average, twice as large as the gap for the baseline protocol data.

text: Distance based knowledge graph embedding methods show promising results on link prediction task, on which two topics have been widely studied: one is the ability to handle complex relations, such as N-to-1, 1-to-N and N-to-N, the other is to encode various relation patterns, such as symmetry/antisymmetry. However, the existing methods fail to solve these two problems at the same time, which leads to unsatisfactory results. To mitigate this problem, we propose PairRE, a model with paired vectors for each relation representation. The paired vectors enable an adaptive adjustment of the margin in loss function to fit for different complex relations. Besides, PairRE is capable of encoding three important relation patterns, symmetry/antisymmetry, inverse and composition. Given simple constraints on relation representations, PairRE can encode subrelation further. Experiments on link prediction benchmarks demonstrate the proposed key capabilities of PairRE. Moreover, We set a new state-of-the-art on two knowledge graph datasets of the challenging Open Graph Benchmark.

text: Distance-based knowledge graph embedding methods have shown promising results in link prediction tasks, with two areas of focus: handling complex relationships, such as N-to-1, 1-to-N, and N-to-N, and encoding various relation patterns, such as symmetry and antisymmetry. However, current methods struggle to address both challenges simultaneously, resulting in subpar performance. To overcome this issue, we introduce PairRE, a model that utilizes paired vectors to represent each relation. The paired vectors allow for an adaptive adjustment of the margin in the loss function, making it suitable for complex relationships. Additionally, PairRE can encode three important relation patterns: symmetry/antisymmetry, inverse, and composition. By imposing simple constraints on relation representations, PairRE can even encode subrelations. Our experiments on link prediction benchmarks showcase the effectiveness of PairRE, setting a new state-of-the-art on two knowledge graph datasets from the challenging Open Graph Benchmark.

label: emnlp
text: We present a data set for evaluating the grammaticality of the predictions of a language model. We automatically construct a large number of minimally different pairs of English sentences, each consisting of a grammatical and an ungrammatical sentence. The sentence pairs represent different variations of structure-sensitive phenomena: subject-verb agreement, reflexive anaphora and negative polarity items. We expect a language model to assign a higher probability to the grammatical sentence than the ungrammatical one. In an experiment using this data set, an LSTM language model performed poorly on many of the constructions. Multi-task training with a syntactic objective (CCG supertagging) improved the LSTM's accuracy, but a large gap remained between its performance and the accuracy of human participants recruited online. This suggests that there is considerable room for improvement over LSTMs in capturing syntax in a language model.

label: emnlp
text: We present a dataset designed to evaluate the grammaticality of language model predictions. This dataset is constructed automatically and features a large number of minimally different pairs of English sentences, each consisting of a grammatically correct sentence and an ungrammatical one. These sentence pairs showcase variations of structure-sensitive phenomena, including subject-verb agreement, reflexive anaphora, and negative polarity items. The goal is for the language model to assign a higher probability to the grammatically correct sentence than the ungrammatical one. Our experiment using this dataset revealed that an LSTM language model performed poorly on many of the constructions. Although multi-task training with a syntactic objective (CCG supertagging) improved the LSTM's accuracy, a significant gap still remained between its performance and the accuracy of human participants recruited online. This highlights the need for further improvements in capturing syntax in language models beyond LSTMs.

label: acl
text: Humans often refer to personal narratives, life experiences, and events to make a conversation more engaging and rich. While persona-grounded dialog models are able to generate responses that follow a given persona, they often miss out on stating detailed experiences or events related to a persona, often leaving conversations shallow and dull. In this work, we equip dialog models with `background stories' related to a persona by leveraging fictional narratives from existing story datasets (e.g. ROCStories). Since current dialog datasets do not contain such narratives as responses, we perform an unsupervised adaptation of a retrieved story for generating a dialog response using a gradient-based rewriting technique. Our proposed method encourages the generated response to be fluent (i.e., highly likely) with the dialog history, minimally different from the retrieved story to preserve event ordering and consistent with the original persona. We demonstrate that our method can generate responses that are more diverse, and are rated more engaging and human-like by human evaluators, compared to outputs from existing dialog models.

label: acl
text: Humans often use personal narratives, life experiences, and events to make conversations more engaging and rich. However, persona-based dialog models, which generate responses based on a given persona, often miss out on including detailed experiences or events. To address this issue, we equip dialog models with `background stories' related to a persona by using fictional narratives from story datasets such as ROCStories. We perform an unsupervised adaptation of a retrieved story to generate a dialog response, using a gradient-based rewriting technique. Our method ensures that the generated response is fluent, minimally different from the retrieved story, and consistent with the original persona. Our results show that our method generates more diverse and engaging responses that are rated as more human-like by human evaluators, compared to existing dialog models.

label: coling
text: Using prompts to utilize language models to perform various downstream tasks, also known as prompt-based learning or prompt-learning, has lately gained significant success in comparison to the pre-train and fine-tune paradigm. Nonetheless, virtually most prompt-based methods are token-level such as PET based on mask language model (MLM). In this paper, we attempt to accomplish several NLP tasks in the zero-shot and few-shot scenarios using a BERT original pre-training task abandoned by RoBERTa and other models——Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). Unlike token-level techniques, our sentence-level prompt-based method NSP-BERT does not need to fix the length of the prompt or the position to be predicted, allowing it to handle tasks such as entity linking with ease. NSP-BERT can be applied to a variety of tasks based on its properties. We present an NSP-tuning approach with binary cross-entropy loss for single-sentence classification tasks that is competitive compared to PET and EFL. By continuing to train BERT on RoBERTa's corpus, the model's performance improved significantly, which indicates that the pre-training corpus is another important determinant of few-shot besides model size and prompt method.

label: coling
text: Recently, prompt-based learning, also known as prompt-based language model utilization, has gained significant success in comparison to the pre-train and fine-tune paradigm for various downstream NLP tasks. However, most prompt-based methods are token-level, such as the mask language model (MLM) based on PET. In this paper, we propose a sentence-level prompt-based method, NSP-BERT, which utilizes the abandoned Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task from the original BERT pre-training process. Unlike token-level techniques, NSP-BERT does not have any restrictions on the length of the prompt or the position to be predicted, making it suitable for tasks such as entity linking. Our NSP-tuning approach, using binary cross-entropy loss for single-sentence classification tasks, is competitive with PET and EFL. Furthermore, our results show that the pre-training corpus is another crucial factor in determining the model's performance, as evident from the significant improvement in NSP-BERT's performance after continuing its training on RoBERTa's corpus.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on short-input summarization. However, they still struggle with summarizing longer text. In this paper, we present DYLE, a novel dynamic latent extraction approach for abstractive long-input summarization. DYLE jointly trains an extractor and a generator and treats the extracted text snippets as the latent variable, allowing dynamic snippet-level attention weights during decoding. To provide adequate supervision, we propose simple yet effective heuristics for oracle extraction as well as a consistency loss term, which encourages the extractor to approximate the averaged dynamic weights predicted by the generator. We evaluate our method on different long-document and long-dialogue summarization tasks: GovReport, QMSum, and arXiv. Experiment results show that DYLE outperforms all existing methods on GovReport and QMSum, with gains up to 6.1 ROUGE, while yielding strong results on arXiv. Further analysis shows that the proposed dynamic weights provide interpretability of our generation process.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in short-input summarization, but they still face challenges in summarizing longer texts. This paper presents a novel approach, DYLE, for abstractive long-input summarization. DYLE trains an extractor and a generator simultaneously and treats extracted text snippets as latent variables, allowing dynamic snippet-level attention weights during the decoding process. We also introduce simple and effective heuristics for oracle extraction and a consistency loss term to provide adequate supervision. Our method was evaluated on three different long-document and long-dialogue summarization tasks: GovReport, QMSum, and arXiv. The results showed that DYLE outperformed all existing methods on GovReport and QMSum, with an improvement of up to 6.1 ROUGE, and produced strong results on arXiv. Analysis showed that the dynamic weights provide interpretability for our generation process.

label: coling
text: Multi-label classification is an important yet challenging task in natural language processing. It is more complex than single-label classification in that the labels tend to be correlated. Existing methods tend to ignore the correlations between labels. Besides, different parts of the text can contribute differently for predicting different labels, which is not considered by existing models. In this paper, we propose to view the multi-label classification task as a sequence generation problem, and apply a sequence generation model with a novel decoder structure to solve it. Extensive experimental results show that our proposed methods outperform previous work by a substantial margin. Further analysis of experimental results demonstrates that the proposed methods not only capture the correlations between labels, but also select the most informative words automatically when predicting different labels.

label: coling
text: Multi-label classification is a complex and challenging task in natural language processing. Unlike single-label classification, the labels in multi-label classification are often correlated, and existing methods tend to overlook these correlations. Moreover, current models fail to consider that different parts of the text may contribute differently to the prediction of different labels. To address these limitations, we propose to treat multi-label classification as a sequence generation problem and use a novel decoder structure in a sequence generation model to solve it. Our results show that our proposed method outperforms previous work by a significant margin. Further analysis of these results indicates that our method not only effectively captures the correlations between labels, but also automatically selects the most relevant words when making predictions for different labels.

label: acl
text: Although parsing to Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has become very popular and AMR has been shown effective on the many sentence-level downstream tasks, little work has studied how to generate AMRs that can represent multi-sentence information. We introduce the first end-to-end AMR coreference resolution model in order to build multi-sentence AMRs. Compared with the previous pipeline and rule-based approaches, our model alleviates error propagation and it is more robust for both in-domain and out-domain situations. Besides, the document-level AMRs obtained by our model can significantly improve over the AMRs generated by a rule-based method (Liu et al., 2015) on text summarization.

label: acl
text: Despite the popularity of parsing to Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) and its effectiveness in many sentence-level downstream tasks, little research has been conducted on generating AMRs that can represent multi-sentence information. To address this gap, we present the first end-to-end AMR coreference resolution model. Our approach is a significant improvement over previous pipeline and rule-based methods, as it eliminates error propagation and is more robust in both in-domain and out-of-domain situations. Additionally, the document-level AMRs generated by our model significantly outperform those generated by a rule-based method (Liu et al., 2015) in text summarization.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we leverage social media platforms such as twitter for developing corpus across multiple languages. The corpus creation methodology is applicable for resource-scarce languages provided the speakers of that particular language are active users on social media platforms. We present an approach to extract social media microblogs such as tweets (Twitter). In this paper, we create corpus for multilingual sentiment analysis and emoji prediction in Hindi, Bengali and Telugu. Further, we perform and analyze multiple NLP tasks utilizing the corpus to get interesting observations.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we utilize social media platforms, such as Twitter, to develop a corpus across multiple languages. Our corpus creation methodology is suitable for resource-scarce languages, provided the speakers of that language are active users on social media platforms. We present an approach to extract social media microblogs, specifically tweets, and use them to create a corpus for multilingual sentiment analysis and emoji prediction in Hindi, Bengali, and Telugu. We then perform various NLP tasks and analyze the results to gain insights.

label: acl
text: Training a referring expression comprehension (ReC) model for a new visual domain requires collecting referring expressions, and potentially corresponding bounding boxes, for images in the domain. While large-scale pre-trained models are useful for image classification across domains, it remains unclear if they can be applied in a zero-shot manner to more complex tasks like ReC. We present ReCLIP, a simple but strong zero-shot baseline that repurposes CLIP, a state-of-the-art large-scale model, for ReC. Motivated by the close connection between ReC and CLIP's contrastive pre-training objective, the first component of ReCLIP is a region-scoring method that isolates object proposals via cropping and blurring, and passes them to CLIP. However, through controlled experiments on a synthetic dataset, we find that CLIP is largely incapable of performing spatial reasoning off-the-shelf. We reduce the gap between zero-shot baselines from prior work and supervised models by as much as 29% on RefCOCOg, and on RefGTA (video game imagery), ReCLIP's relative improvement over supervised ReC models trained on real images is 8%.

label: acl
text: Training a Referring Expression Comprehension (ReC) model for a new visual domain requires collecting referring expressions and their corresponding bounding boxes for images in that domain. It is still unclear if pre-trained models, which are useful for image classification across domains, can be applied in a zero-shot manner to more complex tasks like ReC. To address this challenge, we present ReCLIP, a simple yet strong zero-shot baseline that repurposes the state-of-the-art large-scale model, CLIP, for ReC. The first component of ReCLIP is a region-scoring method that isolates object proposals by cropping and blurring them and passes them to CLIP. However, through controlled experiments on a synthetic dataset, we found that CLIP is limited in its ability to perform spatial reasoning. Despite this, we reduced the gap between zero-shot baselines and supervised models by up to 29% on RefCOCOg and improved the performance of supervised ReC models trained on real images by 8% on RefGTA (video game imagery).

label: acl
text: Language variation and change are driven both by individuals' internal cognitive processes and by the social structures through which language propagates. A wide range of computational frameworks have been proposed to connect these drivers. We compare the strengths and weaknesses of existing approaches and propose a new analytic framework which combines previous network models' ability to capture realistic social structure with practically and more elegant computational properties. The framework privileges the process of language acquisition and embeds learners in a social network but is modular so that population structure can be combined with different acquisition models. We demonstrate two applications for the framework: a test of practical concerns that arise when modeling acquisition in a population setting and an application of the framework to recent work on phonological mergers in progress.

label: acl
text: Language variation and change are driven by both individuals' internal cognitive processes and the social structures that propagate language. A variety of computational frameworks have been developed to bridge these drivers. This article compares the advantages and disadvantages of existing approaches and introduces a new analytical framework that combines the realistic social structure captured by previous network models with more practical and elegant computational properties. This framework prioritizes language acquisition and places learners within a social network, while also allowing for modularity so that population structure can be combined with different acquisition models. The article demonstrates two applications of the framework, including a test of practical considerations for modeling language acquisition in a population setting and an application of the framework to recent research on ongoing phonological mergers.

label: acl
text: Previous approaches to multilingual semantic dependency parsing treat languages independently, without exploiting the similarities between semantic structures across languages. We experiment with a new approach where we combine resources from different languages in the CoNLL 2009 shared task to build a single polyglot semantic dependency parser. Notwithstanding the absence of parallel data, and the dissimilarity in annotations between languages, our approach results in improvement in parsing performance on several languages over a monolingual baseline. Analysis of the polyglot models' performance provides a new understanding of the similarities and differences between languages in the shared task.

label: acl
text: Previous efforts in multilingual semantic dependency parsing have treated each language separately, without taking advantage of the similarities between the semantic structures across languages. In our new approach, we merge resources from different languages in the CoNLL 2009 shared task to create a single polyglot parser. Despite the lack of parallel data and differences in annotations between languages, our approach leads to improved parsing performance on several languages compared to a monolingual baseline. Our analysis of the polyglot models' performance offers new insights into the similarities and differences between the languages in the shared task.

label: acl
text: In this work, we focus on the problem of distinguishing a human written news article from a news article that is created by manipulating entities in a human written news article (e.g., replacing entities with factually incorrect entities). Such manipulated articles can mislead the reader by posing as a human written news article. We propose a neural network based detector that detects manipulated news articles by reasoning about the facts mentioned in the article. Our proposed detector exploits factual knowledge via graph convolutional neural network along with the textual information in the news article. We also create challenging datasets for this task by considering various strategies to generate the new replacement entity (e.g., entity generation from GPT-2). In all the settings, our proposed model either matches or outperforms the state-of-the-art detector in terms of accuracy. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/UBC-NLP/manipulated_entity_detection.

label: acl
text: In this study, we address the challenge of identifying human-written news articles from those that have been manipulated by altering the entities within them (e.g., by replacing them with factually incorrect information). These manipulated articles can deceive the reader by appearing to be written by a human. To tackle this issue, we propose a neural network-based detector that can detect manipulated news articles by evaluating the facts mentioned in the article. Our detector leverages both factual knowledge and textual information in the article through the use of graph convolutional neural networks. We also develop challenging datasets for this task by exploring various methods for generating replacement entities (such as using GPT-2). Our proposed model consistently outperforms or matches the accuracy of the current state-of-the-art detector in all settings. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/UBC-NLP/manipulated_entity_detection.

label: naacl
text: Word embeddings are one of the most fundamental technologies used in natural language processing. Existing word embeddings are high-dimensional and consume considerable computational resources. In this study, we propose WordTour, unsupervised one-dimensional word embeddings. To achieve the challenging goal, we propose a decomposition of the desiderata of word embeddings into two parts, completeness and soundness, and focus on soundness in this paper. Owing to the single dimensionality, WordTour is extremely efficient and provides a minimal means to handle word embeddings. We experimentally confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed method via user study and document classification.

label: naacl
text: In this study, we introduce WordTour - an unsupervised, one-dimensional word embedding approach. This method aims to address the challenges posed by high-dimensional, resource-intensive existing word embeddings. Our approach decomposes the requirements for word embeddings into two parts - completeness and soundness - and focuses on soundness in this paper. The single dimensionality of WordTour makes it highly efficient and provides a minimal solution for handling word embeddings. Our experiments, including a user study and document classification, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.

label: acl
text: Task-oriented dialogue systems typically require manual annotation of dialogue slots in training data, which is costly to obtain. We propose a method that eliminates this requirement: We use weak supervision from existing linguistic annotation models to identify potential slot candidates, then automatically identify domain-relevant slots by using clustering algorithms. Furthermore, we use the resulting slot annotation to train a neural-network-based tagger that is able to perform slot tagging with no human intervention. This tagger is trained solely on the outputs of our method and thus does not rely on any labeled data. Our model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in slot tagging without labeled training data on four different dialogue domains. Moreover, we find that slot annotations discovered by our model significantly improve the performance of an end-to-end dialogue response generation model, compared to using no slot annotation at all.

label: acl
text: Task-oriented dialogue systems usually need manual annotation of dialogue slots in the training data, which can be expensive to obtain. To eliminate this requirement, we present a method that leverages weak supervision from existing linguistic annotation models to identify potential slot candidates and then automatically identifies domain-relevant slots using clustering algorithms. This results in a neural-network-based tagger that is trained solely on the outputs of our method and does not require any human intervention. Our model outperforms state-of-the-art models in slot tagging without labeled training data on four different dialogue domains. Additionally, our model demonstrates that slot annotations discovered by our method significantly improve the performance of an end-to-end dialogue response generation model, compared to using no slot annotation.

label: coling
text: Models of natural language understanding often rely on question answering and logical inference benchmark challenges to evaluate the performance of a system. While informative, such task-oriented evaluations do not assess the broader semantic abilities that humans have as part of their linguistic competence when speaking and interpreting language. We define competence-based (CB) question generation, and focus on queries over lexical semantic knowledge involving implicit argument and subevent structure of verbs. We present a method to generate such questions and a dataset of English cooking recipes we use for implementing the generation method. Our primary experiment shows that even large pretrained language models perform poorly on CB questions until they are provided with additional contextualized semantic information. The data and the source code is available at: https: //github.com/brandeis-llc/CompQG.

label: coling
text: Models evaluating natural language understanding often use question answering and logical inference benchmark challenges to assess the performance of a system. However, these task-oriented evaluations do not consider the broader semantic abilities that humans possess as part of their linguistic competence when speaking and interpreting language. To address this gap, we introduce competence-based (CB) question generation, which focuses on queries over lexical semantic knowledge that involve implicit argument and subevent structure of verbs. Our method generates such questions and we present a dataset of English cooking recipes that we use to implement the generation method. Our primary experiment demonstrates that even large pre-trained language models perform poorly on CB questions until they are provided with additional contextualized semantic information. The data and source code can be found at: https://github.com/brandeis-llc/CompQG.

label: acl
text: Pre-trained language models have achieved human-level performance on many Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) tasks, but it remains unclear whether these models truly understand language or answer questions by exploiting statistical biases in datasets. Here, we demonstrate a simple yet effective method to attack MRC models and reveal the statistical biases in these models. We apply the method to the RACE dataset, for which the answer to each MRC question is selected from 4 options. It is found that several pre-trained language models, including BERT, ALBERT, and RoBERTa, show consistent preference to some options, even when these options are irrelevant to the question. When interfered by these irrelevant options, the performance of MRC models can be reduced from human-level performance to the chance-level performance. Human readers, however, are not clearly affected by these irrelevant options. Finally, we propose an augmented training method that can greatly reduce models' statistical biases.

label: acl
text: Pre-trained language models have demonstrated human-level proficiency in many Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) tasks, but it remains uncertain if they truly comprehend language or simply exploit statistical biases in datasets. In this study, we present a straightforward yet effective approach to expose these biases in MRC models. Our method was applied to the RACE dataset, where each MRC question has four potential answers. Our findings reveal that several pre-trained language models, including BERT, ALBERT, and RoBERTa, exhibit a consistent preference for certain answers, even when these answers are not relevant to the question. This interference from irrelevant options can reduce MRC model performance from human-level to chance-level. In contrast, human readers are not significantly affected by these irrelevant options. Finally, we propose an improved training method that significantly reduces the statistical biases in these models.

label: emnlp
text: Multi-task learning in text classification leverages implicit correlations among related tasks to extract common features and yield performance gains. However, a large body of previous work treats labels of each task as independent and meaningless one-hot vectors, which cause a loss of potential label information. In this paper, we propose Multi-Task Label Embedding to convert labels in text classification into semantic vectors, thereby turning the original tasks into vector matching tasks. Our model utilizes semantic correlations among tasks and makes it convenient to scale or transfer when new tasks are involved. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets for text classification show that our model can effectively improve the performances of related tasks with semantic representations of labels and additional information from each other.

label: emnlp
text: Multi-Task Label Embedding is a novel approach to text classification that leverages the implicit correlations among related tasks to extract common features, leading to improved performance. Unlike existing methods, which treat labels as independent and meaningless one-hot vectors, our model converts labels into semantic vectors, turning the original tasks into vector matching tasks. This allows the model to utilize semantic correlations among tasks and makes it easier to scale or transfer when new tasks are added. Our experiments on five benchmark datasets for text classification demonstrate that our model can effectively improve the performance of related tasks by utilizing semantic representations of labels and incorporating additional information from each task.

label: acl
text: Word identification from continuous input is typically viewed as a segmentation task. Experiments with human adults suggest that familiarity with syntactic structures in their native language also influences word identification in artificial languages; however, the relation between syntactic processing and word identification is yet unclear. This work takes one step forward by exploring a radically different approach of word identification, in which segmentation of a continuous input is viewed as a process isomorphic to unsupervised constituency parsing. Besides formalizing the approach, this study reports simulations of human experiments with DIORA (Drozdov et al., 2020), a neural unsupervised constituency parser. Results show that this model can reproduce human behavior in word identification experiments, suggesting that this is a viable approach to study word identification and its relation to syntactic processing.

label: acl
text: Word recognition from a continuous stream of input is usually considered a segmentation task. Research with adult human subjects indicates that knowledge of the syntactic structures in their native language also affects word recognition in artificial languages. However, the correlation between syntactic processing and word recognition is still unclear. This study advances our understanding by exploring a novel approach to word recognition, where the segmentation of a continuous input is treated as a process equivalent to unsupervised constituency parsing. The study formalizes this approach and uses DIORA (Drozdov et al., 2020), a neural unsupervised constituency parser, to simulate human experiments. The results demonstrate that this model can accurately replicate human behavior in word recognition experiments, suggesting that this is a promising approach for investigating the relationship between syntactic processing and word recognition.

label: emnlp
text: Semantic specialization is a process of fine-tuning pre-trained distributional word vectors using external lexical knowledge (e.g., WordNet) to accentuate a particular semantic relation in the specialized vector space. While post-processing specialization methods are applicable to arbitrary distributional vectors, they are limited to updating only the vectors of words occurring in external lexicons (i.e., seen words), leaving the vectors of all other words unchanged. We propose a novel approach to specializing the full distributional vocabulary. Our adversarial post-specialization method propagates the external lexical knowledge to the full distributional space. We exploit words seen in the resources as training examples for learning a global specialization function. This function is learned by combining a standard L2-distance loss with a adversarial loss: the adversarial component produces more realistic output vectors. We show the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method across three languages and on three tasks: word similarity, dialog state tracking, and lexical simplification. We report consistent improvements over distributional word vectors and vectors specialized by other state-of-the-art specialization frameworks. Finally, we also propose a cross-lingual transfer method for zero-shot specialization which successfully specializes a full target distributional space without any lexical knowledge in the target language and without any bilingual data.

label: emnlp
text: The process of fine-tuning pre-trained distributional word vectors using external lexical knowledge (such as WordNet) to emphasize a specific semantic relationship in the specialized vector space is called semantic specialization. While post-processing specialization methods can be used with any distributional vectors, they are limited to updating only the vectors of words that appear in external lexicons (i.e., known words), leaving the vectors of all other words unchanged. Our novel approach to specializing the full distributional vocabulary involves propagating external lexical knowledge to the full distributional space using an adversarial post-specialization method. This method uses words that are seen in resources as training examples to learn a global specialization function by combining a standard L2-distance loss with an adversarial loss. The adversarial component helps produce more realistic output vectors. Our method has been tested across three languages and three tasks (word similarity, dialog state tracking, and lexical simplification) and has consistently shown improvement over distributional word vectors and vectors specialized by other state-of-the-art specialization frameworks. Finally, we also propose a cross-lingual transfer method for zero-shot specialization, which specializes a full target distributional space without any lexical knowledge in the target language and without any bilingual data.

label: emnlp
text: Current image captioning approaches generate descriptions which lack specific information, such as named entities that are involved in the images. In this paper we propose a new task which aims to generate informative image captions, given images and hashtags as input. We propose a simple but effective approach to tackle this problem. We first train a convolutional neural networks - long short term memory networks (CNN-LSTM) model to generate a template caption based on the input image. Then we use a knowledge graph based collective inference algorithm to fill in the template with specific named entities retrieved via the hashtags. Experiments on a new benchmark dataset collected from Flickr show that our model generates news-style image descriptions with much richer information. Our model outperforms unimodal baselines significantly with various evaluation metrics.

label: emnlp
text: The current methods for image captioning generate descriptions which lack specific details, such as named entities. This paper presents a new task of generating informative image captions, given images and hashtags as inputs. Our approach involves training a CNN-LSTM model to generate a template caption based on the image, and then using a knowledge graph-based collective inference algorithm to fill in the template with specific named entities retrieved from the hashtags. Our experiments on a new benchmark dataset collected from Flickr demonstrate that our model generates news-style image descriptions with more information, outperforming unimodal baselines significantly according to various evaluation metrics.

label: acl
text: We study learning from user feedback for extractive question answering by simulating feedback using supervised data. We cast the problem as contextual bandit learning, and analyze the characteristics of several learning scenarios with focus on reducing data annotation. We show that systems initially trained on few examples can dramatically improve given feedback from users on model-predicted answers, and that one can use existing datasets to deploy systems in new domains without any annotation effort, but instead improving the system on-the-fly via user feedback.

label: acl
text: We investigate the impact of user feedback on extractive question answering by simulating feedback using supervised data. We approach this problem as a contextual bandit learning challenge and analyze different learning scenarios with an emphasis on reducing data annotation. Our results demonstrate that systems trained on a limited number of examples can significantly improve with user feedback on model-generated answers. Additionally, we demonstrate that existing datasets can be leveraged to deploy systems in new domains without any annotation, but instead, the system can be improved incrementally through user feedback.

label: coling
text: This paper reports on a reimplementation of a system on detecting implicit positive meaning from negated statements. In the original regression experiment, different positive interpretations per negation are scored according to their likelihood. We convert the scores to classes and report our results on both the regression and classification tasks. We show that a baseline taking the mean score or most frequent class is hard to beat because of class imbalance in the dataset. Our error analysis indicates that an approach that takes the information structure into account (i.e. which information is new or contrastive) may be promising, which requires looking beyond the syntactic and semantic characteristics of negated statements.

label: coling
text: This paper presents the results of a re-implementation of a system for detecting implicit positive meaning in negated statements. The original regression experiment involved scoring various positive interpretations of negations based on their likelihood. The scores were then converted into classes and the results were analyzed for both the regression and classification tasks. Our findings reveal that due to class imbalance in the dataset, it is challenging to outperform a baseline approach that uses the mean score or the most frequent class.
