Our error analysis suggests that a more promising approach may be to take into account the information structure (i.e. whether the information is new or contrasting) when analyzing negated statements, which requires considering factors beyond their syntactic and semantic characteristics.

label: coling
text: To automatically correct handwritten assignments, the traditional approach is to use an OCR model to recognize characters and compare them to answers. The OCR model easily gets confused on recognizing handwritten Chinese characters, and the textual information of the answers is missing during the model inference. However, teachers always have these answers in mind to review and correct assignments. In this paper, we focus on the Chinese cloze tests correction and propose a multimodal approach(named AiM). The encoded representations of answers interact with the visual information of students' handwriting. Instead of predicting `right' or `wrong', we perform the sequence labeling on the answer text to infer which answer character differs from the handwritten content in a fine-grained way. We take samples of OCR datasets as the positive samples for this task, and develop a negative sample augmentation method to scale up the training data. Experimental results show that AiM outperforms OCR-based methods by a large margin. Extensive studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our multimodal approach.

label: coling
text: The traditional approach to automatically correcting handwritten assignments involves using an OCR model to recognize characters and compare them to answers. However, this model often struggles with recognizing handwritten Chinese characters and lacks the textual information of answers during inference. To address this issue, we propose a multimodal approach called AiM that focuses on correcting Chinese cloze tests. Our approach encodes the answers and interacts with the visual information of students' handwriting, performing sequence labeling on the answer text to identify any fine-grained differences between the answer and the handwriting. We use OCR datasets as positive samples for this task and develop a negative sample augmentation method to increase the training data. Our results show that AiM outperforms OCR-based methods by a significant margin, and extensive studies validate the effectiveness of our multimodal approach.

label: acl
text: Early stopping, which is widely used to prevent overfitting, is generally based on a separate validation set. However, in low resource settings, validation-based stopping can be risky because a small validation set may not be sufficiently representative, and the reduction in the number of samples by validation split may result in insufficient samples for training. In this study, we propose an early stopping method that uses unlabeled samples. The proposed method is based on confidence and class distribution similarities. To further improve the performance, we present a calibration method to better estimate the class distribution of the unlabeled samples. The proposed method is advantageous because it does not require a separate validation set and provides a better stopping point by using a large unlabeled set. Extensive experiments are conducted on five text classification datasets and several stop-methods are compared. Our results show that the proposed model even performs better than using an additional validation set as well as the existing stop-methods, in both balanced and imbalanced data settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/DMCB-GIST/BUS-stop.

label: acl
text: Early stopping is a commonly used technique to prevent overfitting, typically relying on a validation set. However, in low-resource settings, validation-based stopping can be problematic as a small validation set may not be representative, and the reduction in sample size due to the validation split can lead to insufficient training samples. To address these issues, we propose an early stopping method that uses unlabeled samples, based on confidence and class distribution similarities. We also present a calibration method to further improve performance by better estimating the class distribution of the unlabeled samples. This method is beneficial as it does not require a separate validation set and provides a more accurate stopping point by utilizing a larger unlabeled set. Our experiments on five text classification datasets demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms both using a validation set and existing stop-methods, both in balanced and imbalanced data settings. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/DMCB-GIST/BUS-stop.

label: acl
text: Understanding causality has vital importance for various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. Beyond the labeled instances, conceptual explanations of the causality can provide deep understanding of the causal fact to facilitate the causal reasoning process. However, such explanation information still remains absent in existing causal reasoning resources. In this paper, we fill this gap by presenting a human-annotated explainable CAusal REasoning dataset (e-CARE), which contains over 20K causal reasoning questions, together with natural language formed explanations of the causal questions. Experimental results show that generating valid explanations for causal facts still remains especially challenging for the state-of-the-art models, and the explanation information can be helpful for promoting the accuracy and stability of causal reasoning models.

label: acl
text: The importance of understanding causality is crucial for various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. While labeled instances are useful, a deeper understanding of causality can be achieved through conceptual explanations. However, these explanations are currently lacking in existing causal reasoning resources. To address this issue, we present the e-CARE (Explainable CAusal REasoning) dataset, which contains over 20,000 causal reasoning questions and natural language explanations. Our experiments demonstrate that generating valid explanations for causal facts is still a challenge for state-of-the-art models, and that the inclusion of explanation information can improve the accuracy and stability of causal reasoning models.

label: acl
text: Reducing and counter-acting hate speech on Social Media is a significant concern. Most of the proposed automatic methods are conducted exclusively on English and very few consistently labeled, non-English resources have been proposed. Learning to detect hate speech on English and transferring to unseen languages seems an immediate solution. This work is the first to shed light on the limits of this zero-shot, cross-lingual transfer learning framework for hate speech detection. We use benchmark data sets in English, Italian, and Spanish to detect hate speech towards immigrants and women. Investigating post-hoc explanations of the model, we discover that non-hateful, language-specific taboo interjections are misinterpreted as signals of hate speech. Our findings demonstrate that zero-shot, cross-lingual models cannot be used as they are, but need to be carefully designed.

label: acl
text: Reducing and combating hate speech on social media is a pressing issue. Most automatic methods for detecting hate speech are limited to English and there are very few resources available for non-English languages that are consistently labeled. An immediate solution to this problem is to learn to detect hate speech in English and then transfer the knowledge to other languages. This study is the first to investigate the limitations of the zero-shot, cross-lingual transfer learning framework for hate speech detection. We use benchmark datasets in English, Italian, and Spanish to detect hate speech directed towards immigrants and women. Our findings reveal that non-hateful, language-specific taboo interjections are often misinterpreted by the model as signals of hate speech. Our results show that zero-shot, cross-lingual models cannot be used as is, but must be carefully designed to avoid these misinterpretations.

label: acl
text: Bilingual tasks, such as bilingual lexicon induction and cross-lingual classification, are crucial for overcoming data sparsity in the target language. Resources required for such tasks are often out-of-domain, thus domain adaptation is an important problem here. We make two contributions. First, we test a delightfully simple method for domain adaptation of bilingual word embeddings. We evaluate these embeddings on two bilingual tasks involving different domains: cross-lingual twitter sentiment classification and medical bilingual lexicon induction. Second, we tailor a broadly applicable semi-supervised classification method from computer vision to these tasks. We show that this method also helps in low-resource setups. Using both methods together we achieve large improvements over our baselines, by using only additional unlabeled data.

label: acl
text: The bilingual tasks of bilingual lexicon induction and cross-lingual classification are critical for addressing the issue of data sparsity in the target language. However, the resources needed for these tasks are often in different domains, making domain adaptation a significant challenge. In this study, we have made two contributions. Firstly, we have tested a simple method for adapting bilingual word embeddings to different domains. We have evaluated these embeddings on two bilingual tasks, cross-lingual Twitter sentiment classification and medical bilingual lexicon induction, that involve different domains. Secondly, we have adapted a widely applicable semi-supervised classification method from computer vision to these tasks. Our results show that this method can also be effective in low-resource settings. By combining these two methods, we have achieved substantial improvements over our baselines, using only additional unlabeled data.

label: acl
text: As a more natural and intelligent interaction manner, multimodal task-oriented dialog system recently has received great attention and many remarkable progresses have been achieved. Nevertheless, almost all existing studies follow the pipeline to first learn intra-modal features separately and then conduct simple feature concatenation or attention-based feature fusion to generate responses, which hampers them from learning inter-modal interactions and conducting cross-modal feature alignment for generating more intention-aware responses. To address these issues, we propose UniTranSeR, a Unified Transformer Semantic Representation framework with feature alignment and intention reasoning for multimodal dialog systems. Specifically, we first embed the multimodal features into a unified Transformer semantic space to prompt inter-modal interactions, and then devise a feature alignment and intention reasoning (FAIR) layer to perform cross-modal entity alignment and fine-grained key-value reasoning, so as to effectively identify user's intention for generating more accurate responses. Experimental results verify the effectiveness of UniTranSeR, showing that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the representative MMD dataset.

label: acl
text: Multimodal task-oriented dialog systems have recently received great attention for their natural and intelligent interaction manner. Despite the remarkable progress made, existing studies tend to follow a pipeline approach that involves learning intra-modal features separately and then conducting simple feature concatenation or attention-based feature fusion to generate responses. This approach hinders the ability to learn inter-modal interactions and perform cross-modal feature alignment, resulting in less intention-aware responses. To overcome these limitations, we propose UniTranSeR, a Unified Transformer Semantic Representation framework that incorporates feature alignment and intention reasoning. UniTranSeR embeds multimodal features into a unified Transformer semantic space to facilitate inter-modal interactions and uses a feature alignment and intention reasoning (FAIR) layer to perform cross-modal entity alignment and fine-grained key-value reasoning. This enables UniTranSeR to effectively identify the user's intention and generate more accurate responses. The effectiveness of UniTranSeR is verified by experimental results, which demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the representative MMD dataset.

label: coling
text: User-generated content such as the questions on community question answering (CQA) forums does not always come with appropriate headlines, in contrast to the news articles used in various headline generation tasks. In such cases, we cannot use paired supervised data, e.g., pairs of articles and headlines, to learn a headline generation model. To overcome this problem, we propose an extractive headline generation method based on learning to rank for CQA that extracts the most informative substring from each question as its headline. Experimental results show that our method outperforms several baselines, including a prefix-based method, which is widely used in real services.

label: coling
text: The questions on community question-answering (CQA) forums often lack appropriate headlines, unlike news articles used in various headline generation tasks. As a result, we cannot use paired supervised data, such as article-headline pairs, to train a headline generation model. To address this challenge, we propose an extractive headline generation method based on learning to rank for CQA. Our method extracts the most informative substring from each question to serve as its headline. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms several baselines, including the widely used prefix-based method.

label: naacl
text: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) is a fine-grained sentiment classification task. Most recent efforts adopt pre-trained model to classify the sentences with aspects. However, the aspect sentiment bias from pre-trained model brings some noise to the ABSA task. Besides, traditional methods using cross-entropy loss are hard to find the potential associations between sentiment polarities. In this work, we analyze the ABSA task from a novel cognition perspective: humans can often judge the sentiment of an aspect even if they do not know what the aspect is. Moreover, it is easier to distinguish positive and negative sentiments than others for human beings because positive and negative are two opposite sentiments. To this end, we propose a no-aspect differential sentiment (NADS) framework for the ABSA task. We first design a no-aspect template by replacing the aspect with a special unbiased character to eliminate the sentiment bias and obtain a stronger representation. To better get the benefits from the template, we adopt contrastive learning between the no-aspect template and the original sentence. Then we propose a differential sentiment loss instead of the cross-entropy loss to better classify the sentiments by distinguishing the different distances between sentiments. Our proposed model is a general framework and can be combined with almost all traditional ABSA methods. Experiments on SemEval 2014 show that our framework is still able to predict the sentiment of the aspect even we don't konw what the aspect is. Moreover, our NADS framework boosts three typical ABSA methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

label: naacl
text: Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) is a challenging task that requires fine-grained sentiment classification. In recent years, many efforts have been made to adopt pre-trained models for ABSA, but these models often introduce noise due to aspect sentiment bias. Additionally, traditional methods that use cross-entropy loss struggle to find the potential associations between sentiment polarities. To address these challenges, we propose a novel cognition-based approach to ABSA. Our approach is inspired by the observation that humans can often judge the sentiment of an aspect even if they do not know what the aspect is, and that it is easier for humans to distinguish between positive and negative sentiments. To this end, we present a No-Aspect Differential Sentiment (NADS) framework for ABSA. Our framework replaces the aspect with a special unbiased character in a no-aspect template, thus eliminating sentiment bias and obtaining a stronger representation. We then use contrastive learning between the no-aspect template and the original sentence to better leverage the benefits of the template. Finally, we propose a differential sentiment loss to better classify sentiments by distinguishing different distances between sentiments. Our NADS framework can be combined with traditional ABSA methods and is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods on the SemEval 2014 dataset.

label: coling
text: Distributed representations of words play a major role in the field of natural language processing by encoding semantic and syntactic information of words. However, most existing works on learning word representations typically regard words as individual atomic units and thus are blind to subword information in words. This further gives rise to a difficulty in representing out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. In this paper, we present a character-based word representation approach to deal with this limitation. The proposed model learns to generate word representations from characters. In our model, we employ a convolutional neural network and a highway network over characters to extract salient features effectively. Unlike previous models that learn word representations from a large corpus, we take a set of pre-trained word embeddings and generalize it to word entries, including OOV words. To demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model, we perform both an intrinsic and an extrinsic task which are word similarity and language modeling, respectively. Experimental results show clearly that the proposed model significantly outperforms strong baseline models that regard words or their subwords as atomic units. For example, we achieve as much as 18.5% improvement on average in perplexity for morphologically rich languages compared to strong baselines in the language modeling task.

label: coling
text: Distributed representations of words play a crucial role in natural language processing by encoding semantic and syntactic information. However, most existing methods for learning word representations treat words as individual atomic units and ignore subword information, leading to difficulties in representing out-of-vocabulary words. To address this limitation, we propose a character-based word representation approach. Our model uses a convolutional neural network and a highway network to extract salient features from characters. Unlike previous models that learn word representations from a large corpus, we use pre-trained word embeddings and generalize them to word entries, including out-of-vocabulary words. To evaluate the effectiveness of our model, we conduct intrinsic and extrinsic tasks, such as word similarity and language modeling. The results show that our model outperforms strong baseline models that treat words or their subwords as atomic units. For instance, in the language modeling task, our model improves the average perplexity by 18.5% for morphologically rich languages compared to strong baselines.

label: acl
text: We explore the notion of subjectivity, and hypothesize that word embeddings learnt from input corpora of varying levels of subjectivity behave differently on natural language processing tasks such as classifying a sentence by sentiment, subjectivity, or topic. Through systematic comparative analyses, we establish this to be the case indeed. Moreover, based on the discovery of the outsized role that sentiment words play on subjectivity-sensitive tasks such as sentiment classification, we develop a novel word embedding SentiVec which is infused with sentiment information from a lexical resource, and is shown to outperform baselines on such tasks.

label: acl
text: We investigate the concept of subjectivity and propose that word embeddings learned from input corpora with varying levels of subjectivity will exhibit different behavior on natural language processing tasks, such as sentiment, subjectivity, or topic classification. Our systematic comparative analysis confirms this hypothesis. Furthermore, we discover that sentiment words have a significant impact on subjectivity-sensitive tasks, such as sentiment classification. As a result, we develop a new word embedding called SentiVec, which incorporates sentiment information from a lexical resource. This approach outperforms traditional baselines on these tasks.

label: acl
text: In Machine Translation, assessing the quality of a large amount of automatic translations can be challenging. Automatic metrics are not reliable when it comes to high performing systems. In addition, resorting to human evaluators can be expensive, especially when evaluating multiple systems. To overcome the latter challenge, we propose a novel application of online learning that, given an ensemble of Machine Translation systems, dynamically converges to the best systems, by taking advantage of the human feedback available. Our experiments on WMT'19 datasets show that our online approach quickly converges to the top-3 ranked systems for the language pairs considered, despite the lack of human feedback for many translations.

label: acl
text: Assessing the quality of large amounts of automatic translations in Machine Translation can be difficult. Reliable automatic metrics are not always available for high-performing systems. Using human evaluators to assess the translations can be costly, especially when evaluating multiple systems. To address this challenge, we propose a novel application of online learning that dynamically converges to the best systems in an ensemble of Machine Translation systems. Our approach leverages available human feedback to achieve this convergence. Our experiments on WMT'19 datasets demonstrate that our online approach quickly identifies the top-3 ranked systems for the language pairs considered, even without human feedback for many translations.

label: emnlp
text: Understanding and reasoning about cooking recipes is a fruitful research direction towards enabling machines to interpret procedural text. In this work, we introduce RecipeQA, a dataset for multimodal comprehension of cooking recipes. It comprises of approximately 20K instructional recipes with multiple modalities such as titles, descriptions and aligned set of images. With over 36K automatically generated question-answer pairs, we design a set of comprehension and reasoning tasks that require joint understanding of images and text, capturing the temporal flow of events and making sense of procedural knowledge. Our preliminary results indicate that RecipeQA will serve as a challenging test bed and an ideal benchmark for evaluating machine comprehension systems. The data and leaderboard are available at http://hucvl.github.io/recipeqa.

label: emnlp
text: The research direction of understanding and reasoning about cooking recipes is promising, as it aims to enable machines to interpret procedural text. To facilitate this, we present RecipeQA, a multi-modal dataset for comprehending cooking recipes. It contains approximately 20,000 instructional recipes, each with a title, description, and corresponding set of images. The dataset also includes over 36,000 automatically generated question-answer pairs, designed to test a machine's ability to understand the temporal flow of events and grasp procedural knowledge through a joint understanding of text and images. Our initial results show that RecipeQA will be a valuable test bed and benchmark for evaluating machine comprehension systems. The data and leaderboard can be accessed at http://hucvl.github.io/recipeqa.

label: naacl
text: Large-scale cross-lingual pre-trained language models (xPLMs) have shown effective in cross-lingual sequence labeling tasks (xSL), such as machine reading comprehension (xMRC) by transferring knowledge from a high-resource language to low-resource languages.Despite the great success, we draw an empirical observation that there is an training objective gap between pre-training and fine-tuning stages: e.g., mask language modeling objective requires local understanding of the masked token and the span-extraction objective requires understanding and reasoning of the global input passage/paragraph and question, leading to the discrepancy between pre-training and xMRC. In this paper, we first design a pre-training task tailored for xSL named Cross-lingual Language Informative Span Masking (CLISM) to eliminate the objective gap in a self-supervised manner. Second, we present ContrAstive-Consistency Regularization (CACR), which utilizes contrastive learning to encourage the consistency between representations of input parallel sequences via unsupervised cross-lingual instance-wise training signals during pre-training. By these means, our methods not only bridge the gap between pretrain-finetune, but also enhance PLMs to better capture the alignment between different languages. Extensive experiments prove that our method achieves clearly superior results on multiple xSL benchmarks with limited pre-training data. Our methods also surpass the previous state-of-the-art methods by a large margin in few-shot data setting, where only a few hundred training examples are available.

label: naacl
text: Large-scale cross-lingual pre-trained language models (xPLMs) have proven effective in cross-lingual sequence labeling tasks, such as machine reading comprehension (xMRC), by transferring knowledge from high-resource languages to low-resource languages. However, we have observed that there is a gap between the training objectives of the pre-training and fine-tuning stages. For example, the mask language modeling objective requires a local understanding of the masked token, while the span-extraction objective requires an understanding and reasoning of the global input passage/paragraph and question, leading to a discrepancy between pre-training and xMRC. To address this issue, we propose two solutions. First, we design a pre-training task, Cross-lingual Language Informative Span Masking (CLISM), specifically tailored for xSL, to eliminate the objective gap in a self-supervised manner. Second, we introduce ContrAstive-Consistency Regularization (CACR), which uses contrastive learning to encourage consistency between representations of parallel input sequences through unsupervised cross-lingual instance-wise training signals during pre-training. Our methods not only bridge the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning, but also enhance the ability of PLMs to capture the alignment between different languages. Extensive experiments show that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on multiple xSL benchmarks, even with limited pre-training data. In the few-shot data setting, where only a few hundred training examples are available, our method surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a significant margin.

label: acl
text: The discrepancy between maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and task measures such as BLEU score has been studied before for autoregressive neural machine translation (NMT) and resulted in alternative training algorithms (Ranzato et al., 2016; Norouzi et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018). However, MLE training remains the de facto approach for autoregressive NMT because of its computational efficiency and stability. Despite this mismatch between the training objective and task measure, we notice that the samples drawn from an MLE-based trained NMT support the desired distribution – there are samples with much higher BLEU score comparing to the beam decoding output. To benefit from this observation, we train an energy-based model to mimic the behavior of the task measure (i.e., the energy-based model assigns lower energy to samples with higher BLEU score), which is resulted in a re-ranking algorithm based on the samples drawn from NMT: energy-based re-ranking (EBR). We use both marginal energy models (over target sentence) and joint energy models (over both source and target sentences). Our EBR with the joint energy model consistently improves the performance of the Transformer-based NMT: +3.7 BLEU points on IWSLT'14 German-English, +3.37 BELU points on Sinhala-English, +1.4 BLEU points on WMT'16 English-German tasks.

label: acl
text: The discrepancy between the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach and task measures such as BLEU score in autoregressive neural machine translation (NMT) has been previously explored, leading to the development of alternative training algorithms (Ranzato et al., 2016; Norouzi et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018). Despite this mismatch, MLE remains the most widely used training method for autoregressive NMT due to its computational efficiency and stability. However, our observations have shown that the samples generated from an MLE-trained NMT support the desired distribution, with some samples having a much higher BLEU score compared to the beam decoding output. To leverage this observation, we trained an energy-based model to mimic the behavior of the task measure (i.e., assigning lower energy to samples with higher BLEU scores) and developed an energy-based re-ranking (EBR) algorithm based on the samples generated by NMT. We employed both marginal energy models (target sentence only) and joint energy models (source and target sentences) and found that our EBR with the joint energy model consistently improved the performance of Transformer-based NMT, with an increase of +3.7 BLEU points on the IWSLT'14 German-English task, +3.37 BLEU points on the Sinhala-English task, and +1.4 BLEU points on the WMT'16 English-German task.

label: acl
text: Learned self-attention functions in state-of-the-art NLP models often correlate with human attention. We investigate whether self-attention in large-scale pre-trained language models is as predictive of human eye fixation patterns during task-reading as classical cognitive models of human attention. We compare attention functions across two task-specific reading datasets for sentiment analysis and relation extraction. We find the predictiveness of large-scale pre-trained self-attention for human attention depends on `what is in the tail', e.g., the syntactic nature of rare contexts.Further, we observe that task-specific fine-tuning does not increase the correlation with human task-specific reading. Through an input reduction experiment we give complementary insights on the sparsity and fidelity trade-off, showing that lower-entropy attention vectors are more faithful.

label: acl
text: The self-attention functions in current NLP models often mirror human attention patterns. Our research explores whether these functions in large-scale pre-trained language models can predict human eye fixation patterns during task-reading as well as traditional cognitive models of human attention. To do this, we compare attention functions across two datasets for sentiment analysis and relation extraction. Our findings indicate that the predictiveness of pre-trained self-attention for human attention is influenced by the syntactic nature of rare contexts, specifically, "what is in the tail." Additionally, we discovered that task-specific fine-tuning does not improve the correlation with human task-specific reading. Finally, our input reduction experiment sheds light on the sparsity and fidelity trade-off, revealing that lower-entropy attention vectors are more accurate.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we challenge the ACL community to reckon with historical and ongoing colonialism by adopting a set of ethical obligations and best practices drawn from the Indigenous studies literature. While the vast majority of NLP research focuses on a very small number of very high resource languages (English, Chinese, etc), some work has begun to engage with Indigenous languages. No research involving Indigenous language data can be considered ethical without first acknowledging that Indigenous languages are not merely very low resource languages. The toxic legacy of colonialism permeates every aspect of interaction between Indigenous communities and outside researchers. To this end, we propose that the ACL draft and adopt an ethical framework for NLP researchers and computational linguists wishing to engage in research involving Indigenous languages.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we call upon the ACL community to confront the historical and ongoing impacts of colonialism by embracing ethical principles and best practices from Indigenous studies. Despite the majority of NLP research being centered on a few high-resource languages (such as English and Chinese), some efforts have been made to work with Indigenous languages. However, any research that involves Indigenous language data must first acknowledge that these languages are not simply low-resource languages. The harmful legacy of colonialism continues to shape all interactions between Indigenous communities and external researchers. Therefore, we suggest that the ACL establish an ethical framework for NLP researchers and computational linguists who wish to conduct research involving Indigenous languages.

label: naacl
text: During the past decade, neural network models have made tremendous progress on in-domain semantic role labeling (SRL). However, performance drops dramatically under the out-of-domain setting. In order to facilitate research on cross-domain SRL, this paper presents MuCPAD, a multi-domain Chinese predicate-argument dataset, which consists of 30,897 sentences and 92,051 predicates from six different domains. MuCPAD exhibits three important features. 1) Based on a frame-free annotation methodology, we avoid writing complex frames for new predicates. 2) We explicitly annotate omitted core arguments to recover more complete semantic structure, considering that omission of content words is ubiquitous in multi-domain Chinese texts. 3) We compile 53 pages of annotation guidelines and adopt strict double annotation for improving data quality. This paper describes in detail the annotation methodology and annotation process of MuCPAD, and presents in-depth data analysis. We also give benchmark results on cross-domain SRL based on MuCPAD.

label: naacl
text:
The results demonstrate that MuCPAD makes a significant contribution to the development of cross-domain SRL.

Over the past decade, tremendous progress has been made in the development of neural network models for in-domain semantic role labeling (SRL). However, these models suffer from a significant drop in performance when applied to out-of-domain settings. To address this issue, this paper introduces MuCPAD, a multi-domain Chinese predicate-argument dataset consisting of 30,897 sentences and 92,051 predicates from six different domains. MuCPAD is unique in its three key features: 1) it is based on a frame-free annotation methodology, eliminating the need for complex frames for new predicates. 2) It includes explicit annotations for omitted core arguments to provide a more complete semantic structure, as the omission of content words is common in multi-domain Chinese texts. 3) The dataset was created using strict double annotation procedures and 53 pages of annotation guidelines to ensure high-quality data. This paper provides a detailed description of the MuCPAD annotation methodology and process, as well as in-depth data analysis. Results from benchmark cross-domain SRL experiments using MuCPAD demonstrate its significant contribution to the field.

label: acl
text: We present a generative probabilistic model of documents as sequences of sentences, and show that inference in it can lead to extraction of long-range latent discourse structure from a collection of documents. The approach is based on embedding sequences of sentences from longer texts into a 2- or 3-D spatial grids, in which one or two coordinates model smooth topic transitions, while the third captures the sequential nature of the modeled text. A significant advantage of our approach is that the learned models are naturally visualizable and interpretable, as semantic similarity and sequential structure are modeled along orthogonal directions in the grid. We show that the method is effective in capturing discourse structures in narrative text across multiple genres, including biographies, stories, and newswire reports. In particular, our method outperforms or is competitive with state-of-the-art generative approaches on tasks such as predicting the outcome of a story, and sentence ordering.

label: acl
text: We present a generative probabilistic model for documents that views them as sequences of sentences. Our approach shows that inference in this model can extract long-range latent discourse structures from a collection of documents. This is achieved by embedding sequences of sentences into 2- or 3-D spatial grids, where one or two coordinates model smooth topic transitions and the third captures the sequential nature of the text. The learned models are visually interpretable, as semantic similarity and sequential structure are modeled along orthogonal directions in the grid. Our method demonstrates effectiveness in capturing discourse structures in various narrative texts, including biographies, stories, and newswire reports. Furthermore, it outperforms or is competitive with state-of-the-art generative approaches on tasks such as predicting story outcomes and sentence ordering.

label: coling
text: Transformer-based pre-trained language models such as BERT have achieved remarkable results in Semantic Sentence Matching. However, existing models still suffer from insufficient ability to capture subtle differences. Minor noise like word addition, deletion, and modification of sentences may cause flipped predictions. To alleviate this problem, we propose a novel Dual Attention Enhanced BERT (DABERT) to enhance the ability of BERT to capture fine-grained differences in sentence pairs. DABERT comprises (1) Dual Attention module, which measures soft word matches by introducing a new dual channel alignment mechanism to model affinity and difference attention. (2) Adaptive Fusion module, this module uses attention to learn the aggregation of difference and affinity features, and generates a vector describing the matching details of sentence pairs. We conduct extensive experiments on well-studied semantic matching and robustness test datasets, and the experimental results show the effectiveness of our proposed method.

label: coling
text: Transformer-based pre-trained language models such as BERT have demonstrated remarkable success in semantic sentence matching. However, these models still struggle to capture subtle differences, and even minor changes such as adding, deleting, or modifying words can result in incorrect predictions. To address this issue, we introduce a novel Dual Attention Enhanced BERT (DABERT) model that enhances BERT's ability to capture fine-grained differences between sentence pairs. DABERT consists of two main components: (1) a Dual Attention module, which leverages a new dual channel alignment mechanism to measure soft word matches and model both affinity and difference attention, and (2) an Adaptive Fusion module, which uses attention to aggregate difference and affinity features and generate a vector that describes the detailed matching information between sentence pairs. Our extensive experiments on well-known semantic matching and robustness test datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

label: coling
text: We present a system for Answer Selection that integrates fine-grained Question Classification with a Deep Learning model designed for Answer Selection. We detail the necessary changes to the Question Classification taxonomy and system, the creation of a new Entity Identification system and methods of highlighting entities to achieve this objective. Our experiments show that Question Classes are a strong signal to Deep Learning models for Answer Selection, and enable us to outperform the current state of the art in all variations of our experiments except one. In the best configuration, our MRR and MAP scores outperform the current state of the art by between 3 and 5 points on both versions of the TREC Answer Selection test set, a standard dataset for this task.

label: coling
text: A system for Answer Selection is introduced that combines fine-grained Question Classification with a Deep Learning model. The modifications made to the Question Classification taxonomy and system, as well as the development of a new Entity Identification system, are explained. The results of our experiments demonstrate that Question Classes provide a robust signal for Deep Learning models in Answer Selection, leading to improved performance compared to the current state of the art. In the optimal configuration, our MRR and MAP scores outperformed the current state of the art by 3 to 5 points on both versions of the TREC Answer Selection test set, a widely recognized benchmark for this task.

label: acl
text: This paper presents the first study aimed at capturing stylistic similarity between words in an unsupervised manner. We propose extending the continuous bag of words (CBOW) embedding model (Mikolov et al., 2013b) to learn style-sensitive word vectors using a wider context window under the assumption that the style of all the words in an utterance is consistent. In addition, we introduce a novel task to predict lexical stylistic similarity and to create a benchmark dataset for this task. Our experiment with this dataset supports our assumption and demonstrates that the proposed extensions contribute to the acquisition of style-sensitive word embeddings.

label: acl
text: This paper presents the first study aimed at capturing stylistic similarity between words in an unsupervised manner. We propose to extend the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) embedding model (Mikolov et al., 2013b) by incorporating a wider context window to learn style-sensitive word vectors. We assume that the style of all words in an utterance is consistent. Additionally, we introduce a novel task of predicting lexical stylistic similarity and create a benchmark dataset for this purpose. Our experiments using this dataset support our assumption and show that the proposed extensions significantly contribute to the acquisition of style-sensitive word embeddings.

label: acl
text: The transfer or share of knowledge between languages is a potential solution to resource scarcity in NLP. However, the effectiveness of cross-lingual transfer can be challenged by variation in syntactic structures. Frameworks such as Universal Dependencies (UD) are designed to be cross-lingually consistent, but even in carefully designed resources trees representing equivalent sentences may not always overlap. In this paper, we measure cross-lingual syntactic variation, or anisomorphism, in the UD treebank collection, considering both morphological and structural properties. We show that reducing the level of anisomorphism yields consistent gains in cross-lingual transfer tasks. We introduce a source language selection procedure that facilitates effective cross-lingual parser transfer, and propose a typologically driven method for syntactic tree processing which reduces anisomorphism. Our results show the effectiveness of this method for both machine translation and cross-lingual sentence similarity, demonstrating the importance of syntactic structure compatibility for boosting cross-lingual transfer in NLP.

label: acl
text: The transfer of knowledge between languages can be a solution for resource scarcity in NLP, but the effectiveness of cross-lingual transfer can be hindered by variations in syntactic structures. Universal Dependencies (UD) frameworks aim to be cross-lingually consistent, but even in well-designed resources, the trees representing equivalent sentences may not always match. In this paper, we assess cross-lingual syntactic variation, or anisomorphism, in the UD treebank collection, taking into account both morphological and structural properties. Our results demonstrate that reducing anisomorphism leads to consistent improvements in cross-lingual transfer tasks. We present a source language selection procedure that enhances effective cross-lingual parser transfer, and propose a typologically driven method for syntactic tree processing that reduces anisomorphism. Our findings show the effectiveness of this method for both machine translation and cross-lingual sentence similarity, highlighting the significance of syntactic structure compatibility for enhancing cross-lingual transfer in NLP.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we define the task of gender rewriting in contexts involving two users (I and/or You) – first and second grammatical persons with independent grammatical gender preferences. We focus on Arabic, a gender-marking morphologically rich language. We develop a multi-step system that combines the positive aspects of both rule-based and neural rewriting models. Our results successfully demonstrate the viability of this approach on a recently created corpus for Arabic gender rewriting, achieving 88.42 M2 F0.5 on a blind test set. Our proposed system improves over previous work on the first-person-only version of this task, by 3.05 absolute increase in M2 F0.5. We demonstrate a use case of our gender rewriting system by using it to post-edit the output of a commercial MT system to provide personalized outputs based on the users' grammatical gender preferences. We make our code, data, and pretrained models publicly available.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we define the task of gender rewriting in contexts involving two users - the first and second grammatical persons with different grammatical gender preferences. Our focus is on Arabic, a morphologically rich language that marks gender. We present a multi-step system that combines the best aspects of rule-based and neural rewriting models. Our results show the viability of this approach on a newly created corpus for Arabic gender rewriting, achieving a score of 88.42 on M2 F0.5 in a blind test set. Our system outperforms previous work on the first-person-only version of this task, with a 3.05 increase in M2 F0.5. To demonstrate the practical applications of our gender rewriting system, we use it to post-edit the output of a commercial machine translation system, providing personalized outputs based on the users' grammatical gender preferences. Our code, data, and pre-trained models are available to the public.

label: emnlp
text: Most existing studies in text-to-SQL tasks do not require generating complex SQL queries with multiple clauses or sub-queries, and generalizing to new, unseen databases. In this paper we propose SyntaxSQLNet, a syntax tree network to address the complex and cross-domain text-to-SQL generation task. SyntaxSQLNet employs a SQL specific syntax tree-based decoder with SQL generation path history and table-aware column attention encoders. We evaluate SyntaxSQLNet on a new large-scale text-to-SQL corpus containing databases with multiple tables and complex SQL queries containing multiple SQL clauses and nested queries. We use a database split setting where databases in the test set are unseen during training. Experimental results show that SyntaxSQLNet can handle a significantly greater number of complex SQL examples than prior work, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art model by 9.5% in exact matching accuracy. To our knowledge, we are the first to study this complex text-to-SQL task. Our task and models with the latest updates are available at https://yale-lily.github.io/seq2sql/spider.

label: emnlp
text: Most previous studies on text-to-SQL tasks have not tackled the challenge of generating complex SQL queries with multiple clauses or sub-queries, and generalizing to new, unseen databases. To address this, we present SyntaxSQLNet, a syntax tree network that can handle complex and cross-domain text-to-SQL generation tasks. SyntaxSQLNet features a SQL-specific syntax tree-based decoder, with SQL generation path history and table-aware column attention encoders. We evaluate SyntaxSQLNet on a large-scale text-to-SQL corpus that includes databases with multiple tables and complex SQL queries with multiple clauses and nested queries. The evaluation is conducted using a database split setting, where the databases in the test set are unseen during training. Our results show that SyntaxSQLNet outperforms the previous state-of-the-art model by 9.5% in exact matching accuracy, and can handle a significantly greater number of complex SQL examples. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study this complex text-to-SQL task. Our task and models, along with the latest updates, can be accessed at https://yale-lily.github.io/seq2sql/spider.

label: coling
text: This paper introduces a novel Self-supervised Fine-grained Dialogue Evaluation framework (SelF-Eval). The core idea is to model the correlation between turn quality and the entire dialogue quality. We first propose a novel automatic data construction method that can automatically assign fine-grained scores for arbitrarily dialogue data. Then we train SelF-Eval with a multi-level contrastive learning schema which helps to distinguish different score levels. Experimental results on multiple benchmarks show that SelF-Eval is highly consistent with human evaluations and better than the state-of-the-art models. We give a detailed analysis of the experiments in this paper. Our code is available on GitHub.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a new Self-supervised Fine-grained Dialogue Evaluation framework (SelF-Eval) that models the correlation between turn quality and the overall quality of a dialogue. Our approach introduces a novel method for automatic data construction that assigns fine-grained scores to arbitrary dialogue data. SelF-Eval is trained using a multi-level contrastive learning schema that helps distinguish various score levels. Results from experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SelF-Eval is highly consistent with human evaluations and outperforms state-of-the-art models. A thorough analysis of the experiments is provided, and the code is available on GitHub.

label: emnlp
text: Many modern neural document summarization systems based on encoder-decoder networks are designed to produce abstractive summaries. We attempted to verify the degree of abstractiveness of modern neural abstractive summarization systems by calculating overlaps in terms of various types of units. Upon the observation that many abstractive systems tend to be near-extractive in practice, we also implemented a pure copy system, which achieved comparable results as abstractive summarizers while being far more computationally efficient. These findings suggest the possibility for future efforts towards more efficient systems that could better utilize the vocabulary in the original document.

label: emnlp
text: Many modern neural document summarization systems that are based on encoder-decoder networks are designed to create abstractive summaries. To assess the level of abstractiveness of these systems, we calculated the overlap of various types of units. Our findings showed that many abstractive systems tend to be close to extractive in nature. To address this, we implemented a pure copy system that achieved similar results to abstractive summarizers while being much more computationally efficient. These results imply the potential for future development of more efficient systems that can better leverage the vocabulary in the original document.

label: acl
text: We investigate a new commonsense inference task: given an event described in a short free-form text (“X drinks coffee in the morning”), a system reasons about the likely intents (“X wants to stay awake”) and reactions (“X feels alert”) of the event's participants. To support this study, we construct a new crowdsourced corpus of 25,000 event phrases covering a diverse range of everyday events and situations. We report baseline performance on this task, demonstrating that neural encoder-decoder models can successfully compose embedding representations of previously unseen events and reason about the likely intents and reactions of the event participants. In addition, we demonstrate how commonsense inference on people's intents and reactions can help unveil the implicit gender inequality prevalent in modern movie scripts.

label: acl
text: We investigate a new task in commonsense inference: given a short, free-form description of an event (e.g. "X drinks coffee in the morning"), a system must reason about the probable intents (e.g. "X wants to stay awake") and reactions (e.g. "X feels alert") of the event's participants. To support this research, we have created a new corpus of 25,000 event phrases covering a wide range of everyday situations. Our results show that neural encoder-decoder models can effectively generate embedding representations for unseen events and make accurate predictions about the participants' intents and reactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this type of commonsense inference can uncover implicit gender inequalities in modern movie scripts.

label: acl
text: Sequence modeling has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on natural language and document understanding tasks. However, it is challenging to correctly serialize tokens in form-like documents in practice due to their variety of layout patterns. We propose FormNet, a structure-aware sequence model to mitigate the suboptimal serialization of forms. First, we design Rich Attention that leverages the spatial relationship between tokens in a form for more precise attention score calculation. Second, we construct Super-Tokens for each word by embedding representations from their neighboring tokens through graph convolutions. FormNet therefore explicitly recovers local syntactic information that may have been lost during serialization. In experiments, FormNet outperforms existing methods with a more compact model size and less pre-training data, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on CORD, FUNSD and Payment benchmarks.

label: acl
text: The proposed FormNet is a structure-aware sequence model that addresses the challenge of correctly serializing tokens in form-like documents. It leverages the spatial relationship between tokens to calculate more precise attention scores through Rich Attention, and embeds representations from neighboring tokens to construct Super-Tokens that recover local syntactic information. The experiments show that FormNet outperforms existing methods with a smaller model size and less pre-training data, setting new state-of-the-art performance on CORD, FUNSD, and Payment benchmarks.

label: acl
text: We present a new human-human dialogue dataset - PhotoChat, the first dataset that casts light on the photo sharing behavior in online messaging. PhotoChat contains 12k dialogues, each of which is paired with a user photo that is shared during the conversation. Based on this dataset, we propose two tasks to facilitate research on image-text modeling: a photo-sharing intent prediction task that predicts whether one intends to share a photo in the next conversation turn, and a photo retrieval task that retrieves the most relevant photo according to the dialogue context. In addition, for both tasks, we provide baseline models using the state-of-the-art models and report their benchmark performances. The best image retrieval model achieves 10.4% recall@1 (out of 1000 candidates) and the best photo intent prediction model achieves 58.1% F1 score, indicating that the dataset presents interesting yet challenging real-world problems. We are releasing PhotoChat to facilitate future research work among the community.

label: acl
text: We introduce PhotoChat, a new human-human dialogue dataset that sheds light on photo sharing behavior in online messaging. This dataset contains 12,000 dialogues, each paired with a user photo that is shared during the conversation. To encourage research on image-text modeling, we propose two tasks: photo-sharing intent prediction and photo retrieval. The former predicts whether one intends to share a photo in the next conversation turn, while the latter retrieves the most relevant photo based on the dialogue context. We provide baseline models using state-of-the-art models and report their benchmark performances. The best image retrieval model has a recall@1 of 10.4% (out of 1000 candidates), and the best photo intent prediction model has a F1 score of 58.1%, indicating that the dataset presents challenging real-world problems. We hope to facilitate future research work in the community by releasing PhotoChat.

label: coling
text: Medication recommendation is a crucial task for intelligent healthcare systems. Previous studies mainly recommend medications with electronic health records (EHRs). However, some details of interactions between doctors and patients may be ignored or omitted in EHRs, which are essential for automatic medication recommendation. Therefore, we make the first attempt to recommend medications with the conversations between doctors and patients. In this work, we construct DIALMED, the first high-quality dataset for medical dialogue-based medication recommendation task. It contains 11, 996 medical dialogues related to 16 common diseases from 3 departments and 70 corresponding common medications. Furthermore, we propose a Dialogue structure and Disease knowledge aware Network (DDN), where a QA Dialogue Graph mechanism is designed to model the dialogue structure and the knowledge graph is used to introduce external disease knowledge. The extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method is a promising solution to recommend medications with medical dialogues. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/f-window/DialMed.

text: The task of recommending medication is vital for intelligent healthcare systems. While previous studies have primarily relied on electronic health records (EHRs) for medication recommendations, these records can sometimes omit essential details of interactions between doctors and patients. To address this issue, we present the first attempt to recommend medications based on medical dialogues between doctors and patients. We introduce DIALMED, the first high-quality dataset for this task, which includes 11,996 medical dialogues related to 16 common diseases and 70 corresponding medications from three different departments. Additionally, we propose the Dialogue Structure and Disease Knowledge aware Network (DDN), which incorporates a QA Dialogue Graph mechanism to model the dialogue structure and a knowledge graph to incorporate external disease knowledge. Our experimental results show that this method is a promising solution for recommending medications using medical dialogues. The dataset and code can be accessed at https://github.com/f-window/DialMed.

label: emnlp
text: Identifying the salience (i.e. importance) of discourse units is an important task in language understanding. While events play important roles in text documents, little research exists on analyzing their saliency status. This paper empirically studies Event Salience and proposes two salience detection models based on discourse relations. The first is a feature based salience model that incorporates cohesion among discourse units. The second is a neural model that captures more complex interactions between discourse units. In our new large-scale event salience corpus, both methods significantly outperform the strong frequency baseline, while our neural model further improves the feature based one by a large margin. Our analyses demonstrate that our neural model captures interesting connections between salience and discourse unit relations (e.g., scripts and frame structures).

label: emnlp
text:
Our models provide a promising direction for future work in event salience detection.
