Despite recent improvements in coreference resolvers on the CoNLL dataset, they still struggle to generalize to new domains or datasets. In this paper, we examine the role of linguistic features in building more generalizable coreference resolvers. Our findings show that using additional linguistic features only slightly improves generalization. However, by incorporating features and subsets of their values that are informative for coreference resolution, we significantly improve generalization. As a result, our system achieves state-of-the-art performance in out-of-domain evaluations, for example, on WikiCoref, our system trained on CoNLL performs on par with a system specifically designed for that dataset.

label: emnlp
text: Homographic puns have a long history in human writing, widely used in written and spoken literature, which usually occur in a certain syntactic or stylistic structure. How to recognize homographic puns is an important research. However, homographic pun recognition does not solve very well in existing work. In this work, we first use WordNet to understand and expand word embedding for settling the polysemy of homographic puns, and then propose a WordNet-Encoded Collocation-Attention network model (WECA) which combined with the context weights for recognizing the puns. Our experiments on the SemEval2017 Task7 and Pun of the Day demonstrate that the proposed model is able to distinguish between homographic pun and non-homographic pun texts. We show the effectiveness of the model to present the capability of choosing qualitatively informative words. The results show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance on homographic puns recognition.

label: emnlp
text: Homographic puns, a type of word play that uses the same spelling for different meanings, have a long history in human writing and are widely used in written and spoken literature. Recognizing homographic puns is an important area of research, but existing methods are not very effective. In this work, we first use WordNet to expand word embeddings and address the polysemy of homographic puns. Then, we propose a WordNet-Encoded Collocation-Attention network (WECA) model that combines context weights to recognize puns. Our experiments on the SemEval2017 Task7 and Pun of the Day datasets show that the WECA model is able to distinguish between homographic puns and non-homographic puns and outperforms existing methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the model in selecting informative words and achieving state-of-the-art performance in homographic pun recognition.

label: acl
text: We conduct the most comprehensive study to date into translating words via images. To facilitate research on the task, we introduce a large-scale multilingual corpus of images, each labeled with the word it represents. Past datasets have been limited to only a few high-resource languages and unrealistically easy translation settings. In contrast, we have collected by far the largest available dataset for this task, with images for approximately 10,000 words in each of 100 languages. We run experiments on a dozen high resource languages and 20 low resources languages, demonstrating the effect of word concreteness and part-of-speech on translation quality. %We find that while image features work best for concrete nouns, they are sometimes effective on other parts of speech. To improve image-based translation, we introduce a novel method of predicting word concreteness from images, which improves on a previous state-of-the-art unsupervised technique. This allows us to predict when image-based translation may be effective, enabling consistent improvements to a state-of-the-art text-based word translation system. Our code and the Massively Multilingual Image Dataset (MMID) are available at http://multilingual-images.org/.

label: acl
text: We have conducted the most comprehensive study to date on translating words through images. To support our research, we have introduced a large-scale multilingual corpus of images, each labeled with the corresponding word. Previous datasets were limited to only a few high-resource languages and unrealistic translation settings. In contrast, our dataset is by far the largest available, with images for approximately 10,000 words in each of 100 languages. We have conducted experiments on 12 high-resource languages and 20 low-resource languages, demonstrating the impact of word concreteness and part-of-speech on translation quality. Our findings show that while image features are most effective for concrete nouns, they can also be effective for other parts of speech. To enhance image-based translation, we have developed a novel method for predicting word concreteness from images, which outperforms the previous state-of-the-art unsupervised technique. This enables us to predict when image-based translation will be effective, leading to consistent improvements in a state-of-the-art text-based word translation system. Our code and the Massively Multilingual Image Dataset (MMID) can be accessed at http://multilingual-images.org/.

label: acl
text: Few-shot NER needs to effectively capture information from limited instances and transfer useful knowledge from external resources. In this paper, we propose a self-describing mechanism for few-shot NER, which can effectively leverage illustrative instances and precisely transfer knowledge from external resources by describing both entity types and mentions using a universal concept set. Specifically, we design Self-describing Networks (SDNet), a Seq2Seq generation model which can universally describe mentions using concepts, automatically map novel entity types to concepts, and adaptively recognize entities on-demand. We pre-train SDNet with large-scale corpus, and conduct experiments on 8 benchmarks from different domains. Experiments show that SDNet achieves competitive performances on all benchmarks and achieves the new state-of-the-art on 6 benchmarks, which demonstrates its effectiveness and robustness.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we present a self-describing mechanism for few-shot Named Entity Recognition (NER), which effectively captures information from limited instances and transfers useful knowledge from external resources. Our proposed mechanism, Self-describing Networks (SDNet), is a Seq2Seq generation model that describes both entity types and mentions using a universal concept set. SDNet can universally describe mentions using concepts, map novel entity types to concepts, and recognize entities on-demand. We pre-trained SDNet with a large-scale corpus and conducted experiments on eight benchmarks from different domains. The results show that SDNet achieved competitive performance on all benchmarks and set new state-of-the-art results on six of them, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.

label: acl
text: Recent works made significant advances on summarization tasks, facilitated by summarization datasets. Several existing datasets have the form of coherent-paragraph summaries. However, these datasets were curated from academic documents that were written for experts, thus making the essential step of assessing the summarization output through human-evaluation very demanding. To overcome these limitations, we present a dataset based on article summaries appearing on the WikiHow website, composed of how-to articles and coherent-paragraph summaries written in plain language. We compare our dataset attributes to existing ones, including readability and world-knowledge, showing our dataset makes human evaluation significantly easier and thus, more effective. A human evaluation conducted on PubMed and the proposed dataset reinforces our findings.

label: acl
text: Recent advances in summarization tasks have been facilitated by the availability of summarization datasets. Many of these datasets consist of coherent-paragraph summaries that were curated from academic documents written for experts. However, this makes the task of evaluating the summarization output through human-evaluation very challenging. To address this issue, we have created a new dataset based on article summaries from the WikiHow website. These summaries are written in plain language and consist of how-to articles and coherent-paragraph summaries. Our comparison of the attributes of our dataset with existing ones, including readability and world-knowledge, demonstrates that our dataset makes human evaluation easier and more effective. This was confirmed by a human evaluation conducted on both PubMed and our proposed dataset.

label: acl
text: Training datasets for semantic parsing are typically small due to the higher expertise required for annotation than most other NLP tasks. As a result, models for this application usually need additional prior knowledge to be built into the architecture or algorithm. The increased dependency on human experts hinders automation and raises the development and maintenance costs in practice. This work investigates whether a generic transformer-based seq2seq model can achieve competitive performance with minimal code-generation-specific inductive bias design. By exploiting a relatively sizeable monolingual corpus of the target programming language, which is cheap to mine from the web, we achieved 81.03% exact match accuracy on Django and 32.57 BLEU score on CoNaLa. Both are SOTA to the best of our knowledge. This positive evidence highlights a potentially easier path toward building accurate semantic parsers in practice.

label: acl
text: Training datasets for semantic parsing are typically small due to the higher level of expertise required for annotation, compared to other NLP tasks. As a result, models for this application often require additional prior knowledge to be incorporated into their architecture or algorithm. This reliance on human experts makes automation more difficult and increases the development and maintenance costs. This study explores the feasibility of using a generic transformer-based seq2seq model with minimal code-generation-specific inductive bias design to achieve competitive performance. By leveraging a relatively large monolingual corpus of the target programming language, which can be easily mined from the web, we achieved an exact match accuracy of 81.03% on Django and a BLEU score of 32.57 on CoNaLa. These results are state-of-the-art, to the best of our knowledge. Our findings suggest that this approach could provide a more straightforward path to building accurate semantic parsers in practice.

label: coling
text: Fact-checking has gained increasing attention due to the widespread of falsified information. Most fact-checking approaches focus on claims made in English only due to the data scarcity issue in other languages. The lack of fact-checking datasets in low-resource languages calls for an effective cross-lingual transfer technique for fact-checking. Additionally, trustworthy information in different languages can be complementary and helpful in verifying facts. To this end, we present the first fact-checking framework augmented with cross-lingual retrieval that aggregates evidence retrieved from multiple languages through a cross-lingual retriever. Given the absence of cross-lingual information retrieval datasets with claim-like queries, we train the retriever with our proposed Cross-lingual Inverse Cloze Task (X-ICT), a self-supervised algorithm that creates training instances by translating the title of a passage. The goal for X-ICT is to learn cross-lingual retrieval in which the model learns to identify the passage corresponding to a given translated title. On the X-Fact dataset, our approach achieves 2.23% absolute F1 improvement in the zero-shot cross-lingual setup over prior systems. The source code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/khuangaf/CONCRETE.

label: coling
text: Fact-checking has become increasingly important due to the prevalence of false information. Most fact-checking methods focus exclusively on claims made in English, due to the scarcity of data in other languages. To address this issue, a cross-lingual transfer technique is needed for effective fact-checking. Complementary, trustworthy information in different languages can also be useful in verifying facts. To address these challenges, we present a fact-checking framework that incorporates cross-lingual retrieval, aggregating evidence from multiple languages through a cross-lingual retriever. However, there are currently no cross-lingual information retrieval datasets with claim-like queries. To overcome this, we propose the Cross-lingual Inverse Cloze Task (X-ICT), a self-supervised algorithm that trains the retriever by translating the title of a passage. The goal of X-ICT is to learn cross-lingual retrieval, so the model can identify the corresponding passage for a given translated title. Our approach, tested on the X-Fact dataset, achieved a 2.23% absolute F1 improvement in the zero-shot cross-lingual setup compared to previous systems. The source code and data are available for public use at https://github.com/khuangaf/CONCRETE.

label: naacl
text: Pre-trained Language Models (PTLMs) have been shown to perform well on natural language tasks. Many prior works have leveraged structured commonsense present in the form of entities linked through labeled relations in Knowledge Graphs (KGs) to assist PTLMs. Retrieval approaches use KG as a separate static module which limits coverage since KGs contain finite knowledge. Generative methods train PTLMs on KG triples to improve the scale at which knowledge can be obtained. However, training on symbolic KG entities limits their applicability in tasks involving natural language text where they ignore overall context. To mitigate this, we propose a CommonSense Contextualizer (CoSe-Co) conditioned on sentences as input to make it generically usable in tasks for generating knowledge relevant to the overall context of input text. To train CoSe-Co, we propose a novel dataset comprising of sentence and commonsense knowledge pairs. The knowledge inferred by CoSe-Co is diverse and contain novel entities not present in the underlying KG. We augment generated knowledge in Multi-Choice QA and Open-ended CommonSense Reasoning tasks leading to improvements over current best methods on CSQA, ARC, QASC and OBQA datasets. We also demonstrate its applicability in improving performance of a baseline model for paraphrase generation task.

label: naacl
text: Pre-trained Language Models (PTLMs) have been shown to be effective on natural language processing tasks. Many previous studies have utilized structured commonsense information in the form of entities linked through labeled relationships in Knowledge Graphs (KGs) to aid PTLMs. However, retrieval methods use KGs as a separate static module that restricts coverage, as KGs only contain finite knowledge. Generative methods train PTLMs on KG triples to expand the scope of knowledge that can be obtained. However, training on symbolic KG entities limits their usefulness in tasks that involve natural language text, as they ignore the overall context. To address this issue, we propose a CommonSense Contextualizer (CoSe-Co) that is conditioned on sentences as input, making it versatile for generating knowledge that is relevant to the input text's context. To train CoSe-Co, we create a novel dataset consisting of sentence and commonsense knowledge pairs. The knowledge derived from CoSe-Co is diverse and includes novel entities not found in the underlying KG. We apply the generated knowledge to Multi-Choice QA and Open-ended CommonSense Reasoning tasks, resulting in improved performance on CSQA, ARC, QASC, and OBQA datasets compared to current best methods. Additionally, we demonstrate the usefulness of CoSe-Co in improving the performance of a baseline model for paraphrase generation.

label: acl
text: A few approaches have been developed to improve neural machine translation (NMT) models with multiple passes of decoding. However, their performance gains are limited because of lacking proper policies to terminate the multi-pass process. To address this issue, we introduce a novel architecture of Rewriter-Evaluator. Translating a source sentence involves multiple rewriting passes. In every pass, a rewriter generates a new translation to improve the past translation. Termination of this multi-pass process is determined by a score of translation quality estimated by an evaluator. We also propose prioritized gradient descent (PGD) to jointly and efficiently train the rewriter and the evaluator. Extensive experiments on three machine translation tasks show that our architecture notably improves the performances of NMT models and significantly outperforms prior methods. An oracle experiment reveals that it can largely reduce performance gaps to the oracle policy. Experiments confirm that the evaluator trained with PGD is more accurate than prior methods in determining proper numbers of rewriting.

label: acl
text: To improve the performance of neural machine translation (NMT) models, several approaches have been developed that use multiple passes of decoding. However, these approaches have limited success due to a lack of proper policies for terminating the multi-pass process. To address this issue, we present a novel architecture called the Rewriter-Evaluator. This architecture involves multiple rewriting passes in which a rewriter generates a new translation to improve the previous one. The termination of the multi-pass process is determined by an evaluator that scores the translation quality. To train the rewriter and evaluator efficiently, we also propose the use of prioritized gradient descent (PGD). Our experiments on three machine translation tasks show that our architecture significantly improves NMT performance and outperforms prior methods. An oracle experiment shows that it can significantly reduce performance gaps compared to the oracle policy. The results confirm that the evaluator trained with PGD is more accurate in determining the proper number of rewriting passes than prior methods.

label: naacl
text: Each utterance in multi-turn empathetic dialogues has features such as emotion, keywords, and utterance-level meaning. Feature transitions between utterances occur naturally. However, existing approaches fail to perceive the transitions because they extract features for the context at the coarse-grained level. To solve the above issue, we propose a novel approach of recognizing feature transitions between utterances, which helps understand the dialogue flow and better grasp the features of utterance that needs attention. Also, we introduce a response generation strategy to help focus on emotion and keywords related to appropriate features when generating responses. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms baselines and especially, achieves significant improvements on multi-turn dialogues.

label: naacl
text: Each utterance in multi-turn empathetic dialogues has distinct features such as emotions, keywords, and utterance-level meanings. These features transition naturally between utterances, but existing approaches struggle to recognize these transitions as they extract context features at a coarse-grained level. To address this issue, we propose a new method for recognizing feature transitions between utterances. This helps to better understand the flow of the dialogue, and to more effectively identify the features that require attention. Additionally, we introduce a response generation strategy that focuses on emotions and keywords related to the relevant features when generating responses. Our approach outperforms existing methods, particularly in multi-turn dialogues, as demonstrated by our experimental results.

label: coling
text: Named entity recognition has become an increasingly useful tool for digital humanities research, specially when it comes to historical texts. However, historical texts pose a wide range of challenges to both named entity recognition and natural language processing in general that are still difficult to address even with modern neural methods. In this article we focus in named entity recognition for historical French, and in particular for Early Modern French (16th-18th c.), i.e. Ancien Régime French. However, instead of developing a specialised architecture to tackle the particularities of this state of language, we opt for a data-driven approach by developing a new corpus with fine-grained entity annotation, covering three centuries of literature corresponding to the early modern period; we try to annotate as much data as possible producing a corpus that is many times bigger than the most popular NER evaluation corpora for both Contemporary English and French. We then fine-tune existing state-of-the-art architectures for Early Modern and Contemporary French, obtaining results that are on par with those of the current state-of-the-art NER systems for Contemporary English. Both the corpus and the fine-tuned models are released.

label: coling
text: Named entity recognition (NER) has become a valuable tool for digital humanities research, especially when working with historical texts. Despite advancements in NER and natural language processing, historical texts present a wide range of challenges that are still difficult to address using modern neural methods. This article focuses on NER for Early Modern French (16th-18th c.), also known as Ancien Régime French. Instead of creating a specialized architecture, we adopt a data-driven approach by developing a new corpus with fine-grained entity annotation covering three centuries of literature from the early modern period. Our corpus is much larger than the popular NER evaluation corpora for both Contemporary English and French. We fine-tune existing state-of-the-art architectures for Early Modern and Contemporary French and achieve results that are comparable to the current state-of-the-art NER systems for Contemporary English. Both the corpus and the fine-tuned models will be made publicly available.

label: coling
text: Reading comprehension models are based on recurrent neural networks that sequentially process the document tokens. As interest turns to answering more complex questions over longer documents, sequential reading of large portions of text becomes a substantial bottleneck. Inspired by how humans use document structure, we propose a novel framework for reading comprehension. We represent documents as trees, and model an agent that learns to interleave quick navigation through the document tree with more expensive answer extraction. To encourage exploration of the document tree, we propose a new algorithm, based on Deep Q-Network (DQN), which strategically samples tree nodes at training time. Empirically we find our algorithm improves question answering performance compared to DQN and a strong information-retrieval (IR) baseline, and that ensembling our model with the IR baseline results in further gains in performance.

label: coling
text: Reading comprehension models are based on recurrent neural networks that process document tokens sequentially. As the focus shifts towards answering more complex questions in longer documents, sequential reading of large text portions becomes a significant bottleneck. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for reading comprehension that is inspired by human document processing. Our framework represents documents as trees and models an agent that learns to interleave quick navigation through the tree with more intensive answer extraction. To promote exploration of the document tree, we introduce a new algorithm, based on Deep Q-Network (DQN), that strategically samples tree nodes during training. Our results show that our algorithm outperforms DQN and a strong information-retrieval (IR) baseline, and that combining our model with the IR baseline results in even better performance.

label: acl
text: Data-to-text generation focuses on generating fluent natural language responses from structured meaning representations (MRs). Such representations are compositional and it is costly to collect responses for all possible combinations of atomic meaning schemata, thereby necessitating few-shot generalization to novel MRs. In this work, we systematically study the compositional generalization of the state-of-the-art T5 models in few-shot data-to-text tasks. We show that T5 models fail to generalize to unseen MRs, and we propose a template-based input representation that considerably improves the model's generalization capability. To further improve the model's performance, we propose an approach based on self-training using fine-tuned BLEURT for pseudo-response selection. On the commonly-used SGD and Weather benchmarks, the proposed self-training approach improves tree accuracy by C-C-C and reduces the slot error rates by D-D-D over the strong T5 baselines in few-shot settings.

label: acl
text: The focus of data-to-text generation is to produce fluent natural language responses from structured meaning representations (MRs). However, it is challenging to collect responses for all possible combinations of MRs, leading to the need for few-shot generalization. In this study, we examine the compositional generalization of state-of-the-art T5 models in few-shot data-to-text tasks. Our findings indicate that T5 models struggle to generalize to new MRs. To address this issue, we propose a template-based input representation that significantly improves the model's generalization ability. Additionally, we introduce a self-training approach using fine-tuned BLEURT for pseudo-response selection, which further improves the model's performance. On the SGD and Weather benchmarks, our approach improves tree accuracy by C-C-C and reduces slot error rates by D-D-D compared to strong T5 baselines in few-shot settings.

label: acl
text: Users of medical question answering systems often submit long and detailed questions, making it hard to achieve high recall in answer retrieval. To alleviate this problem, we propose a novel Multi-Task Learning (MTL) method with data augmentation for medical question understanding. We first establish an equivalence between the tasks of question summarization and Recognizing Question Entailment (RQE) using their definitions in the medical domain. Based on this equivalence, we propose a data augmentation algorithm to use just one dataset to optimize for both tasks, with a weighted MTL loss. We introduce gradually soft parameter-sharing: a constraint for decoder parameters to be close, that is gradually loosened as we move to the highest layer. We show through ablation studies that our proposed novelties improve performance. Our method outperforms existing MTL methods across 4 datasets of medical question pairs, in ROUGE scores, RQE accuracy and human evaluation. Finally, we show that our method fares better than single-task learning under 4 low-resource settings.

label: acl
text: The users of medical question answering systems often submit long, detailed questions, making it challenging to achieve high recall in answer retrieval. To address this issue, we propose a Multi-Task Learning (MTL) method with data augmentation for medical question understanding. We equate the tasks of question summarization and Recognizing Question Entailment (RQE) using their definitions in the medical domain and use a data augmentation algorithm to optimize for both tasks with a weighted MTL loss. Our method features gradually soft parameter-sharing, a constraint for decoder parameters to be close, which is gradually relaxed as we move to the highest layer. Ablation studies demonstrate that our proposed novelties improve performance, and our method outperforms existing MTL methods across four datasets of medical question pairs in terms of ROUGE scores, RQE accuracy, and human evaluation. Additionally, our method fares better than single-task learning in four low-resource settings.

label: coling
text: Measuring Sentence Textual Similarity (STS) is a classic task that can be applied to many downstream NLP applications such as text generation and retrieval. In this paper, we focus on unsupervised STS that works on various domains but only requires minimal data and computational resources. Theoretically, we propose a light-weighted Expectation-Correction (EC) formulation for STS computation. EC formulation unifies unsupervised STS approaches including the cosine similarity of Additively Composed (AC) sentence embeddings, Optimal Transport (OT), and Tree Kernels (TK). Moreover, we propose the Recursive Optimal Transport Similarity (ROTS) algorithm to capture the compositional phrase semantics by composing multiple recursive EC formulations. ROTS finishes in linear time and is faster than its predecessors. ROTS is empirically more effective and scalable than previous approaches. Extensive experiments on 29 STS tasks under various settings show the clear advantage of ROTS over existing approaches. Detailed ablation studies prove the effectiveness of our approaches.

label: coling
text: Measuring Textual Similarity (STS) in sentences is a classic task that is widely applicable in various NLP applications, such as text generation and retrieval. This paper focuses on unsupervised STS that can be used across different domains while requiring minimal data and computational resources. We propose a lightweight Expectation-Correction (EC) formulation for STS computation that unifies existing unsupervised STS approaches, including the cosine similarity of Additively Composed (AC) sentence embeddings, Optimal Transport (OT), and Tree Kernels (TK). Additionally, we introduce the Recursive Optimal Transport Similarity (ROTS) algorithm, which captures compositional phrase semantics by combining multiple EC formulations recursively. ROTS is faster than previous approaches, with a linear runtime, and is more effective and scalable, as shown by extensive experiments on 29 STS tasks in various settings. Our results are further validated by detailed ablation studies.

label: coling
text: Rationale-based models provide a unique way to provide justifiable results for relation classification models by identifying rationales (key words and phrases that a person can use to justify the relation in the sentence) during the process. However, existing generative networks used to extract rationales come with a trade-off between extracting diversified rationales and achieving good classification results. In this paper, we propose a multilevel heuristic approach to regulate rationale extraction to avoid extracting monotonous rationales without compromising classification performance. In our model, rationale selection is regularized by a semi-supervised process and features from different levels: word, syntax, sentence, and corpus. We evaluate our approach on the SemEval 2010 dataset that includes 19 relation classes and the quality of extracted rationales with our manually-labeled rationales. Experiments show a significant improvement in classification performance and a 20% gain in rationale interpretability compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

label: coling
text: Rationale-based models offer a unique approach to providing justifiable results for relation classification by identifying key words and phrases that justify the relation in a sentence. However, existing generative networks used to extract rationales come with a trade-off between diversity and accuracy. In this paper, we present a multilevel heuristic approach that regulates rationale extraction to prevent the extraction of repetitive rationales while maintaining classification performance. Our model uses a semi-supervised process and features from various levels, including words, syntax, sentences, and corpus. We evaluate our approach on the SemEval 2010 dataset, which includes 19 relation classes, and compare the quality of our extracted rationales to manually-labeled rationales. Our experiments demonstrate a significant improvement in classification performance and a 20% increase in rationale interpretability compared to state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: Open-domain question answering is a challenging task with a wide variety of practical applications. Existing modern approaches mostly follow a standard two-stage paradigm: retriever then reader. In this article, we focus on improving the effectiveness of the reader module and propose a novel copy-augmented generative approach that integrates the merits of both extractive and generative readers. In particular, our model is built upon the powerful generative model FiD (CITATION). We enhance the original generative reader by incorporating a pointer network to encourage the model to directly copy words from the retrieved passages. We conduct experiments on the two benchmark datasets, Natural Questions and TriviaQA, and the empirical results demonstrate the performance gains of our proposed approach.

label: acl
text: Open-domain question answering is a challenging task with numerous practical applications. Most existing approaches follow a standard two-step process: retrieval and then reading. In this article, we focus on enhancing the reader module and propose a novel copy-augmented generative approach that combines the best of both extractive and generative readers. Our model is based on the powerful generative model FiD (CITATION). We have improved the original generative reader by adding a pointer network, which encourages the model to directly copy words from the retrieved passages. We conducted experiments on two benchmark datasets, Natural Questions and TriviaQA, and the results show that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods.

label: naacl
text: We present FactPEGASUS, an abstractive summarization model that addresses the problem of factuality during pre-training and fine-tuning: (1) We augment the sentence selection strategy of PEGASUS's (Zhang et al., 2019) pre-training objective to create pseudo-summaries that are both important and factual; (2) We introduce three complementary components for fine-tuning. The corrector removes hallucinations present in the reference summary, the contrastor uses contrastive learning to better differentiate nonfactual summaries from factual ones, and the connector bridges the gap between the pre-training and fine-tuning for better transfer of knowledge. Experiments on three downstream tasks demonstrate that FactPEGASUS substantially improves factuality evaluated by multiple automatic metrics and humans. Our thorough analysis suggests that FactPEGASUS is more factual than using the original pre-training objective in zero-shot and few-shot settings, retains factual behavior more robustly than strong baselines, and does not rely entirely on becoming more extractive to improve factuality.

label: naacl
text: We introduce FactPEGASUS, a novel abstractive summarization model that addresses the issue of factuality during both pre-training and fine-tuning. Our model enhances the sentence selection strategy of PEGASUS (Zhang et al., 2019) by creating pseudo-summaries that are both important and factual. Additionally, we introduce three complementary components for fine-tuning: the corrector, which removes hallucinations present in the reference summary; the contrastor, which uses contrastive learning to better differentiate factual summaries from nonfactual ones; and the connector, which bridges the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning to facilitate better transfer of knowledge. Our experiments on three downstream tasks demonstrate that FactPEGASUS significantly improves factuality, as evaluated by multiple automatic metrics and human assessments. Our analysis shows that FactPEGASUS outperforms the original pre-training objective in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, and retains its factual behavior more robustly than strong baselines, without relying solely on becoming more extractive to improve factuality.

label: coling
text: Most question answering (QA) systems are based on raw text and structured knowledge graph. However, raw text corpora are hard for QA system to understand, and structured knowledge graph needs intensive manual work, while it is relatively easy to obtain semi-structured tables from many sources directly, or build them automatically. In this paper, we build an end-to-end system to answer multiple choice questions with semi-structured tables as its knowledge. Our system answers queries by two steps. First, it finds the most similar tables. Then the system measures the relevance between each question and candidate table cells, and choose the most related cell as the source of answer. The system is evaluated with TabMCQ dataset, and gets a huge improvement compared to the state of the art.

label: coling
text: Most QA systems are built on raw text and structured knowledge graphs, but these sources can be challenging for the system to understand. Raw text corpora are difficult to interpret, and creating structured knowledge graphs requires significant manual effort. On the other hand, obtaining semi-structured tables is relatively straightforward, either through direct sources or through automatic generation. This paper introduces an end-to-end system that answers multiple choice questions using semi-structured tables as its knowledge base. The system works in two steps: it first identifies the most similar tables, and then determines the relevance between the question and the candidate table cells, ultimately selecting the most relevant cell as the answer source. The system was evaluated using the TabMCQ dataset and showed significant improvement compared to the state-of-the-art.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we firstly empirically find that existing models struggle to handle hard mentions due to their insufficient contexts, which consequently limits their overall typing performance. To this end, we propose to exploit sibling mentions for enhancing the mention representations.Specifically, we present two different metrics for sibling selection and employ an attentive graph neural network to aggregate information from sibling mentions. The proposed graph model is scalable in that unseen test mentions are allowed to be added as new nodes for inference.Exhaustive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our sibling learning strategy, where our model outperforms ten strong baselines. Moreover, our experiments indeed prove the superiority of sibling mentions in helping clarify the types for hard mentions.

label: acl
text: In this study, we first discover through empirical evidence that current models have difficulty handling challenging mentions due to their limited context. To address this issue, we propose a solution that leverages sibling mentions to improve mention representation. We present two metrics for selecting sibling mentions and utilize an attentive graph neural network to gather information from these mentions. Our graph model is scalable, as it allows for the addition of unseen test mentions as new nodes during inference. Our experiments show the effectiveness of our sibling learning approach, with our model outperforming ten strong baselines. Our results also demonstrate the superiority of sibling mentions in clarifying types for challenging mentions.

label: acl
text: Easy access, variety of content, and fast widespread interactions are some of the reasons making social media increasingly popular. However, this rise has also enabled the propagation of fake news, text published by news sources with an intent to spread misinformation and sway beliefs. Detecting it is an important and challenging problem to prevent large scale misinformation and maintain a healthy society. We view fake news detection as reasoning over the relations between sources, articles they publish, and engaging users on social media in a graph framework. After embedding this information, we formulate inference operators which augment the graph edges by revealing unobserved interactions between its elements, such as similarity between documents' contents and users' engagement patterns. Our experiments over two challenging fake news detection tasks show that using inference operators leads to a better understanding of the social media framework enabling fake news spread, resulting in improved performance.

label: acl
text: Social media's popularity is driven by its ease of access, diverse content, and fast interactions. However, this growth has also enabled the spread of fake news, which is text published by news sources with the intention of spreading misinformation and influencing beliefs. Detecting fake news is a crucial and challenging problem to prevent widespread misinformation and maintain a healthy society. In this study, we approach the problem of fake news detection as reasoning over the relationships between sources, articles, and users on social media within a graph framework. By embedding this information, we develop inference operators that enhance the graph edges by uncovering unobserved interactions between its elements, such as the similarity between document contents and user engagement patterns. Our experiments on two challenging fake news detection tasks demonstrate that the use of inference operators leads to a deeper understanding of the social media framework that enables the spread of fake news, resulting in improved performance.

label: naacl
text: Reasoning is a crucial part of natural language argumentation. To comprehend an argument, one must analyze its warrant, which explains why its claim follows from its premises. As arguments are highly contextualized, warrants are usually presupposed and left implicit. Thus, the comprehension does not only require language understanding and logic skills, but also depends on common sense. In this paper we develop a methodology for reconstructing warrants systematically. We operationalize it in a scalable crowdsourcing process, resulting in a freely licensed dataset with warrants for 2k authentic arguments from news comments. On this basis, we present a new challenging task, the argument reasoning comprehension task. Given an argument with a claim and a premise, the goal is to choose the correct implicit warrant from two options. Both warrants are plausible and lexically close, but lead to contradicting claims. A solution to this task will define a substantial step towards automatic warrant reconstruction. However, experiments with several neural attention and language models reveal that current approaches do not suffice.

label: naacl
text: Reasoning is an essential aspect of natural language argumentation. To comprehend an argument, one must analyze its warrant, which explains why the argument's claim follows from its premises. Arguments are highly contextualized, and warrants are often presupposed and left implicit. As a result, comprehending an argument requires not only language understanding and logic skills, but also common sense. In this paper, we present a methodology for systematically reconstructing warrants and implement it in a scalable crowdsourcing process. This results in a freely licensed dataset of 2k authentic arguments from news comments, along with their associated warrants. We also introduce a new challenge task, the argument reasoning comprehension task. Given an argument with a claim and premise, the goal is to choose the correct implicit warrant from two options. Both warrants are plausible and lexically similar, but lead to conflicting claims. Solving this task will represent a significant step towards automatic warrant reconstruction. However, experiments with various neural attention and language models show that current approaches are insufficient.

label: acl
text: Question answering (QA) systems for large document collections typically use pipelines that (i) retrieve possibly relevant documents, (ii) re-rank them, (iii) rank paragraphs or other snippets of the top-ranked documents, and (iv) select spans of the top-ranked snippets as exact answers. Pipelines are conceptually simple, but errors propagate from one component to the next, without later components being able to revise earlier decisions. We present an architecture for joint document and snippet ranking, the two middle stages, which leverages the intuition that relevant documents have good snippets and good snippets come from relevant documents. The architecture is general and can be used with any neural text relevance ranker. We experiment with two main instantiations of the architecture, based on POSIT-DRMM (PDRMM) and a BERT-based ranker. Experiments on biomedical data from BIOASQ show that our joint models vastly outperform the pipelines in snippet retrieval, the main goal for QA, with fewer trainable parameters, also remaining competitive in document retrieval. Furthermore, our joint PDRMM-based model is competitive with BERT-based models, despite using orders of magnitude fewer parameters. These claims are also supported by human evaluation on two test batches of BIOASQ. To test our key findings on another dataset, we modified the Natural Questions dataset so that it can also be used for document and snippet retrieval. Our joint PDRMM-based model again outperforms the corresponding pipeline in snippet retrieval on the modified Natural Questions dataset, even though it performs worse than the pipeline in document retrieval. We make our code and the modified Natural Questions dataset publicly available.

label: acl
text: The typical pipelines for large document collection's Question Answering (QA) systems consist of four stages: (1) retrieval of potentially relevant documents, (2) re-ranking of those documents, (3) ranking of snippets or paragraphs from the top-ranked documents, and (4) selection of spans from the highest-ranked snippets as the final answers. Although these pipelines are straightforward, errors can propagate from one stage to the next, making it difficult for later stages to revise earlier decisions. To address this, we propose an architecture that combines document and snippet ranking into a single stage, leveraging the idea that relevant documents contain good snippets and vice versa. Our architecture is flexible and can be applied to any neural text relevance ranker. We evaluate two implementations of the architecture, using POSIT-DRMM (PDRMM) and a BERT-based ranker. Our experiments on biomedical data from BIOASQ show that our joint models outperform traditional pipelines in snippet retrieval, the primary goal of QA, while also being competitive in document retrieval. Additionally, our PDRMM-based model, which uses significantly fewer parameters, performs similarly to the BERT-based model. These results are confirmed by human evaluations on two test batches of BIOASQ. To further validate our findings, we modified the Natural Questions dataset for document and snippet retrieval and found that our PDRMM-based model outperforms the pipeline in snippet retrieval, although it performs worse in document retrieval. Our code and the modified Natural Questions dataset are publicly available.

label: acl
text: Human language understanding operates at multiple levels of granularity (e.g., words, phrases, and sentences) with increasing levels of abstraction that can be hierarchically combined. However, existing deep models with stacked layers do not explicitly model any sort of hierarchical process. In this paper, we propose a recursive Transformer model based on differentiable CKY style binary trees to emulate this composition process, and we extend the bidirectional language model pre-training objective to this architecture, attempting to predict each word given its left and right abstraction nodes. To scale up our approach, we also introduce an efficient pruning and growing algorithm to reduce the time complexity and enable encoding in linear time. Experimental results on language modeling and unsupervised parsing show the effectiveness of our approach.

label: acl
text: Human language understanding is a process that occurs at multiple levels of granularity, including words, phrases, and sentences, with levels of abstraction that can be combined in a hierarchical manner. However, current deep models with stacked layers do not explicitly model this hierarchical process. In this paper, we present a recursive Transformer model based on differentiable CKY-style binary trees. This model emulates the composition process, and we extend the bidirectional language model pre-training objective to predict each word, given its left and right abstraction nodes. To make our approach scalable, we also develop an efficient pruning and growing algorithm that reduces time complexity and enables encoding in linear time. Our experiments on language modeling and unsupervised parsing demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

label: emnlp
text: Distantly-supervised Relation Extraction (RE) methods train an extractor by automatically aligning relation instances in a Knowledge Base (KB) with unstructured text. In addition to relation instances, KBs often contain other relevant side information, such as aliases of relations (e.g., founded and co-founded are aliases for the relation founderOfCompany). RE models usually ignore such readily available side information. In this paper, we propose RESIDE, a distantly-supervised neural relation extraction method which utilizes additional side information from KBs for improved relation extraction. It uses entity type and relation alias information for imposing soft constraints while predicting relations. RESIDE employs Graph Convolution Networks (GCN) to encode syntactic information from text and improves performance even when limited side information is available. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate RESIDE's effectiveness. We have made RESIDE's source code available to encourage reproducible research.

label: emnlp
text: The Distantly-supervised Relation Extraction (RE) method trains an extractor by aligning relation instances in a Knowledge Base (KB) with unstructured text. However, KBs often contain other useful information, such as relation aliases (e.g. "founded" and "co-founded" are aliases for the "founderOfCompany" relation), which is usually ignored by RE models. In this paper, we present RESIDE, a neural relation extraction method that utilizes additional side information from KBs to improve relation extraction. RESIDE uses entity type and relation alias information to impose soft constraints while predicting relations, and employs Graph Convolution Networks (GCN) to encode syntactic information from text. Our experiments on benchmark datasets show that RESIDE is effective, even when limited side information is available. To promote reproducible research, we have made the source code for RESIDE publicly available.

label: emnlp
text: A news article's title, content and link structure often reveal its political ideology. However, most existing works on automatic political ideology detection only leverage textual cues. Drawing inspiration from recent advances in neural inference, we propose a novel attention based multi-view model to leverage cues from all of the above views to identify the ideology evinced by a news article. Our model draws on advances in representation learning in natural language processing and network science to capture cues from both textual content and the network structure of news articles. We empirically evaluate our model against a battery of baselines and show that our model outperforms state of the art by 10 percentage points F1 score.

label: emnlp
text: The title, content, and link structure of a news article often reveal its political ideology. However, most current methods for automatic political ideology detection only use textual clues. Inspired by recent advancements in neural inference, we propose a new attention-based multi-view model that considers cues from all three sources to identify the ideology expressed in a news article. Our model incorporates the latest advancements in representation learning in NLP and network science to capture both textual content and the network structure of news articles. Our results, compared to state-of-the-art methods, show a 10% improvement in F1 score.

label: coling
text: Cross-lingual Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers are currently evaluated in comparison to gold English AMRs, despite parsing a language other than English, due to the lack of multilingual AMR evaluation metrics. This evaluation practice is problematic because of the established effect of source language on AMR structure. In this work, we present three multilingual adaptations of monolingual AMR evaluation metrics and compare the performance of these metrics to sentence-level human judgments. We then use our most highly correlated metric to evaluate the output of state-of-the-art cross-lingual AMR parsers, finding that Smatch may still be a useful metric in comparison to gold English AMRs, while our multilingual adaptation of S2match (XS2match) is best for comparison with gold in-language AMRs.

label: coling
text: Cross-lingual Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers are currently evaluated against gold English AMRs, even though they parse languages other than English, due to the absence of multilingual AMR evaluation metrics. This evaluation method is flawed because it disregards the impact of the source language on AMR structure. To address this issue, we present three adaptations of monolingual AMR evaluation metrics for multiple languages and compare their performance to sentence-level human judgments. Our results reveal that, while Smatch may still be a useful metric for comparison to gold English AMRs, our most highly correlated metric, XS2match, which is a multilingual adaptation of S2match, is best for evaluating cross-lingual AMR parsers against gold in-language AMRs.

label: coling
text: Recent studies show that the attention heads in Transformer are not equal. We relate this phenomenon to the imbalance training of multi-head attention and the model dependence on specific heads. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple masking method: HeadMask, in two specific ways. Experiments show that translation improvements are achieved on multiple language pairs. Subsequent empirical analyses also support our assumption and confirm the effectiveness of the method.

label: coling
text: Recent studies have revealed that the attention heads in Transformers are not equal in performance. This imbalance is attributed to the unequal training of multi-head attention and the model's reliance on specific heads. To address this issue, we introduce HeadMask, a simple masking technique that has been shown to improve translation results on multiple language pairs through experiments. Our findings are further supported by empirical analyses, which confirm the effectiveness of the HeadMask method.

label: naacl
text: Canonical automatic summary evaluation metrics, such as ROUGE, focus on lexical similarity which cannot well capture semantics nor linguistic quality and require a reference summary which is costly to obtain. Recently, there have been a growing number of efforts to alleviate either or both of the two drawbacks. In this paper, we present a proof-of-concept study to a weakly supervised summary evaluation approach without the presence of reference summaries. Massive data in existing summarization datasets are transformed for training by pairing documents with corrupted reference summaries. In cross-domain tests, our strategy outperforms baselines with promising improvements, and show a great advantage in gauging linguistic qualities over all metrics.

label: naacl
text: Canonical automatic summary evaluation metrics, such as ROUGE, rely solely on lexical similarity and do not effectively capture semantics or linguistic quality. This approach also requires a reference summary, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain. However, there have been recent efforts to address these limitations. In this paper, we present a proof-of-concept study for a weakly supervised summary evaluation approach that does not require reference summaries. By transforming existing summarization datasets and pairing documents with corrupted reference summaries, we are able to train our model effectively. Our results show promising improvements over baseline metrics in cross-domain tests, and demonstrate a significant advantage in measuring linguistic quality over other metrics.

label: acl
text: One of the main bottlenecks in developing discourse dependency parsers is the lack of annotated training data. A potential solution is to utilize abundant unlabeled data by using unsupervised techniques, but there is so far little research in unsupervised discourse dependency parsing. Fortunately, unsupervised syntactic dependency parsing has been studied by decades, which could potentially be adapted for discourse parsing. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method to adapt unsupervised syntactic dependency parsing methodology for unsupervised discourse dependency parsing. We apply the method to adapt two state-of-the-art unsupervised syntactic dependency parsing methods. Experimental results demonstrate that our adaptation is effective. Moreover, we extend the adapted methods to the semi-supervised and supervised setting and surprisingly, we find that they outperform previous methods specially designed for supervised discourse parsing. Further analysis shows our adaptations result in superiority not only in parsing accuracy but also in time and space efficiency.

label: acl
text: One of the main challenges in developing discourse dependency parsers is the limited availability of annotated training data. To overcome this, unsupervised techniques that utilize abundant unlabeled data have been proposed, but there has been limited research in this area. However, unsupervised syntactic dependency parsing has been extensively studied over the years and could potentially be adapted for discourse parsing. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method to adapt unsupervised syntactic dependency parsing techniques for the purpose of unsupervised discourse dependency parsing. We apply this method to two state-of-the-art unsupervised syntactic dependency parsing methods and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our adaptation. Furthermore, we extend the adapted methods to semi-supervised and supervised settings and find that they outperform previously designed methods for supervised discourse parsing, particularly in terms of parsing accuracy, time efficiency and space efficiency.

label: emnlp
text: High-level semantics tasks, e.g., paraphrasing, textual entailment or question answering, involve modeling of text pairs. Before the emergence of neural networks, this has been mostly performed using intra-pair features, which incorporate similarity scores or rewrite rules computed between the members within the same pair. In this paper, we compute scalar products between vectors representing similarity between members of different pairs, in place of simply using a single vector for each pair. This allows us to obtain a representation specific to any pair of pairs, which delivers the state of the art in answer sentence selection. Most importantly, our approach can outperform much more complex algorithms based on neural networks.

label: emnlp
text: High-level semantic tasks, like paraphrasing, textual entailment, or question answering, require the modeling of text pairs. Previously, this was mainly done using intra-pair features that calculated similarity scores or rewrite rules between the members of each pair. In this paper, we introduce a new approach that computes scalar products between vectors representing the similarity between members of different pairs, rather than relying on a single vector for each pair. This results in a representation that is specific to each pair of pairs and outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms based on neural networks. Furthermore, our approach is more efficient than much more complex neural network algorithms.

label: acl
text: Models of narrative schema knowledge have proven useful for a range of event-related tasks, but they typically do not capture the temporal relationships between events. We propose a single model that addresses both temporal ordering, sorting given events into the order they occurred, and event infilling, predicting new events which fit into an existing temporally-ordered sequence. We use a BART-based conditional generation model that can capture both temporality and common event co-occurrence, meaning it can be flexibly applied to different tasks in this space. Our model is trained as a denoising autoencoder: we take temporally-ordered event sequences, shuffle them, delete some events, and then attempt to recover the original event sequence. This task teaches the model to make inferences given incomplete knowledge about the events in an underlying scenario. On the temporal ordering task, we show that our model is able to unscramble event sequences from existing datasets without access to explicitly labeled temporal training data, outperforming both a BERT-based pairwise model and a BERT-based pointer network. On event infilling, human evaluation shows that our model is able to generate events that fit better temporally into the input events when compared to GPT-2 story completion models.

label: acl
text: Narrative schema models have been effective for various event-related tasks, but they often lack the ability to capture the temporal relationships between events. Our proposed model solves this problem by addressing both temporal ordering and event infilling. The model is based on a BART-based conditional generation that can capture both the temporal relationships and common event co-occurrence, making it flexible for different tasks. We trained the model as a denoising autoencoder, where we shuffle and delete events from a temporally-ordered sequence and then try to recover the original order. This task teaches the model to make inferences based on incomplete event knowledge in a scenario. Our model outperforms BERT-based pairwise and pointer network models on the temporal ordering task without access to explicitly labeled temporal training data. In addition, human evaluation shows that our model generates events that better fit into the input events temporally compared to GPT-2 story completion models for event infilling.

label: naacl
text: Common studies of gender bias in NLP focus either on extrinsic bias measured by model performance on a downstream task or on intrinsic bias found in models' internal representations. However, the relationship between extrinsic and intrinsic bias is relatively unknown. In this work, we illuminate this relationship by measuring both quantities together: we debias a model during downstream fine-tuning, which reduces extrinsic bias, and measure the effect on intrinsic bias, which is operationalized as bias extractability with information-theoretic probing. Through experiments on two tasks and multiple bias metrics, we show that our intrinsic bias metric is a better indicator of debiasing than (a contextual adaptation of) the standard WEAT metric, and can also expose cases of superficial debiasing. Our framework provides a comprehensive perspective on bias in NLP models, which can be applied to deploy NLP systems in a more informed manner. Our code and model checkpoints are publicly available.

label: naacl
text: Common studies in NLP that examine gender bias focus either on extrinsic bias, which is measured by the model's performance on a downstream task, or intrinsic bias, which is found in the model's internal representations. However, the relationship between these two types of bias is not well understood. This work aims to shed light on this relationship by measuring both extrinsic and intrinsic bias simultaneously. We debias the model during fine-tuning, which reduces extrinsic bias, and measure the impact on intrinsic bias by using information-theoretic probing to extract bias. Our experiments on two tasks and multiple bias metrics show that our intrinsic bias metric provides a better indicator of debiasing than the standard WEAT metric, and can also reveal cases of superficial debiasing. This framework offers a comprehensive view of bias in NLP models and can be used to deploy NLP systems in a more informed manner. Our code and model checkpoints are publicly available.

label: acl
text: Fake news detection is crucial for preventing the dissemination of misinformation on social media. To differentiate fake news from real ones, existing methods observe the language patterns of the news post and “zoom in” to verify its content with knowledge sources or check its readers' replies. However, these methods neglect the information in the external news environment where a fake news post is created and disseminated. The news environment represents recent mainstream media opinion and public attention, which is an important inspiration of fake news fabrication because fake news is often designed to ride the wave of popular events and catch public attention with unexpected novel content for greater exposure and spread. To capture the environmental signals of news posts, we “zoom out” to observe the news environment and propose the News Environment Perception Framework (NEP). For each post, we construct its macro and micro news environment from recent mainstream news. Then we design a popularity-oriented and a novelty-oriented module to perceive useful signals and further assist final prediction. Experiments on our newly built datasets show that the NEP can efficiently improve the performance of basic fake news detectors.

label: acl
text: Fake news detection is crucial in preventing the spread of misinformation on social media. Current methods to differentiate fake news from real news observe the language patterns of news posts, verify their content with knowledge sources, and check the replies of readers. However, these methods overlook the information in the external news environment, where fake news is created and disseminated. This environment includes recent mainstream media opinion and public attention, which are important inspirations for fake news fabrication. Fake news is often designed to ride the wave of popular events and catch public attention with unexpected novel content for greater exposure and spread. To capture these environmental signals, we propose the News Environment Perception Framework (NEP), which "zooms out" to observe the news environment. We construct the macro and micro news environment for each post from recent mainstream news, and design a popularity-oriented and a novelty-oriented module to perceive useful signals and assist in final prediction. Our experiments on newly built datasets show that the NEP can effectively improve the performance of basic fake news detectors.

label: emnlp
text: Neural sequence-to-sequence models have proven very effective for machine translation, but at the expense of model interpretability. To shed more light into the role played by linguistic structure in the process of neural machine translation, we perform a fine-grained analysis of how various source-side morphological features are captured at different levels of the NMT encoder while varying the target language. Differently from previous work, we find no correlation between the accuracy of source morphology encoding and translation quality. We do find that morphological features are only captured in context and only to the extent that they are directly transferable to the target words.

label: emnlp
text: Neural sequence-to-sequence models have proven highly effective for machine translation, but with the drawback of reduced interpretability. To gain a deeper understanding of the role of linguistic structure in neural machine translation, we conduct a detailed analysis of how various source-side morphological features are captured at different levels of the NMT encoder, while varying the target language. Unlike previous studies, we find that there is no correlation between the accuracy of source morphology encoding and the quality of translation. Instead, we observe that morphological features are only captured in context and to the extent that they can be directly transferred to the target words.

label: acl
text: Solving math word problems requires deductive reasoning over the quantities in the text. Various recent research efforts mostly relied on sequence-to-sequence or sequence-to-tree models to generate mathematical expressions without explicitly performing relational reasoning between quantities in the given context. While empirically effective, such approaches typically do not provide explanations for the generated expressions. In this work, we view the task as a complex relation extraction problem, proposing a novel approach that presents explainable deductive reasoning steps to iteratively construct target expressions, where each step involves a primitive operation over two quantities defining their relation. Through extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets, we show that the proposed model significantly outperforms existing strong baselines. We further demonstrate that the deductive procedure not only presents more explainable steps but also enables us to make more accurate predictions on questions that require more complex reasoning.

label: acl
text: The solution of math word problems requires deductive reasoning regarding the quantities mentioned in the text. Previous research has mostly focused on using sequence-to-sequence or sequence-to-tree models to generate mathematical expressions without performing relational reasoning between the quantities in the context. However, these approaches are often effective but do not provide explanations for the generated expressions. Our novel approach views the task as a complex relation extraction problem and presents explainable deductive reasoning steps to construct target expressions. Each step involves a primitive operation over two quantities, defining their relationship. Through experiments on four benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our model outperforms existing strong baselines. Additionally, our deductive procedure not only provides more explainable steps but also leads to more accurate predictions for questions that require complex reasoning.

label: acl
text: Treebank conversion is a straightforward and effective way to exploit various heterogeneous treebanks for boosting parsing performance. However, previous work mainly focuses on unsupervised treebank conversion and has made little progress due to the lack of manually labeled data where each sentence has two syntactic trees complying with two different guidelines at the same time, referred as bi-tree aligned data. In this work, we for the first time propose the task of supervised treebank conversion. First, we manually construct a bi-tree aligned dataset containing over ten thousand sentences. Then, we propose two simple yet effective conversion approaches (pattern embedding and treeLSTM) based on the state-of-the-art deep biaffine parser. Experimental results show that 1) the two conversion approaches achieve comparable conversion accuracy, and 2) treebank conversion is superior to the widely used multi-task learning framework in multi-treebank exploitation and leads to significantly higher parsing accuracy.

label: acl
text: Treebank conversion is a simple and effective way to use various heterogeneous treebanks to improve parsing performance. However, previous research has mainly focused on unsupervised treebank conversion and has seen limited success due to the lack of bi-tree aligned data - sentences with two syntactic trees that comply with two different guidelines at the same time. In this study, we introduce the task of supervised treebank conversion. We manually create a bi-tree aligned dataset with over 10,000 sentences, and propose two effective conversion methods (pattern embedding and treeLSTM) based on the latest deep biaffine parser. Our results show that the two conversion methods have comparable accuracy, and that treebank conversion outperforms the widely used multi-task learning framework in exploiting multiple treebanks, leading to significantly improved parsing accuracy.

text: Recent research on cross-lingual word embeddings has been dominated by unsupervised mapping approaches that align monolingual embeddings. Such methods critically rely on those embeddings having a similar structure, but it was recently shown that the separate training in different languages causes departures from this assumption. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach that does not have this limitation, while requiring a weak seed dictionary (e.g., a list of identical words) as the only form of supervision. Rather than aligning two fixed embedding spaces, our method works by fixing the target language embeddings, and learning a new set of embeddings for the source language that are aligned with them. To that end, we use an extension of skip-gram that leverages translated context words as anchor points, and incorporates self-learning and iterative restarts to reduce the dependency on the initial dictionary. Our approach outperforms conventional mapping methods on bilingual lexicon induction, and obtains competitive results in the downstream XNLI task.

text: The recent research on cross-lingual word embeddings has been dominated by unsupervised mapping techniques that align monolingual embeddings. However, these methods critically depend on the assumption that the embeddings have a similar structure, which was recently shown to not always be the case due to separate training in different languages. This paper proposes an alternative approach that doesn't have this limitation, while only requiring a weak seed dictionary as supervision. Instead of aligning two fixed embedding spaces, our method fixes the target language embeddings and learns a new set of source language embeddings that are aligned with them. This is achieved through an extension of skip-gram that uses translated context words as anchor points and incorporates self-learning and iterative restarts to reduce dependency on the initial dictionary. Our approach outperforms conventional mapping methods in bilingual lexicon induction and obtains competitive results in the XNLI task.

label: acl
text: In the era of pre-trained language models, Transformers are the de facto choice of model architectures. While recent research has shown promise in entirely convolutional, or CNN, architectures, they have not been explored using the pre-train-fine-tune paradigm. In the context of language models, are convolutional models competitive to Transformers when pre-trained? This paper investigates this research question and presents several interesting findings. Across an extensive set of experiments on 8 datasets/tasks, we find that CNN-based pre-trained models are competitive and outperform their Transformer counterpart in certain scenarios, albeit with caveats. Overall, the findings outlined in this paper suggest that conflating pre-training and architectural advances is misguided and that both advances should be considered independently. We believe our research paves the way for a healthy amount of optimism in alternative architectures.
