The proposed reconciled embedding approach is able to tackle them simultaneously. Experimental results on the MIMIC dataset show that our model outperforms all previous state-of-the-art models by a large margin. The source code is available at https://github.com/discnet2022/discnet2022.

label: coling
text: The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is the cornerstone of global health statistics and epidemiology. It translates health conditions into alphanumeric codes for easier tracking and analysis. However, manual coding is labor-intensive and the shortage of healthcare workers worldwide has led to a search for automatic ICD coding methods. Previous studies have failed to consider the rich contextual information provided by the discourse structure of clinical notes. In this paper, we address this gap by leveraging section type classification and section type embeddings to exploit the discourse structure. Furthermore, we tackle the challenges of class imbalance and heterogeneous writing styles between clinical notes and ICD code definitions through our proposed reconciled embedding approach. Our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated by experimental results on the MIMIC dataset. The source code for our model is available at https://github.com/discnet2022/discnet2022.

label: naacl
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) annotations are often assumed to closely mirror dependency syntax, but AMR explicitly does not require this, and the assumption has never been tested. To test it, we devise an expressive framework to align AMR graphs to dependency graphs, which we use to annotate 200 AMRs. Our annotation explains how 97% of AMR edges are evoked by words or syntax. Previously existing AMR alignment frameworks did not allow for mapping AMR onto syntax, and as a consequence they explained at most 23%. While we find that there are indeed many cases where AMR annotations closely mirror syntax, there are also pervasive differences. We use our annotations to test a baseline AMR-to-syntax aligner, finding that this task is more difficult than AMR-to-string alignment; and to pinpoint errors in an AMR parser. We make our data and code freely available for further research on AMR parsing and generation, and the relationship of AMR to syntax.

label: naacl
text: The assumption that Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) annotations closely mirror dependency syntax has never been tested. To verify this, we have developed an expressive framework to align AMR graphs with dependency graphs and annotated 200 AMRs. Our framework explains 97% of AMR edges, while previous AMR alignment frameworks only managed to explain 23% at most, as they did not allow for mapping AMR to syntax. Our findings show that while there are many cases where AMR annotations align with syntax, there are also significant differences. We used our annotations to evaluate a baseline AMR-to-syntax aligner and found that this task is more challenging than AMR-to-string alignment. Additionally, our annotations were used to identify errors in an AMR parser. Our data and code are available for further research on AMR parsing and generation, and the relationship between AMR and syntax.

label: coling
text: Studies have shown that the sentence's syntactic structures are important for semantic sentence matching. A typical approach is encoding each sentence's syntactic structure into an embedding vector, which can be combined with other features to predict the final matching scores. Though successes have been observed, embedding the whole syntactic structures as one vector inevitably overlooks the fine-grained syntax matching patterns, e.g. the alignment of specific term dependencies relations in the two inputted sentences. In this paper, we formalize the task of semantic sentence matching as a problem of graph matching in which each sentence is represented as a directed graph according to its syntactic structures. The syntax matching patterns (i.e. similar syntactic structures) between two sentences, therefore, can be extracted as the sub-graph structure alignments. The proposed method, referred to as Interacted Syntax Graphs (ISG), represents two sentences' syntactic alignments as well as their semantic matching signals into one association graph. After that, the neural quadratic assignment programming (QAP) is adapted to extract syntactic matching patterns from the association graph. In this way, the syntactic structures fully interact in a fine granularity during the matching process. Experimental results on three public datasets demonstrated that ISG can outperform the state-of-the-art baselines effectively and efficiently. The empirical analysis also showed that ISG can match sentences in an interpretable way.

label: coling
text: Studies have shown that the syntactic structure of sentences is crucial for semantic sentence matching. The typical approach involves encoding each sentence's syntactic structure into an embedding vector, which is then combined with other features to predict the final matching score. However, this approach overlooks the fine-grained syntax matching patterns, such as the alignment of specific term dependencies in the two input sentences. In this paper, we formalize the task of semantic sentence matching as a graph matching problem, where each sentence is represented as a directed graph based on its syntactic structure. This allows us to extract syntax matching patterns as sub-graph structure alignments. Our proposed method, called Interacted Syntax Graphs (ISG), represents both the syntactic alignments and semantic matching signals of two sentences into one association graph. We then use neural quadratic assignment programming (QAP) to extract the syntactic matching patterns from the association graph. This allows for a fine-grained interaction between the syntactic structures during the matching process. Results from experiments on three public datasets show that ISG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines effectively and efficiently. Additionally, the empirical analysis demonstrates that ISG matches sentences in an interpretable manner.

label: coling
text: Scientific papers from all disciplines contain many abbreviations and acronyms. In many cases these acronyms are ambiguous. We present a method to choose the contextual correct definition of an acronym that does not require training for each acronym and thus can be applied to a large number of different acronyms with only few instances. We constructed a set of 19,954 examples of 4,365 ambiguous acronyms from image captions in scientific papers along with their contextually correct definition from different domains. We learn word embeddings for all words in the corpus and compare the averaged context vector of the words in the expansion of an acronym with the weighted average vector of the words in the context of the acronym. We show that this method clearly outperforms (classical) cosine similarity. Furthermore, we show that word embeddings learned from a 1 billion word corpus of scientific texts outperform word embeddings learned on much large general corpora.

label: coling
text: Scientific papers from various disciplines are often filled with abbreviations and acronyms, many of which are ambiguous. To address this issue, we have developed a method to determine the correct definition of an acronym in context without the need for individual training for each acronym. This approach can be applied to a large number of different acronyms with only a few instances. We have compiled a set of 19,954 examples of 4,365 ambiguous acronyms from image captions in scientific papers, along with their contextually correct definitions from different domains. Our method involves learning word embeddings for all words in the corpus and comparing the average context vector of the words in the expansion of an acronym with the weighted average vector of the words in the context of the acronym. Our results indicate that this method outperforms traditional cosine similarity and that word embeddings learned from a 1 billion word corpus of scientific texts are more effective than those learned from much larger general corpora.

label: acl
text: We show that an epsilon-free, chain-free synchronous context-free grammar (SCFG) can be converted into a weakly equivalent synchronous tree-adjoining grammar (STAG) which is prefix lexicalized. This transformation at most doubles the grammar's rank and cubes its size, but we show that in practice the size increase is only quadratic. Our results extend Greibach normal form from CFGs to SCFGs and prove new formal properties about SCFG, a formalism with many applications in natural language processing.

label: acl
text: We demonstrate that an epsilon-free and chain-free synchronous context-free grammar (SCFG) can be transformed into a weakly equivalent synchronous tree-adjoining grammar (STAG) that is prefix lexicalized. This transformation may result in a maximum doubling of the grammar's rank and a cubing of its size. However, we find that in practice, the size increase is only quadratic. Our findings extend Greibach normal form from context-free grammars (CFGs) to SCFGs and establish new formal properties for SCFG, a widely used formalism in natural language processing.

label: naacl
text: We present a novel approach incorporating transformer-based language models into infectious disease modelling. Text-derived features are quantified by tracking high-density clusters of sentence-level representations of Reddit posts within specific US states' COVID-19 subreddits. We benchmark these clustered embedding features against features extracted from other high-quality datasets. In a threshold-classification task, we show that they outperform all other feature types at predicting upward trend signals, a significant result for infectious disease modelling in areas where epidemiological data is unreliable. Subsequently, in a time-series forecasting task, we fully utilise the predictive power of the caseload and compare the relative strengths of using different supplementary datasets as covariate feature sets in a transformer-based time-series model.

label: naacl
text: We introduce a new approach that integrates transformer-based language models into infectious disease modeling. Our approach quantifies text-derived features by tracking high-density clusters of sentence-level representations of Reddit posts within specific COVID-19 subreddits in the US. We compare these clustered embedding features with features extracted from other high-quality datasets and show that they outperform all other feature types in predicting upward trend signals, which is a crucial result for infectious disease modeling in regions where epidemiological data is unreliable. Finally, in a time-series forecasting task, we utilize the full potential of the caseload and evaluate the effectiveness of different supplementary datasets as covariate feature sets in a transformer-based time-series model.

label: naacl
text: Causal inference methods that control for text-based confounders are becoming increasingly important in the social sciences and other disciplines where text is readily available. However, these methods rely on a critical assumption that there is no treatment leakage: that is, the text only contains information about the confounder and no information about treatment assignment. When this assumption does not hold, methods that control for text to adjust for confounders face the problem of post-treatment (collider) bias. However, the assumption that there is no treatment leakage may be unrealistic in real-world situations involving text, as human language is rich and flexible. Language appearing in a public policy document or health records may refer to the future and the past simultaneously, and thereby reveal information about the treatment assignment.In this article, we define the treatment-leakage problem, and discuss the identification as well as the estimation challenges it raises. Second, we delineate the conditions under which leakage can be addressed by removing the treatment-related signal from the text in a pre-processing step we define as text distillation. Lastly, using simulation, we show how treatment leakage introduces a bias in estimates of the average treatment effect (ATE) and how text distillation can mitigate this bias.

label: naacl
text: Causal inference methods that control for text-based confounders are becoming increasingly crucial in disciplines where text is abundant, such as the social sciences. However, these methods depend on a crucial assumption that there is no treatment leakage; meaning, the text only contains information about the confounder and not about treatment assignment. When this assumption is not met, methods that control for text to adjust for confounders face the problem of post-treatment (collider) bias. However, the assumption of no treatment leakage may be unrealistic in real-world text situations, as human language is versatile and flexible. For example, language in public policy documents or health records may refer to both the past and future, thereby revealing information about treatment assignment. In this article, we define the treatment-leakage problem, discuss its identification and estimation challenges, and outline the conditions under which it can be addressed by removing the treatment-related signal from the text through a pre-processing step known as text distillation. Finally, using simulations, we demonstrate how treatment leakage can introduce bias in the estimate of the average treatment effect (ATE) and how text distillation can help to mitigate this bias.

label: acl
text: We study the problem of building entity tagging systems by using a few rules as weak supervision. Previous methods mostly focus on disambiguating entity types based on contexts and expert-provided rules, while assuming entity spans are given. In this work, we propose a novel method TALLOR that bootstraps high-quality logical rules to train a neural tagger in a fully automated manner. Specifically, we introduce compound rules that are composed from simple rules to increase the precision of boundary detection and generate more diverse pseudo labels. We further design a dynamic label selection strategy to ensure pseudo label quality and therefore avoid overfitting the neural tagger. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms other weakly supervised methods and even rivals a state-of-the-art distantly supervised tagger with a lexicon of over 2,000 terms when starting from only 20 simple rules. Our method can serve as a tool for rapidly building taggers in emerging domains and tasks. Case studies show that learned rules can potentially explain the predicted entities.

label: acl
text: We investigate the challenge of constructing entity tagging systems through the use of a limited number of rules as weak supervision. Previous approaches have mainly focused on disambiguating entity types based on contextual information and expert-defined rules, while assuming that the entity spans have already been identified. Our novel method, TALLOR, addresses this issue by automating the process of training a neural tagger using high-quality logical rules. To achieve this, we utilize compound rules, which are derived from simple rules, to improve boundary detection precision and generate a more diverse set of pseudo labels. Our dynamic label selection strategy helps to maintain the quality of the pseudo labels and prevent overfitting of the neural tagger. Our experiments on three datasets show that our method outperforms other weakly supervised methods and even rivals a state-of-the-art distantly supervised tagger with a lexicon of over 2000 terms, even when starting from just 20 simple rules. Our method can be used as a tool for quickly building taggers for new domains and tasks, and our case studies suggest that the learned rules can provide insight into the predicted entities.

label: coling
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has brought out both the best and worst of language technology (LT). On one hand, conversational agents for information dissemination and basic diagnosis have seen widespread use, and arguably, had an important role in fighting against the pandemic. On the other hand, it has also become clear that such technologies are readily available for a handful of languages, and the vast majority of the global south is completely bereft of these benefits. What is the state of LT, especially conversational agents, for healthcare across the world's languages? And, what would it take to ensure global readiness of LT before the next pandemic? In this paper, we try to answer these questions through survey of existing literature and resources, as well as through a rapid chatbot building exercise for 15 Asian and African languages with varying amount of resource-availability. The study confirms the pitiful state of LT even for languages with large speaker bases, such as Sinhala and Hausa, and identifies the gaps that could help us prioritize research and investment strategies in LT for healthcare.

label: coling
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has revealed both the strengths and weaknesses of language technology (LT). On one hand, conversational agents that provide information dissemination and basic diagnosis have been widely used and have played a crucial role in combating the pandemic. On the other hand, it has become evident that these technologies are only available in a limited number of languages, leaving the majority of the global south without access to these benefits. What is the current state of LT, particularly conversational agents, for healthcare in various languages around the world? And, what steps need to be taken to ensure global readiness of LT before the next pandemic? This paper aims to answer these questions through a review of existing literature and resources, as well as a rapid chatbot building exercise for 15 Asian and African languages with varying levels of resource availability. The study highlights the inadequate state of LT even for languages with large speaker populations, such as Sinhala and Hausa, and identifies the gaps that will help us prioritize research and investment strategies in LT for healthcare.

label: naacl
text: When strong partial-input baselines reveal artifacts in crowdsourced NLI datasets, the performance of full-input models trained on such datasets is often dismissed as reliance on spurious correlations. We investigate whether state-of-the-art NLI models are capable of overriding default inferences made by a partial-input baseline. We introduce an evaluation set of 600 examples consisting of perturbed premises to examine a RoBERTa model's sensitivity to edited contexts. Our results indicate that NLI models are still capable of learning to condition on context—a necessary component of inferential reasoning—despite being trained on artifact-ridden datasets.

label: naacl
text: When the strong partial-input baselines reveal artifacts in crowdsourced natural language inference (NLI) datasets, the performance of full-input models trained on such datasets is often criticized for being based on spurious correlations. To examine this issue, we investigate whether state-of-the-art NLI models can overcome the default inferences made by partial-input baselines. To do this, we introduce a set of 600 evaluation examples that consist of perturbed premises to assess the sensitivity of a RoBERTa model to edited contexts. Our findings suggest that despite being trained on datasets that contain artifacts, NLI models are still capable of learning to condition on context, which is a crucial part of inferential reasoning.

label: acl
text: We introduce Latent Vector Grammars (LVeGs), a new framework that extends latent variable grammars such that each nonterminal symbol is associated with a continuous vector space representing the set of (infinitely many) subtypes of the nonterminal. We show that previous models such as latent variable grammars and compositional vector grammars can be interpreted as special cases of LVeGs. We then present Gaussian Mixture LVeGs (GM-LVeGs), a new special case of LVeGs that uses Gaussian mixtures to formulate the weights of production rules over subtypes of nonterminals. A major advantage of using Gaussian mixtures is that the partition function and the expectations of subtype rules can be computed using an extension of the inside-outside algorithm, which enables efficient inference and learning. We apply GM-LVeGs to part-of-speech tagging and constituency parsing and show that GM-LVeGs can achieve competitive accuracies.

label: acl
text: We present Latent Vector Grammars (LVeGs), a novel framework that extends latent variable grammars by associating each nonterminal symbol with a continuous vector space, representing the set of (infinite) subtypes of the nonterminal. By doing so, we demonstrate that previous models, such as latent variable grammars and compositional vector grammars, can be considered as special cases of LVeGs. Additionally, we introduce Gaussian Mixture LVeGs (GM-LVeGs), a specific instance of LVeGs that utilizes Gaussian mixtures to formulate the weights of production rules for subtypes of nonterminals. The use of Gaussian mixtures offers the advantage of being able to compute the partition function and expectations of subtype rules using an extended inside-outside algorithm, leading to efficient inference and learning. We evaluate the performance of GM-LVeGs on part-of-speech tagging and constituency parsing and show that it can achieve comparable accuracy.

label: coling
text: The dialogue-based relation extraction (DialogRE) task aims to predict the relations between argument pairs that appear in dialogue. Most previous studies utilize fine-tuning pre-trained language models (PLMs) only with extensive features to supplement the low information density of the dialogue by multiple speakers. To effectively exploit inherent knowledge of PLMs without extra layers and consider scattered semantic cues on the relation between the arguments, we propose a Guiding model with RelAtional Semantics using Prompt (GRASP). We adopt a prompt-based fine-tuning approach and capture relational semantic clues of a given dialogue with 1) an argument-aware prompt marker strategy and 2) the relational clue detection task. In the experiments, GRASP achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both F1 and F1c scores on a DialogRE dataset even though our method only leverages PLMs without adding any extra layers.

label: coling
text: The DialogRE task aims to identify the relationships between argument pairs in dialogues. Previous studies have used fine-tuned pre-trained language models (PLMs) with extensive features to overcome the low information density of dialogues with multiple speakers. To effectively utilize the inherent knowledge of PLMs and consider scattered semantic cues in the relationships between arguments, we propose the Guiding model with Relational Semantics using Prompt (GRASP). This approach adopts a prompt-based fine-tuning method and captures relational semantic clues in dialogues through 1) an argument-aware prompt marker strategy and 2) the detection of relational clues. Our experiments show that GRASP outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of F1 and F1c scores on a DialogRE dataset, without requiring any additional layers beyond PLMs.

label: naacl
text: In recent years, pre-trained models have become dominant in most natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, in the area of Automated Essay Scoring (AES), pre-trained models such as BERT have not been properly used to outperform other deep learning models such as LSTM. In this paper, we introduce a novel multi-scale essay representation for BERT that can be jointly learned. We also employ multiple losses and transfer learning from out-of-domain essays to further improve the performance. Experiment results show that our approach derives much benefit from joint learning of multi-scale essay representation and obtains almost the state-of-the-art result among all deep learning models in the ASAP task. Our multi-scale essay representation also generalizes well to CommonLit Readability Prize data set, which suggests that the novel text representation proposed in this paper may be a new and effective choice for long-text tasks.

label: naacl
text: Recently, pre-trained models have become the norm for most natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, in the field of Automated Essay Scoring (AES), pre-trained models such as BERT have not yet been effectively utilized to outperform other deep learning models, such as LSTM. In this study, we present a novel multi-scale essay representation for BERT that can be learned jointly. Additionally, we incorporate multiple losses and transfer learning from out-of-domain essays to further enhance performance. Our experiments demonstrate that joint learning of the multi-scale essay representation results in significant improvements, yielding almost state-of-the-art results among all deep learning models in the ASAP task. Our multi-scale essay representation also generalizes well to the CommonLit Readability Prize dataset, suggesting that the novel text representation proposed in this paper may be a new and effective choice for long-text tasks.

label: acl
text: Whereas much of the success of the current generation of neural language models has been driven by increasingly large training corpora, relatively little research has been dedicated to analyzing these massive sources of textual data. In this exploratory analysis, we delve deeper into the Common Crawl, a colossal web corpus that is extensively used for training language models. We find that it contains a significant amount of undesirable content, including hate speech and sexually explicit content, even after filtering procedures. We discuss the potential impacts of this content on language models and conclude with future research directions and a more mindful approach to corpus collection and analysis.

label: acl
text: Despite the impressive results achieved by current neural language models, there has been limited research into the analysis of the vast amounts of text data used for training. In this study, we examine the Common Crawl, a widely-used web corpus for language model training. Our analysis reveals the presence of undesirable content, including hate speech and sexually explicit material, even after filtering efforts. This raises concerns about the impact of such content on language models and highlights the need for more careful corpus collection and analysis in the future.

label: acl
text: Extensive work has argued in favour of paying crowd workers a wage that is at least equivalent to the U.S. federal minimum wage. Meanwhile, research on collecting high quality annotations suggests using a qualification that requires workers to have previously completed a certain number of tasks. If most requesters who pay fairly require workers to have completed a large number of tasks already then workers need to complete a substantial amount of poorly paid work before they can earn a fair wage. Through analysis of worker discussions and guidance for researchers, we estimate that workers spend approximately 2.25 months of full time effort on poorly paid tasks in order to get the qualifications needed for better paid tasks. We discuss alternatives to this qualification and conduct a study of the correlation between qualifications and work quality on two NLP tasks. We find that it is possible to reduce the burden on workers while still collecting high quality data.

label: acl
text: Studies have extensively supported the notion of compensating crowd workers with a wage that meets or exceeds the U.S. federal minimum wage. Research on obtaining high-quality annotations highlights the importance of having workers meet a certain qualification, usually achieved by completing a set number of tasks. Unfortunately, this often means that workers must complete a significant amount of low-paying work before they can attain the qualifications necessary for higher-paying tasks. Our analysis of worker discussions and guidance for researchers suggests that workers typically devote 2.25 months of full-time effort to low-paying tasks to meet the qualifications. We explore alternative qualifications and conduct a correlation study between qualifications and work quality on two NLP tasks. Our findings indicate that it is possible to reduce the burden on workers while still maintaining high-quality data.

label: coling
text: Prompting, which casts downstream applications as language modeling tasks, has shown to be sample efficient compared to standard fine-tuning with pre-trained models. However, one pitfall of prompting is the need of manually-designed patterns, whose outcome can be unintuitive and requires large validation sets to tune. To tackle the challenge, we propose AutoSeq, a fully automatic prompting method: (1) We adopt natural language prompts on sequence-to-sequence models, enabling free-form generation and larger label search space; (2) We propose label sequences – phrases with indefinite lengths to verbalize the labels – which eliminate the need of manual templates and are more expressive than single label words; (3) We use beam search to automatically generate a large amount of label sequence candidates and propose contrastive re-ranking to get the best combinations. AutoSeq significantly outperforms other no-manual-design methods, such as soft prompt tuning, adapter tuning, and automatic search on single label words; the generated label sequences are even better than curated manual ones on a variety of tasks. Our method reveals the potential of sequence-to-sequence models in few-shot learning and sheds light on a path to generic and automatic prompting. The source code of this paper can be obtained from https://github.com/thunlp/Seq2Seq-Prompt.

label: coling
text: The use of prompting, which views downstream applications as language modeling tasks, has been found to be more sample-efficient compared to standard fine-tuning with pre-trained models. However, manual design of prompts is a challenge, as the results can be unpredictable and require large validation sets for tuning. To overcome this, we introduce AutoSeq, a fully automatic prompting method that utilizes natural language prompts on sequence-to-sequence models. This allows for free-form generation and a larger label search space. Our method eliminates the need for manual templates by using label sequences, which are phrases with indefinite lengths that verbalize the labels. We use beam search to generate a large number of label sequence candidates and employ contrastive re-ranking to select the best combinations. Our results show that AutoSeq outperforms other no-manual-design methods, such as soft prompt tuning, adapter tuning, and automatic search on single label words. The generated label sequences are even better than manually curated ones on various tasks. Our work highlights the potential of sequence-to-sequence models for few-shot learning and provides a path towards generic and automatic prompting. The source code for this paper can be found at https://github.com/thunlp/Seq2Seq-Prompt.

label: naacl
text: The common practice for training commonsense models has gone from–human–to–corpus–to–machine: humans author commonsense knowledge graphs in order to train commonsense models. In this work, we investigate an alternative, from–machine–to–corpus–to–machine: general language models author these commonsense knowledge graphs to train commonsense models. Our study leads to a new framework, Symbolic Knowledge Distillation. As with prior art in Knowledge Distillation (Hinton et al. 2015), our approach uses larger models to teach smaller models. A key difference is that we distill knowledge symbolically–as text–in addition to the neural model. We distill only one aspect–the commonsense of a general language model teacher, allowing the student to be a different type, a commonsense model. Altogether, we show that careful prompt engineering and a separately trained critic model allow us to selectively distill high-quality causal commonsense from GPT-3, a general language model. Empirical results demonstrate that, for the first time, a human-authored commonsense knowledge graph is surpassed by our automatically distilled variant in all three criteria: quantity, quality, and diversity. In addition, it results in a neural commonsense model that surpasses the teacher model's commonsense capabilities despite its 100x smaller size. We apply this to the ATOMIC resource, and will share our new symbolic knowledge graph and commonsense models.

label: naacl
text: The training of commonsense models has traditionally been done using human-generated knowledge graphs. However, in this study, we explore an alternative approach, where general language models are used to author these knowledge graphs to train commonsense models. Our new framework, called Symbolic Knowledge Distillation, differs from prior art in that it uses larger models to teach smaller models, but also distills knowledge symbolically as text, in addition to the neural model. Our approach selectively distills high-quality commonsense from a general language model teacher, allowing the student to be a different type of model, a commonsense model. Our results show that with careful prompt engineering and a separately trained critic model, we can surpass a human-authored commonsense knowledge graph in terms of quantity, quality, and diversity. Furthermore, our distilled commonsense model outperforms the teacher model in terms of commonsense capabilities, despite being 100 times smaller in size. We apply this to the ATOMIC resource and will share our new symbolic knowledge graph and commonsense models.

label: acl
text: Automatic evaluation metrics are essential for the rapid development of open-domain dialogue systems as they facilitate hyper-parameter tuning and comparison between models. Although recently proposed trainable conversation-level metrics have shown encouraging results, the quality of the metrics is strongly dependent on the quality of training data. Prior works mainly resort to heuristic text-level manipulations (e.g. utterances shuffling) to bootstrap incoherent conversations (negative examples) from coherent dialogues (positive examples). Such approaches are insufficient to appropriately reflect the incoherence that occurs in interactions between advanced dialogue models and humans. To tackle this problem, we propose DEAM, a Dialogue coherence Evaluation metric that relies on Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) to apply semantic-level Manipulations for incoherent (negative) data generation. AMRs naturally facilitate the injection of various types of incoherence sources, such as coreference inconsistency, irrelevancy, contradictions, and decrease engagement, at the semantic level, thus resulting in more natural incoherent samples. Our experiments show that DEAM achieves higher correlations with human judgments compared to baseline methods on several dialog datasets by significant margins. We also show that DEAM can distinguish between coherent and incoherent dialogues generated by baseline manipulations, whereas those baseline models cannot detect incoherent examples generated by DEAM. Our results demonstrate the potential of AMR-based semantic manipulations for natural negative example generation.

label: acl
text: Automatic evaluation metrics play a crucial role in the rapid development of open-domain dialogue systems by streamlining hyper-parameter tuning and model comparisons. Despite recent advancements in trainable conversation-level metrics, their quality is heavily dependent on the quality of the training data. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic text-level manipulations, such as shuffling utterances, to generate negative examples from positive dialogues. However, these methods are inadequate in reflecting the incoherence that occurs in human-model interactions. To address this issue, we propose DEAM, a Dialogue coherence Evaluation metric that leverages Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) to apply semantic-level manipulations for generating incoherent data. AMRs allow for the injection of various types of incoherence, such as coreference inconsistency, irrelevancy, contradictions, and decreased engagement, at a semantic level, resulting in more natural incoherent samples. Our experiments show that DEAM outperforms baseline methods in terms of correlation with human judgments on multiple dialogue datasets. Additionally, DEAM can distinguish between coherent and incoherent dialogues generated by baseline manipulations, while these baseline models cannot detect examples generated by DEAM. Our results highlight the potential of AMR-based semantic manipulations for generating natural negative examples.

label: naacl
text: Making an informed choice of pre-trained language model (LM) is critical for performance, yet environmentally costly, and as such widely underexplored. The field of Computer Vision has begun to tackle encoder ranking, with promising forays into Natural Language Processing, however they lack coverage of linguistic tasks such as structured prediction. We propose probing to rank LMs, specifically for parsing dependencies in a given language, by measuring the degree to which labeled trees are recoverable from an LM's contextualized embeddings. Across 46 typologically and architecturally diverse LM-language pairs, our probing approach predicts the best LM choice 79% of the time using orders of magnitude less compute than training a full parser. Within this study, we identify and analyze one recently proposed decoupled LM—RemBERT—and find it strikingly contains less inherent dependency information, but often yields the best parser after full fine-tuning. Without this outlier our approach identifies the best LM in 89% of cases.

label: naacl
text: Choosing the right pre-trained language model (LM) is important for optimal performance, but it is also environmentally costly and often overlooked. The field of Computer Vision has started to address the issue of encoder ranking, and there have been some promising advances in Natural Language Processing, but these efforts lack coverage of linguistic tasks such as structured prediction. Our proposal is to rank LMs by measuring the extent to which labeled trees can be recovered from the LM's contextualized embeddings. Our probing method was applied to 46 diverse LM-language pairs and was able to predict the best LM choice 79% of the time using much less computational power than training a full parser. In this study, we also analyzed RemBERT, a recently proposed decoupled LM, and found that it contains less inherent dependency information, but often results in the best parser after fine-tuning. Without RemBERT, our approach was able to identify the best LM in 89% of cases.

label: emnlp
text: Code-switching, the use of more than one language within a single utterance, is ubiquitous in much of the world, but remains a challenge for NLP largely due to the lack of representative data for training models. In this paper, we present a novel model architecture that is trained exclusively on monolingual resources, but can be applied to unseen code-switched text at inference time. The model accomplishes this by jointly maintaining separate word representations for each of the possible languages, or scripts in the case of transliteration, allowing each to contribute to inferences without forcing the model to commit to a language. Experiments on Hindi-English part-of-speech tagging demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard models when training on monolingual text without transliteration, and testing on code-switched text with alternate scripts.

label: emnlp
text: Code-switching, the use of multiple languages in a single utterance, is a common occurrence in many parts of the world, but it remains a challenge for NLP due to the scarcity of representative data for training models. This paper presents a new model architecture that is trained only on monolingual resources but can be applied to unseen code-switched text during inference. The model achieves this by maintaining separate word representations for each of the possible languages or scripts, enabling each to contribute to the inference without forcing the model to choose a language. Our experiments on Hindi-English part-of-speech tagging show that our approach outperforms standard models when trained on monolingual text without transliteration and tested on code-switched text with alternate scripts.

label: coling
text: Text classification is a primary task in natural language processing (NLP). Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have developed rapidly and been applied to text classification tasks. As a special kind of graph data, the tree has a simpler data structure and can provide rich hierarchical information for text classification. Inspired by the structural entropy, we construct the coding tree of the graph by minimizing the structural entropy and propose HINT, which aims to make full use of the hierarchical information contained in the text for the task of text classification. Specifically, we first establish a dependency parsing graph for each text. Then we designed a structural entropy minimization algorithm to decode the key information in the graph and convert each graph to its corresponding coding tree. Based on the hierarchical structure of the coding tree, the representation of the entire graph is obtained by updating the representation of non-leaf nodes in the coding tree layer by layer. Finally, we present the effectiveness of hierarchical information in text classification. Experimental results show that HINT outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on popular benchmarks while having a simple structure and few parameters.

label: coling
text: Text classification, which is a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP), has recently seen the application of rapidly developing graph neural networks (GNNs). Trees, as a special type of graph data, have a simple data structure, and provide abundant hierarchical information that can be leveraged for text classification. To make the most of this information, we introduce HINT, a novel approach that minimizes structural entropy to construct a coding tree of the graph. This coding tree represents the key information in the graph and is used to update the representation of non-leaf nodes layer by layer, providing a hierarchical representation of the entire graph. Our experiments show that HINT outperforms state-of-the-art methods on popular benchmarks, with a simple structure and minimal parameters.

label: coling
text: Neural machine translation (NMT) is a deep learning based approach for machine translation, which yields the state-of-the-art translation performance in scenarios where large-scale parallel corpora are available. Although the high-quality and domain-specific translation is crucial in the real world, domain-specific corpora are usually scarce or nonexistent, and thus vanilla NMT performs poorly in such scenarios. Domain adaptation that leverages both out-of-domain parallel corpora as well as monolingual corpora for in-domain translation, is very important for domain-specific translation. In this paper, we give a comprehensive survey of the state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques for NMT.

label: coling
text: Neural machine translation (NMT) is a deep learning-based approach to machine translation that achieves state-of-the-art results when large-scale parallel corpora are available. However, in real-world scenarios, high-quality, domain-specific translations are crucial and often require domain-specific corpora, which are often scarce or nonexistent. This leads to poor performance from standard NMT models. To address this issue, domain adaptation techniques that utilize both out-of-domain parallel corpora and monolingual corpora for in-domain translation are crucial for improving domain-specific translation. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the latest state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques for NMT.

label: acl
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task to recognize specific types of entities from a given sentence. Depending on how the entities appear in the sentence, it can be divided into three subtasks, namely, Flat NER, Nested NER, and Discontinuous NER. Among the existing approaches, only the generative model can be uniformly adapted to these three subtasks. However, when the generative model is applied to NER, its optimization objective is not consistent with the task, which makes the model vulnerable to the incorrect biases. In this paper, we analyze the incorrect biases in the generation process from a causality perspective and attribute them to two confounders: pre-context confounder and entity-order confounder. Furthermore, we design Intra- and Inter-entity Deconfounding Data Augmentation methods to eliminate the above confounders according to the theory of backdoor adjustment. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of the generative NER model in various datasets.

label: acl
text: Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a crucial task in recognizing specific entities from a given sentence. It can be divided into three sub-tasks: Flat NER, Nested NER, and Discontinuous NER, depending on how the entities appear in the sentence. While the generative model can be adapted to all three sub-tasks, its optimization objective is not aligned with the NER task, leading to incorrect biases. In this paper, we examine these biases from a causality perspective and attribute them to two factors: pre-context confounder and entity-order confounder. To mitigate these biases, we propose Intra- and Inter-entity Deconfounding Data Augmentation methods based on the theory of backdoor adjustment. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our method effectively improves the performance of the generative NER model across various datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Recent work has shown that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can implicitly capture and exploit hierarchical information when trained to solve common natural language processing tasks (Blevins et al., 2018) such as language modeling (Linzen et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) and neural machine translation (Shi et al., 2016). In contrast, the ability to model structured data with non-recurrent neural networks has received little attention despite their success in many NLP tasks (Gehring et al., 2017; Vaswani et al., 2017). In this work, we compare the two architectures—recurrent versus non-recurrent—with respect to their ability to model hierarchical structure and find that recurrency is indeed important for this purpose. The code and data used in our experiments is available at https://github.com/ketranm/fan_vs_rnn.

label: emnlp
text: Recent studies have demonstrated that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can effectively capture and leverage hierarchical information in common Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks such as language modeling and neural machine translation. In contrast, the capability of non-recurrent neural networks to model structured data has received limited attention, despite their success in various NLP tasks. In this study, we compare the two architectures - recurrent and non-recurrent - in terms of their ability to model hierarchical structures and find that recurrency is crucial in this regard. The code and data used in our experiments can be accessed at https://github.com/ketranm/fan_vs_rnn.

label: emnlp
text: We introduce novel dynamic oracles for training two of the most accurate known shift-reduce algorithms for constituent parsing: the top-down and in-order transition-based parsers. In both cases, the dynamic oracles manage to notably increase their accuracy, in comparison to that obtained by performing classic static training. In addition, by improving the performance of the state-of-the-art in-order shift-reduce parser, we achieve the best accuracy to date (92.0 F1) obtained by a fully-supervised single-model greedy shift-reduce constituent parser on the WSJ benchmark.

label: emnlp
text: We introduce innovative dynamic oracles for enhancing the accuracy of two of the most precise known shift-reduce algorithms for constituent parsing: the top-down and in-order transition-based parsers. Our dynamic oracles significantly improve the accuracy of both parsers compared to the results obtained through traditional static training. Furthermore, by improving the performance of the state-of-the-art in-order shift-reduce parser, we attain the highest accuracy to date (92.0 F1) for a fully-supervised single-model greedy shift-reduce constituent parser on the WSJ benchmark.

label: coling
text: Ethical judgment aims to determine if a person in a narrative situation acts under people's social norms under a culture, so it is crucial to understand actions in narratives and achieve machine ethics. Recent works depend on data-driven methods to directly judge the ethics of complex real-world narratives but face two major challenges. First, they cannot well handle dilemma situations due to a lack of basic knowledge about social norms. Second, they focus merely on sparse situation-level judgment regardless of the social norms involved during the judgment, leading to a black box. In this work, inspired by previous knowledge-grounded and -augmented paradigms, we propose to complement a complex situation with grounded social norms. Besides a norm-grounding knowledge model, we present a novel norm-supported ethical judgment model in line with neural module networks to alleviate dilemma situations and improve norm-level explainability. Empirically, our model improves state-of-the-art performance on two narrative judgment benchmarks.

label: coling
text: The purpose of ethical judgment is to determine if a person's actions in a narrative situation align with the social norms of their culture. To achieve machine ethics, it is essential to understand these actions and the norms they are based on. However, recent data-driven methods used to judge the ethics of real-world narratives face two significant challenges. Firstly, they struggle to handle dilemma situations because of a lack of knowledge about social norms. Secondly, they focus only on sparse situation-level judgments, ignoring the social norms involved, resulting in a black box. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach that complements complex situations with grounded social norms. Our model includes a norm-grounding knowledge model and a norm-supported ethical judgment model based on neural module networks. This approach improves the state-of-the-art performance on two narrative judgment benchmarks and provides a more explainable norm-level judgment.

label: coling
text: We present LANTERN, a multi-stage transformer architecture for named-entity recognition (NER) designed to operate on indefinitely large text sequences (i.e.  512 elements). For a given image of a form with structured text, our method uses language and spatial features to predict the entity tags of each text element. It breaks the quadratic computational constraints of the attention mechanism by operating over a learned latent space representation which encodes the input sequence via the cross-attention mechanism while having the multi-stage encoding component as a refinement over the NER predictions. As a proxy task, we propose RADAR, an LSTM classifier operating at character level, which predicts the relevance of a word with respect to the entity-recognition task. Additionally, we formulate a challenging novel NER use case, nutritional information extraction from food product labels. We created a dataset with 11,926 images depicting food product labels entitled TREAT dataset, with fully detailed annotations. Our method achieves superior performance against two competitive models designed for long sequences on the proposed TREAT dataset.

label: coling
text: We present LANTERN, a multi-stage transformer architecture for Named-Entity Recognition (NER) that operates on indefinitely long text sequences (i.e. up to 512 elements). Our approach uses language and spatial features to predict the entity tags of each text element in a given image of a structured form. To overcome the computational constraints of the attention mechanism, our method operates over a learned latent space representation that encodes the input sequence via cross-attention, while the multi-stage encoding component refines the NER predictions. As a proxy task, we propose RADAR, an LSTM classifier that operates at the character level, which predicts the relevance of a word to the entity-recognition task. Furthermore, we introduce a novel NER use case, nutritional information extraction from food product labels, and create a dataset, the TREAT dataset, with 11,926 images of food product labels and fully detailed annotations. Our method outperforms two competitive models designed for long sequences on the proposed TREAT dataset.

label: emnlp
text: Attention mechanism is often used in deep neural networks for distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) to distinguish valid from noisy instances. However, traditional 1-D vector attention model is insufficient for learning of different contexts in the selection of valid instances to predict the relationship for an entity pair. To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel multi-level structured (2-D matrix) self-attention mechanism for DS-RE in a multi-instance learning (MIL) framework using bidirectional recurrent neural networks (BiRNN). In the proposed method, a structured word-level self-attention learns a 2-D matrix where each row vector represents a weight distribution for different aspects of an instance regarding two entities. Targeting the MIL issue, the structured sentence-level attention learns a 2-D matrix where each row vector represents a weight distribution on selection of different valid instances. Experiments conducted on two publicly available DS-RE datasets show that the proposed framework with multi-level structured self-attention mechanism significantly outperform baselines in terms of PR curves, P@N and F1 measures.

label: emnlp
text: The use of attention mechanisms is common in deep neural networks for distant supervision of relation extraction (DS-RE) to distinguish between valid and noisy instances. However, traditional 1-D vector attention models are not adequate for learning the different contexts involved in selecting valid instances for predicting relationships between entities. To address this issue, we propose a novel multi-level structured (2-D matrix) self-attention mechanism for DS-RE in a multi-instance learning (MIL) framework using bidirectional recurrent neural networks (BiRNN). Our proposed method utilizes a structured word-level self-attention to learn a 2-D matrix, with each row vector representing a weight distribution for different aspects of an instance related to the two entities. To address the MIL issue, the structured sentence-level attention learns a 2-D matrix, with each row vector representing a weight distribution for selecting different valid instances. Experiments on two publicly available DS-RE datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework with multi-level structured self-attention mechanism significantly outperforms baselines in terms of PR curves, P@N, and F1 measures.

label: coling
text: Indigenous languages of the American continent are highly diverse. However, they have received little attention from the technological perspective. In this paper, we review the research, the digital resources and the available NLP systems that focus on these languages. We present the main challenges and research questions that arise when distant languages and low-resource scenarios are faced. We would like to encourage NLP research in linguistically rich and diverse areas like the Americas.

label: coling
text: The indigenous languages of the American continent are incredibly diverse, yet they have received limited attention from the technological perspective. In this paper, we review the available research, digital resources, and NLP systems that focus on these languages. We present the key challenges and research questions that arise when dealing with distant languages and low-resource scenarios. Our aim is to stimulate NLP research in linguistically rich and diverse regions like the Americas.

label: acl
text: In this work, we propose a novel constituency parsing scheme. The model first predicts a real-valued scalar, named syntactic distance, for each split position in the sentence. The topology of grammar tree is then determined by the values of syntactic distances. Compared to traditional shift-reduce parsing schemes, our approach is free from the potentially disastrous compounding error. It is also easier to parallelize and much faster. Our model achieves the state-of-the-art single model F1 score of 92.1 on PTB and 86.4 on CTB dataset, which surpasses the previous single model results by a large margin.

label: acl
text: In this study, we introduce a new approach to constituency parsing. Our model starts by predicting a scalar value, referred to as the syntactic distance, for each possible split in a sentence. The resulting values are used to determine the structure of the grammar tree. Compared to traditional shift-reduce parsing methods, our approach eliminates the risk of compounding error and is easier to parallelize, resulting in faster processing times. Our model outperforms previous single model results, achieving a state-of-the-art F1 score of 92.1 on the PTB dataset and 86.4 on the CTB dataset, surpassing previous results by a significant margin.

label: acl
text: Disease is one of the fundamental entities in biomedical research. Recognizing such entities from biomedical text and then normalizing them to a standardized disease vocabulary offer a tremendous opportunity for many downstream applications. Previous studies have demonstrated that joint modeling of the two sub-tasks has superior performance than the pipelined counterpart. Although the neural joint model based on multi-task learning framework has achieved state-of-the-art performance, it suffers from the boundary inconsistency problem due to the separate decoding procedures. Moreover, it ignores the rich information (e.g., the text surface form) of each candidate concept in the vocabulary, which is quite essential for entity normalization. In this work, we propose a neural transition-based joint model to alleviate these two issues. We transform the end-to-end disease recognition and normalization task as an action sequence prediction task, which not only jointly learns the model with shared representations of the input, but also jointly searches the output by state transitions in one search space. Moreover, we introduce attention mechanisms to take advantage of the text surface form of each candidate concept for better normalization performance. Experimental results conducted on two publicly available datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

label: acl
text: Disease recognition and normalization are crucial components of biomedical research. The ability to identify and standardize diseases from biomedical text provides numerous opportunities for downstream applications. Previous studies have shown that joint modeling of these two tasks outperforms a pipelined approach. However, current neural joint models based on multi-task learning frameworks suffer from boundary inconsistency and ignore the important information contained in the text surface form of each candidate concept. To address these issues, we propose a neural transition-based joint model that transforms the end-to-end disease recognition and normalization task into an action sequence prediction task. This approach jointly learns the model and searches the output through state transitions in one search space, and incorporates attention mechanisms to utilize the text surface form of each candidate concept for improved normalization performance. Our experiments on two publicly available datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

label: coling
text: Currently, human-bot symbiosis dialog systems, e.g. pre- and after-sales in E-commerce, are ubiquitous, and the dialog routing component is essential to improve the overall efficiency, reduce human resource cost and increase user experience. To satisfy this requirement, existing methods are mostly heuristic and cannot obtain high-quality performance. In this paper, we investigate the important problem by thoroughly mining both the data-to-task and task-to-task knowledge among various kinds of dialog data. To achieve the above target, we propose a comprehensive and general solution with multi-task learning framework, specifically including a novel dialog encoder and two tailored gated mechanism modules. The proposed Gated Mechanism enhanced Multi-task Model (G3M) can play the role of hierarchical information filtering and is non-invasive to the existing dialog systems. Experiments on two datasets collected from the real world demonstrate our method's effectiveness and the results achieve the state-of-the-art performance by relatively increasing 8.7%/11.8% on RMSE metric and 2.2%/4.4% on F1 metric.

label: coling
text: Human-bot symbiotic dialog systems, such as those used in pre- and after-sales in e-commerce, are becoming increasingly common, and the dialog routing component is critical for improving efficiency, reducing human resource costs, and enhancing user experience. However, existing methods for this purpose are largely heuristic and do not perform well. In this paper, we address this problem by thoroughly mining both data-to-task and task-to-task knowledge from various dialog data. To achieve this, we propose a comprehensive and general solution using a multi-task learning framework, including a novel dialog encoder and two tailored gated mechanism modules. Our proposed Gated Mechanism Enhanced Multi-task Model (G3M) functions as a hierarchical information filter and is non-invasive to existing dialog systems. Our experiments on real-world datasets show that our method is effective, with results that outperform the state-of-the-art by 8.7%/11.8% on the RMSE metric and 2.2%/4.4% on the F1 metric.

label: coling
text: Several studies in the literature on the interpretation of Neural Language Models (NLM) focus on the linguistic generalization abilities of pre-trained models. However, little attention is paid to how the linguistic knowledge of the models changes during the fine-tuning steps. In this paper, we contribute to this line of research by showing to what extent a wide range of linguistic phenomena are forgotten across 50 epochs of fine-tuning, and how the preserved linguistic knowledge is correlated with the resolution of the fine-tuning task. To this end, we considered a quite understudied task where linguistic information plays the main role, i.e. the prediction of the evolution of written language competence of native language learners. In addition, we investigate whether it is possible to predict the fine-tuned NLM accuracy across the 50 epochs solely relying on the assessed linguistic competence. Our results are encouraging and show a high relationship between the model's linguistic competence and its ability to solve a linguistically-based downstream task.

label: coling
text: Several studies in the literature have focused on the linguistic generalization abilities of pre-trained Neural Language Models (NLM). However, little attention has been given to how the models' linguistic knowledge changes during fine-tuning. This paper aims to fill this gap by examining the extent to which a wide range of linguistic phenomena are forgotten during 50 epochs of fine-tuning and how the preserved linguistic knowledge is correlated with the resolution of the fine-tuning task. To achieve this, we consider an understudied task where linguistic information plays a crucial role - predicting the evolution of written language competence in native language learners. Furthermore, we investigate whether it is possible to predict the fine-tuned NLM accuracy across the 50 epochs based solely on the assessed linguistic competence. Our results are promising and demonstrate a strong correlation between the model's linguistic competence and its ability to solve a linguistically-based downstream task.

label: coling
text: Most previous research in text simplification has aimed to develop generic solutions, assuming very homogeneous target audiences with consistent intra-group simplification needs. We argue that this assumption does not hold, and that instead we need to develop simplification systems that adapt to the individual needs of specific users. As a first step towards personalized simplification, we propose a framework for adaptive lexical simplification and introduce Lexi, a free open-source and easily extensible tool for adaptive, personalized text simplification. Lexi is easily installed as a browser extension, enabling easy access to the service for its users.

label: coling
text: Previous studies in text simplification have primarily focused on creating generic solutions for homogeneous target audiences with uniform simplification requirements. However, this assumption is flawed, and we need to create systems that cater to the specific needs of individual users. To achieve this, we propose a framework for adaptive lexical simplification and introduce Lexi, a free, open-source tool for personalized text simplification. Lexi can be easily installed as a browser extension, providing convenient access to its users.

label: emnlp
text: To what extent could the sommelier profession, or wine stewardship, be displaced by machine leaning algorithms? There are at least three essential skills that make a qualified sommelier: wine theory, blind tasting, and beverage service, as exemplified in the rigorous certification processes of certified sommeliers and above (advanced and master) with the most authoritative body in the industry, the Court of Master Sommelier (hereafter CMS). We propose and train corresponding machine learning models that match these skills, and compare algorithmic results with real data collected from a large group of wine professionals. We find that our machine learning models outperform human sommeliers on most tasks — most notably in the section of blind tasting, where hierarchically supervised Latent Dirichlet Allocation outperforms sommeliers' judgment calls by over 6% in terms of F1-score; and in the section of beverage service, especially wine and food pairing, a modified Siamese neural network based on BiLSTM achieves better results than sommeliers by 2%. This demonstrates, contrary to popular opinion in the industry, that the sommelier profession is at least to some extent automatable, barring economic (Kleinberg et al., 2017) and psychological (Dietvorst et al., 2015) complications.

label: emnlp
text: To what degree can sommelier expertise, or wine stewardship, be replaced by machine learning algorithms? Three key abilities define a competent sommelier: wine theory, blind tasting, and beverage service, as demonstrated by the rigorous certification processes of certified sommeliers and higher levels (advanced and master) of the industry's leading authority, the Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS). We have developed and trained machine learning models that correspond to these skills and compared their results with actual data collected from a large group of wine professionals. Our findings show that our machine learning models outperform human sommeliers on most tasks, particularly in the area of blind tasting, where a hierarchically supervised Latent Dirichlet Allocation model outperforms sommeliers' judgments by over 6% in terms of F1-score. In the area of beverage service, particularly wine and food pairing, a modified Siamese neural network based on BiLSTM outperforms sommeliers by 2%. This indicates that, contrary to industry beliefs, the sommelier profession is to some extent automatable, despite economic (Kleinberg et al., 2017) and psychological (Dietvorst et al., 2015) challenges.

label: emnlp
text: Current dialogue systems fail at being engaging for users, especially when trained end-to-end without relying on proactive reengaging scripted strategies. Zhang et al. (2018) showed that the engagement level of end-to-end dialogue models increases when conditioning them on text personas providing some personalized back-story to the model. However, the dataset used in Zhang et al. (2018) is synthetic and only contains around 1k different personas. In this paper we introduce a new dataset providing 5 million personas and 700 million persona-based dialogues. Our experiments show that, at this scale, training using personas still improves the performance of end-to-end systems. In addition, we show that other tasks benefit from the wide coverage of our dataset by fine-tuning our model on the data from Zhang et al. (2018) and achieving state-of-the-art results.

label: emnlp
text: Dialogue systems currently struggle to engage users, particularly when they are trained end-to-end without incorporating proactive reengagement strategies. Zhang et al. (2018) demonstrated that end-to-end dialogue models can be made more engaging by conditioning them on text personas that provide a personalized background story. However, the dataset used by Zhang et al. (2018) was limited, consisting of only 1k synthetic personas. In this paper, we present a new dataset featuring 5 million personas and 700 million persona-based dialogues. Our experiments reveal that, even at this scale, training with personas still enhances the performance of end-to-end systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that other tasks can benefit from the extensive coverage of our dataset by fine-tuning our model on the data from Zhang et al. (2018) and achieving state-of-the-art results.

label: naacl
text: As humans, we can modify our assumptions about a scene by imagining alternative objects or concepts in our minds. For example, we can easily anticipate the implications of the sun being overcast by rain clouds (e.g., the street will get wet) and accordingly prepare for that. In this paper, we introduce a new dataset called Commonsense Reasoning for Counterfactual Scene Imagination (CoSIm) which is designed to evaluate the ability of AI systems to reason about scene change imagination. To be specific, in this multimodal task/dataset, models are given an image and an initial question-response pair about the image. Next, a counterfactual imagined scene change (in textual form) is applied, and the model has to predict the new response to the initial question based on this scene change. We collect 3.5K high-quality and challenging data instances, with each instance consisting of an image, a commonsense question with a response, a description of a counterfactual change, a new response to the question, and three distractor responses. Our dataset contains various complex scene change types (such as object addition/removal/state change, event description, environment change, etc.) that require models to imagine many different scenarios and reason about the changed scenes. We present a baseline model based on a vision-language Transformer (i.e., LXMERT) and ablation studies. Through human evaluation, we demonstrate a large human-model performance gap, suggesting room for promising future work on this challenging, counterfactual multimodal task.

label: naacl
text: As humans, we are able to alter our perceptions of a scene by visualizing alternative objects or concepts in our minds. For instance, if we imagine the sun being covered by rain clouds, we can easily predict the consequent implications (e.g. the street will become wet) and prepare accordingly. This paper introduces a new dataset, called Commonsense Reasoning for Counterfactual Scene Imagination (CoSIm), which is designed to assess the capacity of AI systems to reason about changes in a scene's appearance. In this multimodal task, models are presented with an image and an initial question-answer pair related to the image. A counterfactual change is then introduced in textual form, and the model must predict the new answer to the initial question based on this change. Our dataset includes 3.5K high-quality and challenging instances, each consisting of an image, a commonsense question with a response, a description of a counterfactual change, a new response to the question, and three distractor responses. It encompasses a broad range of complex scene changes (such as object addition/removal/state change, event description, environmental changes, etc.), requiring models to imagine various scenarios and reason about the altered scenes. We present a baseline model using a vision-language Transformer (LXMERT) and conduct ablation studies. Our human evaluation reveals a significant gap between human and model performance, indicating ample opportunities for future research in this challenging counterfactual multimodal task.

label: acl
text: We present a study on leveraging multilingual pre-trained generative language models for zero-shot cross-lingual event argument extraction (EAE). By formulating EAE as a language generation task, our method effectively encodes event structures and captures the dependencies between arguments. We design language-agnostic templates to represent the event argument structures, which are compatible with any language, hence facilitating the cross-lingual transfer. Our proposed model finetunes multilingual pre-trained generative language models to generate sentences that fill in the language-agnostic template with arguments extracted from the input passage. The model is trained on source languages and is then directly applied to target languages for event argument extraction. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms the current state-of-the-art models on zero-shot cross-lingual EAE. Comprehensive studies and error analyses are presented to better understand the advantages and the current limitations of using generative language models for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer EAE.

label: acl
text: We present a study on using multilingual pre-trained generative language models for cross-lingual event argument extraction (EAE) without any additional training data. Our approach views EAE as a language generation task, allowing us to effectively encode event structures and capture argument dependencies. To facilitate cross-lingual transfer, we design language-agnostic templates to represent event argument structures. Our model fine-tunes multilingual pre-trained generative language models to generate sentences that fill in these templates with arguments extracted from input passages. This model is trained on source languages and can be directly applied to target languages for event argument extraction. Our experiments show that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art models in zero-shot cross-lingual EAE. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of our results, highlighting the strengths and limitations of using generative language models for this task.

label: naacl
text: Current pre-trained models applied for summarization are prone to factual inconsistencies that misrepresent the source text. Evaluating the factual consistency of summaries is thus necessary to develop better models. However, the human evaluation setup for evaluating factual consistency has not been standardized. To determine the factors that affect the reliability of the human evaluation, we crowdsource evaluations for factual consistency across state-of-the-art models on two news summarization datasets using the rating-based Likert Scale and ranking-based Best-Worst Scaling. Our analysis reveals that the ranking-based Best-Worst Scaling offers a more reliable measure of summary quality across datasets and that the reliability of Likert ratings highly depends on the target dataset and the evaluation design. To improve crowdsourcing reliability, we extend the scale of the Likert rating and present a scoring algorithm for Best-Worst Scaling that we call value learning. Our crowdsourcing guidelines will be publicly available to facilitate future work on factual consistency in summarization.

label: naacl
text: Pre-trained models used for summarization can result in factual inaccuracies that distort the source text. Therefore, evaluating the factual consistency of summaries is critical for improving these models. However, there is no standard approach for human evaluation of factual consistency. To investigate the factors that impact the reliability of human evaluations, we conduct crowdsourced evaluations of the factual consistency of state-of-the-art models on two news summarization datasets using both the Likert Scale and Best-Worst Scaling. Our findings indicate that the Best-Worst Scaling provides a more reliable measure of summary quality across datasets, while the reliability of Likert ratings is dependent on the target dataset and evaluation design. To enhance the reliability of crowdsourcing, we enhance the Likert rating scale and introduce a value learning algorithm for Best-Worst Scaling. Our crowdsourcing guidelines will be publicly accessible to support future work on factual consistency in summarization.

label: naacl
text: Providing technologies to communities or domains where training data is scarce or protected e.g., for privacy reasons, is becoming increasingly important. To that end, we generalise methods for unsupervised transfer from multiple input models for structured prediction. We show that the means of aggregating over the input models is critical, and that multiplying marginal probabilities of substructures to obtain high-probability structures for distant supervision is substantially better than taking the union of such structures over the input models, as done in prior work. Testing on 18 languages, we demonstrate that the method works in a cross-lingual setting, considering both dependency parsing and part-of-speech structured prediction problems. Our analyses show that the proposed method produces less noisy labels for the distant supervision.

label: naacl
text: Providing technologies to communities or domains where training data is scarce or protected due to privacy concerns is becoming increasingly important. To address this challenge, we have developed a general method for unsupervised transfer from multiple input models for structured prediction. Our research shows that the method of aggregating over the input models is crucial, and that multiplying the marginal probabilities of substructures to obtain high-probability structures for distant supervision is more effective than taking the union of such structures from the input models, as previously done. Our tests on 18 languages demonstrate that the method works well in a cross-lingual setting, covering both dependency parsing and part-of-speech structured prediction problems. Our analysis also shows that the proposed method results in fewer noisy labels for distant supervision.

label: coling
text: Natural language generation (NLG) models can propagate social bias towards particular demography.
