Though several studies investigated bias from data and model, NLG task distinctively uses stochastic decoder that can positively or negatively impact the bias-sensitive tokens initially predicted by the model. To address this gap in research, we present an extensive analysis of bias from decoding techniques for open-domain language generation considering the entire decoding space. We analyze to what extent bias metrics like toxicity and sentiment are impacted by the individual components of decoder algorithms. To this extent, we also analyze the trade-off between bias scores and human-annotated generation quality throughout the decoder space. Together, these methods reveal the imperative of testing inference time bias and provide evidence on the usefulness of inspecting the entire decoding spectrum.

label: coling
text: Natural language generation (NLG) models can perpetuate social bias towards certain demographics. While previous studies have examined bias in data and models, the NLG task is unique in that it uses a stochastic decoder that can amplify or mitigate the bias-sensitive tokens predicted by the model. To bridge the gap in research, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of bias in open-domain language generation resulting from decoding techniques. We examine the extent to which bias metrics such as toxicity and sentiment are affected by the various components of decoder algorithms. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between bias scores and human-annotated generation quality across the entire decoding space. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating inference time bias and demonstrate the value of examining the entire decoding spectrum.

label: coling
text: Meta-learning has emerged as an effective approach for few-shot text classification. However, current studies fail to realize the importance of the semantic interaction between sentence features and neglect to enhance the generalization ability of the model to new tasks. In this paper, we integrate an adversarial network architecture into the meta-learning system and leverage cost-effective modules to build a novel few-shot classification framework named SaAML. Significantly, our approach can exploit the temporal convolutional network to encourage more discriminative representation learning and explore the attention mechanism to promote more comprehensive feature expression, thus resulting in better adaptation for new classes. Through a series of experiments on four benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our new framework acquires considerable superiority over state-of-the-art methods in all datasets, increasing the performance of 1-shot classification and 5-shot classification by 7.15% and 2.89%, respectively.

label: coling
text: Meta-learning has proven to be an effective approach for few-shot text classification, but current studies overlook the importance of semantic interaction between sentence features and fail to improve the model's generalization ability to new tasks. To address this, we introduce SaAML, a novel few-shot classification framework that integrates an adversarial network architecture into the meta-learning system and leverages cost-effective modules. SaAML exploits the temporal convolutional network for more discriminative representation learning and employs the attention mechanism for more comprehensive feature expression, resulting in better adaptation to new classes. Our experiments on four benchmark datasets show that SaAML outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with an increase in performance of 1-shot classification and 5-shot classification by 7.15% and 2.89%, respectively.

label: naacl
text: We study the robustness of machine reading comprehension (MRC) models to entity renaming—do models make more wrong predictions when the same questions are asked about an entity whose name has been changed? Such failures imply that models overly rely on entity information to answer questions, and thus may generalize poorly when facts about the world change or questions are asked about novel entities. To systematically audit this issue, we present a pipeline to automatically generate test examples at scale, by replacing entity names in the original test sample with names from a variety of sources, ranging from names in the same test set, to common names in life, to arbitrary strings. Across five datasets and three pretrained model architectures, MRC models consistently perform worse when entities are renamed, with particularly large accuracy drops on datasets constructed via distant supervision. We also find large differences between models: SpanBERT, which is pretrained with span-level masking, is more robust than RoBERTa, despite having similar accuracy on unperturbed test data. We further experiment with different masking strategies as the continual pretraining objective and find that entity-based masking can improve the robustness of MRC models.

label: naacl
text: These results suggest that MRC models are not robust to entity renaming and that there is room for improvement in the design of models and training regimes. We present a systematic study of the robustness of machine reading comprehension (MRC) models to entity renaming. Our study aims to determine if these models make more incorrect predictions when the same questions are asked about an entity whose name has been changed. Our findings indicate that the models heavily rely on entity information to answer questions and may generalize poorly when facts about the world change or when questions are asked about novel entities. To thoroughly examine this issue, we have developed a pipeline to generate test examples at scale. This pipeline replaces entity names in the original test sample with names from a variety of sources, including names in the same test set, common names in life, and arbitrary strings. Our results show that across five datasets and three pretrained model architectures, MRC models perform worse when entities are renamed, with particularly large accuracy drops on datasets constructed via distant supervision. We also found significant differences between models, with SpanBERT, which is pretrained with span-level masking, being more robust than RoBERTa, despite having similar accuracy on unperturbed test data. Finally, our experiments with different masking strategies as the continual pretraining objective indicate that entity-based masking can improve the robustness of MRC models. These results highlight the need for improvement in the design of MRC models and training regimes.

label: emnlp
text: To disambiguate between closely related concepts, entity linking systems need to effectively distill cues from their context, which may be quite noisy. We investigate several techniques for using these cues in the context of noisy entity linking on short texts. Our starting point is a state-of-the-art attention-based model from prior work; while this model's attention typically identifies context that is topically relevant, it fails to identify some of the most indicative surface strings, especially those exhibiting lexical overlap with the true title. Augmenting the model with convolutional networks over characters still leaves it largely unable to pick up on these cues compared to sparse features that target them directly, indicating that automatically learning how to identify relevant character-level context features is a hard problem. Our final system outperforms past work on the WikilinksNED test set by 2.8% absolute.

label: emnlp
text: To accurately distinguish between closely related concepts, entity linking systems must effectively extract context-based cues, even in noisy environments. We explore various techniques for utilizing these cues in the context of entity linking on short texts. Our starting point is a state-of-the-art attention-based model from prior research, which identifies contextually relevant information through attention mechanisms. However, this model falls short in identifying the most critical surface strings, particularly those with lexical overlap with the true title. Despite augmenting the model with convolutional networks, it still struggles to pick up on these important cues. This highlights the challenging nature of automatically learning to identify relevant character-level context features. Our final system shows a 2.8% improvement over previous work on the WikilinksNED test set.

label: naacl
text: This paper proposes an approach for applying GANs to NMT. We build a conditional sequence generative adversarial net which comprises of two adversarial sub models, a generator and a discriminator. The generator aims to generate sentences which are hard to be discriminated from human-translated sentences ( i.e., the golden target sentences); And the discriminator makes efforts to discriminate the machine-generated sentences from human-translated ones. The two sub models play a mini-max game and achieve the win-win situation when they reach a Nash Equilibrium. Additionally, the static sentence-level BLEU is utilized as the reinforced objective for the generator, which biases the generation towards high BLEU points. During training, both the dynamic discriminator and the static BLEU objective are employed to evaluate the generated sentences and feedback the evaluations to guide the learning of the generator. Experimental results show that the proposed model consistently outperforms the traditional RNNSearch and the newly emerged state-of-the-art Transformer on English-German and Chinese-English translation tasks.

label: naacl
text: This paper proposes a new approach for using GANs in NMT (Neural Machine Translation). The approach involves building a conditional sequence generative adversarial network that consists of two sub-models: a generator and a discriminator. The generator's goal is to generate sentences that are difficult to distinguish from human-translated sentences (i.e. the target sentences), while the discriminator strives to differentiate machine-generated sentences from human-translated ones. The two sub-models engage in a mini-max game and reach a Nash Equilibrium, resulting in a win-win situation. The generator is further reinforced by the static sentence-level BLEU, which biases the generation towards high BLEU scores. During training, both the dynamic discriminator and the static BLEU objective are used to evaluate the generated sentences and guide the learning of the generator. The proposed model consistently outperforms traditional RNNSearch and state-of-the-art Transformer models on English-German and Chinese-English translation tasks, according to the experimental results.

label: naacl
text: Multi-task learning with an unbalanced data distribution skews model learning towards high resource tasks, especially when model capacity is fixed and fully shared across all tasks. Sparse scaling architectures, such as BASELayers, provide flexible mechanisms for different tasks to have a variable number of parameters, which can be useful to counterbalance skewed data distributions. We find that that sparse architectures for multilingual machine translation can perform poorly out of the box and propose two straightforward techniques to mitigate this — a temperature heating mechanism and dense pre-training. Overall, these methods improve performance on two multilingual translation benchmarks compared to standard BASELayers and Dense scaling baselines, and in combination, more than 2x model convergence speed.

label: naacl
text: Multi-task learning with an imbalanced data distribution can result in biased model learning towards high-resource tasks, particularly when the model's capacity is fixed and shared equally across all tasks. To address this issue, sparse scaling architectures such as BASELayers offer flexible options for different tasks to have varying numbers of parameters, which can help counteract the skewed data distribution. Our study shows that using sparse architectures for multilingual machine translation may not always produce optimal results, and we propose two simple techniques for improvement: a temperature heating mechanism and dense pre-training. These methods enhance performance on two multilingual translation benchmarks in comparison to standard BASELayers and dense scaling baselines, and result in more than a 2x increase in model convergence speed when used together.

label: acl
text: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems exhibit problematic biases, such as stereotypical gender bias in the translation of occupation terms into languages with grammatical gender. In this paper we describe a new source of bias prevalent in NMT systems, relating to translations of sentences containing person names. To correctly translate such sentences, a NMT system needs to determine the gender of the name. We show that leading systems are particularly poor at this task, especially for female given names. This bias is deeper than given name gender: we show that the translation of terms with ambiguous sentiment can also be affected by person names, and the same holds true for proper nouns denoting race. To mitigate these biases we propose a simple but effective data augmentation method based on randomly switching entities during translation, which effectively eliminates the problem without any effect on translation quality.

label: acl
text: The translation systems in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) tend to exhibit biases, such as gender bias in the translation of job titles in languages that have grammatical gender. This paper highlights a new source of bias in NMT systems, specifically in the translation of sentences that contain personal names. To accurately translate these sentences, the NMT system must determine the gender of the name. Our research shows that current NMT systems struggle with this task, particularly for female names. This bias goes beyond just the gender of a name and also affects the translation of terms with ambiguous sentiment and proper nouns that denote race. To address these biases, we propose a simple but effective data augmentation method that involves randomly swapping entities during translation. This method effectively eliminates the biases without compromising the quality of the translation.

label: coling
text: This paper proposes an extractive multi-document summarization approach based on an ant colony system to optimize the information coverage of summary sentences. The implemented system was evaluated on both English and Arabic versions of the corpus of the Text Analysis Conference 2011 MultiLing Pilot by using ROUGE metrics. The evaluation results are promising in comparison to those of the participating systems. Indeed, our system achieved the best scores based on several ROUGE metrics.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a proposal for an extractive multi-document summarization approach that leverages an ant colony system to optimize the coverage of summary sentences. The system was evaluated on both English and Arabic versions of the Text Analysis Conference 2011 MultiLing Pilot corpus using ROUGE metrics. The results of the evaluation were encouraging, with our system achieving the best scores based on multiple ROUGE metrics.

label: coling
text: Multi-turn conversation understanding is a major challenge for building intelligent dialogue systems. This work focuses on retrieval-based response matching for multi-turn conversation whose related work simply concatenates the conversation utterances, ignoring the interactions among previous utterances for context modeling. In this paper, we formulate previous utterances into context using a proposed deep utterance aggregation model to form a fine-grained context representation. In detail, a self-matching attention is first introduced to route the vital information in each utterance. Then the model matches a response with each refined utterance and the final matching score is obtained after attentive turns aggregation. Experimental results show our model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on three multi-turn conversation benchmarks, including a newly introduced e-commerce dialogue corpus.

label: coling
text: The challenge of building intelligent dialogue systems is the understanding of multi-turn conversations. This paper focuses on retrieval-based response matching for multi-turn conversations, where previous work has simply concatenated the conversation utterances without considering the interactions among them for context modeling. To address this issue, we formulate previous utterances into context using a proposed deep utterance aggregation model. This model creates a fine-grained context representation by introducing a self-matching attention mechanism to route the vital information in each utterance. The model then matches a response with each refined utterance and aggregates the matching scores after multiple attentive turns. Our experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on three multi-turn conversation benchmarks, including a newly introduced e-commerce dialogue corpus.

label: coling
text: This survey discusses how recent developments in multimodal processing facilitate conceptual grounding of language. We categorize the information flow in multimodal processing with respect to cognitive models of human information processing and analyze different methods for combining multimodal representations. Based on this methodological inventory, we discuss the benefit of multimodal grounding for a variety of language processing tasks and the challenges that arise. We particularly focus on multimodal grounding of verbs which play a crucial role for the compositional power of language.

label: coling
text: The present survey examines the impact of recent advancements in multimodal processing on the conceptual foundation of language. We categorize the flow of information in multimodal processing based on cognitive models of human information processing and examine various methods for combining multimodal representations. After conducting a comprehensive analysis of these methods, we explore the advantages of multimodal grounding for a range of language processing tasks and the challenges that come with it. Our focus is particularly on the multimodal grounding of verbs, which are crucial for the language's compositional ability.

label: naacl
text: There are many ways to express similar things in text, which makes evaluating natural language generation (NLG) systems difficult. Compounding this difficulty is the need to assess varying quality criteria depending on the deployment setting. While the landscape of NLG evaluation has been well-mapped, practitioners' goals, assumptions, and constraints—which inform decisions about what, when, and how to evaluate—are often partially or implicitly stated, or not stated at all. Combining a formative semi-structured interview study of NLG practitioners (N=18) with a survey study of a broader sample of practitioners (N=61), we surface goals, community practices, assumptions, and constraints that shape NLG evaluations, examining their implications and how they embody ethical considerations.

label: naacl
text: There are numerous ways to convey similar ideas in text, making the evaluation of natural language generation (NLG) systems a challenging task. The challenge is further compounded by the need to assess various quality criteria based on the deployment setting. Although the field of NLG evaluation has been thoroughly explored, the goals, assumptions, and constraints of practitioners - which inform their decisions on what, when, and how to evaluate - are often only partially or implicitly stated, or not stated at all. To shed light on these issues, we conducted a formative semi-structured interview study with 18 NLG practitioners and a survey study with a larger sample of 61 practitioners. Our findings highlight the goals, community practices, assumptions, and constraints that shape NLG evaluations, and how they embody ethical considerations.

label: emnlp
text: Self-attention networks have proven to be of profound value for its strength of capturing global dependencies. In this work, we propose to model localness for self-attention networks, which enhances the ability of capturing useful local context. We cast localness modeling as a learnable Gaussian bias, which indicates the central and scope of the local region to be paid more attention. The bias is then incorporated into the original attention distribution to form a revised distribution. To maintain the strength of capturing long distance dependencies while enhance the ability of capturing short-range dependencies, we only apply localness modeling to lower layers of self-attention networks. Quantitative and qualitative analyses on Chinese-English and English-German translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach.

label: emnlp
text: Self-attention networks have demonstrated their profound value in capturing global dependencies. In this work, we propose to enhance their ability to capture useful local context by modeling localness. We cast this modeling as a learnable Gaussian bias, which indicates the center and scope of the local region that should receive more attention. This bias is then incorporated into the original attention distribution to form a revised distribution. To balance the ability to capture both long-distance and short-range dependencies, we only apply localness modeling to the lower layers of the self-attention network. Our quantitative and qualitative analyses on Chinese-English and English-German translation tasks show the effectiveness and universality of our approach.

label: acl
text: Previous math word problem solvers following the encoder-decoder paradigm fail to explicitly incorporate essential math symbolic constraints, leading to unexplainable and unreasonable predictions. Herein, we propose Neural-Symbolic Solver (NS-Solver) to explicitly and seamlessly incorporate different levels of symbolic constraints by auxiliary tasks. Our NS-Solver consists of a problem reader to encode problems, a programmer to generate symbolic equations, and a symbolic executor to obtain answers. Along with target expression supervision, our solver is also optimized via 4 new auxiliary objectives to enforce different symbolic reasoning: a) self-supervised number prediction task predicting both number quantity and number locations; b) commonsense constant prediction task predicting what prior knowledge (e.g. how many legs a chicken has) is required; c) program consistency checker computing the semantic loss between predicted equation and target equation to ensure reasonable equation mapping; d) duality exploiting task exploiting the quasi-duality between symbolic equation generation and problem's part-of-speech generation to enhance the understanding ability of a solver. Besides, to provide a more realistic and challenging benchmark for developing a universal and scalable solver, we also construct a new largescale MWP benchmark CM17K consisting of 4 kinds of MWPs (arithmetic, one-unknown linear, one-unknown non-linear, equation set) with more than 17K samples. Extensive experiments on Math23K and our CM17k demonstrate the superiority of our NS-Solver compared to state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: Previous math word problem solvers that follow the encoder-decoder paradigm don't incorporate essential math symbolic constraints, causing predictions that are unexplainable and unreasonable. To address this, we propose the Neural-Symbolic Solver (NS-Solver), which explicitly and seamlessly incorporates different levels of symbolic constraints through auxiliary tasks. Our NS-Solver includes a problem reader to encode problems, a programmer to generate symbolic equations, and a symbolic executor to obtain answers. In addition to target expression supervision, our solver is optimized through four new auxiliary objectives: (a) a self-supervised number prediction task that predicts both the quantity and location of numbers; (b) a commonsense constant prediction task that predicts what prior knowledge is required; (c) a program consistency checker that calculates the semantic loss between the predicted equation and the target equation to ensure reasonable equation mapping; and (d) a duality exploiting task that exploits the quasi-duality between symbolic equation generation and problem's part-of-speech generation to enhance the solver's understanding ability. To provide a more realistic and challenging benchmark, we also created a new, large-scale MWP benchmark, CM17K, consisting of 4 types of MWPs (arithmetic, one-unknown linear, one-unknown non-linear, equation set) with over 17K samples. Our experiments on Math23K and CM17K show that our NS-Solver outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: In sequence modeling, certain tokens are usually less ambiguous than others, and representations of these tokens require fewer refinements for disambiguation. However, given the nature of attention-based models like Transformer and UT (universal transformer), all tokens are equally processed towards depth. Inspired by the equilibrium phenomenon, we present a lazy transition, a mechanism to adjust the significance of iterative refinements for each token representation. Our lazy transition is deployed on top of UT to build LT (lazy transformer), where all tokens are processed unequally towards depth. Eventually, LT is encouraged to oscillate around a relaxed equilibrium. Our experiments show that LT outperforms baseline models on several tasks of machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute, and LAMBADA.

label: acl
text: In sequence modeling, some tokens tend to be less ambiguous and require fewer refinements for disambiguation, while others are more complex. However, attention-based models like the Transformer and Universal Transformer (UT) treat all tokens equally in terms of processing depth. To address this issue, we introduce the lazy transition mechanism to adjust the significance of iterative refinements for each token representation. This mechanism is integrated into the Universal Transformer to create the Lazy Transformer (LT), where tokens are processed differently in terms of depth. The LT oscillates around a relaxed equilibrium, leading to improved performance on various tasks such as machine translation, pre-training, Learning to Execute, and LAMBADA, as shown by our experiments.

label: acl
text: We study the interpretability issue of task-oriented dialogue systems in this paper. Previously, most neural-based task-oriented dialogue systems employ an implicit reasoning strategy that makes the model predictions uninterpretable to humans. To obtain a transparent reasoning process, we introduce neuro-symbolic to perform explicit reasoning that justifies model decisions by reasoning chains. Since deriving reasoning chains requires multi-hop reasoning for task-oriented dialogues, existing neuro-symbolic approaches would induce error propagation due to the one-phase design. To overcome this, we propose a two-phase approach that consists of a hypothesis generator and a reasoner. We first obtain multiple hypotheses, i.e., potential operations to perform the desired task, through the hypothesis generator. Each hypothesis is then verified by the reasoner, and the valid one is selected to conduct the final prediction. The whole system is trained by exploiting raw textual dialogues without using any reasoning chain annotations. Experimental studies on two public benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach not only achieves better results, but also introduces an interpretable decision process.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we examine the interpretability of task-oriented dialogue systems. Previously, most neural-based systems have employed an implicit reasoning strategy that makes their predictions uninterpretable to humans. To address this, we introduce a neuro-symbolic approach that performs explicit reasoning and justifies model decisions with reasoning chains. However, existing neuro-symbolic methods are prone to error propagation due to their one-phase design, especially when multi-hop reasoning is required for task-oriented dialogues. To overcome this, we propose a two-phase approach consisting of a hypothesis generator and a reasoner. The hypothesis generator obtains multiple potential operations for the desired task, and the reasoner verifies each hypothesis before selecting the valid one for the final prediction. Our system is trained on raw textual dialogues without any reasoning chain annotations. Our experiments on two public benchmark datasets show that our approach not only achieves better results but also provides an interpretable decision process.

label: emnlp
text: In this work, we propose a novel method for training neural networks to perform single-document extractive summarization without heuristically-generated extractive labels. We call our approach BanditSum as it treats extractive summarization as a contextual bandit (CB) problem, where the model receives a document to summarize (the context), and chooses a sequence of sentences to include in the summary (the action). A policy gradient reinforcement learning algorithm is used to train the model to select sequences of sentences that maximize ROUGE score. We perform a series of experiments demonstrating that BanditSum is able to achieve ROUGE scores that are better than or comparable to the state-of-the-art for extractive summarization, and converges using significantly fewer update steps than competing approaches. In addition, we show empirically that BanditSum performs significantly better than competing approaches when good summary sentences appear late in the source document.

label: emnlp
text: We present a novel method for training neural networks to perform single-document extractive summarization without the use of heuristically-generated extractive labels. Our approach, called BanditSum, treats extractive summarization as a contextual bandit problem. In this problem, the model receives a document to summarize (the context) and must choose a sequence of sentences to include in the summary (the action). To train the model, we use a policy gradient reinforcement learning algorithm that helps the model select sequences of sentences that maximize the ROUGE score. Our experiments demonstrate that BanditSum outperforms or is comparable to the state-of-the-art for extractive summarization, and converges faster than competing approaches. Furthermore, our empirical results show that BanditSum performs significantly better than other approaches when good summary sentences appear late in the source document.

label: acl
text: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) currently exhibits biases such as producing translations that are too short and overgenerating frequent words, and shows poor robustness to copy noise in training data or domain shift. Recent work has tied these shortcomings to beam search – the de facto standard inference algorithm in NMT – and Eikema & Aziz (2020) propose to use Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding on unbiased samples instead. In this paper, we empirically investigate the properties of MBR decoding on a number of previously reported biases and failure cases of beam search. We find that MBR still exhibits a length and token frequency bias, owing to the MT metrics used as utility functions, but that MBR also increases robustness against copy noise in the training data and domain shift.

label: acl
text: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is currently facing some biases, such as generating translations that are too short and overusing common words, and it is also not very robust in dealing with copy noise in the training data or domain shift. Recent research has linked these issues to the use of beam search, which is the most commonly used inference algorithm in NMT. To address these problems, Eikema & Aziz (2020) proposed using Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding based on unbiased samples. In this paper, we examine the properties of MBR decoding and its impact on the biases and failure cases of beam search. Our findings show that MBR still has a length and token frequency bias, due to the use of MT metrics as utility functions, but it also improves robustness against copy noise in the training data and domain shift.

label: acl
text: This paper demonstrates how a graph-based semantic parser can be applied to the task of structured sentiment analysis, directly predicting sentiment graphs from text. We advance the state of the art on 4 out of 5 standard benchmark sets. We release the source code, models and predictions.

label: acl
text: This paper showcases the application of a graph-based semantic parser to structured sentiment analysis, with the aim of directly predicting sentiment graphs from text. Our approach advances the state-of-the-art on 4 out of 5 standard benchmark sets. Additionally, we make the source code, models and predictions publicly available.

label: acl
text: Multilingual pre-trained models are able to zero-shot transfer knowledge from rich-resource to low-resource languages in machine reading comprehension (MRC). However, inherent linguistic discrepancies in different languages could make answer spans predicted by zero-shot transfer violate syntactic constraints of the target language. In this paper, we propose a novel multilingual MRC framework equipped with a Siamese Semantic Disentanglement Model (S2DM) to disassociate semantics from syntax in representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. To explicitly transfer only semantic knowledge to the target language, we propose two groups of losses tailored for semantic and syntactic encoding and disentanglement. Experimental results on three multilingual MRC datasets (i.e., XQuAD, MLQA, and TyDi QA) demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach over models based on mBERT and XLM-100.

label: acl
text: Multilingual pre-trained models can transfer knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in machine reading comprehension (MRC) using zero-shot transfer. However, linguistic discrepancies in different languages can result in answer spans predicted by zero-shot transfer that violate the syntactic constraints of the target language. To address this issue, we propose a novel multilingual MRC framework that includes a Siamese Semantic Disentanglement Model (S2DM) to separate semantics from syntax in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. Our approach explicitly transfers only semantic knowledge to the target language by using two groups of losses specifically designed for semantic and syntactic encoding and disentanglement. The effectiveness of our proposed approach is demonstrated through experiments on three multilingual MRC datasets (XQuAD, MLQA, and TyDi QA), which show that it outperforms models based on mBERT and XLM-100.

label: acl
text: Responsing with image has been recognized as an important capability for an intelligent conversational agent. Yet existing works only focus on exploring the multimodal dialogue models which depend on retrieval-based methods, but neglecting generation methods. To fill in the gaps, we first present a new task: multimodal dialogue response generation (MDRG) - given the dialogue history, one model needs to generate a text sequence or an image as response. Learning such a MDRG model often requires multimodal dialogues containing both texts and images which are difficult to obtain. Motivated by the challenge in practice, we consider MDRG under a natural assumption that only limited training examples are available. In such a low-resource setting, we devise a novel conversational agent, Divter, in order to isolate parameters that depend on multimodal dialogues from the entire generation model. By this means, the major part of the model can be learned from a large number of text-only dialogues and text-image pairs respectively, then the whole parameters can be well fitted using the limited training examples. Extensive experiments demonstrate our method achieves state-of-the-art results in both automatic and human evaluation, and can generate informative text and high-resolution image responses.

label: acl
text: Responding with images has been identified as a crucial capability for intelligent conversational agents. However, existing works only concentrate on exploring multimodal dialogue models that rely on retrieval-based methods, neglecting generation methods. To address this gap, we introduce a new task: Multimodal Dialogue Response Generation (MDRG). This task requires a model to generate a text sequence or an image response given the dialogue history. However, learning a MDRG model often requires a large number of multimodal dialogues, which are difficult to obtain. To overcome this challenge, we consider MDRG in a low-resource setting, where only limited training examples are available. To address this challenge, we propose a novel conversational agent, Divter, which isolates parameters that depend on multimodal dialogues from the entire generation model. By doing so, the majority of the model can be learned from a large number of text-only dialogues and text-image pairs, and then the entire parameters can be fine-tuned using limited training examples. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art results in both automatic and human evaluations, generating informative text and high-resolution image responses.

label: naacl
text: Most existing reading comprehension datasets focus on single-span answers, which can be extracted as a single contiguous span from a given text passage. Multi-span questions, i.e., questions whose answer is a series of multiple discontiguous spans in the text, are common real life but are less studied. In this paper, we present MultiSpanQA, a new dataset that focuses on multi-span questions. Raw questions and contexts are extracted from the Natural Questions dataset. After multi-span re-annotation, MultiSpanQA consists of over a total of 6,000 multi-span questions in the basic version, and over 19,000 examples with unanswerable questions, and questions with single-, and multi-span answers in the expanded version. We introduce new metrics for the purposes of multi-span question answering evaluation, and establish several baselines using advanced models. Finally, we propose a new model which beats all baselines and achieves state-of-the-art on our dataset.

label: naacl
text: Most existing reading comprehension datasets concentrate on single-span answers, which can be identified as a single, continuous span in a given text. However, multi-span questions, which require a series of multiple, non-contiguous spans in the text as the answer, are more common in real life but have been less studied. This paper introduces MultiSpanQA, a new dataset that focuses on multi-span questions. The raw questions and contexts were extracted from the Natural Questions dataset, and after multi-span re-annotation, MultiSpanQA consists of over 6,000 multi-span questions in its basic version and over 19,000 examples with unanswerable questions and questions with single- and multi-span answers in its expanded version. We also propose new metrics for multi-span question answering evaluation and establish several baselines using advanced models. Finally, we present a new model that outperforms all baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on our dataset.

label: acl
text: Due to the great potential in facilitating software development, code generation has attracted increasing attention recently. Generally, dominant models are Seq2Tree models, which convert the input natural language description into a sequence of tree-construction actions corresponding to the pre-order traversal of an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). However, such a traversal order may not be suitable for handling all multi-branch nodes. In this paper, we propose to equip the Seq2Tree model with a context-based Branch Selector, which is able to dynamically determine optimal expansion orders of branches for multi-branch nodes. Particularly, since the selection of expansion orders is a non-differentiable multi-step operation, we optimize the selector through reinforcement learning, and formulate the reward function as the difference of model losses obtained through different expansion orders. Experimental results and in-depth analysis on several commonly-used datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of our approach. We have released our code at https://github.com/DeepLearnXMU/CG-RL.

label: acl
text: Due to its potential to simplify software development, code generation has recently gained significant attention. The dominant models in this field are Seq2Tree models, which convert natural language descriptions into sequences of tree-construction actions that correspond to the pre-order traversal of an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). However, this pre-order traversal may not be suitable for handling multi-branch nodes. To address this issue, we propose a Seq2Tree model equipped with a context-based Branch Selector, which dynamically determines the optimal expansion orders of branches for multi-branch nodes. Since the selection of expansion orders is a non-differentiable multi-step operation, we optimize the selector through reinforcement learning and formulate the reward function as the difference in model losses obtained through different expansion orders. Our approach has been demonstrated to be effective and general through experimental results and in-depth analysis on several commonly-used datasets. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/DeepLearnXMU/CG-RL.

label: acl
text: Attention-based long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have proven to be useful in aspect-level sentiment classification. However, due to the difficulties in annotating aspect-level data, existing public datasets for this task are all relatively small, which largely limits the effectiveness of those neural models. In this paper, we explore two approaches that transfer knowledge from document-level data, which is much less expensive to obtain, to improve the performance of aspect-level sentiment classification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches on 4 public datasets from SemEval 2014, 2015, and 2016, and we show that attention-based LSTM benefits from document-level knowledge in multiple ways.

label: acl
text: Rewritten: Attention-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have proven to be effective in aspect-level sentiment classification. However, the limited size of existing public datasets for this task, which is largely due to the difficulties in annotating aspect-level data, hinders the performance of these neural models. To address this issue, we present two approaches that transfer knowledge from document-level data, which is more readily available, to improve the performance of aspect-level sentiment classification. Our approaches are demonstrated to be effective on four public datasets from SemEval 2014, 2015, and 2016, and we show that attention-based LSTMs benefit from document-level knowledge in multiple ways.

label: acl
text: This paper studies a new problem setting of entity alignment for knowledge graphs (KGs). Since KGs possess different sets of entities, there could be entities that cannot find alignment across them, leading to the problem of dangling entities. As the first attempt to this problem, we construct a new dataset and design a multi-task learning framework for both entity alignment and dangling entity detection. The framework can opt to abstain from predicting alignment for the detected dangling entities. We propose three techniques for dangling entity detection that are based on the distribution of nearest-neighbor distances, i.e., nearest neighbor classification, marginal ranking and background ranking. After detecting and removing dangling entities, an incorporated entity alignment model in our framework can provide more robust alignment for remaining entities. Comprehensive experiments and analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. We further discover that the dangling entity detection module can, in turn, improve alignment learning and the final performance. The contributed resource is publicly available to foster further research.

label: acl
text: This paper explores a new area of research: entity alignment for knowledge graphs (KGs). Since KGs contain different entities, some entities may not be aligned across them, resulting in the problem of dangling entities. To address this issue, we introduce a new dataset and a multi-task learning framework for entity alignment and dangling entity detection. Our framework allows for abstaining from predicting alignment for detected dangling entities. We also propose three techniques for dangling entity detection, based on the distribution of nearest-neighbor distances, including nearest neighbor classification, marginal ranking, and background ranking. By removing dangling entities, the incorporated entity alignment model in our framework provides more robust alignment for the remaining entities. Our comprehensive experiments and analyses show the effectiveness of our framework, and we find that the dangling entity detection module can even improve the final performance of the alignment learning. The resources we contribute are publicly available to encourage further research.

label: coling
text: Text infilling aims to restore incomplete texts by filling in blanks, which has attracted more attention recently because of its wide application in ancient text restoration and text rewriting. However, attribute- aware text infilling is yet to be explored, and existing methods seldom focus on the infilling length of each blank or the number/location of blanks. In this paper, we propose an Attribute-aware Text Infilling method via a Pre-trained language model (A-TIP), which contains a text infilling component and a plug- and-play discriminator. Specifically, we first design a unified text infilling component with modified attention mechanisms and intra- and inter-blank positional encoding to better perceive the number of blanks and the infilling length for each blank. Then, we propose a plug-and-play discriminator to guide generation towards the direction of improving attribute relevance without decreasing text fluency. Finally, automatic and human evaluations on three open-source datasets indicate that A-TIP achieves state-of- the-art performance compared with all baselines.

label: coling
text: The aim of text infilling is to fill in the gaps in incomplete texts. This has become increasingly popular due to its use in ancient text restoration and text rewriting. However, there is a lack of research in attribute-aware text infilling, and current methods do not consider the number or location of blanks or the length of the text to be filled in. In this paper, we present a new method, called Attribute-aware Text Infilling via a Pre-trained language model (A-TIP), which combines a text infilling component with a plug-and-play discriminator. Our method uses modified attention mechanisms and positional encoding to better understand the number of blanks and the length of the text to be filled in. The plug-and-play discriminator helps to improve attribute relevance while maintaining text fluency. Our results, obtained through automatic and human evaluations on three datasets, show that A-TIP outperforms existing methods.

label: naacl
text: Ontologies compartmentalize types and relations in a target domain and provide the semantic backbone needed for a plethora of practical applications. Very often different ontologies are developed independently for the same domain. Such “parallel” ontologies raise the need for a process that will establish alignments between their entities in order to unify and extend the existing knowledge. In this work, we present a novel entity alignment method which we dub DeepAlignment. DeepAlignment refines pre-trained word vectors aiming at deriving ontological entity descriptions which are tailored to the ontology matching task. The absence of explicit information relevant to the ontology matching task during the refinement process makes DeepAlignment completely unsupervised. We empirically evaluate our method using standard ontology matching benchmarks. We present significant performance improvements over the current state-of-the-art, demonstrating the advantages that representation learning techniques bring to ontology matching.

label: naacl
text: Ontologies categorize types and relationships within a specific domain and provide the semantic foundation for a wide range of practical applications. However, it is common for different ontologies to be developed independently for the same domain, leading to the need for a process to align their entities and unify existing knowledge. To address this, we introduce a novel entity alignment method called DeepAlignment. This method uses pre-trained word vectors to refine ontological entity descriptions specifically for ontology matching. As there is no explicit information relevant to the ontology matching task during the refinement process, DeepAlignment is completely unsupervised. Our method is evaluated using standard ontology matching benchmarks, and our results show significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the benefits of representation learning techniques in ontology matching.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we address the problem of finding a novel document descriptor based on the covariance matrix of the word vectors of a document. Our descriptor has a fixed length, which makes it easy to use in many supervised and unsupervised applications. We tested our novel descriptor in different tasks including supervised and unsupervised settings. Our evaluation shows that our document covariance descriptor fits different tasks with competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: This paper presents a novel document descriptor based on the covariance matrix of the word vectors of a document. The fixed length of the descriptor makes it easily adaptable for a range of supervised and unsupervised applications. Our evaluation demonstrates that this document covariance descriptor performs competitively against state-of-the-art methods in various tasks, including both supervised and unsupervised settings.

label: coling
text: This paper studies event causality identification, which aims at predicting the causality relation for a pair of events in a sentence. Regarding event causality identification as a supervised classification task, most existing methods suffer from the problem of insufficient annotated data. In this paper, we propose a new derivative prompt joint learning model for event causality identification, which leverages potential causal knowledge in the pre-trained language model to tackle the data scarcity problem. Specifically, rather than external data or knowledge augmentation, we derive two relevant prompt tasks from event causality identification to enhance the model's ability to identify explicit and implicit causality. We evaluate our model on two benchmark datasets and the results show that our model has great advantages over previous methods.

label: coling
text: This paper investigates event causality identification, which aims to predict the causal relationship between events in a sentence. Most existing methods for event causality identification, which are treated as a supervised classification task, are limited by the scarcity of annotated data. To address this challenge, we introduce a new derivative prompt joint learning model for event causality identification. This model leverages the potential causal knowledge from a pre-trained language model to overcome the data scarcity issue. Rather than relying on external data or knowledge augmentation, our model derives two relevant prompt tasks from event causality identification to enhance its ability to identify both explicit and implicit causality. Our experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our model over previous methods.

label: acl
text: Complex word identification (CWI) is a cornerstone process towards proper text simplification. CWI is highly dependent on context, whereas its difficulty is augmented by the scarcity of available datasets which vary greatly in terms of domains and languages. As such, it becomes increasingly more difficult to develop a robust model that generalizes across a wide array of input examples. In this paper, we propose a novel training technique for the CWI task based on domain adaptation to improve the target character and context representations. This technique addresses the problem of working with multiple domains, inasmuch as it creates a way of smoothing the differences between the explored datasets. Moreover, we also propose a similar auxiliary task, namely text simplification, that can be used to complement lexical complexity prediction. Our model obtains a boost of up to 2.42% in terms of Pearson Correlation Coefficients in contrast to vanilla training techniques, when considering the CompLex from the Lexical Complexity Prediction 2021 dataset. At the same time, we obtain an increase of 3% in Pearson scores, while considering a cross-lingual setup relying on the Complex Word Identification 2018 dataset. In addition, our model yields state-of-the-art results in terms of Mean Absolute Error.

label: acl
text: The process of Complex Word Identification (CWI) is crucial for proper text simplification. However, it is challenging because it is highly dependent on context and there is a lack of available datasets that vary greatly in terms of domain and language. This makes it difficult to develop a generalizable model. In this paper, we present a novel technique for training the CWI task that uses domain adaptation to improve the representation of characters and context. This technique helps to bridge the gap between different datasets, making it easier to work with multiple domains. Additionally, we propose an auxiliary task, text simplification, to complement lexical complexity prediction. Our model outperforms traditional training techniques, with a 2.42% increase in Pearson Correlation Coefficients on the CompLex dataset from the Lexical Complexity Prediction 2021 dataset. We also see a 3% increase in Pearson scores when using a cross-lingual setup with the Complex Word Identification 2018 dataset. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of Mean Absolute Error.

label: coling
text: Predicting Machine Translation (MT) quality can help in many practical tasks such as MT post-editing. The performance of Quality Estimation (QE) methods has drastically improved recently with the introduction of neural approaches to the problem. However, thus far neural approaches have only been designed for word and sentence-level prediction. We present a neural framework that is able to accommodate neural QE approaches at these fine-grained levels and generalize them to the level of documents. We test the framework with two sentence-level neural QE approaches: a state of the art approach that requires extensive pre-training, and a new light-weight approach that we propose, which employs basic encoders. Our approach is significantly faster and yields performance improvements for a range of document-level quality estimation tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first neural architecture for document-level QE. In addition, for the first time we apply QE models to the output of both statistical and neural MT systems for a series of European languages and highlight the new challenges resulting from the use of neural MT.

label: coling
text: Predicting the quality of Machine Translation (MT) can be useful in various practical applications, such as MT post-editing. The performance of Quality Estimation (QE) methods has recently been greatly improved by the implementation of neural approaches. However, these neural approaches have only been designed for word and sentence-level predictions. Our paper introduces a neural framework that can incorporate these fine-grained neural QE methods and extend them to the document level. We evaluate the framework using two sentence-level neural QE approaches: a state-of-the-art method that requires extensive pre-training and a new, lightweight approach that we propose, which uses basic encoders. Our approach is significantly faster and delivers improved performance for a variety of document-level quality estimation tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first neural architecture for document-level QE. Additionally, we apply QE models to the outputs of both statistical and neural MT systems for a series of European languages and highlight the new challenges posed by the use of neural MT.

label: acl
text: Few-shot crosslingual transfer has been shown to outperform its zero-shot counterpart with pretrained encoders like multilingual BERT. Despite its growing popularity, little to no attention has been paid to standardizing and analyzing the design of few-shot experiments. In this work, we highlight a fundamental risk posed by this shortcoming, illustrating that the model exhibits a high degree of sensitivity to the selection of few shots. We conduct a large-scale experimental study on 40 sets of sampled few shots for six diverse NLP tasks across up to 40 languages. We provide an analysis of success and failure cases of few-shot transfer, which highlights the role of lexical features. Additionally, we show that a straightforward full model finetuning approach is quite effective for few-shot transfer, outperforming several state-of-the-art few-shot approaches. As a step towards standardizing few-shot crosslingual experimental designs, we make our sampled few shots publicly available.

label: acl
text: Few-shot cross-lingual transfer has been shown to outperform its zero-shot counterpart, thanks to pretrained encoders like multilingual BERT. Despite its growing popularity, there has been little to no focus on standardizing and analyzing the design of few-shot experiments. This lack of attention poses a fundamental risk, as our research illustrates that the model is highly sensitive to the selection of few shots. To address this issue, we conducted a large-scale experimental study on 40 sets of sampled few shots for six NLP tasks across 40 languages. Our analysis of success and failure cases highlights the importance of lexical features and shows that full model finetuning is the most effective approach for few-shot transfer, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. To contribute to the standardization of few-shot cross-lingual experimental designs, we made our sampled few shots publicly available.

text: With the ever growing scale of neural models, knowledge distillation (KD) attracts more attention as a prominent tool for neural model compression. However, there are counter intuitive observations in the literature showing some challenging limitations of KD. A case in point is that the best performing checkpoint of the teacher might not necessarily be the best teacher for training the student in KD. Therefore, one important question would be how to find the best checkpoint of the teacher for distillation? Searching through the checkpoints of the teacher would be a very tedious and computationally expensive process, which we refer to as the checkpoint-search problem. Moreover, another observation is that larger teachers might not necessarily be better teachers in KD, which is referred to as the capacity-gap problem. To address these challenging problems, in this work, we introduce our progressive knowledge distillation (Pro-KD) technique which defines a smoother training path for the student by following the training footprints of the teacher instead of solely relying on distilling from a single mature fully-trained teacher. We demonstrate that our technique is quite effective in mitigating the capacity-gap problem and the checkpoint search problem. We evaluate our technique using a comprehensive set of experiments on different tasks such as image classification (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), natural language understanding tasks of the GLUE benchmark, and question answering (SQuAD 1.1 and 2.0) using BERT-based models and consistently got superior results over state-of-the-art techniques.

text: With the increasing size of neural models, knowledge distillation (KD) has gained attention as a tool for compressing these models. However, some limitations of KD have been observed, including the fact that the best-performing checkpoint of a teacher model may not always be the best teacher for training a student model. This leads to the checkpoint-search problem, which is both time-consuming and computationally expensive. Additionally, larger teacher models may not necessarily be better teachers in KD, which is known as the capacity-gap problem. To address these challenges, we propose the Progressive Knowledge Distillation (Pro-KD) technique, which provides a smoother training path for the student by following the teacher's training footprints, rather than relying solely on distillation from a single, mature teacher. Our experiments on various tasks, such as image classification (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), natural language understanding (GLUE benchmark), and question answering (SQuAD 1.1 and 2.0) using BERT-based models, show that Pro-KD is effective in mitigating the capacity-gap and checkpoint-search problems and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques.

text: Pre-trained language models have shown stellar performance in various downstream tasks. But, this usually comes at the cost of high latency and computation, hindering their usage in resource-limited settings. In this work, we propose a novel approach for reducing the computational cost of BERT with minimal loss in downstream performance. Our method dynamically eliminates less contributing tokens through layers, resulting in shorter lengths and consequently lower computational cost. To determine the importance of each token representation, we train a Contribution Predictor for each layer using a gradient-based saliency method. Our experiments on several diverse classification tasks show speedups up to 22x during inference time without much sacrifice in performance. We also validate the quality of the selected tokens in our method using human annotations in the ERASER benchmark. In comparison to other widely used strategies for selecting important tokens, such as saliency and attention, our proposed method has a significantly lower false positive rate in generating rationales. Our code is freely available at https://github.com/amodaresi/AdapLeR.

text: Pre-trained language models have demonstrated exceptional performance in various downstream tasks, but this often comes at the cost of high latency and computational requirements, making them unsuitable for resource-constrained settings. To address this issue, we present a novel approach that reduces the computational cost of BERT while retaining its downstream performance. Our method dynamically eliminates less important tokens through layers, resulting in shorter lengths and lower computational cost. A Contribution Predictor is trained for each layer to determine the significance of each token representation using a gradient-based saliency method. Our experiments on diverse classification tasks demonstrate speedups of up to 22x during inference time, with minimal loss in performance. Additionally, we validate the quality of the selected tokens using human annotations in the ERASER benchmark. Our method outperforms other widely used strategies for selecting important tokens, such as saliency and attention, with a significantly lower false positive rate in generating rationales. Our code is available for free at https://github.com/amodaresi/AdapLeR.

text: Abstractive dialogue summarization aims to convert a long dialogue content into its short form where the salient information is preserved while the redundant pieces are ignored. Different from the well-structured text, such as news and scientific articles, dialogues often consist of utterances coming from two or more interlocutors, where the conversations are often informal, verbose, and repetitive, sprinkled with false-starts, backchanneling, reconfirmations, hesitations, speaker interruptions and the salient information is often scattered across the whole chat. The above properties of conversations make it difficult to directly concentrate on scattered outstanding utterances and thus present new challenges of summarizing dialogues. In this work, rather than directly forcing a summarization system to merely pay more attention to the salient pieces, we propose to explicitly have the model perceive the redundant parts of an input dialogue history during the training phase. To be specific, we design two strategies to construct examples without salient pieces as negative cues. Then, the sequence-to-sequence likelihood loss is cooperated with the unlikelihood objective to drive the model to focus less on the unimportant information and also pay more attention to the salient pieces. Extensive experiments on the benchmark dataset demonstrate that our simple method significantly outperforms the baselines with regard to both semantic matching and factual consistent based metrics. The human evaluation also proves the performance gains.

label: coling
text: Abstractive dialogue summarization aims to convert lengthy dialogue content into a concise form while preserving important information and ignoring redundant pieces. Unlike well-structured texts, such as news articles and scientific papers, dialogues often consist of informal, verbose, and repetitive utterances from two or more interlocutors. These conversations can contain false-starts, backchanneling, reconfirmations, hesitations, speaker interruptions, and the important information is often scattered throughout the dialogue. This makes it difficult to focus on the salient pieces, presenting new challenges for summarizing dialogues. To address these challenges, we propose to explicitly train the model to perceive redundant parts of the input dialogue history during the training phase. We design two strategies to construct examples without important information as negative cues, and we combine the sequence-to-sequence likelihood loss with the unlikelihood objective to drive the model to focus less on unimportant information and pay more attention to the salient pieces. Our method significantly outperforms baselines on benchmark datasets, as demonstrated by extensive experiments and human evaluations.

label: emnlp
text: Character-based neural models have recently proven very useful for many NLP tasks. However, there is a gap of sophistication between methods for learning representations of sentences and words. While, most character models for learning representations of sentences are deep and complex, models for learning representations of words are shallow and simple. Also, in spite of considerable research on learning character embeddings, it is still not clear which kind of architecture is the best for capturing character-to-word representations. To address these questions, we first investigate the gaps between methods for learning word and sentence representations. We conduct detailed experiments and comparisons on different state-of-the-art convolutional models, and also investigate the advantages and disadvantages of their constituents. Furthermore, we propose IntNet, a funnel-shaped wide convolutional neural architecture with no down-sampling for learning representations of the internal structure of words by composing their characters from limited, supervised training corpora. We evaluate our proposed model on six sequence labeling datasets, including named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and syntactic chunking. Our in-depth analysis shows that IntNet significantly outperforms other character embedding models and obtains new state-of-the-art performance without relying on any external knowledge or resources.

label: emnlp
text: Recently, character-based neural models have proven to be highly effective for many NLP tasks. However, there is a disparity in sophistication between methods for learning sentence and word representations. While character models for sentence representation tend to be deep and complex, models for word representation are shallow and simple. Despite significant research on character embeddings, there is still no consensus on the best architecture for capturing character-to-word representations. To address this issue, we first examine the differences between methods for learning word and sentence representations. We perform a thorough analysis of different state-of-the-art convolutional models, evaluating their strengths and weaknesses. Then, we introduce IntNet, a funnel-shaped, wide convolutional neural architecture that does not use down-sampling for learning the internal structure of words by composing characters from limited, supervised training data. We evaluate IntNet on six sequence labeling datasets, including named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and syntactic chunking, and our results show that it outperforms other character embedding models and achieves new state-of-the-art performance without relying on external knowledge or resources.

text: Pretrained multilingual models are able to perform cross-lingual transfer in a zero-shot setting, even for languages unseen during pretraining. However, prior work evaluating performance on unseen languages has largely been limited to low-level, syntactic tasks, and it remains unclear if zero-shot learning of high-level, semantic tasks is possible for unseen languages. To explore this question, we present AmericasNLI, an extension of XNLI (Conneau et al., 2018) to 10 Indigenous languages of the Americas. We conduct experiments with XLM-R, testing multiple zero-shot and translation-based approaches. Additionally, we explore model adaptation via continued pretraining and provide an analysis of the dataset by considering hypothesis-only models. We find that XLM-R's zero-shot performance is poor for all 10 languages, with an average performance of 38.48%. Continued pretraining offers improvements, with an average accuracy of 43.85%. Surprisingly, training on poorly translated data by far outperforms all other methods with an accuracy of 49.12%.

label: acl
text:
Our results suggest that zero-shot learning is still limited for high-level, semantic tasks, but that training on poorly translated data can still lead to good performance.

Pretrained multilingual models have the ability to perform cross-lingual transfer in a zero-shot setting, even for languages that were not seen during the pretraining phase. However, prior research evaluating the performance of these models on unseen languages has been limited to low-level, syntactic tasks. It is still uncertain if zero-shot learning of high-level, semantic tasks is possible for unseen languages. To address this question, we introduce AmericasNLI, an extension of XNLI to 10 Indigenous languages of the Americas. We conduct experiments using XLM-R and test multiple zero-shot and translation-based approaches, as well as model adaptation through continued pretraining. We also analyze the dataset by examining hypothesis-only models. Our results show that XLM-R's zero-shot performance is inadequate for all 10 languages, with an average accuracy of 38.48%. Although continued pretraining offers some improvement, with an average accuracy of 43.85%, training on poorly translated data outperforms all other methods, with an accuracy of 49.12%. Our findings suggest that zero-shot learning is still limited for high-level, semantic tasks, but that training on poorly translated data can still produce good results.

text: Online hate speech detection has become an important issue due to the growth of online content, but resources in languages other than English are extremely limited. We introduce K-MHaS, a new multi-label dataset for hate speech detection that effectively handles Korean language patterns. The dataset consists of 109k utterances from news comments and provides a multi-label classification using 1 to 4 labels, and handles subjectivity and intersectionality. We evaluate strong baselines on K-MHaS. KR-BERT with a sub-character tokenizer outperforms others, recognizing decomposed characters in each hate speech class.

label: coling
text:
Our results demonstrate the potential of K-MHaS for developing effective hate speech detection models in the Korean language.

The detection of online hate speech has gained significance due to the exponential growth of online content. However, resources for languages other than English are scarce. To address this issue, we present K-MHaS, a novel multi-label dataset for hate speech detection in the Korean language. The dataset comprises 109,000 utterances from news comments and features multi-label classification with 1 to 4 labels, taking into account subjectivity and intersectionality. We evaluate various strong baselines on K-MHaS and find that KR-BERT with a sub-character tokenizer outperforms other models by accurately recognizing decomposed characters in each hate speech class. Our findings demonstrate the potential of K-MHaS in developing effective hate speech detection models for the Korean language.
