text: Due to the presence of both Twitter-specific conventions and non-standard and dialectal language, Twitter presents a significant parsing challenge to current dependency parsing tools. We broaden English dependency parsing to handle social media English, particularly social media African-American English (AAE), by developing and annotating a new dataset of 500 tweets, 250 of which are in AAE, within the Universal Dependencies 2.0 framework. We describe our standards for handling Twitter- and AAE-specific features and evaluate a variety of cross-domain strategies for improving parsing with no, or very little, in-domain labeled data, including a new data synthesis approach. We analyze these methods' impact on performance disparities between AAE and Mainstream American English tweets, and assess parsing accuracy for specific AAE lexical and syntactic features. Our annotated data and a parsing model are available at: http://slanglab.cs.umass.edu/TwitterAAE/.

label: acl
text: Due to the presence of Twitter-specific conventions and non-standard dialectal language, parsing tweets presents a significant challenge for current dependency parsing tools. To address this challenge, we have developed and annotated a new dataset of 500 tweets, 250 of which are in African-American English (AAE) - a type of social media English. Our dataset is based on the Universal Dependencies 2.0 framework and includes standards for handling Twitter- and AAE-specific features. We have evaluated various cross-domain strategies to improve parsing with limited in-domain labeled data, including a new data synthesis approach. Our study analyzes the impact of these methods on performance disparities between AAE and Mainstream American English tweets and assesses parsing accuracy for AAE lexical and syntactic features. Our annotated data and parsing model can be found at: http://slanglab.cs.umass.edu/TwitterAAE/.

label: acl
text: The problem of AMR-to-text generation is to recover a text representing the same meaning as an input AMR graph. The current state-of-the-art method uses a sequence-to-sequence model, leveraging LSTM for encoding a linearized AMR structure. Although being able to model non-local semantic information, a sequence LSTM can lose information from the AMR graph structure, and thus facing challenges with large-graphs, which result in long sequences. We introduce a neural graph-to-sequence model, using a novel LSTM structure for directly encoding graph-level semantics. On a standard benchmark, our model shows superior results to existing methods in the literature.

label: acl
text: The challenge of generating text from an AMR graph involves recovering a text that conveys the same meaning as the input graph. The current state-of-the-art approach utilizes a sequence-to-sequence model that employs LSTMs to encode a linearized AMR structure. While this method can capture non-local semantic information, it can also lose information from the graph structure, making it difficult to handle large graphs that result in long sequences. To address this challenge, we propose a neural graph-to-sequence model that uses a novel LSTM structure to directly encode graph-level semantics. Our model outperforms existing methods on a standard benchmark, demonstrating its superior performance.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based language models benefit from conditioning on contexts of hundreds to thousands of previous tokens. What aspects of these contexts contribute to accurate model prediction? We describe a series of experiments that measure usable information by selectively ablating lexical and structural information in transformer language models trained on English Wikipedia. In both mid- and long-range contexts, we find that several extremely destructive context manipulations—including shuffling word order within sentences and deleting all words other than nouns—remove less than 15% of the usable information. Our results suggest that long contexts, but not their detailed syntactic and propositional content, are important for the low perplexity of current transformer language models.

label: acl
text: Transformer-based language models are enhanced by being conditioned on context that consists of hundreds to thousands of previous tokens. To understand the impact of these contexts on accurate model predictions, we conducted a series of experiments to measure the usable information by selectively removing lexical and structural information in transformer language models trained on English Wikipedia. Our findings indicate that even in both mid- and long-range contexts, several highly disruptive manipulations, such as shuffling word order within sentences and deleting all words except for nouns, result in a removal of less than 15% of the usable information. These results suggest that long contexts, rather than their intricate syntactic and propositional content, play a significant role in the low perplexity of current transformer language models.

label: acl
text: Word embedding models such as GloVe rely on co-occurrence statistics to learn vector representations of word meaning. While we may similarly expect that co-occurrence statistics can be used to capture rich information about the relationships between different words, existing approaches for modeling such relationships are based on manipulating pre-trained word vectors. In this paper, we introduce a novel method which directly learns relation vectors from co-occurrence statistics. To this end, we first introduce a variant of GloVe, in which there is an explicit connection between word vectors and PMI weighted co-occurrence vectors. We then show how relation vectors can be naturally embedded into the resulting vector space.

label: acl
text:
Our approach has the advantage of being able to learn rich relationships between words without relying on pre-trained word vectors.

The GloVe word embedding model uses co-occurrence statistics to learn the meaning of words as vector representations. However, existing methods for modeling relationships between words are limited to manipulating pre-trained word vectors. In this paper, we present a new approach that directly learns relation vectors from co-occurrence statistics. We introduce a variation of GloVe that links word vectors and PMI-weighted co-occurrence vectors. Our method allows us to embed relation vectors into the resulting vector space, providing a more comprehensive understanding of word relationships without relying on pre-trained word vectors.

label: naacl
text: Neural text generation models are typically trained by maximizing log-likelihood with the sequence cross entropy (CE) loss, which encourages an exact token-by-token match between a target sequence with a generated sequence. Such training objective is sub-optimal when the target sequence is not perfect, e.g., when the target sequence is corrupted with noises, or when only weak sequence supervision is available. To address the challenge, we propose a novel Edit-Invariant Sequence Loss (EISL), which computes the matching loss of a target C-C-C-gram with all D-D-D-grams in the generated sequence. EISL is designed to be robust to various noises and edits in the target sequences. Moreover, the EISL computation is essentially an approximate convolution operation with target E-E-E-grams as kernels, which is easy to implement and efficient to compute with existing libraries. To demonstrate the effectiveness of EISL, we conduct experiments on a wide range of tasks, including machine translation with noisy target sequences, unsupervised text style transfer with only weak training signals, and non-autoregressive generation with non-predefined generation order. Experimental results show our method significantly outperforms the common CE loss and other strong baselines on all the tasks. EISL has a simple API that can be used as a drop-in replacement of the CE loss: https://github.com/guangyliu/EISL.

text: The training of neural text generation models is typically performed by maximizing log-likelihood with the sequence cross-entropy (CE) loss. This method encourages an exact match between the target sequence and the generated sequence. However, this approach is not optimal when the target sequence is not perfect, for example, when it is corrupted with noise or when weak sequence supervision is available. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Edit-Invariant Sequence Loss (EISL), which calculates the matching loss between a target C-C-C-gram and all D-D-D-grams in the generated sequence. This design makes EISL robust to various noises and edits in target sequences. Additionally, the computation of EISL is essentially an approximate convolution operation with target E-E-E-grams as kernels, which is easy to implement and computationally efficient. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EISL by conducting experiments on a wide range of tasks, including machine translation with noisy target sequences, unsupervised text style transfer with weak training signals, and non-autoregressive generation with non-predefined generation order. Our results show that EISL outperforms the common CE loss and other strong baselines on all tasks. Our implementation of EISL is available as a simple API that can be used as a drop-in replacement for the CE loss: https://github.com/guangyliu/EISL.

label: naacl
text: Question answering (QA) and question generation (QG) are closely related tasks that could improve each other; however, the connection of these two tasks is not well explored in literature. In this paper, we give a systematic study that seeks to leverage the connection to improve both QA and QG. We present a training algorithm that generalizes both Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) and Generative Domain-Adaptive Nets (GDAN) under the question answering scenario. The two key ideas are improving the QG model with QA through incorporating additional QA-specific signal as the loss function, and improving the QA model with QG through adding artificially generated training instances. We conduct experiments on both document based and knowledge based question answering tasks. We have two main findings. Firstly, the performance of a QG model (e.g in terms of BLEU score) could be easily improved by a QA model via policy gradient. Secondly, directly applying GAN that regards all the generated questions as negative instances could not improve the accuracy of the QA model. Learning when to regard generated questions as positive instances could bring performance boost.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we explore the connection between question answering (QA) and question generation (QG) to improve both tasks. We present a training algorithm that combines the features of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) and Generative Domain-Adaptive Nets (GDAN) in a question answering scenario. The algorithm improves the QG model by incorporating additional QA-specific signals as loss functions, and improves the QA model by adding artificially generated training instances. Our experiments on document-based and knowledge-based question answering tasks reveal two key findings: (1) the performance of a QG model can be easily improved by a QA model through policy gradient, and (2) directly applying GAN that regards all generated questions as negative instances does not improve the accuracy of the QA model. However, learning when to consider generated questions as positive instances can lead to a significant performance boost.

label: naacl
text: We present neural syntactic generative models with exact marginalization that support both dependency parsing and language modeling. Exact marginalization is made tractable through dynamic programming over shift-reduce parsing and minimal RNN-based feature sets. Our algorithms complement previous approaches by supporting batched training and enabling online computation of next word probabilities. For supervised dependency parsing, our model achieves a state-of-the-art result among generative approaches. We also report empirical results on unsupervised syntactic models and their role in language modeling. We find that our model formulation of latent dependencies with exact marginalization do not lead to better intrinsic language modeling performance than vanilla RNNs, and that parsing accuracy is not correlated with language modeling perplexity in stack-based models.

label: naacl
text: We present neural syntactic generative models that support both dependency parsing and language modeling. Our models are based on exact marginalization, which is made tractable through the use of dynamic programming over shift-reduce parsing and minimal RNN-based feature sets. Our algorithms offer several advantages over previous approaches, including support for batched training and the ability to compute next word probabilities online. Our model outperforms other generative models in supervised dependency parsing and we report empirical results on unsupervised syntactic models and their impact on language modeling. Our findings show that our model formulation of latent dependencies with exact marginalization does not result in improved language modeling performance compared to vanilla RNNs, and that parsing accuracy and language modeling perplexity are not correlated in stack-based models.

text: The process by which sections in a document are demarcated and labeled is known as section identification. Such sections are helpful to the reader when searching for information and contextualizing specific topics. The goal of this work is to segment the sections of clinical medical domain documentation. The primary contribution of this work is MedSecId, a publicly available set of 2,002 fully annotated medical notes from the MIMIC-III. We include several baselines, source code, a pretrained model and analysis of the data showing a relationship between medical concepts across sections using principal component analysis.

label: coling
text: The process of labeling and identifying sections in a document is referred to as section identification. These sections are beneficial for the reader, as they aid in locating information and contextualizing specific topics. The aim of this work is to segment sections in clinical medical domain documentation. Our primary contribution is MedSecId, a publicly available dataset of 2,002 fully annotated medical notes from MIMIC-III. This includes several baselines, source code, a pre-trained model, and an analysis of the data that highlights the relationship between medical concepts across sections using principal component analysis.

text: Conversational machine reading comprehension (CMRC) aims to assist computers to understand an natural language text and thereafter engage in a multi-turn conversation to answer questions related to the text. Existing methods typically require three steps: (1) decision making based on entailment reasoning; (2) span extraction if required by the above decision; (3) question rephrasing based on the extracted span. However, for nearly all these methods, the span extraction and question rephrasing steps cannot fully exploit the fine-grained entailment reasoning information in decision making step because of their relative independence, which will further enlarge the information gap between decision making and question phrasing. Thus, to tackle this problem, we propose a novel end-to-end framework for conversational machine reading comprehension based on shared parameter mechanism, called entailment reasoning T5 (ET5). Despite the lightweight of our proposed framework, experimental results show that the proposed ET5 achieves new state-of-the-art results on the ShARC leaderboard with the BLEU-4 score of 55.2. Our model and code are publicly available.

label: coling
text: The objective of conversational machine reading comprehension (CMRC) is to help computers comprehend natural language text and engage in multi-turn conversations to answer questions related to the text. Existing methods usually involve three steps: (1) decision making based on entailment reasoning, (2) span extraction if necessary, and (3) question rephrasing based on the extracted span. However, these methods often fail to fully exploit the information from the decision making step in the span extraction and question rephrasing steps due to their independence, leading to a gap in information between decision making and question phrasing. To address this issue, we present a novel end-to-end framework called Entailment Reasoning T5 (ET5), which utilizes a shared parameter mechanism. Despite its simplicity, our proposed ET5 framework outperforms existing methods, achieving a BLEU-4 score of 55.2 on the ShARC leaderboard. Our model and code are freely available.

label: acl
text: Information integration from different modalities is an active area of research. Human beings and, in general, biological neural systems are quite adept at using a multitude of signals from different sensory perceptive fields to interact with the environment and each other. Recent work in deep fusion models via neural networks has led to substantial improvements over unimodal approaches in areas like speech recognition, emotion recognition and analysis, captioning and image description. However, such research has mostly focused on architectural changes allowing for fusion of different modalities while keeping the model complexity manageable.Inspired by neuroscientific ideas about multisensory integration and processing, we investigate the effect of introducing neural dependencies in the loss functions. Experiments on multimodal sentiment analysis tasks with different models show that our approach provides a consistent performance boost.

label: acl
text: The integration of information from various modalities is a current area of research focus. Humans and biological neural systems are skilled at utilizing multiple signals from different sensory fields to interact with their environment and each other. Recent advancements in deep fusion models through neural networks have resulted in significant improvements over unimodal approaches in areas such as speech recognition, emotion recognition and analysis, captioning, and image description. However, most of these studies have focused on architectural modifications that enable the fusion of different modalities while maintaining manageable model complexity. We explore the impact of incorporating neural dependencies in loss functions, drawing inspiration from neuroscientific concepts of multisensory integration and processing. Our experiments on multimodal sentiment analysis tasks with different models demonstrate that our approach consistently enhances performance.

label: naacl
text: Factual consistency is an essential quality of text summarization models in practical settings. Existing work in evaluating this dimension can be broadly categorized into two lines of research, entailment-based and question answering (QA)-based metrics, and different experimental setups often lead to contrasting conclusions as to which paradigm performs the best. In this work, we conduct an extensive comparison of entailment and QA-based metrics, demonstrating that carefully choosing the components of a QA-based metric, especially question generation and answerability classification, is critical to performance. Building on those insights, we propose an optimized metric, which we call QAFactEval, that leads to a 14% average improvement over previous QA-based metrics on the SummaC factual consistency benchmark, and also outperforms the best-performing entailment-based metric. Moreover, we find that QA-based and entailment-based metrics can offer complementary signals and be combined into a single metric for a further performance boost.

label: naacl
text: The quality of consistency in text summarization models is crucial in practical settings. There are two main categories of evaluation research in this area: entailment-based and question answering (QA)-based metrics. However, different experimental setups often result in conflicting conclusions about which paradigm is superior. In our study, we compare entailment and QA-based metrics and find that the choice of components, particularly question generation and answerability classification, is crucial to performance. Based on these findings, we introduce an optimized metric, QAFactEval, which results in a 14% improvement in performance over previous QA-based metrics on the SummaC factual consistency benchmark and outperforms the best-performing entailment-based metric. Additionally, we discover that combining QA-based and entailment-based metrics can provide even better results.

label: emnlp
text: WikiSQL is a newly released dataset for studying the natural language sequence to SQL translation problem. The SQL queries in WikiSQL are simple: Each involves one relation and does not have any join operation. Despite of its simplicity, none of the publicly reported structured query generation models can achieve an accuracy beyond 62%, which is still far from enough for practical use. In this paper, we ask two questions, “Why is the accuracy still low for such simple queries?” and “What does it take to achieve 100% accuracy on WikiSQL?” To limit the scope of our study, we focus on the WHERE clause in SQL. The answers will help us gain insights about the directions we should explore in order to further improve the translation accuracy. We will then investigate alternative solutions to realize the potential ceiling performance on WikiSQL. Our proposed solution can reach up to 88.6% condition accuracy on the WikiSQL dataset.

label: emnlp
text: The newly released WikiSQL dataset provides a platform for studying the problem of natural language sequence to SQL translation. Despite its simplicity, with only one relation and no join operations, publicly reported structured query generation models have not been able to achieve more than a 62% accuracy, which is insufficient for practical use. This paper addresses two questions: why is accuracy still low for such simple queries, and what steps are necessary to achieve 100% accuracy on WikiSQL? Our study focuses specifically on the WHERE clause in SQL, as the answers to these questions will provide valuable insights into future improvements in translation accuracy. We propose an alternative solution that reaches up to 88.6% accuracy for conditions in the WikiSQL dataset.

label: naacl
text: User sessions empower many search and recommendation tasks on a daily basis. Such session data are semi-structured, which encode heterogeneous relations between queries and products, and each item is described by the unstructured text. Despite recent advances in self-supervised learning for text or graphs, there lack of self-supervised learning models that can effectively capture both intra-item semantics and inter-item interactions for semi-structured sessions. To fill this gap, we propose CERES, a graph-based transformer model for semi-structured session data. CERES learns representations that capture both inter- and intra-item semantics with (1) a graph-conditioned masked language pretraining task that jointly learns from item text and item-item relations; and (2) a graph-conditioned transformer architecture that propagates inter-item contexts to item-level representations. We pretrained CERES using ~468 million Amazon sessions and find that CERES outperforms strong pretraining baselines by up to 9% in three session search and entity linking tasks.

label: naacl
text: User sessions play a crucial role in many search and recommendation tasks that are performed on a daily basis. These sessions generate semi-structured data that encode the heterogeneous relationships between queries and products. Each item is described by unstructured text. Despite the recent advancements in self-supervised learning for text or graphs, there is still a lack of models that can effectively capture both the intra-item semantics and inter-item interactions in semi-structured sessions. To address this issue, we introduce CERES, a graph-based transformer model designed specifically for semi-structured session data. CERES learns representations that consider both the inter- and intra-item semantics through a combination of (1) a graph-conditioned masked language pre-training task that learns from both item text and item-item relationships, and (2) a graph-conditioned transformer architecture that spreads inter-item context to item-level representations. We pre-trained CERES using approximately 468 million Amazon sessions and found that it outperformed strong pre-training baselines by up to 9% in three session search and entity linking tasks.

label: naacl
text: We introduce DocTime - a novel temporal dependency graph (TDG) parser that takes as input a text document and produces a temporal dependency graph. It outperforms previous BERT-based solutions by a relative 4-8% on three datasets from modeling the problem as a graph network with path-prediction loss to incorporate longer range dependencies. This work also demonstrates how the TDG graph can be used to improve the downstream tasks of temporal questions answering and NLI by a relative 4-10% with a new framework that incorporates the temporal dependency graph into the self-attention layer of Transformer models (Time-transformer). Finally, we develop and evaluate on a new temporal dependency graph dataset for the domain of contractual documents, which has not been previously explored in this setting.

label: naacl
text: We present DocTime, a pioneering temporal dependency graph (TDG) parser that transforms a text document into a TDG. Compared to previous BERT-based solutions, DocTime outperforms them by 4-8% on three datasets. This is achieved by modeling the problem as a graph network with path-prediction loss, which incorporates longer-range dependencies. Our work also shows how the TDG graph can enhance the performance of temporal questions answering and NLI by 4-10% through a new framework, Time-transformer, that incorporates the TDG into the self-attention layer of Transformer models. Additionally, we create and evaluate a new TDG dataset for contractual documents, a domain that has not been previously explored in this context.

label: acl
text: Code search is to search reusable code snippets from source code corpus based on natural languages queries. Deep learning-based methods on code search have shown promising results. However, previous methods focus on retrieval accuracy, but lacked attention to the efficiency of the retrieval process. We propose a novel method CoSHC to accelerate code search with deep hashing and code classification, aiming to perform efficient code search without sacrificing too much accuracy. To evaluate the effectiveness of CoSHC, we apply our methodon five code search models. Extensive experimental results indicate that compared with previous code search baselines, CoSHC can save more than 90% of retrieval time meanwhile preserving at least 99% of retrieval accuracy.

label: acl
text: Code search aims to find reusable code snippets from a source code corpus using natural language queries. Previous deep learning-based methods have shown promising results, but they have a focus on retrieval accuracy and neglect the efficiency of the process. We introduce a new method, CoSHC, which uses deep hashing and code classification to speed up code search without sacrificing accuracy. To test its effectiveness, we apply CoSHC to five code search models and the results show that it can save over 90% of retrieval time while maintaining at least 99% of retrieval accuracy compared to previous code search baselines.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we investigate the use of discourse-aware rewards with reinforcement learning to guide a model to generate long, coherent text. In particular, we propose to learn neural rewards to model cross-sentence ordering as a means to approximate desired discourse structure. Empirical results demonstrate that a generator trained with the learned reward produces more coherent and less repetitive text than models trained with cross-entropy or with reinforcement learning with commonly used scores as rewards.

label: naacl
text: In this research, we explore the application of discourse-aware rewards in reinforcement learning to generate long, coherent text. Our approach involves learning neural rewards to model cross-sentence ordering for the purpose of approximating the desired discourse structure. Our empirical findings show that the generator trained with the learned rewards produces text that is more coherent and less repetitive compared to models trained using cross-entropy or reinforcement learning with commonly used scores as rewards.

label: coling
text: Machine reading comprehension (MRC) poses new challenges to logical reasoning, which aims to understand the implicit logical relations entailed in the given contexts and perform inference over them. Due to the complexity of logic, logical connections exist at different granularity levels. However, most existing methods of logical reasoning individually focus on either entity-aware or discourse-based information but ignore the hierarchical relations that may even have mutual effects. This paper proposes a holistic graph network (HGN) that deals with context at both discourse-level and word-level as the basis for logical reasoning to provide a more fine-grained relation extraction. Specifically, node-level and type-level relations, which can be interpreted as bridges in the reasoning process, are modeled by a hierarchical interaction mechanism to improve the interpretation of MRC systems. Experimental results on logical reasoning QA datasets (ReClor and LogiQA) and natural language inference datasets (SNLI and ANLI) show the effectiveness and generalization of our method, and in-depth analysis verifies its capability to understand complex logical relations.

label: coling
text: Machine reading comprehension (MRC) presents new challenges for logical reasoning, which aims to comprehend the implicit logical relations in the given context and perform inferences over them. However, due to the complexity of logic, logical connections exist at different levels of granularity. Most existing logical reasoning methods focus on either entity-aware or discourse-based information, but ignore the hierarchical relations that may have mutual effects. To address this issue, this paper proposes a holistic graph network (HGN) that deals with context at both the discourse-level and word-level as the basis for logical reasoning. This provides a more fine-grained relation extraction by modeling node-level and type-level relations as bridges in the reasoning process through a hierarchical interaction mechanism. The effectiveness and generalization of the proposed method are demonstrated through experimental results on logical reasoning QA datasets (ReClor and LogiQA) and natural language inference datasets (SNLI and ANLI). In-depth analysis verifies the ability of the HGN to understand complex logical relations.

label: coling
text: Conversational recommendation systems (CRS) aim to determine a goal item by sequentially tracking users' interests through multi-turn conversation. In CRS, implicit patterns of user interest sequence guide the smooth transition of dialog utterances to the goal item. However, with the convenient explicit knowledge of knowledge graph (KG), existing KG-based CRS methods over-rely on the explicit separate KG links to model the user interests but ignore the rich goal-aware implicit interest sequence patterns in a dialog. In addition, interest sequence is also not fully used to generate smooth transited utterances. We propose CR-GIS with a parallel star framework. First, an interest-level star graph is designed to model the goal-aware implicit user interest sequence. Second, a hierarchical Star Transformer is designed to guide the multi-turn utterances generation with the interest-level star graph. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of CR-GIS in achieving more accurate recommended items with more fluent and coherent dialog utterances.

label: coling
text: Conversational Recommendation Systems (CRS) aim to identify a target item through a multi-turn conversation that tracks users' interests. The implicit patterns of user interest sequences in CRS help guide the smooth transition of dialog utterances to the target item. However, current KG-based CRS methods rely too heavily on explicit knowledge graph (KG) links to model user interests and ignore the rich implicit interest sequence patterns in dialogs. They also do not fully utilize interest sequences to generate smooth transitions in utterances. To address these issues, we propose CR-GIS, a parallel star framework that incorporates an interest-level star graph to model goal-aware implicit user interest sequences and a hierarchical Star Transformer to guide multi-turn utterance generation. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of CR-GIS in delivering more accurate recommendations and producing more fluent and coherent dialog utterances.

label: coling
text: Deep prompt tuning (DPT) has gained great success in most natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, it is not well-investigated in dense retrieval where fine-tuning (FT) still dominates. When deploying multiple retrieval tasks using the same backbone model (e.g., RoBERTa), FT-based methods are unfriendly in terms of deployment cost: each new retrieval model needs to repeatedly deploy the backbone model without reuse. To reduce the deployment cost in such a scenario, this work investigates applying DPT in dense retrieval. The challenge is that directly applying DPT in dense retrieval largely underperforms FT methods. To compensate for the performance drop, we propose two model-agnostic and task-agnostic strategies for DPT-based retrievers, namely retrieval-oriented intermediate pretraining and unified negative mining, as a general approach that could be compatible with any pre-trained language model and retrieval task. The experimental results show that the proposed method (called DPTDR) outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on both MS-MARCO and Natural Questions. We also conduct ablation studies to examine the effectiveness of each strategy in DPTDR. We believe this work facilitates the industry, as it saves enormous efforts and costs of deployment and increases the utility of computing resources. Our code is available at https://github.com/tangzhy/DPTDR.

label: coling
text: The success of Deep Prompt Tuning (DPT) in most Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks has been widely acknowledged. However, its application in dense retrieval, where Fine-tuning (FT) still dominates, has not been thoroughly explored. When using the same backbone model (e.g. RoBERTa) for multiple retrieval tasks, FT-based methods are costly in terms of deployment, as each new retrieval model requires repeated deployment without reuse. To reduce this cost, this study investigates the use of DPT in dense retrieval. The challenge is that direct application of DPT in dense retrieval often underperforms FT methods. To address this, we propose two model-agnostic and task-agnostic strategies, namely Retrieval-oriented Intermediate Pretraining and Unified Negative Mining, as a general approach that can be applied to any pre-trained language model and retrieval task. Our results show that the proposed method (DPTDR) outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on both MS-MARCO and Natural Questions. Ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of each strategy in DPTDR. This work offers significant benefits to the industry, as it reduces deployment costs and increases the efficiency of computing resources. Our code is available at https://github.com/tangzhy/DPTDR.

label: coling
text: Existing research for argument representation learning mainly treats tokens in the sentence equally and ignores the implied structure information of argumentative context. In this paper, we propose to separate tokens into two groups, namely framing tokens and topic ones, to capture structural information of arguments. In addition, we consider high-level structure by incorporating paragraph-level position information. A novel structure-aware argument encoder is proposed for literature discourse analysis. Experimental results on both a self-constructed corpus and a public corpus show the effectiveness of our model. Resources are available at https://github.com/lemuria-wchen/SAE.

label: coling
text: The current research on argument representation learning primarily focuses on treating all sentence tokens equally and disregards the inherent structural information of argumentative context. In an effort to address this, we propose to categorize tokens into two groups: framing tokens and topic tokens, in order to capture the structural information of arguments. Furthermore, we incorporate paragraph-level position information to consider high-level structure. Our novel structure-aware argument encoder is designed specifically for literature discourse analysis and has been proven effective through experiments on both a self-constructed corpus and a public corpus. The resources used in our research are available for public use at https://github.com/lemuria-wchen/SAE.

label: acl
text: Existing solutions to task-oriented dialogue systems follow pipeline designs which introduces architectural complexity and fragility. We propose a novel, holistic, extendable framework based on a single sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model which can be optimized with supervised or reinforcement learning. A key contribution is that we design text spans named belief spans to track dialogue believes, allowing task-oriented dialogue systems to be modeled in a seq2seq way. Based on this, we propose a simplistic Two Stage CopyNet instantiation which emonstrates good scalability: significantly reducing model complexity in terms of number of parameters and training time by a magnitude. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art pipeline-based methods on large datasets and retains a satisfactory entity match rate on out-of-vocabulary (OOV) cases where pipeline-designed competitors totally fail.

label: acl
text: Existing task-oriented dialogue systems follow pipeline designs that result in architectural complexity and fragility. We introduce a novel, holistic, and extendable framework based on a single sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model that can be trained using either supervised or reinforcement learning. Our key contribution is the design of text spans, known as belief spans, to track dialogue beliefs. This allows task-oriented dialogue systems to be modeled using a seq2seq approach. We propose a simple Two Stage CopyNet instantiation that demonstrates good scalability by reducing the model complexity and training time by a significant magnitude. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art pipeline-based methods on large datasets, and it also maintains a satisfactory entity match rate in out-of-vocabulary (OOV) cases, where pipeline-based competitors fail completely.

label: naacl
text: How reliably an automatic summarization evaluation metric replicates human judgments of summary quality is quantified by system-level correlations. We identify two ways in which the definition of the system-level correlation is inconsistent with how metrics are used to evaluate systems in practice and propose changes to rectify this disconnect. First, we calculate the system score for an automatic metric using the full test set instead of the subset of summaries judged by humans, which is currently standard practice. We demonstrate how this small change leads to more precise estimates of system-level correlations. Second, we propose to calculate correlations only on pairs of systems that are separated by small differences in automatic scores which are commonly observed in practice. This allows us to demonstrate that our best estimate of the correlation of ROUGE to human judgments is near 0 in realistic scenarios. The results from the analyses point to the need to collect more high-quality human judgments and to improve automatic metrics when differences in system scores are small.

label: naacl
text: The reliability of an automatic summarization evaluation metric in replicating human judgments of summary quality is quantified through system-level correlations. However, we have identified two inconsistencies in the definition of these correlations that affect the accuracy of the evaluation. To address these issues, we propose changes in the calculation of system scores. Firstly, we use the full test set instead of a subset of human-judged summaries to calculate the system score for an automatic metric. This leads to more accurate estimates of system-level correlations. Secondly, we suggest calculating correlations only between systems that have small differences in automatic scores, which are commonly observed in practice. Our results indicate that the correlation of ROUGE to human judgments is close to zero in realistic scenarios. These findings emphasize the need for further collection of high-quality human judgments and improvement of automatic metrics, especially when there are small differences in system scores.

label: coling
text: We present a novel collection of news articles originating from fake and real news media sources for the analysis and prediction of news virality. Unlike existing fake news datasets which either contain claims, or news article headline and body, in this collection each article is supported with a Facebook engagement count which we consider as an indicator of the article virality. In addition we also provide the article description and thumbnail image with which the article was shared on Facebook. These images were automatically annotated with object tags and color attributes. Using cloud based vision analysis tools, thumbnail images were also analyzed for faces and detected faces were annotated with facial attributes. We empirically investigate the use of this collection on an example task of article virality prediction.

label: coling
text: We present a novel collection of news articles, comprising both fake and real sources, for analyzing and predicting news virality. This collection is unique in that each article is accompanied by a Facebook engagement count, which we use as a measure of its virality. The articles also come with descriptions, as well as thumbnail images that were shared on Facebook. These images have been annotated with object tags and color attributes, and analyzed using cloud-based vision tools to detect faces, which were further annotated with facial attributes. Our collection will be used to conduct an empirical investigation into the prediction of article virality.

label: naacl
text: Neural machine translation requires large amount of parallel training text to learn a reasonable quality translation model. This is particularly inconvenient for language pairs for which enough parallel text is not available. In this paper, we use monolingual linguistic resources in the source side to address this challenging problem based on a multi-task learning approach. More specifically, we scaffold the machine translation task on auxiliary tasks including semantic parsing, syntactic parsing, and named-entity recognition. This effectively injects semantic and/or syntactic knowledge into the translation model, which would otherwise require a large amount of training bitext to learn from. We empirically analyze and show the effectiveness of our multitask learning approach on three translation tasks: English-to-French, English-to-Farsi, and English-to-Vietnamese.

label: naacl
text: Neural machine translation requires vast amounts of parallel training text to produce a high-quality translation model. This can be a significant challenge for language pairs for which sufficient parallel text is not available. To address this issue, we propose a multi-task learning approach that utilizes monolingual linguistic resources in the source language. Our approach involves scaffolding the machine translation task with auxiliary tasks, including semantic parsing, syntactic parsing, and named-entity recognition, which effectively incorporates semantic and syntactic knowledge into the translation model. This eliminates the need for a large amount of training bitext. We evaluate the effectiveness of our multi-task learning approach on three translation tasks: English to French, English to Farsi, and English to Vietnamese.

label: acl
text: The retriever-reader framework is popular for open-domain question answering (ODQA) due to its ability to use explicit knowledge.Although prior work has sought to increase the knowledge coverage by incorporating structured knowledge beyond text, accessing heterogeneous knowledge sources through a unified interface remains an open question. While data-to-text generation has the potential to serve as a universal interface for data and text, its feasibility for downstream tasks remains largely unknown. In this work, we bridge this gap and use the data-to-text method as a means for encoding structured knowledge for open-domain question answering. Specifically, we propose a verbalizer-retriever-reader framework for ODQA over data and text where verbalized tables from Wikipedia and graphs from Wikidata are used as augmented knowledge sources. We show that our Unified Data and Text QA, UDT-QA, can effectively benefit from the expanded knowledge index, leading to large gains over text-only baselines. Notably, our approach sets the single-model state-of-the-art on Natural Questions. Furthermore, our analyses indicate that verbalized knowledge is preferred for answer reasoning for both adapted and hot-swap settings.

label: acl
text: The Retriever-Reader framework is widely used for open-domain question answering (ODQA) because of its ability to leverage explicit knowledge. Despite previous efforts to enhance knowledge coverage by incorporating structured information beyond text, there is still a need for a unified interface to access heterogeneous knowledge sources. Data-to-text generation has the potential to serve as a universal interface for both data and text, but its suitability for downstream tasks is still largely unknown. To address this gap, we propose a Verbalizer-Retriever-Reader framework for ODQA that uses data-to-text generation to encode structured knowledge. Our approach integrates verbalized tables from Wikipedia and graphs from Wikidata as augmented knowledge sources. Our experiments demonstrate that our Unified Data and Text QA (UDT-QA) system significantly outperforms text-only baselines, setting a new state-of-the-art on the Natural Questions benchmark. Our results also suggest that verbalized knowledge is preferred for answer reasoning in both adapted and hot-swap settings.

label: naacl
text: The task of natural language inference (NLI), to decide if a hypothesis entails or contradicts a premise, received considerable attention in recent years. All competitive systems build on top of contextualized representations and make use of transformer architectures for learning an NLI model. When somebody is faced with a particular NLI task, they need to select the best model that is available. This is a time-consuming and resource-intense endeavour. To solve this practical problem, we propose a simple method for predicting the performance without actually fine-tuning the model. We do this by testing how well the pre-trained models perform on the aNLI task when just comparing sentence embeddings with cosine similarity to what kind of performance is achieved when training a classifier on top of these embeddings. We show that the accuracy of the cosine similarity approach correlates strongly with the accuracy of the classification approach with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.65. Since the similarity is orders of magnitude faster to compute on a given dataset (less than a minute vs. hours), our method can lead to significant time savings in the process of model selection.

label: naacl
text: The task of Natural Language Inference (NLI), which involves deciding if a hypothesis entails or contradicts a premise, has received significant attention in recent years. Competitive systems for this task are built on top of contextualized representations and rely on transformer architectures to learn an NLI model. Choosing the best model for a particular NLI task can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. To address this practical challenge, we propose a simple method for predicting performance without fine-tuning the model. Our method involves testing the pre-trained models' performance on the aNLI task by comparing sentence embeddings using cosine similarity, and comparing this to the performance achieved when training a classifier on top of these embeddings. The results show that the accuracy of the cosine similarity approach is strongly correlated with the accuracy of the classification approach, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.65. Our method offers significant time savings, as computing similarity is orders of magnitude faster (less than a minute compared to hours) in the process of model selection.

label: acl
text: While online conversations can cover a vast amount of information in many different formats, abstractive text summarization has primarily focused on modeling solely news articles. This research gap is due, in part, to the lack of standardized datasets for summarizing online discussions. To address this gap, we design annotation protocols motivated by an issues–viewpoints–assertions framework to crowdsource four new datasets on diverse online conversation forms of news comments, discussion forums, community question answering forums, and email threads. We benchmark state-of-the-art models on our datasets and analyze characteristics associated with the data. To create a comprehensive benchmark, we also evaluate these models on widely-used conversation summarization datasets to establish strong baselines in this domain. Furthermore, we incorporate argument mining through graph construction to directly model the issues, viewpoints, and assertions present in a conversation and filter noisy input, showing comparable or improved results according to automatic and human evaluations.

label: acl
text: Online conversations can encompass a vast array of information and formats, but abstractive text summarization has mainly focused on modeling news articles. This research gap is partly due to the absence of standardized datasets for summarizing online discussions. To address this, we design annotation protocols based on an "issues-viewpoints-assertions" framework to create four new datasets on diverse online conversation forms, including news comments, discussion forums, community question-answering forums, and email threads. We benchmark the latest models on our datasets and analyze the data's characteristics. Additionally, we evaluate these models on widely-used conversation summarization datasets to establish strong baselines in this field. Finally, we incorporate argument mining through graph construction to directly model the issues, viewpoints, and assertions in a conversation and eliminate noisy input, resulting in comparable or improved results according to both automatic and human evaluations.

label: acl
text: Models pre-trained with a language modeling objective possess ample world knowledge and language skills, but are known to struggle in tasks that require reasoning. In this work, we propose to leverage semi-structured tables, and automatically generate at scale question-paragraph pairs, where answering the question requires reasoning over multiple facts in the paragraph. We add a pre-training step over this synthetic data, which includes examples that require 16 different reasoning skills such as number comparison, conjunction, and fact composition. To improve data efficiency, we sample examples from reasoning skills where the model currently errs. We evaluate our approach on three reasoning-focused reading comprehension datasets, and show that our model, PReasM, substantially outperforms T5, a popular pre-trained encoder-decoder model. Moreover, sampling examples based on model errors leads to faster training and higher performance.

label: acl
text: Models that have been pre-trained with a language modeling objective have a wealth of world knowledge and language skills, but they often struggle with tasks requiring reasoning. To address this issue, we propose leveraging semi-structured tables to generate question-paragraph pairs at scale, where answering the question requires reasoning over multiple facts in the paragraph. We introduce a pre-training step using this synthetic data, which covers 16 different reasoning skills, such as number comparison, conjunction, and fact composition. To improve data efficiency, we sample examples based on the model's errors, to focus on areas where the model needs improvement. Our approach, called PReasM, is evaluated on three reasoning-focused reading comprehension datasets, and it outperforms T5, a widely used pre-trained encoder-decoder model. Furthermore, our approach of sampling examples based on model errors results in faster training and better performance.

label: acl
text: Machine reading comprehension is a heavily-studied research and test field for evaluating new pre-trained language models (PrLMs) and fine-tuning strategies, and recent studies have enriched the pre-trained language models with syntactic, semantic and other linguistic information to improve the performance of the models. In this paper, we imitate the human reading process in connecting the anaphoric expressions and explicitly leverage the coreference information of the entities to enhance the word embeddings from the pre-trained language model, in order to highlight the coreference mentions of the entities that must be identified for coreference-intensive question answering in QUOREF, a relatively new dataset that is specifically designed to evaluate the coreference-related performance of a model. We use two strategies to fine-tune a pre-trained language model, namely, placing an additional encoder layer after a pre-trained language model to focus on the coreference mentions or constructing a relational graph convolutional network to model the coreference relations. We demonstrate that the explicit incorporation of coreference information in the fine-tuning stage performs better than the incorporation of the coreference information in pre-training a language model.

label: acl
text: Machine reading comprehension is a well-studied area in evaluating new pre-trained language models (PrLMs) and their fine-tuning strategies. Recent studies have enriched PrLMs with linguistic information such as syntax and semantics to improve their performance. In this paper, we imitate the human reading process by connecting anaphoric expressions and leveraging coreference information to enhance the word embeddings from the pre-trained language model. Our goal is to enhance the coreference mentions of entities for coreference-intensive question answering in QUOREF, a new dataset designed to evaluate coreference-related performance. We use two fine-tuning strategies: adding an encoder layer to focus on coreference mentions or constructing a relational graph convolutional network to model coreference relations. Our results show that explicit incorporation of coreference information in the fine-tuning stage outperforms incorporating it in pre-training the language model.

label: acl
text: Bilingual lexicons map words in one language to their translations in another, and are typically induced by learning linear projections to align monolingual word embedding spaces. In this paper, we show it is possible to produce much higher quality lexicons with methods that combine (1) unsupervised bitext mining and (2) unsupervised word alignment. Directly applying a pipeline that uses recent algorithms for both subproblems significantly improves induced lexicon quality and further gains are possible by learning to filter the resulting lexical entries, with both unsupervised and semi-supervised schemes. Our final model outperforms the state of the art on the BUCC 2020 shared task by 14 F1 points averaged over 12 language pairs, while also providing a more interpretable approach that allows for rich reasoning of word meaning in context. Further analysis of our output and the standard reference lexicons suggests they are of comparable quality, and new benchmarks may be needed to measure further progress on this task.

label: acl
text: Bilingual lexicons are dictionaries that map words from one language to their translations in another language. They are usually generated by learning linear projections that align monolingual word embedding spaces. In this paper, we demonstrate that higher quality lexicons can be produced by combining unsupervised bitext mining and unsupervised word alignment. Directly applying recent algorithms to both subproblems leads to significant improvement in the quality of the induced lexicon, and further gains can be achieved by filtering the resulting lexical entries using unsupervised and semi-supervised methods. Our final model outperforms the state-of-the-art on the BUCC 2020 shared task by 14 F1 points, on average, across 12 language pairs. Additionally, our approach provides a more interpretable solution that enables rich reasoning of word meaning in context. Further analysis of our output and the standard reference lexicons suggests that they are of comparable quality, and new benchmarks may be required to measure further progress in this area.

label: emnlp
text: The encode-decoder framework has shown recent success in image captioning. Visual attention, which is good at detailedness, and semantic attention, which is good at comprehensiveness, have been separately proposed to ground the caption on the image. In this paper, we propose the Stepwise Image-Topic Merging Network (simNet) that makes use of the two kinds of attention at the same time. At each time step when generating the caption, the decoder adaptively merges the attentive information in the extracted topics and the image according to the generated context, so that the visual information and the semantic information can be effectively combined. The proposed approach is evaluated on two benchmark datasets and reaches the state-of-the-art performances.

label: emnlp
text: The recent success of the encode-decoder framework in image captioning has been attributed to the integration of visual and semantic attention. Visual attention provides detailed representations of the image while semantic attention offers a comprehensive understanding. In this paper, we present the Stepwise Image-Topic Merging Network (simNet), which combines both forms of attention to generate captions. The decoder adaptively merges the attentive information from the extracted topics and image based on the generated context at each time step, thus effectively combining visual and semantic information. Our proposed approach has been evaluated on two benchmark datasets and achieved state-of-the-art results.

label: coling
text: Entity linking, which aims at aligning ambiguous entity mentions to their referent entities in a knowledge base, plays a key role in multiple natural language processing tasks. Recently, zero-shot entity linking task has become a research hotspot, which links mentions to unseen entities to challenge the generalization ability. For this task, the training set and test set are from different domains, and thus entity linking models tend to be overfitting due to the tendency of memorizing the properties of entities that appear frequently in the training set. We argue that general ultra-fine-grained type information can help the linking models to learn contextual commonality and improve their generalization ability to tackle the overfitting problem. However, in the zero-shot entity linking setting, any type information is not available and entities are only identified by textual descriptions. Thus, we first extract the ultra-fine entity type information from the entity textual descriptions. Then, we propose a hierarchical multi-task model to improve the high-level zero-shot entity linking candidate generation task by utilizing the entity typing task as an auxiliary low-level task, which introduces extracted ultra-fine type information into the candidate generation task. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing the ultra-fine entity type information and our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

label: coling
text: Entity linking, which aligns ambiguous entity mentions with their referent entities in a knowledge base, is crucial for many natural language processing tasks. Zero-shot entity linking, which links mentions to unseen entities, is a current research focus. This task is challenging because the training and test sets come from different domains, causing entity linking models to overfit due to memorizing the properties of frequently appearing entities. We believe that ultra-fine-grained entity type information can help these models learn contextual commonality and improve generalization, overcoming the overfitting problem. However, in zero-shot entity linking, type information is not available, and entities are only identified by textual descriptions. To address this issue, we extract ultra-fine entity type information from these descriptions and propose a hierarchical multi-task model that improves the high-level zero-shot entity linking candidate generation task by utilizing the entity typing task as an auxiliary low-level task. This introduces the extracted ultra-fine type information into the candidate generation task. Our experiments show the effectiveness of using ultra-fine entity type information, and our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

label: naacl
text: This paper presents a novel, data-driven language model that produces entire lyrics for a given input melody. Previously proposed models for lyrics generation suffer from the inability of capturing the relationship between lyrics and melody partly due to the unavailability of lyrics-melody aligned data. In this study, we first propose a new practical method for creating a large collection of lyrics-melody aligned data and then create a collection of 1,000 lyrics-melody pairs augmented with precise syllable-note alignments and word/sentence/paragraph boundaries. We then provide a quantitative analysis of the correlation between word/sentence/paragraph boundaries in lyrics and melodies. We then propose an RNN-based lyrics language model conditioned on a featurized melody. Experimental results show that the proposed model generates fluent lyrics while maintaining the compatibility between boundaries of lyrics and melody structures.

label: naacl
text: This paper introduces a novel, data-driven language model that generates complete lyrics for a given melody. Previous models for lyrics generation have struggled to capture the relationship between lyrics and melody, largely due to the lack of lyrics-melody aligned data. To address this issue, we present a new method for creating a large collection of lyrics-melody aligned data. Our collection includes 1,000 lyrics-melody pairs, augmented with precise syllable-note alignments and word/sentence/paragraph boundaries. We also provide a quantitative analysis of the correlation between these boundaries in lyrics and melodies. Our model is based on an RNN and is conditioned on a featurized melody. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model generates fluent lyrics while preserving the compatibility between the boundaries of lyrics and melody structures.

label: coling
text: Data-to-Text Generation (D2T) problems can be considered as a stream of time-stamped events with a text summary being produced for each. The problem becomes more challenging when event summaries contain complex insights derived from multiple records either within an event, or across several events from the event stream. It is important to understand the different types of content present in the summary to help us better define the system requirements so that we can build better systems. In this paper, we propose a novel typology of content types, that we use to classify the contents of event summaries. Using the typology, a profile of a dataset is generated as the distribution of the aggregated content types which captures the specific characteristics of the dataset and gives a measure of the complexity present in the problem. Extensive experimentation on different D2T datasets is performed and these demonstrate that neural systems struggle in generating contents of complex types.

label: coling
text:
The proposed typology provides a clear understanding of the different types of content present in the event summaries and can be used to inform the development of better systems.

Data-to-Text Generation (D2T) involves generating text summaries for time-stamped events. This task becomes more challenging when the event summaries contain complex insights derived from multiple records within or across several events. To build better systems, it's important to understand the different types of content in the summaries. This paper proposes a novel typology of content types, which we use to classify the contents of event summaries. This typology generates a profile of the dataset by aggregating the distribution of content types, capturing the specific characteristics of the dataset and providing a measure of its complexity. Our experiments on various D2T datasets demonstrate that neural systems struggle with generating complex content types. The proposed typology provides a clear understanding of the different types of content in event summaries, informing the development of better systems.

text: Correct natural language understanding requires computers to distinguish the literal and metaphorical senses of a word. Recent neu- ral models achieve progress on verb metaphor detection by viewing it as sequence labeling. In this paper, we argue that it is appropriate to view this task as relation classification between a verb and its various contexts. We propose the Metaphor-relation BERT (Mr-BERT) model, which explicitly models the relation between a verb and its grammatical, sentential and semantic contexts. We evaluate our method on the VUA, MOH-X and TroFi datasets. Our method gets competitive results compared with state-of-the-art approaches.

label: acl
text: Correct natural language understanding requires computers to differentiate between the literal and metaphorical senses of words. Recent neural models have made progress in detecting verb metaphors by treating it as a sequence labeling task. However, in this paper, we argue that it is more appropriate to view this task as a relation classification between a verb and its different contexts. To this end, we introduce the Metaphor-relation BERT (Mr-BERT) model, which explicitly considers the relationship between a verb and its grammatical, sentential, and semantic contexts. Our method is evaluated on the VUA, MOH-X, and TroFi datasets, and our results show that it is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.

label: naacl
text: Training data for sentiment analysis are abundant in multiple domains, yet scarce for other domains. It is useful to leveraging data available for all existing domains to enhance performance on different domains. We investigate this problem by learning domain-specific representations of input sentences using neural network. In particular, a descriptor vector is learned for representing each domain, which is used to map adversarially trained domain-general Bi-LSTM input representations into domain-specific representations. Based on this model, we further expand the input representation with exemplary domain knowledge, collected by attending over a memory network of domain training data. Results show that our model outperforms existing methods on multi-domain sentiment analysis significantly, giving the best accuracies on two different benchmarks.

label: naacl
text: Training data for sentiment analysis is abundant in many domains, but scarce in others. To overcome this challenge, we aim to utilize data from all available domains to improve performance in different domains. To achieve this, we use a neural network to learn domain-specific representations of input sentences. We do this by creating a descriptor vector for each domain, which is used to map adversarially trained domain-General Bi-LSTM input representations into domain-specific representations. Additionally, we enhance the input representation by incorporating domain-specific knowledge, which is obtained by attending to a memory network of domain training data. Our results show that our model outperforms existing methods in multi-domain sentiment analysis and achieves the highest accuracy on two different benchmarks.

label: coling
text: We present bot#1337: a dialog system developed for the 1st NIPS Conversational Intelligence Challenge 2017 (ConvAI). The aim of the competition was to implement a bot capable of conversing with humans based on a given passage of text. To enable conversation, we implemented a set of skills for our bot, including chit-chat, topic detection, text summarization, question answering and question generation. The system has been trained in a supervised setting using a dialogue manager to select an appropriate skill for generating a response. The latter allows a developer to focus on the skill implementation rather than the finite state machine based dialog manager. The proposed system bot#1337 won the competition with an average dialogue quality score of 2.78 out of 5 given by human evaluators. Source code and trained models for the bot#1337 are available on GitHub.

label: coling
text: We present Bot#1337, a dialog system developed for the 1st NIPS Conversational Intelligence Challenge 2017 (ConvAI). This competition aimed to create a bot capable of engaging in conversation with humans based on a given text passage. To facilitate this, we equipped our bot with a set of skills, including chit-chat, topic detection, text summarization, question answering, and question generation. The system was trained in a supervised setting, utilizing a dialogue manager to select the appropriate skill for generating a response. This approach allows developers to focus on skill implementation rather than the finite state machine-based dialog manager. Bot#1337 emerged as the winner of the competition, with an average dialogue quality score of 2.78 out of 5, as evaluated by human evaluators. The source code and trained models for Bot#1337 are available on GitHub.

text: Learning disentangled representations of textual data is essential for many natural language tasks such as fair classification, style transfer and sentence generation, among others. The existent dominant approaches in the context of text data either rely on training an adversary (discriminator) that aims at making attribute values difficult to be inferred from the latent code or rely on minimising variational bounds of the mutual information between latent code and the value attribute. However, the available methods suffer of the impossibility to provide a fine-grained control of the degree (or force) of disentanglement. In contrast to adversarial methods, which are remarkably simple, although the adversary seems to be performing perfectly well during the training phase, after it is completed a fair amount of information about the undesired attribute still remains. This paper introduces a novel variational upper bound to the mutual information between an attribute and the latent code of an encoder. Our bound aims at controlling the approximation error via the Renyi's divergence, leading to both better disentangled representations and in particular, a precise control of the desirable degree of disentanglement than state-of-the-art methods proposed for textual data. Furthermore, it does not suffer from the degeneracy of other losses in multi-class scenarios. We show the superiority of this method on fair classification and on textual style transfer tasks. Additionally, we provide new insights illustrating various trade-offs in style transfer when attempting to learn disentangled representations and quality of the generated sentence.

text: Learning disentangled representations of textual data is crucial for various natural language tasks, such as fair classification, style transfer, and sentence generation. Currently, the dominant approaches either train an adversarial discriminator to make attribute values difficult to infer from the latent code or minimize variational bounds of the mutual information between the latent code and attribute values. However, these methods lack the ability to control the degree of disentanglement precisely. Adversarial methods, while simple, still retain a significant amount of information about undesired attributes even after training. This paper presents a novel variational upper bound that controls the approximation error via Renyi's divergence, leading to improved disentangled representations and precise control over the desired degree of disentanglement compared to state-of-the-art methods for textual data. Additionally, this method is not prone to degeneracy in multi-class scenarios. Our results demonstrate the superiority of this method on fair classification and style transfer tasks and provide new insights on the trade-offs between disentangled representations and sentence quality in style transfer.

label: naacl
text: Most previous studies aim at extracting events from a single sentence, while document-level event extraction still remains under-explored. In this paper, we focus on extracting event arguments from an entire document, which mainly faces two critical problems: a) the long-distance dependency between trigger and arguments over sentences; b) the distracting context towards an event in the document. To address these issues, we propose a Two-Stream Abstract meaning Representation enhanced extraction model (TSAR). TSAR encodes the document from different perspectives by a two-stream encoding module, to utilize local and global information and lower the impact of distracting context. Besides, TSAR introduces an AMR-guided interaction module to capture both intra-sentential and inter-sentential features, based on the locally and globally constructed AMR semantic graphs. An auxiliary boundary loss is introduced to enhance the boundary information for text spans explicitly. Extensive experiments illustrate that TSAR outperforms previous state-of-the-art by a large margin, with 2.54 F1 and 5.13 F1 performance gain on the public RAMS and WikiEvents datasets respectively, showing the superiority in the cross-sentence arguments extraction. We release our code in https://github.com/ PKUnlp-icler/TSAR.

label: naacl
text: Most studies have focused on extracting events from individual sentences, leaving document-level event extraction under-explored. This paper addresses two critical issues in document-level event extraction: the long-distance dependency between triggers and arguments across sentences and the impact of distracting context. To overcome these challenges, we propose the Two-Stream Abstract Meaning Representation enhanced extraction model (TSAR). This model encodes the document from different perspectives using a two-stream encoding module, which leverages local and global information to reduce the impact of distracting context. Additionally, TSAR includes an AMR-guided interaction module to capture both intra-sentential and inter-sentential features, based on locally and globally constructed AMR semantic graphs. The model also includes an auxiliary boundary loss to enhance the boundary information for text spans. Our experiments show that TSAR outperforms previous state-of-the-art models with a 2.54 F1 performance gain on the RAMS dataset and a 5.13 F1 performance gain on the WikiEvents dataset, demonstrating its superiority in cross-sentence argument extraction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ PKUnlp-icler/TSAR.

label: acl
text: Large multilingual pretrained language models such as mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa have been found to be surprisingly effective for cross-lingual transfer of syntactic parsing models Wu and Dredze (2019), but only between related languages. However, source and training languages are rarely related, when parsing truly low-resource languages. To close this gap, we adopt a method from multi-task learning, which relies on automated curriculum learning, to dynamically optimize for parsing performance on outlier languages. We show that this approach is significantly better than uniform and size-proportional sampling in the zero-shot setting.

label: acl
text: Multilingual pretrained language models, such as mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa, have demonstrated remarkable success in cross-lingual transfer of syntactic parsing models between related languages, as noted by Wu and Dredze (2019). However, this method is limited when parsing low-resource languages that are not related to the source or training languages. To address this challenge, we propose a multi-task learning method that utilizes automated curriculum learning to dynamically optimize parsing performance for outlier languages. Our results demonstrate that this approach outperforms uniform and size-proportional sampling in the zero-shot setting.

label: acl
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is a well-studied task in natural language processing. Traditional NER research only deals with flat entities and ignores nested entities. The span-based methods treat entity recognition as a span classification task. Although these methods have the innate ability to handle nested NER, they suffer from high computational cost, ignorance of boundary information, under-utilization of the spans that partially match with entities, and difficulties in long entity recognition. To tackle these issues, we propose a two-stage entity identifier. First we generate span proposals by filtering and boundary regression on the seed spans to locate the entities, and then label the boundary-adjusted span proposals with the corresponding categories. Our method effectively utilizes the boundary information of entities and partially matched spans during training. Through boundary regression, entities of any length can be covered theoretically, which improves the ability to recognize long entities. In addition, many low-quality seed spans are filtered out in the first stage, which reduces the time complexity of inference. Experiments on nested NER datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms previous state-of-the-art models.
