text: Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a well-researched area in Natural Language Processing. Traditional NER research focuses only on flat entities, ignoring nested entities. Span-based methods treat entity recognition as a span classification task, but suffer from high computational costs, ignoring boundary information, underutilizing partially matching spans, and difficulties in recognizing long entities. To address these issues, we propose a two-stage entity identifier that first generates span proposals by filtering and boundary regression on seed spans, then labels the boundary-adjusted span proposals with the corresponding categories. Our method effectively utilizes boundary information and partially matching spans during training, and through boundary regression, entities of any length can be recognized, improving the ability to recognize long entities. The first stage also filters out many low-quality seed spans, reducing inference time complexity. Experiments on nested NER datasets show that our proposed method outperforms previous state-of-the-art models.

label: naacl
text: Grounding dialogue on external knowledge and interpreting linguistic patterns in dialogue history context, such as ellipsis, anaphora, and co-reference is critical for dialogue comprehension and generation. In this paper, we present a novel open-domain dialogue generation model which effectively utilizes the large-scale commonsense and named entity based knowledge in addition to the unstructured topic-specific knowledge associated with each utterance. We enhance the commonsense knowledge with named entity-aware structures using co-references. Our proposed model utilizes a multi-hop attention layer to preserve the most accurate and critical parts of the dialogue history and the associated knowledge. In addition, we employ a Commonsense and Named Entity Enhanced Attention Module, which starts with the extracted triples from various sources and gradually finds the relevant supporting set of triples using multi-hop attention with the query vector obtained from the interactive dialogue-knowledge module. Empirical results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both automatic evaluation metrics and human judgment. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/deekshaVarshney/CNTF; https://www.iitp.ac.in/-ai-nlp-ml/resources/codes/CNTF.zip.

label: naacl
text: Grounding dialogue on external knowledge and interpreting linguistic patterns, such as ellipsis, anaphora, and co-reference, is crucial for effective dialogue comprehension and generation. In this paper, we propose a novel open-domain dialogue generation model that leverages large-scale commonsense and named entity-based knowledge, as well as topic-specific knowledge associated with each utterance. Our model enhances commonsense knowledge with named entity-aware structures using co-references and employs a multi-hop attention layer to preserve the most relevant parts of the dialogue history and knowledge. The Commonsense and Named Entity Enhanced Attention Module starts with extracted triples from various sources and gradually finds the relevant supporting set of triples using multi-hop attention with the query vector from the interactive dialogue-knowledge module. Our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of automatic evaluation metrics and human judgment, as demonstrated by empirical results on two benchmark datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/deekshaVarshney/CNTF and https://www.iitp.ac.in/-ai-nlp-ml/resources/codes/CNTF.zip.

label: acl
text: We present a framework for learning hierarchical policies from demonstrations, using sparse natural language annotations to guide the discovery of reusable skills for autonomous decision-making. We formulate a generative model of action sequences in which goals generate sequences of high-level subtask descriptions, and these descriptions generate sequences of low-level actions. We describe how to train this model using primarily unannotated demonstrations by parsing demonstrations into sequences of named high-level sub-tasks, using only a small number of seed annotations to ground language in action. In trained models, natural language commands index a combinatorial library of skills; agents can use these skills to plan by generating high-level instruction sequences tailored to novel goals. We evaluate this approach in the ALFRED household simulation environment, providing natural language annotations for only 10% of demonstrations. It achieves performance comparable state-of-the-art models on ALFRED success rate, outperforming several recent methods with access to ground-truth plans during training and evaluation.

label: acl
text: We introduce a framework for learning hierarchical policies from demonstrations, where sparse natural language annotations are used to discover reusable skills for autonomous decision-making. Our approach involves a generative model of action sequences, where goals generate high-level subtask descriptions, which then generate low-level actions. The model is trained primarily using unannotated demonstrations, with only a small number of seed annotations to link language to action. In the trained models, natural language commands index a library of skills, allowing agents to plan by generating high-level instruction sequences for novel goals. We evaluate this approach in the ALFRED household simulation environment, using only 10% of demonstrations with natural language annotations. The results show that our approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art models in terms of ALFRED success rate, outperforming recent methods that have access to ground-truth plans during training and evaluation.

text: Effective textual communication depends on readers being proficient enough to comprehend texts, and texts being clear enough to be understood by the intended audience, in a reading task. When the meaning of textual information and instructions is not well conveyed, many losses and damages may occur. Among the solutions to alleviate this problem is the automatic evaluation of sentence readability, task which has been receiving a lot of attention due to its large applicability. However, a shortage of resources, such as corpora for training and evaluation, hinders the full development of this task. In this paper, we generate a nontrivial sentence corpus in Portuguese. We evaluate three scenarios for building it, taking advantage of a parallel corpus of simplification, in which each sentence triplet is aligned and has simplification operations annotated, being ideal for justifying possible mistakes of future methods. The best scenario of our corpus PorSimplesSent is composed of 4,888 pairs, which is bigger than a similar corpus for English; all the three versions of it are publicly available. We created four baselines for PorSimplesSent and made available a pairwise ranking method, using 17 linguistic and psycholinguistic features, which correctly identifies the ranking of sentence pairs with an accuracy of 74.2%.

label: coling
text:
The results of this paper demonstrate the potential of PorSimplesSent as a resource for automatic evaluation of sentence readability in Portuguese.

Improved: The effectiveness of textual communication depends on both the reader's proficiency in comprehending texts and the clarity of the texts themselves, to be understood by the intended audience. When the meaning of textual information and instructions is not effectively conveyed, it can result in significant losses and damages. To address this issue, automatic evaluation of sentence readability has received a lot of attention as a solution, but a shortage of resources, such as training and evaluation corpora, has hindered its full development. In this paper, we generate a new sentence corpus in Portuguese, evaluating three scenarios for its construction, using a parallel corpus of simplification. The best scenario, PorSimplesSent, consists of 4,888 sentence pairs, which is larger than a similar corpus for English, and is publicly available. We also create four baselines and provide a pairwise ranking method using 17 linguistic and psycholinguistic features, achieving an accuracy of 74.2% in correctly identifying the ranking of sentence pairs. Our results demonstrate the potential of PorSimplesSent as a valuable resource for automatic evaluation of sentence readability in Portuguese.

label: acl
text: During the last years, there has been a lot of interest in achieving some kind of complex reasoning using deep neural networks. To do that, models like Memory Networks (MemNNs) have combined external memory storages and attention mechanisms. These architectures, however, lack of more complex reasoning mechanisms that could allow, for instance, relational reasoning. Relation Networks (RNs), on the other hand, have shown outstanding results in relational reasoning tasks. Unfortunately, their computational cost grows quadratically with the number of memories, something prohibitive for larger problems. To solve these issues, we introduce the Working Memory Network, a MemNN architecture with a novel working memory storage and reasoning module. Our model retains the relational reasoning abilities of the RN while reducing its computational complexity from quadratic to linear. We tested our model on the text QA dataset bAbI and the visual QA dataset NLVR. In the jointly trained bAbI-10k, we set a new state-of-the-art, achieving a mean error of less than 0.5%. Moreover, a simple ensemble of two of our models solves all 20 tasks in the joint version of the benchmark.

label: acl
text: Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing deep neural networks capable of complex reasoning. To achieve this, Memory Networks (MemNNs) have been designed to incorporate external memory storages and attention mechanisms. However, these architectures lack more advanced reasoning mechanisms that would allow for relational reasoning. Relation Networks (RNs) have demonstrated exceptional results in relational reasoning tasks, but their computational cost increases quadratically with the number of memories, making it challenging for larger problems. To address these limitations, we present the Working Memory Network - a MemNN architecture that features a novel working memory storage and reasoning module. Our model retains the relational reasoning capabilities of RNs while reducing its computational complexity from quadratic to linear. We evaluated our model on the text QA dataset bAbI and the visual QA dataset NLVR, and achieved a new state-of-the-art mean error of less than 0.5% in the jointly trained bAbI-10k. Furthermore, a simple ensemble of two of our models was able to solve all 20 tasks in the joint version of the benchmark.

label: coling
text: A Multilingual model relies on language encodings to identify input languages because the multilingual model has to distinguish between the input and output languages or among all the languages for cross-lingual tasks. Furthermore, we find that language encodings potentially refine multiple morphologies of different languages to form a better isomorphic space for multilinguality. To leverage this observation, we present a method to compute a vocabulary-informed language encoding as the language representation, for a required language, considering a local vocabulary covering an acceptable amount of the most frequent word embeddings in this language. In our experiments, our method can consistently improve the performance of multilingual models on unsupervised neural machine translation and cross-lingual embedding.

label: coling
text: A multilingual model depends on language encodings to recognize input languages, as it must differentiate between the input and output languages or among all languages for cross-lingual tasks. We discovered that language encodings can refine multiple morphologies of different languages to create a more isomorphic space for multilinguality. To take advantage of this insight, we propose a method to compute a vocabulary-informed language encoding as the language representation for a specific language, taking into account a local vocabulary that covers a sufficient number of the most frequent word embeddings in that language. Our experiments show that this method can significantly enhance the performance of multilingual models in unsupervised neural machine translation and cross-lingual embedding.

label: coling
text: Both humans and neural language models are able to perform subject verb number agreement (SVA). In principle, semantics shouldn't interfere with this task, which only requires syntactic knowledge. In this work we test whether meaning interferes with this type of agreement in English in syntactic structures of various complexities. To do so, we generate both semantically well-formed and nonsensical items. We compare the performance of BERT-base to that of humans, obtained with a psycholinguistic online crowdsourcing experiment. We find that BERT and humans are both sensitive to our semantic manipulation: They fail more often when presented with nonsensical items, especially when their syntactic structure features an attractor (a noun phrase between the subject and the verb that has not the same number as the subject). We also find that the effect of meaningfulness on SVA errors is stronger for BERT than for humans, showing higher lexical sensitivity of the former on this task.

label: coling
text: Both humans and neural language models are capable of performing subject-verb agreement. This task only requires syntactic knowledge, and semantics should not interfere with it. In this study, we examine if meaning affects this type of agreement in English in syntactic structures of varying complexities. To do so, we generate both semantically well-formed and nonsensical items and compare the performance of BERT-base with that of humans obtained through an online crowdsourcing experiment. Our results reveal that both BERT and humans are sensitive to our semantic manipulation, with a higher failure rate when presented with nonsensical items, especially when the syntactic structure features an attractor (a noun phrase between the subject and the verb that does not have the same number as the subject). Additionally, our findings show that the effect of meaningfulness on subject-verb agreement errors is stronger for BERT than for humans, demonstrating the higher lexical sensitivity of the former in this task.

label: acl
text: With the development of several multilingual datasets used for semantic parsing, recent research efforts have looked into the problem of learning semantic parsers in a multilingual setup. However, how to improve the performance of a monolingual semantic parser for a specific language by leveraging data annotated in different languages remains a research question that is under-explored. In this work, we present a study to show how learning distributed representations of the logical forms from data annotated in different languages can be used for improving the performance of a monolingual semantic parser. We extend two existing monolingual semantic parsers to incorporate such cross-lingual distributed logical representations as features. Experiments show that our proposed approach is able to yield improved semantic parsing results on the standard multilingual GeoQuery dataset.

label: acl
text: With the growth of multilingual datasets for semantic parsing, recent research has focused on learning semantic parsers in a multilingual setting. However, the question of how to enhance the performance of a monolingual semantic parser for a specific language by utilizing data annotated in different languages has yet to be fully explored. This study investigates the use of cross-lingual distributed logical representations to improve the performance of a monolingual semantic parser. We modify two existing monolingual semantic parsers by incorporating these representations as features. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach leads to improved semantic parsing results on the GeoQuery dataset, a widely used multilingual benchmark.

label: acl
text: Static word embeddings that represent words by a single vector cannot capture the variability of word meaning in different linguistic and extralinguistic contexts. Building on prior work on contextualized and dynamic word embeddings, we introduce dynamic contextualized word embeddings that represent words as a function of both linguistic and extralinguistic context. Based on a pretrained language model (PLM), dynamic contextualized word embeddings model time and social space jointly, which makes them attractive for a range of NLP tasks involving semantic variability. We highlight potential application scenarios by means of qualitative and quantitative analyses on four English datasets.

label: acl
text: Dynamic word embeddings that are represented by a single vector are insufficient in capturing the variability of a word's meaning across different linguistic and extralinguistic contexts. Our work builds upon prior research in contextualized and dynamic word embeddings and introduces dynamic contextualized word embeddings. These embeddings represent words as a function of both linguistic and extralinguistic context, making them suitable for a range of NLP tasks that deal with semantic variability. Our dynamic contextualized word embeddings, which are based on a pre-trained language model (PLM), model time and social space jointly. To demonstrate their potential applications, we conduct qualitative and quantitative analyses on four English datasets.

label: naacl
text: Despite being a common figure of speech, hyperbole is under-researched in Figurative Language Processing. In this paper, we tackle the challenging task of hyperbole generation to transfer a literal sentence into its hyperbolic paraphrase. To address the lack of available hyperbolic sentences, we construct HYPO-XL, the first large-scale English hyperbole corpus containing 17,862 hyperbolic sentences in a non-trivial way. Based on our corpus, we propose an unsupervised method for hyperbole generation that does not require parallel literal-hyperbole pairs. During training, we fine-tune BART to infill masked hyperbolic spans of sentences from HYPO-XL. During inference, we mask part of an input literal sentence and over-generate multiple possible hyperbolic versions. Then a BERT-based ranker selects the best candidate by hyperbolicity and paraphrase quality. Automatic and human evaluation results show that our model is effective at generating hyperbolic paraphrase sentences and outperforms several baseline systems.

label: naacl
text: Despite being a commonly used figure of speech, hyperbole is under-researched in Figurative Language Processing. This paper aims to tackle the challenging task of generating hyperbolic paraphrases of literal sentences. To address the shortage of available hyperbolic sentences, we created HYPO-XL, the first large-scale English hyperbole corpus consisting of 17,862 hyperbolic sentences. Our unsupervised method for hyperbole generation does not require parallel literal-hyperbole pairs. We fine-tune BART to infill masked hyperbolic spans using HYPO-XL during training. During inference, we mask part of the input literal sentence and generate multiple possible hyperbolic versions, then a BERT-based ranker selects the best candidate based on hyperbolicity and paraphrase quality. Our results from automatic and human evaluations show that our model is effective in generating hyperbolic paraphrase sentences and outperforms several baseline systems.

label: acl
text: Discovering Out-of-Domain(OOD) intents is essential for developing new skills in a task-oriented dialogue system. The key challenge is how to transfer prior IND knowledge to OOD clustering. Different from existing work based on shared intent representation, we propose a novel disentangled knowledge transfer method via a unified multi-head contrastive learning framework. We aim to bridge the gap between IND pre-training and OOD clustering. Experiments and analysis on two benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of our method.

label: acl
text: Discovering Out-of-Domain (OOD) intents is crucial for advancing the capabilities of task-oriented dialogue systems. The central challenge lies in how to transfer prior in-domain (IND) knowledge to OOD clustering. Unlike existing approaches that rely on shared intent representations, we propose a novel method of transferring knowledge through a unified multi-head contrastive learning framework. Our goal is to close the gap between IND pre-training and OOD clustering. Our experiments and analysis on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

label: coling
text: Language modelling and machine translation tasks mostly use subword or character inputs, but syllables are seldom used. Syllables provide shorter sequences than characters, require less-specialised extracting rules than morphemes, and their segmentation is not impacted by the corpus size. In this study, we first explore the potential of syllables for open-vocabulary language modelling in 21 languages. We use rule-based syllabification methods for six languages and address the rest with hyphenation, which works as a syllabification proxy. With a comparable perplexity, we show that syllables outperform characters and other subwords. Moreover, we study the importance of syllables on neural machine translation for a non-related and low-resource language-pair (Spanish–Shipibo-Konibo). In pairwise and multilingual systems, syllables outperform unsupervised subwords, and further morphological segmentation methods, when translating into a highly synthetic language with a transparent orthography (Shipibo-Konibo). Finally, we perform some human evaluation, and discuss limitations and opportunities.

text: Language modeling and machine translation tasks typically use subword or character inputs, but syllables are rarely used. Syllables offer shorter sequences than characters, require less specialized extraction rules than morphemes, and their segmentation is not impacted by the corpus size. This study investigates the potential of syllables for open-vocabulary language modeling in 21 languages. We use rule-based syllabification methods for six languages and employ hyphenation as a syllabification proxy for the remaining languages. Our results demonstrate that syllables outperform characters and other subwords in terms of comparable perplexity. Additionally, we examine the impact of syllables on neural machine translation for Spanish-Shipibo-Konibo, a non-related and low-resource language pair. Our findings show that syllables outperform unsupervised subwords and further morphological segmentation methods when translating into Shipibo-Konibo, a highly synthetic language with a transparent orthography. Finally, we conduct human evaluation, discuss limitations, and highlight opportunities for future research.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a corpus and experimental results to extract possession relations over time. We work with Wikipedia articles about artworks, and extract possession relations along with temporal information indicating when these relations are true. The annotation scheme yields many possessors over time for a given artwork, and experimental results show that an LSTM ensemble can automate the task.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a corpus and experimental results for extracting possession relations over time in Wikipedia articles about artworks. Our approach involves the extraction of possession relations along with temporal information that indicates the validity of these relations. Our annotation scheme generates multiple possessors over time for a given artwork, and our experimental results demonstrate that an LSTM ensemble can effectively automate this task.

label: coling
text: Discourse parsing has proven to be useful for a number of NLP tasks that require complex reasoning. However, over a decade since the advent of the Penn Discourse Treebank, predicting implicit discourse relations in text remains challenging. There are several possible reasons for this, and we hypothesize that models should be exposed to more context as it plays an important role in accurate human annotation; meanwhile adding uncertainty measures can improve model accuracy and calibration. To thoroughly investigate this phenomenon, we perform a series of experiments to determine 1) the effects of context on human judgments, and 2) the effect of quantifying uncertainty with annotator confidence ratings on model accuracy and calibration (which we measure using the Brier score (Brier et al, 1950)). We find that including annotator accuracy and confidence improves model accuracy, and incorporating confidence in the model's temperature function can lead to models with significantly better-calibrated confidence measures. We also find some insightful qualitative results regarding human and model behavior on these datasets.

label: coling
text: The usefulness of discourse parsing has been demonstrated for various NLP tasks that involve intricate reasoning. Despite the emergence of the Penn Discourse Treebank over a decade ago, predicting implicit discourse relations in text remains a significant challenge. There could be various reasons for this, and we believe that exposing models to more context, which plays a crucial role in accurate human annotation, and incorporating uncertainty measures can enhance model accuracy and calibration. To explore this phenomenon, we conduct a series of experiments to assess the impact of context on human judgments and the effect of incorporating annotator confidence ratings on model accuracy and calibration, as measured by the Brier score (Brier et al, 1950). Our findings indicate that including annotator accuracy and confidence improves model accuracy and that incorporating confidence in the model's temperature function results in models with better-calibrated confidence measures. Additionally, we uncover some noteworthy qualitative results regarding human and model behavior on these datasets.

label: acl
text: Zero-shot sequence labeling aims to build a sequence labeler without human-annotated datasets. One straightforward approach is utilizing existing systems (source models) to generate pseudo-labeled datasets and train a target sequence labeler accordingly. However, due to the gap between the source and the target languages/domains, this approach may fail to recover the true labels. In this paper, we propose a novel unified framework for zero-shot sequence labeling with minimum risk training and design a new decomposable risk function that models the relations between the predicted labels from the source models and the true labels. By making the risk function trainable, we draw a connection between minimum risk training and latent variable model learning. We propose a unified learning algorithm based on the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm. We extensively evaluate our proposed approaches on cross-lingual/domain sequence labeling tasks over twenty-one datasets. The results show that our approaches outperform state-of-the-art baseline systems.

label: acl
text: The goal of zero-shot sequence labeling is to build a sequence labeler without the need for human-annotated datasets. One common approach is to use existing systems (source models) to generate pseudo-labeled datasets and train a target sequence labeler. However, this method can fail to accurately recover true labels due to differences between the source and target languages/domains. To address this issue, we present a novel, unified framework for zero-shot sequence labeling that incorporates minimum risk training and a new decomposable risk function. This function models the relationship between the predicted labels from the source models and the true labels, allowing for the risk function to be trained. Our framework draws a connection between minimum risk training and latent variable model learning and is based on the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm. Our approach is evaluated on 21 datasets for cross-lingual/domain sequence labeling tasks and outperforms existing baseline systems.

label: acl
text: Negative sampling is an important component in word2vec for distributed word representation learning. We hypothesize that taking into account global, corpus-level information and generating a different noise distribution for each target word better satisfies the requirements of negative examples for each training word than the original frequency-based distribution. In this purpose we pre-compute word co-occurrence statistics from the corpus and apply to it network algorithms such as random walk. We test this hypothesis through a set of experiments whose results show that our approach boosts the word analogy task by about 5% and improves the performance on word similarity tasks by about 1% compared to the skip-gram negative sampling baseline.

label: acl
text: Negative sampling is a crucial aspect in the learning of distributed word representation through word2vec. Our hypothesis is that considering global corpus-level information and generating a unique noise distribution for each target word will provide more suitable negative examples for each training word than the original frequency-based distribution. To achieve this, we first compute word co-occurrence statistics from the corpus and then apply network algorithms such as random walk to it. Our hypothesis is confirmed through a series of experiments, which show that our approach enhances the word analogy task by around 5% and improves the performance on word similarity tasks by approximately 1% compared to the skip-gram negative sampling baseline.

label: coling
text: Standard word embedding algorithms learn vector representations from large corpora of text documents in an unsupervised fashion. However, the quality of word embeddings learned from these algorithms is affected by the size of training data sets. Thus, applications of these algorithms in domains with only moderate amounts of available data is limited. In this paper we introduce an algorithm that learns word embeddings jointly with a classifier. Our algorithm is called SWESA (Supervised Word Embeddings for Sentiment Analysis). SWESA leverages document label information to learn vector representations of words from a modest corpus of text documents by solving an optimization problem that minimizes a cost function with respect to both word embeddings and the weight vector used for classification. Experiments on several real world data sets show that SWESA has superior performance on domains with limited data, when compared to previously suggested approaches to word embeddings and sentiment analysis tasks.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we present a novel algorithm, SWESA (Supervised Word Embeddings for Sentiment Analysis), that learns word embeddings in a supervised manner. Unlike traditional unsupervised algorithms, which learn vector representations from large text corpora, the quality of our word embeddings is not impacted by the size of the training data set. SWESA solves an optimization problem that minimizes a cost function with respect to both word embeddings and the weight vector used for classification, leveraging document label information to learn vector representations of words from a modest corpus of text documents. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SWESA outperforms previous approaches to word embeddings and sentiment analysis on domains with limited data.

label: acl
text: Typed entailment graphs try to learn the entailment relations between predicates from text and model them as edges between predicate nodes. The construction of entailment graphs usually suffers from severe sparsity and unreliability of distributional similarity. We propose a two-stage method, Entailment Graph with Textual Entailment and Transitivity (EGT2). EGT2 learns the local entailment relations by recognizing the textual entailment between template sentences formed by typed CCG-parsed predicates. Based on the generated local graph, EGT2 then uses three novel soft transitivity constraints to consider the logical transitivity in entailment structures. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that EGT2 can well model the transitivity in entailment graph to alleviate the sparsity, and leads to signifcant improvement over current state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: Typed entailment graphs aim to learn the relationships between predicates in text and represent them as edges between nodes representing predicates. However, the construction of these graphs is often hampered by the sparsity and unreliability of distributional similarity. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage method called Entailment Graph with Textual Entailment and Transitivity (EGT2). EGT2 first recognizes the local entailment relationships by identifying the textual entailment between template sentences formed from typed, CCG-parsed predicates. It then uses three innovative soft transitivity constraints to account for logical transitivity in the entailment structure. Results from experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that EGT2 effectively models transitivity in entailment graphs, reducing sparsity, and outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a local coherence model that captures the flow of what semantically connects adjacent sentences in a text. We represent the semantics of a sentence by a vector and capture its state at each word of the sentence. We model what relates two adjacent sentences based on the two most similar semantic states, each of which is in one of the sentences. We encode the perceived coherence of a text by a vector, which represents patterns of changes in salient information that relates adjacent sentences. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach is beneficial for two downstream tasks: Readability assessment, in which our model achieves new state-of-the-art results; and essay scoring, in which the combination of our coherence vectors and other task-dependent features significantly improves the performance of a strong essay scorer.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a local coherence model that captures the flow of semantically-connected information between adjacent sentences in a text. We represent the semantics of each sentence as a vector and capture its state at each word. Our model relates two adjacent sentences based on the two most similar semantic states, one in each sentence. We encode the perceived coherence of a text as a vector, which represents patterns of changes in salient information that connects adjacent sentences. Our experiments show that our approach is effective for two downstream tasks: readability assessment, where our model achieves new state-of-the-art results; and essay scoring, where the combination of our coherence vectors and other task-specific features significantly improves the performance of a strong essay scorer.

label: emnlp
text: We present a corpus that encompasses the complete history of conversations between contributors to Wikipedia, one of the largest online collaborative communities. By recording the intermediate states of conversations - including not only comments and replies, but also their modifications, deletions and restorations - this data offers an unprecedented view of online conversation. Our framework is designed to be language agnostic, and we show that it extracts high quality data in both Chinese and English. This level of detail supports new research questions pertaining to the process (and challenges) of large-scale online collaboration. We illustrate the corpus' potential with two case studies on English Wikipedia that highlight new perspectives on earlier work. First, we explore how a person's conversational behavior depends on how they relate to the discussion's venue. Second, we show that community moderation of toxic behavior happens at a higher rate than previously estimated.

label: emnlp
text: We present a comprehensive corpus that captures the entire history of conversations between contributors to Wikipedia, one of the largest online collaborative communities. Our corpus records the intermediate states of conversations, including not only comments and replies, but also modifications, deletions, and restorations, providing an unparalleled view of online conversation. Our framework is language-agnostic and has been successfully applied to both Chinese and English, extracting high-quality data. This level of detail enables new research into the process and challenges of large-scale online collaboration. To demonstrate the potential of our corpus, we present two case studies on English Wikipedia that offer new insights into previous research. The first study explores the relationship between a person's conversational behavior and the discussion venue. The second study shows that community moderation of toxic behavior occurs at a higher rate than previously estimated.

label: acl
text: Many deep learning architectures have been proposed to model the compositionality in text sequences, requiring substantial number of parameters and expensive computations. However, there has not been a rigorous evaluation regarding the added value of sophisticated compositional functions. In this paper, we conduct a point-by-point comparative study between Simple Word-Embedding-based Models (SWEMs), consisting of parameter-free pooling operations, relative to word-embedding-based RNN/CNN models. Surprisingly, SWEMs exhibit comparable or even superior performance in the majority of cases considered. Based upon this understanding, we propose two additional pooling strategies over learned word embeddings: (i) a max-pooling operation for improved interpretability; and (ii) a hierarchical pooling operation, which preserves spatial (C-C-C-gram) information within text sequences. We present experiments on 17 datasets encompassing three tasks: (i) (long) document classification; (ii) text sequence matching; and (iii) short text tasks, including classification and tagging.

label: acl
text:
Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed pooling strategies, yielding state-of-the-art results in several benchmark datasets.

 A large number of deep learning architectures have been developed to model the compositionality in text sequences, but they require a significant number of parameters and computationally expensive operations. However, there has been a lack of rigorous evaluation of the added value of these sophisticated compositional functions. In this paper, we compare Simple Word-Embedding-based Models (SWEMs), which consist of parameter-free pooling operations, to word-embedding-based RNN/CNN models. To our surprise, SWEMs perform comparably or even better than the latter models in most cases. Based on this understanding, we propose two additional pooling strategies using learned word embeddings: (i) a max-pooling operation for improved interpretability and (ii) a hierarchical pooling operation that preserves spatial information within text sequences. We evaluate our proposed pooling strategies on 17 datasets across three tasks: (i) document classification, (ii) text sequence matching, and (iii) short text classification and tagging. Our results show the effectiveness of our proposed pooling strategies, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.

label: naacl
text: We address the detection of abusive words. The task is to identify such words among a set of negative polar expressions. We propose novel features employing information from both corpora and lexical resources. These features are calibrated on a small manually annotated base lexicon which we use to produce a large lexicon. We show that the word-level information we learn cannot be equally derived from a large dataset of annotated microposts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our (domain-independent) lexicon in the cross-domain detection of abusive microposts.

label: naacl
text: We aim to detect abusive words by identifying them among a set of negative expressions. To achieve this, we introduce novel features that leverage information from both corpora and lexical resources. Our features are calibrated using a small, manually annotated base lexicon, which we then use to generate a larger lexicon. Our results show that the word-level information we derived cannot be obtained from a large annotated dataset of microposts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our domain-independent lexicon in detecting abusive microposts across different domains.

label: acl
text: Tuning pre-trained language models (PLMs) with task-specific prompts has been a promising approach for text classification. Particularly, previous studies suggest that prompt-tuning has remarkable superiority in the low-data scenario over the generic fine-tuning methods with extra classifiers. The core idea of prompt-tuning is to insert text pieces, i.e., template, to the input and transform a classification problem into a masked language modeling problem, where a crucial step is to construct a projection, i.e., verbalizer, between a label space and a label word space. A verbalizer is usually handcrafted or searched by gradient descent, which may lack coverage and bring considerable bias and high variances to the results. In this work, we focus on incorporating external knowledge into the verbalizer, forming a knowledgeable prompttuning (KPT), to improve and stabilize prompttuning. Specifically, we expand the label word space of the verbalizer using external knowledge bases (KBs) and refine the expanded label word space with the PLM itself before predicting with the expanded label word space. Extensive experiments on zero and few-shot text classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of knowledgeable prompt-tuning.

label: acl
text: The use of prompt-tuning for text classification has been shown to be a promising approach, particularly in low-data scenarios, where it outperforms generic fine-tuning methods with extra classifiers. The core concept of prompt-tuning involves transforming a classification problem into a masked language modeling problem by inserting text pieces (templates) into the input. A crucial step in this process is to construct a projection, known as a verbalizer, between the label space and the label word space. However, the verbalizer is often handcrafted or found through gradient descent, which can result in bias, high variance, and a lack of coverage. In this work, we aim to improve and stabilize prompt-tuning by incorporating external knowledge into the verbalizer, forming a knowledgeable prompt-tuning (KPT) approach. We expand the label word space of the verbalizer using external knowledge bases and refine the expanded label word space with the pre-trained language model before making predictions. Our experiments on zero and few-shot text classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of knowledgeable prompt-tuning.

label: acl
text: Despite the prominence of neural abstractive summarization models, we know little about how they actually form summaries and how to understand where their decisions come from. We propose a two-step method to interpret summarization model decisions. We first analyze the model's behavior by ablating the full model to categorize each decoder decision into one of several generation modes: roughly, is the model behaving like a language model, is it relying heavily on the input, or is it somewhere in between? After isolating decisions that do depend on the input, we explore interpreting these decisions using several different attribution methods. We compare these techniques based on their ability to select content and reconstruct the model's predicted token from perturbations of the input, thus revealing whether highlighted attributions are truly important for the generation of the next token. While this machinery can be broadly useful even beyond summarization, we specifically demonstrate its capability to identify phrases the summarization model has memorized and determine where in the training pipeline this memorization happened, as well as study complex generation phenomena like sentence fusion on a per-instance basis.

label: acl
text: Despite the popularity of neural abstractive summarization models, little is known about how they form summaries and the reasoning behind their decisions. To address this issue, we propose a two-step approach to interpret the decisions made by these models. Firstly, we analyze the model's behavior by breaking it down into several generation modes, such as language model-like behavior, heavy reliance on the input, or a combination of both. Secondly, we use different attribution methods to interpret the decisions that depend on the input. We evaluate these techniques based on their ability to reconstruct the model's predicted tokens from perturbations of the input, and to determine the content that is truly important for the next token generation. This methodology can be applied to a wide range of applications, including summarization. We demonstrate its effectiveness by identifying memorized phrases, determining where they were memorized, and studying sentence fusion on a per-instance basis.

label: acl
text: With the recent success of pre-trained models in NLP, a significant focus was put on interpreting their representations. One of the most prominent approaches is structural probing (Hewitt and Manning, 2019), where a linear projection of word embeddings is performed in order to approximate the topology of dependency structures. In this work, we introduce a new type of structural probing, where the linear projection is decomposed into 1. iso-morphic space rotation; 2. linear scaling that identifies and scales the most relevant dimensions. In addition to syntactic dependency, we evaluate our method on two novel tasks (lexical hypernymy and position in a sentence). We jointly train the probes for multiple tasks and experimentally show that lexical and syntactic information is separated in the representations. Moreover, the orthogonal constraint makes the Structural Probes less vulnerable to memorization.

label: acl
text: Recently, with the success of pre-trained models in NLP, much focus has been placed on interpreting their representations. One of the most widely used methods is structural probing (Hewitt and Manning, 2019), where word embeddings are linearly projected to approximate the topology of dependency structures. In this study, we present a new type of structural probing, where the linear projection is decomposed into 1) an iso-morphic space rotation and 2) a linear scaling that identifies and scales the most relevant dimensions. We evaluate our method on two novel tasks (lexical hypernymy and sentence position) in addition to syntactic dependency. Our results show that by jointly training the probes for multiple tasks, lexical and syntactic information is separated in the representations. Furthermore, the orthogonal constraint makes the structural probes less susceptible to memorization.

label: coling
text: Recently, neural machine translation (NMT) has been extended to multilinguality, that is to handle more than one translation direction with a single system. Multilingual NMT showed competitive performance against pure bilingual systems. Notably, in low-resource settings, it proved to work effectively and efficiently, thanks to shared representation space that is forced across languages and induces a sort of transfer-learning. Furthermore, multilingual NMT enables so-called zero-shot inference across language pairs never seen at training time. Despite the increasing interest in this framework, an in-depth analysis of what a multilingual NMT model is capable of and what it is not is still missing. Motivated by this, our work (i) provides a quantitative and comparative analysis of the translations produced by bilingual, multilingual and zero-shot systems; (ii) investigates the translation quality of two of the currently dominant neural architectures in MT, which are the Recurrent and the Transformer ones; and (iii) quantitatively explores how the closeness between languages influences the zero-shot translation. Our analysis leverages multiple professional post-edits of automatic translations by several different systems and focuses both on automatic standard metrics (BLEU and TER) and on widely used error categories, which are lexical, morphology, and word order errors.

label: coling
text: Recently, neural machine translation (NMT) has been expanded to include multilinguality, allowing for the handling of multiple translation directions with a single system. Multilingual NMT has demonstrated competitive performance compared to pure bilingual systems, particularly in low-resource settings, due to the shared representation space that enables transfer-learning across languages. Additionally, multilingual NMT enables zero-shot inference across language pairs never seen during training. Despite the growing interest in this framework, a comprehensive analysis of its capabilities and limitations is still lacking. To address this, our work provides a quantitative and comparative analysis of translations produced by bilingual, multilingual, and zero-shot systems. We investigate the translation quality of two dominant neural architectures in MT - Recurrent and Transformer - and quantitatively explore the impact of language closeness on zero-shot translation. Our analysis is based on multiple professional post-edits of automatic translations and focuses on both automatic standard metrics (BLEU and TER) and widely used error categories, including lexical, morphological, and word order errors.

label: acl
text: Decipherment of historical ciphers is a challenging problem. The language of the target plaintext might be unknown, and ciphertext can have a lot of noise. State-of-the-art decipherment methods use beam search and a neural language model to score candidate plaintext hypotheses for a given cipher, assuming the plaintext language is known. We propose an end-to-end multilingual model for solving simple substitution ciphers. We test our model on synthetic and real historical ciphers and show that our proposed method can decipher text without explicit language identification while still being robust to noise.

label: acl
text: The decipherment of historical ciphers poses a significant challenge, as the target plaintext language may be unknown and the ciphertext can contain a significant amount of noise. To address this challenge, current state-of-the-art decipherment methods utilize beam search and a neural language model to score potential plaintext hypotheses based on the given cipher, assuming the language of the plaintext is known. Our proposed solution is an end-to-end multilingual model specifically designed to solve simple substitution ciphers. Our results demonstrate that our method can successfully decipher text without the need for explicit language identification, while still maintaining robustness in the presence of noise.

label: acl
text: NER model has achieved promising performance on standard NER benchmarks. However, recent studies show that previous approaches may over-rely on entity mention information, resulting in poor performance on out-of-vocabulary(OOV) entity recognition. In this work, we propose MINER, a novel NER learning framework, to remedy this issue from an information-theoretic perspective. The proposed approach contains two mutual information based training objectives: i) generalizing information maximization, which enhances representation via deep understanding of context and entity surface forms; ii) superfluous information minimization, which discourages representation from rotate memorizing entity names or exploiting biased cues in data. Experiments on various settings and datasets demonstrate that it achieves better performance in predicting OOV entities.

label: acl
text: The NER model has shown promising results on standard NER benchmarks, but recent studies indicate that previous approaches may have over-relied on entity mention information, leading to poor performance in recognizing out-of-vocabulary (OOV) entities. To address this issue, we present MINER, a new NER learning framework that takes an information-theoretic approach. MINER consists of two mutual information-based training objectives: (i) maximizing generalizing information, which improves representation by providing a deeper understanding of context and entity surface forms; and (ii) minimizing superfluous information, which discourages representation from simply memorizing entity names or exploiting biased cues in the data. Our experiments on various settings and datasets show that MINER outperforms existing methods in predicting OOV entities.

label: emnlp
text: Capturing the semantic relations of words in a vector space contributes to many natural language processing tasks. One promising approach exploits lexico-syntactic patterns as features of word pairs. In this paper, we propose a novel model of this pattern-based approach, neural latent relational analysis (NLRA). NLRA can generalize co-occurrences of word pairs and lexico-syntactic patterns, and obtain embeddings of the word pairs that do not co-occur. This overcomes the critical data sparseness problem encountered in previous pattern-based models. Our experimental results on measuring relational similarity demonstrate that NLRA outperforms the previous pattern-based models. In addition, when combined with a vector offset model, NLRA achieves a performance comparable to that of the state-of-the-art model that exploits additional semantic relational data.

label: emnlp
text: Capturing the semantic relationships between words in a vector space is beneficial for various natural language processing tasks. One promising approach involves using lexico-syntactic patterns as features for word pairs. In this paper, we introduce a new model for this pattern-based approach, called Neural Latent Relational Analysis (NLRA). NLRA generalizes co-occurrences of word pairs and lexico-syntactic patterns, and produces embeddings for word pairs that don't co-occur, thereby overcoming the data sparsity problem encountered in previous pattern-based models. The results of our experiments measuring relational similarity show that NLRA outperforms previous pattern-based models, and when combined with a vector offset model, it achieves performance comparable to that of the state-of-the-art models that use additional semantic relational data.

label: acl
text: Vision-language pre-training (VLP) on large-scale image-text pairs has achieved huge success for the cross-modal downstream tasks. The most existing pre-training methods mainly adopt a two-step training procedure, which firstly employs a pre-trained object detector to extract region-based visual features, then concatenates the image representation and text embedding as the input of Transformer to train. However, these methods face problems of using task-specific visual representation of the specific object detector for generic cross-modal understanding, and the computation inefficiency of two-stage pipeline. In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end vision-language pre-trained model for both V+L understanding and generation, namely E2E-VLP, where we build a unified Transformer framework to jointly learn visual representation, and semantic alignments between image and text. We incorporate the tasks of object detection and image captioning into pre-training with a unified Transformer encoder-decoder architecture for enhancing visual learning. An extensive set of experiments have been conducted on well-established vision-language downstream tasks to demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel VLP paradigm.

label: acl
text: The proposed E2E-VLP is the first end-to-end vision-language pre-training model for both visual and language understanding and generation. It addresses the limitations of existing methods by incorporating object detection and image captioning into the pre-training process with a unified Transformer encoder-decoder architecture. This enhances visual learning and eliminates the need for a two-step training procedure. The effectiveness of this novel approach has been demonstrated through a comprehensive set of experiments on well-established vision-language downstream tasks.

label: coling
text: OntoLex-Lemon has become a de facto standard for lexical resources in the web of data. This paper provides the first overall description of the emerging OntoLex module for Frequency, Attestations, and Corpus-Based Information (OntoLex-FrAC) that is intended to complement OntoLex-Lemon with the necessary vocabulary to represent major types of information found in or automatically derived from corpora, for applications in both language technology and the language sciences.

label: coling
text: OntoLex-Lemon has established itself as the standard for lexical resources in the web of data. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive overview of the developing OntoLex-FrAC module, which aims to complement OntoLex-Lemon by providing the necessary vocabulary to represent the main types of information found in or generated from corpora. This module is intended for use in both language technology and language sciences applications.

label: acl
text: QA models based on pretrained language models have achieved remarkable performance on various benchmark datasets. However, QA models do not generalize well to unseen data that falls outside the training distribution, due to distributional shifts. Data augmentation (DA) techniques which drop/replace words have shown to be effective in regularizing the model from overfitting to the training data. Yet, they may adversely affect the QA tasks since they incur semantic changes that may lead to wrong answers for the QA task. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple yet effective DA method based on a stochastic noise generator, which learns to perturb the word embedding of the input questions and context without changing their semantics. We validate the performance of the QA models trained with our word embedding perturbation on a single source dataset, on five different target domains. The results show that our method significantly outperforms the baseline DA methods. Notably, the model trained with ours outperforms the model trained with more than 240K artificially generated QA pairs.

label: acl
text: Remarkable results have been achieved by QA models that are based on pretrained language models on various benchmark datasets. However, these models struggle to generalize to new data that falls outside the training distribution due to distributional shifts. To tackle this problem, data augmentation (DA) techniques have been used, such as dropping or replacing words, which have been shown to be effective in preventing overfitting to the training data. However, these techniques may negatively impact the QA task by causing semantic changes that lead to incorrect answers. To address this issue, we propose a simple and effective DA method that uses a stochastic noise generator to perturb the word embeddings of the input questions and context without altering their semantics. Our method was validated on a single source dataset and five different target domains, and the results show that it significantly outperforms the baseline DA methods. Notably, the model trained with our method outperforms the model trained with over 240,000 artificially generated QA pairs.

label: acl
text: A growing body of literature has focused on detailing the linguistic knowledge embedded in large, pretrained language models. Existing work has shown that non-linguistic biases in models can drive model behavior away from linguistic generalizations. We hypothesized that competing linguistic processes within a language, rather than just non-linguistic model biases, could obscure underlying linguistic knowledge. We tested this claim by exploring a single phenomenon in four languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, and Italian. While human behavior has been found to be similar across languages, we find cross-linguistic variation in model behavior. We show that competing processes in a language act as constraints on model behavior and demonstrate that targeted fine-tuning can re-weight the learned constraints, uncovering otherwise dormant linguistic knowledge in models. Our results suggest that models need to learn both the linguistic constraints in a language and their relative ranking, with mismatches in either producing non-human-like behavior.

label: acl
text: A growing body of literature has been dedicated to exploring the linguistic knowledge embedded in large, pretrained language models. Previous research has demonstrated that non-linguistic biases in models can steer model behavior away from linguistic generalizations. However, we hypothesized that the competition between different linguistic processes within a language, rather than just non-linguistic biases, could hinder the underlying linguistic knowledge. To test this claim, we conducted an investigation into a single phenomenon in four languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, and Italian. Although human behavior has been found to be similar across languages, our study reveals cross-linguistic variations in model behavior. Our findings indicate that the competition between linguistic processes within a language acts as a constraint on model behavior and that targeted fine-tuning can adjust the learned constraints, thus uncovering previously hidden linguistic knowledge in models. Our results suggest that models need to learn both the linguistic constraints in a language and their relative importance, as mismatches in either can result in non-human-like behavior.

label: acl
text: Research on distributed word representations is focused on widely-used languages such as English. Although the same methods can be used for other languages, language-specific knowledge can enhance the accuracy and richness of word vector representations. In this paper, we look at improving distributed word representations for Korean using knowledge about the unique linguistic structure of Korean. Specifically, we decompose Korean words into the jamo-level, beyond the character-level, allowing a systematic use of subword information. To evaluate the vectors, we develop Korean test sets for word similarity and analogy and make them publicly available. The results show that our simple method outperforms word2vec and character-level Skip-Grams on semantic and syntactic similarity and analogy tasks and contributes positively toward downstream NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis.

label: acl
text: The research on distributed word representations focuses on popular languages such as English. Despite the fact that the same methods can be applied to other languages, incorporating language-specific knowledge can improve the accuracy and richness of word vector representations. In this paper, we aim to enhance the distributed word representations for Korean by utilizing the unique linguistic structure of the language. We decompose Korean words into jamo-level units, beyond the character-level, to systematically incorporate subword information. To evaluate the effectiveness of our vectors, we created Korean test sets for word similarity and analogy and made them publicly available. Our results indicate that our simple method outperforms word2vec and character-level Skip-Grams on semantic and syntactic similarity and analogy tasks, and has a positive impact on downstream NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis.

label: coling
text: Back-translation has been proven to be effective in unsupervised domain adaptation of neural machine translation (NMT). However, the existing back-translation methods mainly improve domain adaptability by generating in-domain pseudo-parallel data that contains sentence-structural knowledge, paying less attention to the in-domain lexical knowledge, which may lead to poor translation of unseen in-domain words. In this paper, we propose an Iterative Constrained Back-Translation (ICBT) method to incorporate in-domain lexical knowledge on the basis of BT for unsupervised domain adaptation of NMT. Specifically, we apply lexical constraints into back-translation to generate pseudo-parallel data with in-domain lexical knowledge, and then perform round-trip iterations to incorporate more lexical knowledge. Based on this, we further explore sampling strategies of constrained words in ICBT to introduce more targeted lexical knowledge, via domain specificity and confidence estimation. Experimental results on four domains show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results, improving the BLEU score by up to 3.08 compared to the strongest baseline, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

label: coling
text: Back-translation has been shown to be effective in improving the unsupervised domain adaptation of neural machine translation (NMT). However, existing back-translation methods primarily focus on generating in-domain pseudo-parallel data that contains sentence-structural knowledge, neglecting the importance of in-domain lexical knowledge. This can result in poor translation of unseen in-domain words. To address this issue, we propose an Iterative Constrained Back-Translation (ICBT) method that incorporates in-domain lexical knowledge into the back-translation process. Our approach applies lexical constraints to generate pseudo-parallel data that includes in-domain lexical knowledge, and then performs round-trip iterations to further refine this knowledge. Additionally, we explore different sampling strategies for constrained words in ICBT, allowing us to introduce targeted lexical knowledge based on domain specificity and confidence estimation. Our experiments on four domains show that our approach outperforms the strongest baseline, improving the BLEU score by up to 3.08. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

label: coling
text: Predicting difficulty of questions is crucial for technical interviews. However, such questions are long-form and more open-ended than factoid and multiple choice questions explored so far for question difficulty prediction. Existing models also require large volumes of candidate response data for training. We study weak-supervision and use unsupervised algorithms for both question generation and difficulty prediction. We create a dataset of interview questions with difficulty scores for deep learning and use it to evaluate SOTA models for question difficulty prediction trained using weak supervision. Our analysis brings out the task's difficulty as well as the promise of weak supervision for it.

label: coling
text: Predicting the difficulty of technical interview questions is critical, but these questions are more open-ended and longer than the factoid and multiple choice questions that have been explored previously for difficulty prediction. Existing models also require a significant amount of candidate response data for training. To address these challenges, we employ weak supervision and unsupervised algorithms for both question generation and difficulty prediction. We have created a dataset of interview questions with difficulty scores for deep learning and used it to evaluate state-of-the-art models for question difficulty prediction trained using weak supervision. Our analysis highlights the difficulty of the task, as well as the potential of weak supervision for improving it.

label: acl
text: As more and more product reviews are posted in both text and images, Multimodal Review Analysis (MRA) becomes an attractive research topic. Among the existing review analysis tasks, helpfulness prediction on review text has become predominant due to its importance for e-commerce platforms and online shops, i.e. helping customers quickly acquire useful product information. This paper proposes a new task Multimodal Review Helpfulness Prediction (MRHP) aiming to analyze the review helpfulness from text and visual modalities. Meanwhile, a novel Multi-perspective Coherent Reasoning method (MCR) is proposed to solve the MRHP task, which conducts joint reasoning over texts and images from both the product and the review, and aggregates the signals to predict the review helpfulness. Concretely, we first propose a product-review coherent reasoning module to measure the intra- and inter-modal coherence between the target product and the review. In addition, we also devise an intra-review coherent reasoning module to identify the coherence between the text content and images of the review, which is a piece of strong evidence for review helpfulness prediction. To evaluate the effectiveness of MCR, we present two newly collected multimodal review datasets as benchmark evaluation resources for the MRHP task. Experimental results show that our MCR method can lead to a performance increase of up to 8.5% as compared to the best performing text-only model. The source code and datasets can be obtained from https://github.com/jhliu17/MCR.

label: acl
text: As the number of product reviews posted with both text and images increases, the field of Multimodal Review Analysis (MRA) becomes increasingly relevant. Of the various review analysis tasks, the prediction of review helpfulness, based solely on text, has become the most prominent due to its significance for e-commerce platforms and online shops. This paper introduces a new task, Multimodal Review Helpfulness Prediction (MRHP), which aims to analyze the helpfulness of reviews using both text and visual modalities. To address this task, we propose a novel Multi-perspective Coherent Reasoning method (MCR) that integrates reasoning over product and review text and images. The MCR method includes two modules: the product-review coherent reasoning module, which measures the coherence between the product and review, and the intra-review coherent reasoning module, which evaluates the coherence between the review's text and images. We also present two newly collected multimodal review datasets as benchmark resources for MRHP. Our experiments show that the MCR method outperforms the best text-only model by up to 8.5%. The source code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/jhliu17/MCR.

label: emnlp
text: Gang-involved youth in cities such as Chicago have increasingly turned to social media to post about their experiences and intents online. In some situations, when they experience the loss of a loved one, their online expression of emotion may evolve into aggression towards rival gangs and ultimately into real-world violence. In this paper, we present a novel system for detecting Aggression and Loss in social media. Our system features the use of domain-specific resources automatically derived from a large unlabeled corpus, and contextual representations of the emotional and semantic content of the user's recent tweets as well as their interactions with other users. Incorporating context in our Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) leads to a significant improvement.

label: emnlp
text: Gang-affiliated youth in cities like Chicago are increasingly using social media to express their experiences and intentions. In some cases, the loss of a loved one can escalate their online emotional expression into aggression towards rival gangs, leading to real-world violence. This paper introduces a new system for identifying Aggression and Loss in social media. The system utilizes domain-specific resources derived from a large corpus and contextual representations of the emotional and semantic content of the user's recent tweets, as well as their interactions with other users. Our Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model, incorporating context, demonstrates a significant improvement.

label: emnlp
text: We propose Odd-Man-Out, a novel task which aims to test different properties of word representations. An Odd-Man-Out puzzle is composed of 5 (or more) words, and requires the system to choose the one which does not belong with the others. We show that this simple setup is capable of teasing out various properties of different popular lexical resources (like WordNet and pre-trained word embeddings), while being intuitive enough to annotate on a large scale. In addition, we propose a novel technique for training multi-prototype word representations, based on unsupervised clustering of ELMo embeddings, and show that it surpasses all other representations on all Odd-Man-Out collections.

label: emnlp
text: We propose Odd-Man-Out, a novel task that tests various properties of word representations. This task consists of 5 (or more) words, with the goal of identifying the word that does not belong with the others. Our findings demonstrate that this straightforward setup can effectively reveal the strengths and weaknesses of popular lexical resources, such as WordNet and pre-trained word embeddings, while also being feasible for large-scale annotation. Furthermore, we introduce a new method for training multi-prototype word representations using unsupervised clustering of ELMo embeddings. Our results indicate that this technique outperforms all other representations on all Odd-Man-Out collections.

label: coling
text: Although the Conditional Variational Auto-Encoder (CVAE) model can generate more diversified responses than the traditional Seq2Seq model, the responses often have low relevance with the input words or are illogical with the question. A causal analysis is carried out to study the reasons behind, and a methodology of searching for the mediators and mitigating the confounding bias in dialogues is provided. Specifically, we propose to predict the mediators to preserve relevant information and auto-regressively incorporate the mediators into generating process. Besides, a dynamic topic graph guided conditional variational auto-encoder (TGG-CVAE) model is utilized to complement the semantic space and reduce the confounding bias in responses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed model is able to generate both relevant and informative responses, and outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of automatic metrics and human evaluations.

label: coling
text: The Conditional Variational Auto-Encoder (CVAE) model generates more diverse responses compared to the traditional Seq2Seq model, but these responses often lack relevance to the input words or are illogical in relation to the question. To understand the reasons behind this, we conducted a causal analysis and developed a methodology for identifying mediators and reducing confounding biases in dialogues. Our approach involves predicting mediators to maintain relevant information and incorporating them auto-regressively into the response generation process. Additionally, we employ a dynamic topic graph-guided conditional variational auto-encoder (TGG-CVAE) model to enhance the semantic space and minimize confounding biases in the generated responses. Our experiments show that our proposed model generates both relevant and informative responses, outperforming the state-of-the-art in terms of both automatic metrics and human evaluations.

label: emnlp
text: The task of sentiment modification requires reversing the sentiment of the input and preserving the sentiment-independent content. However, aligned sentences with the same content but different sentiments are usually unavailable. Due to the lack of such parallel data, it is hard to extract sentiment independent content and reverse the sentiment in an unsupervised way. Previous work usually can not reconcile sentiment transformation and content preservation. In this paper, motivated by the fact the non-emotional context (e.g., “staff”) provides strong cues for the occurrence of emotional words (e.g., “friendly”), we propose a novel method that automatically extracts appropriate sentiment information from learned sentiment memories according to the specific context. Experiments show that our method substantially improves the content preservation degree and achieves the state-of-the-art performance.

label: emnlp
text: The challenge of sentiment modification involves flipping the sentiment of the input while maintaining the sentiment-free content. However, obtaining parallel sentences with the same content but differing sentiments is often not possible. The lack of such data makes it difficult to extract sentiment-free content and reverse the sentiment in an unsupervised manner. Previous approaches have struggled to balance sentiment transformation and content preservation. This paper presents a novel method that leverages learned sentiment memories to automatically extract relevant sentiment information based on the specific context. Our experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves content preservation and achieves the highest performance compared to existing methods.

label: acl
text: We present ProtoTEx, a novel white-box NLP classification architecture based on prototype networks (Li et al., 2018). ProtoTEx faithfully explains model decisions based on prototype tensors that encode latent clusters of training examples. At inference time, classification decisions are based on the distances between the input text and the prototype tensors, explained via the training examples most similar to the most influential prototypes. We also describe a novel interleaved training algorithm that effectively handles classes characterized by ProtoTEx indicative features. On a propaganda detection task, ProtoTEx accuracy matches BART-large and exceeds BERTlarge with the added benefit of providing faithful explanations. A user study also shows that prototype-based explanations help non-experts to better recognize propaganda in online news.

label: acl
text: We introduce ProtoTEx, a new NLP classification architecture based on prototype networks that provides a transparent explanation of its decisions. The model uses prototype tensors to encode latent clusters of training examples, and at inference time, it classifies text based on the distances between the input and the prototype tensors. The closest training examples to the most influential prototypes provide the explanation. Additionally, we propose a novel interleaved training algorithm that effectively handles classes with ProtoTEx indicative features. In a propaganda detection task, ProtoTEx achieved comparable accuracy to BART-large and outperformed BERT-large, while also providing clear explanations. A user study confirmed that prototype-based explanations help non-experts better understand propaganda in online news.

label: acl
text: Charts are commonly used for exploring data and communicating insights. Generating natural language summaries from charts can be very helpful for people in inferring key insights that would otherwise require a lot of cognitive and perceptual efforts. We present Chart-to-text, a large-scale benchmark with two datasets and a total of 44,096 charts covering a wide range of topics and chart types. We explain the dataset construction process and analyze the datasets.
