We also introduce a number of state-of-the-art neural models as baselines that utilize image captioning and data-to-text generation techniques to tackle two problem variations: one assumes the underlying data table of the chart is available while the other needs to extract data from chart images. Our analysis with automatic and human evaluation shows that while our best models usually generate fluent summaries and yield reasonable BLEU scores, they also suffer from hallucinations and factual errors as well as difficulties in correctly explaining complex patterns and trends in charts.

label: acl
text: Charts are a popular tool for analyzing data and communicating insights. To make it easier to understand the information they contain, natural language summaries can be generated. We introduce Chart-to-text, a benchmark that includes two datasets with a total of 44,096 charts covering a wide range of topics and chart types. The dataset construction process is explained, and the datasets are analyzed. We also present several state-of-the-art neural models as baselines that use image captioning and data-to-text generation techniques to address two different variations of the problem: one that assumes the data table is available, and one that requires data to be extracted from the chart images. Our analysis, which includes both automatic and human evaluations, shows that while the best models often produce fluent summaries and have reasonable BLEU scores, they also have limitations, such as hallucinations, factual errors, and difficulties in explaining complex patterns and trends in charts.

label: acl
text: Event language models represent plausible sequences of events. Most existing approaches train autoregressive models on text, which successfully capture event co-occurrence but unfortunately constrain the model to follow the discourse order in which events are presented. Other domains may employ different discourse orders, and for many applications, we may care about different notions of ordering (e.g., temporal) or not care about ordering at all (e.g., when predicting related events in a schema). We propose a simple yet surprisingly effective strategy for improving event language models by perturbing event sequences so we can relax model dependence on text order. Despite generating completely synthetic event orderings, we show that this technique improves the performance of the event language models on both applications and out-of-domain events data.

label: acl
text: Event models that represent sequences of events are called event language models. Most existing methods train autoregressive models on text, capturing the co-occurrence of events, but are limited by their dependence on the discourse order presented in the text. This constraint is problematic in other domains where different discourse orders may be used, and for applications where different notions of ordering (e.g. temporal) or no ordering at all (e.g. predicting related events in a schema) are desired. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective strategy to improve event language models by perturbing event sequences and relaxing the model's dependence on text order. Our technique generates completely synthetic event orderings, and we show that it leads to improved performance on both applications and out-of-domain event data.

label: acl
text: Recently, there has been significant progress in studying neural networks to translate text descriptions into SQL queries. Despite achieving good performance on some public benchmarks, existing text-to-SQL models typically rely on the lexical matching between words in natural language (NL) questions and tokens in table schemas, which may render the models vulnerable to attacks that break the schema linking mechanism. In this work, we investigate the robustness of text-to-SQL models to synonym substitution. In particular, we introduce Spider-Syn, a human-curated dataset based on the Spider benchmark for text-to-SQL translation. NL questions in Spider-Syn are modified from Spider, by replacing their schema-related words with manually selected synonyms that reflect real-world question paraphrases. We observe that the accuracy dramatically drops by eliminating such explicit correspondence between NL questions and table schemas, even if the synonyms are not adversarially selected to conduct worst-case attacks. Finally, we present two categories of approaches to improve the model robustness. The first category of approaches utilizes additional synonym annotations for table schemas by modifying the model input, while the second category is based on adversarial training. We demonstrate that both categories of approaches significantly outperform their counterparts without the defense, and the first category of approaches are more effective.

label: acl
text: Recently, there has been significant progress in the study of neural networks for translating text descriptions into SQL queries. Despite good performance on some public benchmarks, existing text-to-SQL models rely heavily on lexical matching between words in natural language (NL) questions and tokens in table schemas, which can make the models vulnerable to attacks that break the schema linking mechanism. In this study, we examine the robustness of these models to synonym substitution. We introduce Spider-Syn, a human-curated dataset based on the Spider benchmark for text-to-SQL translation. The NL questions in Spider-Syn are modified from the original Spider dataset by replacing schema-related words with manually selected synonyms that reflect common real-world question paraphrases. Our results show that accuracy dramatically decreases when explicit correspondence between NL questions and table schemas is eliminated, even if synonyms are not selected to conduct worst-case attacks. Finally, we present two categories of approaches to improve model robustness: those that utilize additional synonym annotations for the table schemas by modifying the model input, and those that are based on adversarial training. We demonstrate that both categories of approaches significantly outperform their counterparts without defense, with the first category being more effective.

label: acl
text: Feed-forward networks are widely used in cross-modal applications to bridge modalities by mapping distributed vectors of one modality to the other, or to a shared space. The predicted vectors are then used to perform e.g., retrieval or labeling. Thus, the success of the whole system relies on the ability of the mapping to make the neighborhood structure (i.e., the pairwise similarities) of the predicted vectors akin to that of the target vectors. However, whether this is achieved has not been investigated yet. Here, we propose a new similarity measure and two ad hoc experiments to shed light on this issue. In three cross-modal benchmarks we learn a large number of language-to-vision and vision-to-language neural network mappings (up to five layers) using a rich diversity of image and text features and loss functions. Our results reveal that, surprisingly, the neighborhood structure of the predicted vectors consistently resembles more that of the input vectors than that of the target vectors. In a second experiment, we further show that untrained nets do not significantly disrupt the neighborhood (i.e., semantic) structure of the input vectors.

label: acl
text: Feed-forward networks are commonly used in cross-modal applications to map distributed vectors from one modality to another or to a shared space. The predicted vectors are then utilized for tasks such as retrieval or labeling. The success of the system depends on the mapping's ability to preserve the neighborhood structure (pairwise similarities) of the target vectors in the predicted vectors. However, this has not yet been investigated. In this paper, we propose a new similarity measure and conduct two experiments to shed light on this issue. We learn a large number of language-to-vision and vision-to-language neural network mappings using diverse image and text features and loss functions in three cross-modal benchmarks. Our results show that the neighborhood structure of the predicted vectors more closely resembles that of the input vectors rather than that of the target vectors. In a second experiment, we demonstrate that untrained nets do not significantly alter the neighborhood structure of the input vectors.

label: coling
text: Given a set of instances of some relation, the relation induction task is to predict which other word pairs are likely to be related in the same way. While it is natural to use word embeddings for this task, standard approaches based on vector translations turn out to perform poorly. To address this issue, we propose two probabilistic relation induction models. The first model is based on translations, but uses Gaussians to explicitly model the variability of these translations and to encode soft constraints on the source and target words that may be chosen. In the second model, we use Bayesian linear regression to encode the assumption that there is a linear relationship between the vector representations of related words, which is considerably weaker than the assumption underlying translation based models.

label: coling
text: The task of relation induction involves predicting which word pairs are likely to have the same relationship as the instances in a given set. Utilizing word embeddings is a natural approach, however, standard vector translation methods have proven to be insufficient. To overcome this, we present two probabilistic models for relation induction. The first model is based on translations, but incorporates Gaussians to model the variability of translations and to encode flexible constraints on the source and target words. The second model uses Bayesian linear regression to represent the assumption that there is a linear relationship between the vector representations of related words, which is weaker than the assumption made by translation-based models.

label: coling
text: Semantic parsing converts natural language utterances into structured logical expressions. We consider two such formal representations: Propositional Logic (PL) and First-order Logic (FOL). The paucity of labeled data is a major challenge in this field. In previous works, dual reinforcement learning has been proposed as an approach to reduce dependence on labeled data. However, this method has the following limitations: 1) The reward needs to be set manually and is not applicable to all kinds of logical expressions. 2) The training process easily collapses when models are trained with only the reward from dual reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose a scoring model to automatically learn a model-based reward, and an effective training strategy based on curriculum learning is further proposed to stabilize the training process. In addition to the technical contribution, a Chinese-PL/FOL dataset is constructed to compensate for the paucity of labeled data in this field. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms competitors on several datasets. Furthermore, by introducing PL/FOL generated by our model, the performance of existing Natural Language Inference (NLI) models is further enhanced.

label: coling
text: Semantic parsing transforms natural language expressions into structured logical forms, such as Propositional Logic (PL) and First-order Logic (FOL). Despite its importance, the field faces a significant challenge: a lack of labeled data. Previous studies have attempted to address this issue by using dual reinforcement learning, but this method has several limitations, including the need for manual reward setting and a tendency to collapse during training. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a scoring model to learn a model-based reward and a curriculum learning-based training strategy to stabilize the process. Additionally, a Chinese-PL/FOL dataset is created to alleviate the shortage of labeled data. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms other methods on several datasets and improves the performance of existing Natural Language Inference (NLI) models when using PL/FOL generated by our model.

label: coling
text: Can we build multi-view decoders that can decode concepts from brain recordings corresponding to any view (picture, sentence, word cloud) of stimuli? Can we build a system that can use brain recordings to automatically describe what a subject is watching using keywords or sentences? How about a system that can automatically extract important keywords from sentences that a subject is reading? Previous brain decoding efforts have focused only on single view analysis and hence cannot help us build such systems. As a first step toward building such systems, inspired by Natural Language Processing literature on multi-lingual and cross-lingual modeling, we propose two novel brain decoding setups: (1) multi-view decoding (MVD) and (2) cross-view decoding (CVD). In MVD, the goal is to build an MV decoder that can take brain recordings for any view as input and predict the concept. In CVD, the goal is to train a model which takes brain recordings for one view as input and decodes a semantic vector representation of another view. Specifically, we study practically useful CVD tasks like image captioning, image tagging, keyword extraction, and sentence formation. Our extensive experiments lead to MVD models with ~0.68 average pairwise accuracy across view pairs, and also CVD models with ~0.8 average pairwise accuracy across tasks. Analysis of the contribution of different brain networks reveals exciting cognitive insights: (1) Models trained on picture or sentence view of stimuli are better MV decoders than a model trained on word cloud view. (2) Our extensive analysis across 9 broad regions, 11 language sub-regions and 16 visual sub-regions of the brain help us localize, for the first time, the parts of the brain involved in cross-view tasks like image captioning, image tagging, sentence formation and keyword extraction. We make the code publicly available.

label: coling
text: Can we design multi-view decoders that can decode concepts from brain recordings, regardless of the view of the stimuli (such as a picture, sentence, or word cloud)? Can we create a system that can automatically describe what a subject is viewing based on their brain recordings, using keywords or sentences? And what about a system that can extract important keywords from sentences that a subject is reading? Previous brain decoding efforts have only focused on single-view analysis, which limits our ability to build these systems. As a first step in this direction, we propose two novel brain decoding approaches, inspired by Natural Language Processing research on multi-lingual and cross-lingual modeling: (1) Multi-View Decoding (MVD) and (2) Cross-View Decoding (CVD). In MVD, the goal is to develop an MV decoder that can take brain recordings from any view as input and predict the concept. In CVD, the goal is to train a model that takes brain recordings from one view and decodes a semantic vector representation of another view. We study practical CVD tasks, such as image captioning, image tagging, keyword extraction, and sentence formation. Our experiments result in MVD models with an average pairwise accuracy of ~0.68 across all view pairs, and CVD models with an average pairwise accuracy of ~0.8 across all tasks. Our analysis of the contribution of different brain networks provides exciting cognitive insights: (1) Models trained on picture or sentence views of stimuli are better MV decoders than a model trained on the word cloud view. (2) Our extensive analysis of 9 broad regions, 11 language sub-regions, and 16 visual sub-regions of the brain helps us pinpoint, for the first time, the parts of the brain involved in cross-view tasks such as image captioning, image tagging, sentence formation, and keyword extraction. The code is publicly available.

label: naacl
text: The rapid spread of information over social media influences quantitative trading and investments. The growing popularity of speculative trading of highly volatile assets such as cryptocurrencies and meme stocks presents a fresh challenge in the financial realm. Investigating such “bubbles” - periods of sudden anomalous behavior of markets are critical in better understanding investor behavior and market dynamics. However, high volatility coupled with massive volumes of chaotic social media texts, especially for underexplored assets like cryptocoins pose a challenge to existing methods. Taking the first step towards NLP for cryptocoins, we present and publicly release CryptoBubbles, a novel multi- span identification task for bubble detection, and a dataset of more than 400 cryptocoins from 9 exchanges over five years spanning over two million tweets. Further, we develop a set of sequence-to-sequence hyperbolic models suited to this multi-span identification task based on the power-law dynamics of cryptocurrencies and user behavior on social media. We further test the effectiveness of our models under zero-shot settings on a test set of Reddit posts pertaining to 29 “meme stocks”, which see an increase in trade volume due to social media hype. Through quantitative, qualitative, and zero-shot analyses on Reddit and Twitter spanning cryptocoins and meme-stocks, we show the practical applicability of CryptoBubbles and hyperbolic models.

label: naacl
text: The rapid dissemination of information on social media has a significant impact on quantitative trading and investment. The increasing popularity of speculative trading in highly volatile assets, such as cryptocurrencies and meme stocks, presents a new challenge in the financial world. Investigating these "bubbles" - periods of sudden and abnormal market behavior - is crucial in improving our understanding of investor behavior and market dynamics. However, the high volatility and massive amounts of chaotic social media text, particularly for under-explored assets like cryptocurrencies, pose a challenge to traditional methods. To address this, we introduce CryptoBubbles, a novel multi-span identification task for bubble detection, and a dataset of over 400 cryptocurrencies from 9 exchanges over five years and two million tweets. Additionally, we develop a set of sequence-to-sequence hyperbolic models specifically designed for this multi-span identification task, taking into account the power-law dynamics of cryptocurrencies and user behavior on social media. We also evaluate the effectiveness of our models in zero-shot settings on a test set of Reddit posts related to 29 "meme stocks," which have seen an increase in trading volume due to social media hype. Our quantitative, qualitative, and zero-shot analyses on Reddit and Twitter, spanning cryptocurrencies and meme stocks, demonstrate the practicality of CryptoBubbles and hyperbolic models.

label: coling
text: We evaluated various compositional models, from bag-of-words representations to compositional RNN-based models, on several extrinsic supervised and unsupervised evaluation benchmarks. Our results confirm that weighted vector averaging can outperform context-sensitive models in most benchmarks, but structural features encoded in RNN models can also be useful in certain classification tasks. We analyzed some of the evaluation datasets to identify the aspects of meaning they measure and the characteristics of the various models that explain their performance variance.

label: coling
text: We evaluated different compositional models, ranging from bag-of-word representations to RNN-based models, on both supervised and unsupervised evaluation benchmarks. Our findings indicate that weighted vector averaging often outperforms context-sensitive models, but RNN models that encode structural features can be beneficial for certain classification tasks. We also examined the evaluation datasets to determine the meaning they measure and the reasons for the performance variance among the models.

label: acl
text: Computing precise evidences, namely minimal sets of sentences that support or refute a given claim, rather than larger evidences is crucial in fact verification (FV), since larger evidences may contain conflicting pieces some of which support the claim while the other refute, thereby misleading FV. Despite being important, precise evidences are rarely studied by existing methods for FV. It is challenging to find precise evidences due to a large search space with lots of local optimums. Inspired by the strong exploration ability of the deep Q-learning network (DQN), we propose a DQN-based approach to retrieval of precise evidences. In addition, to tackle the label bias on Q-values computed by DQN, we design a post-processing strategy which seeks best thresholds for determining the true labels of computed evidences. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of DQN in computing precise evidences and demonstrate improvements in achieving accurate claim verification.

label: acl
text: Computing precise and minimal sets of sentences that either support or refute a given claim is crucial in fact verification (FV), as larger sets of evidence may contain conflicting information that can mislead the FV process. Despite its importance, the study of precise evidence is often neglected by existing FV methods. Finding precise evidence is challenging due to the vast search space and numerous local optimums. To tackle this issue, we propose a deep Q-learning network (DQN) based approach for retrieving precise evidence. To counteract any label bias in the Q-values computed by the DQN, we also design a post-processing strategy that identifies the best thresholds for determining the true labels of computed evidence. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our DQN-based approach in computing precise evidence and show improvements in achieving accurate fact verification.

label: coling
text: One typical approach to long-form document matching is first conducting alignment between cross-document sentence pairs, and then aggregating all of the sentence-level matching signals. However, this approach could be problematic because the alignment between documents is partial — despite two documents as a whole are well-matched, most of the sentences could still be dissimilar. Those dissimilar sentences lead to spurious sentence-level matching signals which may overwhelm the real ones, increasing the difficulties of learning the matching function. Therefore, accurately selecting the key sentences for document matching is becoming a challenging issue. To address the issue, we propose a novel matching approach that equips existing document matching models with an Optimal Partial Transport (OPT) based component, namely OPT-Match, which selects the sentences that play a major role in matching. Enjoying the partial transport properties of OPT, the selected key sentences can not only effectively enhance the matching accuracy, but also be explained as the rationales for the matching results. Extensive experiments on four publicly available datasets demonstrated that existing methods equipped with OPT-Match consistently outperformed the corresponding underlying methods. Evaluations also showed that the key sentences selected by OPT-Match were consistent with human-provided rationales.

label: coling
text: A typical method for matching long-form documents involves aligning cross-document sentence pairs and aggregating the resulting sentence-level matching signals. However, this approach can be problematic as the alignment between documents is often partial, meaning that even though two documents may match well as a whole, most of their individual sentences may still be dissimilar. These dissimilar sentences can lead to false matching signals, making it difficult to learn the matching function. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach, called OPT-Match, which uses Optimal Partial Transport to select the key sentences that play a major role in the matching process. The selected key sentences can significantly improve the accuracy of the matching results and can also be used to explain the rationales behind the match. Our experiments on four publicly available datasets show that methods equipped with OPT-Match consistently outperform their underlying methods. The key sentences selected by OPT-Match were also found to be consistent with human-provided rationales.

label: coling
text: Systematic Offensive stereotyping (SOS) in word embeddings could lead to associating marginalised groups with hate speech and profanity, which might lead to blocking and silencing those groups, especially on social media platforms. In this [id=stk]work, we introduce a quantitative measure of the SOS bias, [id=stk]validate it in the most commonly used word embeddings, and investigate if it explains the performance of different word embeddings on the task of hate speech detection. Results show that SOS bias exists in almost all examined word embeddings and that [id=stk]the proposed SOS bias metric correlates positively with the statistics of published surveys on online extremism. We also show that the [id=stk]proposed metric reveals distinct information [id=stk]compared to established social bias metrics. However, we do not find evidence that SOS bias explains the performance of hate speech detection models based on the different word embeddings.

label: coling
text: Systematic Offensive Stereotyping (SOS) in word embeddings can lead to the association of marginalized groups with hate speech and profanity, resulting in the silencing of these groups on social media platforms. This study introduces a quantitative measure of SOS bias, validates it in commonly used word embeddings, and examines if it affects the performance of hate speech detection models. The results indicate that SOS bias is present in almost all analyzed word embeddings and that the proposed SOS bias metric is positively correlated with statistics from online extremism surveys. Additionally, the proposed metric provides distinct information compared to established social bias metrics. However, there is no evidence that SOS bias impacts the performance of hate speech detection models based on different word embeddings.

text: In this paper, we present an improved model for voicing silent speech, where audio is synthesized from facial electromyography (EMG) signals. To give our model greater flexibility to learn its own input features, we directly use EMG signals as input in the place of hand-designed features used by prior work. Our model uses convolutional layers to extract features from the signals and Transformer layers to propagate information across longer distances. To provide better signal for learning, we also introduce an auxiliary task of predicting phoneme labels in addition to predicting speech audio features. On an open vocabulary intelligibility evaluation, our model improves the state of the art for this task by an absolute 25.8%.

label: acl
text: We present an improved model for synthesizing audio from facial electromyography (EMG) signals for silent speech in this paper. Our model is designed to have greater flexibility in learning its own input features by using EMG signals directly as input, instead of hand-designed features used in previous work. The model employs convolutional layers to extract features from the signals and Transformer layers to transfer information across longer distances. To enhance the learning process, we introduce an auxiliary task of predicting phoneme labels in addition to predicting speech audio features. Our model outperforms the state of the art by 25.8% in an open vocabulary intelligibility evaluation.

text: Self-training has proven effective for improving NMT performance by augmenting model training with synthetic parallel data. The common practice is to construct synthetic data based on a randomly sampled subset of large-scale monolingual data, which we empirically show is sub-optimal. In this work, we propose to improve the sampling procedure by selecting the most informative monolingual sentences to complement the parallel data. To this end, we compute the uncertainty of monolingual sentences using the bilingual dictionary extracted from the parallel data. Intuitively, monolingual sentences with lower uncertainty generally correspond to easy-to-translate patterns which may not provide additional gains. Accordingly, we design an uncertainty-based sampling strategy to efficiently exploit the monolingual data for self-training, in which monolingual sentences with higher uncertainty would be sampled with higher probability. Experimental results on large-scale WMT English⇒German and English⇒Chinese datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses suggest that emphasizing the learning on uncertain monolingual sentences by our approach does improve the translation quality of high-uncertainty sentences and also benefits the prediction of low-frequency words at the target side.

label: acl
text: Self-training has been shown to be effective in improving NMT performance by incorporating synthetic parallel data into model training. The typical method is to generate synthetic data using a random subset of large monolingual data, which we have found to be sub-optimal. Our proposal is to enhance this sampling process by identifying the most informative monolingual sentences to complement the parallel data. To achieve this, we calculate the uncertainty of monolingual sentences using a bilingual dictionary derived from the parallel data. Monolingual sentences with lower uncertainty are generally easier to translate and may not provide significant benefits. Therefore, we have designed an uncertainty-based sampling strategy that prioritizes monolingual sentences with higher uncertainty, sampling them with a higher probability. Our approach has been tested on large-scale WMT English⇒German and English⇒Chinese datasets and has been shown to be effective. Our results also indicate that prioritizing the learning of uncertain monolingual sentences leads to improved translation quality of high-uncertainty sentences and benefits the prediction of low-frequency words in the target language.

label: coling
text: Generative dialog models usually adopt beam search as the inference method to generate responses. However, small-width beam search only focuses on the limited current optima. This deficiency named as myopic bias ultimately suppresses the diversity and probability of generated responses. Although increasing the beam width mitigates the myopic bias, it also proportionally slows down the inference efficiency. To alleviate the myopic bias in small-width beam search, this paper proposes a Prospective-Performance Network (PPN) to predict the future reward of the given partially-generated response, and the future reward is defined by the expectation of the partial response appearing in the top-ranked responses given by a larger-width beam search. Enhanced by PPN, the decoder can promote the results with great potential during the beam search phase. The experimental results on both Chinese and English corpora show that our method is promising to increase the quality and diversity of generated responses, with inference efficiency well maintained.

label: coling
text: Generative dialog models typically rely on beam search as their inference method for generating responses. However, small-width beam search only considers limited current optima, leading to a deficiency known as myopic bias, which reduces the diversity and probability of generated responses. Although increasing the beam width can alleviate this issue, it also slows down the inference efficiency. To address the myopic bias in small-width beam search, this paper proposes a Prospective-Performance Network (PPN) that predicts the future reward of a partially-generated response. The future reward is defined as the expectation of the partial response appearing in the top-ranked responses generated by a larger-width beam search. With the help of PPN, the decoder can prioritize results with great potential during the beam search phase. The results of our experiments on Chinese and English corpora demonstrate that our method effectively improves the quality and diversity of generated responses, while maintaining inference efficiency.

label: acl
text: We propose NeuralWOZ, a novel dialogue collection framework that uses model-based dialogue simulation. NeuralWOZ has two pipelined models, Collector and Labeler. Collector generates dialogues from (1) user's goal instructions, which are the user context and task constraints in natural language, and (2) system's API call results, which is a list of possible query responses for user requests from the given knowledge base. Labeler annotates the generated dialogue by formulating the annotation as a multiple-choice problem, in which the candidate labels are extracted from goal instructions and API call results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in the zero-shot domain transfer learning for dialogue state tracking. In the evaluation, the synthetic dialogue corpus generated from NeuralWOZ achieves a new state-of-the-art with improvements of 4.4% point joint goal accuracy on average across domains, and improvements of 5.7% point of zero-shot coverage against the MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset.

label: acl
text: The NeuralWOZ is a novel dialogue collection framework that uses model-based dialogue simulation. It consists of two models, the Collector and the Labeler. The Collector generates dialogues based on the user's goal instructions, which are the user context and task constraints in natural language, and the system's API call results, which are lists of possible query responses to user requests from the knowledge base. The Labeler annotates these dialogues by formulating the annotation as a multiple-choice problem, using candidate labels extracted from the goal instructions and API call results. The proposed method has been demonstrated to be effective in zero-shot domain transfer learning for dialogue state tracking. In evaluations, the synthetic dialogue corpus generated by NeuralWOZ achieved a new state-of-the-art, with an average improvement of 4.4% in joint goal accuracy across domains and a 5.7% improvement in zero-shot coverage compared to the MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset.

label: coling
text: Consistency identification in task-oriented dialog (CI-ToD) usually consists of three subtasks, aiming to identify inconsistency between current system response and current user response, dialog history and the corresponding knowledge base. This work aims to solve CI-ToD task by introducing an explicit interaction paradigm, Cycle Guided Interactive learning Model (CGIM), which achieves to make information exchange explicitly from all the three tasks. Specifically, CGIM relies on two core insights, referred to as guided multi-head attention module and cycle interactive mechanism, that collaborate from each other. On the one hand, each two tasks are linked with the guided multi-head attention module, aiming to explicitly model the interaction across two related tasks. On the other hand, we further introduce cycle interactive mechanism that focuses on facilitating model to exchange information among the three correlated sub-tasks via a cycle interaction manner. Experimental results on CI-ToD benchmark show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance, pushing the overall score to 56.3% (5.0% point absolute improvement). In addition, we find that CGIM is robust to the initial task flow order.

label: coling
text: The Consistency Identification in Task-Oriented Dialog (CI-ToD) typically involves three subtasks aimed at identifying inconsistencies between the current system response, the current user response, the dialog history, and the knowledge base. This study introduces the Cycle Guided Interactive Learning Model (CGIM) to solve the CI-ToD task by explicitly modeling information exchange among the three subtasks. CGIM leverages two core insights, the guided multi-head attention module and the cycle interactive mechanism, to link the two tasks and facilitate information exchange among the three subtasks, respectively. Experimental results on the CI-ToD benchmark show that our model outperforms the state of the art, with an overall score of 56.3% (a 5.0% point absolute improvement). Furthermore, our model demonstrates robustness to the initial task flow order.

label: acl
text: Deep learning models have achieved great success on the task of Natural Language Inference (NLI), though only a few attempts try to explain their behaviors. Existing explanation methods usually pick prominent features such as words or phrases from the input text. However, for NLI, alignments among words or phrases are more enlightening clues to explain the model. To this end, this paper presents AREC, a post-hoc approach to generate alignment rationale explanations for co-attention based models in NLI. The explanation is based on feature selection, which keeps few but sufficient alignments while maintaining the same prediction of the target model. Experimental results show that our method is more faithful and human-readable compared with many existing approaches. We further study and re-evaluate three typical models through our explanation beyond accuracy, and propose a simple method that greatly improves the model robustness.

label: acl
text: Deep learning models have achieved significant success in the field of Natural Language Inference (NLI), but few attempts have been made to explain their behaviors. Existing explanation methods usually focus on selecting prominent features such as words or phrases from the input text. However, for NLI, alignments between words or phrases provide more insightful explanations of the model's behavior. To address this issue, we present AREC, a post-hoc approach that generates alignment rationale explanations for co-attention-based models in NLI. Our explanation is based on feature selection, keeping only the most important alignments while preserving the model's prediction. Our experiments show that our method provides more accurate and human-readable explanations compared to existing approaches. Additionally, we study and re-evaluate three typical models through our explanation beyond accuracy and propose a simple method that significantly improves the model's robustness.

label: coling
text: In this research, we present pilot experiments to distil monolingual models from a jointly trained model for 102 languages (mBERT). We demonstrate that it is possible for the target language to outperform the original model, even with a basic distillation setup. We evaluate our methodology for 6 languages with varying amounts of resources and language families.

label: coling
text: In this study, we present the results of pilot experiments aimed at distilling monolingual models from a joint model trained on 102 languages (mBERT). Our findings show that, even with a simple distillation setup, the target language can outperform the original model. We evaluate our approach for six languages, considering the varying availability of resources and language families.

label: acl
text: Sentence compression reduces the length of text by removing non-essential content while preserving important facts and grammaticality. Unsupervised objective driven methods for sentence compression can be used to create customized models without the need for ground-truth training data, while allowing flexibility in the objective function(s) that are used for learning and inference. Recent unsupervised sentence compression approaches use custom objectives to guide discrete search; however, guided search is expensive at inference time. In this work, we explore the use of reinforcement learning to train effective sentence compression models that are also fast when generating predictions. In particular, we cast the task as binary sequence labelling and fine-tune a pre-trained transformer using a simple policy gradient approach. Our approach outperforms other unsupervised models while also being more efficient at inference time.

label: acl
text: Sentence compression shortens text by retaining important facts and grammaticality while eliminating non-essential content. Unsupervised sentence compression models can be customized without ground-truth training data using objective-driven methods. However, these methods often use guided search, which can be time-consuming during inference. In this study, we examine the use of reinforcement learning to train efficient sentence compression models that generate predictions quickly. We approach the task as a binary sequence labelling problem and fine-tune a pre-trained transformer using a policy gradient method. Our approach outperforms other unsupervised models and is more efficient during inference.

label: coling
text: Neural network based multi-task learning has achieved great success on many NLP problems, which focuses on sharing knowledge among tasks by linking some layers to enhance the performance. However, most existing approaches suffer from the interference between tasks because they lack of selection mechanism for feature sharing. In this way, the feature spaces of tasks may be easily contaminated by helpless features borrowed from others, which will confuse the models for making correct prediction. In this paper, we propose a multi-task convolutional neural network with the Leaky Unit, which has memory and forgetting mechanism to filter the feature flows between tasks. Experiments on five different datasets for text classification validate the benefits of our approach.

label: coling
text: The multi-task learning approach based on neural networks has been highly successful in addressing many NLP problems. This approach focuses on sharing knowledge among tasks by linking some layers to improve performance. However, most existing methods suffer from interference between tasks due to the lack of a feature-sharing selection mechanism. This can result in contamination of the feature spaces of tasks with irrelevant features borrowed from other tasks, which can confuse the model and lead to incorrect predictions. To address this issue, we propose a multi-task convolutional neural network with a Leaky Unit, which has a memory and forgetting mechanism to filter the flow of features between tasks. The benefits of our approach are validated by experiments on five different text classification datasets.

label: naacl
text: As using they/them as personal pronouns becomes increasingly common in English, it is important that coreference resolution systems work as well for individuals who use personal “they” as they do for those who use gendered personal pronouns. We introduce a new benchmark for coreference resolution systems which evaluates singular personal “they” recognition. Using these WinoNB schemas, we evaluate a number of publicly available coreference resolution systems and confirm their bias toward resolving “they” pronouns as plural.

label: naacl
text: With the growing prevalence of using "they/them" as personal pronouns in English, it is crucial that coreference resolution systems are effective in recognizing and resolving personal "they" just as they are with gendered personal pronouns. To address this, we have created a new benchmark for evaluating coreference resolution systems, specifically focused on recognizing singular personal "they". By utilizing WinoNB schemas, we have tested several publicly available coreference resolution systems and found that they tend to resolve "they" pronouns as plural.

label: emnlp
text: This paper proposes a new neural architecture that exploits readily available sentiment lexicon resources. The key idea is that that incorporating a word-level prior can aid in the representation learning process, eventually improving model performance. To this end, our model employs two distinctly unique components, i.e., (1) we introduce a lexicon-driven contextual attention mechanism to imbue lexicon words with long-range contextual information and (2), we introduce a contrastive co-attention mechanism that models contrasting polarities between all positive and negative words in a sentence. Via extensive experiments, we show that our approach outperforms many other neural baselines on sentiment classification tasks on multiple benchmark datasets.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a novel neural architecture that leverages readily accessible sentiment lexicon resources. The central idea is that incorporating a word-level prior can enhance the representation learning process and improve model performance. Our model features two unique components: (1) a lexicon-driven contextual attention mechanism that imbues lexicon words with long-range contextual information, and (2) a contrastive co-attention mechanism that models contrasting polarities among positive and negative words in a sentence. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms numerous neural baselines on sentiment classification tasks across multiple benchmark datasets.

label: naacl
text: Contrastive learning (CL) has achieved astonishing progress in computer vision, speech, and natural language processing fields recently with self-supervised learning. However, CL approach to the supervised setting is not fully explored, especially for the natural language understanding classification task. Intuitively, the class label itself has the intrinsic ability to perform hard positive/negative mining, which is crucial for CL. Motivated by this, we propose a novel label anchored contrastive learning approach (denoted as LaCon) for language understanding. Specifically, three contrastive objectives are devised, including a multi-head instance-centered contrastive loss (ICL), a label-centered contrastive loss (LCL), and a label embedding regularizer (LER). Our approach does not require any specialized network architecture or any extra data augmentation, thus it can be easily plugged into existing powerful pre-trained language models. Compared to the state-of-the-art baselines, LaCon obtains up to 4.1% improvement on the popular datasets of GLUE and CLUE benchmarks. Besides, LaCon also demonstrates significant advantages under the few-shot and data imbalance settings, which obtains up to 9.4% improvement on the FewGLUE and FewCLUE benchmarking tasks.

label: naacl
text: Recently, Contrastive Learning (CL) has made remarkable advances in computer vision, speech, and natural language processing through self-supervised learning. However, its application to supervised settings, especially for natural language understanding classification tasks, has not been fully explored. Our intuition is that the class label itself has the intrinsic ability to perform hard positive/negative mining, which is crucial for CL. To this end, we propose a novel Label Anchored Contrastive Learning (LaCon) approach for language understanding. LaCon consists of three contrastive objectives: a multi-head instance-centered contrastive loss (ICL), a label-centered contrastive loss (LCL), and a label embedding regularizer (LER). Unlike other approaches, LaCon does not require any specialized network architecture or data augmentation and can be easily integrated into existing pre-trained language models. Our experiments show that LaCon outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 4.1% on popular datasets such as GLUE and CLUE. Additionally, LaCon demonstrates strong performance in few-shot and imbalanced data settings, achieving up to 9.4% improvement on FewGLUE and FewCLUE benchmarking tasks.

label: acl
text: Transferring the knowledge to a small model through distillation has raised great interest in recent years. Prevailing methods transfer the knowledge derived from mono-granularity language units (e.g., token-level or sample-level), which is not enough to represent the rich semantics of a text and may lose some vital knowledge. Besides, these methods form the knowledge as individual representations or their simple dependencies, neglecting abundant structural relations among intermediate representations. To overcome the problems, we present a novel knowledge distillation framework that gathers intermediate representations from multiple semantic granularities (e.g., tokens, spans and samples) and forms the knowledge as more sophisticated structural relations specified as the pair-wise interactions and the triplet-wise geometric angles based on multi-granularity representations. Moreover, we propose distilling the well-organized multi-granularity structural knowledge to the student hierarchically across layers. Experimental results on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our method outperforms advanced distillation methods.

label: acl
text: The transfer of knowledge to a small model through distillation has gained significant attention in recent years. However, current methods transfer knowledge derived from mono-granularity language units, such as tokens or samples, which is inadequate for representing the rich semantics of text and may result in the loss of important information. These methods also form knowledge as individual representations or simple dependencies, ignoring the abundant structural relations between intermediate representations. To address these issues, we introduce a novel knowledge distillation framework that gathers intermediate representations from multiple semantic granularities, such as tokens, spans, and samples, and forms the knowledge as more sophisticated structural relations. These relations are specified as pair-wise interactions and triplet-wise geometric angles based on multi-granularity representations. Additionally, we propose distilling this well-organized multi-granularity structural knowledge to the student model hierarchically across layers. Our experiments on the GLUE benchmark show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods.

label: acl
text: Revealing the implicit semantic relation between the constituents of a noun-compound is important for many NLP applications. It has been addressed in the literature either as a classification task to a set of pre-defined relations or by producing free text paraphrases explicating the relations. Most existing paraphrasing methods lack the ability to generalize, and have a hard time interpreting infrequent or new noun-compounds. We propose a neural model that generalizes better by representing paraphrases in a continuous space, generalizing for both unseen noun-compounds and rare paraphrases. Our model helps improving performance on both the noun-compound paraphrasing and classification tasks.

label: acl
text: Revealing the implicit semantic relationship between the constituents of a noun-compound is crucial for various NLP applications. This has been tackled in previous studies either by classifying the relationship into a set of pre-defined categories or by generating free-text paraphrases that explain the relationship. However, most existing paraphrasing methods lack generalization capabilities and struggle with interpreting infrequent or new noun-compounds. To address these limitations, we propose a neural model that represents paraphrases in a continuous space, allowing for better generalization for both unseen noun-compounds and rare paraphrases. This model can significantly improve performance on both noun-compound paraphrasing and classification tasks.

label: emnlp
text: Multi-modal sentiment analysis offers various challenges, one being the effective combination of different input modalities, namely text, visual and acoustic. In this paper, we propose a recurrent neural network based multi-modal attention framework that leverages the contextual information for utterance-level sentiment prediction. The proposed approach applies attention on multi-modal multi-utterance representations and tries to learn the contributing features amongst them. We evaluate our proposed approach on two multi-modal sentiment analysis benchmark datasets, viz. CMU Multi-modal Opinion-level Sentiment Intensity (CMU-MOSI) corpus and the recently released CMU Multi-modal Opinion Sentiment and Emotion Intensity (CMU-MOSEI) corpus. Evaluation results show the effectiveness of our proposed approach with the accuracies of 82.31% and 79.80% for the MOSI and MOSEI datasets, respectively. These are approximately 2 and 1 points performance improvement over the state-of-the-art models for the datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Multi-modal sentiment analysis presents several challenges, including the effective integration of text, visual, and acoustic input modalities. In this paper, we introduce a recurrent neural network-based multi-modal attention framework that utilizes contextual information to predict sentiment at the utterance level. Our approach applies attention to multi-modal, multi-utterance representations and learns the contributing features among them. We evaluate our framework on two benchmark datasets: the CMU Multi-modal Opinion-level Sentiment Intensity (CMU-MOSI) corpus and the recently released CMU Multi-modal Opinion Sentiment and Emotion Intensity (CMU-MOSEI) corpus. Our results show that our approach is effective, with accuracy rates of 82.31% and 79.80% for the MOSI and MOSEI datasets, respectively. This represents an improvement of 2 and 1 points over the state-of-the-art models for these datasets.

label: naacl
text: Current text-image approaches (e.g., CLIP) typically adopt dual-encoder architecture using pre-trained vision-language representation. However, these models still pose non-trivial memory requirements and substantial incremental indexing time, which makes them less practical on mobile devices. In this paper, we present an effective two-stage framework to compress large pre-trained dual-encoder for lightweight text-image retrieval. The resulting model is smaller (39% of the original), faster (1.6x/2.9x for processing image/text respectively), yet performs on par with or better than the original full model on Flickr30K and MSCOCO benchmarks. We also open-source an accompanying realistic mobile image search application.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we present a two-stage framework for compressing large pre-trained dual-encoder models for text-image retrieval. This is in response to the non-trivial memory requirements and substantial incremental indexing time posed by current text-image approaches (e.g., CLIP). Our framework results in a smaller model (39% of the original), which is faster (1.6x/2.9x for processing images/text, respectively) and performs on par with or better than the original model on Flickr30K and MSCOCO benchmarks. Additionally, we have open-sourced a realistic mobile image search application to accompany this research.

label: acl
text: The general format of natural language inference (NLI) makes it tempting to be used for zero-shot text classification by casting any target label into a sentence of hypothesis and verifying whether or not it could be entailed by the input, aiming at generic classification applicable on any specified label space. In this opinion piece, we point out a few overlooked issues that are yet to be discussed in this line of work. We observe huge variance across different classification datasets amongst standard BERT-based NLI models and surprisingly find that pre-trained BERT without any fine-tuning can yield competitive performance against BERT fine-tuned for NLI. With the concern that these models heavily rely on spurious lexical patterns for prediction, we also experiment with preliminary approaches for more robust NLI, but the results are in general negative. Our observations reveal implicit but challenging difficulties in entailment-based zero-shot text classification.

label: acl
text: The natural language inference (NLI) format is often used for zero-shot text classification because it is easy to cast any target label into a sentence of hypothesis and verify if it can be entailed by the input. This approach aims to create a generic classification system that can be applied to any specified label space. However, this article highlights some overlooked issues that have not been discussed in this field. Despite the widespread use of standard BERT-based NLI models, we find significant variance across different classification datasets. Surprisingly, we also discover that pre-trained BERT without fine-tuning can perform as well as BERT fine-tuned for NLI. We are concerned that these models rely on unreliable lexical patterns for predictions, so we experiment with preliminary approaches to make NLI more robust. Unfortunately, our results are generally negative. Our findings highlight the implicit and challenging difficulties in using entailment-based zero-shot text classification.

label: naacl
text: Extracting temporal relations (before, after, overlapping, etc.) is a key aspect of understanding events described in natural language. We argue that this task would gain from the availability of a resource that provides prior knowledge in the form of the temporal order that events usually follow. This paper develops such a resource – a probabilistic knowledge base acquired in the news domain – by extracting temporal relations between events from the New York Times (NYT) articles over a 20-year span (1987–2007). We show that existing temporal extraction systems can be improved via this resource. As a byproduct, we also show that interesting statistics can be retrieved from this resource, which can potentially benefit other time-aware tasks. The proposed system and resource are both publicly available.

label: naacl
text: Extracting temporal relationships between events, such as "before," "after," and "overlapping," is critical for comprehending natural language descriptions. Our proposal is that this task would benefit from a resource that provides prior knowledge in the form of the typical temporal order of events. This paper presents such a resource, a probabilistic knowledge base, which was acquired by extracting temporal relationships from 20 years of New York Times articles (1987-2007). Our results demonstrate that this resource can improve existing temporal extraction systems, and also reveals interesting statistics that can be applied to other time-aware tasks. Both the proposed system and resource are publicly accessible.

label: emnlp
text: Word embedding models have become a fundamental component in a wide range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. However, embeddings trained on human-generated corpora have been demonstrated to inherit strong gender stereotypes that reflect social constructs. To address this concern, in this paper, we propose a novel training procedure for learning gender-neutral word embeddings. Our approach aims to preserve gender information in certain dimensions of word vectors while compelling other dimensions to be free of gender influence. Based on the proposed method, we generate a Gender-Neutral variant of GloVe (GN-GloVe). Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that GN-GloVe successfully isolates gender information without sacrificing the functionality of the embedding model.

label: emnlp
text: Word embedding models are a critical component in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. However, these models, which are trained on human-generated corpora, have been shown to carry strong gender stereotypes that reflect social constructs. To address this issue, we propose a new training procedure for learning gender-neutral word embeddings. Our approach aims to preserve gender information in certain dimensions of the word vectors while ensuring that other dimensions are free from gender influence. We have generated a Gender-Neutral variant of GloVe (GN-GloVe) based on this method. Our experiments show that GN-GloVe effectively separates gender information without sacrificing the functionality of the embedding model.

label: coling
text: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires reasoning over multiple documents to answer a complex question and provide interpretable supporting evidence. However, providing supporting evidence is not enough to demonstrate that a model has performed the desired reasoning to reach the correct answer. Most existing multi-hop QA methods fail to answer a large fraction of sub-questions, even if their parent questions are answered correctly. In this paper, we propose the Prompt-based Conservation Learning (PCL) framework for multi-hop QA, which acquires new knowledge from multi-hop QA tasks while conserving old knowledge learned on single-hop QA tasks, mitigating forgetting. Specifically, we first train a model on existing single-hop QA tasks, and then freeze this model and expand it by allocating additional sub-networks for the multi-hop QA task. Moreover, to condition pre-trained language models to stimulate the kind of reasoning required for specific multi-hop questions, we learn soft prompts for the novel sub-networks to perform type-specific reasoning. Experimental results on the HotpotQA benchmark show that PCL is competitive for multi-hop QA and retains good performance on the corresponding single-hop sub-questions, demonstrating the efficacy of PCL in mitigating knowledge loss by forgetting.

label: coling
text: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires reasoning over multiple documents to provide interpretable supporting evidence for a complex question. However, simply providing supporting evidence is not enough to prove that a model has performed the necessary reasoning to reach a correct answer. Many existing multi-hop QA methods fail to answer a significant number of sub-questions correctly, even when their parent questions are answered correctly. To address this challenge, we introduce the Prompt-based Conservation Learning (PCL) framework for multi-hop QA. This framework acquires new knowledge from multi-hop QA tasks while preserving the old knowledge learned from single-hop QA tasks, thus reducing the risk of forgetting. We first train a model on single-hop QA tasks, then freeze it and expand it by adding sub-networks for the multi-hop QA task. Additionally, to condition pre-trained language models to perform the type of reasoning required for specific multi-hop questions, we learn soft prompts for the new sub-networks to perform type-specific reasoning. Our experiments on the HotpotQA benchmark show that PCL is effective for multi-hop QA and retains good performance on single-hop sub-questions, demonstrating its ability to prevent knowledge loss through forgetting.

label: coling
text: Emotion Representation Mapping (ERM) has the goal to convert existing emotion ratings from one representation format into another one, e.g., mapping Valence-Arousal-Dominance annotations for words or sentences into Ekman's Basic Emotions and vice versa. ERM can thus not only be considered as an alternative to Word Emotion Induction (WEI) techniques for automatic emotion lexicon construction but may also help mitigate problems that come from the proliferation of emotion representation formats in recent years. We propose a new neural network approach to ERM that not only outperforms the previous state-of-the-art. Equally important, we present a refined evaluation methodology and gather strong evidence that our model yields results which are (almost) as reliable as human annotations, even in cross-lingual settings. Based on these results we generate new emotion ratings for 13 typologically diverse languages and claim that they have near-gold quality, at least.

label: coling
text: The goal of Emotion Representation Mapping (ERM) is to convert existing emotion ratings from one format to another, such as mapping Valence-Arousal-Dominance annotations for words or sentences into Ekman's Basic Emotions and vice versa. This not only offers an alternative to Word Emotion Induction (WEI) techniques for automatic emotion lexicon construction, but also helps address the challenges posed by the proliferation of emotion representation formats in recent years. We propose a new neural network approach to ERM that outperforms the previous state-of-the-art. Additionally, we present a refined evaluation methodology and provide strong evidence that our model produces results that are nearly as reliable as human annotations, even in cross-lingual settings. Based on these findings, we generate new emotion ratings for 13 typologically diverse languages and assert that they have near-gold quality.

label: emnlp
text: We introduce an effective and efficient method that grounds (i.e., localizes) natural sentences in long, untrimmed video sequences. Specifically, a novel Temporal GroundNet (TGN) is proposed to temporally capture the evolving fine-grained frame-by-word interactions between video and sentence. TGN sequentially scores a set of temporal candidates ended at each frame based on the exploited frame-by-word interactions, and finally grounds the segment corresponding to the sentence. Unlike traditional methods treating the overlapping segments separately in a sliding window fashion, TGN aggregates the historical information and generates the final grounding result in one single pass. We extensively evaluate our proposed TGN on three public datasets with significant improvements over the state-of-the-arts. We further show the consistent effectiveness and efficiency of TGN through an ablation study and a runtime test.

label: emnlp
text: We present an efficient and effective method for localizing natural sentences in untrimmed video sequences. Our novel Temporal GroundNet (TGN) captures the evolving fine-grained interactions between video and sentence frames on a frame-by-word basis. TGN scores a set of temporal candidates at each frame end, based on these interactions, and selects the segment corresponding to the sentence. Unlike traditional methods that treat overlapping segments separately, TGN aggregates historical information and generates the final grounding result in a single pass. Our TGN has been extensively evaluated on three public datasets and has shown significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The effectiveness and efficiency of TGN have been confirmed through an ablation study and a runtime test.

text: We introduce PRIMERA, a pre-trained model for multi-document representation with a focus on summarization that reduces the need for dataset-specific architectures and large amounts of fine-tuning labeled data. PRIMERA uses our newly proposed pre-training objective designed to teach the model to connect and aggregate information across documents. It also uses efficient encoder-decoder transformers to simplify the processing of concatenated input documents. With extensive experiments on 6 multi-document summarization datasets from 3 different domains on zero-shot, few-shot and full-supervised settings, PRIMERA outperforms current state-of-the-art dataset-specific and pre-trained models on most of these settings with large margins.

text: Introducing PRIMERA, a pre-trained model for multi-document representation that focuses on summarization, reducing the need for dataset-specific architectures and large amounts of fine-tuning data. label: emnlp
text: We construct a multilingual common semantic space based on distributional semantics, where words from multiple languages are projected into a shared space via which all available resources and knowledge can be shared across multiple languages. Beyond word alignment, we introduce multiple cluster-level alignments and enforce the word clusters to be consistently distributed across multiple languages. We exploit three signals for clustering: (1) neighbor words in the monolingual word embedding space; (2) character-level information; and (3) linguistic properties (e.g., apposition, locative suffix) derived from linguistic structure knowledge bases available for thousands of languages. We introduce a new cluster-consistent correlational neural network to construct the common semantic space by aligning words as well as clusters. Intrinsic evaluation on monolingual and multilingual QVEC tasks shows our approach achieves significantly higher correlation with linguistic features which are extracted from manually crafted lexical resources than state-of-the-art multi-lingual embedding learning methods do. Using low-resource language name tagging as a case study for extrinsic evaluation, our approach achieves up to 14.6% absolute F-score gain over the state of the art on cross-lingual direct transfer. Our approach is also shown to be robust even when the size of bilingual dictionary is small.

text: We construct a multilingual common semantic space using distributional semantics, where words from multiple languages are projected into a shared space. Our approach exploits three signals for clustering: (1) neighboring words in the monolingual word embedding space, (2) character-level information, and (3) linguistic properties (e.g. apposition, locative suffix) derived from linguistic structure knowledge bases available for thousands of languages. Our new cluster-consistent correlational neural network aligns words and clusters to construct the common semantic space. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art multilingual embedding learning methods in intrinsic evaluations on monolingual and multilingual QVEC tasks, achieving a significantly higher correlation with linguistic features extracted from manually crafted lexical resources. text: Interpretable methods to reveal the internal reasoning processes behind machine learning models have attracted increasing attention in recent years. To quantify the extent to which the identified interpretations truly reflect the intrinsic decision-making mechanisms, various faithfulness evaluation metrics have been proposed. However, we find that different faithfulness metrics show conflicting preferences when comparing different interpretations. Motivated by this observation, we aim to conduct a comprehensive and comparative study of the widely adopted faithfulness metrics. In particular, we introduce two assessment dimensions, namely diagnosticity and complexity. Diagnosticity refers to the degree to which the faithfulness metric favors relatively faithful interpretations over randomly generated ones, and complexity is measured by the average number of model forward passes. According to the experimental results, we find that sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics have higher diagnosticity and lower complexity than the other faithfulness metrics.

text: Interpretable methods for revealing the internal reasoning processes of machine learning models have gained growing attention in recent years. To address this issue, we aim to conduct a comprehensive and comparative study of the widely used faithfulness metrics. We introduce two assessment dimensions: diagnosticity, which measures the degree to which the metric favors faithful interpretations over randomly generated ones, and complexity, which is determined by the average number of model forward passes. Our experimental results show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics have higher diagnosticity and lower complexity compared to other faithfulness metrics.

text: Code-mixing refers to the mixed use of multiple languages. It is prevalent in multilingual societies and is also one of the most challenging natural language processing tasks. In this paper, we study Bahasa Rojak, a dialect popular in Malaysia that consists of English, Malay, and Chinese. Aiming to establish a model to deal with the code-mixing phenomena of Bahasa Rojak, we use data augmentation to automatically construct the first Bahasa Rojak corpus for pre-training language models, which we name the Bahasa Rojak Crawled Corpus (BRCC). We also develop a new pre-trained model called “Mixed XLM”. The model can tag the language of the input token automatically to process code-mixing input. Finally, to test the effectiveness of the Mixed XLM model pre-trained on BRCC for social media scenarios where code-mixing is found frequently, we compile a new Bahasa Rojak sentiment analysis dataset, SentiBahasaRojak, with a Kappa value of 0.77.

Code-mixing, the use of multiple languages in a single sentence or conversation, is a common phenomenon in multilingual societies and poses a significant challenge for natural language processing. In this study, we focus on Bahasa Rojak, a dialect popular in Malaysia that combines English, Malay, and Chinese. To tackle the code-mixing challenges of Bahasa Rojak, we created the first Bahasa Rojak Crawled Corpus (BRCC) using data augmentation and developed a new pre-trained model called “Mixed XLM”. This model is able to automatically tag the language of the input token, making it well-suited for processing code-mixed input. To evaluate the effectiveness of the Mixed XLM model in social media scenarios where code-mixing is prevalent, we created a new sentiment analysis dataset, SentiBahasaRojak, with a Kappa value of 0.77. The results show that the Mixed XLM model outperforms the baseline XLM model by 2.9% in terms of accuracy.

text: Aspect-level sentiment classification aims to determine the sentiment polarity of a review sentence towards an opinion target. A sentence could contain multiple sentiment-target pairs; thus the main challenge of this task is to separate different opinion contexts for different targets. To this end, attention mechanism has played an important role in previous state-of-the-art neural models. The mechanism is able to capture the importance of each context word towards a target by modeling their semantic associations. We build upon this line of research and propose two novel approaches for improving the effectiveness of attention. First, we propose a method for target representation that better captures the semantic meaning of the opinion target. Second, we introduce an attention model that incorporates syntactic information into the attention mechanism. We experiment on attention-based LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) models using the datasets from SemEval 2014, 2015, and 2016. The experimental results show that the conventional attention-based LSTM can be substantially improved by incorporating the two approaches.

text: The objective of aspect-level sentiment classification is to identify the sentiment polarity of a review sentence towards a specific opinion target. This task is challenging as a sentence may contain multiple sentiment-target pairs, requiring the separation of different opinion contexts for different targets. Attention mechanism has been a crucial factor in previous state-of-the-art neural models, as it helps in capturing the significance of each context word towards a target by modeling their semantic connections. To enhance the effectiveness of attention, we propose two novel methods. Our first approach is a method for target representation that better reflects the semantic meaning of the opinion target. Our second approach is an attention model that incorporates syntactic information into the attention mechanism. We evaluate our models using the datasets from SemEval 2014, 2015, and 2016 and demonstrate the improvement of the conventional attention-based LSTM models by incorporating these two methods through experimental results.

text: The phenomenon of compounding is ubiquitous in Sanskrit. It serves for achieving brevity in expressing thoughts, while simultaneously enriching the lexical and structural formation of the language. In this work, we focus on the Sanskrit Compound Type Identification (SaCTI) task, where we consider the problem of identifying semantic relations between the components of a compound word. Earlier approaches solely rely on the lexical information obtained from the components and ignore the most crucial contextual and syntactic information useful for SaCTI. However, the SaCTI task is challenging primarily due to the implicitly encoded context-sensitive semantic relation between the compound components. Thus, we propose a novel multi-task learning architecture which incorporates the contextual information and enriches the complementary syntactic information using morphological tagging and dependency parsing as two auxiliary tasks. Experiments on the benchmark datasets for SaCTI show 6.1 points (Accuracy) and 7.7 points (F1-score) absolute gain compared to the state-of-the-art system. Further, our multi-lingual experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed architecture in English and Marathi languages.

text: The phenomenon of compounding is widespread in Sanskrit, serving to both shorten expressions and enrich the language's lexical and structural formation. In this study, we concentrate on the Sanskrit Compound Type Identification (SaCTI) task, which involves identifying the semantic relationships between the components of a compound word. Previous approaches have only considered the lexical information from the components and neglected the crucial contextual and syntactic information that is essential for SaCTI. The SaCTI task is challenging due to the implicit encoding of context-sensitive semantic relationships between the components. To address this, we propose a novel multi-task learning architecture that incorporates contextual information and enhances the complementary syntactic information using morphological tagging and dependency parsing as auxiliary tasks. Our experiments on benchmark datasets for SaCTI show an improvement of 6.1 points in accuracy and 7.7 points in F1-score compared to the state-of-the-art system. Our multi-lingual experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture in English and Marathi.

text: In this paper we explore the improvement of intent recognition in conversational systems by the use of meta-knowledge embedded in intent identifiers. Developers often include such knowledge, structure as taxonomies, in the documentation of chatbots. By using neuro-symbolic algorithms to incorporate those taxonomies into embeddings of the output space, we were able to improve accuracy in intent recognition. In datasets with intents and example utterances from 200 professional chatbots, we saw decreases in the equal error rate (EER) in more than 40% of the chatbots in comparison to the baseline of the same algorithm without the meta-knowledge. The meta-knowledge proved also to be effective in detecting out-of-scope utterances, improving the false acceptance rate (FAR) in two thirds of the chatbots, with decreases of 0.05 or more in FAR in almost 40% of the chatbots. When considering only the well-developed workspaces with a high level use of taxonomies, FAR decreased more than 0.05 in 77% of them, and more than 0.1 in 39% of the chatbots.

text: In this paper, we examine the enhancement of intent recognition in conversational systems through the integration of meta-knowledge embedded in intent identifiers.
