text: Deep convolutional neural networks excel at sentiment polarity classification, but tend to require substantial amounts of training data, which moreover differs quite significantly between domains. In this work, we present an approach to feed generic cues into the training process of such networks, leading to better generalization abilities given limited training data. We propose to induce sentiment embeddings via supervision on extrinsic data, which are then fed into the model via a dedicated memory-based component. We observe significant gains in effectiveness on a range of different datasets in seven different languages.

label: acl
text: Deep convolutional neural networks are highly effective in sentiment polarity classification but require a significant amount of training data, which can vary significantly between domains. To address this issue, we present a new approach that incorporates generic cues into the training process, resulting in improved generalization with limited training data. Our approach involves inducing sentiment embeddings through supervised extrinsic data and feeding them into the model using a memory-based component. Our results show significant improvement in effectiveness across a range of datasets in seven different languages.

label: emnlp
text: Computational modeling of human multimodal language is an emerging research area in natural language processing spanning the language, visual and acoustic modalities. Comprehending multimodal language requires modeling not only the interactions within each modality (intra-modal interactions) but more importantly the interactions between modalities (cross-modal interactions). In this paper, we propose the Recurrent Multistage Fusion Network (RMFN) which decomposes the fusion problem into multiple stages, each of them focused on a subset of multimodal signals for specialized, effective fusion. Cross-modal interactions are modeled using this multistage fusion approach which builds upon intermediate representations of previous stages. Temporal and intra-modal interactions are modeled by integrating our proposed fusion approach with a system of recurrent neural networks. The RMFN displays state-of-the-art performance in modeling human multimodal language across three public datasets relating to multimodal sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, and speaker traits recognition. We provide visualizations to show that each stage of fusion focuses on a different subset of multimodal signals, learning increasingly discriminative multimodal representations.

text: Computational modeling of human multimodal language is a rapidly growing field of research in natural language processing that encompasses language, visual, and acoustic modalities. Understanding multimodal language requires the modeling of both intra-modal interactions (within each modality) and cross-modal interactions (between modalities). In this paper, we introduce the Recurrent Multistage Fusion Network (RMFN), which decomposes the fusion process into multiple stages, each of which focuses on a specific subset of multimodal signals for specialized and effective fusion. Cross-modal interactions are modeled through this multistage approach, which is built upon intermediate representations from previous stages. Temporal and intra-modal interactions are modeled by integrating our fusion approach with a recurrent neural network system. The RMFN demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in modeling human multimodal language across three public datasets related to multimodal sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, and speaker traits recognition. We provide visualizations to show that each stage of fusion focuses on a different subset of multimodal signals and learns increasingly discriminative multimodal representations.

text: Knowledge-grounded dialogue generation consists of two subtasks: knowledge selection and response generation. The knowledge selector generally constructs a query based on the dialogue context and selects the most appropriate knowledge to help response generation. Recent work finds that realizing who (the user or the agent) holds the initiative and utilizing the role-initiative information to instruct the query construction can help select knowledge. It depends on whether the knowledge connection between two adjacent rounds is smooth to assign the role. However, whereby the user takes the initiative only when there is a strong semantic transition between two rounds, probably leading to initiative misjudgment. Therefore, it is necessary to seek a more sensitive reason beyond the initiative role for knowledge selection. To address the above problem, we propose a Topic-shift Aware Knowledge sElector(TAKE). Specifically, we first annotate the topic shift and topic inheritance labels in multi-round dialogues with distant supervision. Then, we alleviate the noise problem in pseudo labels through curriculum learning and knowledge distillation. Extensive experiments on WoW show that TAKE performs better than strong baselines.

text: The subtasks of knowledge-grounded dialogue generation are knowledge selection and response generation. The knowledge selector usually creates a query based on the dialogue context and selects the most relevant knowledge to assist in response generation. Recent research has shown that considering who holds the initiative (the user or the agent) and using this role-initiative information to guide query construction can improve knowledge selection. However, assigning the initiative role depends on the smoothness of the knowledge connection between two adjacent rounds, which can lead to inaccurate initiative misjudgment. To overcome this issue, we propose the Topic-shift Aware Knowledge sElector (TAKE). We annotate topic shift and inheritance labels in multi-round dialogues using distant supervision and reduce noise in these labels through curriculum learning and knowledge distillation. Our experiments on the WoW dataset demonstrate that TAKE outperforms strong baselines.

text: Open pit mines left many regions worldwide inhospitable or uninhabitable. Many sites are left behind in a hazardous or contaminated state, show remnants of waste, or have other restrictions imposed upon them, e.g., for the protection of human or nature. Such information has to be permanently managed in order to reuse those areas in the future. In this work we present and evaluate an automated workflow for supporting the post-mining management of former lignite open pit mines in the eastern part of Germany, where prior to any planned land reuse, aforementioned information has to be acquired to ensure the safety and validity of such an endeavor. Usually, this information is found in expert reports, either in the form of paper documents, or in the best case as digitized unstructured text—all of them in German language. However, due to the size and complexity of these documents, any inquiry is tedious and time-consuming, thereby slowing down or even obstructing the reuse of related areas. Since no training data is available, we employ active learning in order to perform multi-label sentence classification for two categories of restrictions and seven categories of topics. The final system integrates optical character recognition (OCR), active-learning-based text classification, and geographic information system visualization in order to effectively extract, query, and visualize this information for any area of interest. Active learning and text classification results are twofold: Whereas the restriction categories were reasonably accurate (0.85 F1), the seven topic-oriented categories seemed to be complex even for human annotators and achieved mediocre evaluation scores (0.70 F1).

The system is able to provide a comprehensive overview of the information available in the reports and thus supports the post-mining management process in the eastern part of Germany.

text: Thanks to the strong representation power of neural encoders, neural chart-based parsers have achieved highly competitive performance by using local features. Recently, it has been shown that non-local features in CRF structures lead to improvements. In this paper, we investigate injecting non-local features into the training process of a local span-based parser, by predicting constituent C-C-C-gram non-local patterns and ensuring consistency between non-local patterns and local constituents. Results show that our simple method gives better results than the self-attentive parser on both PTB and CTB. Besides, our method achieves state-of-the-art BERT-based performance on PTB (95.92 F1) and strong performance on CTB (92.31 F1). Our parser also outperforms the self-attentive parser in multi-lingual and zero-shot cross-domain settings.

text: Thanks to the strong representation power of neural encoders, chart-based parsers that use local features have achieved highly competitive performance. However, recent research has shown that incorporating non-local features in CRF structures can lead to further improvements. In this paper, we explore the impact of injecting non-local features into the training process of a local span-based parser. Our approach involves predicting constituent C-C-C-gram non-local patterns and ensuring consistency between these non-local patterns and local constituents. Our results demonstrate that this simple method outperforms the self-attentive parser on both the PTB and CTB datasets. Furthermore, our parser achieves state-of-the-art BERT-based performance on the PTB dataset (95.92 F1) and strong performance on CTB (92.31 F1). text: Idioms are unlike most phrases in two important ways. First, words in an idiom have non-canonical meanings. Second, the non-canonical meanings of words in an idiom are contingent on the presence of other words in the idiom. Linguistic theories differ on whether these properties depend on one another, as well as whether special theoretical machinery is needed to accommodate idioms. We define two measures that correspond to the properties above, and we show that idioms fall at the expected intersection of the two dimensions, but that the dimensions themselves are not correlated. Our results suggest that introducing special machinery to handle idioms may not be warranted.

text: Idioms are distinct from most phrases in two significant ways. Firstly, the words in an idiom have meanings that deviate from their standard or conventional meanings. Secondly, these non-standard meanings of words within an idiom are dependent on the presence of other words within the idiom. There is disagreement among linguistic theories as to whether these properties are interrelated and whether specialized theoretical tools are necessary to understand idioms. Our study defines two metrics that align with the aforementioned properties and demonstrates that idioms occupy the expected intersection of these two dimensions. However, the dimensions themselves are not correlated. Our findings indicate that the need for specialized machinery to deal with idioms may not be justified.

label: acl
text: With the need of fast retrieval speed and small memory footprint, document hashing has been playing a crucial role in large-scale information retrieval. To generate high-quality hashing code, both semantics and neighborhood information are crucial. However, most existing methods leverage only one of them or simply combine them via some intuitive criteria, lacking a theoretical principle to guide the integration process. In this paper, we encode the neighborhood information with a graph-induced Gaussian distribution, and propose to integrate the two types of information with a graph-driven generative model. To deal with the complicated correlations among documents, we further propose a tree-structured approximation method for learning. Under the approximation, we prove that the training objective can be decomposed into terms involving only singleton or pairwise documents, enabling the model to be trained as efficiently as uncorrelated ones. Extensive experimental results on three benchmark datasets show that our method achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed model for simultaneously preserving semantic and neighborhood information.

text: With the requirement for fast retrieval speed and a small memory footprint, document hashing has become a crucial aspect in large-scale information retrieval. In this paper, we encode the neighborhood information using a graph-induced Gaussian distribution and propose a graph-driven generative model to integrate the two types of information. This approximation allows us to decompose the training objective into terms that only involve singleton or pairwise documents, making the model trainable as efficiently as uncorrelated ones. text: Modelling prosody variation is critical for synthesizing natural and expressive speech in end-to-end text-to-speech (TTS) systems. In this paper, a cross-utterance conditional VAE (CUC-VAE) is proposed to estimate a posterior probability distribution of the latent prosody features for each phoneme by conditioning on acoustic features, speaker information, and text features obtained from both past and future sentences. At inference time, instead of the standard Gaussian distribution used by VAE, CUC-VAE allows sampling from an utterance-specific prior distribution conditioned on cross-utterance information, which allows the prosody features generated by the TTS system to be related to the context and is more similar to how humans naturally produce prosody. The performance of CUC-VAE is evaluated via a qualitative listening test for naturalness, intelligibility and quantitative measurements, including word error rates and the standard deviation of prosody attributes. Experimental results on LJ-Speech and LibriTTS data show that the proposed CUC-VAE TTS system improves naturalness and prosody diversity with clear margins.

text: The modeling of prosody variation is crucial for synthesizing natural and expressive speech in end-to-end text-to-speech (TTS) systems. In this paper, we propose a cross-utterance conditional VAE (CUC-VAE) that estimates the posterior probability distribution of latent prosody features for each phoneme. This is achieved by conditioning on acoustic features, speaker information, and text features obtained from past and future sentences. Unlike the standard Gaussian distribution used by VAE, CUC-VAE allows for sampling from an utterance-specific prior distribution that is conditioned on cross-utterance information. This results in prosody features that are more contextually related and closer to how humans naturally produce prosody. The performance of CUC-VAE is evaluated through qualitative listening tests for naturalness, intelligibility, and quantitative measurements, including word error rates and the standard deviation of prosody attributes. Results from experiments on LJ-Speech and LibriTTS data show that the proposed CUC-VAE TTS system significantly improves naturalness and prosody diversity.

text: We reproduce the Structurally Constrained Recurrent Network (SCRN) model, and then regularize it using the existing widespread techniques, such as naive dropout, variational dropout, and weight tying. We show that when regularized and optimized appropriately the SCRN model can achieve performance comparable with the ubiquitous LSTM model in language modeling task on English data, while outperforming it on non-English data.

text: We replicate the Structurally Constrained Recurrent Network (SCRN) model and enhance it with popular regularization techniques, including naive dropout, variational dropout, and weight tying. Our results demonstrate that, when optimized and regularized correctly, the SCRN model can perform similarly to the widely used LSTM model in language modeling tasks using English data, and even surpass it when applied to non-English data.

text: We propose a large margin criterion for training neural language models. Conventionally, neural language models are trained by minimizing perplexity (PPL) on grammatical sentences. However, we demonstrate that PPL may not be the best metric to optimize in some tasks, and further propose a large margin formulation. The proposed method aims to enlarge the margin between the “good” and “bad” sentences in a task-specific sense. It is trained end-to-end and can be widely applied to tasks that involve re-scoring of generated text. Compared with minimum-PPL training, our method gains up to 1.1 WER reduction for speech recognition and 1.0 BLEU increase for machine translation.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a new training criterion for neural language models called the large margin criterion. This is a departure from the traditional method of training these models, which is to minimize perplexity on grammatically correct sentences. Our research shows that perplexity may not be the best metric to optimize for all tasks, and we therefore propose the large margin formulation. The goal of this method is to increase the difference between "good" and "bad" sentences in a task-specific manner. The training process is end-to-end and can be applied to a wide range of text generation tasks. Our method has been shown to result in up to a 1.1 reduction in word error rate for speech recognition and a 1.0 increase in BLEU score for machine translation, compared to traditional minimum-perplexity training.

label: naacl
text: Although sequence-to-sequence models often achieve good performance in semantic parsing for i.i.d. data, their performance is still inferior in compositional generalization. Several data augmentation methods have been proposed to alleviate this problem. However, prior work only leveraged superficial grammar or rules for data augmentation, which resulted in limited improvement. We propose to use subtree substitution for compositional data augmentation, where we consider subtrees with similar semantic functions as exchangeable. Our experiments showed that such augmented data led to significantly better performance on Scan and GeoQuery, and reached new SOTA on compositional split of GeoQuery.

To address this issue, various data augmentation methods have been proposed. However, previous approaches only utilized shallow grammar or rules for augmentation, resulting in limited improvement. Our solution is to use subtree substitution for compositional data augmentation, by treating subtrees with similar semantic functions as interchangeable. Our experiments demonstrated that this augmented data produced significantly improved results on the Scan and GeoQuery datasets and achieved new state-of-the-art results on the compositional split of GeoQuery.

text: Metadata attributes (e.g., user and product IDs from reviews) can be incorporated as additional inputs to neural-based NLP models, by expanding the architecture of the models to improve performance. However, recent models rely on pretrained language models (PLMs), in which previously used techniques for attribute injection are either nontrivial or cost-ineffective. In this paper, we introduce a benchmark for evaluating attribute injection models, which comprises eight datasets across a diverse range of tasks and domains and six synthetically sparsified ones. We also propose a lightweight and memory-efficient method to inject attributes into PLMs. We extend adapters, i.e. tiny plug-in feed-forward modules, to include attributes both independently of or jointly with the text. We use approximation techniques to parameterize the model efficiently for domains with large attribute vocabularies, and training mechanisms to handle multi-labeled and sparse attributes. Extensive experiments and analyses show that our method outperforms previous attribute injection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on all datasets.

text: Metadata attributes, such as user and product IDs from reviews, can enhance the performance of neural-based NLP models by expanding their architecture. However, the use of pretrained language models (PLMs) in recent models makes incorporating these attributes challenging, as traditional techniques for attribute injection are either complex or cost-ineffective. To address this issue, this paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating attribute injection models, consisting of eight diverse datasets and six synthetically sparsified ones. A lightweight and memory-efficient method is also proposed to inject attributes into PLMs, using adapters - tiny plug-in feed-forward modules - to incorporate attributes both independently and jointly with the text. The proposed method utilizes approximation techniques to efficiently parameterize the model for domains with large attribute vocabularies, and training mechanisms to handle multi-labeled and sparse attributes. The results of extensive experiments and analyses show that the proposed method outperforms previous attribute injection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on all datasets.

text: We carry out experiments with deep learning models of summarization across the domains of news, personal stories, meetings, and medical articles in order to understand how content selection is performed. We find that many sophisticated features of state of the art extractive summarizers do not improve performance over simpler models. These results suggest that it is easier to create a summarizer for a new domain than previous work suggests and bring into question the benefit of deep learning models for summarization for those domains that do have massive datasets (i.e., news). At the same time, they suggest important questions for new research in summarization; namely, new forms of sentence representations or external knowledge sources are needed that are better suited to the sumarization task.

label: emnlp
text: We conduct experiments on deep learning models for summarization across various domains, including news, personal stories, meetings, and medical articles, to gain insights into the content selection process. Our findings reveal that many advanced features of state-of-the-art extractive summarizers do not enhance performance compared to simpler models. These results indicate that creating a summarizer for a new domain may be easier than previously thought and call into question the value of deep learning models for summarization in domains with large datasets, such as news. Our findings also raise important questions for future research in summarization, including the need for new sentence representations or external knowledge sources that are more appropriate for the summarization task.

text: Building dialogue generation systems in a zero-shot scenario remains a huge challenge, since the typical zero-shot approaches in dialogue generation rely heavily on large-scale pre-trained language generation models such as GPT-3 and T5. The research on zero-shot dialogue generation without cumbersome language models is limited due to lacking corresponding parallel dialogue corpora. In this paper, we propose a simple but effective Multilingual learning framework for Zero-shot Dialogue Generation (dubbed as MulZDG) that can effectively transfer knowledge from an English corpus with large-scale training samples to a non-English corpus with zero samples. Besides, MulZDG can be viewed as a multilingual data augmentation method to improve the performance of the resource-rich language. First, we construct multilingual code-switching dialogue datasets via translation utterances randomly selected from monolingual English datasets. Then we employ MulZDG to train a unified multilingual dialogue model based on the code-switching datasets. The MulZDG can conduct implicit semantic alignment between different languages. Experiments on DailyDialog and DSTC7 datasets demonstrate that MulZDG not only achieve competitive performance under zero-shot case compared to training with sufficient examples but also greatly improve the performance of the source language.

text: Building dialogue generation systems in a zero-shot scenario remains a challenge, as typical zero-shot approaches are heavily dependent on large-scale pre-trained language generation models, such as GPT-3 and T5. However, research on zero-shot dialogue generation without these models is limited due to a lack of corresponding parallel dialogue corpora. In this paper, we propose a simple but effective Multilingual learning framework for Zero-shot Dialogue Generation (MulZDG) that effectively transfers knowledge from an English corpus with many training samples to a non-English corpus with no samples. Additionally, MulZDG can be used as a multilingual data augmentation method to improve the performance of resource-rich languages. We construct multilingual code-switching dialogue datasets by translating randomly selected utterances from monolingual English datasets. Then, we use MulZDG to train a unified multilingual dialogue model based on these code-switching datasets. MulZDG conducts implicit semantic alignment between different languages. Experiments on the DailyDialog and DSTC7 datasets show that MulZDG not only performs competitively in zero-shot cases compared to models trained with sufficient examples but also greatly improves the performance of the source language.

text: We consider the problem of collectively detecting multiple events, particularly in cross-sentence settings. The key to dealing with the problem is to encode semantic information and model event inter-dependency at a document-level. In this paper, we reformulate it as a Seq2Seq task and propose a Multi-Layer Bidirectional Network (MLBiNet) to capture the document-level association of events and semantic information simultaneously. Specifically, a bidirectional decoder is firstly devised to model event inter-dependency within a sentence when decoding the event tag vector sequence. Secondly, an information aggregation module is employed to aggregate sentence-level semantic and event tag information. Finally, we stack multiple bidirectional decoders and feed cross-sentence information, forming a multi-layer bidirectional tagging architecture to iteratively propagate information across sentences. We show that our approach provides significant improvement in performance compared to the current state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: We address the challenge of collectively detecting multiple events in cross-sentence settings. To tackle this issue, we focus on encoding semantic information and modeling event inter-dependency at a document-level. We propose a Multi-Layer Bidirectional Network (MLBiNet) that simultaneously captures the document-level association of events and semantic information. Our MLBiNet consists of a bidirectional decoder that models event inter-dependency within a sentence and an information aggregation module that aggregates sentence-level semantic and event tag information. Multiple bidirectional decoders are stacked to iteratively propagate information across sentences, forming a multi-layer bidirectional tagging architecture. Our approach significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art results.

text: Dense retrieval has achieved impressive advances in first-stage retrieval from a large-scale document collection, which is built on bi-encoder architecture to produce single vector representation of query and document. However, a document can usually answer multiple potential queries from different views. So the single vector representation of a document is hard to match with multi-view queries, and faces a semantic mismatch problem. This paper proposes a multi-view document representation learning framework, aiming to produce multi-view embeddings to represent documents and enforce them to align with different queries. First, we propose a simple yet effective method of generating multiple embeddings through viewers. Second, to prevent multi-view embeddings from collapsing to the same one, we further propose a global-local loss with annealed temperature to encourage the multiple viewers to better align with different potential queries. Experiments show our method outperforms recent works and achieves state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: Dense retrieval has made remarkable progress in the first stage of retrieving information from large-scale document collections. This is achieved through the use of a bi-encoder architecture that creates a single vector representation of both the query and document. However, a document can often answer multiple queries from different perspectives, making it difficult for the single vector representation to match with these multi-view queries, resulting in a semantic mismatch problem. To address this issue, this paper introduces a multi-view document representation learning framework, which aims to produce multiple embeddings to represent documents and align them with different queries. Our framework includes a simple yet effective method for generating multiple embeddings through viewers and a global-local loss with annealed temperature to prevent the multi-view embeddings from collapsing into a single representation. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms recent works and achieves state-of-the-art results.

text: Most works on financial forecasting use information directly associated with individual companies (e.g., stock prices, news on the company) to predict stock returns for trading. We refer to such company-specific information as local information. Stock returns may also be influenced by global information (e.g., news on the economy in general), and inter-company relationships. Capturing such diverse information is challenging due to the low signal-to-noise ratios, different time-scales, sparsity and distributions of global and local information from different modalities. In this paper, we propose a model that captures both global and local multimodal information for investment and risk management-related forecasting tasks. Our proposed Guided Attention Multimodal Multitask Network (GAME) model addresses these challenges by using novel attention modules to guide learning with global and local information from different modalities and dynamic inter-company relationship networks. Our extensive experiments show that GAME outperforms other state-of-the-art models in several forecasting tasks and important real-world application case studies.

text: Most studies on financial forecasting use company-specific information, such as stock prices and news, to predict stock returns for trading purposes. This type of information is referred to as local information. However, stock returns can also be impacted by global information, such as news about the economy and inter-company relationships. It can be challenging to capture this diverse information due to the low signal-to-noise ratios, varying time-scales, and sparse distributions of both global and local information from different sources. To tackle these challenges, we present a model called the Guided Attention Multimodal Multitask Network (GAME). This model uses innovative attention modules to guide the learning process with both global and local information from multiple sources and dynamic inter-company relationship networks. Our experiments demonstrate that GAME outperforms other state-of-the-art models in various forecasting tasks and real-world applications.

text: Social media platforms have become new battlegrounds for anti-social elements, with misinformation being the weapon of choice. Fact-checking organizations try to debunk as many claims as possible while staying true to their journalistic processes but cannot cope with its rapid dissemination. We believe that the solution lies in partial automation of the fact-checking life cycle, saving human time for tasks which require high cognition. We propose a new workflow for efficiently detecting previously fact-checked claims that uses abstractive summarization to generate crisp queries. These queries can then be executed on a general-purpose retrieval system associated with a collection of previously fact-checked claims. We curate an abstractive text summarization dataset comprising noisy claims from Twitter and their gold summaries. It is shown that retrieval performance improves 2x by using popular out-of-the-box summarization models and 3x by fine-tuning them on the accompanying dataset compared to verbatim querying. Our approach achieves Recall@5 and MRR of 35% and 0.3, compared to baseline values of 10% and 0.1, respectively. Our dataset, code, and models are available publicly: https://github.com/varadhbhatnagar/FC-Claim-Det/.

text: Anti-social elements have taken to social media platforms, using misinformation as their weapon of choice. Fact-checking organizations are struggling to keep up with the rapid spread of false information, despite their efforts to debunk as many claims as possible while adhering to their journalistic processes. To address this issue, we propose a partial automation of the fact-checking process, freeing up human time for tasks that require higher cognitive skills. Our solution involves a new workflow for efficiently detecting previously fact-checked claims, utilizing abstractive summarization to generate concise queries. These queries are executed on a general-purpose retrieval system linked to a collection of previously fact-checked claims. Our abstractive text summarization dataset includes noisy claims from Twitter, along with their accurate summaries. Our results show that using popular summarization models and fine-tuning them on our accompanying dataset can improve retrieval performance by 2x, compared to using verbatim querying. Our approach has a Recall@5 and MRR of 35% and 0.3, compared to baseline values of 10% and 0.1, respectively. Our dataset, code, and models are publicly available at https://github.com/varadhbhatnagar/FC-Claim-Det/.

text: Event Causality Identification (ECI), which aims to detect whether a causality relation exists between two given textual events, is an important task for event causality understanding. However, the ECI task ignores crucial event structure and cause-effect causality component information, making it struggle for downstream applications. In this paper, we introduce a novel task, namely Event Causality Extraction (ECE), aiming to extract the cause-effect event causality pairs with their structured event information from plain texts. The ECE task is more challenging since each event can contain multiple event arguments, posing fine-grained correlations between events to decide the cause-effect event pair. Hence, we propose a method with a dual grid tagging scheme to capture the intra- and inter-event argument correlations for ECE. Further, we devise a event type-enhanced model architecture to realize the dual grid tagging scheme. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, and extensive analyses point out several future directions for ECE.

text: The Event Causality Identification (ECI) task aims to detect whether there is a causal relationship between two given events in text. However, this task ignores important information about the structure of the events and the cause-and-effect relationship, making it difficult to use for downstream applications. In this paper, we present a new task called Event Causality Extraction (ECE), which involves extracting cause-and-effect event pairs along with their structured event information from plain text. The ECE task is more challenging because each event can have multiple event arguments, making it difficult to determine the cause-and-effect relationship between events. To address this challenge, we propose a method that uses a dual grid tagging scheme to capture the correlations between event arguments both within and between events. We also develop a model architecture that is enhanced with event type information to implement the dual grid tagging scheme. Our experiments show the effectiveness of our method, and our analysis highlights potential future directions for ECE.

text: A desirable dialog system should be able to continually learn new skills without forgetting old ones, and thereby adapt to new domains or tasks in its life cycle. However, continually training a model often leads to a well-known catastrophic forgetting issue. In this paper, we present Continual Prompt Tuning, a parameter-efficient framework that not only avoids forgetting but also enables knowledge transfer between tasks. To avoid forgetting, we only learn and store a few prompt tokens' embeddings for each task while freezing the backbone pre-trained model. To achieve bi-directional knowledge transfer among tasks, we propose several techniques (continual prompt initialization, query fusion, and memory replay) to transfer knowledge from preceding tasks and a memory-guided technique to transfer knowledge from subsequent tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method on continual learning for dialog state tracking, compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

text: A desirable dialog system should continually learn new skills without forgetting old ones, adapting to new domains or tasks throughout its life cycle. However, continuous training often leads to catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we introduce Continual Prompt Tuning, a parameter-efficient framework that avoids forgetting and enables knowledge transfer between tasks. To prevent forgetting, we only learn and store the embeddings of a few prompt tokens for each task, while freezing the pre-trained backbone model. We propose several techniques, including continual prompt initialization, query fusion, and memory replay, to transfer knowledge from previous tasks and a memory-guided technique to transfer knowledge from future tasks. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method in continual learning for dialog state tracking, compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

text: Comprehending procedural text, e.g., a paragraph describing photosynthesis, requires modeling actions and the state changes they produce, so that questions about entities at different timepoints can be answered. Although several recent systems have shown impressive progress in this task, their predictions can be globally inconsistent or highly improbable. In this paper, we show how the predicted effects of actions in the context of a paragraph can be improved in two ways: (1) by incorporating global, commonsense constraints (e.g., a non-existent entity cannot be destroyed), and (2) by biasing reading with preferences from large-scale corpora (e.g., trees rarely move). Unlike earlier methods, we treat the problem as a neural structured prediction task, allowing hard and soft constraints to steer the model away from unlikely predictions. We show that the new model significantly outperforms earlier systems on a benchmark dataset for procedural text comprehension (+8% relative gain), and that it also avoids some of the nonsensical predictions that earlier systems make.

text: Understanding procedural texts, such as a paragraph describing photosynthesis, involves modeling actions and the changes they bring about, so that questions about entities at different points in time can be answered. Although recent systems have made impressive progress in this task, their predictions can be globally inconsistent or highly implausible. In this paper, we demonstrate how the predicted effects of actions in the context of a paragraph can be improved through two approaches: (1) by incorporating global commonsense constraints, such as the fact that a non-existent entity cannot be destroyed, and (2) by biasing reading with preferences from large-scale corpora, such as the fact that trees rarely move. Unlike previous methods, we treat this as a neural structured prediction task, allowing both hard and soft constraints to guide the model away from unlikely predictions. Our results show that the new model outperforms previous systems by 8% on a benchmark dataset for procedural text comprehension, and reduces nonsensical predictions made by earlier systems.

text: In this paper, we study the problem of geometric reasoning (a form of visual reasoning) in the context of question-answering. We introduce Dynamic Spatial Memory Network (DSMN), a new deep network architecture that specializes in answering questions that admit latent visual representations, and learns to generate and reason over such representations. Further, we propose two synthetic benchmarks, FloorPlanQA and ShapeIntersection, to evaluate the geometric reasoning capability of QA systems. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our proposed DSMN for visual thinking tasks.

label: acl
text: In this study, we investigate the issue of geometric reasoning in the realm of question-answering. To tackle this challenge, we present the Dynamic Spatial Memory Network (DSMN), a novel deep network architecture designed specifically to answer questions that require latent visual representations, and capable of learning to generate and reason over these representations. Additionally, we introduce two synthetic benchmarks, FloorPlanQA and ShapeIntersection, to assess the geometric reasoning ability of QA systems. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DSMN in performing visual thinking tasks.

text: Within textual emotion classification, the set of relevant labels depends on the domain and application scenario and might not be known at the time of model development. This conflicts with the classical paradigm of supervised learning in which the labels need to be predefined. A solution to obtain a model with a flexible set of labels is to use the paradigm of zero-shot learning as a natural language inference task, which in addition adds the advantage of not needing any labeled training data. This raises the question how to prompt a natural language inference model for zero-shot learning emotion classification. Options for prompt formulations include the emotion name anger alone or the statement “This text expresses anger”. With this paper, we analyze how sensitive a natural language inference-based zero-shot-learning classifier is to such changes to the prompt under consideration of the corpus: How carefully does the prompt need to be selected? We perform experiments on an established set of emotion datasets presenting different language registers according to different sources (tweets, events, blogs) with three natural language inference models and show that indeed the choice of a particular prompt formulation needs to fit to the corpus. We show that this challenge can be tackled with combinations of multiple prompts. Such ensemble is more robust across corpora than individual prompts and shows nearly the same performance as the individual best prompt for a particular corpus.

label: coling
text: In the field of textual emotion classification, the relevant labels for a given model may not be known at the time of development, which conflicts with the traditional approach of supervised learning, where labels must be predefined. To overcome this challenge, the zero-shot learning paradigm can be used as a natural language inference task, which also eliminates the need for labeled training data. However, this raises the question of how to prompt a natural language inference model for zero-shot emotion classification. This paper analyzes the sensitivity of such a classifier to different prompt formulations, such as "This text expresses anger" or simply "anger," while considering the corpus being used. Our experiments on established emotion datasets from various sources (tweets, events, blogs) and using three natural language inference models show that the choice of prompt formulation must fit the corpus and that using a combination of multiple prompts can provide a more robust solution. Our results demonstrate that such an ensemble approach performs nearly as well as the best individual prompt for a given corpus.

text: Concepts, which represent a group of different instances sharing common properties, are essential information in knowledge representation. Most conventional knowledge embedding methods encode both entities (concepts and instances) and relations as vectors in a low dimensional semantic space equally, ignoring the difference between concepts and instances. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge graph embedding model named TransC by differentiating concepts and instances. Specifically, TransC encodes each concept in knowledge graph as a sphere and each instance as a vector in the same semantic space. We use the relative positions to model the relations between concepts and instances (i.e.,instanceOf), and the relations between concepts and sub-concepts (i.e., subClassOf). We evaluate our model on both link prediction and triple classification tasks on the dataset based on YAGO. Experimental results show that TransC outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and captures the semantic transitivity for instanceOf and subClassOf relation. Our codes and datasets can be obtained from https://github.com/davidlvxin/TransC.

text: Concepts, which represent a group of instances with similar properties, play a crucial role in knowledge representation. Conventional knowledge embedding methods encode both entities (concepts and instances) and relationships as vectors in a low-dimensional semantic space, disregarding the difference between concepts and instances. In this paper, we present a novel knowledge graph embedding model named TransC, which differentiates between concepts and instances. TransC encodes each concept in the knowledge graph as a sphere and each instance as a vector in the same semantic space. We model the relationships between concepts and instances (instanceOf) and between concepts and sub-concepts (subClassOf) using the relative positions of the vectors. We evaluate our model on link prediction and triple classification tasks using the YAGO dataset and show that TransC outperforms state-of-the-art methods and captures the semantic transitivity for the instanceOf and subClassOf relationships. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/davidlvxin/TransC.

text: Recent neural sequence-to-sequence models have shown significant progress on short text summarization. However, for document summarization, they fail to capture the long-term structure of both documents and multi-sentence summaries, resulting in information loss and repetitions. In this paper, we propose to leverage the structural information of both documents and multi-sentence summaries to improve the document summarization performance. Specifically, we import both structural-compression and structural-coverage regularization into the summarization process in order to capture the information compression and information coverage properties, which are the two most important structural properties of document summarization. Experimental results demonstrate that the structural regularization improves the document summarization performance significantly, which enables our model to generate more informative and concise summaries, and thus significantly outperforms state-of-the-art neural abstractive methods.

text: Recent advances in neural sequence-to-sequence models have made significant strides in short text summarization. However, these models fall short in capturing the long-term structure of both documents and multi-sentence summaries, leading to information loss and repetition. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the structural information of both documents and multi-sentence summaries to improve document summarization performance. Our approach incorporates structural-compression and structural-coverage regularization into the summarization process, capturing the two most important structural properties of document summarization: information compression and coverage. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the structural regularization significantly improves document summarization performance, generating more informative and concise summaries that outperform state-of-the-art neural abstractive methods.

text: Existing approaches to mitigate demographic biases evaluate on monolingual data, however, multilingual data has not been examined. In this work, we treat the gender as domains (e.g., male vs. female) and present a standard domain adaptation model to reduce the gender bias and improve performance of text classifiers under multilingual settings. We evaluate our approach on two text classification tasks, hate speech detection and rating prediction, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with three fair-aware baselines.

label: naacl
text: To address demographic biases, current methods mainly focus on evaluating monolingual data, neglecting the potential of multilingual data. In our study, we categorize gender as domains (i.e., male and female) and propose a domain adaptation model to reduce gender bias and enhance the performance of text classifiers in multilingual settings. Our approach is evaluated on two text classification tasks, namely hate speech detection and rating prediction, and compared with three fair-aware baselines, showing its effectiveness.

text: Although neural machine translation with the encoder-decoder framework has achieved great success recently, it still suffers drawbacks of forgetting distant information, which is an inherent disadvantage of recurrent neural network structure, and disregarding relationship between source words during encoding step. Whereas in practice, the former information and relationship are often useful in current step. We target on solving these problems and thus introduce relation networks to learn better representations of the source. The relation networks are able to facilitate memorization capability of recurrent neural network via associating source words with each other, this would also help retain their relationships. Then the source representations and all the relations are fed into the attention component together while decoding, with the main encoder-decoder framework unchanged. Experiments on several datasets show that our method can improve the translation performance significantly over the conventional encoder-decoder model and even outperform the approach involving supervised syntactic knowledge.

text: The encoder-decoder framework in neural machine translation has achieved great success, but it still has limitations such as forgetting distant information and disregarding the relationships between source words during encoding. These limitations are inherent in recurrent neural network structures. However, in practice, distant information and relationships between source words are often useful. To address these issues, we introduce relation networks to learn better representations of the source. These networks enhance the memorization capability of the recurrent neural network by associating source words with each other, preserving their relationships. The source representations and relationships are fed into the attention component along with the main encoder-decoder framework during decoding. Experiments on multiple datasets show that our method significantly improves translation performance compared to the conventional encoder-decoder model, and even outperforms approaches that incorporate supervised syntactic knowledge.

text: Knowledge Graph (KG) and attention mechanism have been demonstrated effective in introducing and selecting useful information for weakly supervised methods. However, only qualitative analysis and ablation study are provided as evidence. In this paper, we contribute a dataset and propose a paradigm to quantitatively evaluate the effect of attention and KG on bag-level relation extraction (RE). We find that (1) higher attention accuracy may lead to worse performance as it may harm the model's ability to extract entity mention features; (2) the performance of attention is largely influenced by various noise distribution patterns, which is closely related to real-world datasets; (3) KG-enhanced attention indeed improves RE performance, while not through enhanced attention but by incorporating entity prior; and (4) attention mechanism may exacerbate the issue of insufficient training data. Based on these findings, we show that a straightforward variant of RE model can achieve significant improvements (6% AUC on average) on two real-world datasets as compared with three state-of-the-art baselines. Our codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/zig-kwin-hu/how-KG-ATT-help.

label: acl
text: The effectiveness of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and attention mechanisms in introducing and selecting relevant information for weakly-supervised methods has been demonstrated through qualitative analysis and ablation studies. However, in this paper, we introduce a dataset and a paradigm to quantitatively evaluate the impact of attention and KGs on bag-level relation extraction. Our findings show that: (1) higher attention accuracy may negatively impact the model's ability to extract entity mention features; (2) attention performance is highly influenced by various noise distribution patterns, which are closely related to real-world datasets; (3) KG-enhanced attention does improve relation extraction performance, but not through enhanced attention, but by incorporating entity prior; and (4) attention mechanisms may exacerbate the issue of insufficient training data. Our results demonstrate that a straightforward variant of the relation extraction model can achieve significant improvements (6% AUC on average) on two real-world datasets compared to three state-of-the-art baselines. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/zig-kwin-hu/how-KG-ATT-help.

label: coling
text: Language evolves over time, and word meaning changes accordingly. This is especially true in social media, since its dynamic nature leads to faster semantic shifts, making it challenging for NLP models to deal with new content and trends. However, the number of datasets and models that specifically address the dynamic nature of these social platforms is scarce. To bridge this gap, we present TempoWiC, a new benchmark especially aimed at accelerating research in social media-based meaning shift. Our results show that TempoWiC is a challenging benchmark, even for recently-released language models specialized in social media.

label: coling
text: The evolution of language over time leads to changes in word meaning, particularly in the dynamic environment of social media where semantic shifts occur at a faster pace. This presents a challenge for NLP models to effectively deal with new content and trends. Currently, there is a scarcity of datasets and models that address the dynamic nature of social media. To address this gap, we introduce TempoWiC, a new benchmark designed to advance research in meaning shift in social media. Our results demonstrate that TempoWiC is a challenging benchmark, even for language models that specialize in social media.

label: naacl
text: State-of-the-art pretrained NLP models contain a hundred million to trillion parameters. Adapters provide a parameter-efficient alternative for the full finetuning in which we can only finetune lightweight neural network layers on top of pretrained weights. Adapter layers are initialized randomly. However, existing work uses the same adapter architecture—i.e., the same adapter layer on top of each layer of the pretrained model—for every dataset, regardless of the properties of the dataset or the amount of available training data. In this work, we introduce adaptable adapters that contain (1) learning different activation functions for different layers and different input data, and (2) a learnable switch to select and only use the beneficial adapter layers. We show that adaptable adapters achieve on-par performances with the standard adapter architecture while using a considerably smaller number of adapter layers. In addition, we show that the selected adapter architecture by adaptable adapters transfers well across different data settings and similar tasks. We propose to use adaptable adapters for designing efficient and effective adapter architectures. The resulting adapters (a) contain about 50% of the learning parameters of the standard adapter and are therefore more efficient at training and inference, and require less storage space, and (b) achieve considerably higher performances in low-data settings.

label: naacl
text: The state-of-the-art NLP models contain a massive number of parameters, ranging from 100 million to trillions. Adapters provide a parameter-efficient alternative to full finetuning by only finetuning lightweight neural network layers on top of the pretrained weights. Adapters are initialized randomly, but existing work uses the same adapter architecture for every dataset, regardless of its properties or the amount of training data available. In this work, we introduce adaptable adapters that can learn different activation functions for different layers and input data, and also have a learnable switch to select only the beneficial adapter layers. Our results show that adaptable adapters achieve comparable performance to the standard adapter architecture while using a significantly smaller number of adapter layers. Furthermore, the adaptable adapters transfer well across different data settings and similar tasks, resulting in adapters that are more efficient and effective. With approximately 50% fewer learning parameters than the standard adapter, the adaptable adapters require less storage space and achieve higher performance in low-data settings.

label: naacl
text: Real-world datasets often encode stereotypes and societal biases. Such biases can be implicitly captured by trained models, leading to biased predictions and exacerbating existing societal preconceptions. Existing debiasing methods, such as adversarial training and removing protected information from representations, have been shown to reduce bias. However, a disconnect between fairness criteria and training objectives makes it difficult to reason theoretically about the effectiveness of different techniques. In this work, we propose two novel training objectives which directly optimise for the widely-used criterion of equal opportunity, and show that they are effective in reducing bias while maintaining high performance over two classification tasks.

text: Real-world datasets often contain encoded stereotypes and societal biases, which can be implicitly captured by trained models and result in biased predictions that exacerbate existing societal preconceptions. To mitigate this, various debiasing methods have been developed, including adversarial training and removing protected information from representations, which have been shown to effectively reduce bias. However, there is a lack of connection between fairness criteria and training objectives, making it challenging to understand the effectiveness of different debiasing techniques. To address this, we present two novel training objectives that directly optimize for the widely-used criterion of equal opportunity, and demonstrate their effectiveness in reducing bias while maintaining high performance on two classification tasks.

label: acl
text: Despite the achievements of large-scale multimodal pre-training approaches, cross-modal retrieval, e.g., image-text retrieval, remains a challenging task. To bridge the semantic gap between the two modalities, previous studies mainly focus on word-region alignment at the object level, lacking the matching between the linguistic relation among the words and the visual relation among the regions. The neglect of such relation consistency impairs the contextualized representation of image-text pairs and hinders the model performance and the interpretability. In this paper, we first propose a novel metric, Intra-modal Self-attention Distance (ISD), to quantify the relation consistency by measuring the semantic distance between linguistic and visual relations. In response, we present Inter-modal Alignment on Intra-modal Self-attentions (IAIS), a regularized training method to optimize the ISD and calibrate intra-modal self-attentions from the two modalities mutually via inter-modal alignment. The IAIS regularizer boosts the performance of prevailing models on Flickr30k and MS COCO datasets by a considerable margin, which demonstrates the superiority of our approach.

label: acl
text: Despite the success of large-scale multimodal pre-training approaches, cross-modal retrieval, such as image-text retrieval, remains a challenging task. Previous studies have mainly focused on aligning the word and region levels of the two modalities, but have neglected the matching of the linguistic relationships among words and the visual relationships among regions. This neglect of relation consistency impairs the contextualized representation of image-text pairs and negatively impacts model performance and interpretability. In this paper, we propose a novel metric, the Intra-modal Self-attention Distance (ISD), which quantifies relation consistency by measuring the semantic distance between linguistic and visual relationships. We also present the Inter-modal Alignment on Intra-modal Self-attentions (IAIS) method, which optimizes the ISD and aligns intra-modal self-attentions between the two modalities. Our IAIS regularizer significantly improves the performance of existing models on the Flickr30k and MS COCO datasets, showcasing the superiority of our approach.

label: acl
text: Statutory reasoning is the task of determining whether a legal statute, stated in natural language, applies to the text description of a case. Prior work introduced a resource that approached statutory reasoning as a monolithic textual entailment problem, with neural baselines performing nearly at-chance. To address this challenge, we decompose statutory reasoning into four types of language-understanding challenge problems, through the introduction of concepts and structure found in Prolog programs. Augmenting an existing benchmark, we provide annotations for the four tasks, and baselines for three of them. Models for statutory reasoning are shown to benefit from the additional structure, improving on prior baselines. Further, the decomposition into subtasks facilitates finer-grained model diagnostics and clearer incremental progress.

label: acl
text: Statutory reasoning involves determining whether a legal statute expressed in natural language applies to a text description of a case. Previous research introduced a resource that treated statutory reasoning as a single textual entailment problem, with neural baselines performing poorly. To overcome this challenge, we have decomposed statutory reasoning into four distinct language-understanding tasks by incorporating concepts and structure found in Prolog programs. By enhancing an existing benchmark, we have provided annotations for these four tasks and established baselines for three of them. Our results show that models for statutory reasoning benefit from the additional structure and outperform previous baselines. Additionally, breaking down statutory reasoning into subtasks allows for more detailed model diagnostics and clearer progress.

label: coling
text: Modern neural machine translation (NMT) models have achieved competitive performance in standard benchmarks. However, they have recently been shown to suffer limitation in compositional generalization, failing to effectively learn the translation of atoms (e.g., words) and their semantic composition (e.g., modification) from seen compounds (e.g., phrases), and thus suffering from significantly weakened translation performance on unseen compounds during inference.We address this issue by introducing categorization to the source contextualized representations. The main idea is to enhance generalization by reducing sparsity and overfitting, which is achieved by finding prototypes of token representations over the training set and integrating their embeddings into the source encoding. Experiments on a dedicated MT dataset (i.e., CoGnition) show that our method reduces compositional generalization error rates by 24% error reduction. In addition, our conceptually simple method gives consistently better results than the Transformer baseline on a range of general MT datasets.

label: coling
text: Modern neural machine translation (NMT) models have performed competitively in standard benchmarks, but have been shown to have limitations in compositional generalization. They struggle to effectively learn the translation of words and their semantic composition from seen phrases, leading to weakened performance on unseen phrases during inference. To address this issue, we introduce categorization to the source contextualized representations. Our approach enhances generalization by reducing sparsity and overfitting by finding prototypes of token representations in the training set and integrating their embeddings into the source encoding. Our experiments on the CoGnition MT dataset show that our method reduces compositional generalization error rates by 24%. Additionally, our conceptually simple method outperforms the Transformer baseline on a range of general MT datasets.

label: acl
text: In this paper we present the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder network (EED), a novel conversation model that learns to utilize similar examples from training data to generate responses. Similar conversation examples (context-response pairs) from training data are retrieved using a traditional TF-IDF based retrieval model and the corresponding responses are used by our decoder to generate the ground truth response. The contribution of each retrieved response is weighed by the similarity of corresponding context with the input context. As a result, our model learns to assign higher similarity scores to those retrieved contexts whose responses are crucial for generating the final response. We present detailed experiments on two large data sets and we find that our method out-performs state of the art sequence to sequence generative models on several recently proposed evaluation metrics.

label: acl
text: This paper introduces the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder Network (EED), a new conversation model that leverages similar examples from training data to generate responses. The model retrieves conversation examples (context-response pairs) from training data using a traditional TF-IDF-based retrieval model, and the decoder uses the corresponding responses to generate the ground truth response. The contribution of each retrieved response is determined by the similarity of its corresponding context with the input context. As a result, the model learns to assign higher similarity scores to those retrieved contexts whose responses are crucial for generating the final response. Through detailed experiments on two large datasets, we demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence generative models on several recently proposed evaluation metrics.

label: emnlp
text: Sequence-to-sequence neural generation models have achieved promising performance on short text conversation tasks. However, they tend to generate generic/dull responses, leading to unsatisfying dialogue experience. We observe that in the conversation tasks, each query could have multiple responses, which forms a 1-to-n or m-to-n relationship in the view of the total corpus. The objective function used in standard sequence-to-sequence models will be dominated by loss terms with generic patterns. Inspired by this observation, we introduce a statistical re-weighting method that assigns different weights for the multiple responses of the same query, and trains the common neural generation model with the weights. Experimental results on a large Chinese dialogue corpus show that our method improves the acceptance rate of generated responses compared with several baseline models and significantly reduces the number of generated generic responses.

label: emnlp
text: Sequence-to-sequence neural generation models have shown promising results in short text conversation tasks, but they frequently produce generic and uninteresting responses, leading to an unsatisfactory dialogue experience. Our analysis reveals that in the context of conversation tasks, queries often have multiple possible responses, resulting in a 1-to-n or m-to-n relationship with the total corpus. The standard objective function used in these models tends to prioritize generic patterns, which contributes to the dull responses. To address this issue, we propose a statistical re-weighting method that assigns different weights to the multiple responses of a single query and trains the neural generation model using these weights. Our experiments on a large Chinese dialogue corpus demonstrate that our method leads to an improvement in the acceptance rate of generated responses when compared to several baseline models and significantly reduces the number of generic responses generated.

label: acl
text: Fast and reliable evaluation metrics are key to R&D progress. While traditional natural language generation metrics are fast, they are not very reliable. Conversely, new metrics based on large pretrained language models are much more reliable, but require significant computational resources. In this paper, we propose FrugalScore, an approach to learn a fixed, low cost version of any expensive NLG metric, while retaining most of its original performance. Experiments with BERTScore and MoverScore on summarization and translation show that FrugalScore is on par with the original metrics (and sometimes better), while having several orders of magnitude less parameters and running several times faster. On average over all learned metrics, tasks, and variants, FrugalScore retains 96.8% of the performance, runs 24 times faster, and has 35 times less parameters than the original metrics. We make our trained metrics publicly available, to benefit the entire NLP community and in particular researchers and practitioners with limited resources.

label: acl
text: Fast and reliable evaluation metrics are crucial for advancing R&D. Although traditional natural language generation metrics are fast, they lack reliability. On the other hand, new metrics based on large pretrained language models are more reliable but require substantial computational resources. To address this issue, we present FrugalScore, a method for learning a low-cost version of any expensive NLG metric while preserving most of its performance. Our experiments with BERTScore and MoverScore on summarization and translation demonstrate that FrugalScore is comparable to the original metrics, and in some cases, even better. It also has several orders of magnitude fewer parameters and runs faster. On average, FrugalScore retains 96.8% of the performance, runs 24 times faster, and has 35 times fewer parameters than the original metrics. We make our trained metrics publicly available to benefit the NLP community, particularly researchers and practitioners with limited resources.

label: acl
text: With state-of-the-art systems having finally attained estimated human performance, Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) has now joined the array of Natural Language Processing tasks that have seemingly been solved, thanks to the vast amounts of knowledge encoded into Transformer-based pre-trained language models. And yet, if we look below the surface of raw figures, it is easy to realize that current approaches still make trivial mistakes that a human would never make. In this work, we provide evidence showing why the F1 score metric should not simply be taken at face value and present an exhaustive analysis of the errors that seven of the most representative state-of-the-art systems for English all-words WSD make on traditional evaluation benchmarks.In addition, we produce and release a collection of test sets featuring (a) an amended version of the standard evaluation benchmark that fixes its lexical and semantic inaccuracies, (b) 42D, a challenge set devised to assess the resilience of systems with respect to least frequent word senses and senses not seen at training time, and (c) hardEN, a challenge set made up solely of instances which none of the investigated state-of-the-art systems can solve. We make all of the test sets and model predictions available to the research community at https://github.com/SapienzaNLP/wsd-hard-benchmark.

label: acl
text: With the latest state-of-the-art systems achieving estimated human performance, Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) has been added to the list of Natural Language Processing tasks that have been seemingly solved, thanks to the vast amounts of knowledge encoded into Transformer-based pre-trained language models. However, if we delve deeper, we find that current approaches still make mistakes that a human would never make. In this study, we provide evidence that the F1 score metric should not be taken at face value and conduct a comprehensive analysis of the errors made by seven of the most representative state-of-the-art systems for English all-words WSD on traditional evaluation benchmarks. Furthermore, we create and release a collection of test sets, including an amended version of the standard evaluation benchmark, a challenge set designed to test the resilience of systems with respect to least frequent word senses and unseen senses, and a set of instances that none of the investigated state-of-the-art systems can solve. All of these test sets and model predictions are available to the research community at https://github.com/SapienzaNLP/wsd-hard-benchmark.

label: acl
text: One of the main challenges in conversational question answering (CQA) is to resolve the conversational dependency, such as anaphora and ellipsis. However, existing approaches do not explicitly train QA models on how to resolve the dependency, and thus these models are limited in understanding human dialogues. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, ExCorD (Explicit guidance on how to resolve Conversational Dependency) to enhance the abilities of QA models in comprehending conversational context. ExCorD first generates self-contained questions that can be understood without the conversation history, then trains a QA model with the pairs of original and self-contained questions using a consistency-based regularizer. In our experiments, we demonstrate that ExCorD significantly improves the QA models' performance by up to 1.2 F1 on QuAC, and 5.2 F1 on CANARD, while addressing the limitations of the existing approaches.

label: acl
text: One of the main challenges in conversational question answering (CQA) is resolving conversational dependencies such as anaphora and ellipsis. However, current approaches do not provide explicit training for QA models on how to resolve these dependencies, limiting the models' ability to understand human dialogues. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework, ExCorD (Explicit guidance on resolving Conversational Dependency), which enhances QA models' comprehension of conversational context. ExCorD starts by generating self-contained questions that can be understood without the conversation history, then trains a QA model using a consistency-based regularizer with the pairs of original and self-contained questions. Our experiments show that ExCorD significantly improves QA model performance, with up to a 1.2 F1 increase on QuAC and a 5.2 F1 increase on CANARD, compared to existing approaches.

label: emnlp
text: We propose to generalize language models for conversational speech recognition to allow them to operate across utterance boundaries and speaker changes, thereby capturing conversation-level phenomena such as adjacency pairs, lexical entrainment, and topical coherence. The model consists of a long-short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent network that reads the entire word-level history of a conversation, as well as information about turn taking and speaker overlap, in order to predict each next word. The model is applied in a rescoring framework, where the word history prior to the current utterance is approximated with preliminary recognition results. In experiments in the conversational telephone speech domain (Switchboard) we find that such a model gives substantial perplexity reductions over a standard LSTM-LM with utterance scope, as well as improvements in word error rate.

label: emnlp
text: We propose to enhance language models for conversational speech recognition to capture conversation-level phenomena such as adjacency pairs, lexical entrainment, and topical coherence by allowing them to operate beyond utterance boundaries and speaker changes. Our model features a long-short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent network that considers the entire word-level history of the conversation, including information about turn taking and speaker overlap, to predict each subsequent word. The model is tested in a rescoring framework, where the word history prior to the current utterance is estimated using preliminary recognition results. Our experiments in the conversational telephone speech domain (Switchboard) demonstrate substantial reductions in perplexity compared to a standard LSTM-LM with utterance scope, as well as improved word error rate.

label: emnlp
text: This paper proposes a modularized sense induction and representation learning model that jointly learns bilingual sense embeddings that align well in the vector space, where the cross-lingual signal in the English-Chinese parallel corpus is exploited to capture the collocation and distributed characteristics in the language pair. The model is evaluated on the Stanford Contextual Word Similarity (SCWS) dataset to ensure the quality of monolingual sense embeddings. In addition, we introduce Bilingual Contextual Word Similarity (BCWS), a large and high-quality dataset for evaluating cross-lingual sense embeddings, which is the first attempt of measuring whether the learned embeddings are indeed aligned well in the vector space. The proposed approach shows the superior quality of sense embeddings evaluated in both monolingual and bilingual spaces.

label: emnlp
text: This paper introduces a modularized sense induction and representation learning model that jointly learns bilingual sense embeddings that are aligned in the vector space. The model uses the cross-lingual signal from the English-Chinese parallel corpus to capture the collocation and distributed characteristics of the language pair. To evaluate the quality of the monolingual sense embeddings, the model is tested on the Stanford Contextual Word Similarity (SCWS) dataset. Additionally, a new dataset, Bilingual Contextual Word Similarity (BCWS), is introduced to evaluate cross-lingual sense embeddings. This is the first attempt to measure the alignment of the learned embeddings in the vector space. The results show that the proposed approach produces high-quality sense embeddings in both monolingual and bilingual spaces.

label: emnlp
text: Rapid growth of multi-modal documents on the Internet makes multi-modal summarization research necessary. Most previous research summarizes texts or images separately. Recent neural summarization research shows the strength of the Encoder-Decoder model in text summarization.
