This paper proposes an abstractive text-image summarization model using the attentional hierarchical Encoder-Decoder model to summarize a text document and its accompanying images simultaneously, and then to align the sentences and images in summaries. A multi-modal attentional mechanism is proposed to attend original sentences, images, and captions when decoding. The DailyMail dataset is extended by collecting images and captions from the Web. Experiments show our model outperforms the neural abstractive and extractive text summarization methods that do not consider images. In addition, our model can generate informative summaries of images.

label: emnlp
text: The rapid growth of multi-modal documents on the Internet necessitates research in multi-modal summarization. Previous research has primarily focused on summarizing texts or images separately. However, recent neural summarization research has demonstrated the effectiveness of the Encoder-Decoder model in text summarization. This paper presents an abstractive text-image summarization model that utilizes the attentional hierarchical Encoder-Decoder model to summarize both a text document and its accompanying images simultaneously, and aligns the sentences and images in the summaries. Our model incorporates a multi-modal attention mechanism, which attends to original sentences, images, and captions during decoding. To validate our model, we extend the DailyMail dataset by collecting images and captions from the Web. Our experiments show that our model outperforms neural abstractive and extractive text summarization methods that do not consider images and can generate informative summaries of images.

label: coling
text: Retrieval-based conversational systems learn to rank response candidates for a given dialogue context by computing the similarity between their vector representations. However, training on a single textual form of the multi-turn context limits the ability of a model to learn representations that generalize to natural perturbations seen during inference. In this paper we propose a framework that incorporates augmented versions of a dialogue context into the learning objective. We utilize contrastive learning as an auxiliary objective to learn robust dialogue context representations that are invariant to perturbations injected through the augmentation method. We experiment with four benchmark dialogue datasets and demonstrate that our framework combines well with existing augmentation methods and can significantly improve over baseline BERT-based ranking architectures. Furthermore, we propose a novel data augmentation method, ConMix, that adds token level perturbations through stochastic mixing of tokens from other contexts in the batch. We show that our proposed augmentation method outperforms previous data augmentation approaches, and provides dialogue representations that are more robust to common perturbations seen during inference.

label: coling
text: Retrieval-based conversational systems learn to rank response candidates by computing the similarity between the vector representations of a given dialogue context and the response candidates. However, training the model on a single textual form of the multi-turn context limits its ability to generalize to natural perturbations seen during inference. To address this, we propose a framework that incorporates augmented versions of the dialogue context into the learning objective. Our framework utilizes contrastive learning as an auxiliary objective to learn robust dialogue context representations that are invariant to perturbations introduced through the augmentation method. We conduct experiments on four benchmark dialogue datasets and show that our framework, when combined with existing augmentation methods, significantly improves over baseline BERT-based ranking architectures. Additionally, we propose a novel data augmentation method, ConMix, that adds token-level perturbations by stochastically mixing tokens from other contexts in the batch. Our results demonstrate that our proposed augmentation method outperforms previous data augmentation approaches and provides dialogue representations that are more robust to common perturbations seen during inference.

label: coling
text: Few-shot Named Entity Recognition (NER) is imperative for entity tagging in limited resource domains and thus received proper attention in recent years. Existing approaches for few-shot NER are evaluated mainly under in-domain settings. In contrast, little is known about how these inherently faithful models perform in cross-domain NER using a few labeled in-domain examples. This paper proposes a two-step rationale-centric data augmentation method to improve the model's generalization ability. Results on several datasets show that our model-agnostic method significantly improves the performance of cross-domain NER tasks compared to previous state-of-the-art methods compared to the counterfactual data augmentation and prompt-tuning methods.

label: coling
text: The importance of Few-shot Named Entity Recognition (NER) for entity tagging in resource-constrained domains has received significant attention in recent years. Most existing approaches for few-shot NER have been evaluated under in-domain settings, leaving little information on how these models perform in cross-domain scenarios with only a few in-domain labeled examples. To address this issue, this paper proposes a two-step rationale-centric data augmentation method to enhance the model's generalization ability. Our results on multiple datasets demonstrate that this model-agnostic method significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, including counterfactual data augmentation and prompt-tuning methods, in cross-domain NER tasks.

label: acl
text: State-of-the-art relation extraction approaches are only able to recognize relationships between mentions of entity arguments stated explicitly in the text and typically localized to the same sentence. However, the vast majority of relations are either implicit or not sententially localized. This is a major problem for Knowledge Base Population, severely limiting recall. In this paper we propose a new methodology to identify relations between two entities, consisting of detecting a very large number of unary relations, and using them to infer missing entities. We describe a deep learning architecture able to learn thousands of such relations very efficiently by using a common deep learning based representation. Our approach largely outperforms state of the art relation extraction technology on a newly introduced web scale knowledge base population benchmark, that we release to the research community.

label: acl
text: State-of-the-art relation extraction methods can only recognize relationships between entities that are explicitly stated in the same sentence within the text. However, the majority of relationships are either implicit or not confined to a single sentence, presenting a significant challenge for Knowledge Base Population and limiting recall. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach for identifying relations between entities by detecting a large number of unary relations and using them to infer missing entities. Our deep learning architecture is capable of learning thousands of these relationships efficiently, utilizing a common deep learning-based representation. Our method outperforms current state-of-the-art relation extraction technology on a new web-scale knowledge base population benchmark, which we are making available to the research community.

label: coling
text: Despite the success of state-of-the-art pre-trained language models (PLMs) on a series of multi-hop reasoning tasks, they still suffer from their limited abilities to transfer learning from simple to complex tasks and vice-versa. We argue that one step forward to overcome this limitation is to better understand the behavioral trend of PLMs at each hop over the inference chain. Our critical underlying idea is to mimic human-style reasoning: we envision the multi-hop reasoning process as a sequence of explicit single-hop reasoning steps. To endow PLMs with incremental reasoning skills, we propose a set of inference strategies on relevant facts and distractors allowing us to build automatically generated training datasets. Using the SHINRA and ConceptNet resources jointly, we empirically show the effectiveness of our proposal on multiple-choice question answering and reading comprehension, with a relative improvement in terms of accuracy of 68.4% and 16.0% w.r.t. classic PLMs, respectively.

label: coling
text: Despite the success of state-of-the-art pre-trained language models (PLMs) in multiple-hop reasoning tasks, they still have limitations when it comes to transferring learning from simple to complex tasks and vice versa. To overcome this, we need to better understand the behavior of PLMs at each step of the inference chain. Our approach mimics human-style reasoning by envisioning the multi-hop reasoning process as a sequence of explicit single-hop reasoning steps. To enhance PLMs with incremental reasoning skills, we propose a set of inference strategies for relevant facts and distractions, which will allow us to automatically generate training datasets. Using both the SHINRA and ConceptNet resources, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal through experiments in multiple-choice question answering and reading comprehension, resulting in a 68.4% improvement in accuracy compared to classic PLMs in the former and a 16.0% improvement in the latter.

label: emnlp
text: When parsing morphologically-rich languages with neural models, it is beneficial to model input at the character level, and it has been claimed that this is because character-level models learn morphology. We test these claims by comparing character-level models to an oracle with access to explicit morphological analysis on twelve languages with varying morphological typologies. Our results highlight many strengths of character-level models, but also show that they are poor at disambiguating some words, particularly in the face of case syncretism. We then demonstrate that explicitly modeling morphological case improves our best model, showing that character-level models can benefit from targeted forms of explicit morphological modeling.

label: emnlp
text: Parsing morphologically-rich languages with neural models is more effective when input is modeled at the character level. This is because it is believed that character-level models learn the morphology of the language. To test these claims, we compare character-level models to an oracle that has access to explicit morphological analysis in twelve languages with different morphological typologies. Our findings highlight the strengths of character-level models, but also reveal that they struggle to disambiguate certain words, particularly in the presence of case syncretism. To address this issue, we show that incorporating explicit morphological case modeling into the best model leads to improvement, demonstrating that character-level models can benefit from targeted forms of explicit morphological modeling.

label: acl
text: Recently, various response generation models for two-party conversations have achieved impressive improvements, but less effort has been paid to multi-party conversations (MPCs) which are more practical and complicated. Compared with a two-party conversation where a dialogue context is a sequence of utterances, building a response generation model for MPCs is more challenging, since there exist complicated context structures and the generated responses heavily rely on both interlocutors (i.e., speaker and addressee) and history utterances. To address these challenges, we present HeterMPC, a heterogeneous graph-based neural network for response generation in MPCs which models the semantics of utterances and interlocutors simultaneously with two types of nodes in a graph. Besides, we also design six types of meta relations with node-edge-type-dependent parameters to characterize the heterogeneous interactions within the graph. Through multi-hop updating, HeterMPC can adequately utilize the structural knowledge of conversations for response generation. Experimental results on the Ubuntu Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channel benchmark show that HeterMPC outperforms various baseline models for response generation in MPCs.

label: acl
text: Recently, response generation models for two-party conversations have achieved impressive improvements, but less attention has been paid to multi-party conversations (MPCs), which are more practical and complex. Compared to two-party conversations, where the dialogue context is a sequence of utterances, building a response generation model for MPCs is more challenging due to the complicated context structures and the need to consider both interlocutors and historical utterances. To overcome these challenges, we introduce HeterMPC, a heterogeneous graph-based neural network for response generation in MPCs. HeterMPC models the semantics of utterances and interlocutors simultaneously through two types of nodes in a graph, and it uses six types of meta-relations with node-edge-type-dependent parameters to characterize the heterogeneous interactions. Through multi-hop updating, HeterMPC can effectively utilize the structural knowledge of conversations for response generation. Experimental results on the Ubuntu Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channel benchmark demonstrate that HeterMPC outperforms various baseline models for response generation in MPCs.

label: coling
text: The literature frequently addresses the differences in receptive and productive vocabulary, but grammar is often left unacknowledged in second language acquisition studies. In this paper, we used two corpora to investigate the divergences in the behavior of pedagogically relevant grammatical structures in reception and production texts. We further improved the divergence scores observed in this investigation by setting a polarity to them that indicates whether there is overuse or underuse of a grammatical structure by language learners. This led to the compilation of a language profile that was later combined with vocabulary and readability features for classifying reception and production texts in three classes: beginner, intermediate, and advanced. The results of the automatic classification task in both production (0.872 of F-measure) and reception (0.942 of F-measure) were comparable to the current state of the art. We also attempted to automatically attribute a score to texts produced by learners, and the correlation results were encouraging, but there is still a good amount of room for improvement in this task. The developed language profile will serve as input for a system that helps language learners to activate more of their passive knowledge in writing texts.

label: coling
text: The literature often discusses the differences between receptive and productive vocabulary, but it often overlooks the role of grammar in second language acquisition. In this paper, we used two corpora to examine the differences in the usage of pedagogically relevant grammatical structures in reception and production texts. We enhanced our findings by assigning a polarity, indicating whether there was overuse or underuse of a grammatical structure by language learners, to the divergence scores. This led to the creation of a language profile, which was then combined with vocabulary and readability features to classify reception and production texts into three categories: beginner, intermediate, and advanced. The results of the automatic classification task in production (0.872 F-measure) and reception (0.942 F-measure) were comparable to the current state of the art. We also attempted to automatically score texts produced by learners, and while the correlation results were promising, there is still room for improvement. The language profile will be used as input for a system aimed at helping language learners to activate more of their passive knowledge when writing texts.

label: naacl
text: Multimodal machine learning algorithms aim to learn visual-textual correspondences. Previous work suggests that concepts with concrete visual manifestations may be easier to learn than concepts with abstract ones. We give an algorithm for automatically computing the visual concreteness of words and topics within multimodal datasets. We apply the approach in four settings, ranging from image captions to images/text scraped from historical books. In addition to enabling explorations of concepts in multimodal datasets, our concreteness scores predict the capacity of machine learning algorithms to learn textual/visual relationships. We find that 1) concrete concepts are indeed easier to learn; 2) the large number of algorithms we consider have similar failure cases; 3) the precise positive relationship between concreteness and performance varies between datasets. We conclude with recommendations for using concreteness scores to facilitate future multimodal research.

label: naacl
text: Multimodal machine learning algorithms aim to learn the relationships between visual and textual information. Previous research has shown that concepts with concrete visual representations are easier to learn than those with abstract representations. Our algorithm calculates the visual concreteness of words and topics in multimodal datasets automatically. We have tested our approach in four different settings, from image captions to historical book images and texts. Our concreteness scores not only allow for the exploration of concepts in multimodal datasets, but also predict the ability of machine learning algorithms to learn the relationships between text and visual information. Our findings indicate that 1) concrete concepts are indeed easier to learn; 2) the majority of the algorithms we tested have similar limitations; 3) the relationship between concreteness and performance varies between datasets. Finally, we provide recommendations for using concreteness scores to enhance future research in the field of multimodal machine learning.

label: emnlp
text: Exponential growth in the number of scientific publications yields the need for effective automatic analysis of rhetorical aspects of scientific writing. Acknowledging the argumentative nature of scientific text, in this work we investigate the link between the argumentative structure of scientific publications and rhetorical aspects such as discourse categories or citation contexts. To this end, we (1) augment a corpus of scientific publications annotated with four layers of rhetoric annotations with argumentation annotations and (2) investigate neural multi-task learning architectures combining argument extraction with a set of rhetorical classification tasks. By coupling rhetorical classifiers with the extraction of argumentative components in a joint multi-task learning setting, we obtain significant performance gains for different rhetorical analysis tasks.

label: emnlp
text: The exponential increase in the number of scientific publications necessitates the need for an efficient automatic analysis of the rhetorical aspects of scientific writing. Recognizing the argumentative nature of scientific text, this study explores the relationship between the argumentative structure of scientific publications and rhetorical aspects such as discourse categories and citation contexts. To achieve this, we (1) enhance a corpus of scientific publications with four layers of rhetoric annotations and argumentation annotations and (2) examine neural multi-task learning models that combine argument extraction with various rhetorical classification tasks. By incorporating rhetorical classifiers and argumentative components in a multi-task learning setting, we achieve notable improvements in the performance of various rhetorical analysis tasks.

label: acl
text: The definition generation task can help language learners by providing explanations for unfamiliar words. This task has attracted much attention in recent years. We propose a novel task of Simple Definition Generation (SDG) to help language learners and low literacy readers. A significant challenge of this task is the lack of learner's dictionaries in many languages, and therefore the lack of data for supervised training. We explore this task and propose a multitasking framework SimpDefiner that only requires a standard dictionary with complex definitions and a corpus containing arbitrary simple texts. We disentangle the complexity factors from the text by carefully designing a parameter sharing scheme between two decoders. By jointly training these components, the framework can generate both complex and simple definitions simultaneously. We demonstrate that the framework can generate relevant, simple definitions for the target words through automatic and manual evaluations on English and Chinese datasets. Our method outperforms the baseline model by a 1.77 SARI score on the English dataset, and raises the proportion of the low level (HSK level 1-3) words in Chinese definitions by 3.87%.

label: acl
text: The task of definition generation can assist language learners by offering explanations for unfamiliar words. In recent years, this task has gained considerable attention. To further aid language learners and low literacy readers, we introduce a new task, Simple Definition Generation (SDG). A significant challenge in this task is the absence of learner's dictionaries in many languages, which results in a lack of data for supervised training. To overcome this, we propose a multitasking framework, SimpDefiner, which only requires a standard dictionary with complex definitions and a corpus containing simple texts. Our framework disentangles complexity factors from the text by designing a parameter sharing scheme between two decoders. By jointly training these components, the framework can generate both complex and simple definitions simultaneously. Our method was evaluated on English and Chinese datasets, and the results showed that it outperforms the baseline model by 1.77 SARI score on the English dataset, and increases the proportion of low-level (HSK level 1-3) words in Chinese definitions by 3.87%.

label: acl
text: Recently, many studies are emerging towards building a retrieval-based dialogue system that is able to effectively leverage background knowledge (e.g., documents) when conversing with humans. However, it is non-trivial to collect large-scale dialogues that are naturally grounded on the background documents, which hinders the effective and adequate training of knowledge selection and response matching. To overcome the challenge, we consider decomposing the training of the knowledge-grounded response selection into three tasks including: 1) query-passage matching task; 2) query-dialogue history matching task; 3) multi-turn response matching task, and joint learning all these tasks in a unified pre-trained language model. The former two tasks could help the model in knowledge selection and comprehension, while the last task is designed for matching the proper response with the given query and background knowledge (dialogue history). By this means, the model can be learned to select relevant knowledge and distinguish proper response, with the help of ad-hoc retrieval corpora and a large number of ungrounded multi-turn dialogues. Experimental results on two benchmarks of knowledge-grounded response selection indicate that our model can achieve comparable performance with several existing methods that rely on crowd-sourced data for training.

label: acl
text: Recently, numerous studies have been conducted to develop a retrieval-based dialogue system that can effectively utilize background knowledge (e.g., documents) during conversations with humans. However, it is challenging to collect large-scale dialogues that are naturally grounded in the background documents, which limits the effective training of knowledge selection and response matching. To address this issue, we propose a three-task training approach that includes: 1) query-passage matching; 2) query-dialogue history matching; and 3) multi-turn response matching. These tasks are jointly learned in a unified pre-trained language model. The first two tasks help the model with knowledge selection and comprehension, while the last task is designed to match the appropriate response with the given query and background knowledge (dialogue history). This approach allows the model to learn how to select relevant knowledge and distinguish proper responses with the help of ad-hoc retrieval corpora and a large number of ungrounded multi-turn dialogues. Our experimental results on two benchmarks for knowledge-grounded response selection show that our model performs comparably to existing methods that rely on crowd-sourced data for training.

label: acl
text: Finding codes given natural language query is beneficial to the productivity of software developers. Future progress towards better semantic matching between query and code requires richer supervised training resources. To remedy this, we introduce CoSQA dataset. It includes 20,604 labels for pairs of natural language queries and codes, each annotated by at least 3 human annotators. We further introduce a contrastive learning method dubbed CoCLR to enhance text-code matching, which works as a data augmenter to bring more artificially generated training instances. We show that, evaluated on CodeXGLUE with the same CodeBERT model, training on CoSQA improves the accuracy of code question answering by 5.1% and incorporating CoCLR brings a further improvement of 10.5%.

label: acl
text: The ability to find codes for natural language queries is crucial for improving the efficiency of software developers. In order to achieve better semantic matching between queries and codes, there is a need for more comprehensive supervised training resources. To address this challenge, we introduce the CoSQA dataset, which includes 20,604 labels for pairs of natural language queries and codes, each annotated by at least three human annotators. Additionally, we propose a new contrastive learning method, called CoCLR, which acts as a data augmenter to generate more training instances and improve the text-code matching process. Our results, based on the CodeXGLUE dataset and using the CodeBERT model, show that training on the CoSQA dataset improves the accuracy of code question answering by 5.1%, and incorporating CoCLR results in a further improvement of 10.5%.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we first utilize the word embedding that focuses on sub-word units to the Mongolian Phrase Break (PB) prediction task by using Long-Short-Term-Memory (LSTM) model. Mongolian is an agglutinative language. Each root can be followed by several suffixes to form probably millions of words, but the existing Mongolian corpus is not enough to build a robust entire word embedding, thus it suffers a serious data sparse problem and brings a great difficulty for Mongolian PB prediction. To solve this problem, we look at sub-word units in Mongolian word, and encode their information to a meaningful representation, then fed it to LSTM to decode the best corresponding PB label. Experimental results show that the proposed model significantly outperforms traditional CRF model using manually features and obtains 7.49% F-Measure gain.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a solution to the Mongolian Phrase Break (PB) prediction task using a Long-Short-Term-Memory (LSTM) model with a focus on sub-word units. Mongolian is an agglutinative language, where a root word can be followed by multiple suffixes to form a potentially unlimited number of words. The existing Mongolian corpus, however, is insufficient to create a comprehensive word embedding, resulting in a serious data sparsity problem and hindering the PB prediction process. To overcome this, we encode the information of sub-word units in Mongolian words into a meaningful representation and use it as input for the LSTM model to predict the corresponding PB label. The results of our experiment show that the proposed model outperforms the traditional CRF model with manually designed features, with a 7.49% increase in F-Measure.

label: acl
text: Recent work on controlled text generation has either required attribute-based fine-tuning of the base language model (LM), or has restricted the parameterization of the attribute discriminator to be compatible with the base autoregressive LM. In this work, we propose Mix and Match LM, a global score-based alternative for controllable text generation that combines arbitrary pre-trained black-box models for achieving the desired attributes in the generated text without involving any fine-tuning or structural assumptions about the black-box models. We interpret the task of controllable generation as drawing samples from an energy-based model whose energy values are a linear combination of scores from black-box models that are separately responsible for fluency, the control attribute, and faithfulness to any conditioning context. We use a Metropolis-Hastings sampling scheme to sample from this energy-based model using bidirectional context and global attribute features. We validate the effectiveness of our approach on various controlled generation and style-based text revision tasks by outperforming recently proposed methods that involve extra training, fine-tuning, or restrictive assumptions over the form of models.

label: acl
text: In recent work on controlled text generation, either attribute-based fine-tuning of the base language model (LM) was required, or the parameterization of the attribute discriminator was restricted to be compatible with the base autoregressive LM. To address this issue, we present Mix and Match LM, a global score-based approach for controllable text generation that combines pre-trained black-box models without requiring fine-tuning or making structural assumptions about the black-box models. Our approach views controllable generation as drawing samples from an energy-based model, whose energy values are a linear combination of scores from black-box models responsible for fluency, control attributes, and faithfulness to the conditioning context. We use a Metropolis-Hastings sampling scheme with bidirectional context and global attribute features to sample from this energy-based model. Our approach outperforms recently proposed methods that require extra training, fine-tuning, or restrictive assumptions about the form of models in various controlled generation and style-based text revision tasks.

label: coling
text: Word sense disambiguation (WSD), identifying the most suitable meaning of ambiguous words in the given contexts according to a predefined sense inventory, is one of the most classical and challenging tasks in natural language processing. Benefiting from the powerful ability of deep neural networks, WSD has achieved a great advancement in recent years. Reformulating WSD as a text span extraction task is an effective approach, which accepts a sentence context of an ambiguous word together with all definitions of its candidate senses simultaneously, and requires to extract the text span corresponding with the right sense. However, the approach merely depends on a short definition to learn sense representation, which neglects abundant semantic knowledge from related senses and leads to data-inefficient learning and suboptimal WSD performance. To address the limitations, we propose a novel WSD method with Knowledge-Enhanced and Local Self-Attention-based Extractive Sense Comprehension (KELESC). Specifically, a knowledge-enhanced method is proposed to enrich semantic representation by incorporating additional examples and definitions of the related senses in WordNet. Then, in order to avoid the huge computing complexity induced by the additional information, a local self-attention mechanism is utilized to constrain attention to be local, which allows longer input texts without large-scale computing burdens. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that KELESC achieves better performance than baseline models on public benchmark datasets.

label: coling
text: The task of word sense disambiguation (WSD), which involves identifying the most suitable meaning of ambiguous words in a given context based on a predefined sense inventory, is a classical and challenging aspect of natural language processing. With the powerful capabilities of deep neural networks, recent advancements have been made in WSD. One effective approach to WSD is to reformulate it as a text span extraction task, where a sentence context of an ambiguous word and all definitions of its candidate senses are simultaneously accepted, and the text span corresponding to the correct sense is extracted. However, this approach only relies on a short definition to learn sense representation, neglecting the abundance of semantic knowledge from related senses, leading to inefficiencies in data learning and suboptimal WSD performance. To address these limitations, we propose a novel WSD method, Knowledge-Enhanced and Local Self-Attention-based Extractive Sense Comprehension (KELESC), which enriches semantic representation by incorporating additional examples and definitions of related senses in WordNet. A local self-attention mechanism is used to constrain attention and avoid the large computing complexity that additional information would bring. Extensive experimental results show that KELESC outperforms baseline models on public benchmark datasets.

label: coling
text: Existing neural models usually predict the tag of the current token independent of the neighboring tags. The popular LSTM-CRF model considers the tag dependencies between every two consecutive tags. However, it is hard for existing neural models to take longer distance dependencies between tags into consideration. The scalability is mainly limited by the complex model structures and the cost of dynamic programming during training. In our work, we first design a new model called “high order LSTM” to predict multiple tags for the current token which contains not only the current tag but also the previous several tags. We call the number of tags in one prediction as “order”. Then we propose a new method called Multi-Order BiLSTM (MO-BiLSTM) which combines low order and high order LSTMs together. MO-BiLSTM keeps the scalability to high order models with a pruning technique. We evaluate MO-BiLSTM on all-phrase chunking and NER datasets. Experiment results show that MO-BiLSTM achieves the state-of-the-art result in chunking and highly competitive results in two NER datasets.

label: coling
text: Existing neural models typically predict the tag of a token independently of the neighboring tags. The popular LSTM-CRF model, however, considers the dependencies between every two consecutive tags. Yet, it can be challenging for these models to take into account longer-distance dependencies between tags. This is due to their complex model structures and the cost of dynamic programming during training, which limits their scalability. In our work, we introduce a novel model called "high-order LSTM" that predicts multiple tags for a token, including not only the current tag but also previous tags. The number of tags in each prediction is referred to as the "order." We then propose a new method, Multi-Order BiLSTM (MO-BiLSTM), which combines low- and high-order LSTMs. MO-BiLSTM maintains scalability with a pruning technique. We evaluate MO-BiLSTM on all-phrase chunking and NER datasets and find that it achieves state-of-the-art results in chunking and highly competitive results in two NER datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Sequence-to-Sequence (seq2seq) models have become overwhelmingly popular in building end-to-end trainable dialogue systems. Though highly efficient in learning the backbone of human-computer communications, they suffer from the problem of strongly favoring short generic responses. In this paper, we argue that a good response should smoothly connect both the preceding dialogue history and the following conversations. We strengthen this connection by mutual information maximization. To sidestep the non-differentiability of discrete natural language tokens, we introduce an auxiliary continuous code space and map such code space to a learnable prior distribution for generation purpose. Experiments on two dialogue datasets validate the effectiveness of our model, where the generated responses are closely related to the dialogue context and lead to more interactive conversations.

label: emnlp
text: The popularity of Sequence-to-Sequence (seq2seq) models in building end-to-end trainable dialogue systems has increased significantly. Despite their efficiency in learning the basics of human-computer communication, they tend to favor short, generic responses. This paper proposes a solution to this issue by maximizing mutual information to strengthen the connection between the preceding dialogue history and the following conversations. To overcome the non-differentiability of discrete natural language tokens, the authors introduce a continuous code space that is mapped to a learnable prior distribution for generating responses. The effectiveness of the model is validated through experiments on two dialogue datasets, resulting in more interactive conversations with responses closely related to the dialogue context.

label: acl
text: We propose a novel neural method to extract drug-drug interactions (DDIs) from texts using external drug molecular structure information. We encode textual drug pairs with convolutional neural networks and their molecular pairs with graph convolutional networks (GCNs), and then we concatenate the outputs of these two networks. In the experiments, we show that GCNs can predict DDIs from the molecular structures of drugs in high accuracy and the molecular information can enhance text-based DDI extraction by 2.39 percent points in the F-score on the DDIExtraction 2013 shared task data set.

label: acl
text: We propose a novel neural technique for extracting drug-drug interactions (DDIs) from text by incorporating external information on drug molecular structures. Our approach involves encoding textual drug pairs using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and molecular pairs using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). The outputs from both networks are then concatenated. Our experiments demonstrate that GCNs can accurately predict DDIs from drug molecular structures and incorporating molecular information can improve text-based DDI extraction by 2.39% in terms of F-score on the DDIExtraction 2013 shared task dataset.

label: emnlp
text: It has been argued that humans rapidly adapt their lexical and syntactic expectations to match the statistics of the current linguistic context. We provide further support to this claim by showing that the addition of a simple adaptation mechanism to a neural language model improves our predictions of human reading times compared to a non-adaptive model. We analyze the performance of the model on controlled materials from psycholinguistic experiments and show that it adapts not only to lexical items but also to abstract syntactic structures.

label: emnlp
text: The argument that humans quickly adjust their lexical and syntactic expectations to align with the statistics of the current linguistic context has been made. Our study provides additional support for this argument by demonstrating that incorporating a straightforward adaptation mechanism into a neural language model leads to improved predictions of human reading times compared to a non-adaptive model. Our analysis of the model's performance on controlled materials from psycholinguistic experiments reveals that it adapts not only to specific lexical items, but also to abstract syntactic structures.

label: acl
text: This paper focuses on detection tasks in information extraction, where positive instances are sparsely distributed and models are usually evaluated using F-measure on positive classes. These characteristics often result in deficient performance of neural network based detection models. In this paper, we propose adaptive scaling, an algorithm which can handle the positive sparsity problem and directly optimize over F-measure via dynamic cost-sensitive learning. To this end, we borrow the idea of marginal utility from economics and propose a theoretical framework for instance importance measuring without introducing any additional hyper-parameters. Experiments show that our algorithm leads to a more effective and stable training of neural network based detection models.

label: acl
text: This paper focuses on information extraction detection tasks, where positive instances are scarce and models are typically evaluated using the F-measure on positive classes. These conditions often result in subpar performance from neural network-based detection models. To address this issue, we introduce adaptive scaling, an algorithm that can handle the positive sparsity problem and directly optimize the F-measure through dynamic cost-sensitive learning. Our approach is based on the concept of marginal utility from economics and provides a theoretical framework for measuring instance importance without adding any extra hyperparameters. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our algorithm leads to a more effective and consistent training of neural network-based detection models.

label: naacl
text: Clinical notes are text documents that are created by clinicians for each patient encounter. They are typically accompanied by medical codes, which describe the diagnosis and treatment. Annotating these codes is labor intensive and error prone; furthermore, the connection between the codes and the text is not annotated, obscuring the reasons and details behind specific diagnoses and treatments. We present an attentional convolutional network that predicts medical codes from clinical text. Our method aggregates information across the document using a convolutional neural network, and uses an attention mechanism to select the most relevant segments for each of the thousands of possible codes. The method is accurate, achieving precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 of 0.54, which are both better than the prior state of the art. Furthermore, through an interpretability evaluation by a physician, we show that the attention mechanism identifies meaningful explanations for each code assignment.

label: naacl
text: Clinical notes are text documents that are created by healthcare providers during patient encounters, and they usually come with medical codes that describe the diagnosis and treatment. However, annotating these codes can be time-consuming and prone to errors, and the connection between codes and text is not always clear, making it difficult to understand the reasoning behind specific diagnoses and treatments. To address this issue, we have developed an attentional convolutional network that predicts medical codes from clinical text. Our system uses a convolutional neural network to gather information from the entire document, and an attention mechanism to highlight the most relevant segments for each of the thousands of possible codes. Our method is highly accurate, achieving a precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 of 0.54, which outperforms prior state-of-the-art results. Additionally, through a physician-led interpretability evaluation, we have demonstrated that the attention mechanism provides meaningful explanations for each code assignment.

label: acl
text: We present a targeted, scaled-up comparison of incremental processing in humans and neural language models by collecting by-word reaction time data for sixteen different syntactic test suites across a range of structural phenomena. Human reaction time data comes from a novel online experimental paradigm called the Interpolated Maze task. We compare human reaction times to by-word probabilities for four contemporary language models, with different architectures and trained on a range of data set sizes. We find that across many phenomena, both humans and language models show increased processing difficulty in ungrammatical sentence regions with human and model `accuracy' scores a la Marvin and Linzen (2018) about equal. However, although language model outputs match humans in direction, we show that models systematically under-predict the difference in magnitude of incremental processing difficulty between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences. Specifically, when models encounter syntactic violations they fail to accurately predict the longer reading times observed in the human data. These results call into question whether contemporary language models are approaching human-like performance for sensitivity to syntactic violations.

label: acl
text: We present a comprehensive comparison of incremental processing in humans and neural language models by collecting by-word reaction time data for 16 different syntactic test suites covering a range of structural phenomena. The human reaction time data was obtained through a novel online experimental paradigm called the Interpolated Maze task. We compared human reaction times to the by-word probabilities of four contemporary language models with varying architectures, trained on different data set sizes. Our results indicate that both humans and language models exhibit increased processing difficulty in ungrammatical sentence regions, with human and model accuracy scores being roughly equal. However, while the language models match human performance in terms of direction, they systematically under-predict the difference in magnitude of incremental processing difficulty between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences. Specifically, when encountering syntactic violations, the models fail to accurately predict the longer reading times observed in the human data. These findings raise questions about whether contemporary language models are truly achieving human-like performance in their sensitivity to syntactic violations.

label: emnlp
text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have met great success in abstractive summarization, but they cannot effectively generate summaries of desired lengths. Because generated summaries are used in difference scenarios which may have space or length constraints, the ability to control the summary length in abstractive summarization is an important problem. In this paper, we propose an approach to constrain the summary length by extending a convolutional sequence to sequence model. The results show that this approach generates high-quality summaries with user defined length, and outperforms the baselines consistently in terms of ROUGE score, length variations and semantic similarity.

label: emnlp
text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved great success in abstractive summarization, but they struggle to effectively generate summaries of a desired length. This is a significant challenge as generated summaries are used in various scenarios, which may have space or length constraints. To address this issue, we propose an approach to control the summary length by extending a convolutional sequence to sequence model. Our results demonstrate that this approach generates high-quality summaries of the desired length, consistently outperforming baselines in terms of ROUGE score, length variations, and semantic similarity.

label: acl
text: One of possible ways of obtaining continuous-space sentence representations is by training neural machine translation (NMT) systems. The recent attention mechanism however removes the single point in the neural network from which the source sentence representation can be extracted. We propose several variations of the attentive NMT architecture bringing this meeting point back. Empirical evaluation suggests that the better the translation quality, the worse the learned sentence representations serve in a wide range of classification and similarity tasks.

label: acl
text: One approach to obtaining continuous-space sentence representations is through training neural machine translation (NMT) systems. However, the recent attention mechanism eliminates the single point in the neural network from which the source sentence representation can be extracted. To address this issue, we propose several variations of the attentive NMT architecture that restore this meeting point. Our empirical evaluation shows that while the quality of translations improves, the learned sentence representations are less effective for a variety of classification and similarity tasks.

label: acl
text: On social media platforms, hateful and offensive language negatively impact the mental well-being of users and the participation of people from diverse backgrounds. Automatic methods to detect offensive language have largely relied on datasets with categorical labels. However, comments can vary in their degree of offensiveness. We create the first dataset of English language Reddit comments that has fine-grained, real-valued scores between -1 (maximally supportive) and 1 (maximally offensive). The dataset was annotated using Best–Worst Scaling, a form of comparative annotation that has been shown to alleviate known biases of using rating scales. We show that the method produces highly reliable offensiveness scores. Finally, we evaluate the ability of widely-used neural models to predict offensiveness scores on this new dataset.

label: acl
text: On social media platforms, the use of hateful and offensive language can have a negative impact on the mental well-being of users and hinder the participation of people from diverse backgrounds. To address this issue, automatic methods for detecting offensive language have largely relied on datasets with categorical labels. However, comments can vary greatly in their degree of offensiveness. To address this challenge, we have created the first dataset of English language Reddit comments that has fine-grained, real-valued scores between -1 (maximally supportive) and 1 (maximally offensive). This dataset was annotated using Best–Worst Scaling, a form of comparative annotation that has been proven to reduce biases that can arise from using rating scales. Our results show that this method is highly reliable in producing offensiveness scores. Finally, we have evaluated the ability of popular neural models to predict these offensiveness scores on this new dataset.

label: acl
text: AI technologies for Natural Languages have made tremendous progress recently. However, commensurate progress has not been made on Sign Languages, in particular, in recognizing signs as individual words or as complete sentences. We introduce OpenHands, a library where we take four key ideas from the NLP community for low-resource languages and apply them to sign languages for word-level recognition. First, we propose using pose extracted through pretrained models as the standard modality of data in this work to reduce training time and enable efficient inference, and we release standardized pose datasets for different existing sign language datasets. Second, we train and release checkpoints of 4 pose-based isolated sign language recognition models across 6 languages (American, Argentinian, Chinese, Greek, Indian, and Turkish), providing baselines and ready checkpoints for deployment. Third, to address the lack of labelled data, we propose self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled data. We curate and release the largest pose-based pretraining dataset on Indian Sign Language (Indian-SL). Fourth, we compare different pretraining strategies and for the first time establish that pretraining is effective for sign language recognition by demonstrating (a) improved fine-tuning performance especially in low-resource settings, and (b) high crosslingual transfer from Indian-SL to few other sign languages. We open-source all models and datasets in OpenHands with a hope that it makes research in sign languages reproducible and more accessible.

label: acl
text: The recent advancements in AI technologies for Natural Languages have not been matched by similar progress in Sign Languages, particularly in terms of recognizing individual words or complete sentences. To address this issue, we present OpenHands, a library that incorporates four key principles from NLP for low-resource languages and applies them to Sign Languages for word-level recognition. Firstly, we use pose extracted through pretrained models as the standard modality of data to reduce training time and improve efficiency. We also provide standardized pose datasets for various Sign Language datasets. Secondly, we train and release checkpoints for four pose-based isolated Sign Language recognition models across six languages, including American, Argentinian, Chinese, Greek, Indian, and Turkish. This provides baselines and ready-to-use checkpoints for deployment. Thirdly, to overcome the lack of labeled data, we propose self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled data. We have curated the largest pose-based pretraining dataset on Indian Sign Language (Indian-SL) and made it available. Finally, we compare different pretraining strategies and demonstrate, for the first time, that pretraining is effective for Sign Language recognition through improved fine-tuning performance, especially in low-resource settings, and high cross-lingual transfer from Indian-SL to other Sign Languages. All models and datasets in OpenHands are open-sourced in the hope of making research in Sign Languages more accessible and reproducible.

label: acl
text: Finetuning large pre-trained language models with a task-specific head has advanced the state-of-the-art on many natural language understanding benchmarks. However, models with a task-specific head require a lot of training data, making them susceptible to learning and exploiting dataset-specific superficial cues that do not generalize to other datasets.Prompting has reduced the data requirement by reusing the language model head and formatting the task input to match the pre-training objective. Therefore, it is expected that few-shot prompt-based models do not exploit superficial cues.This paper presents an empirical examination of whether few-shot prompt-based models also exploit superficial cues.Analyzing few-shot prompt-based models on MNLI, SNLI, HANS, and COPA has revealed that prompt-based models also exploit superficial cues. While the models perform well on instances with superficial cues, they often underperform or only marginally outperform random accuracy on instances without superficial cues.

label: acl
text: Fine-tuning large pre-trained language models with task-specific heads has significantly improved the state of the art on various natural language understanding benchmarks. However, these models are highly dependent on large amounts of training data and can easily learn and exploit superficial cues that are specific to the dataset, resulting in poor generalization to other datasets. To reduce the data requirements, prompting has been introduced, which reuses the language model head and formats the task input to align with the pre-training objective. It was believed that this approach would prevent the exploitation of superficial cues. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of whether few-shot prompt-based models also exploit superficial cues. The analysis of these models on MNLI, SNLI, HANS, and COPA shows that they indeed exploit superficial cues. Despite performing well on instances with superficial cues, they either underperform or only slightly outperform random accuracy on instances without such cues.

label: acl
text: In linguistics, there are two main perspectives on negation: a semantic and a pragmatic view. So far, research in NLP on negation has almost exclusively adhered to the semantic view. In this article, we adopt the pragmatic paradigm to conduct a study of negation understanding focusing on transformer-based PLMs. Our results differ from previous, semantics-based studies and therefore help to contribute a more comprehensive – and, given the results, much more optimistic – picture of the PLMs' negation understanding.

label: acl
text: In linguistics, two main perspectives on negation exist: a semantic perspective and a pragmatic perspective. To date, research on negation in NLP has almost exclusively followed the semantic view. This article takes a pragmatic approach to studying negation understanding in transformer-based PLMs. Our findings, which differ from previous studies that relied on a semantic perspective, contribute to a more comprehensive and optimistic understanding of PLMs' negation capabilities.

label: naacl
text: Automatic evaluation systems in the field of automatic summarization have been relying on the availability of gold standard summaries for over ten years. Gold standard summaries are expensive to obtain and often require the availability of domain experts to achieve high quality. In this paper, we propose an alternative evaluation approach based on pairwise preferences of sentences. In comparison to gold standard summaries, they are simpler and cheaper to obtain. In our experiments, we show that humans are able to provide useful feedback in the form of pairwise preferences. The new framework performs better than the three most popular versions of ROUGE with less expensive human input. We also show that our framework can reuse already available evaluation data and achieve even better results.

label: naacl
text: Automatic summarization systems have relied on the use of gold standard summaries for over a decade. However, these summaries are both costly to obtain and require the input of domain experts to ensure their quality. In this paper, we present an alternative evaluation approach that uses pairwise sentence preferences. This method is simpler and more cost-effective than the use of gold standard summaries. Our experiments demonstrate that human feedback in the form of pairwise preferences is valuable, and our framework outperforms the three most widely used versions of ROUGE with less human input required. Additionally, our framework can leverage existing evaluation data to achieve even better results.

label: naacl
text: We present a content-based method for recommending citations in an academic paper draft. We embed a given query document into a vector space, then use its nearest neighbors as candidates, and rerank the candidates using a discriminative model trained to distinguish between observed and unobserved citations. Unlike previous work, our method does not require metadata such as author names which can be missing, e.g., during the peer review process. Without using metadata, our method outperforms the best reported results on PubMed and DBLP datasets with relative improvements of over 18% in F1@20 and over 22% in MRR. We show empirically that, although adding metadata improves the performance on standard metrics, it favors self-citations which are less useful in a citation recommendation setup. We release an online portal for citation recommendation based on our method, (URL: http://bit.ly/citeDemo) and a new dataset OpenCorpus of 7 million research articles to facilitate future research on this task.

label: naacl
text: We propose a content-based method for recommending citations in academic paper drafts. Our method embeds the query document into a vector space and uses its nearest neighbors as candidates. These candidates are then reranked using a discriminative model trained to distinguish between observed and unobserved citations. Unlike previous work, our approach does not rely on metadata such as author names, which can be missing during the peer review process. Our method outperforms the existing results on PubMed and DBLP datasets, delivering relative improvements of over 18% in F1@20 and over 22% in MRR. Our experiments also demonstrate that, while metadata can improve the performance on standard metrics, it tends to favor self-citations, which are less useful in a citation recommendation setup. To facilitate future research in this area, we have created an online portal for citation recommendation (http://bit.ly/citeDemo) and a new dataset, OpenCorpus, consisting of 7 million research articles.

label: coling
text: The spread of fake news can have devastating ramifications, and recent advancements to neural fake news generators have made it challenging to understand how misinformation generated by these models may best be confronted. We conduct a feature-based study to gain an interpretative understanding of the linguistic attributes that neural fake news generators may most successfully exploit. When comparing models trained on subsets of our features and confronting the models with increasingly advanced neural fake news, we find that stylistic features may be the most robust. We discuss our findings, subsequent analyses, and broader implications in the pages within.

label: coling
text: The proliferation of fake news can cause devastating consequences, and recent advancements in neural fake news generators have made it difficult to determine the best way to counter misinformation generated by these models. To gain a better understanding of the linguistic attributes that neural fake news generators may exploit, we conducted a feature-based study. Our results showed that stylistic features may be the most robust when comparing models trained on different subsets of features and facing increasingly advanced neural fake news. In the following pages, we will delve into our findings, further analysis, and broader implications.

label: naacl
text: Natural language processing researchers have identified limitations of evaluation methodology for generation tasks, with new questions raised about the validity of automatic metrics and of crowdworker judgments. Meanwhile, efforts to improve generation models tend to depend on simple n-gram overlap metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE). We argue that new advances on models and metrics should each more directly benefit and inform the other. We therefore propose a generalization of leaderboards, bidimensional leaderboards (Billboards), that simultaneously tracks progress in language generation models and metrics for their evaluation. Unlike conventional unidimensional leaderboards that sort submitted systems by predetermined metrics, a Billboard accepts both generators and evaluation metrics as competing entries. A Billboard automatically creates an ensemble metric that selects and linearly combines a few metrics based on a global analysis across generators. Further, metrics are ranked based on their correlation with human judgments. We release four Billboards for machine translation, summarization, and image captioning. We demonstrate that a linear ensemble of a few diverse metrics sometimes substantially outperforms existing metrics in isolation. Our mixed-effects model analysis shows that most automatic metrics, especially the reference-based ones, overrate machine over human generation, demonstrating the importance of updating metrics as generation models become stronger (and perhaps more similar to humans) in the future.

label: naacl
text: The limitations of evaluation methodology for natural language processing generation tasks have been identified by researchers, leading to questions about the validity of automatic metrics and crowdworker judgments. To improve generation models, simple n-gram overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE are often used. The authors propose a new approach, bidimensional leaderboards (Billboards), that tracks progress in both language generation models and metrics for their evaluation. Unlike traditional leaderboards, Billboards accept both generators and evaluation metrics as competing entries and create an ensemble metric based on a global analysis across generators. The metrics are ranked based on their correlation with human judgments. The authors release four Billboards for machine translation, summarization, and image captioning and demonstrate that a linear ensemble of a few diverse metrics can outperform existing metrics in isolation. A mixed-effects model analysis shows that most automatic metrics overrate machine over human generation, highlighting the need to update metrics as generation models become stronger and more human-like.

label: acl
text: A recent study by Feldman (2020) proposed a long-tail theory to explain the memorization behavior of deep learning models. However, memorization has not been empirically verified in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work. In this paper, we use three different NLP tasks to check if the long-tail theory holds. Our experiments demonstrate that top-ranked memorized training instances are likely atypical, and removing the top-memorized training instances leads to a more serious drop in test accuracy compared with removing training instances randomly. Furthermore, we develop an attribution method to better understand why a training instance is memorized. We empirically show that our memorization attribution method is faithful, and share our interesting finding that the top-memorized parts of a training instance tend to be features negatively correlated with the class label.

label: acl
text: A recent study by Feldman (2020) put forth a long-tail theory to explain the deep learning models' memorization behavior. However, the theory has not been tested in the context of NLP, a gap that this study aims to address. This paper uses three NLP tasks to verify if the long-tail theory holds. Our experiments show that the top-ranked memorized training instances are likely atypical, and removing them leads to a greater decrease in test accuracy compared to removing training instances randomly. Additionally, we introduce an attribution method to better understand why a training instance is memorized. Our results demonstrate that the method is reliable, and we also find that the top-memorized parts of a training instance tend to be features negatively correlated with the class label.

label: acl
text: This paper presents a novel method for nested named entity recognition. As a layered method, our method extends the prior second-best path recognition method by explicitly excluding the influence of the best path. Our method maintains a set of hidden states at each time step and selectively leverages them to build a different potential function for recognition at each level. In addition, we demonstrate that recognizing innermost entities first results in better performance than the conventional outermost entities first scheme. We provide extensive experimental results on ACE2004, ACE2005, and GENIA datasets to show the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method.

label: acl
text: This paper introduces a new approach to nested named entity recognition. Our method, which is based on a layered approach, extends the previous second-best path recognition method by eliminating the impact of the best path. Our method utilizes a set of hidden states at each time step to construct a unique potential function for recognition at each level. Furthermore, our findings suggest that recognizing the innermost entities first leads to improved performance compared to the traditional approach of recognizing the outermost entities first. Through extensive experiments on the ACE2004, ACE2005, and GENIA datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method.

label: coling
text: Within the natural language processing community, English is by far the most resource-rich language. There is emerging interest in conducting translation via computational approaches to conform its dialects or creole languages back to standard English. This computational approach paves the way to leverage generic English language backbones, which are beneficial for various downstream tasks. However, in practical online communication scenarios, the use of language varieties is often accompanied by noisy user-generated content, making this translation task more challenging. In this work, we introduce a joint paraphrasing task of creole translation and text normalization of Singlish messages, which can shed light on how to process other language varieties and dialects. We formulate the task in three different linguistic dimensions: lexical level normalization, syntactic level editing, and semantic level rewriting. We build an annotated dataset of Singlish-to-Standard English messages, and report performance on a perturbation-resilient sequence-to-sequence model. Experimental results show that the model produces reasonable generation results, and can improve the performance of downstream tasks like stance detection.

label: coling
text: The natural language processing community has a wealth of resources for English, but there is growing interest in using computational approaches to translate dialects or creole languages back to standard English. This approach utilizes generic English language backbones, which are useful for various NLP tasks. However, online communication scenarios often involve noisy user-generated content, making the translation task more challenging. This work presents a joint paraphrasing task of creole translation and text normalization for Singlish messages, which can inform the processing of other language varieties and dialects. The task is formulated in three linguistic dimensions: lexical-level normalization, syntactic-level editing, and semantic-level rewriting. The authors build an annotated dataset of Singlish-to-Standard English messages and evaluate the performance of a perturbation-resilient sequence-to-sequence model. The results show that the model generates reasonable results and improves the performance of downstream tasks, such as stance detection.

label: acl
text: Paraphrase generation has been widely used in various downstream tasks. Most tasks benefit mainly from high quality paraphrases, namely those that are semantically similar to, yet linguistically diverse from, the original sentence. Generating high-quality paraphrases is challenging as it becomes increasingly hard to preserve meaning as linguistic diversity increases. Recent works achieve nice results by controlling specific aspects of the paraphrase, such as its syntactic tree. However, they do not allow to directly control the quality of the generated paraphrase, and suffer from low flexibility and scalability. Here we propose QCPG, a quality-guided controlled paraphrase generation model, that allows directly controlling the quality dimensions. Furthermore, we suggest a method that given a sentence, identifies points in the quality control space that are expected to yield optimal generated paraphrases. We show that our method is able to generate paraphrases which maintain the original meaning while achieving higher diversity than the uncontrolled baseline. The models, the code, and the data can be found in https://github.com/IBM/quality-controlled-paraphrase-generation.

label: acl
text: The use of paraphrase generation has become widespread in a variety of downstream tasks, with most tasks benefiting from high-quality paraphrases that are semantically similar to the original sentence but linguistically diverse. However, generating high-quality paraphrases is challenging, as it becomes more difficult to preserve meaning as linguistic diversity increases. While recent works have achieved good results by controlling specific aspects of the paraphrase, such as its syntactic tree, they do not allow direct control over the quality of the generated paraphrase and have limitations in terms of flexibility and scalability. To address this issue, we propose a quality-guided controlled paraphrase generation model (QCPG) that enables direct control over quality dimensions. Additionally, we present a method that identifies optimal points in the quality control space for a given sentence. Our results demonstrate that our method can generate paraphrases that maintain the original meaning while achieving higher diversity than the uncontrolled baseline. The models, code, and data can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/quality-controlled-paraphrase-generation.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a set of dimensions to characterize the association between two people. We distinguish between interactions (when somebody refers to somebody in a conversation) and relationships (a sequence of interactions). We work with dialogue scripts from the TV show Friends, and do not impose any restrictions on the interactions and relationships. We introduce and analyze a new corpus, and present experimental results showing that the task can be automated.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a comprehensive set of dimensions for characterizing the association between two individuals. We differentiate between interactions, which refer to instances where one person mentions another in a conversation, and relationships, which are comprised of a series of interactions. Using dialogue scripts from the popular TV show Friends, we conduct our analysis without imposing any limitations on the interactions and relationships. We introduce and analyze a new corpus, and present experimental results demonstrating the feasibility of automating the task.

label: coling
text: This paper describes CzEngClass, a bilingual lexical resource being built to investigate verbal synonymy in bilingual context and to relate semantic roles common to one synonym class to verb arguments (verb valency). In addition, the resource is linked to existing resources with the same of a similar aim: English and Czech WordNet, FrameNet, PropBank, VerbNet (SemLink), and valency lexicons for Czech and English (PDT-Vallex, Vallex, and EngVallex). There are several goals of this work and resource: (a) to provide gold standard data for automatic experiments in the future (such as automatic discovery of synonym classes, word sense disambiguation, assignment of classes to occurrences of verbs in text, coreferential linking of verb and event arguments in text, etc.), (b) to build a core (bilingual) lexicon linked to existing resources, for comparative studies and possibly for training automatic tools, and (c) to enrich the annotation of a parallel treebank, the Prague Czech English Dependency Treebank, which so far contained valency annotation but has not linked synonymous senses of verbs together. The method used for extracting the synonym classes is a semi-automatic process with a substantial amount of manual work during filtering, role assignment to classes and individual Class members' arguments, and linking to the external lexical resources. We present the first version with 200 classes (about 1800 verbs) and evaluate interannotator agreement using several metrics.

label: coling
text:
The results show that the agreement is good, with a mean of 0.70 for the F1 measure. The resource is available online and open access.

This paper presents CzEngClass, a bilingual lexical resource aimed at investigating verbal synonymy in a bilingual context. The resource links semantic roles common to one synonym class to verb arguments (verb valency) and is connected to existing resources, such as English and Czech WordNet, FrameNet, PropBank, VerbNet (SemLink), and valency lexicons for Czech and English (PDT-Vallex, Vallex, and EngVallex). The goals of this work and resource are to provide gold standard data for future automatic experiments (such as automatic discovery of synonym classes, word sense disambiguation, assignment of classes to verb occurrences in text, coreferential linking of verb and event arguments in text, etc.), to build a core (bilingual) lexicon linked to existing resources for comparative studies and possible training of automatic tools, and to enrich the annotation of the Prague Czech English Dependency Treebank. The method used to extract synonym classes is a semi-automatic process with substantial manual filtering, role assignment, and linking to external lexical resources. The first version of CzEngClass includes 200 classes (approximately 1800 verbs) and the interannotator agreement was evaluated using several metrics, with a mean F1 measure of 0.70. The resource is open access and available online.

label: coling
text: Event detection aims to detect events from the text by identifying and classifying event triggers (the most representative words). Most of the existing works rely heavily on complex downstream networks and require sufficient training data. Thus, those models may be structurally redundant and perform poorly when data is scarce. Prompt-based models are easy to build and are promising for few-shot tasks. However, current prompt-based methods may suffer from low precision because they have not introduced event-related semantic knowledge (e.g., part of speech, semantic correlation, etc.). To address these problems, this paper proposes a Knowledge-injected Prompt Tuning (KiPT) model. Specifically, the event detection task is formulated into a condition generation task. Then, knowledge-injected prompts are constructed using external knowledge bases, and a prompt tuning strategy is leveraged to optimize the prompts. Extensive experiments indicate that KiPT outperforms strong baselines, especially in few-shot scenarios.

label: coling
text: The aim of event detection is to identify and classify event triggers in text, represented by the most representative words. Most existing methods rely heavily on complex downstream networks and require a large amount of training data, making them structurally redundant and prone to poor performance when data is limited. A promising alternative is prompt-based models, which are easy to construct and well-suited for few-shot tasks. However, these methods may have low precision due to the lack of event-related semantic knowledge, such as part of speech and semantic correlation. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a Knowledge-injected Prompt Tuning (KiPT) model. The event detection task is transformed into a condition generation task, and external knowledge bases are utilized to construct knowledge-injected prompts. A prompt tuning strategy is also employed to optimize the prompts. The results of our experiments show that KiPT outperforms strong baselines, particularly in few-shot scenarios.

label: coling
text: Unsupervised contrastive sentence embedding models, e.g., unsupervised SimCSE, use the InfoNCE loss function in training. Theoretically, we expect to use larger batches to get more adequate comparisons among samples and avoid overfitting. However, increasing batch size leads to performance degradation when it exceeds a threshold, which is probably due to the introduction of false-negative pairs through statistical observation. To alleviate this problem, we introduce a simple smoothing strategy upon the InfoNCE loss function, termed Gaussian Smoothed InfoNCE (GS-InfoNCE). In other words, we add random Gaussian noise as an extension to the negative pairs without increasing the batch size. Through experiments on the semantic text similarity tasks, though simple, the proposed smoothing strategy brings improvements to unsupervised SimCSE.

label: coling
text: Unsupervised contrastive sentence embedding models, such as unsupervised SimCSE, use the InfoNCE loss function during training. In theory, larger batches are expected to provide more accurate comparisons among samples and prevent overfitting.
