However, when the batch size exceeds a certain threshold, performance begins to degrade, likely due to the introduction of false-negative pairs through statistical observation. To address this issue, we propose a simple smoothing strategy, called Gaussian Smoothed InfoNCE (GS-InfoNCE), which extends the InfoNCE loss function by adding random Gaussian noise to the negative pairs without increasing the batch size. Through experiments on semantic text similarity tasks, our simple smoothing strategy demonstrates improved results for unsupervised SimCSE.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a sequence to sequence (seq2seq) dependency parser by directly predicting the relative position of head for each given word, which therefore results in a truly end-to-end seq2seq dependency parser for the first time. Enjoying the advantage of seq2seq modeling, we enrich a series of embedding enhancement, including firstly introduced subword and node2vec augmentation. Meanwhile, we propose a beam search decoder with tree constraint and subroot decomposition over the sequence to furthermore enhance our seq2seq parser. Our parser is evaluated on benchmark treebanks, being on par with the state-of-the-art parsers by achieving 94.11% UAS on PTB and 88.78% UAS on CTB, respectively.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a novel sequence to sequence (seq2seq) dependency parser by directly predicting the relative position of the head for each word. This results in a truly end-to-end seq2seq parser for the first time. The seq2seq model is enhanced with various embedding techniques, including the introduction of subword and node2vec augmentations. Additionally, a beam search decoder with tree constraint and subroot decomposition is proposed to further improve the parser. The parser is evaluated on benchmark treebanks and performs on par with state-of-the-art parsers, achieving 94.11% UAS on PTB and 88.78% UAS on CTB.

label: coling
text: Incrementality is ubiquitous in human-human interaction and beneficial for human-computer interaction. It has been a topic of research in different parts of the NLP community, mostly with focus on the specific topic at hand even though incremental systems have to deal with similar challenges regardless of domain. In this survey, I consolidate and categorize the approaches, identifying similarities and differences in the computation and data, and show trade-offs that have to be considered. A focus lies on evaluating incremental systems because the standard metrics often fail to capture the incremental properties of a system and coming up with a suitable evaluation scheme is non-trivial.

label: coling
text: The concept of incrementality is prevalent in human-human interactions and can also be beneficial in human-computer interactions. Despite being a widely researched topic in various areas of the NLP community, most studies focus on specific topics without considering the common challenges faced by incremental systems across domains. This survey aims to consolidate and categorize existing approaches, highlighting similarities and differences in computation and data, and exploring the trade-offs that must be considered. A significant emphasis is placed on evaluating incremental systems, as standard metrics often fail to capture the incremental properties of these systems, and developing a suitable evaluation scheme is challenging.

label: naacl
text: Recursive noun phrases (NPs) have interesting semantic properties. For example, “my favorite new movie” is not necessarily my favorite movie, whereas “my new favorite movie” is. This is common sense to humans, yet it is unknown whether language models have such knowledge. We introduce the Recursive Noun Phrase Challenge (RNPC), a dataset of three textual inference tasks involving textual entailment and event plausibility comparison, precisely targeting the understanding of recursive NPs. When evaluated on RNPC, state-of-the-art Transformer models only perform around chance. Still, we show that such knowledge is learnable with appropriate data. We further probe the models for relevant linguistic features that can be learned from our tasks, including modifier semantic category and modifier scope. Finally, models trained on RNPC achieve strong zero-shot performance on an extrinsic Harm Detection evaluation task, showing the usefulness of the understanding of recursive NPs in downstream applications.

label: naacl
text: Recursive noun phrases (NPs) have intriguing semantic properties, such as the fact that "my favorite new movie" is not necessarily my favorite movie, while "my new favorite movie" is. Despite this being common sense to humans, it is unclear if language models possess this knowledge. To address this, we introduce the Recursive Noun Phrase Challenge (RNPC), a dataset of three textual inference tasks that test understanding of recursive NPs through textual entailment and event plausibility comparison. When evaluated on RNPC, state-of-the-art Transformer models perform only at chance levels, but we demonstrate that this knowledge is learnable with the right data. We examine the models for the presence of relevant linguistic features, including modifier semantic category and scope, and find that models trained on RNPC exhibit strong zero-shot performance on an extrinsic Harm Detection task, demonstrating the practical applications of understanding recursive NPs.

label: naacl
text: Automatic identification of spurious instances (those with potentially wrong labels in datasets) can improve the quality of existing language resources, especially when annotations are obtained through crowdsourcing or automatically generated based on coded rankings. In this paper, we present effective approaches inspired by queueing theory and psychology of learning to automatically identify spurious instances in datasets. Our approaches discriminate instances based on their “difficulty to learn,” determined by a downstream learner. Our methods can be applied to any dataset assuming the existence of a neural network model for the target task of the dataset. Our best approach outperforms competing state-of-the-art baselines and has a MAP of 0.85 and 0.22 in identifying spurious instances in synthetic and carefully-crowdsourced real-world datasets respectively.

label: naacl
text: The automatic identification of potentially incorrect instances in datasets, commonly referred to as "spurious instances," can significantly enhance the quality of language resources, especially when annotations are obtained through crowdsourcing or generated automatically through coded rankings. This paper presents innovative approaches, inspired by the principles of queueing theory and learning psychology, for automatically identifying such instances. Our methods differentiate instances based on their "difficulty to learn," as determined by a downstream learner, and can be applied to any dataset that has a neural network model for the target task. Our best approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with a MAP of 0.85 and 0.22 for identifying spurious instances in synthetic and real-world datasets, respectively.

label: acl
text: Mechanisms for encoding positional information are central for transformer-based language models. In this paper, we analyze the position embeddings of existing language models, finding strong evidence of translation invariance, both for the embeddings themselves and for their effect on self-attention. The degree of translation invariance increases during training and correlates positively with model performance. Our findings lead us to propose translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), which accounts for the relative position between tokens in an interpretable fashion without needing conventional position embeddings. Our proposal has several theoretical advantages over existing position-representation approaches. Proof-of-concept experiments show that it improves on regular ALBERT on GLUE tasks, while only adding orders of magnitude less positional parameters.

label: acl
text: The encoding of positional information is crucial for transformer-based language models. In this study, we examine the position embeddings of existing language models and discover robust evidence of translation invariance for both the embeddings and their impact on self-attention. This translation invariance increases during training and is positively correlated with improved model performance. Based on these findings, we introduce the concept of Translation-Invariant Self-Attention (TISA), which represents the relative position between tokens in a clear and concise manner, without relying on traditional position embeddings. Our proposal offers several theoretical advantages over current position representation methods and proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate its effectiveness, as it enhances the performance of regular ALBERT on GLUE tasks while requiring significantly fewer positional parameters.

label: acl
text: Recent work in neural machine translation has demonstrated both the necessity and feasibility of using inter-sentential context, context from sentences other than those currently being translated. However, while many current methods present model architectures that theoretically can use this extra context, it is often not clear how much they do actually utilize it at translation time. In this paper, we introduce a new metric, conditional cross-mutual information, to quantify usage of context by these models. Using this metric, we measure how much document-level machine translation systems use particular varieties of context. We find that target context is referenced more than source context, and that including more context has a diminishing affect on results. We then introduce a new, simple training method, context-aware word dropout, to increase the usage of context by context-aware models. Experiments show that our method not only increases context usage, but also improves the translation quality according to metrics such as BLEU and COMET, as well as performance on anaphoric pronoun resolution and lexical cohesion contrastive datasets.

label: acl
text: Recent studies in neural machine translation have shown the importance and practicality of using inter-sentential context, which refers to context from sentences other than those currently being translated. Despite the availability of model architectures that can theoretically incorporate this extra context, it remains unclear how much they actually use it during translation. To address this issue, we introduce a new metric, conditional cross-mutual information, to quantify the usage of context by these models. Our findings indicate that target context is used more frequently than source context, and that the impact of adding more context decreases over time. To enhance the usage of context, we propose a new training method, called context-aware word dropout, which not only increases context usage but also results in improved translation quality based on metrics such as BLEU and COMET, as well as improved performance on datasets for anaphoric pronoun resolution and lexical cohesion contrast.

label: emnlp
text: Causal understanding is essential for many kinds of decision-making, but causal inference from observational data has typically only been applied to structured, low-dimensional datasets. While text classifiers produce low-dimensional outputs, their use in causal inference has not previously been studied. To facilitate causal analyses based on language data, we consider the role that text classifiers can play in causal inference through established modeling mechanisms from the causality literature on missing data and measurement error. We demonstrate how to conduct causal analyses using text classifiers on simulated and Yelp data, and discuss the opportunities and challenges of future work that uses text data in causal inference.

label: emnlp
text: Causal understanding is crucial for effective decision-making in various fields, yet causal inference from observational data has traditionally only been applied to structured datasets with low dimensionality. The use of text classifiers in causal inference has not been explored previously, despite the low-dimensional outputs produced by these models. In this study, we examine how text classifiers can be utilized in causal inference by incorporating established modeling techniques from the causality literature on missing data and measurement error. Through simulations and analysis of Yelp data, we demonstrate the feasibility of conducting causal analyses using text classifiers and highlight the potential and challenges of future work in this area.

label: emnlp
text: Universal sentence encoding is a hot topic in recent NLP research. Attention mechanism has been an integral part in many sentence encoding models, allowing the models to capture context dependencies regardless of the distance between the elements in the sequence. Fully attention-based models have recently attracted enormous interest due to their highly parallelizable computation and significantly less training time. However, the memory consumption of their models grows quadratically with the sentence length, and the syntactic information is neglected. To this end, we propose Phrase-level Self-Attention Networks (PSAN) that perform self-attention across words inside a phrase to capture context dependencies at the phrase level, and use the gated memory updating mechanism to refine each word's representation hierarchically with longer-term context dependencies captured in a larger phrase. As a result, the memory consumption can be reduced because the self-attention is performed at the phrase level instead of the sentence level. At the same time, syntactic information can be easily integrated in the model. Experiment results show that PSAN can achieve the state-of-the-art performance across a plethora of NLP tasks including binary and multi-class classification, natural language inference and sentence similarity.

label: emnlp
text: Universal sentence encoding is a current topic of interest in NLP research. Attention mechanisms have been a crucial component in many sentence encoding models, allowing them to capture context dependencies, regardless of the distance between elements in a sequence. Recently, fully attention-based models have gained significant attention due to their highly parallelizable computation and reduced training time. However, these models have a drawback in that their memory consumption increases quadratically with sentence length and they neglect syntactic information. To address these issues, we propose Phrase-level Self-Attention Networks (PSAN), which perform self-attention across words within a phrase to capture context dependencies at the phrase level. Additionally, our model uses a gated memory updating mechanism to refine each word's representation, hierarchically incorporating longer-term context dependencies captured in larger phrases. This results in reduced memory consumption, as self-attention is performed at the phrase level rather than the sentence level, and enables the integration of syntactic information into the model. Our experiments show that PSAN achieves state-of-the-art performance across a range of NLP tasks, including binary and multi-class classification, natural language inference, and sentence similarity.

label: acl
text: We propose an effective context-sensitive neural model for time to event (TTE) prediction task, which aims to predict the amount of time to/from the occurrence of given events in streaming content. We investigate this problem in the context of a multi-task learning framework, which we enrich with time difference embeddings. In addition, we develop a multi-genre dataset of English events about soccer competitions and academy awards ceremonies, and their relevant tweets obtained from Twitter. Our model is 1.4 and 3.3 hours more accurate than the current state-of-the-art model in estimating TTE on English and Dutch tweets respectively. We examine different aspects of our model to illustrate its source of improvement.

label: acl
text: We propose an efficient context-sensitive neural model for predicting time to event (TTE) in streaming content. Our aim is to accurately estimate the amount of time until or since the occurrence of specified events. Our approach involves multi-task learning and the incorporation of time difference embeddings. To validate our model, we have created a multi-genre dataset of English events related to soccer competitions and academy awards ceremonies, as well as their corresponding tweets from Twitter. Our model outperforms the current state-of-the-art model by 1.4 and 3.3 hours in estimating TTE for English and Dutch tweets respectively. We also analyze various aspects of our model to showcase its improvement.

label: emnlp
text: Most text-classification approaches represent the input based on textual features, either feature-based or continuous. However, this ignores strong non-linguistic similarities like homophily: people within a demographic group use language more similar to each other than to non-group members. We use homophily cues to retrofit text-based author representations with non-linguistic information, and introduce a trade-off parameter. This approach increases in-class similarity between authors, and improves classification performance by making classes more linearly separable. We evaluate the effect of our method on two author-attribute prediction tasks with various training-set sizes and parameter settings. We find that our method can significantly improve classification performance, especially when the number of labels is large and limited labeled data is available. It is potentially applicable as preprocessing step to any text-classification task.

label: emnlp
text: Most text-classification approaches only consider textual features, either feature-based or continuous, ignoring non-linguistic similarities such as homophily. Homophily refers to the idea that people within a demographic group tend to use language that is more similar to each other than to non-group members. To address this issue, we propose a method that retrofits text-based author representations with non-linguistic information and introduces a trade-off parameter. This enhances the in-class similarity between authors, making classes more linearly separable and improving classification performance. Our method was evaluated on two author-attribute prediction tasks with various training-set sizes and parameter settings, and the results showed significant improvement in classification performance, especially when the number of labels is large and there is limited labeled data available. This method can potentially be used as a preprocessing step for any text-classification task.

label: coling
text: We investigate the birth and diffusion of lexical innovations in a large dataset of online social communities. We build on sociolinguistic theories and focus on the relation between the spread of a novel term and the social role of the individuals who use it, uncovering characteristics of innovators and adopters. Finally, we perform a prediction task that allows us to anticipate whether an innovation will successfully spread within a community.

label: coling
text: We delve into the origins and dissemination of lexical innovations in a vast collection of online social networks. Our study is based on sociolinguistic principles and concentrates on the correlation between the spread of a new term and the social status of those who employ it. By doing so, we uncover the defining traits of both innovators and adopters. Ultimately, we carry out a predictive analysis to determine the likelihood of a lexical innovation's successful diffusion within a specific community.

label: acl
text: Shi, Huang, and Lee (2017a) obtained state-of-the-art results for English and Chinese dependency parsing by combining dynamic-programming implementations of transition-based dependency parsers with a minimal set of bidirectional LSTM features. However, their results were limited to projective parsing. In this paper, we extend their approach to support non-projectivity by providing the first practical implementation of the MH₄ algorithm, an C-C-C mildly nonprojective dynamic-programming parser with very high coverage on non-projective treebanks. To make MH₄ compatible with minimal transition-based feature sets, we introduce a transition-based interpretation of it in which parser items are mapped to sequences of transitions. We thus obtain the first implementation of global decoding for non-projective transition-based parsing, and demonstrate empirically that it is effective than its projective counterpart in parsing a number of highly non-projective languages.

label: acl
text: Shi, Huang, and Lee (2017a) achieved state-of-the-art results for English and Chinese dependency parsing by combining dynamic-programming implementations of transition-based parsers with minimal bidirectional LSTM features. However, their results were restricted to projective parsing. In this paper, we expand their approach to support non-projectivity by implementing the MH₄ algorithm, a C-C-C mild non-projective dynamic-programming parser with high coverage on non-projective treebanks. To integrate the MH₄ algorithm with minimal transition-based features, we present a transition-based interpretation of it, mapping parser items to sequences of transitions. This results in the first implementation of global decoding for non-projective transition-based parsing, which we demonstrate to be more effective than its projective counterpart when parsing highly non-projective languages.

label: naacl
text: Both scientific progress and individual researcher careers depend on the quality of peer review, which in turn depends on paper-reviewer matching. Surprisingly, this problem has been mostly approached as an automated recommendation problem rather than as a matter where different stakeholders (area chairs, reviewers, authors) have accumulated experience worth taking into account. We present the results of the first survey of the NLP community, identifying common issues and perspectives on what factors should be considered by paper-reviewer matching systems. This study contributes actionable recommendations for improving future NLP conferences, and desiderata for interpretable peer review assignments.

label: naacl
text: The quality of peer review, which is essential for both scientific progress and individual researcher careers, relies heavily on the effective matching of papers to reviewers. However, this problem has been primarily approached as an automated recommendation task, disregarding the valuable experience and insights of stakeholders such as area chairs, reviewers, and authors. Our study, which is the first survey of the NLP community, sheds light on the common issues and perspectives surrounding paper-reviewer matching. Our findings offer practical recommendations for enhancing future NLP conferences and provide a roadmap for developing interpretable peer review assignments.

label: coling
text: Semantic parsers critically rely on accurate and high-coverage lexicons. However, traditional semantic parsers usually utilize annotated logical forms to learn the lexicon, which often suffer from the lexicon coverage problem. In this paper, we propose a graph-based semi-supervised learning framework that makes use of large text corpora and lexical resources. This framework first constructs a graph with a phrase similarity model learned by utilizing many text corpora and lexical resources. Next, graph propagation algorithm identifies the label distribution of unlabeled phrases from labeled ones. We evaluate our approach on two benchmarks: Webquestions and Free917. The results show that, in both datasets, our method achieves substantial improvement when comparing to the base system that does not utilize the learned lexicon, and gains competitive results when comparing to state-of-the-art systems.

label: coling
text: Semantic parsers require accurate and high-coverage lexicons to function effectively. However, traditional semantic parsers often face the lexicon coverage problem as they use annotated logical forms to learn the lexicon. To address this issue, we propose a graph-based semi-supervised learning framework that leverages large text corpora and lexical resources. Our framework starts by constructing a graph using a phrase similarity model trained on multiple text corpora and lexical resources. Then, a graph propagation algorithm is applied to identify the label distribution of unlabeled phrases from labeled ones. We evaluate our approach on two benchmark datasets: Webquestions and Free917. The results demonstrate that our method significantly improves performance compared to the base system that does not use the learned lexicon and achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art systems.

label: acl
text: Clinical trials offer a fundamental opportunity to discover new treatments and advance the medical knowledge. However, the uncertainty of the outcome of a trial can lead to unforeseen costs and setbacks. In this study, we propose a new method to predict the effectiveness of an intervention in a clinical trial. Our method relies on generating an informative summary from multiple documents available in the literature about the intervention under study. Specifically, our method first gathers all the abstracts of PubMed articles related to the intervention. Then, an evidence sentence, which conveys information about the effectiveness of the intervention, is extracted automatically from each abstract. Based on the set of evidence sentences extracted from the abstracts, a short summary about the intervention is constructed. Finally, the produced summaries are used to train a BERT-based classifier, in order to infer the effectiveness of an intervention. To evaluate our proposed method, we introduce a new dataset which is a collection of clinical trials together with their associated PubMed articles. Our experiments, demonstrate the effectiveness of producing short informative summaries and using them to predict the effectiveness of an intervention.

label: acl
text: Clinical trials provide a crucial opportunity to uncover new treatments and advance medical knowledge. However, the unpredictability of trial outcomes can result in unexpected costs and setbacks. In this study, we introduce a novel method to predict the efficacy of an intervention in clinical trials. Our approach is based on synthesizing informative summaries from multiple literature sources related to the intervention under investigation. Our method starts by collecting all abstracts from PubMed articles relevant to the intervention. Then, it automatically extracts a sentence conveying information about the intervention's efficacy from each abstract. The set of extracted sentences is used to construct a short summary about the intervention. Finally, the generated summaries are used to train a BERT-based classifier, enabling us to predict the efficacy of the intervention. To validate our method, we introduce a new dataset, consisting of a collection of clinical trials and their associated PubMed articles. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating short, informative summaries and using them to predict the efficacy of an intervention.

label: coling
text: The stance detection task aims to classify the stance toward given documents and topics. Since the topics can be implicit in documents and unseen in training data for zero-shot settings, we propose to boost the transferability of the stance detection model by using sentiment and commonsense knowledge, which are seldom considered in previous studies. Our model includes a graph autoencoder module to obtain commonsense knowledge and a stance detection module with sentiment and commonsense. Experimental results show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on the zero-shot and few-shot benchmark dataset–VAST. Meanwhile, ablation studies prove the significance of each module in our model. Analysis of the relations between sentiment, common sense, and stance indicates the effectiveness of sentiment and common sense.

label: coling
text: The objective of the stance detection task is to classify the stance of given documents and topics. Given that the topics in documents can be implicit and unseen in the training data in zero-shot settings, we aim to enhance the transferability of the stance detection model by incorporating sentiment and commonsense knowledge, which has been overlooked in previous studies. Our model comprises a graph autoencoder module to extract commonsense knowledge, and a stance detection module that leverages sentiment and commonsense. Our experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the VAST benchmark dataset, both in zero-shot and few-shot settings. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the importance of each module in our model. Our analysis of the relationship between sentiment, common sense, and stance highlights the effectiveness of sentiment and common sense in enhancing stance detection.

label: naacl
text: Exemplification is a process by which writers explain or clarify a concept by providing an example. While common in all forms of writing, exemplification is particularly useful in the task of long-form question answering (LFQA), where a complicated answer can be made more understandable through simple examples. In this paper, we provide the first computational study of exemplification in QA, performing a fine-grained annotation of different types of examples (e.g., hypotheticals, anecdotes) in three corpora. We show that not only do state-of-the-art LFQA models struggle to generate relevant examples, but also that standard evaluation metrics such as ROUGE are insufficient to judge exemplification quality. We propose to treat exemplification as a retrieval problem in which a partially-written answer is used to query a large set of human-written examples extracted from a corpus. Our approach allows a reliable ranking-type automatic metrics that correlates well with human evaluation. A human evaluation shows that our model's retrieved examples are more relevant than examples generated from a state-of-the-art LFQA model.

label: naacl
text: Exemplification is a writing technique where a concept is explained or clarified through the use of examples. This method is commonly used in all forms of writing, but is particularly helpful in long-form question answering (LFQA), where complex answers can be made easier to understand with simple examples. This paper presents the first computational study of exemplification in QA, with a detailed annotation of various types of examples (e.g., hypothetical scenarios, anecdotes) in three different corpora. Our study shows that current LFQA models struggle to generate relevant examples, and that standard evaluation metrics like ROUGE are inadequate for judging exemplification quality. To address this, we propose treating exemplification as a retrieval problem, where a partially written answer is used to query a large collection of human-written examples from a corpus. This approach enables the use of reliable, ranking-based automatic metrics that correlate well with human evaluations. Our human evaluations show that the examples retrieved by our model are more relevant than those generated by state-of-the-art LFQA models.

label: acl
text: The performance of deep learning models in NLP and other fields of machine learning has led to a rise in their popularity, and so the need for explanations of these models becomes paramount. Attention has been seen as a solution to increase performance, while providing some explanations. However, a debate has started to cast doubt on the explanatory power of attention in neural networks. Although the debate has created a vast literature thanks to contributions from various areas, the lack of communication is becoming more and more tangible. In this paper, we provide a clear overview of the insights on the debate by critically confronting works from these different areas. This holistic vision can be of great interest for future works in all the communities concerned by this debate. We sum up the main challenges spotted in these areas, and we conclude by discussing the most promising future avenues on attention as an explanation.

label: acl
text: The popularity of deep learning models in NLP and other machine learning fields has risen due to their impressive performance, leading to an increased demand for explanations of these models. Attention mechanisms have been seen as a way to improve performance while providing some level of explanation. However, a debate has arisen about the explanatory power of attention in neural networks. Despite the extensive literature generated by contributions from various fields, a lack of communication between these areas is becoming increasingly apparent. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of the debate by critically examining works from these different fields. This holistic approach can be of great value to future works in all communities involved in the debate. We highlight the main challenges and conclude by discussing the most promising future directions for attention as an explanation.

label: acl
text: GPT is an auto-regressive Transformer-based pre-trained language model which has attracted a lot of attention in the natural language processing (NLP) domain. The success of GPT is mostly attributed to its pre-training on huge amount of data and its large number of parameters. Despite the superior performance of GPT, this overparameterized nature of GPT can be very prohibitive for deploying this model on devices with limited computational power or memory. This problem can be mitigated using model compression techniques; however, compressing GPT models has not been investigated much in the literature. In this work, we use Kronecker decomposition to compress the linear mappings of the GPT-2 model. Our Kronecker GPT-2 model (KnGPT2) is initialized based on the Kronecker decomposed version of the GPT-2 model and then is undergone a very light pre- training on only a small portion of the training data with intermediate layer knowledge distillation (ILKD). Finally, our KnGPT2 is fine-tuned on downstream tasks using ILKD as well. We evaluate our model on both language modeling and General Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark tasks and show that with more efficient pre-training and similar number of parameters, our KnGPT2 outperforms the existing DistilGPT2 model significantly.

label: acl
text: GPT is an auto-regressive Transformer-based language model that has gained significant attention in the field of natural language processing (NLP). Its success is largely due to its pre-training on vast amounts of data and its large number of parameters. However, this overparameterized nature of GPT can be a hindrance when deploying the model on devices with limited computational power or memory. To mitigate this problem, model compression techniques can be used, but compressing GPT models has not been extensively explored in the literature. In this study, we use Kronecker decomposition to compress the linear mappings of the GPT-2 model. Our Kronecker GPT-2 model (KnGPT2) is initialized using the Kronecker decomposed version of the GPT-2 model and undergoes a light pre-training on a small portion of the data with intermediate layer knowledge distillation (ILKD). Finally, we fine-tune our KnGPT2 on downstream tasks using ILKD. We evaluate our model on language modeling and General Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark tasks and demonstrate that, with more efficient pre-training and a similar number of parameters, our KnGPT2 outperforms the existing DistilGPT2 model significantly.

label: naacl
text: Endowing the protagonist with a specific personality is essential for writing an engaging story. In this paper, we aim to control the protagonist's persona in story generation, i.e., generating a story from a leading context and a persona description, where the protagonist should exhibit the specified personality through a coherent event sequence. Considering that personas are usually embodied implicitly and sparsely in stories, we propose a planning-based generation model named ConPer to explicitly model the relationship between personas and events. ConPer first plans events of the protagonist's behavior which are motivated by the specified persona through predicting one target sentence, then plans the plot as a sequence of keywords with the guidance of the predicted persona-related events and commonsense knowledge, and finally generates the whole story. Both automatic and manual evaluation results demonstrate that ConPer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for generating more coherent and persona-controllable stories. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-coai/ConPer.

label: naacl
text: Endowing the protagonist with a specific personality is crucial for writing an engaging story. In this paper, we aim to control the protagonist's persona in story generation by generating a story from a given context and persona description. The protagonist's personality should be evident throughout the story and expressed coherently through a series of events. Personas are often implicitly and sparsely embodied in stories. To address this issue, we present a planning-based generation model, ConPer, which explicitly models the relationship between personas and events. ConPer begins by planning the protagonist's behavior, motivated by the specified persona, through predicting one target sentence. It then plans the plot as a sequence of keywords, guided by the predicted persona-related events and commonsense knowledge, before finally generating the entire story. Our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines, as demonstrated by both automatic and manual evaluations, by producing more coherent and persona-controlled stories. The code for ConPer is available at https://github.com/thu-coai/ConPer.

label: coling
text: In this paper we present InferES - an original corpus for Natural Language Inference (NLI) in European Spanish. We propose, implement, and analyze a variety of corpus-creating strategies utilizing expert linguists and crowd workers. The objectives behind InferES are to provide high-quality data, and at the same time to facilitate the systematic evaluation of automated systems. Specifically, we focus on measuring and improving the performance of machine learning systems on negation-based adversarial examples and their ability to generalize across out-of-distribution topics. We train two transformer models on InferES (8,055 gold examples) in a variety of scenarios. Our best model obtains 72.8% accuracy, leaving a lot of room for improvement. The “hypothesis-only” baseline performs only 2%-5% higher than majority, indicating much fewer annotation artifacts than prior work. We show that models trained on InferES generalize very well across topics (both in- and out-of-distribution) and perform moderately well on negation-based adversarial examples.

label: coling
text: This paper introduces InferES, a unique corpus for Natural Language Inference (NLI) in European Spanish. We have devised, implemented, and analyzed multiple corpus-creation strategies that involve the collaboration of expert linguists and crowd workers. The goal of InferES is to provide high-quality data that can be used to evaluate the performance of automated systems for NLI. Our focus is on measuring and enhancing the performance of machine learning systems on negation-based adversarial examples and their ability to generalize to out-of-distribution topics. We trained two transformer models on InferES (8,055 gold examples) in various scenarios, with the best model achieving 72.8% accuracy, leaving room for improvement. The "hypothesis-only" baseline performed only 2% to 5% higher than the majority, which demonstrates fewer annotation artifacts compared to previous work. Our results show that models trained on InferES generalize well across topics (both in- and out-of-distribution) and perform moderately well on negation-based adversarial examples.

label: coling
text: Understanding news content is critical to improving the quality of news recommendation. To achieve this goal, recent studies have attempted to apply pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT for semantic-enhanced news recommendation. Despite their great success in offline evaluation, it is still a challenge to apply such large PLMs in real-time ranking model due to the stringent requirement in inference and updating time. To bridge this gap, we propose a plug-and-play pre-trainer, namely PREC, to learn both user and news encoders through multi-task pre-training. Instead of directly leveraging sophisticated PLMs for end-to-end inference, we focus on how to use the derived user and item representations to boost the performance of conventional lightweight models for click-through-rate prediction. This enables efficient online inference as well as compatibility to conventional models, which would significantly ease the practical deployment. We validate the effectiveness of PREC through both offline evaluation on public datasets and online A/B testing in an industrial application.

label: coling
text: Understanding news content is crucial for enhancing the quality of news recommendations.
