Although these models have achieved great success in offline evaluations, they still pose a challenge when it comes to real-time ranking due to their high inference and updating time requirements. To address this issue, we introduce PREC, a plug-and-play pre-trainer that learns both user and news encoders through multi-task pre-training. Instead of relying on complex PLMs for end-to-end inference, we focus on using the derived user and item representations to improve the performance of conventional, lightweight models for click-through-rate prediction. This approach enables efficient online inference and compatibility with conventional models, making it easier to deploy in practical settings. We validate the effectiveness of PREC through both offline evaluations on public datasets and online A/B testing in an industrial application.

label: acl
text: Aspect category detection (ACD) in sentiment analysis aims to identify the aspect categories mentioned in a sentence. In this paper, we formulate ACD in the few-shot learning scenario. However, existing few-shot learning approaches mainly focus on single-label predictions. These methods can not work well for the ACD task since a sentence may contain multiple aspect categories. Therefore, we propose a multi-label few-shot learning method based on the prototypical network. To alleviate the noise, we design two effective attention mechanisms. The support-set attention aims to extract better prototypes by removing irrelevant aspects. The query-set attention computes multiple prototype-specific representations for each query instance, which are then used to compute accurate distances with the corresponding prototypes. To achieve multi-label inference, we further learn a dynamic threshold per instance by a policy network. Extensive experimental results on three datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms strong baselines.

label: acl
text: The Aspect Category Detection (ACD) in Sentiment Analysis aims to identify the aspect categories mentioned in a sentence. This paper presents a novel approach to ACD in the context of few-shot learning. Existing few-shot learning methods primarily focus on single-label predictions, but this is not suitable for ACD. As a sentence may contain multiple aspect categories, we propose a multi-label few-shot learning method based on the prototypical network. To enhance the performance, two effective attention mechanisms are designed. The support-set attention aims to eliminate irrelevant aspects and extract better prototypes, while the query-set attention computes multiple prototype-specific representations for each query instance. This results in accurate distances computed with the corresponding prototypes. Additionally, a policy network is used to learn a dynamic threshold per instance for multi-label inference. The proposed method is tested on three datasets and results show that it significantly outperforms strong baselines.

label: coling
text: The task of shallow discourse parsing in the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) framework has traditionally been restricted to identifying those relations that are signaled by a discourse connective (“explicit”) and those that have no signal at all (“implicit”). The third type, the more flexible group of “AltLex” realizations has been neglected because of its small amount of occurrences in the PDTB2 corpus. Their number has grown significantly in the recent PDTB3, and in this paper, we present the first approaches for recognizing these “alternative lexicalizations”. We compare the performance of a pattern-based approach and a sequence labeling model, add an experiment on the pre-classification of candidate sentences, and provide an initial qualitative analysis of the error cases made by both models.

label: coling
text: The task of shallow discourse parsing in the framework of the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) has typically been limited to identifying explicit relationships that are signaled by a discourse connective and implicit relationships that have no signal. The third group of "AltLex" realizations, which are more flexible, have been overlooked due to their limited occurrence in the PDTB2 corpus. However, the number of these realizations has significantly increased in the recent PDTB3, and this paper presents the first attempts at recognizing these "alternative lexicalizations." We compare the performance of a pattern-based approach and a sequence labeling model, conduct an experiment on pre-classifying candidate sentences, and provide an initial qualitative analysis of the errors made by both models.

label: coling
text: This paper explores the task of identifying the overall sentiment expressed towards volitional entities (persons and organizations) in a document - what we refer to as Entity-Level Sentiment Analysis (ELSA). While identifying sentiment conveyed towards an entity is well researched for shorter texts like tweets, we find little to no research on this specific task for longer texts with multiple mentions and opinions towards the same entity. This lack of research would be understandable if ELSA can be derived from existing tasks and models. To assess this, we annotate a set of professional reviews for their overall sentiment towards each volitional entity in the text. We sample from data already annotated for document-level, sentence-level, and target-level sentiment in a multi-domain review corpus, and our results indicate that there is no single proxy task that provides this overall sentiment we seek for the entities at a satisfactory level of performance. We present a suite of experiments aiming to assess the contribution towards ELSA provided by document-, sentence-, and target-level sentiment analysis, and provide a discussion of their shortcomings. We show that sentiment in our dataset is expressed not only with an entity mention as target, but also towards targets with a sentiment-relevant relation to a volitional entity. In our data, these relations extend beyond anaphoric coreference resolution, and our findings call for further research of the topic. Finally, we also present a survey of previous relevant work.

label: coling
text: This paper investigates the challenge of determining the overall sentiment expressed towards volitional entities, such as people and organizations, in a document, which we refer to as Entity-Level Sentiment Analysis (ELSA). Although sentiment analysis towards entities has been well researched for shorter texts, such as tweets, little to no research has been conducted on this specific task for longer texts with multiple mentions and opinions towards the same entity. To determine if ELSA can be derived from existing tasks and models, we annotated a set of professional reviews for their overall sentiment towards each volitional entity in the text. Our results show that there is no single proxy task that provides the overall sentiment for entities at a satisfactory level of performance. We present a series of experiments to assess the contribution of document-, sentence-, and target-level sentiment analysis towards ELSA and discuss their shortcomings. Our findings indicate that sentiment in our dataset is expressed not only with an entity mention as a target but also towards targets with a sentiment-relevant relation to a volitional entity. These relations extend beyond anaphoric coreference resolution, and our results call for further research in this area. Additionally, we provide a review of previous relevant work.

label: naacl
text: Cross-lingual Hypernymy Detection involves determining if a word in one language (“fruit”) is a hypernym of a word in another language (“pomme” i.e. apple in French). The ability to detect hypernymy cross-lingually can aid in solving cross-lingual versions of tasks such as textual entailment and event coreference. We propose BiSparse-Dep, a family of unsupervised approaches for cross-lingual hypernymy detection, which learns sparse, bilingual word embeddings based on dependency contexts. We show that BiSparse-Dep can significantly improve performance on this task, compared to approaches based only on lexical context. Our approach is also robust, showing promise for low-resource settings: our dependency-based embeddings can be learned using a parser trained on related languages, with negligible loss in performance. We also crowd-source a challenging dataset for this task on four languages – Russian, French, Arabic, and Chinese. Our embeddings and datasets are publicly available.

label: naacl
text: Cross-lingual Hypernymy Detection determines if a word in one language (such as "fruit") is a hypernym of a word in another language (such as "pomme," which means "apple" in French). This ability can assist in solving cross-lingual versions of tasks like textual entailment and event coreference. We present BiSparse-Dep, a family of unsupervised approaches for cross-lingual hypernymy detection, which learns sparse, bilingual word embeddings based on dependency contexts. Our results show that BiSparse-Dep outperforms approaches that rely solely on lexical context. Additionally, our approach is robust and shows promise for low-resource settings; our dependency-based embeddings can be learned using a parser trained on related languages with minimal loss in performance. To further support our research, we have also created a challenging dataset for this task in four languages: Russian, French, Arabic, and Chinese. This dataset, along with our embeddings, is publicly available.

label: acl
text: Inductive transfer learning has greatly impacted computer vision, but existing approaches in NLP still require task-specific modifications and training from scratch. We propose Universal Language Model Fine-tuning (ULMFiT), an effective transfer learning method that can be applied to any task in NLP, and introduce techniques that are key for fine-tuning a language model. Our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on six text classification tasks, reducing the error by 18-24% on the majority of datasets. Furthermore, with only 100 labeled examples, it matches the performance of training from scratch on 100 times more data. We open-source our pretrained models and code.

label: acl
text: The impact of Inductive Transfer Learning on Computer Vision has been substantial, however, existing NLP approaches still necessitate task-specific modifications and the need for training from scratch. To address this, we introduce Universal Language Model Fine-tuning (ULMFiT), a transfer learning method that can be applied to any NLP task. Our method incorporates crucial techniques for fine-tuning a language model, resulting in significant performance improvements. On six text classification tasks, ULMFiT outperforms the state-of-the-art by reducing the error by 18-24% on most datasets. Moreover, with only 100 labeled examples, ULMFiT matches the performance of training from scratch with 100 times more data. Our pretrained models and code are freely available as open-source.

label: naacl
text: Although Transformers with fully connected self-attentions are powerful to model long-term dependencies, they are struggling to scale to long texts with thousands of words in language modeling. One of the solutions is to equip the model with a recurrence memory. However, existing approaches directly reuse hidden states from the previous segment that encodes contexts in a uni-directional way. As a result, this prohibits the memory to dynamically interact with the current context that provides up-to-date information for token prediction. To remedy this issue, we propose Look-Ahead Memory (LaMemo) that enhances the recurrence memory by incrementally attending to the right-side tokens and interpolating with the old memory states to maintain long-term information in the history. LaMemo embraces bi-directional attention and segment recurrence with an additional computation overhead only linearly proportional to the memory length. Experiments on widely used language modeling benchmarks demonstrate its superiority over the baselines equipped with different types of memory mechanisms.

label: naacl
text: Transformers with fully-connected self-attentions are powerful in modeling long-term dependencies, but they struggle to scale to long texts with thousands of words in language modeling. To address this issue, a solution is to equip the model with a recurrent memory. However, existing approaches reuse hidden states from previous segments in a unidirectional way, which prevents the memory from dynamically interacting with the current context for token prediction. To overcome this limitation, we propose Look-Ahead Memory (LaMemo), which enhances the recurrent memory by incrementally attending to right-side tokens and interpolating with old memory states to maintain long-term information. LaMemo combines bi-directional attention and segment recurrence with a computation overhead that is linearly proportional to the memory length. Our experiments on widely-used language modeling benchmarks demonstrate LaMemo's superiority over baselines with different types of memory mechanisms.

label: naacl
text: Few-shot language learners adapt knowledge from a pre-trained model to recognize novel classes from a few-labeled sentences. In such settings, fine-tuning a pre-trained language model can cause severe over-fitting. In this paper, we propose an Embedding Hallucination (EmbedHalluc) method, which generates auxiliary embedding-label pairs to expand the fine-tuning dataset. The hallucinator is trained by playing an adversarial game with the discriminator, such that the hallucinated embedding is indiscriminative to the real ones in the fine-tuning dataset. By training with the extended dataset, the language learner effectively learns from the diverse hallucinated embeddings to overcome the over-fitting issue. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed method is effective in a wide range of language tasks, outperforming current fine-tuning methods. Further, we show that EmbedHalluc outperforms other methods that address this over-fitting problem, such as common data augmentation, semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, and regularization.

label: naacl
text: Few-shot language learners can recognize novel classes from a few labeled sentences by adapting knowledge from a pre-trained model. However, fine-tuning a pre-trained language model in these scenarios can result in severe over-fitting. To overcome this issue, we propose the Embedding Hallucination (EmbedHalluc) method, which generates auxiliary embedding-label pairs to expand the fine-tuning dataset. The hallucinator is trained through an adversarial game with the discriminator, ensuring that the hallucinated embeddings are indistinguishable from real ones in the fine-tuning dataset. By training with the expanded dataset, the language learner can learn from diverse hallucinated embeddings and overcome over-fitting. Our experiments show that EmbedHalluc is effective in a wide range of language tasks and outperforms current fine-tuning methods and other methods that address over-fitting, such as data augmentation, semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, and regularization.

label: acl
text: While BERT is an effective method for learning monolingual sentence embeddings for semantic similarity and embedding based transfer learning BERT based cross-lingual sentence embeddings have yet to be explored. We systematically investigate methods for learning multilingual sentence embeddings by combining the best methods for learning monolingual and cross-lingual representations including: masked language modeling (MLM), translation language modeling (TLM), dual encoder translation ranking, and additive margin softmax. We show that introducing a pre-trained multilingual language model dramatically reduces the amount of parallel training data required to achieve good performance by 80%. Composing the best of these methods produces a model that achieves 83.7% bi-text retrieval accuracy over 112 languages on Tatoeba, well above the 65.5% achieved by LASER, while still performing competitively on monolingual transfer learning benchmarks. Parallel data mined from CommonCrawl using our best model is shown to train competitive NMT models for en-zh and en-de. We publicly release our best multilingual sentence embedding model for 109+ languages at https://tfhub.dev/google/LaBSE.

label: acl
text: The effectiveness of BERT in learning monolingual sentence embeddings for semantic similarity and embedding-based transfer learning has been established. However, BERT-based cross-lingual sentence embeddings have yet to be explored. Our research systematically investigates methods for learning multilingual sentence embeddings by combining the best techniques for monolingual and cross-lingual representations, including masked language modeling (MLM), translation language modeling (TLM), dual encoder translation ranking, and additive margin softmax. We demonstrate that incorporating a pre-trained multilingual language model significantly reduces the amount of parallel training data required to achieve good performance by 80%. By combining the best of these methods, we produce a model that achieves 83.7% bi-text retrieval accuracy over 112 languages on Tatoeba, surpassing the 65.5% achieved by LASER while still performing competitively on monolingual transfer learning benchmarks. Our best model, trained on parallel data mined from CommonCrawl, is capable of training competitive NMT models for en-zh and en-de. We publicly release our best multilingual sentence embedding model for 109+ languages at https://tfhub.dev/google/LaBSE.

label: acl
text: Scarcity of parallel data causes formality style transfer models to have scarce success in preserving content. We show that fine-tuning pre-trained language (GPT-2) and sequence-to-sequence (BART) models boosts content preservation, and that this is possible even with limited amounts of parallel data. Augmenting these models with rewards that target style and content –the two core aspects of the task– we achieve a new state-of-the-art.

label: acl
text: The scarcity of parallel data is a major obstacle to the success of formal style transfer models in preserving the content of the text. Our research demonstrates that fine-tuning pre-trained language models such as GPT-2 and sequence-to-sequence models like BART can significantly improve content preservation, even with limited parallel data. By incorporating rewards that target both style and content, the two critical components of the task, we have achieved a new state-of-the-art performance.

label: coling
text: Pre-Training (PT) of text representations has been successfully applied to low-resource Neural Machine Translation (NMT). However, it usually fails to achieve notable gains (some- times, even worse) on resource-rich NMT on par with its Random-Initialization (RI) counterpart. We take the first step to investigate the complementarity between PT and RI in resource-rich scenarios via two probing analyses, and find that: 1) PT improves NOT the accuracy, but the generalization by achieving flatter loss landscapes than that of RI; 2) PT improves NOT the confidence of lexical choice, but the negative diversity by assigning smoother lexical probability distributions than that of RI. Based on these insights, we propose to combine their complementarities with a model fusion algorithm that utilizes optimal transport to align neurons between PT and RI. Experiments on two resource-rich translation benchmarks, WMT'17 English-Chinese (20M) and WMT'19 English-German (36M), show that PT and RI could be nicely complementary to each other, achieving substantial improvements considering both translation accuracy, generalization, and negative diversity. Probing tools and code are released at: https://github.com/zanchangtong/PTvsRI.

label: coling
text: The pre-training of text representations has been successfully applied to low-resource neural machine translation (NMT) systems. However, it often fails to produce significant gains, and in some cases, even performs worse than random initialization (RI) in resource-rich NMT. To address this issue, we conducted two probing analyses to explore the complementarity between PT and RI in resource-rich scenarios. Our findings indicate that PT improves generalization, rather than accuracy, by creating flatter loss landscapes compared to RI. Additionally, PT improves negative diversity, instead of confidence in lexical choice, by producing smoother lexical probability distributions compared to RI. Based on these insights, we propose a model fusion algorithm that uses optimal transport to align neurons between PT and RI. Our experiments on two resource-rich translation benchmarks, WMT'17 English-Chinese (20M) and WMT'19 English-German (36M), demonstrate that PT and RI can complement each other, resulting in substantial improvements in translation accuracy, generalization, and negative diversity. Our probing tools and code are available at https://github.com/zanchangtong/PTvsRI.

label: emnlp
text: Recently, there has been a surge of interest in reading comprehension-based (RC) question answering (QA). However, current approaches suffer from an impractical assumption that every question has a valid answer in the associated passage. A practical QA system must possess the ability to determine whether a valid answer exists in a given text passage. In this paper, we focus on developing QA systems that can extract an answer for a question if and only if the associated passage contains an answer. If the associated passage does not contain any valid answer, the QA system will correctly return Nil. We propose a novel nil-aware answer span extraction framework that is capable of returning Nil or a text span from the associated passage as an answer in a single step. We show that our proposed framework can be easily integrated with several recently proposed QA models developed for reading comprehension and can be trained in an end-to-end fashion. Our proposed nil-aware answer extraction neural network decomposes pieces of evidence into relevant and irrelevant parts and then combines them to infer the existence of any answer. Experiments on the NewsQA dataset show that the integration of our proposed framework significantly outperforms several strong baseline systems that use pipeline or threshold-based approaches.

label: emnlp
text: Recently, there has been an increased interest in reading comprehension-based (RC) question answering (QA) systems. However, current approaches have a major drawback in that they assume that every question has a valid answer within the associated text passage. To address this issue, we propose a novel nil-aware answer span extraction framework that is capable of determining whether a valid answer exists in the text passage and returning either Nil or a text span as the answer. Our framework can be easily integrated with existing RC-QA models and trained in an end-to-end manner. It decomposes the evidence into relevant and irrelevant parts, which are then combined to infer the presence of an answer. Our experiments on the NewsQA dataset show that the integration of our framework significantly outperforms existing pipeline or threshold-based approaches.

label: coling
text: Multilingual neural machine translation can translate unseen language pairs during training, i.e. zero-shot translation. However, the zero-shot translation is always unstable. Although prior works attributed the instability to the domination of central language, e.g. English, we supplement this viewpoint with the strict dependence of non-centered languages. In this work, we propose a simple, lightweight yet effective language-specific modeling method by adapting to non-centered languages and combining the shared information and the language-specific information to counteract the instability of zero-shot translation. Experiments with Transformer on IWSLT17, Europarl, TED talks, and OPUS-100 datasets show that our method not only performs better than strong baselines in centered data conditions but also can easily fit non-centered data conditions. By further investigating the layer attribution, we show that our proposed method can disentangle the coupled representation in the correct direction.

label: coling
text: Multilingual neural machine translation can translate unseen language pairs during the training phase, known as zero-shot translation. However, this type of translation is often unstable. While previous studies have attributed this instability to the dominance of central languages, such as English, this paper adds to this viewpoint by emphasizing the strict dependence of non-center languages. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight, yet effective language-specific modeling method that adapts to non-center languages and balances shared information with language-specific information. Our experiments, using the Transformer model on the IWSLT17, Europarl, TED talks, and OPUS-100 datasets, show that our method outperforms strong baselines in both centered and non-centered data conditions. Furthermore, our analysis of layer attribution demonstrates that our approach effectively disentangles the coupled representation.

label: acl
text: Pretrained language models (PLM) achieve surprising performance on the Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) task. However, whether PLMs have truly acquired the ability of causal reasoning remains a question. In this paper, we investigate the problem of semantic similarity bias and reveal the vulnerability of current COPA models by certain attacks. Previous solutions that tackle the superficial cues of unbalanced token distribution still encounter the same problem of semantic bias, even more seriously due to the utilization of more training data. We mitigate this problem by simply adding a regularization loss and experimental results show that this solution not only improves the model's generalization ability, but also assists the models to perform more robustly on a challenging dataset, BCOPA-CE, which has unbiased token distribution and is more difficult for models to distinguish cause and effect.

label: acl
text: Pretrained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance on the Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) task. However, the question of whether these models have truly acquired the ability to reason causally remains unanswered. This paper investigates the issue of semantic similarity bias and exposes the vulnerability of current COPA models to certain attacks. Previous attempts to address the superficial cues of unbalanced token distribution still suffer from the same problem of semantic bias, even more so due to the increased use of training data. To mitigate this issue, we propose a simple solution of adding a regularization loss. Our experimental results show that this approach not only enhances the model's generalization ability but also makes the models more robust on the challenging BCOPA-CE dataset, which has an unbiased token distribution and requires a higher degree of distinction between cause and effect.

label: coling
text: Traditional intent classification models are based on a pre-defined intent set and only recognize limited in-domain (IND) intent classes. But users may input out-of-domain (OOD) queries in a practical dialogue system. Such OOD queries can provide directions for future improvement. In this paper, we define a new task, Generalized Intent Discovery (GID), which aims to extend an IND intent classifier to an open-world intent set including IND and OOD intents. We hope to simultaneously classify a set of labeled IND intent classes while discovering and recognizing new unlabeled OOD types incrementally. We construct three public datasets for different application scenarios and propose two kinds of frameworks, pipeline-based and end-to-end for future work. Further, we conduct exhaustive experiments and qualitative analysis to comprehend key challenges and provide new guidance for future GID research.

label: coling
text: Traditional intent classification models are limited in that they are based on a pre-defined set of intents and can only recognize a limited number of in-domain (IND) intent classes. However, in a practical dialogue system, users may input out-of-domain (OOD) queries that can provide valuable insight into areas for improvement. To address this limitation, this paper introduces the task of Generalized Intent Discovery (GID), which aims to extend an IND intent classifier to an open-world intent set that includes both IND and OOD intents. Our goal is to simultaneously classify a set of labeled IND intent classes while incrementally discovering and recognizing new, unlabeled OOD types. To support this work, we have constructed three public datasets for different application scenarios and have proposed two frameworks—pipeline-based and end-to-end—for future research. Through exhaustive experiments and qualitative analysis, we aim to understand the key challenges of GID and provide guidance for future research in this area.

label: coling
text: Generating character-level features is an important step for achieving good results in various natural language processing tasks. To alleviate the need for human labor in generating hand-crafted features, methods that utilize neural architectures such as Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) or Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to automatically extract such features have been proposed and have shown great results. However, CNN generates position-independent features, and RNN is slow since it needs to process the characters sequentially. In this paper, we propose a novel method of using a densely connected network to automatically extract character-level features. The proposed method does not require any language or task specific assumptions, and shows robustness and effectiveness while being faster than CNN- or RNN-based methods. Evaluating this method on three sequence labeling tasks - slot tagging, Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, and Named-Entity Recognition (NER) - we obtain state-of-the-art performance with a 96.62 F1-score and 97.73% accuracy on slot tagging and POS tagging, respectively, and comparable performance to the state-of-the-art 91.13 F1-score on NER.

label: coling
text: Generating character-level features is crucial for obtaining optimal results in various natural language processing tasks. To reduce the dependency on human-generated hand-crafted features, neural architecture-based methods such as Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) have been proposed to automatically extract these features, and have demonstrated remarkable results. However, CNN's features are position-independent, and RNN is slow due to its sequential processing of characters. In this study, we present a novel method of using a densely connected network to automatically extract character-level features. This method is flexible and does not require any language or task-specific assumptions, and it demonstrates robustness, efficiency, and speed compared to CNN and RNN-based methods. We evaluate this method on three sequence labeling tasks, including slot tagging, Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, and Named-Entity Recognition (NER). Our results show state-of-the-art performance, with a 96.62 F1-score and 97.73% accuracy on slot tagging and POS tagging, respectively, and comparable results to the state-of-the-art 91.13 F1-score on NER.

label: acl
text: Multi-encoder models are a broad family of context-aware neural machine translation systems that aim to improve translation quality by encoding document-level contextual information alongside the current sentence. The context encoding is undertaken by contextual parameters, trained on document-level data. In this work, we discuss the difficulty of training these parameters effectively, due to the sparsity of the words in need of context (i.e., the training signal), and their relevant context. We propose to pre-train the contextual parameters over split sentence pairs, which makes an efficient use of the available data for two reasons. Firstly, it increases the contextual training signal by breaking intra-sentential syntactic relations, and thus pushing the model to search the context for disambiguating clues more frequently. Secondly, it eases the retrieval of relevant context, since context segments become shorter. We propose four different splitting methods, and evaluate our approach with BLEU and contrastive test sets. Results show that it consistently improves learning of contextual parameters, both in low and high resource settings.

label: acl
text: Multi-encoder models are a type of context-aware neural machine translation system that aim to enhance translation quality by encoding document-level contextual information along with the current sentence. These models use contextual parameters, which are trained on document-level data, to perform the context encoding. However, the challenge of effectively training these parameters arises due to the scarcity of words that require context and their relevant context. To address this issue, we propose pre-training the contextual parameters using split sentence pairs. This approach is efficient as it increases the contextual training signal by breaking down intra-sentential syntactic relations and encourages the model to search for disambiguating clues in the context more often. Additionally, it simplifies the retrieval of relevant context as the context segments become shorter. We evaluate four different splitting methods and assess our approach using BLEU and contrastive test sets. The results indicate that our approach consistently improves the learning of contextual parameters in both low and high resource settings.

label: acl
text: Motivated by the positive impact of empty category on syntactic parsing, we study neural models for pre- and in-parsing detection of empty category, which has not previously been investigated. We find several non-obvious facts: (a) BiLSTM can capture non-local contextual information which is essential for detecting empty categories, (b) even with a BiLSTM, syntactic information is still able to enhance the detection, and (c) automatic detection of empty categories improves parsing quality for overt words. Our neural ECD models outperform the prior state-of-the-art by significant margins.

label: acl
text: Inspired by the beneficial effects of empty categories on syntactic parsing, we conduct a study on neural models for detecting empty categories during pre- and in-parsing. This area has not been explored previously. Our findings reveal several surprising insights: (a) BiLSTMs can effectively capture non-local contextual information, which is crucial for detecting empty categories; (b) even with a BiLSTM, incorporating syntactic information further improves the detection; and (c) automatically detecting empty categories leads to a higher quality of parsing for overt words. Our neural ECD models surpass the previous state-of-the-art by a significant margin.

label: acl
text: Determining the relative importance of the elements in a sentence is a key factor for effortless natural language understanding. For human language processing, we can approximate patterns of relative importance by measuring reading fixations using eye-tracking technology. In neural language models, gradient-based saliency methods indicate the relative importance of a token for the target objective. In this work, we compare patterns of relative importance in English language processing by humans and models and analyze the underlying linguistic patterns. We find that human processing patterns in English correlate strongly with saliency-based importance in language models and not with attention-based importance. Our results indicate that saliency could be a cognitively more plausible metric for interpreting neural language models. The code is available on github: https://github.com/beinborn/relative_importance.

label: acl
text: Determining the relative importance of elements in a sentence is crucial for effortless natural language understanding. To approximate human language processing, we use eye-tracking technology to measure reading fixations, which provide patterns of relative importance. In neural language models, gradient-based saliency methods reveal the relative importance of a token for the target objective. In this study, we compare patterns of relative importance in English language processing between human and model results and analyze the underlying linguistic patterns. Our findings reveal that human processing patterns in English strongly correlate with saliency-based importance in language models, but not with attention-based importance. These results suggest that saliency could be a more cognitively plausible metric for interpreting the results of neural language models. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/beinborn/relative_importance.

label: naacl
text: Media news framing bias can increase political polarization and undermine civil society. The need for automatic mitigation methods is therefore growing. We propose a new task, a neutral summary generation from multiple news articles of the varying political leaningsto facilitate balanced and unbiased news reading.In this paper, we first collect a new dataset, illustrate insights about framing bias through a case study, and propose a new effective metric and model (NeuS-Title) for the task. Based on our discovery that title provides a good signal for framing bias, we present NeuS-Title that learns to neutralize news content in hierarchical order from title to article. Our hierarchical multi-task learning is achieved by formatting our hierarchical data pair (title, article) sequentially with identifier-tokens (“TITLE=”, “ARTICLE=”) and fine-tuning the auto-regressive decoder with the standard negative log-likelihood objective.We then analyze and point out the remaining challenges and future directions. One of the most interesting observations is that neural NLG models can hallucinate not only factually inaccurate or unverifiable content but also politically biased content.

label: naacl
text: The media's news framing bias can lead to increased political polarization and harm civil society. This highlights the need for automatic methods to mitigate this issue. Our proposed solution is a new task of generating neutral summaries from news articles with varying political leanings, to promote balanced and unbiased news consumption. This paper presents a new dataset and a case study to illustrate the insights into framing bias. We also propose a new metric and model, NeuS-Title, which neutralizes news content in a hierarchical manner, starting with the title and moving to the article. Our model uses hierarchical multi-task learning and is trained using a standard negative log-likelihood objective. Despite the effectiveness of our model, there are still challenges and future directions to be explored. One of the key observations is that neural natural language generation models can create not only factually inaccurate or unverifiable content, but also politically biased content.

label: acl
text: We propose Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR) for answering open-domain questions, which augments a query through text generation of heuristically discovered relevant contexts without external resources as supervision. We demonstrate that the generated contexts substantially enrich the semantics of the queries and GAR with sparse representations (BM25) achieves comparable or better performance than state-of-the-art dense retrieval methods such as DPR. We show that generating diverse contexts for a query is beneficial as fusing their results consistently yields better retrieval accuracy. Moreover, as sparse and dense representations are often complementary, GAR can be easily combined with DPR to achieve even better performance. GAR achieves state-of-the-art performance on Natural Questions and TriviaQA datasets under the extractive QA setup when equipped with an extractive reader, and consistently outperforms other retrieval methods when the same generative reader is used.

label: acl
text: We propose Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR), a novel approach to answering open-domain questions. GAR enriches query semantics by generating relevant contexts without relying on external resources as supervision. Our results show that GAR with sparse representations (BM25) outperforms state-of-the-art dense retrieval methods, such as DPR. We also demonstrate the benefits of generating diverse contexts for a query, as fusing their results consistently leads to improved retrieval accuracy. Additionally, GAR can be easily combined with DPR to achieve even better performance, as sparse and dense representations are often complementary. GAR achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Natural Questions and TriviaQA datasets under the extractive QA setup when equipped with an extractive reader and outperforms other retrieval methods when the same generative reader is used.

label: naacl
text: This paper introduces the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MultiNLI) corpus, a dataset designed for use in the development and evaluation of machine learning models for sentence understanding. At 433k examples, this resource is one of the largest corpora available for natural language inference (a.k.a. recognizing textual entailment), improving upon available resources in both its coverage and difficulty. MultiNLI accomplishes this by offering data from ten distinct genres of written and spoken English, making it possible to evaluate systems on nearly the full complexity of the language, while supplying an explicit setting for evaluating cross-genre domain adaptation. In addition, an evaluation using existing machine learning models designed for the Stanford NLI corpus shows that it represents a substantially more difficult task than does that corpus, despite the two showing similar levels of inter-annotator agreement.

label: naacl
text: This paper presents the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MultiNLI) corpus, a comprehensive dataset designed for the development and evaluation of machine learning models for sentence comprehension. With 433k examples, it is one of the largest corpora available for natural language inference (a.k.a. recognizing textual entailment), surpassing existing resources in both its scope and difficulty. MultiNLI offers data from ten diverse genres of written and spoken English, enabling the evaluation of systems on the full complexity of the language and facilitating cross-genre domain adaptation. Furthermore, an evaluation using existing machine learning models designed for the Stanford NLI corpus reveals that MultiNLI is a substantially more challenging task, despite both corpora demonstrating similar levels of inter-annotator agreement.

label: acl
text: Commonsense reasoning aims to incorporate sets of commonsense facts, retrieved from Commonsense Knowledge Graphs (CKG), to draw conclusion about ordinary situations. The dynamic nature of commonsense knowledge postulates models capable of performing multi-hop reasoning over new situations. This feature also results in having large-scale sparse Knowledge Graphs, where such reasoning process is needed to predict relations between new events. However, existing approaches in this area are limited by considering CKGs as a limited set of facts, thus rendering them unfit for reasoning over new unseen situations and events. In this paper, we present a neural-symbolic reasoner, which is capable of reasoning over large-scale dynamic CKGs. The logic rules for reasoning over CKGs are learned during training by our model. In addition to providing interpretable explanation, the learned logic rules help to generalise prediction to newly introduced events. Experimental results on the task of link prediction on CKGs prove the effectiveness of our model by outperforming the state-of-the-art models.

label: acl
text: Commonsense reasoning aims to draw conclusions about ordinary situations using sets of commonsense facts retrieved from Commonsense Knowledge Graphs (CKG). The dynamic nature of commonsense knowledge requires models capable of performing multi-hop reasoning over new situations, which results in large-scale sparse Knowledge Graphs. However, existing approaches are limited by considering CKGs as a limited set of facts and are thus unfit for reasoning over new, unseen situations and events. In this paper, we present a neural-symbolic reasoner that can perform reasoning over large-scale dynamic CKGs. The logic rules for reasoning are learned during training, and the learned rules provide interpretable explanations and help generalize predictions to newly introduced events. Experimental results on the task of link prediction on CKGs show the effectiveness of our model, outperforming state-of-the-art models.

label: emnlp
text: Answering compositional questions requiring multi-step reasoning is challenging. We introduce an end-to-end differentiable model for interpreting questions about a knowledge graph (KG), which is inspired by formal approaches to semantics. Each span of text is represented by a denotation in a KG and a vector that captures ungrounded aspects of meaning. Learned composition modules recursively combine constituent spans, culminating in a grounding for the complete sentence which answers the question. For example, to interpret “not green”, the model represents “green” as a set of KG entities and “not” as a trainable ungrounded vector—and then uses this vector to parameterize a composition function that performs a complement operation. For each sentence, we build a parse chart subsuming all possible parses, allowing the model to jointly learn both the composition operators and output structure by gradient descent from end-task supervision. The model learns a variety of challenging semantic operators, such as quantifiers, disjunctions and composed relations, and infers latent syntactic structure. It also generalizes well to longer questions than seen in its training data, in contrast to RNN, its tree-based variants, and semantic parsing baselines.

label: emnlp
text: Our end-to-end differentiable model for interpreting questions about a knowledge graph (KG) is challenging to use. However, it is inspired by formal approaches to semantics and offers a unique solution to answering compositional questions that require multi-step reasoning. The model represents each span of text with a denotation in the KG and a vector that captures ungrounded aspects of meaning. The learned composition modules then recursively combine the constituent spans to ground the complete sentence and answer the question. For instance, to interpret "not green," the model represents "green" as a set of KG entities and "not" as a trainable ungrounded vector, which is then used to parameterize a composition function that performs a complement operation. The parse chart for each sentence is built, subsuming all possible parses, allowing the model to jointly learn both the composition operators and output structure through gradient descent from end-task supervision. The model is capable of learning a wide range of challenging semantic operators, such as quantifiers, disjunctions, and composed relations, and infers latent syntactic structure. Furthermore, it generalizes well to longer questions than those seen in its training data, outperforming RNNs, tree-based variants, and semantic parsing baselines.

label: acl
text: Pretrained language models such as BERT have achieved remarkable success in several NLP tasks. With the wide adoption of BERT in real-world applications, researchers begin to investigate the implicit biases encoded in the BERT. In this paper, we assess the implicit stock market preferences in BERT and its finance domain-specific model FinBERT. We find some interesting patterns. For example, the language models are overall more positive towards the stock market, but there are significant differences in preferences between a pair of industry sectors, or even within a sector. Given the prevalence of NLP models in financial decision making systems, this work raises the awareness of their potential implicit preferences in the stock markets. Awareness of such problems can help practitioners improve robustness and accountability of their financial NLP pipelines .

label: acl
text: Pretrained language models, such as BERT, have achieved remarkable success in various NLP tasks. With the widespread adoption of BERT in real-world applications, researchers have started exploring the implicit biases encoded in the model. This paper evaluates the implicit stock market preferences of BERT and its finance-specific model, FinBERT. The results reveal some intriguing patterns, such as the models' overall positive attitude towards the stock market, but with significant differences in preferences between industry sectors or even within a single sector. Given the widespread use of NLP models in financial decision-making systems, this study highlights the importance of considering their potential implicit preferences in the stock market. By raising awareness of these issues, practitioners can improve the robustness and accountability of their financial NLP pipelines.

label: acl
text: Adversarial robustness has attracted much attention recently, and the mainstream solution is adversarial training. However, the tradition of generating adversarial perturbations for each input embedding (in the settings of NLP) scales up the training computational complexity by the number of gradient steps it takes to obtain the adversarial samples. To address this problem, we leverage Flooding method which primarily aims at better generalization and we find promising in defending adversarial attacks. We further propose an effective criterion to bring hyper-parameter-dependent flooding into effect with a narrowed-down search space by measuring how the gradient steps taken within one epoch affect the loss of each batch. Our approach requires zero adversarial sample for training, and its time consumption is equivalent to fine-tuning, which can be 2-15 times faster than standard adversarial training. We experimentally show that our method improves BERT's resistance to textual adversarial attacks by a large margin, and achieves state-of-the-art robust accuracy on various text classification and GLUE tasks.

label: acl
text: Recently, adversarial robustness has received a lot of attention and the most common solution is adversarial training. However, generating adversarial perturbations for each input embedding in NLP settings increases the computational complexity of training by the number of gradient steps required to obtain the adversarial samples. To overcome this challenge, we propose the use of the Flooding method, which focuses on improving generalization and has shown promise in defending against adversarial attacks. We also introduce an effective criterion for controlling hyper-parameters in the Flooding method by measuring the impact of gradient steps taken within one epoch on the loss of each batch. Our approach eliminates the need for adversarial samples during training and has a time consumption equivalent to fine-tuning, which is 2-15 times faster than traditional adversarial training. Our experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves the resistance of BERT to textual adversarial attacks and achieves state-of-the-art robust accuracy on various text classification and GLUE tasks.

label: naacl
text: NLP-powered automatic question generation (QG) techniques carry great pedagogical potential of saving educators' time and benefiting student learning. Yet, QG systems have not been widely adopted in classrooms to date. In this work, we aim to pinpoint key impediments and investigate how to improve the usability of automatic QG techniques for educational purposes by understanding how instructors construct questions and identifying touch points to enhance the underlying NLP models. We perform an in-depth need finding study with 11 instructors across 7 different universities, and summarize their thought processes and needs when creating questions. While instructors show great interests in using NLP systems to support question design, none of them has used such tools in practice. They resort to multiple sources of information, ranging from domain knowledge to students' misconceptions, all of which missing from today's QG systems. We argue that building effective human-NLP collaborative QG systems that emphasize instructor control and explainability is imperative for real-world adoption. We call for QG systems to provide process-oriented support, use modular design, and handle diverse sources of input.

text: The use of NLP-powered automatic question generation (QG) techniques has the potential to save educators' time and improve student learning. However, despite its potential, QG systems have not been widely adopted in classrooms. This research aims to identify the key obstacles to the adoption of QG techniques and improve their usability for educational purposes. The study was conducted with 11 instructors from 7 universities and analyzed their thought processes and needs when creating questions. The instructors showed interest in using NLP systems to support question design, but none of them had used such tools in practice. They rely on multiple sources of information, including domain knowledge and students' misconceptions, which are missing from current QG systems. The authors argue that building human-NLP collaborative QG systems that empower instructors and provide explainability is crucial for real-world adoption. These systems should provide process-oriented support, use modular design, and handle diverse sources of input.

text: Intrinsic evaluations of OIE systems are carried out either manually—with human evaluators judging the correctness of extractions—or automatically, on standardized benchmarks. The latter, while much more cost-effective, is less reliable, primarily because of the incompleteness of the existing OIE benchmarks: the ground truth extractions do not include all acceptable variants of the same fact, leading to unreliable assessment of the models' performance. Moreover, the existing OIE benchmarks are available for English only. In this work, we introduce BenchIE: a benchmark and evaluation framework for comprehensive evaluation of OIE systems for English, Chinese, and German. In contrast to existing OIE benchmarks, BenchIE is fact-based, i.e., it takes into account informational equivalence of extractions: our gold standard consists of fact synsets, clusters in which we exhaustively list all acceptable surface forms of the same fact. Moreover, having in mind common downstream applications for OIE, we make BenchIE multi-faceted; i.e., we create benchmark variants that focus on different facets of OIE evaluation, e.g., compactness or minimality of extractions. We benchmark several state-of-the-art OIE systems using BenchIE and demonstrate that these systems are significantly less effective than indicated by existing OIE benchmarks. We make BenchIE (data and evaluation code) publicly available.

text: Intrinsic evaluations of OIE systems are performed either manually, with human evaluators assessing the accuracy of extractions, or automatically using standardized benchmarks. However, the latter method is less reliable due to the incompleteness of existing OIE benchmarks, which do not include all possible variations of a fact. This leads to inaccurate assessments of the models' performance. Additionally, existing benchmarks are only available in English. To address these issues, we introduce BenchIE, a benchmark and evaluation framework that provides comprehensive evaluation of OIE systems in English, Chinese, and German. Unlike existing benchmarks, BenchIE is fact-based, taking into account the informational equivalence of extractions. Our gold standard consists of fact synsets, which exhaustively list all acceptable surface forms of the same fact. Additionally, to cater to common downstream applications of OIE, we make BenchIE multi-faceted, offering benchmark variants that focus on different aspects of OIE evaluation, such as compactness or minimality of extractions. We evaluate several state-of-the-art OIE systems using BenchIE and demonstrate that these systems are less effective than previously indicated by existing benchmarks. BenchIE (data and evaluation code) is publicly available.

text: Document-level neural machine translation (DocNMT) achieves coherent translations by incorporating cross-sentence context. However, for most language pairs there's a shortage of parallel documents, although parallel sentences are readily available. In this paper, we study whether and how contextual modeling in DocNMT is transferable via multilingual modeling. We focus on the scenario of zero-shot transfer from teacher languages with document level data to student languages with no documents but sentence level data, and for the first time treat document-level translation as a transfer learning problem. Using simple concatenation-based DocNMT, we explore the effect of 3 factors on the transfer: the number of teacher languages with document level data, the balance between document and sentence level data at training, and the data condition of parallel documents (genuine vs. back-translated). Our experiments on Europarl-7 and IWSLT-10 show the feasibility of multilingual transfer for DocNMT, particularly on document-specific metrics. We observe that more teacher languages and adequate data balance both contribute to better transfer quality. Surprisingly, the transfer is less sensitive to the data condition, where multilingual DocNMT delivers decent performance with either back-translated or genuine document pairs.

label: acl
text: Our study shows that contextual modeling in Document-level Neural Machine Translation (DocNMT) can be transferred via multilingual modeling. We focus on the scenario of zero-shot transfer from teacher languages with document-level data to student languages with sentence-level data only. This is a novel approach to treating document-level translation as a transfer learning problem. Using simple concatenation-based DocNMT, we explore the impact of three factors on transfer: the number of teacher languages, the balance between document and sentence-level data, and the quality of parallel documents (genuine vs. back-translated). Our experiments on the Europarl-7 and IWSLT-10 datasets demonstrate the feasibility of multilingual transfer for DocNMT, particularly on document-specific metrics. We find that more teacher languages and a balanced data distribution improve transfer quality, and that the transfer is relatively insensitive to the quality of parallel documents, with decent results achieved using either genuine or back-translated documents.

text: We introduce the new Multimodal Named Entity Disambiguation (MNED) task for multimodal social media posts such as Snapchat or Instagram captions, which are composed of short captions with accompanying images. Social media posts bring significant challenges for disambiguation tasks because 1) ambiguity not only comes from polysemous entities, but also from inconsistent or incomplete notations, 2) very limited context is provided with surrounding words, and 3) there are many emerging entities often unseen during training. To this end, we build a new dataset called SnapCaptionsKB, a collection of Snapchat image captions submitted to public and crowd-sourced stories, with named entity mentions fully annotated and linked to entities in an external knowledge base. We then build a deep zeroshot multimodal network for MNED that 1) extracts contexts from both text and image, and 2) predicts correct entity in the knowledge graph embeddings space, allowing for zeroshot disambiguation of entities unseen in training set as well. The proposed model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art text-only NED models, showing efficacy and potentials of the MNED task.

label: acl
text: We present the new Multimodal Named Entity Disambiguation (MNED) task, which involves disambiguating named entities in multimodal social media posts such as Snapchat or Instagram captions. These captions are short and accompanied by images. Social media posts present significant challenges for disambiguation tasks, including ambiguity from polysemous entities and inconsistent or incomplete notations, limited context from surrounding words, and the presence of emerging entities not seen during training. To address these challenges, we have created the SnapCaptionsKB dataset, a collection of Snapchat captions submitted to public and crowd-sourced stories, with named entity mentions fully annotated and linked to entities in an external knowledge base. We also developed a deep zeroshot multimodal network for MNED that extracts context from both text and images and predicts the correct entity in the knowledge graph embeddings space, allowing for disambiguation of entities unseen during training. Our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art text-only NED models, demonstrating the efficacy and potential of the MNED task.

text: Training large-scale image captioning (IC) models demands access to a rich and diverse set of training examples that are expensive to curate both in terms of time and man-power. Instead, alt-text based captions gathered from the web is a far cheaper alternative to scale with the downside of being noisy. Recent modeling approaches to IC often fall short in terms of performance in leveraging these noisy datasets in favor of clean annotations. We address this problem with a simple yet effective technique of breaking down the task into two smaller, more controllable tasks – skeleton prediction and skeleton-based caption generation. Specifically, we show that sub-selecting content words as skeletons helps in generating improved and denoised captions when leveraging rich yet noisy alt-text–based uncurated datasets. We also show that the predicted English skeletons can further cross-lingually be leveraged to generate non-English captions, and present experimental results covering caption generation in French, Italian, German, Spanish and Hindi. We also show that skeleton-based prediction allows for better control of certain caption properties, such as length, content, and gender expression, providing a handle to perform human-in-the-loop interpretable semi-automatic corrections.

label: coling
text: Training large-scale image captioning models is a time-consuming and resource-intensive task that requires access to a rich and diverse set of training examples. To scale this process, using alt-text-based captions from the web is a cheaper alternative, but it comes with the downside of being noisy. Traditional image captioning models struggle to leverage these noisy datasets effectively. To address this issue, we propose a two-step approach that breaks down the task into skeleton prediction and skeleton-based caption generation. By sub-selecting content words as skeletons, we can generate improved and denoised captions from noisy alt-text-based datasets. Our approach also allows for cross-lingual caption generation in multiple languages, including French, Italian, German, Spanish, and Hindi. Additionally, skeleton-based prediction gives us greater control over caption properties such as length, content, and gender expression, enabling human-in-the-loop corrections for greater interpretability.

text: Early rumor detection is a key challenging task to prevent rumors from spreading widely. Sociological research shows that social bots' behavior in the early stage has become the main reason for rumors' wide spread. However, current models do not explicitly distinguish genuine users from social bots, and their failure in identifying rumors timely. Therefore, this paper aims at early rumor detection by accounting for social bots' behavior, and presents a Social Bot-Aware Graph Neural Network, named SBAG. SBAG firstly pre-trains a multi-layer perception network to capture social bot features, and then constructs multiple graph neural networks by embedding the features to model the early propagation of posts, which is further used to detect rumors. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that SBAG achieves significant improvements against the baselines and also identifies rumors within 3 hours while maintaining more than 90% accuracy.

text: Early detection of rumors is a crucial but challenging task in preventing their widespread dissemination. Sociological research has revealed that social bots' behavior in the early stages of rumor propagation is a major contributor to the rapid spread of rumors. However, current models do not effectively distinguish between genuine users and social bots, resulting in a failure to timely detect rumors. This paper proposes a Social Bot-Aware Graph Neural Network (SBAG) to address this issue. SBAG starts by pre-training a multi-layer perception network to capture social bot features, and then uses these features to construct multiple graph neural networks that model the early propagation of posts. This information is then used to detect rumors. Our experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that SBAG outperforms existing methods and can detect rumors within three hours with over 90% accuracy.

text: Chinese spelling correction (CSC) is a task to detect and correct spelling errors in texts. CSC is essentially a linguistic problem, thus the ability of language understanding is crucial to this task. In this paper, we propose a Pre-trained masked Language model with Misspelled knowledgE (PLOME) for CSC, which jointly learns how to understand language and correct spelling errors. To this end, PLOME masks the chosen tokens with similar characters according to a confusion set rather than the fixed token “[MASK]” as in BERT. Besides character prediction, PLOME also introduces pronunciation prediction to learn the misspelled knowledge on phonic level. Moreover, phonological and visual similarity knowledge is important to this task. PLOME utilizes GRU networks to model such knowledge based on characters' phonics and strokes. Experiments are conducted on widely used benchmarks. Our method achieves superior performance against state-of-the-art approaches by a remarkable margin. We release the source code and pre-trained model for further use by the community (https://github.com/liushulinle/PLOME).

label: acl
text: The Chinese Spelling Correction (CSC) task involves detecting and correcting spelling errors in texts. As a linguistic problem, language understanding is key to its successful completion. In this paper, we propose a new approach, the Pre-trained masked Language model with Misspelled knowledge (PLOME), which combines language understanding with the ability to correct spelling errors. Unlike other models that use the fixed token "[MASK]", PLOME uses a confusion set to mask chosen tokens with similar characters. Additionally, PLOME incorporates pronunciation prediction to learn misspelled knowledge at the phonetic level and uses GRU networks to model phonological and visual similarity knowledge based on character phonetics and strokes. Our experiments on widely-used benchmarks show that PLOME outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. The source code and pre-trained model are available for community use at https://github.com/liushulinle/PLOME.

label: acl
text: Most of the neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models for grammatical error correction (GEC) have two limitations: (1) a seq2seq model may not be well generalized with only limited error-corrected data; (2) a seq2seq model may fail to completely correct a sentence with multiple errors through normal seq2seq inference. We attempt to address these limitations by proposing a fluency boost learning and inference mechanism. Fluency boosting learning generates fluency-boost sentence pairs during training, enabling the error correction model to learn how to improve a sentence's fluency from more instances, while fluency boosting inference allows the model to correct a sentence incrementally with multiple inference steps until the sentence's fluency stops increasing. Experiments show our approaches improve the performance of seq2seq models for GEC, achieving state-of-the-art results on both CoNLL-2014 and JFLEG benchmark datasets.

label: acl
text: Most neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models for grammatical error correction (GEC) have two major limitations. Firstly, these models may not generalize well with limited error-corrected data. Secondly, they may struggle to fully correct sentences with multiple errors through normal seq2seq inference. To address these limitations, we propose a fluency boost learning and inference mechanism. The fluency boost learning generates fluency-boosted sentence pairs during training, enabling the model to learn how to improve fluency from more examples. Fluency boosting inference allows the model to correct sentences incrementally, with multiple inference steps, until the fluency stops improving. Our approach improves the performance of seq2seq models for GEC, achieving state-of-the-art results on both CoNLL-2014 and JFLEG benchmark datasets.

text: Text style transfer (TST) is a well-known task whose goal is to convert the style of the text (e.g., from formal to informal) while preserving its content. Recently, it has been shown that both syntactic and semantic similarities between the source and the converted text are important for TST. However, the interaction between these two concepts has not been modeled. In this work, we propose a novel method based on Optimal Transport for TST to simultaneously incorporate syntactic and semantic information into similarity computation between the source and the converted text. We evaluate the proposed method in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Our analysis reveal the superiority of the proposed model in both settings.

label: naacl
text: The task of Text Style Transfer (TST) is well-known and aims to convert the style of text (e.g. from formal to informal) while retaining its content. Recent studies have demonstrated that both syntactic and semantic similarities are crucial for successful TST. However, the relationship between these two concepts has yet to be explored. This work introduces a novel approach, based on Optimal Transport, for TST that takes into account both syntactic and semantic information in computing the similarity between the source and converted text. Our method is evaluated in both supervised and unsupervised settings, and the results reveal its superiority in both scenarios.

text: We present an efficient BERT-based multi-task (MT) framework that is particularly suitable for iterative and incremental development of the tasks. The proposed framework is based on the idea of partial fine-tuning, i.e. only fine-tune some top layers of BERT while keep the other layers frozen. For each task, we train independently a single-task (ST) model using partial fine-tuning. Then we compress the task-specific layers in each ST model using knowledge distillation. Those compressed ST models are finally merged into one MT model so that the frozen layers of the former are shared across the tasks. We exemplify our approach on eight GLUE tasks, demonstrating that it is able to achieve 99.6% of the performance of the full fine-tuning method, while reducing up to two thirds of its overhead.

label: acl
text: We present an efficient BERT-based multi-task framework that is ideal for incremental and iterative task development. This framework is based on the concept of partial fine-tuning, where only the top layers of BERT are fine-tuned while the other layers remain frozen. For each task, we train a single-task model using partial fine-tuning, then compress the task-specific layers using knowledge distillation. These compressed single-task models are then combined into a single multi-task model, sharing the frozen layers across all tasks. Our approach is demonstrated on eight GLUE tasks and shows that it can achieve 99.6% of the performance of full fine-tuning, while reducing up to two-thirds of its overhead.

text: C-C-C-Nearest-Neighbor Machine Translation (D-D-DNN-MT) has been recently proposed as a non-parametric solution for domain adaptation in neural machine translation (NMT). It aims to alleviate the performance degradation of advanced MT systems in translating out-of-domain sentences by coordinating with an additional token-level feature-based retrieval module constructed from in-domain data. Previous studies (Khandelwal et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021) have already demonstrated that non-parametric NMT is even superior to models fine-tuned on out-of-domain data. In spite of this success, E-E-ENN retrieval is at the expense of high latency, in particular for large datastores. To make it practical, in this paper, we explore a more efficient F-F-FNN-MT and propose to use clustering to improve the retrieval efficiency. Concretely, we first propose a cluster-based Compact Network for feature reduction in a contrastive learning manner to compress context features into 90+% lower dimensional vectors. We then suggest a cluster-based pruning solution to filter out 10% 40% redundant nodes in large datastores while retaining translation quality. Our proposed methods achieve better or comparable performance while reducing up to 57% inference latency against the advanced non-parametric MT model on several machine translation benchmarks. Experimental results indicate that the proposed methods maintain the most useful information of the original datastore and the Compact Network shows good generalization on unseen domains. Codes are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/PCKMT.

text: The recently proposed C-C-C-Nearest-Neighbor Machine Translation (D-D-DNN-MT) is a non-parametric solution that addresses the performance degradation of advanced neural machine translation (NMT) systems when translating out-of-domain sentences. This is achieved through the use of an additional token-level feature-based retrieval module, constructed from in-domain data. Previous studies have shown that non-parametric NMT can outperform models fine-tuned on out-of-domain data (Khandelwal et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021). However, the high latency of E-E-ENN retrieval can be a challenge, particularly for large data stores. To overcome this, this paper explores a more efficient F-F-FNN-MT and proposes the use of clustering to improve retrieval efficiency. Specifically, we introduce a cluster-based Compact Network for feature reduction, which compresses context features into 90+% lower dimensional vectors in a contrastive learning manner. We also suggest a cluster-based pruning solution to filter out 10-40% of redundant nodes in large data stores, while retaining translation quality. Our proposed methods achieve better or comparable performance, reducing inference latency by up to 57% compared to the advanced non-parametric MT model on several machine translation benchmarks. The results indicate that our methods maintain the most useful information from the original data store and the Compact Network demonstrates good generalization on unseen domains. The code is available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/PCKMT.

text: Recognizing named entities in a document is a key task in many NLP applications. Although current state-of-the-art approaches to this task reach a high performance on clean text (e.g. newswire genres), those algorithms dramatically degrade when they are moved to noisy environments such as social media domains. We present two systems that address the challenges of processing social media data using character-level phonetics and phonology, word embeddings, and Part-of-Speech tags as features. The first model is a multitask end-to-end Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BLSTM)-Conditional Random Field (CRF) network whose output layer contains two CRF classifiers. The second model uses a multitask BLSTM network as feature extractor that transfers the learning to a CRF classifier for the final prediction. Our systems outperform the current F1 scores of the state of the art on the Workshop on Noisy User-generated Text 2017 dataset by 2.45% and 3.69%, establishing a more suitable approach for social media environments.

text: The recognition of named entities in documents is a crucial aspect in various NLP applications. Despite the high performance of current state-of-the-art techniques in clean text environments (such as newswire genres), their effectiveness significantly decreases when applied to noisy environments like social media. To tackle this challenge, we propose two systems that utilize character-level phonetics and phonology, word embeddings, and Part-of-Speech tags as features. The first system is a multitask Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BLSTM)-Conditional Random Field (CRF) network with two CRF classifiers in its output layer. The second system employs a multitask BLSTM network as a feature extractor, which transfers its learning to a CRF classifier for the final prediction. Our systems surpass the current state-of-the-art F1 scores on the Workshop on Noisy User-generated Text 2017 dataset by 2.45% and 3.69%, providing a more effective solution for social media environments.

text: Out-of-Domain (OOD) detection is a key component in a task-oriented dialog system, which aims to identify whether a query falls outside the predefined supported intent set. Previous softmax-based detection algorithms are proved to be overconfident for OOD samples. In this paper, we analyze overconfident OOD comes from distribution uncertainty due to the mismatch between the training and test distributions, which makes the model can't confidently make predictions thus probably causes abnormal softmax scores. We propose a Bayesian OOD detection framework to calibrate distribution uncertainty using Monte-Carlo Dropout. Our method is flexible and easily pluggable to existing softmax-based baselines and gains 33.33% OOD F1 improvements with increasing only 0.41% inference time compared to MSP. Further analyses show the effectiveness of Bayesian learning for OOD detection.
