text: The detection of Out-of-Domain (OOD) is a crucial aspect of task-oriented dialog systems, which aims to determine if a query falls outside the predefined set of supported intents. Previous softmax-based detection algorithms have been shown to be overly confident when dealing with OOD samples. This paper explores the cause of this overconfidence, which is attributed to the mismatch between the training and test distributions, leading to distribution uncertainty and resulting in abnormal softmax scores. To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian OOD detection framework that utilizes Monte-Carlo Dropout to calibrate distribution uncertainty. Our approach is flexible and can be easily integrated into existing softmax-based models, resulting in a 33.33% improvement in OOD F1 scores while only increasing inference time by 0.41% compared to the MSP method. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Bayesian learning for OOD detection.

label: acl
text: Text representation models are prone to exhibit a range of societal biases, reflecting the non-controlled and biased nature of the underlying pretraining data, which consequently leads to severe ethical issues and even bias amplification. Recent work has predominantly focused on measuring and mitigating bias in pretrained language models. Surprisingly, the landscape of bias measurements and mitigation resources and methods for conversational language models is still very scarce: it is limited to only a few types of bias, artificially constructed resources, and completely ignores the impact that debiasing methods may have on the final perfor mance in dialog tasks, e.g., conversational response generation. In this work, we present REDDITBIAS, the first conversational data set grounded in the actual human conversations from Reddit, allowing for bias measurement and mitigation across four important bias dimensions: gender,race,religion, and queerness. Further, we develop an evaluation framework which simultaneously 1)measures bias on the developed REDDITBIAS resource, and 2)evaluates model capability in dialog tasks after model debiasing. We use the evaluation framework to benchmark the widely used conversational DialoGPT model along with the adaptations of four debiasing methods. Our results indicate that DialoGPT is biased with respect to religious groups and that some debiasing techniques can remove this bias while preserving downstream task performance.

text: Text representation models are often biased due to the non-controlled and biased nature of the underlying pretraining data, leading to severe ethical issues and even bias amplification. Despite recent efforts to measure and mitigate bias in pretrained language models, the landscape of bias measurements and mitigation resources and methods for conversational language models remains limited, with a focus on only a few types of bias, artificially constructed resources, and ignoring the impact of debiasing methods on the final performance in dialog tasks. To address this, we introduce REDDITBIAS, the first conversational data set grounded in actual human conversations from Reddit, allowing for bias measurement and mitigation across four important dimensions: gender, race, religion, and queerness. Our evaluation framework measures bias on the REDDITBIAS resource while simultaneously evaluating model capability in dialog tasks after debiasing. We use this framework to benchmark the widely used DialoGPT model and evaluate the impact of four debiasing methods on its performance. Our results show that DialoGPT is biased with respect to religious groups, and that some debiasing techniques can effectively remove this bias while preserving downstream task performance.

text: Sentiment analysis is used as a proxy to measure human emotion, where the objective is to categorize text according to some predefined notion of sentiment. Sentiment analysis datasets are typically constructed with gold-standard sentiment labels, assigned based on the results of manual annotations. When working with such annotations, it is common for dataset constructors to discard “noisy” or “controversial” data where there is significant disagreement on the proper label. In datasets constructed for the purpose of Twitter sentiment analysis (TSA), these controversial examples can compose over 30% of the originally annotated data. We argue that the removal of such data is a problematic trend because, when performing real-time sentiment classification of short-text, an automated system cannot know a priori which samples would fall into this category of disputed sentiment. We therefore propose the notion of a “complicated” class of sentiment to categorize such text, and argue that its inclusion in the short-text sentiment analysis framework will improve the quality of automated sentiment analysis systems as they are implemented in real-world settings. We motivate this argument by building and analyzing a new publicly available TSA dataset of over 7,000 tweets annotated with 5x coverage, named MTSA. Our analysis of classifier performance over our dataset offers insights into sentiment analysis dataset and model design, how current techniques would perform in the real world, and how researchers should handle difficult data.

label: naacl
text: The objective of sentiment analysis is to categorize text based on predefined emotions. Datasets used for sentiment analysis are usually built with gold-standard sentiment labels, which are assigned through manual annotations. However, during the construction of these datasets, "noisy" or "controversial" data is often discarded if there is significant disagreement on the proper label. In the case of Twitter sentiment analysis datasets, these controversial examples can make up over 30% of the original annotated data. The removal of such data is a problem because, when performing real-time sentiment classification of short text, an automated system cannot know beforehand which samples would fall into the disputed sentiment category. To address this, we propose the creation of a "complicated" class of sentiment to categorize such text. This will improve the quality of automated sentiment analysis systems in real-world settings. To support this argument, we have built and analyzed a new TSA dataset of over 7,000 tweets, annotated with 5x coverage, named MTSA. Our analysis of classifier performance provides insights into sentiment analysis dataset and model design, the performance of current techniques in real-world settings, and how researchers should handle difficult data.

text: We present a graph-based Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG) parser that uses BiLSTMs, highway connections, and character-level CNNs. Our best end-to-end parser, which jointly performs supertagging, POS tagging, and parsing, outperforms the previously reported best results by more than 2.2 LAS and UAS points. The graph-based parsing architecture allows for global inference and rich feature representations for TAG parsing, alleviating the fundamental trade-off between transition-based and graph-based parsing systems. We also demonstrate that the proposed parser achieves state-of-the-art performance in the downstream tasks of Parsing Evaluation using Textual Entailments (PETE) and Unbounded Dependency Recovery. This provides further support for the claim that TAG is a viable formalism for problems that require rich structural analysis of sentences.

label: naacl
text: We present a graph-based Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG) parser that utilizes BiLSTMs, highway connections, and character-level CNNs. Our top-performing end-to-end parser, which combines supertagging, POS tagging, and parsing, surpasses the previously reported best results by over 2.2 LAS and UAS points. The graph-based parsing architecture enables global inference and provides rich feature representations for TAG parsing, resolving the traditional trade-off between transition-based and graph-based parsing systems. Additionally, our parser demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in the downstream tasks of Parsing Evaluation using Textual Entailments (PETE) and Unbounded Dependency Recovery, further supporting the argument that TAG is an effective formalism for problems requiring in-depth structural analysis of sentences.

label: emnlp
text: The use of connectionist approaches in conversational agents has been progressing rapidly due to the availability of large corpora. However current generative dialogue models often lack coherence and are content poor. This work proposes an architecture to incorporate unstructured knowledge sources to enhance the next utterance prediction in chit-chat type of generative dialogue models. We focus on Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) conversational agents trained with the Reddit News dataset, and consider incorporating external knowledge from Wikipedia summaries as well as from the NELL knowledge base. Our experiments show faster training time and improved perplexity when leveraging external knowledge.

label: emnlp
text: The rapid progression of connectionist approaches in conversational agents is due to the abundance of large corpora. However, current generative dialogue models often suffer from a lack of coherence and content. This study proposes an architecture that incorporates unstructured knowledge sources to improve the next utterance prediction in chit-chat type generative dialogue models. The focus is on Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) conversational agents trained with the Reddit News dataset and incorporating external knowledge from Wikipedia summaries and the NELL knowledge base. The results of our experiments demonstrate faster training times and improved perplexity when utilizing external knowledge.

label: acl
text: To defend against machine-generated fake news, an effective mechanism is urgently needed. We contribute a novel benchmark for fake news detection at the knowledge element level, as well as a solution for this task which incorporates cross-media consistency checking to detect the fine-grained knowledge elements making news articles misinformative. Due to training data scarcity, we also formulate a novel data synthesis method by manipulating knowledge elements within the knowledge graph to generate noisy training data with specific, hard to detect, known inconsistencies. Our detection approach outperforms the state-of-the-art (up to 16.8% accuracy gain), and more critically, yields fine-grained explanations.

label: acl
text: To counteract the threat posed by machine-generated fake news, an efficient solution is imperative. We present a groundbreaking benchmark for fake news detection that focuses on individual knowledge elements. Our solution incorporates cross-media consistency checking to identify the specific knowledge elements that make news articles misleading. To address the issue of limited training data, we have also developed a novel data synthesis method that generates noisy training data with known inconsistencies by manipulating knowledge elements within a knowledge graph. Our detection approach surpasses the current state-of-the-art, achieving up to 16.8% accuracy improvement, and provides detailed explanations for its results.

label: acl
text: Since language models are used to model a wide variety of languages, it is natural to ask whether the neural architectures used for the task have inductive biases towards modeling particular types of languages. Investigation of these biases has proved complicated due to the many variables that appear in the experimental setup. Languages vary in many typological dimensions, and it is difficult to single out one or two to investigate without the others acting as confounders. We propose a novel method for investigating the inductive biases of language models using artificial languages. These languages are constructed to allow us to create parallel corpora across languages that differ only in the typological feature being investigated, such as word order. We then use them to train and test language models. This constitutes a fully controlled causal framework, and demonstrates how grammar engineering can serve as a useful tool for analyzing neural models. Using this method, we find that commonly used neural architectures exhibit different inductive biases: LSTMs display little preference with respect to word ordering, while transformers display a clear preference for some orderings over others. Further, we find that neither the inductive bias of the LSTM nor that of the transformer appear to reflect any tendencies that we see in attested natural languages.

This suggests that the inductive biases of language models are not simply a reflection of the linguistic knowledge they have been exposed to during training, but are instead a result of the architecture of the model itself.

Language models are commonly used to model a wide range of languages, leading to the question of whether the neural architectures utilized for this task have an inherent bias towards modeling specific language types. However, it is challenging to investigate these biases due to the various variables involved in the experimental setup. Languages differ in many typological dimensions, and it is difficult to isolate one or two to study without considering the others as confounding factors. To address this issue, we propose a novel method for investigating the inductive biases of language models using artificial languages. These languages are designed to allow us to create parallel corpora across languages that only vary in the typological feature being examined, such as word order. By training and testing language models using these artificial languages, we create a controlled causal framework to demonstrate how grammar engineering can be a useful tool for analyzing neural models. Our results show that commonly used neural architectures have different inductive biases: LSTMs show little preference for word ordering, while transformers exhibit a clear preference for certain orderings. Additionally, we find that neither the inductive bias of LSTMs nor that of transformers align with tendencies observed in natural languages, suggesting that the inductive biases of language models are not solely a reflection of the linguistic knowledge they have been exposed to during training, but are also influenced by the architecture of the model itself.

text: Review text has been widely studied in traditional tasks such as sentiment analysis and aspect extraction. However, to date, no work is towards the abstractive review summarization that is essential for business organizations and individual consumers to make informed decisions. This work takes the lead to study the aspect/sentiment-aware abstractive review summarization by exploring multi-factor attentions. Specifically, we propose an interactive attention mechanism to interactively learns the representations of context words, sentiment words and aspect words within the reviews, acted as an encoder. The learned sentiment and aspect representations are incorporated into the decoder to generate aspect/sentiment-aware review summaries via an attention fusion network. In addition, the abstractive summarizer is jointly trained with the text categorization task, which helps learn a category-specific text encoder, locating salient aspect information and exploring the variations of style and wording of content with respect to different text categories. The experimental results on a real-life dataset demonstrate that our model achieves impressive results compared to other strong competitors.

text: This work explores the aspect/sentiment-aware abstractive review summarization by introducing a multi-factor attention mechanism. Our proposed interactive attention mechanism learns the representations of context words, sentiment words, and aspect words within the reviews, which act as an encoder. The sentiment and aspect representations are then used in the decoder to generate aspect/sentiment-aware review summaries through an attention fusion network. Additionally, our abstractive summarizer is trained jointly with a text categorization task to learn a category-specific text encoder and to identify salient aspect information, as well as to understand the variations in style and wording of content across different text categories. The results of our experiments on a real-life dataset show that our model outperforms other strong competitors.

label: emnlp
text: Generating a text abstract from a set of documents remains a challenging task. The neural encoder-decoder framework has recently been exploited to summarize single documents, but its success can in part be attributed to the availability of large parallel data automatically acquired from the Web. In contrast, parallel data for multi-document summarization are scarce and costly to obtain. There is a pressing need to adapt an encoder-decoder model trained on single-document summarization data to work with multiple-document input. In this paper, we present an initial investigation into a novel adaptation method. It exploits the maximal marginal relevance method to select representative sentences from multi-document input, and leverages an abstractive encoder-decoder model to fuse disparate sentences to an abstractive summary. The adaptation method is robust and itself requires no training data. Our system compares favorably to state-of-the-art extractive and abstractive approaches judged by automatic metrics and human assessors.

label: emnlp
text: The task of generating a text abstract from a set of documents remains challenging. The neural encoder-decoder framework has been utilized to summarize single documents, but its success is largely due to the availability of large parallel data obtained automatically from the web. In contrast, parallel data for multi-document summarization is scarce and expensive to obtain. There is an urgent need to adapt the encoder-decoder model trained on single-document summarization data to work with multi-document input. In this paper, we present a novel adaptation method that leverages the maximal marginal relevance method to select representative sentences from multi-document input and fuses them into an abstractive summary using an abstractive encoder-decoder model. This adaptation method requires no training data and is robust. Our system outperforms state-of-the-art extractive and abstractive approaches as evaluated by both automatic metrics and human assessors.

label: naacl
text: Current measures for evaluating text simplification systems focus on evaluating lexical text aspects, neglecting its structural aspects. In this paper we propose the first measure to address structural aspects of text simplification, called SAMSA. It leverages recent advances in semantic parsing to assess simplification quality by decomposing the input based on its semantic structure and comparing it to the output. SAMSA provides a reference-less automatic evaluation procedure, avoiding the problems that reference-based methods face due to the vast space of valid simplifications for a given sentence. Our human evaluation experiments show both SAMSA's substantial correlation with human judgments, as well as the deficiency of existing reference-based measures in evaluating structural simplification.

label: naacl
text: The current methods for evaluating text simplification systems concentrate solely on the lexical aspects of the text, ignoring its structural aspects. This paper introduces the first measure, SAMSA, which addresses the structural aspects of text simplification. SAMSA uses cutting-edge semantic parsing techniques to evaluate the quality of simplification by breaking down the input text based on its semantic structure and comparing it to the output. This reference-less automatic evaluation method eliminates the problems encountered by reference-based methods, which are faced with a vast number of valid simplifications for a given sentence. Our human evaluation experiments demonstrate SAMSA's strong correlation with human judgments and the limitations of existing reference-based measures in evaluating structural simplification.

label: naacl
text: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved remarkable success on various natural language understanding tasks. Simple fine-tuning of PLMs, on the other hand, might be suboptimal for domain-specific tasks because they cannot possibly cover knowledge from all domains. While adaptive pre-training of PLMs can help them obtain domain-specific knowledge, it requires a large training cost. Moreover, adaptive pre-training can harm the PLM's performance on the downstream task by causing catastrophic forgetting of its general knowledge. To overcome such limitations of adaptive pre-training for PLM adaption, we propose a novel domain adaption framework for PLMs coined as Knowledge-Augmented Language model Adaptation (KALA), which modulates the intermediate hidden representations of PLMs with domain knowledge, consisting of entities and their relational facts. We validate the performance of our KALA on question answering and named entity recognition tasks on multiple datasets across various domains. The results show that, despite being computationally efficient, our KALA largely outperforms adaptive pre-training.

label: naacl
text: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved great success in various natural language understanding tasks. Adaptive pre-training of PLMs can provide domain-specific knowledge, but it is costly and can lead to catastrophic forgetting of the general knowledge of PLMs. To address these limitations, we propose a novel domain adaptation framework for PLMs called Knowledge-Augmented Language Model Adaptation (KALA). This framework modulates the intermediate hidden representations of PLMs with domain knowledge, which includes entities and their relational facts. Our KALA is tested on question answering and named entity recognition tasks across multiple datasets and domains and shows that, despite being computationally efficient, it outperforms adaptive pre-training.

text: Visual question answering (VQA) is a challenging task that requires a computer system to understand both a question and an image. While there is much research on VQA in English, there is a lack of datasets for other languages, and English annotation is not directly applicable in those languages. To deal with this, we have created a Japanese VQA dataset by using crowdsourced annotation with images from the Visual Genome dataset. This is the first such dataset in Japanese. As another contribution, we propose a cross-lingual method for making use of English annotation to improve a Japanese VQA system. The proposed method is based on a popular VQA method that uses an attention mechanism. We use attention maps generated from English questions to help improve the Japanese VQA task. The proposed method experimentally performed better than simply using a monolingual corpus, which demonstrates the effectiveness of using attention maps to transfer cross-lingual information.

text: The task of Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a challenging one, as it requires a computer system to comprehend both a question and an image. Despite the abundance of research conducted on VQA in English, there is a scarcity of datasets for other languages and English annotations are not directly transferable. To address this issue, we have created the first Japanese VQA dataset by utilizing crowdsourced annotations and images from the Visual Genome dataset. Additionally, we propose a cross-lingual approach to enhance the Japanese VQA system by utilizing English annotations. Our method is based on a popular VQA approach that employs an attention mechanism, and uses the attention maps generated from English questions to improve the Japanese VQA task. Our experiments show that this method outperforms a monolingual corpus, demonstrating the effectiveness of using attention maps to transfer cross-lingual information.

text: Essay exams have been attracting attention as a way of measuring the higher-order abilities of examinees, but they have two major drawbacks in that grading them is expensive and raises questions about fairness. As an approach to overcome these problems, automated essay scoring (AES) is in increasing need. Many AES models based on deep neural networks have been proposed in recent years and have achieved high accuracy, but most of these models are designed to predict only a single overall score. However, to provide detailed feedback in practical situations, we often require not only the overall score but also analytic scores corresponding to various aspects of the essay.Several neural AES models that can predict both the analytic scores and the overall score have also been proposed for this very purpose. However, conventional models are designed to have complex neural architectures for each analytic score, which makes interpreting the score prediction difficult. To improve the interpretability of the prediction while maintaining scoring accuracy, we propose a new neural model for automated analytic scoring that integrates a multidimensional item response theory model, which is a popular psychometric model.

label: coling

Our proposed model can predict both the overall score and the analytic scores in a simple and interpretable manner, and it has been shown to have high accuracy in experiments.

Essay exams are attracting attention as a way to measure higher-order abilities, but they have two main drawbacks: the cost of grading and questions about fairness. To address these issues, the use of Automated Essay Scoring (AES) is becoming increasingly necessary. Recent years have seen the development of many AES models based on deep neural networks, which have achieved high accuracy. However, these models are primarily designed to predict a single overall score and not the various aspects of an essay. To provide detailed feedback, there is a need for AES models that can predict both an overall score and analytic scores. Some models have been proposed to meet this need, but they have complex neural architectures, making it difficult to interpret the prediction. With the aim of improving interpretability while maintaining accuracy, we propose a new neural model that integrates multidimensional item response theory. Our model can predict both overall and analytic scores in a simple, interpretable way and has been shown to be highly accurate in experiments.

text: The proliferation of misleading information in everyday access media outlets such as social media feeds, news blogs, and online newspapers have made it challenging to identify trustworthy news sources, thus increasing the need for computational tools able to provide insights into the reliability of online content. In this paper, we focus on the automatic identification of fake content in online news. Our contribution is twofold. First, we introduce two novel datasets for the task of fake news detection, covering seven different news domains. We describe the collection, annotation, and validation process in detail and present several exploratory analyses on the identification of linguistic differences in fake and legitimate news content. Second, we conduct a set of learning experiments to build accurate fake news detectors, and show that we can achieve accuracies of up to 76%. In addition, we provide comparative analyses of the automatic and manual identification of fake news.

text: The increasing prevalence of false information in everyday access media outlets such as social media, news blogs, and online newspapers has made it difficult to determine trustworthy news sources, thereby creating a need for computational tools that can help assess the reliability of online content. This paper focuses on the automatic detection of fake news. Our contribution is twofold: we introduce two new datasets for the task of fake news detection, covering seven different news domains, and describe the collection, annotation, and validation process in detail. We also present exploratory analyses of linguistic differences in fake and legitimate news content. Furthermore, we conduct learning experiments to build accurate fake news detectors, achieving up to 76% accuracy. Finally, we compare the results of automatic and manual identification of fake news.

label: naacl
text: Language representations are an efficient tool used across NLP, but they are strife with encoded societal biases. These biases are studied extensively, but with a primary focus on English language representations and biases common in the context of Western society. In this work, we investigate the biases present in Hindi language representations such as caste and religion associated biases. We demonstrate how biases are unique to specific language representations based on the history and culture of the region they are widely spoken in, and also how the same societal bias (such as binary gender associated biases) when investigated across languages is encoded by different words and text spans. With this work, we emphasize on the necessity of social-awareness along with linguistic and grammatical artefacts when modeling language representations, in order to understand the biases encoded.

label: naacl
text: Language representations, which are widely used in NLP, are unfortunately plagued by societal biases that are encoded in them. While these biases have been studied extensively, the focus has primarily been on English language representations and the biases prevalent in Western society. This study aims to examine the biases present in Hindi language representations, such as those related to caste and religion. Our findings show that biases in language representations are unique to specific languages and are influenced by the history and culture of the region in which they are widely spoken. Additionally, we observe that the same societal biases, such as those related to binary gender, can be encoded differently across languages. This highlights the importance of considering social awareness, linguistic, and grammatical factors when modeling language representations to better understand the biases encoded in them.

label: acl
text: Reranking models enable the integration of rich features to select a better output hypothesis within an n-best list or lattice. These models have a long history in NLP, and we revisit discriminative reranking for modern neural machine translation models by training a large transformer architecture. This takes as input both the source sentence as well as a list of hypotheses to output a ranked list. The reranker is trained to predict the observed distribution of a desired metric, e.g. BLEU, over the n-best list. Since such a discriminator contains hundreds of millions of parameters, we improve its generalization using pre-training and data augmentation techniques. Experiments on four WMT directions show that our discriminative reranking approach is effective and complementary to existing generative reranking approaches, yielding improvements of up to 4 BLEU over the beam search output.

label: acl
text: Reranking models allow for the integration of rich features to select the best output hypothesis from an n-best list or lattice. With a long history in NLP, we revisit discriminative reranking for modern neural machine translation models. Our approach involves training a large transformer architecture, which takes both the source sentence and a list of hypotheses as input and outputs a ranked list. The reranker is trained to predict the distribution of a desired metric, such as BLEU, over the n-best list. To improve its generalization, we employ pre-training and data augmentation techniques, as the discriminator contains hundreds of millions of parameters. Our experiments on four WMT directions show that our discriminative reranking approach is effective and complementary to existing generative reranking methods, resulting in improvements of up to 4 BLEU over the beam search output.

label: coling
text: This paper introduces a new data augmentation method for neural machine translation that can enforce stronger semantic consistency both within and across languages. Our method is based on Conditional Masked Language Model (CMLM) which is bi-directional and can be conditional on both left and right context, as well as the label. We demonstrate that CMLM is a good technique for generating context-dependent word distributions. In particular, we show that CMLM is capable of enforcing semantic consistency by conditioning on both source and target during substitution. In addition, to enhance diversity, we incorporate the idea of soft word substitution for data augmentation which replaces a word with a probabilistic distribution over the vocabulary. Experiments on four translation datasets of different scales show that the overall solution results in more realistic data augmentation and better translation quality. Our approach consistently achieves the best performance in comparison with strong and recent works and yields improvements of up to 1.90 BLEU points over the baseline.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a novel data augmentation method for neural machine translation that enhances semantic consistency both within and across languages. Our method, based on the Conditional Masked Language Model (CMLM), is bi-directional and can be conditioned on both the left and right context as well as the label. Our results demonstrate that CMLM is a robust technique for generating context-dependent word distributions and enforcing semantic consistency by conditioning on both the source and target during substitution. To further diversify the data, we also implement the idea of soft word substitution, which replaces a word with a probabilistic distribution of the vocabulary. Our experiments on four translation datasets of varying sizes show that our approach leads to more realistic data augmentation and improved translation quality. In comparison with recent and strong works, our solution consistently achieves the best performance, with improvements of up to 1.90 BLEU points over the baseline.

label: coling
text: Despite the great progress of Visual Question Answering (VQA), current VQA models heavily rely on the superficial correlation between the question type and its corresponding frequent answers (i.e., language priors) to make predictions, without really understanding the input. In this work, we define the training instances with the same question type but different answers as superficially similar instances, and attribute the language priors to the confusion of VQA model on such instances. To solve this problem, we propose a novel training framework that explicitly encourages the VQA model to distinguish between the superficially similar instances. Specifically, for each training instance, we first construct a set that contains its superficially similar counterparts. Then we exploit the proposed distinguishing module to increase the distance between the instance and its counterparts in the answer space. In this way, the VQA model is forced to further focus on the other parts of the input beyond the question type, which helps to overcome the language priors. Experimental results show that our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP v2. Codes are available at Distinguishing-VQA.

text: Despite significant advancements in Visual Question Answering (VQA), current models still heavily rely on the superficial relationship between question type and frequent answers, known as language priors. This leads to confusion in the model when presented with superficially similar instances, using the same question type but with different answers. To address this issue, we have developed a novel training framework that explicitly encourages the VQA model to distinguish between superficially similar instances. By constructing a set of superficially similar instances for each training instance, our framework uses a distinguishing module to increase the distance between the instance and its counterparts in the answer space. This forces the VQA model to focus on other aspects of the input beyond the question type, effectively overcoming the limitations of language priors. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on VQA-CP v2, and the code is available at Distinguishing-VQA.

label: naacl
text: Detecting Out-of-Domain (OOD) or unknown intents from user queries is essential in a task-oriented dialog system. A key challenge of OOD detection is the overconfidence of neural models. In this paper, we comprehensively analyze overconfidence and classify it into two perspectives: over-confident OOD and in-domain (IND). Then according to intrinsic reasons, we respectively propose a novel reassigned contrastive learning (RCL) to discriminate IND intents for over-confident OOD and an adaptive class-dependent local threshold mechanism to separate similar IND and OOD intents for over-confident IND. Experiments and analyses show the effectiveness of our proposed method for both aspects of overconfidence issues.

text: Detection of Out-of-Domain (OOD) or unknown intents from user queries is crucial in task-oriented dialog systems. A major challenge in OOD detection is the overconfidence of neural models. In this paper, we thoroughly analyze this overconfidence and classify it into two categories: over-confident OOD and in-domain (IND). To address the intrinsic reasons behind this overconfidence, we present a new Reassigned Contrastive Learning (RCL) approach to differentiate IND intents from over-confident OOD and an Adaptive Class-Dependent Local Threshold Mechanism to distinguish similar IND and OOD intents for over-confident IND. Our results from experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in addressing both aspects of overconfidence.

text: Recent research shows that pre-trained language models, built to generate text conditioned on some context, learn to encode syntactic knowledge to a certain degree. This has motivated researchers to move beyond the sentence-level and look into their ability to encode less studied discourse-level phenomena. In this paper, we add to the body of probing research by investigating discourse entity representations in large pre-trained language models in English. Motivated by early theories of discourse and key pieces of previous work, we focus on the information-status of entities as discourse-new or discourse-old. We present two probing models, one based on binary classification and another one on sequence labeling. The results of our experiments show that pre-trained language models do encode information on whether an entity has been introduced before or not in the discourse. However, this information alone is not sufficient to find the entities in a discourse, opening up interesting questions about the definition of entities for future work.

text: Recent studies have revealed that pre-trained language models, designed to generate text based on a given context, possess a certain level of syntactic knowledge. This has prompted researchers to expand their focus beyond sentence-level analysis and investigate the models' ability to encode discourse-level phenomena. This paper contributes to the existing body of research by examining the representation of discourse entities in large pre-trained language models in English. Drawing upon early theories of discourse and previous work, we concentrate on the information-status of entities, specifically whether they are discourse-new or discourse-old. To this end, we employ two probing models, one based on binary classification and the other on sequence labeling. Our experiments demonstrate that pre-trained language models do encode information about whether an entity has been introduced previously in the discourse. However, this information alone is not enough to locate entities within a discourse, raising intriguing questions about entity definition for future research.

text: Simile is a special type of metaphor, where comparators such as like and as are used to compare two objects. Simile recognition is to recognize simile sentences and extract simile components, i.e., the tenor and the vehicle. This paper presents a study of simile recognition in Chinese. We construct an annotated corpus for this research, which consists of 11.3k sentences that contain a comparator. We propose a neural network framework for jointly optimizing three tasks: simile sentence classification, simile component extraction and language modeling. The experimental results show that the neural network based approaches can outperform all rule-based and feature-based baselines. Both simile sentence classification and simile component extraction can benefit from multitask learning. The former can be solved very well, while the latter is more difficult.

The language modeling task can also improve the overall performance.
Simile is a specific form of metaphor where comparators, such as "like" and "as," are utilized to compare two objects. Recognizing similes involves identifying simile sentences and extracting the tenor and vehicle components. This study focuses on simile recognition in the Chinese language. Multitask learning was found to improve both simile sentence classification and simile component extraction, with the former being easier to solve than the latter. text: Word ordering is a constrained language generation task taking unordered words as input. Existing work uses linear models and neural networks for the task, yet pre-trained language models have not been studied in word ordering, let alone why they help. We use BART as an instance and show its effectiveness in the task. To explain why BART helps word ordering, we extend analysis with probing and empirically identify that syntactic dependency knowledge in BART is a reliable explanation. We also report performance gains with BART in the related partial tree linearization task, which readily extends our analysis.

label: coling
text: The task of word ordering involves generating a language from unordered words as input. Previous research has utilized linear models and neural networks, but the impact of pre-trained language models has not been investigated. In this study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of BART (as an example) in word ordering and explain why it helps through probing and empirical analysis, which reveals that its syntactic dependency knowledge is a reliable factor. Additionally, we show improved performance in the related task of partial tree linearization, further supporting our analysis.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a model for tagging unstructured texts with an arbitrary number of terms drawn from a tree-structured vocabulary (i.e., an ontology). We treat this as a special case of sequence-to-sequence learning in which the decoder begins at the root node of an ontological tree and recursively elects to expand child nodes as a function of the input text, the current node, and the latent decoder state. We demonstrate that this method yields state-of-the-art results on the important task of assigning MeSH terms to biomedical abstracts.

label: emnlp
text: We propose a model for tagging unstructured texts with an arbitrary number of terms from a tree-structured vocabulary (i.e. an ontology). This is treated as a sequence-to-sequence learning problem, where the decoder starts at the root node of the ontological tree and recursively expands child nodes based on the input text, current node, and latent decoder state. Our approach results in state-of-the-art performance in assigning MeSH terms to biomedical abstracts.

label: coling
text: Keyphrase Prediction (KP) is an established NLP task, aiming to yield representative phrases to summarize the main content of a given document. Despite major progress in recent years, existing works on KP have mainly focused on formal texts such as scientific papers or weblogs. The challenges of KP in informal-text domains are not yet fully studied. To this end, this work studies new challenges of KP in transcripts of videos, an understudied domain for KP that involves informal texts and non-cohesive presentation styles. A bottleneck for KP research in this domain involves the lack of high-quality and large-scale annotated data that hinders the development of advanced KP models. To address this issue, we introduce a large-scale manually-annotated KP dataset in the domain of live-stream video transcripts obtained by automatic speech recognition tools. Concretely, transcripts of 500+ hours of videos streamed on the behance.net platform are manually labeled with important keyphrases. Our analysis of the dataset reveals the challenging nature of KP in transcripts. Moreover, for the first time in KP, we demonstrate the idea of improving KP for long documents (i.e., transcripts) by feeding models with paragraph-level keyphrases, i.e., hierarchical extraction. To foster future research, we will publicly release the dataset and code.

text: Keyphrase Prediction (KP) is a well-known NLP task with the goal of identifying representative phrases that summarize the content of a given document. Despite significant advancements in recent years, existing KP research has mainly focused on formal texts like scientific papers or weblogs. This work aims to address this gap by studying the new challenges of KP in video transcripts, an understudied domain that involves informal texts and non-cohesive presentation styles. The biggest obstacle to KP research in this domain is the lack of high-quality, large-scale annotated data, which hinders the development of advanced KP models. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a large-scale, manually annotated KP dataset for live-stream video transcripts obtained through automatic speech recognition tools. text: Story generation is a challenging problem in artificial intelligence (AI) and has received a lot of interests in the natural language processing (NLP) community. Most previous work tried to solve this problem using Sequence to Sequence (Seq2Seq) model trained with Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). However, the pure MLE training objective much limits the power of Seq2Seq model in generating high-quality storys. In this paper, we propose using adversarial training augmented Seq2Seq model to generate reasonable and diversified story endings given a story context. Our model includes a generator that defines the policy of generating a story ending, and a discriminator that labels story endings as human-generated or machine-generated. Carefully designed human and automatic evaluation metrics demonstrate that our adversarial training augmented Seq2Seq model can generate more reasonable and diversified story endings compared to purely MLE-trained Seq2Seq model. Moreover, our model achieves better performance on the task of Story Cloze Test with an accuracy of 62.6% compared with state-of-the-art baseline methods.

text: Story generation is a difficult problem in artificial intelligence (AI) and has gained a lot of attention in the natural language processing (NLP) community. Most previous work attempted to solve this problem using a Sequence to Sequence (Seq2Seq) model trained with Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). However, the MLE training objective limits the potential of the Seq2Seq model to generate high-quality stories. This paper proposes using an adversarial training augmented Seq2Seq model to generate diverse and reasonable story endings given a story context. The model consists of a generator that guides the creation of a story ending, and a discriminator that distinguishes between human-generated and machine-generated endings. Our results, based on both human and automated evaluations, show that the adversarial training augmented Seq2Seq model generates more diverse and reasonable story endings compared to the purely MLE-trained Seq2Seq model. Furthermore, our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods with a Story Cloze Test accuracy of 62.6%.

label: emnlp
text: Developing agents to engage in complex goal-oriented dialogues is challenging partly because the main learning signals are very sparse in long conversations. In this paper, we propose a divide-and-conquer approach that discovers and exploits the hidden structure of the task to enable efficient policy learning. First, given successful example dialogues, we propose the Subgoal Discovery Network (SDN) to divide a complex goal-oriented task into a set of simpler subgoals in an unsupervised fashion. We then use these subgoals to learn a multi-level policy by hierarchical reinforcement learning. We demonstrate our method by building a dialogue agent for the composite task of travel planning. Experiments with simulated and real users show that our approach performs competitively against a state-of-the-art method that requires human-defined subgoals. Moreover, we show that the learned subgoals are often human comprehensible.

label: emnlp
text: Developing agents for complex, goal-oriented dialogues is a challenge due to the sparse learning signals in long conversations. This paper introduces a divide-and-conquer approach that leverages the hidden structure of the task for efficient policy learning. We propose the Subgoal Discovery Network (SDN), which divides the complex task into simpler subgoals using successful example dialogues in an unsupervised fashion. This allows us to learn a multi-level policy using hierarchical reinforcement learning. Our method is demonstrated by creating a dialogue agent for travel planning and shows competitive results against a state-of-the-art method that requires human-defined subgoals. Additionally, the learned subgoals are often easily understandable by humans.

label: acl
text: Although current state-of-the-art Transformer-based solutions succeeded in a wide range for single-document NLP tasks, they still struggle to address multi-input tasks such as multi-document summarization. Many solutions truncate the inputs, thus ignoring potential summary-relevant contents, which is unacceptable in the medical domain where each information can be vital. Others leverage linear model approximations to apply multi-input concatenation, worsening the results because all information is considered, even if it is conflicting or noisy with respect to a shared background. Despite the importance and social impact of medicine, there are no ad-hoc solutions for multi-document summarization. For this reason, we propose a novel discriminative marginalized probabilistic method (DAMEN) trained to discriminate critical information from a cluster of topic-related medical documents and generate a multi-document summary via token probability marginalization. Results prove we outperform the previous state-of-the-art on a biomedical dataset for multi-document summarization of systematic literature reviews. Moreover, we perform extensive ablation studies to motivate the design choices and prove the importance of each module of our method.

label: acl
text: Despite the success of state-of-the-art Transformer-based solutions in a wide range of single-document NLP tasks, they still struggle with multi-input tasks such as multi-document summarization. Many solutions truncate the inputs, ignoring potentially important information, which is unacceptable in the medical field where every piece of information is critical. Other solutions use linear model approximations to concatenate multi-inputs, resulting in poor performance as all information is considered, even if it is conflicting or noisy. There are currently no specialized solutions for multi-document summarization in the medical field. To address this, we propose a novel method called DAMEN (Discriminative Marginalized Probabilistic Method) which is trained to discriminate critical information from a cluster of topic-related medical documents and generate a multi-document summary by marginalizing token probabilities. Our results show that we outperform the previous state-of-the-art in multi-document summarization of systematic literature reviews on a biomedical dataset. Additionally, we conduct extensive ablation studies to justify our design choices and demonstrate the importance of each component of our method.

label: acl
text: Understanding temporal and causal relations between events is a fundamental natural language understanding task. Because a cause must occur earlier than its effect, temporal and causal relations are closely related and one relation often dictates the value of the other. However, limited attention has been paid to studying these two relations jointly. This paper presents a joint inference framework for them using constrained conditional models (CCMs). Specifically, we formulate the joint problem as an integer linear programming (ILP) problem, enforcing constraints that are inherent in the nature of time and causality. We show that the joint inference framework results in statistically significant improvement in the extraction of both temporal and causal relations from text.

label: acl
text: The ability to comprehend the temporal and causal relationships between events is a crucial aspect of natural language understanding. These two relations are closely linked, as a cause must occur before its effect. Despite this, there has been limited research on studying these two relations together. This paper presents a joint inference framework, using Constrained Conditional Models (CCMs), to address this issue. We formulate the problem as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem, incorporating inherent constraints related to time and causality. Our results demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in the extraction of both temporal and causal relations from text.

label: emnlp
text: Simultaneous speech translation aims to maintain translation quality while minimizing the delay between reading input and incrementally producing the output. We propose a new general-purpose prediction action which predicts future words in the input to improve quality and minimize delay in simultaneous translation. We train this agent using reinforcement learning with a novel reward function. Our agent with prediction has better translation quality and less delay compared to an agent-based simultaneous translation system without prediction.

label: emnlp
text: Simultaneous speech translation strives to preserve the quality of translation while minimizing the time lag between the input being read and the output being produced incrementally. We introduce a new general-purpose prediction action that predicts future words in the input, thus enhancing quality and reducing the delay in simultaneous translation. We train this agent using a reinforcement learning approach and a unique reward function. Our prediction-based agent outperforms a traditional simultaneous translation system, delivering both improved translation quality and reduced delay.

label: coling
text: A Visual Question Answering (VQA) model processes images and questions simultaneously with rich semantic information. The attention mechanism can highlight fine-grained features with critical information, thus ensuring that feature extraction emphasizes the objects related to the questions. However, unattended coarse-grained information is also essential for questions involving global elements. We believe that global coarse-grained information and local fine-grained information can complement each other to provide richer comprehensive information. In this paper, we propose a dual capsule attention mask network with mutual learning for VQA. Specifically, it contains two branches processing coarse-grained features and fine-grained features, respectively. We also design a novel stackable dual capsule attention module to fuse features and locate evidence. The two branches are combined to make final predictions for VQA. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the baselines in terms of VQA performance and interpretability and achieves new SOTA performance on the VQA-v2 dataset.

label: coling
text: A Visual Question Answering (VQA) model processes both images and questions while incorporating rich semantic information. The attention mechanism is able to focus on fine-grained features that contain critical information, ensuring that feature extraction is centered around objects relevant to the questions. However, it is also important to consider unattended coarse-grained information for questions that involve global elements. We believe that a combination of global coarse-grained information and local fine-grained information can provide a more comprehensive understanding. In this study, we present a novel Dual Capsule Attention Mask Network with Mutual Learning for VQA. This model consists of two branches, one for processing coarse-grained features and one for processing fine-grained features. We have also developed a unique Stackable Dual Capsule Attention Module to effectively fuse features and identify evidence. The results of our final predictions are obtained by combining the output of both branches. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines in terms of VQA performance and interpretability, achieving new state-of-the-art performance on the VQA-v2 dataset.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we present a conceptually simple while empirically powerful framework for abstractive summarization, SimCLS, which can bridge the gap between the learning objective and evaluation metrics resulting from the currently dominated sequence-to-sequence learning framework by formulating text generation as a reference-free evaluation problem (i.e., quality estimation) assisted by contrastive learning. Experimental results show that, with minor modification over existing top-scoring systems, SimCLS can improve the performance of existing top-performing models by a large margin. Particularly, 2.51 absolute improvement against BART and 2.50 over PEGASUS w.r.t ROUGE-1 on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, driving the state-of-the-art performance to a new level. We have open-sourced our codes and results: https://github.com/yixinL7/SimCLS. Results of our proposed models have been deployed into ExplainaBoard platform, which allows researchers to understand our systems in a more fine-grained way.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we introduce SimCLS, a conceptually simple yet empirically effective framework for abstractive summarization. SimCLS addresses the gap between the learning objective and evaluation metrics in the dominant sequence-to-sequence framework by formulating text generation as a reference-free evaluation problem (i.e., quality estimation) aided by contrastive learning. Our experiments demonstrate that SimCLS can significantly improve the performance of existing top-performing models with minimal modifications. Specifically, SimCLS achieved 2.51 absolute improvement over BART and 2.50 over PEGASUS in terms of ROUGE-1 on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, setting a new state-of-the-art performance. Our codes and results are available on GitHub at https://github.com/yixinL7/SimCLS. Additionally, our proposed models have been integrated into the ExplainaBoard platform, providing researchers with a more detailed understanding of our systems.

label: acl
text: Incorporating syntax into neural approaches in NLP has a multitude of practical and scientific benefits. For instance, a language model that is syntax-aware is likely to be able to produce better samples; even a discriminative model like BERT with a syntax module could be used for core NLP tasks like unsupervised syntactic parsing. Rapid progress in recent years was arguably spurred on by the empirical success of the Parsing-Reading-Predict architecture of (Shen et al., 2018a), later simplified by the Order Neuron LSTM of (Shen et al., 2019). Most notably, this is the first time neural approaches were able to successfully perform unsupervised syntactic parsing (evaluated by various metrics like F-1 score). However, even heuristic (much less fully mathematical) understanding of why and when these architectures work is lagging severely behind. In this work, we answer representational questions raised by the architectures in (Shen et al., 2018a, 2019), as well as some transition-based syntax-aware language models (Dyer et al., 2016): what kind of syntactic structure can current neural approaches to syntax represent? Concretely, we ground this question in the sandbox of probabilistic context-free-grammars (PCFGs), and identify a key aspect of the representational power of these approaches: the amount and directionality of context that the predictor has access to when forced to make parsing decision. We show that with limited context (either bounded, or unidirectional), there are PCFGs, for which these approaches cannot represent the max-likelihood parse; conversely, if the context is unlimited, they can represent the max-likelihood parse of any PCFG.
