text: Incorporating syntax into NLP approaches has numerous practical and scientific benefits. For example, a language model that is syntax-aware is likely to produce better samples. Even a discriminative model like BERT with a syntax module can be used for core NLP tasks like unsupervised syntactic parsing. The recent rapid progress in this field was largely due to the empirical success of the Parsing-Reading-Predict architecture (Shen et al., 2018a) and the Order Neuron LSTM (Shen et al., 2019). These architectures were the first to successfully perform unsupervised syntactic parsing, as evaluated by various metrics such as the F-1 score. However, there is a lack of understanding of why and when these architectures work. In this work, we address the representational questions raised by the architectures in (Shen et al., 2018a, 2019) and some transition-based syntax-aware language models (Dyer et al., 2016). Specifically, we examine what kind of syntactic structure current neural approaches to syntax can represent. To do this, we focus on probabilistic context-free-grammars (PCFGs) and explore the key aspect of the representational power of these approaches: the amount and directionality of context available to the predictor when making parsing decisions. We show that with limited context (either bounded or unidirectional), there are PCFGs that these approaches cannot represent the max-likelihood parse. Conversely, if the context is unlimited, they can represent the max-likelihood parse of any PCFG.

label: coling
text: Dependency tree-based methods might be susceptible to the dependency tree due to that they inevitably introduce noisy information and neglect the rich relation information between words. In this paper, we propose a learnable dependency-based double graph (LD2G) model for aspect-based sentiment classification. We use multi-task learning for domain adaptive pretraining, which combines Biaffine Attention and Mask Language Model by incorporating features such as structure, relations and linguistic features in the sentiment text. Then we utilize the dependency enhanced double graph-based MPNN to deeply fuse structure features and relation features that are affected with each other for ASC. Experiment on four benchmark datasets shows that our model is superior to the state-of-the-art approaches.

label: coling
text: Dependency tree-based methods for aspect-based sentiment classification (ASC) may be limited by the introduction of noisy information and the neglect of rich relation information between words in the dependency tree. To address this issue, we present a learnable dependency-based double graph (LD2G) model. Our model leverages multi-task learning for domain adaptive pretraining, which combines Biaffine Attention and Mask Language Model to incorporate structure, relation, and linguistic features in the sentiment text. We then employ a dependency-enhanced double graph-based MPNN to deeply fuse structure and relation features, which interact with each other in ASC. Our experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

label: coling
text: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to distinguish sentiment polarity of every specific aspect in a given sentence. Previous researches have realized the importance of interactive learning with context and aspects. However, these methods are ill-studied to learn complex sentence with multiple aspects due to overlapped polarity feature. And they do not consider the correlation between aspects to distinguish overlapped feature. In order to solve this problem, we propose a new method called Recurrent Inverse Learning Guided Network (RILGNet). Our RILGNet has two points to improve the modeling of aspect correlation and the selecting of aspect feature. First, we use Recurrent Mechanism to improve the joint representation of aspects, which enhances the aspect correlation modeling iteratively. Second, we propose Inverse Learning Guidance to improve the selection of aspect feature by considering aspect correlation, which provides more useful information to determine polarity. Experimental results on SemEval 2014 Datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of RILGNet, and we further prove that RILGNet is state-of-the-art method in multiaspect scenarios.

label: coling
text: Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) aims to identify the sentiment polarity of each specific aspect within a given sentence. Previous research has emphasized the importance of interactive learning with context and aspects. However, these methods are limited in their ability to learn complex sentences with multiple aspects due to overlapping polarity features. They also fail to consider the correlation between aspects when distinguishing overlapping features. To address these limitations, we propose a new method called Recurrent Inverse Learning Guided Network (RILGNet). Our RILGNet improves upon the modeling of aspect correlation and aspect feature selection in two ways. Firstly, it uses a Recurrent Mechanism to enhance the joint representation of aspects, thereby iteratively improving aspect correlation modeling. Secondly, it employs Inverse Learning Guidance to improve aspect feature selection by considering aspect correlation, providing more useful information to determine polarity. Experimental results on the SemEval 2014 Datasets show the effectiveness of RILGNet and demonstrate that it is a state-of-the-art method for multiaspect scenarios.

label: acl
text: Estimating the expected output quality of generation systems is central to NLG. This paper qualifies the notion that automatic metrics are not as good as humans in estimating system-level quality. Statistically, humans are unbiased, high variance estimators, while metrics are biased, low variance estimators. We compare these estimators by their error in pairwise prediction (which generation system is better?) using the bootstrap. Measuring this error is complicated: predictions are evaluated against noisy, human predicted labels instead of the ground truth, and metric predictions fluctuate based on the test sets they were calculated on. By applying a bias-variance-noise decomposition, we adjust this error to a noise-free, infinite test set setting. Our analysis compares the adjusted error of metrics to humans and a derived, perfect segment-level annotator, both of which are unbiased estimators dependent on the number of judgments collected. In MT, we identify two settings where metrics outperform humans due to a statistical advantage in variance: when the number of human judgments used is small, and when the quality difference between compared systems is small.

label: acl
text:
In NLG, metrics outperform humans in both settings.

Estimating the quality of output generated by NLG systems is crucial. This paper challenges the notion that automatic metrics are inferior to human evaluation in determining system-level quality. Statistically, humans are unbiased with high variance, whereas metrics are biased with low variance. We compare these estimators by evaluating their error in pairwise prediction (which system is better?) using the bootstrap method. However, this evaluation is complicated as predictions are assessed against human-predicted labels that are noisy, instead of the ground truth, and metric predictions vary based on the test sets they were calculated from. We adjust this error by applying a bias-variance-noise decomposition, which enables us to compare the error of metrics to humans and a perfect segment-level annotator in a noise-free, infinite test set setting. Our analysis shows that in MT, metrics outperform human evaluation in two scenarios: when the number of human judgments is small and when the quality difference between the compared systems is small. In NLG, metrics outperform human evaluation in both scenarios.

label: coling
text: A scene graph is a semantic representation that expresses the objects, attributes, and relationships between objects in a scene. Scene graphs play an important role in many cross modality tasks, as they are able to capture the interactions between images and texts. In this paper, we focus on scene graph modification (SGM), where the system is required to learn how to update an existing scene graph based on a natural language query. Unlike previous approaches that rebuilt the entire scene graph, we frame SGM as a graph expansion task by introducing the incremental structure expanding (ISE). ISE constructs the target graph by incrementally expanding the source graph without changing the unmodified structure. Based on ISE, we further propose a model that iterates between nodes prediction and edges prediction, inferring more accurate and harmonious expansion decisions progressively. In addition, we construct a challenging dataset that contains more complicated queries and larger scene graphs than existing datasets. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which surpasses the previous state-of-the-art model by large margins.

label: coling
text: A scene graph is a semantic representation that expresses the objects, attributes, and relationships between objects in a scene. Scene graphs play a crucial role in many cross-modality tasks, as they capture the interactions between images and texts. In this paper, we focus on Scene Graph Modification (SGM), where the system is required to learn how to update an existing scene graph based on a natural language query. Unlike previous approaches that rebuilt the entire scene graph, we frame SGM as a graph expansion task with the introduction of Incremental Structure Expanding (ISE). ISE expands the target graph incrementally from the source graph, preserving the unmodified structure. We propose a model that iteratively predicts nodes and edges, leading to progressively more accurate and harmonious expansion decisions. Furthermore, we construct a challenging dataset with more complex queries and larger scene graphs than existing datasets. Our experiments on four benchmarks show the superiority of our approach, outperforming the current state-of-the-art model by a significant margin.

label: naacl
text: Dialogue state tracking (DST) aims to predict the current dialogue state given the dialogue history. Existing methods generally exploit the utterances of all dialogue turns to assign value for each slot. This could lead to suboptimal results due to the information introduced from irrelevant utterances in the dialogue history, which may be useless and can even cause confusion. To address this problem, we propose LUNA, a SLot-TUrN Alignment enhanced approach. It first explicitly aligns each slot with its most relevant utterance, then further predicts the corresponding value based on this aligned utterance instead of all dialogue utterances. Furthermore, we design a slot ranking auxiliary task to learn the temporal correlation among slots which could facilitate the alignment. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on three multi-domain task-oriented dialogue datasets, MultiWOZ 2.0, MultiWOZ 2.1, and MultiWOZ 2.2. The results show that LUNA achieves new state-of-the-art results on these datasets.

label: naacl
text: Dialogue State Tracking (DST) aims to predict the current state of a dialogue based on its history. Existing methods use all dialogue turns to assign values to each slot, which can lead to suboptimal results due to irrelevant information and confusion from irrelevant utterances. To overcome this, we introduce LUNA, a Slot-Turn Alignment enhanced approach. LUNA aligns each slot with its most relevant utterance and predicts its corresponding value based on this alignment, instead of all dialogue utterances. Additionally, we design a slot ranking auxiliary task to learn the temporal correlation among slots, which enhances the alignment. Our experiments on three multi-domain task-oriented dialogue datasets, MultiWOZ 2.0, MultiWOZ 2.1, and MultiWOZ 2.2, show that LUNA achieves new state-of-the-art results.

label: emnlp
text: Text normalization is an important enabling technology for several NLP tasks. Recently, neural-network-based approaches have outperformed well-established models in this task. However, in languages other than English, there has been little exploration in this direction. Both the scarcity of annotated data and the complexity of the language increase the difficulty of the problem. To address these challenges, we use a sequence-to-sequence model with character-based attention, which in addition to its self-learned character embeddings, uses word embeddings pre-trained with an approach that also models subword information. This provides the neural model with access to more linguistic information especially suitable for text normalization, without large parallel corpora. We show that providing the model with word-level features bridges the gap for the neural network approach to achieve a state-of-the-art F1 score on a standard Arabic language correction shared task dataset.

label: emnlp
text: Text normalization is a crucial technology that enables various NLP tasks. Recently, neural network-based methods have outperformed traditional models in this area. However, there has been limited exploration of this technology in languages other than English, due to the scarcity of annotated data and the complexity of the language. To overcome these challenges, we employ a sequence-to-sequence model with character-based attention. This model leverages self-learned character embeddings and pre-trained word embeddings that also incorporate subword information, providing the neural network with more linguistic information specifically suited for text normalization. Our results demonstrate that incorporating word-level features can significantly improve the neural network's performance, achieving a state-of-the-art F1 score on a standard Arabic language correction dataset.

label: acl
text: Multilingual neural machine translation with a single model has drawn much attention due to its capability to deal with multiple languages. However, the current multilingual translation paradigm often makes the model tend to preserve the general knowledge, but ignore the language-specific knowledge. Some previous works try to solve this problem by adding various kinds of language-specific modules to the model, but they suffer from the parameter explosion problem and require specialized manual design. To solve these problems, we propose to divide the model neurons into general and language-specific parts based on their importance across languages. The general part is responsible for preserving the general knowledge and participating in the translation of all the languages, while the language-specific part is responsible for preserving the language-specific knowledge and participating in the translation of some specific languages. Experimental results on several language pairs, covering IWSLT and Europarl corpus datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed method.

label: acl
text: The attention drawn towards multilingual neural machine translation using a single model is due to its ability to handle multiple languages. However, the current approach often results in the model prioritizing general knowledge over language-specific knowledge. Previous attempts to address this issue by incorporating language-specific modules have faced challenges, such as parameter explosion and the need for specialized manual design. To overcome these limitations, we propose a solution that separates the model neurons into general and language-specific components based on their significance across languages. The general component is responsible for preserving general knowledge and participating in the translation of all languages, while the language-specific component focuses on preserving language-specific knowledge and participating in the translation of specific languages. Our experimental results, using datasets from IWSLT and Europarl corpus, demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of our proposed method.

label: acl
text: Video Question Answering is a task which requires an AI agent to answer questions grounded in video. This task entails three key challenges: (1) understand the intention of various questions, (2) capturing various elements of the input video (e.g., object, action, causality), and (3) cross-modal grounding between language and vision information. We propose Motion-Appearance Synergistic Networks (MASN), which embed two cross-modal features grounded on motion and appearance information and selectively utilize them depending on the question's intentions. MASN consists of a motion module, an appearance module, and a motion-appearance fusion module. The motion module computes the action-oriented cross-modal joint representations, while the appearance module focuses on the appearance aspect of the input video. Finally, the motion-appearance fusion module takes each output of the motion module and the appearance module as input, and performs question-guided fusion. As a result, MASN achieves new state-of-the-art performance on the TGIF-QA and MSVD-QA datasets. We also conduct qualitative analysis by visualizing the inference results of MASN.

label: acl
text: The task of Video Question Answering (VQA) requires an AI agent to answer questions that are grounded in video content. This task presents three significant challenges: (1) understanding the intent behind various questions, (2) capturing various elements of the video input such as objects, actions, and causality, and (3) cross-modal grounding between language and vision information. To address these challenges, we propose the Motion-Appearance Synergistic Networks (MASN). MASN embeds two cross-modal features, grounded in motion and appearance information, and selectively utilizes them based on the question's intent. The network consists of three modules: a motion module, an appearance module, and a motion-appearance fusion module. The motion module calculates action-oriented cross-modal joint representations, while the appearance module focuses on the appearance aspect of the video input. Finally, the motion-appearance fusion module takes the outputs of both the motion and appearance modules as inputs and performs question-guided fusion. As a result, MASN achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on the TGIF-QA and MSVD-QA datasets. We also perform qualitative analysis by visualizing the results of MASN's inference.

label: acl
text: Inspired by how humans summarize long documents, we propose an accurate and fast summarization model that first selects salient sentences and then rewrites them abstractively (i.e., compresses and paraphrases) to generate a concise overall summary. We use a novel sentence-level policy gradient method to bridge the non-differentiable computation between these two neural networks in a hierarchical way, while maintaining language fluency. Empirically, we achieve the new state-of-the-art on all metrics (including human evaluation) on the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, as well as significantly higher abstractiveness scores. Moreover, by first operating at the sentence-level and then the word-level, we enable parallel decoding of our neural generative model that results in substantially faster (10-20x) inference speed as well as 4x faster training convergence than previous long-paragraph encoder-decoder models. We also demonstrate the generalization of our model on the test-only DUC-2002 dataset, where we achieve higher scores than a state-of-the-art model.

label: acl
text: Inspired by human summarization techniques, we propose a fast and accurate summarization model that selects key sentences and then rewrites them abstractively to create a concise overall summary. We use a novel sentence-level policy gradient method to connect two neural networks in a hierarchical manner, ensuring language fluency. Our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on all metrics, including human evaluation, on the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, and achieves significantly higher abstractiveness scores. Additionally, our model operates at both the sentence and word level, allowing for parallel decoding and resulting in a 10-20x faster inference speed and 4x faster training convergence compared to previous encoder-decoder models. Our model also demonstrates its generalization capabilities on the test-only DUC-2002 dataset, outperforming a state-of-the-art model.

label: coling
text: The keyphrase generation task is a challenging work that aims to generate a set of keyphrases for a piece of text. Many previous studies based on the sequence-to-sequence model were used to generate keyphrases, and they introduce a copy mechanism to achieve good results. However, we observed that most of the keyphrases are composed of some important words (seed words) in the source text, and if these words can be identified accurately and copied to create more keyphrases, the performance of the model might be improved. To address this challenge, we propose a DualCopyNet model, which introduces an additional sequence labeling layer for identifying seed words, and further copies the words for generating new keyphrases by dual copy mechanisms. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms the baseline models and achieves an obvious performance improvement.

label: coling
text: The generation of keyphrases is a challenging task that aims to produce a set of relevant keyphrases for a given text. Previous studies have utilized sequence-to-sequence models, incorporating a copy mechanism to achieve good results. However, we have noticed that many keyphrases are composed of important words (referred to as seed words) in the text. If these seed words can be accurately identified and copied to generate new keyphrases, the performance of the model can be improved. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the DualCopyNet model, which incorporates an additional sequence labeling layer to identify seed words, and utilizes dual copy mechanisms to generate new keyphrases. Our experimental results show that the DualCopyNet model outperforms baseline models and demonstrates a significant improvement in performance.

label: coling
text: With the aid of recently proposed word embedding algorithms, the study of semantic similarity has progressed and advanced rapidly. However, many natural language processing tasks need sense level representation. To address this issue, some researches propose sense embedding learning algorithms. In this paper, we present a generalized model from existing sense retrofitting model. The generalization takes three major components: semantic relations between the senses, the relation strength and the semantic strength. In the experiment, we show that the generalized model can outperform previous approaches in three types of experiment: semantic relatedness, contextual word similarity and semantic difference.

label: coling
text: With the advancement of recently proposed word embedding algorithms, the study of semantic similarity has made significant progress. However, many natural language processing tasks require sense-level representation. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed sense embedding learning algorithms. In this paper, we present a generalized model based on existing sense retrofitting models. This generalization incorporates three key components: semantic relationships between senses, the strength of these relationships, and the semantic strength. Our experiments demonstrate that the generalized model outperforms previous approaches in three types of experiments: semantic relatedness, contextual word similarity, and semantic difference.

label: acl
text: Privacy plays a crucial role in preserving democratic ideals and personal autonomy. The dominant legal approach to privacy in many jurisdictions is the “Notice and Choice” paradigm, where privacy policies are the primary instrument used to convey information to users. However, privacy policies are long and complex documents that are difficult for users to read and comprehend. We discuss how language technologies can play an important role in addressing this information gap, reporting on initial progress towards helping three specific categories of stakeholders take advantage of digital privacy policies: consumers, enterprises, and regulators. Our goal is to provide a roadmap for the development and use of language technologies to empower users to reclaim control over their privacy, limit privacy harms, and rally research efforts from the community towards addressing an issue with large social impact. We highlight many remaining opportunities to develop language technologies that are more precise or nuanced in the way in which they use the text of privacy policies.

label: acl
text: Privacy is a crucial aspect in maintaining democratic values and personal freedom. The commonly used legal approach to privacy in various jurisdictions is the "Notice and Choice" principle, where privacy policies serve as the primary means of conveying information to users. However, these policies are often lengthy and complicated, making it difficult for users to understand them. This paper discusses the role of language technologies in bridging this information gap and improving digital privacy for consumers, enterprises, and regulators. Our aim is to provide a roadmap for the development and utilization of language technologies that will give users more control over their privacy, reduce privacy risks, and encourage research efforts to address this socially significant issue. We also highlight the potential for further advancements in language technologies to make privacy policies more precise and user-friendly.

label: naacl
text: The dominant paradigm for neural text generation is left-to-right decoding from autoregressive language models. Constrained or controllable generation under complex lexical constraints, however, requires foresight to plan ahead feasible future paths. Drawing inspiration from the C-C-C search algorithm, we propose NeuroLogic A*esque, a decoding algorithm that incorporates heuristic estimates of future cost. We develop lookahead heuristics that are efficient for large-scale language models, making our method a drop-in replacement for common techniques such as beam search and top-D-D-D sampling. To enable constrained generation, we build on NeuroLogic decoding (Lu et al., 2021), combining its flexibility in incorporating logical constraints with A*esque estimates of future constraint satisfaction. Our approach outperforms competitive baselines on five generation tasks, and achieves new state-of-the-art performance on table-to-text generation, constrained machine translation, and keyword-constrained generation. The improvements are particularly notable on tasks that require complex constraint satisfaction or in few-shot or zero-shot settings. NeuroLogic A*esque illustrates the power of decoding for improving and enabling new capabilities of large-scale language models.

label: naacl
text: The dominant approach for neural text generation is left-to-right decoding from autoregressive language models. However, generating text that meets complex lexical constraints requires foresight to plan ahead feasible future paths. To address this challenge, we introduce NeuroLogic A*esque, a decoding algorithm that incorporates heuristic estimates of future cost. Our method is based on the C-C-C search algorithm and is designed to be an efficient drop-in replacement for common techniques such as beam search and top-D-D-D sampling. By combining the flexibility of NeuroLogic decoding (Lu et al., 2021) with A*esque estimates of future constraint satisfaction, our approach enables constrained generation. Our method outperforms competitive baselines on five generation tasks and achieves new state-of-the-art performance on table-to-text generation, constrained machine translation, and keyword-constrained generation. This is particularly evident in tasks that require complex constraint satisfaction or in few-shot or zero-shot settings. NeuroLogic A*esque demonstrates the potential of decoding algorithms to enhance and expand the capabilities of large-scale language models.

label: acl
text: Neural semantic parsers have obtained acceptable results in the context of parsing DRSs (Discourse Representation Structures). In particular models with character sequences as input showed remarkable performance for English. But how does this approach perform on languages with a different writing system, like Chinese, a language with a large vocabulary of characters? Does rule-based tokenisation of the input help, and which granularity is preferred: characters, or words? The results are promising. Even with DRSs based on English, good results for Chinese are obtained. Tokenisation offers a small advantage for English, but not for Chinese. Overall, characters are preferred as input, both for English and Chinese.

label: acl
text: Neural semantic parsers have demonstrated acceptable performance in parsing Discourse Representation Structures (DRSs). Particularly, models using character sequences as input have shown remarkable results for English. However, it remains unclear how this approach would perform on languages with a different writing system, such as Chinese, which has a vast vocabulary of characters. To address this issue, this study investigates the impact of rule-based tokenization on the input and the preferred granularity, either characters or words. The results are promising, revealing that even with DRSs based on English, good results can be obtained for Chinese. Although tokenization provides some improvement for English, it does not significantly affect the results for Chinese. Ultimately, the preferred input granularity is found to be characters for both English and Chinese.

label: naacl
text: We introduce a new type of deep contextualized word representation that models both (1) complex characteristics of word use (e.g., syntax and semantics), and (2) how these uses vary across linguistic contexts (i.e., to model polysemy). Our word vectors are learned functions of the internal states of a deep bidirectional language model (biLM), which is pre-trained on a large text corpus. We show that these representations can be easily added to existing models and significantly improve the state of the art across six challenging NLP problems, including question answering, textual entailment and sentiment analysis. We also present an analysis showing that exposing the deep internals of the pre-trained network is crucial, allowing downstream models to mix different types of semi-supervision signals.

label: naacl
text: We present a novel type of deep contextualized word representation that captures both the complex characteristics of word usage (such as syntax and semantics) and their variations across linguistic contexts (to model polysemy). Our results demonstrate that these representations can be easily integrated into existing models, resulting in a significant improvement in the state of the art for six challenging NLP tasks, including question answering, textual entailment, and sentiment analysis. text: We propose a method to distill language-agnostic meaning embeddings from multilingual sentence encoders for unsupervised quality estimation of machine translation. Our method facilitates that the meaning embeddings focus on semantics by adversarial training that attempts to eliminate language-specific information. Experimental results on unsupervised quality estimation reveal that our method achieved higher correlations with human evaluations.

label: coling
text: We propose a method for distilling language-agnostic meaning embeddings from multilingual sentence encoders, to perform unsupervised quality estimation of machine translation. Our method focuses on semantics by adversarial training, which eliminates language-specific information. Our experimental results show that our method achieved higher correlations with human evaluations in unsupervised quality estimation.

label: acl
text: The cross-lingual language models are typically pretrained with masked language modeling on multilingual text or parallel sentences. In this paper, we introduce denoising word alignment as a new cross-lingual pre-training task. Specifically, the model first self-label word alignments for parallel sentences. Then we randomly mask tokens in a bitext pair. Given a masked token, the model uses a pointer network to predict the aligned token in the other language. We alternately perform the above two steps in an expectation-maximization manner. Experimental results show that our method improves cross-lingual transferability on various datasets, especially on the token-level tasks, such as question answering, and structured prediction. Moreover, the model can serve as a pretrained word aligner, which achieves reasonably low error rate on the alignment benchmarks. The code and pretrained parameters are available at github.com/CZWin32768/XLM-Align.

text: Cross-lingual language models are typically pre-trained with masked language modeling on multilingual text or parallel sentences. The model uses a pointer network to predict the aligned token in the other language, given a masked token. This process is repeated in an expectation-maximization manner. Our method shows improvement in cross-lingual transferability on various datasets, particularly for token-level tasks such as question answering and structured prediction. text: We introduce a weakly supervised approach for inferring the property of abstractness of words and expressions in the complete absence of labeled data. Exploiting only minimal linguistic clues and the contextual usage of a concept as manifested in textual data, we train sufficiently powerful classifiers, obtaining high correlation with human labels. The results imply the applicability of this approach to additional properties of concepts, additional languages, and resource-scarce scenarios.

label: emnlp
text: We present a weakly supervised method for determining the abstractness of words and phrases in the absence of labeled data. By utilizing only minimal linguistic cues and the contextual usage of concepts within text, we train effective classifiers and achieve a high correlation with human-labeled data. Our results demonstrate the potential for this approach to be applied to other properties of concepts, other languages, and in resource-constrained environments.

text: The point of departure of this article is the claim that sense-specific vectors provide an advantage over normal vectors due to the polysemy that they presumably represent. This claim is based on performance gains observed in gold standard evaluation tests such as word similarity tasks. We demonstrate that this claim, at least as it is instantiated in prior art, is unfounded in two ways. Furthermore, we provide empirical data and an analytic discussion that may account for the previously reported improved performance. First, we show that ground-truth polysemy degrades performance in word similarity tasks. Therefore word similarity tasks are not suitable as an evaluation test for polysemy representation. Second, random assignment of words to senses is shown to improve performance in the same task. This and additional results point to the conclusion that performance gains as reported in previous work may be an artifact of random sense assignment, which is equivalent to sub-sampling and multiple estimation of word vector representations. Theoretical analysis shows that this may on its own be beneficial for the estimation of word similarity, by reducing the bias in the estimation of the cosine distance.

The starting point of this article is the argument that sense-specific vectors offer an advantage over traditional vectors due to the polysemy they supposedly represent. This argument is based on improved performance seen in standard evaluation tests such as word similarity tasks. However, we show that this argument, as it has been presented in previous research, is flawed in two ways. We provide empirical evidence and a detailed analysis to explain the previously reported improved performance. Firstly, we demonstrate that actual polysemy decreases performance in word similarity tasks, making them an unreliable evaluation test for polysemy representation. Secondly, we show that randomly assigning words to senses actually improves performance in these tasks. These findings, along with additional results, lead us to the conclusion that the improved performance reported in previous studies may be a result of random sense assignment, which is equivalent to sub-sampling and multiple estimation of word vector representations. Our theoretical analysis suggests that this can be beneficial for estimating word similarity by reducing the bias in cosine distance estimation. However, this does not apply to the main goal of polysemy representation, which is to estimate word meaning.

label: emnlp
text: One way to interpret neural model predictions is to highlight the most important input features—for example, a heatmap visualization over the words in an input sentence. In existing interpretation methods for NLP, a word's importance is determined by either input perturbation—measuring the decrease in model confidence when that word is removed—or by the gradient with respect to that word. To understand the limitations of these methods, we use input reduction, which iteratively removes the least important word from the input. This exposes pathological behaviors of neural models: the remaining words appear nonsensical to humans and are not the ones determined as important by interpretation methods. As we confirm with human experiments, the reduced examples lack information to support the prediction of any label, but models still make the same predictions with high confidence. To explain these counterintuitive results, we draw connections to adversarial examples and confidence calibration: pathological behaviors reveal difficulties in interpreting neural models trained with maximum likelihood. To mitigate their deficiencies, we fine-tune the models by encouraging high entropy outputs on reduced examples. Fine-tuned models become more interpretable under input reduction, without accuracy loss on regular examples.

label: coling
text: Controllable story generation is a challenging task in the field of NLP, which has attracted increasing research interest in recent years. However, most existing works generate a whole story conditioned on the appointed keywords or emotions, ignoring the psychological changes of the protagonist. Inspired by psychology theories, we introduce global psychological state chains, which include the needs and emotions of the protagonists, to help a story generation system create more controllable and well-planned stories. In this paper, we propose a Psychology-guided Controllable Story Generation System (PICS) to generate stories that adhere to the given leading context and desired psychological state chains for the protagonist. Specifically, psychological state trackers are employed to memorize the protagonist's local psychological states to capture their inner temporal relationships. In addition, psychological state planners are adopted to gain the protagonist's global psychological states for story planning. Eventually, a psychology controller is designed to integrate the local and global psychological states into the story context representation for composing psychology-guided stories. Automatic and manual evaluations demonstrate that PICS outperforms baselines, and each part of PICS shows effectiveness for writing stories with more consistent psychological changes.

label: coling
text: Controllable story generation is a challenging task in NLP, attracting increasing research attention in recent years. However, most existing solutions generate a complete story based on assigned keywords or emotions, ignoring the psychological changes of the protagonist. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of global psychological state chains, which consider the needs and emotions of the protagonist to generate more controlled and well-planned stories. Our proposed Psychology-guided Controllable Story Generation System (PICS) generates stories that follow the given context and desired psychological state chains for the protagonist. This is achieved by using psychological state trackers to remember the protagonist's local psychological states, psychological state planners to determine their global psychological states, and a psychology controller to integrate these states into the story context representation. The results of both automatic and manual evaluations show that PICS outperforms existing solutions and each component of the system is effective in producing stories with consistent psychological changes.

label: naacl
text: This paper introduces a model for incomplete utterance restoration (IUR) called JET (Joint learning token Extraction and Text generation). Different from prior studies that only work on extraction or abstraction datasets, we design a simple but effective model, working for both scenarios of IUR. Our design simulates the nature of IUR, where omitted tokens from the context contribute to restoration. From this, we construct a Picker that identifies the omitted tokens. To support the picker, we design two label creation methods (soft and hard labels), which can work in cases of no annotation data for the omitted tokens. The restoration is done by using a Generator with the help of the Picker on joint learning. Promising results on four benchmark datasets in extraction and abstraction scenarios show that our model is better than the pretrained T5 and non-generative language model methods in both rich and limited training data settings.

label: naacl
text: This paper presents a novel model for Incomplete Utterance Restoration (IUR), called JET (Joint learning Token Extraction and Text Generation). Unlike prior studies that only focus on extraction or abstraction datasets, our model is simple yet effective, working for both scenarios of IUR. Our approach mimics the nature of IUR, where missing tokens from the context contribute to restoration. To achieve this, we have developed a Picker that identifies the missing tokens and two label creation methods (soft and hard labels) to support the Picker in cases where annotation data for the missing tokens is not available. The restoration is performed by the Generator in conjunction with the Picker through joint learning. Our results on four benchmark datasets in extraction and abstraction scenarios demonstrate that our model outperforms pretrained T5 and non-generative language model methods in both rich and limited training data settings.

label: emnlp
text: When the semantics of a sentence are not representable in a semantic parser's output schema, parsing will inevitably fail. Detection of these instances is commonly treated as an out-of-domain classification problem. However, there is also a more subtle scenario in which the test data is drawn from the same domain. In addition to formalizing this problem of domain-adjacency, we present a comparison of various baselines that could be used to solve it. We also propose a new simple sentence representation that emphasizes words which are unexpected. This approach improves the performance of a downstream semantic parser run on in-domain and domain-adjacent instances.

label: emnlp
text: The inability of a semantic parser to represent the semantics of a sentence results in parsing failure. This is often viewed as an out-of-domain classification problem. However, there may be cases where the test data comes from the same domain. To address this issue of domain-adjacency, we compare various baselines and present a new, simple sentence representation that focuses on unexpected words. This approach enhances the performance of semantic parsers in both in-domain and domain-adjacent instances.

label: naacl
text: We present a new approach to the design of deep networks for natural language processing (NLP), based on the general technique of Tensor Product Representations (TPRs) for encoding and processing symbol structures in distributed neural networks. A network architecture — the Tensor Product Generation Network (TPGN) — is proposed which is capable in principle of carrying out TPR computation, but which uses unconstrained deep learning to design its internal representations. Instantiated in a model for image-caption generation, TPGN outperforms LSTM baselines when evaluated on the COCO dataset. The TPR-capable structure enables interpretation of internal representations and operations, which prove to contain considerable grammatical content. Our caption-generation model can be interpreted as generating sequences of grammatical categories and retrieving words by their categories from a plan encoded as a distributed representation.

label: naacl
text: We propose a new method for designing deep networks for Natural Language Processing (NLP) using Tensor Product Representations (TPRs) for encoding and processing symbols in distributed neural networks. Our proposed network architecture, the Tensor Product Generation Network (TPGN), has the potential to perform TPR computation, but utilizes deep learning to design its internal representations. When tested on the COCO dataset, our TPGN model for image-caption generation outperforms LSTM baselines. The TPR-capable structure also allows for the interpretation of internal representations and operations, which have been found to contain significant grammatical content. Our caption-generation model operates by generating sequences of grammatical categories and retrieving words based on their categories from a plan encoded as a distributed representation.

label: naacl
text: Peer reviewing is a central component in the scientific publishing process. We present the first public dataset of scientific peer reviews available for research purposes (PeerRead v1),1 providing an opportunity to study this important artifact. The dataset consists of 14.7K paper drafts and the corresponding accept/reject decisions in top-tier venues including ACL, NIPS and ICLR. The dataset also includes 10.7K textual peer reviews written by experts for a subset of the papers. We describe the data collection process and report interesting observed phenomena in the peer reviews. We also propose two novel NLP tasks based on this dataset and provide simple baseline models. In the first task, we show that simple models can predict whether a paper is accepted with up to 21% error reduction compared to the majority baseline. In the second task, we predict the numerical scores of review aspects and show that simple models can outperform the mean baseline for aspects with high variance such as `originality' and `impact'.

label: naacl
text: Peer reviewing is a critical aspect of the scientific publishing process. The first public dataset of scientific peer reviews, PeerRead v1, is now available for research purposes. The dataset, consisting of 14.7K paper drafts and the corresponding accept/reject decisions from top-tier venues such as ACL, NIPS, and ICLR, offers a unique opportunity to study this important aspect of scientific publishing. In addition to the paper drafts and decisions, the dataset also includes 10.7K textual peer reviews written by experts for a subset of the papers. This article describes the data collection process and highlights some of the interesting observations made from the peer reviews. Furthermore, two new NLP tasks have been proposed based on this dataset, and simple baseline models have been developed. The first task involves predicting whether a paper will be accepted, with a 21% reduction in error compared to the majority baseline. The second task involves predicting the numerical scores for various aspects of the review, such as originality and impact, with simple models outperforming the mean baseline for aspects with high variance.

label: coling
text: Representation learning is the foundation of machine reading comprehension. In state-of-the-art models, deep learning methods broadly use word and character level representations. However, character is not naturally the minimal linguistic unit. In addition, with a simple concatenation of character and word embedding, previous models actually give suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose to use subword rather than character for word embedding enhancement. We also empirically explore different augmentation strategies on subword-augmented embedding to enhance the cloze-style reading comprehension model (reader). In detail, we present a reader that uses subword-level representation to augment word embedding with a short list to handle rare words effectively. A thorough examination is conducted to evaluate the comprehensive performance and generalization ability of the proposed reader. Experimental results show that the proposed approach helps the reader significantly outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on various public datasets.

label: coling
text: The foundation of machine reading comprehension is representation learning, and state-of-the-art models use deep learning methods that employ word and character-level representations. However, character is not always the smallest linguistic unit, and simply combining character and word embeddings can result in suboptimal solutions. In this paper, we propose using subwords instead of characters for word embedding enhancement. We also examine different augmentation strategies for subword-augmented embeddings to enhance the performance of a cloze-style reading comprehension model (reader). Our proposed reader uses subword-level representation to augment word embeddings with a short list to handle rare words effectively. We conduct a thorough examination of the proposed reader's performance and generalization ability, and experimental results show that it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on various public datasets.

label: emnlp
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is an important task in natural language processing area, which needs to determine entities boundaries and classify them into pre-defined categories. For Chinese NER task, there is only a very small amount of annotated data available. Chinese NER task and Chinese word segmentation (CWS) task have many similar word boundaries. There are also specificities in each task. However, existing methods for Chinese NER either do not exploit word boundary information from CWS or cannot filter the specific information of CWS. In this paper, we propose a novel adversarial transfer learning framework to make full use of task-shared boundaries information and prevent the task-specific features of CWS. Besides, since arbitrary character can provide important cues when predicting entity type, we exploit self-attention to explicitly capture long range dependencies between two tokens. Experimental results on two different widely used datasets show that our proposed model significantly and consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial task in natural language processing that involves identifying the boundaries of entities and categorizing them into pre-defined categories. However, there is a limited amount of annotated data available for the Chinese NER task. The Chinese NER task shares many similarities with the Chinese word segmentation (CWS) task in terms of word boundaries, but each task also has its unique characteristics. Previous methods for Chinese NER either fail to utilize the boundary information from CWS or are unable to filter out the task-specific features of CWS. In this paper, we introduce a novel adversarial transfer learning framework that leverages the shared boundary information and eliminates the task-specific features of CWS. Additionally, we utilize self-attention to explicitly capture the long-range dependencies between characters, as individual characters can provide important cues for predicting entity type. Our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two widely used datasets, with significant and consistent improvements.

label: acl
text: Tangled multi-party dialogue contexts lead to challenges for dialogue reading comprehension, where multiple dialogue threads flow simultaneously within a common dialogue record, increasing difficulties in understanding the dialogue history for both human and machine. Previous studies mainly focus on utterance encoding methods with carefully designed features but pay inadequate attention to characteristic features of the structure of dialogues. We specially take structure factors into account and design a novel model for dialogue disentangling. Based on the fact that dialogues are constructed on successive participation and interactions between speakers, we model structural information of dialogues in two aspects: 1)speaker property that indicates whom a message is from, and 2) reference dependency that shows whom a message may refer to. The proposed method achieves new state-of-the-art on the Ubuntu IRC benchmark dataset and contributes to dialogue-related comprehension.

label: acl
text: The complexity of multi-party dialogue contexts presents challenges for dialogue reading comprehension, as multiple dialogue threads flow simultaneously within a single dialogue record, making it difficult for both humans and machines to understand the dialogue history. Previous studies have primarily focused on utterance encoding methods with carefully designed features, but have not given enough attention to the structural characteristics of dialogues. Our novel model addresses this issue by taking these structure factors into account. We model the structural information of dialogues by considering two aspects: 1) the speaker property that indicates the source of a message, and 2) the reference dependency that shows to whom a message may refer. The proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art on the Ubuntu IRC benchmark dataset and advances our understanding of dialogue-related comprehension.

text: We examine the inducement of rare but severe errors in English-Chinese and Chinese-English in-domain neural machine translation by minimal deletion of source text with character-based models. By deleting a single character, we can induce severe translation errors. We categorize these errors and compare the results of deleting single characters and single words. We also examine the effect of training data size on the number and types of pathological cases induced by these minimal perturbations, finding significant variation. We find that deleting a word hurts overall translation score more than deleting a character, but certain errors are more likely to occur when deleting characters, with language direction also influencing the effect.

label: coling
text: We investigate the impact of minimal character deletion on inducing rare but severe errors in English-Chinese and Chinese-English in-domain neural machine translation. By removing a single character, we observe significant errors in the translation output. We categorize these errors and compare the results of deleting single characters and single words. We also study the effect of training data size on the number and types of errors induced by these minimal perturbations and find significant variations. Our findings indicate that deleting a word has a greater overall negative impact on translation score compared to deleting a character. However, certain errors are more likely to occur when deleting characters, and the language direction also influences the effect.

label: naacl
text: Content-based collaborative filtering (CCF) predicts user-item interactions based on both users' interaction history and items' content information. Recently, pre-trained language models (PLM) have been used to extract high-quality item encodings for CCF. However, it is resource-intensive to train a PLM-based CCF model in an end-to-end (E2E) manner, since optimization involves back-propagating through every content encoding within a given user interaction sequence. To tackle this issue, we propose GRAM (GRadient Accumulation for Multi-modality in CCF), which exploits the fact that a given item often appears multiple times within a batch of interaction histories. Specifically, Single-step GRAM aggregates each item encoding's gradients for back-propagation, with theoretic equivalence to the standard E2E training. As an extension of Single-step GRAM, we propose Multi-step GRAM, which increases the gradient update latency, achieving a further speedup with drastically less GPU memory. GRAM significantly improves training efficiency (up to 146x) on five datasets from two task domains of Knowledge Tracing and News Recommendation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yoonseok312/GRAM.

label: naacl
text: Content-based collaborative filtering (CCF) predicts user-item interactions based on a combination of users' interaction history and the content information of the items. Recently, pre-trained language models (PLMs) have been utilized to extract high-quality item encodings for use in CCF. However, training a PLM-based CCF model in an end-to-end (E2E) manner can be resource-intensive due to the need to back-propagate through every content encoding within a user interaction sequence. To address this challenge, we present GRAM (Gradient Accumulation for Multi-modality in CCF), which leverages the fact that a given item frequently appears multiple times within a batch of interaction histories. GRAM uses a single-step approach to aggregate each item encoding's gradients for back-propagation, which is theoretically equivalent to standard E2E training. Additionally, we propose a multi-step approach, which increases gradient update latency and provides further speedup with significantly reduced GPU memory usage. Our results show that GRAM significantly improves training efficiency (up to 146x) on five datasets across two task domains, including Knowledge Tracing and News Recommendation. Our code is available for download at https://github.com/yoonseok312/GRAM.

label: acl
text: The success of many natural language processing (NLP) tasks is bound by the number and quality of annotated data, but there is often a shortage of such training data. In this paper, we ask the question: “Can we combine a neural network (NN) with regular expressions (RE) to improve supervised learning for NLP?”. In answer, we develop novel methods to exploit the rich expressiveness of REs at different levels within a NN, showing that the combination significantly enhances the learning effectiveness when a small number of training examples are available. We evaluate our approach by applying it to spoken language understanding for intent detection and slot filling. Experimental results show that our approach is highly effective in exploiting the available training data, giving a clear boost to the RE-unaware NN.

label: acl
text: The success of many natural language processing (NLP) tasks is limited by the quantity and quality of annotated data, but this data is often in short supply. This paper explores the potential of combining a neural network (NN) with regular expressions (RE) to enhance supervised learning for NLP. To do this, we develop new methods to utilize the rich expressiveness of REs within a NN, demonstrating that this combination significantly improves learning effectiveness when only a small amount of training data is available. Our approach is evaluated by applying it to spoken language understanding for intent detection and slot filling. The results show that our approach effectively leverages the available training data, providing a noticeable boost to the NN that is unaware of REs.

label: acl
text: Semantic specialization of distributional word vectors, referred to as retrofitting, is a process of fine-tuning word vectors using external lexical knowledge in order to better embed some semantic relation. Existing retrofitting models integrate linguistic constraints directly into learning objectives and, consequently, specialize only the vectors of words from the constraints. In this work, in contrast, we transform external lexico-semantic relations into training examples which we use to learn an explicit retrofitting model (ER). The ER model allows us to learn a global specialization function and specialize the vectors of words unobserved in the training data as well. We report large gains over original distributional vector spaces in (1) intrinsic word similarity evaluation and on (2) two downstream tasks − lexical simplification and dialog state tracking. Finally, we also successfully specialize vector spaces of new languages (i.e., unseen in the training data) by coupling ER with shared multilingual distributional vector spaces.

label: acl
text: The process of fine-tuning word vectors using external lexical knowledge to better embed semantic relations is referred to as retrofitting. Unlike existing retrofitting models that integrate linguistic constraints directly into learning objectives and specialize only the vectors of words from the constraints, this work transforms external lexico-semantic relations into training examples to learn an explicit retrofitting model (ER). This allows for a global specialization function to be learned and the vectors of words unobserved in the training data to be specialized as well. The results show significant improvements in intrinsic word similarity evaluation and two downstream tasks (lexical simplification and dialog state tracking). Additionally, ER can be used to specialize vector spaces of new languages by coupling it with shared multilingual distributional vector spaces.

label: acl
text: Multimodal sentiment analysis is the challenging research area that attends to the fusion of multiple heterogeneous modalities. The main challenge is the occurrence of some missing modalities during the multimodal fusion procedure. However, the existing techniques require all modalities as input, thus are sensitive to missing modalities at predicting time. In this work, the coupled-translation fusion network (CTFN) is firstly proposed to model bi-direction interplay via couple learning, ensuring the robustness in respect to missing modalities. Specifically, the cyclic consistency constraint is presented to improve the translation performance, allowing us directly to discard decoder and only embraces encoder of Transformer. This could contribute to a much lighter model. Due to the couple learning, CTFN is able to conduct bi-direction cross-modality intercorrelation parallelly. Based on CTFN, a hierarchical architecture is further established to exploit multiple bi-direction translations, leading to double multimodal fusing embeddings compared with traditional translation methods. Moreover, the convolution block is utilized to further highlight explicit interactions among those translations. For evaluation, CTFN was verified on two multimodal benchmarks with extensive ablation studies. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art or often competitive performance. Additionally, CTFN still maintains robustness when considering missing modality.

label: acl
text: Multimodal sentiment analysis is a challenging research area that focuses on the integration of multiple, heterogeneous modalities. The main challenge is the potential for missing modalities during the fusion process. Existing techniques require all modalities as input, making them sensitive to the absence of any modality during prediction. To address this issue, we propose the Coupled-Translation Fusion Network (CTFN), which models bi-directional interplay through couple learning, ensuring robustness in the presence of missing modalities. The cyclic consistency constraint is introduced to improve translation performance, allowing us to discard the decoder and only use the encoder of the Transformer. This results in a lighter model. The couple learning in CTFN enables parallel bi-directional cross-modality correlation. A hierarchical architecture is established based on CTFN to exploit multiple bi-directional translations, leading to double multimodal fusing embeddings compared to traditional translation methods. The convolution block is used to further highlight explicit interactions among these translations. CTFN was evaluated on two multimodal benchmarks with extensive ablation studies, demonstrating state-of-the-art or often competitive performance. Additionally, CTFN remains robust even when considering missing modalities.

text: Moderating user comments and promoting healthy understanding is a challenging task, especially in the context of polarized topics such as climate change. We propose a moderation tool to assist moderators in promoting mutual understanding in regard to this topic. The approach is twofold. First, we train classifiers to label incoming posts for the arguments they entail, with a specific focus on minority arguments. We apply active learning to further supplement the training data with rare arguments. Second, we dive deeper into singular arguments and extract the lexical patterns that distinguish each argument from the others. Our findings indicate that climate change arguments form clearly separable clusters in the embedding space. These classes are characterized by their own unique lexical patterns that provide a quick insight in an argument's key concepts. Additionally, supplementing our training data was necessary for our classifiers to be able to adequately recognize rare arguments. We argue that this detailed rundown of each argument provides insight into where others are coming from. These computational approaches can be part of the toolkit for content moderators and researchers struggling with polarized topics.

text: Moderating user comments and promoting healthy understanding is a challenging task, especially when it comes to polarized topics such as climate change. To address this challenge, we propose a moderation tool to help moderators foster mutual understanding. Our approach involves two steps. Firstly, we train classifiers to label incoming posts based on the arguments they present, with a particular focus on minority arguments. We use active learning to further enhance our training data with rare arguments. Secondly, we delve deeper into individual arguments and identify the lexical patterns that distinguish each argument from others. Our findings show that climate change arguments form distinct clusters in the embedding space, each characterized by its own unique lexical patterns. These patterns provide a quick insight into each argument's key concepts. Furthermore, we found that supplementing our training data was crucial for our classifiers to effectively recognize rare arguments. Our research suggests that this in-depth analysis of each argument can help moderators and researchers gain a better understanding of where others are coming from, and it can be a valuable tool for those grappling with polarized topics.

text: The recent advance in deep learning and semantic parsing has significantly improved the translation accuracy of natural language questions to structured queries. However, further improvement of the existing approaches turns out to be quite challenging. Rather than solely relying on algorithmic innovations, in this work, we introduce DialSQL, a dialogue-based structured query generation framework that leverages human intelligence to boost the performance of existing algorithms via user interaction. DialSQL is capable of identifying potential errors in a generated SQL query and asking users for validation via simple multi-choice questions. User feedback is then leveraged to revise the query. We design a generic simulator to bootstrap synthetic training dialogues and evaluate the performance of DialSQL on the WikiSQL dataset. Using SQLNet as a black box query generation tool, DialSQL improves its performance from 61.3% to 69.0% using only 2.4 validation questions per dialogue.

text: The recent advancements in deep learning and semantic parsing have significantly improved the accuracy of translating natural language questions into structured queries. However, further improvement of these existing approaches is challenging. To address this issue, we have developed DialSQL, a dialogue-based structured query generation framework that leverages human intelligence to enhance the performance of existing algorithms. DialSQL identifies potential errors in generated SQL queries and asks users for validation through simple multiple-choice questions. User feedback is then used to revise the query. We have also created a generic simulator to generate synthetic training dialogues, and evaluated DialSQL on the WikiSQL dataset. With SQLNet as the black box query generation tool, DialSQL improved its performance from 61.3% to 69.0% with only 2.4 validation questions per dialogue.

text: In this work, we introduce : the largest publicly available multilingual dataset for factual verification of naturally existing real-world claims. The dataset contains short statements in 25 languages and is labeled for veracity by expert fact-checkers. The dataset includes a multilingual evaluation benchmark that measures both out-of-domain generalization, and zero-shot capabilities of the multilingual models. Using state-of-the-art multilingual transformer-based models, we develop several automated fact-checking models that, along with textual claims, make use of additional metadata and evidence from news stories retrieved using a search engine. Empirically, our best model attains an F-score of around 40%, suggesting that our dataset is a challenging benchmark for the evaluation of multilingual fact-checking models.

label: acl
text: In this work, we present the largest publicly available multilingual dataset for the factual verification of real-world claims. The dataset features short statements in 25 languages, each labeled for accuracy by expert fact-checkers. Additionally, the dataset includes a multilingual evaluation benchmark that assesses both out-of-domain generalization and zero-shot capabilities of multilingual models. To develop automated fact-checking models, we utilize state-of-the-art multilingual transformer-based models and incorporate additional metadata and evidence from news stories retrieved through a search engine. Our results demonstrate that our best model achieves an F-score of approximately 40%, highlighting the challenge posed by our dataset as a benchmark for evaluating multilingual fact-checking models.

label: acl
text: The rapid development of conversational assistants accelerates the study on conversational question answering (QA). However, the existing conversational QA systems usually answer users' questions with a single knowledge source, e.g., paragraphs or a knowledge graph, but overlook the important visual cues, let alone multiple knowledge sources of different modalities. In this paper, we hence define a novel research task, i.e., multimodal conversational question answering (MMCoQA), aiming to answer users' questions with multimodal knowledge sources via multi-turn conversations. This new task brings a series of research challenges, including but not limited to priority, consistency, and complementarity of multimodal knowledge. To facilitate the data-driven approaches in this area, we construct the first multimodal conversational QA dataset, named MMConvQA. Questions are fully annotated with not only natural language answers but also the corresponding evidence and valuable decontextualized self-contained questions. Meanwhile, we introduce an end-to-end baseline model, which divides this complex research task into question understanding, multi-modal evidence retrieval, and answer extraction. Moreover, we report a set of benchmarking results, and the results indicate that there is ample room for improvement.

label: acl
text: The fast growth of conversational assistants has boosted research into conversational question answering (QA). However, current conversational QA systems often rely on a single source of knowledge, such as paragraphs or a knowledge graph, ignoring important visual cues and multiple knowledge sources of different modalities. To address this issue, we propose a new research task: multimodal conversational question answering (MMCoQA), which aims to answer questions using multiple knowledge sources through multi-turn conversations. This task presents several challenges, including the prioritization, consistency, and complementarity of multimodal knowledge. To support data-driven approaches, we introduce the first multimodal conversational QA dataset, MMConvQA, which includes fully annotated questions with natural language answers, evidence, and valuable self-contained questions. We also provide an end-to-end baseline model that breaks down the complex task into question understanding, multi-modal evidence retrieval, and answer extraction. Our benchmarking results reveal ample room for improvement.

label: emnlp
text: We leverage a popularity measure in social media as a distant label for extractive summarization of online conversations. In social media, users can vote, share, or bookmark a post they prefer. The number of these actions is regarded as a measure of popularity. However, popularity is not determined solely by content of a post, e.g., a text or an image it contains, but is highly based on its contexts, e.g., timing, and authority. We propose Disjunctive model that computes the contribution of content and context separately. For evaluation, we build a dataset where the informativeness of comments is annotated. We evaluate the results with ranking metrics, and show that our model outperforms the baseline models which directly use popularity as a measure of informativeness.

label: emnlp
text: We use a measure of popularity in social media as a distant label to extract key information from online conversations. Social media users can vote, share, or bookmark posts they like, and the number of these actions is used as a measure of popularity. However, popularity is not only determined by the content of a post (e.g. text or image), but also by contextual factors such as timing and authority. To address this, we have developed a Disjunctive model that separates the impact of content and context on popularity. To evaluate our model, we have created a dataset where the informative value of comments is annotated. Our results, as evaluated using ranking metrics, show that our model outperforms baseline models that rely solely on popularity as a measure of informative value.

label: naacl
text: Analyzing ideology and polarization is of critical importance in advancing our grasp of modern politics. Recent research has made great strides towards understanding the ideological bias (i.e., stance) of news media along the left-right spectrum. In this work, we instead take a novel and more nuanced approach for the study of ideology based on its left or right positions on the issue being discussed. Aligned with the theoretical accounts in political science, we treat ideology as a multi-dimensional construct, and introduce the first diachronic dataset of news articles whose ideological positions are annotated by trained political scientists and linguists at the paragraph level. We showcase that, by controlling for the author's stance, our method allows for the quantitative and temporal measurement and analysis of polarization as a multidimensional ideological distance. We further present baseline models for ideology prediction, outlining a challenging task distinct from stance detection.

label: naacl
text: The analysis of ideology and polarization is crucial in improving our understanding of modern politics. Recent research has made significant progress in comprehending the ideological bias of news media along the political spectrum. However, we take a unique and more nuanced approach to studying ideology by examining its left or right positions on specific issues. Our approach aligns with the political science theory and views ideology as a multi-dimensional construct. Our team of political scientists and linguists has created the first dataset of news articles annotated with their ideological positions at the paragraph level. Our method allows for the quantifiable and temporal measurement and analysis of polarization as a multidimensional ideological distance, even when controlling for the author's stance. Finally, we present baseline models for ideology prediction, highlighting the distinct challenge of this task compared to stance detection.
