text: Despite the significant interest in developing general-purpose fact-checking models, constructing a large-scale, realistic fact-verification dataset is challenging. Existing datasets are either created by crowdworkers, introducing subtle biases that are difficult to control, or verified by professional fact-checkers, making them expensive and limited in scale. To address this challenge, we have constructed a large-scale, challenging fact-verification dataset called FAVIQ, consisting of 188,000 claims derived from an existing corpus of ambiguous information-seeking questions. The ambiguities in these questions allow for the automatic construction of true and false claims that reflect user confusion (e.g., the year a movie was filmed vs. released). The claims in FAVIQ are verified to be natural, contain minimal lexical bias, and require a comprehensive understanding of the evidence for verification. Our experiments demonstrate that current state-of-the-art models are far from solving this task. Furthermore, training on our data leads to improved performance in professional fact-checking, outperforming models trained on the widely used FEVER dataset or in-domain data by up to 17% absolute. Our dataset serves as a challenging benchmark for natural language understanding and will support future progress in professional fact-checking.

label: emnlp
text: We present a neural network-based joint approach for emotion classification and emotion cause detection, which attempts to capture mutual benefits across the two sub-tasks of emotion analysis. Considering that emotion classification and emotion cause detection need different kinds of features (affective and event-based separately), we propose a joint encoder which uses a unified framework to extract features for both sub-tasks and a joint model trainer which simultaneously learns two models for the two sub-tasks separately. Our experiments on Chinese microblogs show that the joint approach is very promising.

label: emnlp
text: We present a neural network-based joint approach for emotion classification and emotion cause detection, which leverages the mutual benefits of both sub-tasks in emotion analysis. Our approach utilizes a joint encoder that extracts both affective and event-based features, and a joint model trainer that simultaneously trains two models for emotion classification and emotion cause detection. The results of our experiments on Chinese microblogs demonstrate the promising potential of our joint approach.

label: coling
text: Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) is the task of labeling semantic arguments for marked semantic predicates. Semantic arguments and their predicates are related in various distinct manners, of which certain semantic arguments are a necessity while others serve as an auxiliary to their predicates. To consider such roles and relations of the arguments in the labeling order, we introduce iterative argument identification (IAI), which combines global decoding and iterative identification for the semantic arguments. In experiments, we first realize that the model with random argument labeling orders outperforms other heuristic orders such as the conventional left-to-right labeling order. Combined with simple reinforcement learning, the proposed model spontaneously learns the optimized labeling orders that are different from existing heuristic orders. The proposed model with the IAI algorithm achieves competitive or outperforming results from the existing models in the standard benchmark datasets of span-based SRL: CoNLL-2005 and CoNLL-2012.

label: coling
text: The task of Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) involves labeling the semantic arguments for marked semantic predicates. The relationship between semantic arguments and their predicates can vary, with some arguments being necessary while others serve as auxiliary components. To properly account for these roles and relationships during the labeling process, we introduce the Iterative Argument Identification (IAI) method, which combines global decoding and iterative identification for the semantic arguments. Our experiments show that a model with randomly assigned argument labeling orders outperforms other heuristic methods such as the traditional left-to-right labeling order. With the addition of simple reinforcement learning, the proposed model is able to learn and implement the optimal labeling orders, which differ from existing heuristic methods. The IAI algorithm results in competitive or improved performance compared to existing models in the standard benchmark datasets for span-based SRL, including CoNLL-2005 and CoNLL-2012.

label: naacl
text: In conversational speech, the acoustic signal provides cues that help listeners disambiguate difficult parses. For automatically parsing spoken utterances, we introduce a model that integrates transcribed text and acoustic-prosodic features using a convolutional neural network over energy and pitch trajectories coupled with an attention-based recurrent neural network that accepts text and prosodic features. We find that different types of acoustic-prosodic features are individually helpful, and together give statistically significant improvements in parse and disfluency detection F1 scores over a strong text-only baseline. For this study with known sentence boundaries, error analyses show that the main benefit of acoustic-prosodic features is in sentences with disfluencies, attachment decisions are most improved, and transcription errors obscure gains from prosody.

label: naacl
text: In conversational speech, the acoustic signal provides cues that aid listeners in resolving ambiguous parses. To improve the automatic parsing of spoken utterances, we have developed a model that combines transcribed text and acoustic-prosodic features using a convolutional neural network that processes energy and pitch trajectories, in conjunction with an attention-based recurrent neural network that considers both text and prosodic features. Our findings indicate that different types of acoustic-prosodic features are beneficial on their own, and when combined, they result in statistically significant improvements in parse and disfluency detection F1 scores, compared to a strong text-only baseline. In this study, which had known sentence boundaries, our error analysis revealed that the main advantage of acoustic-prosodic features is in sentences with disfluencies. The model showed the greatest improvement in attachment decisions, but transcription errors hindered the gains from prosody.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a simple framework for characterizing morphological complexity and how it encodes syntactic information. In particular, we propose a new measure of morpho-syntactic complexity in terms of governor-dependent preferential attachment that explains parsing performance. Through experiments on dependency parsing with data from Universal Dependencies (UD), we show that representations derived from morphological attributes deliver important parsing performance improvements over standard word form embeddings when trained on the same datasets. We also show that the new morpho-syntactic complexity measure is predictive of the gains provided by using morphological attributes over plain forms on parsing scores, making it a tool to distinguish languages using morphology as a syntactic marker from others.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a straightforward framework for analyzing morphological complexity and its role in encoding syntactic information. We propose a novel measure of morpho-syntactic complexity that is based on governor-dependent preferential attachment, which helps to explain parsing performance. Our experiments on dependency parsing with data from Universal Dependencies (UD) demonstrate that utilizing morphological attributes in representations leads to significant improvements in parsing performance compared to traditional word form embeddings, even when trained on the same datasets. Additionally, our new morpho-syntactic complexity measure is shown to be predictive of the benefits gained from using morphological attributes over plain forms in parsing scores, making it a useful tool for distinguishing languages that use morphology as a syntactic marker from others.

label: acl
text: Recent advances in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) have made it possible to reliably produce automatic transcripts of clinician-patient conversations. However, access to clinical datasets is heavily restricted due to patient privacy, thus slowing down normal research practices. We detail the development of a public access, high quality dataset comprising of 57 mocked primary care consultations, including audio recordings, their manual utterance-level transcriptions, and the associated consultation notes. Our work illustrates how the dataset can be used as a benchmark for conversational medical ASR as well as consultation note generation from transcripts.

label: acl
text: Recent advancements in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology have made it possible to produce accurate transcripts of clinician-patient conversations. However, access to clinical datasets is limited due to strict patient privacy regulations, impeding research progress. To address this issue, we have developed a publicly accessible, high-quality dataset consisting of 57 simulated primary care consultations, including audio recordings, manual utterance-level transcriptions, and related consultation notes. Our dataset serves as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of conversational medical ASR systems and generating consultation notes from transcripts.

label: acl
text: Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) have shown superior performance on various downstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. However, conventional pre-training objectives do not explicitly model relational facts in text, which are crucial for textual understanding. To address this issue, we propose a novel contrastive learning framework ERICA to obtain a deep understanding of the entities and their relations in text. Specifically, we define two novel pre-training tasks to better understand entities and relations: (1) the entity discrimination task to distinguish which tail entity can be inferred by the given head entity and relation; (2) the relation discrimination task to distinguish whether two relations are close or not semantically, which involves complex relational reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that ERICA can improve typical PLMs (BERT and RoBERTa) on several language understanding tasks, including relation extraction, entity typing and question answering, especially under low-resource settings.

label: acl
text: Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. However, traditional pre-training objectives do not account for the modeling of relational facts in text, which are crucial for comprehensive understanding. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel contrastive learning framework, ERICA, to facilitate a deeper understanding of entities and their relationships in text. Our framework includes two novel pre-training tasks designed to enhance the understanding of entities and relationships: (1) the Entity Discrimination Task, which distinguishes the tail entity that can be inferred from a given head entity and relation, and (2) the Relation Discrimination Task, which determines the semantic proximity of two relations, requiring complex relational reasoning. Our experiments show that ERICA can improve the performance of typical PLMs (BERT and RoBERTa) on various language understanding tasks, including relation extraction, entity typing, and question answering, particularly in low-resource settings.

label: acl
text: A well-known limitation in pretrain-finetune paradigm lies in its inflexibility caused by the one-size-fits-all vocabulary.This potentially weakens the effect when applying pretrained models into natural language generation (NLG) tasks, especially for the subword distributions between upstream and downstream tasks with significant discrepancy. Towards approaching this problem, we extend the vanilla pretrain-finetune pipeline with an extra embedding transfer step. Specifically, a plug-and-play embedding generator is introduced to produce the representation of any input token, according to pre-trained embeddings of its morphologically similar ones.Thus, embeddings of mismatch tokens in downstream tasks can also be efficiently initialized.We conduct experiments on a variety of NLG tasks under the pretrain-finetune fashion. Experimental results and extensive analyses show that the proposed strategy offers us opportunities to feel free to transfer the vocabulary, leading to more efficient and better performed downstream NLG models.

label: acl
text: One limitation of the pretrain-finetune paradigm is its inflexibility caused by the one-size-fits-all vocabulary. This can weaken its effectiveness in natural language generation (NLG) tasks, especially when there is significant discrepancy between the subword distributions in upstream and downstream tasks. To address this issue, we extend the pretrain-finetune pipeline with an extra embedding transfer step. We introduce a plug-and-play embedding generator that produces representations for any input token based on pre-trained embeddings of its morphologically similar tokens. This allows for the efficient initialization of embeddings for mismatch tokens in downstream tasks. We conduct experiments on various NLG tasks using the pretrain-finetune approach and find that our proposed strategy offers greater flexibility in transferring the vocabulary, leading to more efficient and higher-performing downstream NLG models.

label: acl
text: Hierarchical text classification is an important yet challenging task due to the complex structure of the label hierarchy. Existing methods ignore the semantic relationship between text and labels, so they cannot make full use of the hierarchical information. To this end, we formulate the text-label semantics relationship as a semantic matching problem and thus propose a hierarchy-aware label semantics matching network (HiMatch). First, we project text semantics and label semantics into a joint embedding space. We then introduce a joint embedding loss and a matching learning loss to model the matching relationship between the text semantics and the label semantics. Our model captures the text-label semantics matching relationship among coarse-grained labels and fine-grained labels in a hierarchy-aware manner. The experimental results on various benchmark datasets verify that our model achieves state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: Hierarchical text classification is a complex task due to the intricate structure of label hierarchies. Existing methods fail to consider the semantic relationship between text and labels, hindering their ability to make the most of the hierarchical information. To address this issue, we present a hierarchy-aware label semantics matching network (HiMatch) that formulates the text-label relationship as a semantic matching problem. HiMatch projects text semantics and label semantics into a joint embedding space and uses a joint embedding loss and a matching learning loss to model the matching relationship between the two. As a result, our model captures the text-label semantics relationship among both coarse-grained and fine-grained labels in a hierarchy-aware manner. Our experiments on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that HiMatch outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: Knowledge of difficulty level of questions helps a teacher in several ways, such as estimating students' potential quickly by asking carefully selected questions and improving quality of examination by modifying trivial and hard questions. Can we extract such benefits of instance difficulty in Natural Language Processing? To this end, we conduct Instance-Level Difficulty Analysis of Evaluation data (ILDAE) in a large-scale setup of 23 datasets and demonstrate its five novel applications: 1) conducting efficient-yet-accurate evaluations with fewer instances saving computational cost and time, 2) improving quality of existing evaluation datasets by repairing erroneous and trivial instances, 3) selecting the best model based on application requirements, 4) analyzing dataset characteristics for guiding future data creation, 5) estimating Out-of-Domain performance reliably. Comprehensive experiments for these applications lead to several interesting results, such as evaluation using just 5% instances (selected via ILDAE) achieves as high as 0.93 Kendall correlation with evaluation using complete dataset and computing weighted accuracy using difficulty scores leads to 5.2% higher correlation with Out-of-Domain performance. We release the difficulty scores and hope our work will encourage research in this important yet understudied field of leveraging instance difficulty in evaluations.

label: acl
text: The knowledge of the difficulty level of questions can greatly benefit a teacher by allowing for a quick estimation of students' potential and improving the quality of exams through the modification of trivial and challenging questions. Can the same benefits be achieved in Natural Language Processing through the use of Instance-Level Difficulty Analysis of Evaluation data (ILDAE)? We conducted a large-scale ILDAE study on 23 datasets and discovered five novel applications: 1) conducting efficient evaluations with fewer instances, saving time and computational cost, 2) improving the quality of existing evaluation datasets by repairing trivial and erroneous instances, 3) selecting the best model based on application requirements, 4) analyzing dataset characteristics for future data creation, and 5) estimating Out-of-Domain performance reliably. Our experiments showed several interesting results, such as evaluating only 5% of instances (selected via ILDAE) achieving a 0.93 Kendall correlation with complete evaluations, and computing weighted accuracy using difficulty scores resulting in a 5.2% higher correlation with Out-of-Domain performance. We have released the difficulty scores and hope that our work will inspire further research in this important but understudied field of leveraging instance difficulty in evaluations.

label: acl
text: Constituency parsing and nested named entity recognition (NER) are similar tasks since they both aim to predict a collection of nested and non-crossing spans. In this work, we cast nested NER to constituency parsing and propose a novel pointing mechanism for bottom-up parsing to tackle both tasks. The key idea is based on the observation that if we traverse a constituency tree in post-order, i.e., visiting a parent after its children, then two consecutively visited spans would share a boundary. Our model tracks the shared boundaries and predicts the next boundary at each step by leveraging a pointer network. As a result, it needs only linear steps to parse and thus is efficient. It also maintains a parsing configuration for structural consistency, i.e., always outputting valid trees. Experimentally, our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance on PTB among all BERT-based models (96.01 F1 score) and competitive performance on CTB7 in constituency parsing; and it also achieves strong performance on three benchmark datasets of nested NER: ACE2004, ACE2005, and GENIA. Our code will be available at https://github.com/xxxxx.

label: acl
text: Constituency parsing and nested named entity recognition are related tasks, as both aim to predict a collection of non-crossing, nested spans. In this work, we adapt nested NER to constituency parsing and present a new pointing mechanism for bottom-up parsing to address both tasks. The key insight is that when traversing a constituency tree in post-order, two consecutive spans will share a boundary. Our model uses a pointer network to track shared boundaries and predict the next boundary in linear steps, ensuring structural consistency and efficient parsing. Our results show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art BERT-based models on the PTB dataset (96.01 F1 score) and achieves competitive results on the CTB7 constituency parsing dataset. Additionally, our model shows strong performance on the ACE2004, ACE2005, and GENIA nested NER datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/xxxxx.

label: acl
text: Given a set of related publications, related work section generation aims to provide researchers with an overview of the specific research area by summarizing these works and introducing them in a logical order. Most of existing related work generation models follow the inflexible extractive style, which directly extract sentences from multiple original papers to form a related work discussion. Hence, in this paper, we propose a Relation-aware Related work Generator (RRG), which generates an abstractive related work from the given multiple scientific papers in the same research area. Concretely, we propose a relation-aware multi-document encoder that relates one document to another according to their content dependency in a relation graph. The relation graph and the document representation are interacted and polished iteratively, complementing each other in the training process. We also contribute two public datasets composed of related work sections and their corresponding papers. Extensive experiments on the two datasets show that the proposed model brings substantial improvements over several strong baselines. We hope that this work will promote advances in related work generation task.

label: acl
text: The goal of the related work section generation is to provide researchers with a comprehensive overview of a specific research area by summarizing related publications and presenting them in a logical order. Most existing related work generation models adopt an extractive approach, which simply extracts sentences from multiple papers to form the related work discussion. To address this limitation, we present the Relation-aware Related Work Generator (RRG), which generates an abstractive related work summary from multiple scientific papers in the same research area. Our model features a relation-aware multi-document encoder that relates one document to another based on their content dependency in a relation graph. The relation graph and document representation are refined and polished through an iterative process during training. Additionally, we contribute two publicly available datasets consisting of related work sections and their corresponding papers. Our experiments on these datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms several strong baselines. We believe that this work will drive further advancements in the related work generation task.

label: emnlp
text: Neural text generation, including neural machine translation, image captioning, and summarization, has been quite successful recently. However, during training time, typically only one reference is considered for each example, even though there are often multiple references available, e.g., 4 references in NIST MT evaluations, and 5 references in image captioning data. We first investigate several different ways of utilizing multiple human references during training. But more importantly, we then propose an algorithm to generate exponentially many pseudo-references by first compressing existing human references into lattices and then traversing them to generate new pseudo-references. These approaches lead to substantial improvements over strong baselines in both machine translation (+1.5 BLEU) and image captioning (+3.1 BLEU / +11.7 CIDEr).

label: emnlp
text: The recent advancements in neural text generation, including neural machine translation, image captioning, and summarization, have been quite successful. However, during training, only one reference is usually considered for each example, even though multiple references are often available. For instance, NIST MT evaluations have 4 references and image captioning data has 5 references. To address this issue, we first explore various approaches to utilize multiple human references during training. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm to generate an exponential number of pseudo-references by compressing existing human references into lattices and then traversing them. This leads to significant improvements over strong baselines in both machine translation (1.5 BLEU) and image captioning (3.1 BLEU and 11.7 CIDEr).

label: acl
text: Modern deep learning models are notoriously opaque, which has motivated the development of methods for interpreting how deep models predict.This goal is usually approached with attribution method, which assesses the influence of features on model predictions. As an explanation method, the evaluation criteria of attribution methods is how accurately it reflects the actual reasoning process of the model (faithfulness). Meanwhile, since the reasoning process of deep models is inaccessible, researchers design various evaluation methods to demonstrate their arguments.However, some crucial logic traps in these evaluation methods are ignored in most works, causing inaccurate evaluation and unfair comparison.This paper systematically reviews existing methods for evaluating attribution scores and summarizes the logic traps in these methods.We further conduct experiments to demonstrate the existence of each logic trap.Through both theoretical and experimental analysis, we hope to increase attention on the inaccurate evaluation of attribution scores. Moreover, with this paper, we suggest stopping focusing on improving performance under unreliable evaluation systems and starting efforts on reducing the impact of proposed logic traps.

label: acl
text: The opaqueness of modern deep learning models has spurred the development of methods for interpreting their predictions, such as attribution methods, which evaluate the impact of features on model predictions. The effectiveness of these methods is judged by their ability to accurately reflect the reasoning process of the model, however, many existing evaluation methods have overlooked crucial logic traps, leading to inaccurate evaluations and unfair comparisons. This paper systematically reviews existing evaluation methods for attribution scores and identifies the logic traps present in these methods. Our experiments demonstrate the existence of these traps, and through both theoretical and experimental analysis, we aim to raise awareness of the issue of inaccurate evaluations and encourage a shift away from focusing on improving performance under unreliable evaluation systems towards reducing the impact of these logic traps.

label: acl
text: We introduce VoxPopuli, a large-scale multilingual corpus providing 400K hours of unlabeled speech data in 23 languages. It is the largest open data to date for unsupervised representation learning as well as semi-supervised learning. VoxPopuli also contains 1.8K hours of transcribed speeches in 15 languages and their aligned oral interpretations into 15 target languages totaling 17.3K hours. We provide speech recognition (ASR) baselines and validate the versatility of VoxPopuli unlabeled data in semi-supervised ASR and speech-to-text translation under challenging out-of-domain settings. The corpus is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/voxpopuli.

label: acl
text: We present VoxPopuli, a massive multilingual corpus offering 400,000 hours of unlabeled speech data in 23 languages. It is the largest open data source available for unsupervised representation learning and semi-supervised learning. The corpus also includes 1,800 hours of transcribed speeches in 15 languages, with their oral interpretations aligned into 15 target languages, for a total of 17,300 hours. We provide ASR baselines and demonstrate the usefulness of VoxPopuli's unlabeled data in semi-supervised ASR and speech-to-text translation, even in challenging out-of-domain scenarios. The corpus can be accessed at https://github.com/facebookresearch/voxpopuli.

label: acl
text: Recent active learning (AL) approaches in Natural Language Processing (NLP) proposed using off-the-shelf pretrained language models (LMs). In this paper, we argue that these LMs are not adapted effectively to the downstream task during AL and we explore ways to address this issue. We suggest to first adapt the pretrained LM to the target task by continuing training with all the available unlabeled data and then use it for AL. We also propose a simple yet effective fine-tuning method to ensure that the adapted LM is properly trained in both low and high resource scenarios during AL. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach provides substantial data efficiency improvements compared to the standard fine-tuning approach, suggesting that a poor training strategy can be catastrophic for AL.

label: acl
text: Recent advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have brought forth the use of off-the-shelf pretrained language models (LMs) in active learning (AL) approaches. However, this paper argues that these LMs are not optimally adapted to the downstream task during AL. To address this issue, we propose a two-step approach: first, adapt the pretrained LM to the target task by continuing its training with all available unlabeled data, and then use it for AL. Additionally, we introduce a simple yet effective fine-tuning method to guarantee proper training of the adapted LM in both low and high resource scenarios during AL. Our experiments show that our approach leads to substantial improvements in data efficiency compared to standard fine-tuning methods, highlighting the importance of proper training strategies for AL.

label: acl
text: Large pre-trained models such as BERT are known to improve different downstream NLP tasks, even when such a model is trained on a generic domain. Moreover, recent studies have shown that when large domain-specific corpora are available, continued pre-training on domain-specific data can further improve the performance of in-domain tasks. However, this practice requires significant domain-specific data and computational resources which may not always be available. In this paper, we aim to adapt a generic pretrained model with a relatively small amount of domain-specific data. We demonstrate that by explicitly incorporating multi-granularity information of unseen and domain-specific words via the adaptation of (word based) n-grams, the performance of a generic pretrained model can be greatly improved. Specifically, we introduce a Transformer-based Domain-aware N-gram Adaptor, T-DNA, to effectively learn and incorporate the semantic representation of different combinations of words in the new domain. Experimental results illustrate the effectiveness of T-DNA on eight low-resource downstream tasks from four domains. We show that T-DNA is able to achieve significant improvements compared to existing methods on most tasks using limited data with lower computational costs. Moreover, further analyses demonstrate the importance and effectiveness of both unseen words and the information of different granularities. Our code is available at https://github.com/shizhediao/T-DNA.

label: acl
text: Large pre-trained models such as BERT have been shown to enhance the performance of various NLP tasks, even when trained on a generic domain. However, recent studies have demonstrated that continued pre-training on domain-specific data can lead to even better performance on in-domain tasks, but this approach requires a large amount of domain-specific data and computational resources. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a method to adapt a generic pre-trained model with a relatively small amount of domain-specific data. Our approach, called the Transformer-based Domain-aware N-gram Adaptor (T-DNA), incorporates multi-granularity information of unseen and domain-specific words via the adaptation of word-based n-grams. The results of our experiments on eight low-resource downstream tasks from four domains show that T-DNA significantly outperforms existing methods using limited data with lower computational costs. Our findings also indicate the importance and effectiveness of both unseen words and the information of different granularities. Our code is available at https://github.com/shizhediao/T-DNA.

label: coling
text: Understanding spatial and visual information is essential for a navigation agent who follows natural language instructions. The current Transformer-based VLN agents entangle the orientation and vision information, which limits the gain from the learning of each information source. In this paper, we design a neural agent with explicit Orientation and Vision modules. Those modules learn to ground spatial information and landmark mentions in the instructions to the visual environment more effectively. To strengthen the spatial reasoning and visual perception of the agent, we design specific pre-training tasks to feed and better utilize the corresponding modules in our final navigation model. We evaluate our approach on both Room2room (R2R) and Room4room (R4R) datasets and achieve the state of the art results on both benchmarks.

label: coling
text: A navigation agent must be able to comprehend spatial and visual information to effectively follow natural language instructions. However, current Transformer-based VLN agents lack the ability to separate orientation and vision information, hindering the learning process. To address this issue, we have designed a neural agent with explicit Orientation and Vision modules that are capable of grounding spatial information and landmarks mentioned in the instructions to the visual environment more efficiently. To enhance the agent's spatial reasoning and visual perception, we have created specific pre-training tasks that optimize the use of the Orientation and Vision modules in the final navigation model. Our approach has been evaluated on both Room2room (R2R) and Room4room (R4R) datasets and has achieved state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks.

label: acl
text: Existing pre-trained transformer analysis works usually focus only on one or two model families at a time, overlooking the variability of the architecture and pre-training objectives. In our work, we utilize the oLMpics bench- mark and psycholinguistic probing datasets for a diverse set of 29 models including T5, BART, and ALBERT. Additionally, we adapt the oLMpics zero-shot setup for autoregres- sive models and evaluate GPT networks of different sizes. Our findings show that none of these models can resolve compositional questions in a zero-shot fashion, suggesting that this skill is not learnable using existing pre-training objectives. Furthermore, we find that global model decisions such as architecture, directionality, size of the dataset, and pre-training objective are not predictive of a model's linguistic capabilities.

label: acl
text: Existing pre-trained transformer analysis studies typically only focus on one or two model families, neglecting the diversity of architecture and pre-training objectives. In our research, we use the oLMpics benchmark and psycholinguistic probing datasets to evaluate 29 models, including T5, BART, and ALBERT. We also adapt the oLMpics zero-shot setup for autoregressive models and evaluate GPT networks of varying sizes. Our results demonstrate that none of these models can perform compositional questions in a zero-shot setting, indicating that this ability cannot be learned through existing pre-training objectives. Furthermore, we conclude that global model factors such as architecture, directionality, dataset size, and pre-training objective are not indicative of a model's linguistic competencies.

label: emnlp
text: Conventional solutions to automatic related work summarization rely heavily on human-engineered features. In this paper, we develop a neural data-driven summarizer by leveraging the seq2seq paradigm, in which a joint context-driven attention mechanism is proposed to measure the contextual relevance within full texts and a heterogeneous bibliography graph simultaneously. Our motivation is to maintain the topic coherency between a related work section and its target document, where both the textual and graphic contexts play a big role in characterizing the relationship among scientific publications accurately. Experimental results on a large dataset show that our approach achieves a considerable improvement over a typical seq2seq summarizer and five classical summarization baselines.

label: emnlp
text: The conventional methods for automatic related work summarization rely heavily on human-engineered features. In this paper, we present a data-driven summarizer that leverages the seq2seq paradigm. Our summarizer incorporates a joint context-driven attention mechanism, which measures the contextual relevance both within full texts and across a heterogeneous bibliography graph. Our goal is to ensure that the related work section is coherent with the target document, taking into account both textual and graphical contexts to accurately characterize the relationships among scientific publications. Our experiments on a large dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms a typical seq2seq summarizer and five classical summarization baselines.

label: acl
text: Every natural text is written in some style. Style is formed by a complex combination of different stylistic factors, including formality markers, emotions, metaphors, etc. One cannot form a complete understanding of a text without considering these factors. The factors combine and co-vary in complex ways to form styles. Studying the nature of the covarying combinations sheds light on stylistic language in general, sometimes called cross-style language understanding. This paper provides the benchmark corpus (XSLUE) that combines existing datasets and collects a new one for sentence-level cross-style language understanding and evaluation. The benchmark contains text in 15 different styles under the proposed four theoretical groupings: figurative, personal, affective, and interpersonal groups. For valid evaluation, we collect an additional diagnostic set by annotating all 15 styles on the same text. Using XSLUE, we propose three interesting cross-style applications in classification, correlation, and generation. First, our proposed cross-style classifier trained with multiple styles together helps improve overall classification performance against individually-trained style classifiers. Second, our study shows that some styles are highly dependent on each other in human-written text. Finally, we find that combinations of some contradictive styles likely generate stylistically less appropriate text. We believe our benchmark and case studies help explore interesting future directions for cross-style research. The preprocessed datasets and code are publicly available.

label: acl
text: Every natural text is composed in a particular style that is shaped by a range of stylistic factors, including formality markers, emotions, metaphors, and others. To fully comprehend a text, one must take into account all of these factors, which interact and co-vary in complex ways to form the text's style. Understanding the nature of these co-varying combinations is crucial for studying stylistic language in general, also known as cross-style language understanding. This paper presents the XSLUE benchmark corpus, which combines existing datasets and collects new data to support sentence-level cross-style language understanding and evaluation. The corpus features 15 different styles, grouped into four theoretical categories: figurative, personal, affective, and interpersonal. To ensure accurate evaluation, we have also created a diagnostic set by annotating the same text in all 15 styles. Using XSLUE, we have explored three exciting cross-style applications in classification, correlation, and generation. Our findings show that a cross-style classifier trained on multiple styles outperforms classifiers trained on individual styles. Additionally, we have discovered that certain styles are highly dependent on one another in human-written text. Finally, we have found that combinations of seemingly contradictory styles can result in stylistically inappropriate text. We believe the XSLUE benchmark and our case studies will open up new avenues for future cross-style research. The preprocessed datasets and code are publicly available.

label: coling
text: Multi-Document Summarization (MDS) commonly employs the 2-stage extract-then-abstract paradigm, which first extracts a relatively short meta-document, then feeds it into the deep neural networks to generate an abstract. Previous work usually takes the ROUGE score as the label for training a scoring model to evaluate source documents. However, the trained scoring model is prone to under-fitting for low-resource settings, as it relies on the training data. To extract documents effectively, we construct prompting templates that invoke the underlying knowledge in Pre-trained Language Model (PLM) to calculate the document and keyword's perplexity, which can assess the document's semantic salience. Our unsupervised approach can be applied as a plug-in to boost other metrics for evaluating a document's salience, thus improving the subsequent abstract generation. We get positive results on 2 MDS datasets, 2 data settings, and 2 abstractive backbone models, showing our method's effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/UPER.

label: coling
text: Multi-Document Summarization (MDS) typically uses the 2-stage extract-then-abstract paradigm, which starts by extracting a concise meta-document and then feeding it into deep neural networks to generate an abstract. Previous work often relies on the ROUGE score as the label for training a scoring model to evaluate source documents, but this approach is prone to under-fitting in low-resource settings, as it depends on the training data. To improve document extraction, we devised prompting templates that tap into the knowledge of a Pre-trained Language Model (PLM) to calculate the perplexity of documents and keywords, which can assess the semantic salience of documents. Our unsupervised approach acts as a plug-in that enhances other metrics for evaluating document salience, thereby improving abstract generation. Our method has been tested and proven effective on 2 MDS datasets, 2 data settings, and 2 abstractive backbone models, achieving positive results. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/UPER.

label: acl
text: We propose fill-in-the-blanks as a video understanding evaluation framework and introduce FIBER – a novel dataset consisting of 28,000 videos and descriptions in support of this evaluation framework. The fill-in-the-blanks setting tests a model's understanding of a video by requiring it to predict a masked noun phrase in the caption of the video, given the video and the surrounding text. The FIBER benchmark does not share the weaknesses of the current state-of-the-art language-informed video understanding tasks, namely: (1) video question answering using multiple-choice questions, where models perform relatively well because they exploit linguistic biases in the task formulation, thus making our framework challenging for the current state-of-the-art systems to solve; and (2) video captioning, which relies on an open-ended evaluation framework that is often inaccurate because system answers may be perceived as incorrect if they differ in form from the ground truth. The FIBER dataset and our code are available at https://lit.eecs.umich.edu/fiber/.

label: acl
text: We propose a video understanding evaluation framework using fill-in-the-blanks and present FIBER, a novel dataset of 28,000 videos and descriptions, to support this framework. The fill-in-the-blank setting assesses a model's understanding of a video by requiring it to predict a masked noun phrase in the video's caption, given the video and surrounding text. Unlike current state-of-the-art language-informed video understanding tasks, such as video question answering with multiple-choice questions, which can be easily solved by exploiting linguistic biases, and video captioning, which relies on an open-ended evaluation framework that can lead to inaccurate results, the FIBER benchmark presents a challenging test for current state-of-the-art systems. The FIBER dataset and code can be accessed at https://lit.eecs.umich.edu/fiber/.

label: naacl
text: We examine the extent to which, in principle, different syntactic and semantic graph representations can complement and improve neural language modeling. Specifically, by conditioning on a subgraph encapsulating the locally relevant sentence history, can a model make better next-word predictions than a pretrained sequential language model alone? With an ensemble setup consisting of GPT-2 and ground-truth graphs from one of 7 different formalisms, we find that the graph information indeed improves perplexity and other metrics. Moreover, this architecture provides a new way to compare different frameworks of linguistic representation. In our oracle graph setup, training and evaluating on English WSJ, semantic constituency structures prove most useful to language modeling performance—outpacing syntactic constituency structures as well as syntactic and semantic dependency structures.

label: naacl
text: We investigate how different syntactic and semantic graph representations can enhance neural language modeling. Specifically, we examine if a model that takes into account a subgraph encapsulating the locally relevant sentence history can make better next-word predictions than a standalone pretrained sequential language model. Our ensemble setup, consisting of GPT-2 and ground-truth graphs from 7 different formalisms, shows that the graph information indeed improves perplexity and other metrics. Additionally, this architecture provides a new method for comparing different frameworks of linguistic representation. In our oracle graph setup, using English WSJ for training and evaluation, we find that semantic constituency structures are the most useful for language modeling performance, outperforming syntactic constituency structures and both syntactic and semantic dependency structures.

label: acl
text: Integrating extracted knowledge from the Web to knowledge graphs (KGs) can facilitate tasks like question answering. We study relation integration that aims to align free-text relations in subject-relation-object extractions to relations in a target KG. To address the challenge that free-text relations are ambiguous, previous methods exploit neighbor entities and relations for additional context. However, the predictions are made independently, which can be mutually inconsistent. We propose a two-stage Collective Relation Integration (CoRI) model, where the first stage independently makes candidate predictions, and the second stage employs a collective model that accesses all candidate predictions to make globally coherent predictions. We further improve the collective model with augmented data from the portion of the target KG that is otherwise unused. Experiment results on two datasets show that CoRI can significantly outperform the baselines, improving AUC from .677 to .748 and from .716 to .780, respectively.

label: acl
text: Integrating Web-extracted knowledge into knowledge graphs (KGs) can enhance question answering tasks. Our study focuses on relation integration, which aligns free-text relations in subject-relation-object extractions with target KG relations. The challenge lies in the ambiguity of free-text relations, which previous methods attempted to overcome by using neighbor entities and relations as contextual information. However, these methods made predictions independently, leading to mutual inconsistencies. Our proposed two-stage Collective Relation Integration (CoRI) model overcomes this issue by first making independent candidate predictions and then using a collective model to make globally coherent predictions. We further improve the collective model with augmented data from the unused portion of the target KG. Our experiments on two datasets show that CoRI outperforms the baselines, with an improvement in AUC from .677 to .748 and from .716 to .780, respectively.

label: acl
text: End-to-end task-oriented dialog systems usually suffer from the challenge of incorporating knowledge bases. In this paper, we propose a novel yet simple end-to-end differentiable model called memory-to-sequence (Mem2Seq) to address this issue. Mem2Seq is the first neural generative model that combines the multi-hop attention over memories with the idea of pointer network. We empirically show how Mem2Seq controls each generation step, and how its multi-hop attention mechanism helps in learning correlations between memories. In addition, our model is quite general without complicated task-specific designs. As a result, we show that Mem2Seq can be trained faster and attain the state-of-the-art performance on three different task-oriented dialog datasets.

label: acl
text: End-to-end task-oriented dialog systems often face the challenge of integrating knowledge bases. To address this issue, we introduce a novel, yet straightforward end-to-end differentiable model called Memory-to-Sequence (Mem2Seq). Mem2Seq is the first neural generative model that combines the multi-hop attention mechanism with the pointer network concept. Our empirical results demonstrate how Mem2Seq controls each generation step and how its multi-hop attention mechanism enhances the learning of correlations between memories. Furthermore, our model is highly versatile, lacking any complex, task-specific design. As a result, we show that Mem2Seq can be trained more efficiently and achieve state-of-the-art performance on three diverse task-oriented dialog datasets.

label: naacl
text: Spoken language understanding (SLU) tasks involve mapping from speech signals to semantic labels. Given the complexity of such tasks, good performance is expected to require large labeled datasets, which are difficult to collect for each new task and domain. However, recent advances in self-supervised speech representations have made it feasible to consider learning SLU models with limited labeled data. In this work, we focus on low-resource spoken named entity recognition (NER) and address the question: Beyond self-supervised pre-training, how can we use external speech and/or text data that are not annotated for the task? We consider self-training, knowledge distillation, and transfer learning for end-to-end (E2E) and pipeline (speech recognition followed by text NER) approaches. We find that several of these approaches improve performance in resource-constrained settings beyond the benefits from pre-trained representations. Compared to prior work, we find relative improvements in F1 of up to 16%. While the best baseline model is a pipeline approach, the best performance using external data is ultimately achieved by an E2E model. We provide detailed comparisons and analyses, developing insights on, for example, the effects of leveraging external data on (i) different categories of NER errors and (ii) the switch in performance trends between pipeline and E2E models.

label: naacl
text: Spoken language understanding (SLU) tasks involve mapping speech signals to semantic labels, which can be challenging due to the complexity of the task. Good performance in SLU tasks requires large labeled datasets, which are difficult to collect, especially for new tasks and domains. However, recent advancements in self-supervised speech representations have made it possible to learn SLU models with limited labeled data. In this study, we focus on low-resource spoken named entity recognition (NER) and investigate ways to use external speech and/or text data that are not annotated for the task. We explore self-training, knowledge distillation, and transfer learning for both end-to-end (E2E) and pipeline (speech recognition followed by text NER) approaches. Our findings indicate that several of these approaches improve performance in resource-constrained settings beyond the benefits of pre-trained representations, resulting in up to a 16% relative improvement in F1 compared to prior work. The best baseline model is a pipeline approach, but the best performance using external data is ultimately achieved by an E2E model. We provide detailed comparisons and analyses, offering insights into the effects of leveraging external data on different categories of NER errors and the switch in performance trends between pipeline and E2E models.

label: acl
text: Word alignment, which aims to align translationally equivalent words between source and target sentences, plays an important role in many natural language processing tasks. Current unsupervised neural alignment methods focus on inducing alignments from neural machine translation models, which does not leverage the full context in the target sequence. In this paper, we propose Mask-Align, a self-supervised word alignment model that takes advantage of the full context on the target side. Our model masks out each target token and predicts it conditioned on both source and the remaining target tokens. This two-step process is based on the assumption that the source token contributing most to recovering the masked target token should be aligned. We also introduce an attention variant called leaky attention, which alleviates the problem of unexpected high cross-attention weights on special tokens such as periods. Experiments on four language pairs show that our model outperforms previous unsupervised neural aligners and obtains new state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: Word alignment, which aligns translationally equivalent words between source and target sentences, is crucial in many natural language processing tasks. Currently, unsupervised neural alignment methods concentrate on inducing alignments from neural machine translation models, which do not make the most of the full context in the target sequence. In this paper, we present Mask-Align, a self-supervised word alignment model that utilizes the full context on the target side. Our model masks each target token and predicts it based on both the source and the remaining target tokens. This two-step process is founded on the belief that the source token that contributes the most to predicting the masked target token should be aligned. We also introduce a variant of attention called leaky attention, which addresses the issue of high cross-attention weights on special tokens, such as periods. Our experiments on four language pairs demonstrate that our model surpasses previous unsupervised neural aligners, achieving new state-of-the-art results.

label: acl
text: We show that unsupervised sequence-segmentation performance can be transferred to extremely low-resource languages by pre-training a Masked Segmental Language Model (Downey et al., 2021) multilingually. Further, we show that this transfer can be achieved by training over a collection of low-resource languages that are typologically similar (but phylogenetically unrelated) to the target language. In our experiments, we transfer from a collection of 10 Indigenous American languages (AmericasNLP, Mager et al., 2021) to K'iche', a Mayan language. We compare our multilingual model to a monolingual (from-scratch) baseline, as well as a model pre-trained on Quechua only. We show that the multilingual pre-trained approach yields consistent segmentation quality across target dataset sizes, exceeding the monolingual baseline in 6/10 experimental settings. Our model yields especially strong results at small target sizes, including a zero-shot performance of 20.6 F1. These results have promising implications for low-resource NLP pipelines involving human-like linguistic units, such as the sparse transcription framework proposed by Bird (2020).

label: acl
text: We demonstrate that the performance of unsupervised sequence segmentation can be transferred to low-resource languages by pre-training a Masked Segmental Language Model (Downey et al., 2021) multilingually. Our experiments show that this transfer can be achieved by training over a collection of typologically similar, but phylogenetically unrelated, low-resource languages. To demonstrate this, we transfer from a collection of 10 Indigenous American languages (AmericasNLP, Mager et al., 2021) to K'iche', a Mayan language. We compare our multilingual model to a monolingual (from-scratch) baseline and a model pre-trained on Quechua only. Our results show that the multilingual pre-trained approach consistently outperforms the monolingual baseline in 6 out of 10 experimental settings, especially at small target sizes. Our model even achieved a zero-shot performance of 20.6 F1, which has promising implications for low-resource NLP pipelines that involve human-like linguistic units, such as the sparse transcription framework proposed by Bird (2020).

label: acl
text: Personalization of natural language generation plays a vital role in a large spectrum of tasks, such as explainable recommendation, review summarization and dialog systems. In these tasks, user and item IDs are important identifiers for personalization. Transformer, which is demonstrated with strong language modeling capability, however, is not personalized and fails to make use of the user and item IDs since the ID tokens are not even in the same semantic space as the words. To address this problem, we present a PErsonalized Transformer for Explainable Recommendation (PETER), on which we design a simple and effective learning objective that utilizes the IDs to predict the words in the target explanation, so as to endow the IDs with linguistic meanings and to achieve personalized Transformer. Besides generating explanations, PETER can also make recommendations, which makes it a unified model for the whole recommendation-explanation pipeline. Extensive experiments show that our small unpretrained model outperforms fine-tuned BERT on the generation task, in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency, which highlights the importance and the nice utility of our design.

label: acl
text: The personalization of natural language generation plays a crucial role in a wide range of tasks, including explainable recommendation, review summarization, and dialog systems. In these tasks, user and item IDs are essential for personalization. However, the Transformer model, which has strong language modeling capabilities, is not personalized and fails to utilize user and item IDs as the ID tokens are not in the same semantic space as the words. To solve this issue, we introduce the PErsonalized Transformer for Explainable Recommendation (PETER), which utilizes the IDs to predict the words in the target explanation. This design endows the IDs with linguistic meanings, resulting in a personalized Transformer. PETER not only generates explanations but also makes recommendations, making it a unified model for the entire recommendation-explanation pipeline. Our experiments show that our small unpretrained model outperforms fine-tuned BERT in terms of effectiveness and efficiency, highlighting the significance and usefulness of our design.

label: acl
text: This paper describes and tests a method for carrying out quantified reproducibility assessment (QRA) that is based on concepts and definitions from metrology. QRA produces a single score estimating the degree of reproducibility of a given system and evaluation measure, on the basis of the scores from, and differences between, different reproductions. We test QRA on 18 different system and evaluation measure combinations (involving diverse NLP tasks and types of evaluation), for each of which we have the original results and one to seven reproduction results. The proposed QRA method produces degree-of-reproducibility scores that are comparable across multiple reproductions not only of the same, but also of different, original studies. We find that the proposed method facilitates insights into causes of variation between reproductions, and as a result, allows conclusions to be drawn about what aspects of system and/or evaluation design need to be changed in order to improve reproducibility.

label: acl
text: This paper presents a method for conducting quantified reproducibility assessments (QRA) based on metrology concepts and definitions. QRA calculates a single score that reflects the degree of reproducibility of a given system and evaluation measure, taking into account the scores and differences from multiple reproductions. The proposed method was tested on 18 different combinations of systems and evaluation measures, which involved various NLP tasks and types of evaluation. The original results and one to seven reproduction results were used to evaluate the proposed QRA method. The results showed that the proposed method produces degree-of-reproducibility scores that can be compared across multiple reproductions, regardless of whether they are from the same or different original studies. Additionally, this method provides insights into the causes of variation between reproductions and helps to identify the aspects of system and/or evaluation design that need to be improved to increase reproducibility.

label: naacl
text: Little attention has been paid on EArly Rumor Detection (EARD), and EARD performance was evaluated inappropriately on a few datasets where the actual early-stage information is largely missing. To reverse such situation, we construct BEARD, a new Benchmark dataset for EARD, based on claims from fact-checking websites by trying to gather as many early relevant posts as possible. We also propose HEARD, a novel model based on neural Hawkes process for EARD, which can guide a generic rumor detection model to make timely, accurate and stable predictions. Experiments show that HEARD achieves effective EARD performance on two commonly used general rumor detection datasets and our BEARD dataset.

label: naacl
text: Little attention has been given to Early Rumor Detection (EARD), and evaluations of its performance are limited to a few datasets that lack actual early-stage information. To address this issue, we have created BEARD, a new benchmark dataset for EARD, which is based on claims from fact-checking websites and aims to gather as many relevant early posts as possible. Additionally, we introduce HEARD, a novel neural Hawkes process-based model for EARD that can guide a generic rumor detection model to make timely, accurate, and stable predictions. Our experiments demonstrate that HEARD achieves effective performance on two commonly used general rumor detection datasets and our newly created BEARD dataset.

label: acl
text: Document-level MT models are still far from satisfactory. Existing work extend translation unit from single sentence to multiple sentences. However, study shows that when we further enlarge the translation unit to a whole document, supervised training of Transformer can fail. In this paper, we find such failure is not caused by overfitting, but by sticking around local minima during training. Our analysis shows that the increased complexity of target-to-source attention is a reason for the failure. As a solution, we propose G-Transformer, introducing locality assumption as an inductive bias into Transformer, reducing the hypothesis space of the attention from target to source. Experiments show that G-Transformer converges faster and more stably than Transformer, achieving new state-of-the-art BLEU scores for both nonpretraining and pre-training settings on three benchmark datasets.

label: acl
text: Document-level machine translation (MT) models still have a long way to go before they are considered satisfactory. Previous work has extended the translation unit from a single sentence to multiple sentences. However, studies have shown that when the translation unit is further enlarged to encompass an entire document, the supervised training of a Transformer model can fail. This paper identifies that this failure is not due to overfitting, but rather to the model getting stuck in local minima during training. Our analysis reveals that the increased complexity of the target-to-source attention mechanism is the root cause of the problem. To address this issue, we propose the G-Transformer, which incorporates a locality assumption as an inductive bias into the Transformer model, reducing the hypothesis space of the target-to-source attention. Our experiments demonstrate that the G-Transformer converges faster and more stably than the Transformer model and achieves new state-of-the-art BLEU scores on three benchmark datasets, both in non-pretrained and pre-trained settings.

label: naacl
text: Recently, neural machine translation (NMT) has emerged as a powerful alternative to conventional statistical approaches. However, its performance drops considerably in the presence of morphologically rich languages (MRLs). Neural engines usually fail to tackle the large vocabulary and high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word rate of MRLs. Therefore, it is not suitable to exploit existing word-based models to translate this set of languages. In this paper, we propose an extension to the state-of-the-art model of Chung et al. (2016), which works at the character level and boosts the decoder with target-side morphological information. In our architecture, an additional morphology table is plugged into the model. Each time the decoder samples from a target vocabulary, the table sends auxiliary signals from the most relevant affixes in order to enrich the decoder's current state and constrain it to provide better predictions. We evaluated our model to translate English into German, Russian, and Turkish as three MRLs and observed significant improvements.

label: naacl
text: Recently, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has gained popularity as a powerful alternative to traditional statistical approaches. However, its performance decreases significantly when dealing with morphologically rich languages (MRLs) due to the challenge of handling the large vocabulary and high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word rate. Conventional word-based models are not suitable for translating MRLs. To address this issue, we propose an extension to the state-of-the-art model by Chung et al. (2016) that operates at the character level and incorporates target-side morphological information into the decoder. Our architecture includes an additional morphology table, which sends auxiliary signals from the most relevant affixes to the decoder, enriching its current state and guiding it to make better predictions. Our model was evaluated in translating English into German, Russian, and Turkish, and we observed significant improvements in performance.

label: acl
text: Word and sentence embeddings are useful feature representations in natural language processing. However, intrinsic evaluation for embeddings lags far behind, and there has been no significant update since the past decade. Word and sentence similarity tasks have become the de facto evaluation method. It leads models to overfit to such evaluations, negatively impacting embedding models' development. This paper first points out the problems using semantic similarity as the gold standard for word and sentence embedding evaluations. Further, we propose a new intrinsic evaluation method called EvalRank, which shows a much stronger correlation with downstream tasks. Extensive experiments are conducted based on 60+ models and popular datasets to certify our judgments. Finally, the practical evaluation toolkit is released for future benchmarking purposes.

label: acl
text: Word and sentence embeddings are powerful tools in natural language processing, but their intrinsic evaluation has not been updated in over a decade and relies heavily on word and sentence similarity tasks. This over-reliance on semantic similarity can result in models overfitting to these evaluations, hindering their development. In this paper, we identify the limitations of using semantic similarity as the gold standard for word and sentence embedding evaluations and introduce a new evaluation method, EvalRank, which has a stronger correlation with downstream tasks. Our extensive experiments, conducted on 60+ models and popular datasets, support our findings. We also provide a practical evaluation toolkit for future benchmarking.

label: coling
text: Nowadays, deep-learning based NLP models are usually trained with large-scale third-party data which can be easily injected with malicious backdoors. Thus, BackDoor Attack (BDA) study has become a trending research to help promote the robustness of an NLP system. Text-based BDA aims to train a poisoned model with both clean and poisoned texts to perform normally on clean inputs while being misled to predict those trigger-embedded texts as target labels set by attackers. Previous works usually choose fixed Positions-to-Poison (P2P) first, then add triggers upon those positions such as letter insertion or deletion. However, considering the positions of words with important semantics may vary in different contexts, fixed P2P models are severely limited in flexibility and performance. We study the text-based BDA from the perspective of automatically and dynamically selecting P2P from contexts. We design a novel Locator model which can predict P2P dynamically without human intervention. Based on the predicted P2P, four effective strategies are introduced to show the BDA performance. Experiments on two public datasets show both tinier test accuracy gap on clean data and higher attack success rate on poisoned ones. Human evaluation with volunteers also shows the P2P predicted by our model are important for classification. Source code is available at https://github.com/jncsnlp/LocatorModel.

label: coling
text: Deep-learning based NLP models are commonly trained with large-scale third-party data, which can be easily contaminated with malicious backdoors. As a result, the study of BackDoor Attacks (BDA) has become a popular area of research to improve the robustness of NLP systems. Text-based BDA involves training a poisoned model with both clean and contaminated text, so that it performs normally on clean inputs while being misled to predict target labels set by attackers for trigger-embedded texts. Previous studies have typically used fixed Positions-to-Poison (P2P) and added triggers to these positions, such as through letter insertion or deletion. However, this approach is limited in flexibility and performance as the positions of words with important semantics can vary in different contexts. In this study, we investigate text-based BDA from the perspective of automatically and dynamically selecting P2P from context. We propose a novel Locator model that can predict P2P dynamically without human intervention. Four effective strategies are introduced based on the predicted P2P to demonstrate the BDA performance. Results from experiments on two public datasets show a smaller test accuracy gap on clean data and a higher attack success rate on contaminated data. Human evaluations with volunteers also indicate that the P2P predicted by our model are important for classification. The source code is available at https://github.com/jncsnlp/LocatorModel.

text: Medical Relation Extraction (MRE) task aims to extract relations between entities in medical texts. Traditional relation extraction methods achieve impressive success by exploring the syntactic information, e.g., dependency tree. However, the quality of the 1-best dependency tree for medical texts produced by an out-of-domain parser is relatively limited so that the performance of medical relation extraction method may degenerate. To this end, we propose a method to jointly model semantic and syntactic information from medical texts based on causal explanation theory. We generate dependency forests consisting of the semantic-embedded 1-best dependency tree. Then, a task-specific causal explainer is adopted to prune the dependency forests, which are further fed into a designed graph convolutional network to learn the corresponding representation for downstream task. Empirically, the various comparisons on benchmark medical datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

label: coling
text: The Medical Relation Extraction (MRE) task aims to extract relationships between entities in medical texts. Traditional relation extraction methods have achieved impressive results by utilizing syntactic information, such as dependency trees. However, the quality of the 1-best dependency tree generated by out-of-domain parsers for medical texts is limited, which can negatively impact the performance of medical relation extraction methods. To address this issue, we propose a method that jointly models semantic and syntactic information from medical texts based on the theory of causal explanation. Our method generates dependency forests that consist of semantic-embedded 1-best dependency trees. A task-specific causal explainer is then used to prune the dependency forests, which are fed into a graph convolutional network for representation learning and downstream tasks. The results of various comparisons on benchmark medical datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

label: emnlp
text: Sequence-to-sequence (SEQ2SEQ) models have been successfully applied to automatic math word problem solving. Despite its simplicity, a drawback still remains: a math word problem can be correctly solved by more than one equations. This non-deterministic transduction harms the performance of maximum likelihood estimation. In this paper, by considering the uniqueness of expression tree, we propose an equation normalization method to normalize the duplicated equations. Moreover, we analyze the performance of three popular SEQ2SEQ models on the math word problem solving. We find that each model has its own specialty in solving problems, consequently an ensemble model is then proposed to combine their advantages. Experiments on dataset Math23K show that the ensemble model with equation normalization significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods.

label: emnlp
text: SEQ2SEQ models have been effectively used in automatic math word problem solving, but they still have a drawback: a single math word problem can be solved by multiple equations, which negatively impacts the performance of maximum likelihood estimation. To address this issue, this paper proposes an equation normalization method that considers the uniqueness of the expression tree. Additionally, the performance of three popular SEQ2SEQ models is analyzed, and an ensemble model is proposed to take advantage of each model's strengths. Results from experiments on the Math23K dataset demonstrate that the ensemble model with equation normalization outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods significantly.

label: acl
text: Generating open-domain conversational responses in the desired style usually suffers from the lack of parallel data in the style. Meanwhile, using monolingual stylistic data to increase style intensity often leads to the expense of decreasing content relevance. In this paper, we propose to disentangle the content and style in latent space by diluting sentence-level information in style representations. Combining the desired style representation and a response content representation will then obtain a stylistic response. Our approach achieves a higher BERT-based style intensity score and comparable BLEU scores, compared with baselines. Human evaluation results show that our approach significantly improves style intensity and maintains content relevance.

label: acl
text: Generating open-domain conversational responses in a desired style often faces a challenge due to the scarcity of parallel data in that style. Attempts to increase style intensity using monolingual stylistic data often result in a reduction of content relevance. To address this issue, we propose a method to disentangle content and style in the latent space by diluting sentence-level information in style representations. Our approach combines the desired style representation with a response content representation to produce a stylistically-rich response. Our results show that our approach outperforms baselines in terms of style intensity, as measured by BERT-based scores, while maintaining comparable BLEU scores. Furthermore, human evaluations confirm that our approach significantly enhances style intensity while preserving content relevance.

text: A challenging task when generating summaries of legal documents is the ability to address their argumentative nature. We introduce a simple technique to capture the argumentative structure of legal documents by integrating argument role labeling into the summarization process. Experiments with pretrained language models show that our proposed approach improves performance over strong baselines.

label: coling
text: Generating summaries of legal documents can be a challenging task due to their argumentative nature. To address this challenge, we introduce a technique that incorporates argument role labeling into the summarization process. Our approach has been tested using pretrained language models and has shown improvement over strong baselines.

text: The human recognition system has presented the remarkable ability to effortlessly learn novel knowledge from only a few trigger events based on prior knowledge, which is called insight learning. Mimicking such behavior on Knowledge Graph Reasoning (KGR) is an interesting and challenging research problem with many practical applications. Simultaneously, existing works, such as knowledge embedding and few-shot learning models, have been limited to conducting KGR in either “seen-to-seen” or “unseen-to-unseen” scenarios. To this end, we propose a neural insight learning framework named Eureka to bridge the “seen” to “unseen” gap. Eureka is empowered to learn the seen relations with sufficient training triples while providing the flexibility of learning unseen relations given only one trigger without sacrificing its performance on seen relations. Eureka meets our expectation of the model to acquire seen and unseen relations at no extra cost, and eliminate the need to retrain when encountering emerging unseen relations. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework also outperforms various state-of-the-art baselines on datasets of both seen and unseen relations.
