Our analysis provides new insights into the importance of attention alignment score calculation during the training phase of VL tasks, which is often overlooked in attention-based cross-modal models and pretrained models. Our code is available at https://github.com/adlnlp/Attention_VL.

label: coling
text: Discourse parsing on multi-party dialogues is an important but difficult task in dialogue systems and conversational analysis. It is believed that speaker interactions are helpful for this task. However, most previous research ignores speaker interactions between different speakers. To this end, we present a speaker-aware model for this task. Concretely, we propose a speaker-context interaction joint encoding (SCIJE) approach, using the interaction features between different speakers. In addition, we propose a second-stage pre-training task, same speaker prediction (SSP), enhancing the conversational context representations by predicting whether two utterances are from the same speaker. Experiments on two standard benchmark datasets show that the proposed model achieves the best-reported performance in the literature. We will release the codes of this paper to facilitate future research.

label: coling
text: Discourse parsing in multi-party dialogues is a critical but challenging task in conversational analysis and dialogue systems. It is believed that speaker interactions play a crucial role in this task. However, most previous research has neglected the interactions between speakers. To address this issue, we present a speaker-aware model for discourse parsing. The proposed model, called speaker-context interaction joint encoding (SCIJE), leverages interaction features between different speakers. Additionally, we introduce a second-stage pre-training task, called same speaker prediction (SSP), which enhances the representations of conversational context by predicting whether two utterances are from the same speaker. Our experiments on two standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms previous methods, achieving the best performance reported in the literature. To encourage further research, we will make the code for this paper publicly available.

label: coling
text: Today the pre-trained language models achieve great success for question generation (QG) task and significantly outperform traditional sequence-to-sequence approaches. However, the pre-trained models treat the input passage as a flat sequence and are thus not aware of the text structure of input passage. For QG task, we model text structure as answer position and syntactic dependency, and propose answer localness modeling and syntactic mask attention to address these limitations. Specially, we present localness modeling with a Gaussian bias to enable the model to focus on answer-surrounded context, and propose a mask attention mechanism to make the syntactic structure of input passage accessible in question generation process. Experiments on SQuAD dataset show that our proposed two modules improve performance over the strong pre-trained model ProphetNet, and combing them together achieves very competitive results with the state-of-the-art pre-trained model.

label: coling
text: Today, pre-trained language models have achieved great success in the question generation (QG) task and outperform traditional sequence-to-sequence approaches significantly. However, these models treat the input passage as a flat sequence and are not aware of its text structure. To address this limitation, we propose answer localness modeling and syntactic mask attention to model the text structure as answer position and syntactic dependency. Our localness modeling uses a Gaussian bias to focus on the answer-surrounded context, while our mask attention mechanism makes the syntactic structure of the input passage accessible in the question generation process. Our experiments on the SQuAD dataset show that our proposed modules outperform the strong pre-trained model ProphetNet, and combining them results in very competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art pre-trained model.

label: acl
text: Recent neural text generation models have shown significant improvement in generating descriptive text from structured data such as table formats. One of the remaining important challenges is generating more analytical descriptions that can be inferred from facts in a data source. The use of a template-based generator and a pointer-generator is among the potential alternatives for table-to-text generators. In this paper, we propose a framework consisting of a pre-trained model and a copy mechanism. The pre-trained models are fine-tuned to produce fluent text that is enriched with numerical reasoning. However, it still lacks fidelity to the table contents. The copy mechanism is incorporated in the fine-tuning step by using general placeholders to avoid producing hallucinated phrases that are not supported by a table while preserving high fluency. In summary, our contributions are (1) a new dataset for numerical table-to-text generation using pairs of a table and a paragraph of a table description with richer inference from scientific papers, and (2) a table-to-text generation framework enriched with numerical reasoning.

label: acl
text: Recent neural text generation models have demonstrated significant advancements in creating descriptive text from structured data, such as tables. However, a significant challenge remains in generating more analytical descriptions that can be inferred from the facts in a data source. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that combines a pre-trained model and a copy mechanism. The pre-trained model is fine-tuned to generate fluent text that is enriched with numerical reasoning. However, it still lacks accuracy in reproducing the table contents. To address this issue, the copy mechanism is integrated into the fine-tuning process using general placeholders. This helps to avoid generating unsupported phrases while preserving high fluency. Our framework makes two main contributions: (1) a new dataset for numerical table-to-text generation, which includes pairs of tables and table descriptions with richer inferences from scientific papers, and (2) a table-to-text generation framework that is enriched with numerical reasoning.

label: coling
text: Prompt-based fine-tuning for pre-trained models has proven effective for many natural language processing tasks under few-shot settings in general domain. However, tuning with prompt in biomedical domain has not been investigated thoroughly. Biomedical words are often rare in general domain, but quite ubiquitous in biomedical contexts, which dramatically deteriorates the performance of pre-trained models on downstream biomedical applications even after fine-tuning, especially in low-resource scenarios. We propose a simple yet effective approach to helping models learn rare biomedical words during tuning with prompt. Experimental results show that our method can achieve up to 6% improvement in biomedical natural language inference task without any extra parameters or training steps using few-shot vanilla prompt settings.

label: coling
text: Fine-tuning pre-trained models using prompts has been shown to be effective for many natural language processing tasks in general domains, under few-shot settings. However, the impact of prompt-based tuning in the biomedical domain has not been thoroughly explored. Biomedical words are often rare in general domains, but are commonly used in biomedical contexts, which can significantly lower the performance of pre-trained models in biomedical applications, even after fine-tuning, particularly in low-resource scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a simple and effective approach for helping models learn rare biomedical words during prompt-based tuning. Our results show that this method can improve performance by up to 6% in biomedical natural language inference tasks, without the need for additional parameters or training steps, using only few-shot vanilla prompt settings.

label: naacl
text: Can attention- or gradient-based visualization techniques be used to infer token-level labels for binary sequence tagging problems, using networks trained only on sentence-level labels? We construct a neural network architecture based on soft attention, train it as a binary sentence classifier and evaluate against token-level annotation on four different datasets. Inferring token labels from a network provides a method for quantitatively evaluating what the model is learning, along with generating useful feedback in assistance systems. Our results indicate that attention-based methods are able to predict token-level labels more accurately, compared to gradient-based methods, sometimes even rivaling the supervised oracle network.

label: naacl
text: Can attention-based or gradient-based visualization techniques be applied to predict token-level labels for binary sequence tagging problems using networks trained only on sentence-level labels? We have developed a neural network architecture that is based on soft attention and trained it as a binary sentence classifier. We then evaluated its performance against token-level annotations on four different datasets. This method of inferring token labels from a network provides a way to quantify what the model is learning, and also provides useful feedback in assistance systems. Our results show that attention-based methods outperform gradient-based methods in predicting token-level labels, sometimes even achieving results that rival those of a supervised oracle network.

label: acl
text: Parsing spoken dialogue poses unique difficulties, including disfluencies and unmarked boundaries between sentence-like units. Previous work has shown that prosody can help with parsing disfluent speech (Tran et al. 2018), but has assumed that the input to the parser is already segmented into sentence-like units (SUs), which isn't true in existing speech applications. We investigate how prosody affects a parser that receives an entire dialogue turn as input (a turn-based model), instead of gold standard pre-segmented SUs (an SU-based model). In experiments on the English Switchboard corpus, we find that when using transcripts alone, the turn-based model has trouble segmenting SUs, leading to worse parse performance than the SU-based model. However, prosody can effectively replace gold standard SU boundaries: with prosody, the turn-based model performs as well as the SU-based model (91.38 vs. 91.06 F1 score, respectively), despite performing two tasks (SU segmentation and parsing) rather than one (parsing alone). Analysis shows that pitch and intensity features are the most important for this corpus, since they allow the model to correctly distinguish an SU boundary from a speech disfluency – a distinction that the model otherwise struggles to make.

label: acl
text: Parsing spoken dialogue is challenging, particularly due to the presence of disfluencies and unmarked boundaries between sentence-like units. Previous studies have demonstrated that prosody can aid in parsing disfluent speech (Tran et al. 2018), but these studies have assumed that the input to the parser is already divided into sentence-like units (SUs). In this study, we examine the impact of prosody on a parser that takes an entire dialogue turn as input (turn-based model), instead of pre-segmented SUs (SU-based model). Our experiments on the English Switchboard corpus show that when relying solely on transcripts, the turn-based model struggles to segment SUs, leading to lower parse performance compared to the SU-based model. However, incorporating prosody can effectively replace gold standard SU boundaries, resulting in the turn-based model performing similarly to the SU-based model (91.38 vs. 91.06 F1 score). Analysis indicates that pitch and intensity features are crucial for this corpus, as they enable the model to differentiate between an SU boundary and a speech disfluency, which the model otherwise finds difficult to distinguish.

label: emnlp
text: There is growing interest in the language developed by agents interacting in emergent-communication settings. Earlier studies have focused on the agents' symbol usage, rather than on their representation of visual input. In this paper, we consider the referential games of Lazaridou et al. (2017), and investigate the representations the agents develop during their evolving interaction. We find that the agents establish successful communication by inducing visual representations that almost perfectly align with each other, but, surprisingly, do not capture the conceptual properties of the objects depicted in the input images. We conclude that, if we care about developing language-like communication systems, we must pay more attention to the visual semantics agents associate to the symbols they use.

label: emnlp
text: There is increasing attention being paid to the language that emerges from agent interactions in emergent communication settings. Previous research has mainly focused on the symbols used by the agents, rather than their representation of visual input. This paper examines the referential games from Lazaridou et al. (2017) and investigates the representations that the agents form during their evolving interaction. Our findings reveal that the agents establish effective communication by inducing visual representations that are nearly identical to each other, but surprisingly, do not reflect the underlying concepts of the objects depicted in the input images. Our conclusion is that, in order to develop language-like communication systems, greater consideration must be given to the visual semantics that agents associate with the symbols they use.

label: acl
text: There have been various types of pretraining architectures including autoencoding models (e.g., BERT), autoregressive models (e.g., GPT), and encoder-decoder models (e.g., T5). However, none of the pretraining frameworks performs the best for all tasks of three main categories including natural language understanding (NLU), unconditional generation, and conditional generation. We propose a General Language Model (GLM) based on autoregressive blank infilling to address this challenge. GLM improves blank filling pretraining by adding 2D positional encodings and allowing an arbitrary order to predict spans, which results in performance gains over BERT and T5 on NLU tasks. Meanwhile, GLM can be pretrained for different types of tasks by varying the number and lengths of blanks. On a wide range of tasks across NLU, conditional and unconditional generation, GLM outperforms BERT, T5, and GPT given the same model sizes and data, and achieves the best performance from a single pretrained model with 1.25C-C-C parameters of BERT Large , demonstrating its generalizability to different downstream tasks.

label: acl
text: There have been several pretraining architectures developed, including autoencoding models (e.g. BERT), autoregressive models (e.g. GPT), and encoder-decoder models (e.g. T5). However, no single pretraining framework has been found to perform optimally for all three main categories of tasks: natural language understanding (NLU), unconditional generation, and conditional generation. To address this challenge, we propose a General Language Model (GLM) based on autoregressive blank infilling. GLM improves upon blank filling pretraining by incorporating 2D positional encodings and allowing for the prediction of spans in an arbitrary order, resulting in improved performance on NLU tasks compared to BERT and T5. Additionally, GLM can be pretrained for different types of tasks by varying the number and lengths of blanks. Across a wide range of tasks in NLU, conditional, and unconditional generation, GLM outperforms BERT, T5, and GPT with the same model size and data, achieving the best performance from a single pretrained model with only 1.25 times the parameters of BERT Large, demonstrating its versatility and generalizability to different downstream tasks.

label: acl
text: Dialog response generation in open domain is an important research topic where the main challenge is to generate relevant and diverse responses. In this paper, we propose a new dialog pre-training framework called DialogVED, which introduces continuous latent variables into the enhanced encoder-decoder pre-training framework to increase the relevance and diversity of responses. With the help of a large dialog corpus (Reddit), we pre-train the model using the following 4 tasks, used in training language models (LMs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) literature: 1) masked language model; 2) response generation; 3) bag-of-words prediction; and 4) KL divergence reduction. We also add additional parameters to model the turn structure in dialogs to improve the performance of the pre-trained model. We conduct experiments on PersonaChat, DailyDialog, and DSTC7-AVSD benchmarks for response generation. Experimental results show that our model achieves the new state-of-the-art results on all these datasets.

label: acl
text: The generation of dialog responses in open domains is a significant research area where the primary challenge is to produce relevant and varied responses. In this study, we present a novel dialog pre-training framework, DialogVED, which incorporates continuous latent variables into the enhanced encoder-decoder pre-training framework to enhance the relevance and diversity of responses. We pre-train the model using a large dialog corpus (Reddit) and four tasks commonly utilized in language model (LM) and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) training literature: masked language model, response generation, bag-of-words prediction, and KL divergence reduction. Additionally, we incorporate additional parameters to model dialog turn structure, thereby improving the pre-trained model's performance. Our experiments on the PersonaChat, DailyDialog, and DSTC7-AVSD benchmarks for response generation demonstrate that our model achieves new state-of-the-art results on all datasets.

label: acl
text: Text style transfer aims to alter the style (e.g., sentiment) of a sentence while preserving its content. A common approach is to map a given sentence to content representation that is free of style, and the content representation is fed to a decoder with a target style. Previous methods in filtering style completely remove tokens with style at the token level, which incurs the loss of content information. In this paper, we propose to enhance content preservation by implicitly removing the style information of each token with reverse attention, and thereby retain the content. Furthermore, we fuse content information when building the target style representation, making it dynamic with respect to the content. Our method creates not only style-independent content representation, but also content-dependent style representation in transferring style. Empirical results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines by a large margin in terms of content preservation. In addition, it is also competitive in terms of style transfer accuracy and fluency.

label: acl
text: Text style transfer aims to change the sentiment of a sentence while keeping its content intact. One popular method is to convert the original sentence into a content representation that is free of style, which is then fed into a decoder with a target style. However, previous techniques for filtering style often result in the loss of content information since they completely remove style-related tokens at the token level. In this paper, we propose a new approach that improves content preservation by using reverse attention to implicitly remove style information from each token, thereby retaining the content. Additionally, we integrate content information when constructing the target style representation, making it dynamic in relation to the content. Our method not only creates a style-independent content representation, but also a content-dependent style representation, resulting in improved style transfer accuracy and fluency. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin in terms of content preservation, while also being competitive in terms of style transfer accuracy and fluency.

label: acl
text: Inquiry is fundamental to communication, and machines cannot effectively collaborate with humans unless they can ask questions. In this work, we build a neural network model for the task of ranking clarification questions. Our model is inspired by the idea of expected value of perfect information: a good question is one whose expected answer will be useful. We study this problem using data from StackExchange, a plentiful online resource in which people routinely ask clarifying questions to posts so that they can better offer assistance to the original poster. We create a dataset of clarification questions consisting of 77K posts paired with a clarification question (and answer) from three domains of StackExchange: askubuntu, unix and superuser. We evaluate our model on 500 samples of this dataset against expert human judgments and demonstrate significant improvements over controlled baselines.

label: acl
text: The fundamental aspect of communication is inquiry, and without the ability to ask questions, machines cannot collaborate efficiently with humans. This study presents a neural network model for ranking clarification questions. The model is based on the concept of expected value of perfect information, which states that a good question is one whose expected answer will be valuable. The research uses data from StackExchange, an abundant online platform where individuals frequently ask clarifying questions to posts in order to provide better support to the original poster. A dataset of 77K clarification questions from three domains (askubuntu, Unix, and superuser) was created and evaluated on 500 samples using expert human judgments. The results showed significant improvement over controlled baselines.

label: acl
text: The goal-oriented document-grounded dialogue aims at responding to the user query based on the dialogue context and supporting document. Existing studies tackle this problem by decomposing it into two sub-tasks: knowledge identification and response generation. However, such pipeline methods would unavoidably suffer from the error propagation issue. This paper proposes to unify these two sub-tasks via sequentially generating the grounding knowledge and the response. We further develop a prompt-connected multi-task learning strategy to model the characteristics and connections of different tasks and introduce linear temperature scheduling to reduce the negative effect of irrelevant document information. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

label: acl
text: The goal of the goal-oriented, document-grounded dialogue is to respond to the user's query based on the context of the dialogue and the supporting document. Previous studies have approached this problem by breaking it down into two sub-tasks: knowledge identification and response generation. However, this pipeline method can lead to error propagation. Our paper proposes a solution by unifying these two sub-tasks through sequential generation of the grounding knowledge and response. We also employ a prompt-connected multi-task learning strategy to model the relationships between different tasks, and use linear temperature scheduling to reduce the negative impact of irrelevant document information. Our framework has been proven effective through experimental results.

label: acl
text: Pretrained contextualized embeddings are powerful word representations for structured prediction tasks. Recent work found that better word representations can be obtained by concatenating different types of embeddings. However, the selection of embeddings to form the best concatenated representation usually varies depending on the task and the collection of candidate embeddings, and the ever-increasing number of embedding types makes it a more difficult problem. In this paper, we propose Automated Concatenation of Embeddings (ACE) to automate the process of finding better concatenations of embeddings for structured prediction tasks, based on a formulation inspired by recent progress on neural architecture search. Specifically, a controller alternately samples a concatenation of embeddings, according to its current belief of the effectiveness of individual embedding types in consideration for a task, and updates the belief based on a reward. We follow strategies in reinforcement learning to optimize the parameters of the controller and compute the reward based on the accuracy of a task model, which is fed with the sampled concatenation as input and trained on a task dataset. Empirical results on 6 tasks and 21 datasets show that our approach outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance with fine-tuned embeddings in all the evaluations.

label: acl
text: Pretrained contextualized embeddings are effective representations for structured prediction tasks. Recent studies have shown that better word representations can be obtained by combining different types of embeddings. However, the selection of embeddings to form the optimal combination can vary depending on the task and the available candidate embeddings, and the growing number of embedding types makes this a more challenging problem. To address this challenge, we introduce Automated Concatenation of Embeddings (ACE), a method that automates the process of finding the best combination of embeddings for structured prediction tasks. Our approach, inspired by recent advances in neural architecture search, uses a controller to alternate between sampling combinations of embeddings and updating its belief about the effectiveness of individual embedding types. The parameters of the controller are optimized using reinforcement learning strategies, and the accuracy of the task model, fed with the sampled combination as input, is used to compute the reward. Results from 6 tasks and 21 datasets show that our approach outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance with fine-tuned embeddings in all evaluations.

label: coling
text: Persuasion is rarely achieved through a loose set of arguments alone. Rather, an effective delivery of arguments follows a rhetorical strategy, combining logical reasoning with appeals to ethics and emotion. We argue that such a strategy means to select, arrange, and phrase a set of argumentative discourse units. In this paper, we model rhetorical strategies for the computational synthesis of effective argumentation. In a study, we let 26 experts synthesize argumentative texts with different strategies for 10 topics. We find that the experts agree in the selection significantly more when following the same strategy. While the texts notably vary for different strategies, especially their arrangement remains stable. The results suggest that our model enables a strategical synthesis.

label: coling
text: Persuasion is not often achieved through a disjointed collection of arguments. Rather, a successful delivery of arguments requires a well-structured rhetorical strategy that blends logical reasoning with appeals to ethics and emotion. Our argument is that such a strategy involves the careful selection, arrangement, and phrasing of argumentative discourse units. In this paper, we propose a computational model for synthesizing effective argumentation by incorporating rhetorical strategies. To test our model, we conducted a study in which 26 experts synthesized argumentative texts using different strategies for 10 different topics. The results showed that experts agreed more significantly on the selection of arguments when following the same strategy. Although the texts produced varied depending on the strategy used, their arrangement remained consistent. These findings suggest that our model effectively enables the strategic synthesis of arguments.

label: coling
text: Despite having achieved great success for sentiment analysis, existing neural models struggle with implicit sentiment analysis. It is because they may latch onto spurious correlations (“shortcuts”, e.g., focusing only on explicit sentiment words), resulting in undermining the effectiveness and robustness of the learned model. In this work, we propose a CausaL intervention model for implicit sEntiment ANalysis using instrumental variable (CLEAN). We first review sentiment analysis from a causal perspective and analyze the confounders existing in this task. Then, we introduce instrumental variable to eliminate the confounding causal effects, thus extracting the pure causal effect between sentence and sentiment. We compare the proposed CLEAN with several strong baselines on both the general implicit sentiment analysis and aspect-based implicit sentiment analysis tasks. The results indicate the great advantages of our model and the efficacy of implicit sentiment reasoning.

label: coling
text: Despite its success, existing neural models for sentiment analysis struggle with implicit sentiment analysis due to their tendency to latch onto spurious correlations, or "shortcuts," such as focusing only on explicit sentiment words. This undermines the effectiveness and robustness of the learned model. To address this issue, we propose the CausaL intervention model for implicit sEntiment ANalysis using instrumental variable (CLEAN). Our approach first reviews sentiment analysis from a causal perspective and identifies the confounders present in this task. We then use instrumental variables to eliminate these confounding effects, allowing us to extract the pure causal effect between sentence and sentiment. Our model is compared to several strong baselines on both general and aspect-based implicit sentiment analysis tasks, and the results demonstrate its advantages and the effectiveness of implicit sentiment reasoning.

label: acl
text: Evaluating Natural Language Generation (NLG) systems is a challenging task. Firstly, the metric should ensure that the generated hypothesis reflects the reference's semantics. Secondly, it should consider the grammatical quality of the generated sentence. Thirdly, it should be robust enough to handle various surface forms of the generated sentence. Thus, an effective evaluation metric has to be multifaceted. In this paper, we propose an automatic evaluation metric incorporating several core aspects of natural language understanding (language competence, syntactic and semantic variation). Our proposed metric, RoMe, is trained on language features such as semantic similarity combined with tree edit distance and grammatical acceptability, using a self-supervised neural network to assess the overall quality of the generated sentence. Moreover, we perform an extensive robustness analysis of the state-of-the-art methods and RoMe. Empirical results suggest that RoMe has a stronger correlation to human judgment over state-of-the-art metrics in evaluating system-generated sentences across several NLG tasks.

label: acl
text: Evaluating Natural Language Generation (NLG) systems is a difficult task. The evaluation metric must be multifaceted, taking into account the following aspects: the generated hypothesis must reflect the reference's semantics, the grammatical quality of the generated sentence must be considered, and the metric must be robust enough to handle various surface forms of the generated sentence. In this paper, we propose an automatic evaluation metric, RoMe, that incorporates several core aspects of natural language understanding, such as language competence, syntactic and semantic variation. RoMe is trained on language features such as semantic similarity and tree edit distance, combined with grammatical acceptability, using a self-supervised neural network. We also perform a thorough robustness analysis of the state-of-the-art methods and RoMe. Our empirical results show that RoMe has a stronger correlation with human judgment and outperforms state-of-the-art metrics in evaluating system-generated sentences across various NLG tasks.

label: acl
text: Cognitively plausible visual dialogue models should keep a mental scoreboard of shared established facts in the dialogue context. We propose a theory-based evaluation method for investigating to what degree models pretrained on the VisDial dataset incrementally build representations that appropriately do scorekeeping. Our conclusion is that the ability to make the distinction between shared and privately known statements along the dialogue is moderately present in the analysed models, but not always incrementally consistent, which may partially be due to the limited need for grounding interactions in the original task.

label: acl
text: Cognitively plausible visual dialogue models should maintain a mental record of established facts shared in the dialogue context. We propose a theory-based evaluation method to determine the extent to which models pre-trained on the VisDial dataset incrementally construct representations that accurately track these shared facts. Our findings indicate that the ability to differentiate between shared and privately known statements during the dialogue is moderately present in the analyzed models, although not always consistently. This may be due, in part, to the limited requirement for grounding interactions in the original task.

label: acl
text: Intelligent and adaptive online education systems aim to make high-quality education available for a diverse range of students. However, existing systems usually depend on a pool of hand-made questions, limiting how fine-grained and open-ended they can be in adapting to individual students. We explore targeted question generation as a controllable sequence generation task. We first show how to fine-tune pre-trained language models for deep knowledge tracing (LM-KT). This model accurately predicts the probability of a student answering a question correctly, and generalizes to questions not seen in training. We then use LM-KT to specify the objective and data for training a model to generate questions conditioned on the student and target difficulty. Our results show we succeed at generating novel, well-calibrated language translation questions for second language learners from a real online education platform.

label: acl
text: Intelligent and adaptive online education systems are designed to make high-quality education accessible to a diverse range of students. However, the existing systems often rely on a pool of pre-made questions, limiting their ability to adapt to individual students' needs. To address this issue, we investigate targeted question generation as a controllable sequence generation task. Our approach involves fine-tuning pre-trained language models for deep knowledge tracing (LM-KT). This model accurately predicts the probability of a student correctly answering a question and can generalize to questions not seen during training. We then use LM-KT to define the objective and data for training a model to generate questions that are customized to the student and their target difficulty level. Our results demonstrate that we are successful in generating new and well-calibrated language translation questions for second language learners from a real online education platform.

label: emnlp
text: Recent studies have shown that reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective approach for improving the performance of neural machine translation (NMT) system. However, due to its instability, successfully RL training is challenging, especially in real-world systems where deep models and large datasets are leveraged. In this paper, taking several large-scale translation tasks as testbeds, we conduct a systematic study on how to train better NMT models using reinforcement learning. We provide a comprehensive comparison of several important factors (e.g., baseline reward, reward shaping) in RL training. Furthermore, to fill in the gap that it remains unclear whether RL is still beneficial when monolingual data is used, we propose a new method to leverage RL to further boost the performance of NMT systems trained with source/target monolingual data. By integrating all our findings, we obtain competitive results on WMT14 English-German, WMT17 English-Chinese, and WMT17 Chinese-English translation tasks, especially setting a state-of-the-art performance on WMT17 Chinese-English translation task.

label: emnlp
text: Recent studies have indicated that reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective method for enhancing the performance of neural machine translation (NMT) systems. However, the instability of RL training makes it challenging, particularly when using deep models and large datasets in real-world applications. This paper presents a systematic study on how to train NMT models using reinforcement learning, using several large-scale translation tasks as testbeds. Our study compares several key factors in RL training, including baseline reward and reward shaping. Additionally, to address the lack of clarity on the benefits of RL when using monolingual data, we propose a new method to leverage RL to further improve NMT systems trained with source/target monolingual data. Our findings result in competitive performance on the WMT14 English-German, WMT17 English-Chinese, and WMT17 Chinese-English translation tasks, with a state-of-the-art performance on the WMT17 Chinese-English translation task.

label: naacl
text: k-nearest-neighbor machine translation (C-C-CNN-MT), proposed by Khandelwal et al. (2021), has achieved many state-of-the-art results in machine translation tasks. Although effective, D-D-DNN-MT requires conducting E-E-ENN searches through the large datastore for each decoding step during inference, prohibitively increasing the decoding cost and thus leading to the difficulty for the deployment in real-world applications. In this paper, we propose to move the time-consuming F-F-FNN search forward to the preprocessing phase, and then introduce G-G-G Nearest Neighbor Knowledge Distillation (B-B-BNN-KD) that trains the base NMT model to directly learn the knowledge of C-C-CNN. Distilling knowledge retrieved by D-D-DNN can encourage the NMT model to take more reasonable target tokens into consideration, thus addressing the overcorrection problem. Extensive experimental results show that, the proposed method achieves consistent improvement over the state-of-the-art baselines including E-E-ENN-MT, while maintaining the same training and decoding speed as the standard NMT model.

label: naacl
text: The k-nearest-neighbor machine translation (C-C-CNN-MT) proposed by Khandelwal et al. (2021) has achieved remarkable results in machine translation tasks. However, its use of the D-D-DNN-MT approach, which requires conducting an exhaustive search through a large data store for each decoding step during inference, results in prohibitively high decoding costs, making it challenging to deploy in real-world applications. In this paper, we introduce a new approach, G-G-G Nearest Neighbor Knowledge Distillation (B-B-BNN-KD), which moves the time-consuming F-F-FNN search to the preprocessing phase and trains the base NMT model to directly learn the knowledge of C-C-CNN. By distilling the knowledge retrieved by D-D-DNN, the NMT model is encouraged to consider more reasonable target tokens, thus addressing the overcorrection problem. Our experiments show that this new approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, including E-E-ENN-MT, while still retaining the same training and decoding speed as a standard NMT model.

label: acl
text: This paper explores the task of Difficulty-Controllable Question Generation (DCQG), which aims at generating questions with required difficulty levels. Previous research on this task mainly defines the difficulty of a question as whether it can be correctly answered by a Question Answering (QA) system, lacking interpretability and controllability. In our work, we redefine question difficulty as the number of inference steps required to answer it and argue that Question Generation (QG) systems should have stronger control over the logic of generated questions. To this end, we propose a novel framework that progressively increases question difficulty through step-by-step rewriting under the guidance of an extracted reasoning chain. A dataset is automatically constructed to facilitate the research, on which extensive experiments are conducted to test the performance of our method.

label: acl
text: This paper investigates the task of Difficulty-Controllable Question Generation (DCQG), which aims to generate questions with specific difficulty levels. Previous studies in this field primarily define the difficulty of a question based on its ability to be answered correctly by a Question Answering (QA) system, which lacks interpretability and control. In our work, we redefine question difficulty as the number of inference steps required to answer it and maintain that Question Generation (QG) systems should have greater control over the logic of generated questions. To achieve this, we introduce a novel framework that gradually increases question difficulty through a step-by-step rewriting process, guided by an extracted reasoning chain. A dataset is automatically generated to support our research, and extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach.

label: coling
text: In knowledge-grounded dialogue generation, pre-trained language models (PLMs) can be expected to deepen the fusing of dialogue context and knowledge because of their superior ability of semantic understanding. Unlike adopting the plain text knowledge, it is thorny to leverage the structural commonsense knowledge when using PLMs because most PLMs can only operate plain texts. Thus, linearizing commonsense knowledge facts into plan text is a compulsory trick. However, a dialogue is always aligned to a lot of retrieved fact candidates; as a result, the linearized text is always lengthy and then significantly increases the burden of using PLMs. To address this issue, we propose a novel two-stage framework SAKDP. In the first pre-screening stage, we use a ranking network PriorRanking to estimate the relevance of a retrieved knowledge fact. Thus, facts can be clustered into three sections of different priorities. As priority decreases, the relevance decreases, and the number of included facts increases. In the next dialogue generation stage, we use section-aware strategies to encode the linearized knowledge. The powerful but expensive PLM is only used for a few facts in the higher priority sections, reaching the performance-efficiency balance. Both the automatic and human evaluation demonstrate the superior performance of this work.

label: coling
text: In knowledge-grounded dialogue generation, the use of pre-trained language models (PLMs) can enhance the integration of dialogue context and knowledge due to their exceptional semantic understanding abilities. However, incorporating structured commonsense knowledge into PLMs can be challenging as most PLMs only operate on plain text. As a result, the linearization of commonsense knowledge into plain text is a necessary step. This linearization process, however, results in lengthy text, which increases the computational burden of using PLMs, especially when there are multiple retrieved fact candidates. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel two-stage framework, SAKDP. In the first stage, a ranking network (PriorRanking) is used to estimate the relevance of retrieved knowledge facts, allowing them to be divided into three sections based on priority. In the second stage, section-aware strategies are used to encode the linearized knowledge, balancing performance and efficiency by only utilizing the powerful, but computationally expensive, PLM for the most relevant facts in the highest priority section. Our approach outperforms existing methods, as demonstrated by both automatic and human evaluations.

label: coling
text: Existing studies on the analysis of persuasion in online discussions focus on investigating the effectiveness of comments in discussions and ignore the analysis of the effectiveness of debaters over multiple discussions. In this paper, we propose to quantify debaters effectiveness in the online discussion platform: “ChangeMyView” in order to explore diverse insights into their persuasion strategies. In particular, targeting debaters with different levels of effectiveness (e.g., good vs. bad), various behavioral characteristics (e..g, engagement) and text stylistic features (e.g., used frames) of debaters are carefully examined, leading to several outcomes that can be the backbone of writing assistants and persuasive text generation.

label: coling
text: Previous research on the analysis of persuasion in online discussions has primarily focused on evaluating the impact of comments within individual discussions, neglecting the examination of debaters' effectiveness across multiple discussions. In this study, we aim to quantify the effectiveness of debaters on the online discussion platform "ChangeMyView" and gain a deeper understanding of their persuasion strategies. By analyzing debaters with varying levels of effectiveness (e.g. good vs. bad), engagement, and text stylistic features (e.g. framing), we aim to uncover key outcomes that could inform the development of writing assistants and persuasive text generation tools.

label: acl
text: Many joint entity relation extraction models setup two separated label spaces for the two sub-tasks (i.e., entity detection and relation classification). We argue that this setting may hinder the information interaction between entities and relations. In this work, we propose to eliminate the different treatment on the two sub-tasks' label spaces. The input of our model is a table containing all word pairs from a sentence. Entities and relations are represented by squares and rectangles in the table. We apply a unified classifier to predict each cell's label, which unifies the learning of two sub-tasks. For testing, an effective (yet fast) approximate decoder is proposed for finding squares and rectangles from tables. Experiments on three benchmarks (ACE04, ACE05, SciERC) show that, using only half the number of parameters, our model achieves competitive accuracy with the best extractor, and is faster.

label: acl
text: Many joint entity relation extraction models establish two separate label spaces for the entity detection and relation classification sub-tasks. This setup may limit the interaction of information between entities and relations. Our proposed model eliminates this differentiation between the two sub-tasks' label spaces. The input to our model is a table containing all word pairs from a sentence, with entities and relations represented by squares and rectangles. Our unified classifier predicts the label of each cell, unifying the learning of the two sub-tasks. To test the model, we propose an effective and fast approximate decoder for finding squares and rectangles in the table. Our experiments on three benchmark datasets (ACE04, ACE05, and SciERC) show that our model, using half the number of parameters, achieves competitive accuracy with the best extractor and is faster.

label: coling
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) offers a unified semantic representation for natural language sentences. Thus transformation between AMR and text yields two transition tasks in opposite directions, i.e., Text-to-AMR parsing and AMR-to-Text generation. Existing AMR studies only focus on one-side improvements despite the duality of the two tasks, and their improvements are greatly attributed to the inclusion of large extra training data or complex structure modifications which harm the inference speed. Instead, we propose data-efficient Bidirectional Bayesian learning (BiBL) to facilitate bidirectional information transition by adopting a single-stage multitasking strategy so that the resulting model may enjoy much lighter training at the same time. Evaluation on benchmark datasets shows that our proposed BiBL outperforms strong previous seq2seq refinements without the help of extra data which is indispensable in existing counterpart models. We release the codes of BiBL at: https://github.com/KHAKhazeus/BiBL.

label: coling
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) provides a unified semantic representation for natural language sentences. This results in two transition tasks, Text-to-AMR parsing and AMR-to-Text generation, which are in opposite directions. Despite the duality of these tasks, existing AMR studies only focus on improving one side, often relying on large amounts of extra training data or complex structural modifications, which can negatively impact inference speed. To address this issue, we propose a data-efficient Bidirectional Bayesian learning (BiBL) approach that facilitates bidirectional information transition through a single-stage multitasking strategy. This allows for lighter training while still achieving improved performance. Evaluation on benchmark datasets shows that our BiBL outperforms previous seq2seq refinements without the need for additional data. The code for BiBL is available at https://github.com/KHAKhazeus/BiBL.

label: naacl
text: In recent years, transformer-based coreference resolution systems have achieved remarkable improvements on the CoNLL dataset. However, how coreference resolvers can benefit from discourse coherence is still an open question. In this paper, we propose to incorporate centering transitions derived from centering theory in the form of a graph into a neural coreference model. Our method improves the performance over the SOTA baselines, especially on pronoun resolution in long documents, formal well-structured text, and clusters with scattered mentions.

label: naacl
text: Recently, transformer-based coreference resolution systems have made remarkable advancements on the CoNLL dataset. However, the question of how coreference resolvers can benefit from discourse coherence remains unanswered. This paper presents a novel approach to incorporating centering transitions, derived from centering theory, into a neural coreference model in the form of a graph. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in pronoun resolution in long documents, formal, well-structured text, and clusters with scattered mentions.

label: coling
text: Lack of repeatability and generalisability are two significant threats to continuing scientific development in Natural Language Processing. Language models and learning methods are so complex that scientific conference papers no longer contain enough space for the technical depth required for replication or reproduction. Taking Target Dependent Sentiment Analysis as a case study, we show how recent work in the field has not consistently released code, or described settings for learning methods in enough detail, and lacks comparability and generalisability in train, test or validation data. To investigate generalisability and to enable state of the art comparative evaluations, we carry out the first reproduction studies of three groups of complementary methods and perform the first large-scale mass evaluation on six different English datasets. Reflecting on our experiences, we recommend that future replication or reproduction experiments should always consider a variety of datasets alongside documenting and releasing their methods and published code in order to minimise the barriers to both repeatability and generalisability. We have released our code with a model zoo on GitHub with Jupyter Notebooks to aid understanding and full documentation, and we recommend that others do the same with their papers at submission time through an anonymised GitHub account.

label: coling
text: The lack of repeatability and generalizability pose significant challenges to the ongoing development of Natural Language Processing. The complexity of language models and learning methods means that scientific conference papers no longer have enough space to provide the technical depth necessary for replication or reproduction. Using Target Dependent Sentiment Analysis as an example, we demonstrate that recent work in the field often lacks comparability and generalizability in training, testing, and validation data, and does not consistently release code or provide sufficient detail on learning method settings. To address these issues, we conduct the first reproduction studies of three complementary methods and perform a large-scale evaluation on six English datasets. Our results highlight the importance of considering multiple datasets and providing full documentation and code when conducting replication or reproduction experiments. To facilitate this, we have made our code and model zoo available on GitHub with Jupyter Notebooks and detailed documentation. We encourage others to follow this example and submit their code and documentation through an anonymized GitHub account at the time of paper submission.

label: coling
text: Dense video captioning aims to identify the events of interest in an input video, and generate descriptive captions for each event. Previous approaches usually follow a two-stage generative process, which first proposes a segment for each event, then renders a caption for each identified segment. Recent advances in large-scale sequence generation pretraining have seen great success in unifying task formulation for a great variety of tasks, but so far, more complex tasks such as dense video captioning are not able to fully utilize this powerful paradigm. In this work, we show how to model the two subtasks of dense video captioning jointly as one sequence generation task, and simultaneously predict the events and the corresponding descriptions. Experiments on YouCook2 and ViTT show encouraging results and indicate the feasibility of training complex tasks such as end-to-end dense video captioning integrated into large-scale pretrained models.

label: coling
text: Dense video captioning aims to identify significant events in an input video and generate descriptive captions for each event. The conventional approach involves a two-step generative process, which first segments the video to identify events and then generates captions for each segment. However, recent advances in large-scale sequence generation pretraining have been successful in unifying task formulation for various tasks, but complex tasks like dense video captioning have not yet been able to fully benefit from this powerful paradigm. In this study, we demonstrate how to model both subtasks of dense video captioning as a single sequence generation task, enabling the simultaneous prediction of events and their corresponding descriptions. The results of our experiments on YouCook2 and ViTT datasets are promising and indicate the viability of integrating end-to-end dense video captioning into large-scale pretrained models.

label: naacl
text: Analyzing language in context, both from a theoretical and from a computational perspective, is receiving increased interest. Complementing the research in linguistics on discourse and information structure, in computational linguistics identifying discourse concepts was also shown to improve the performance of certain applications, for example, Short Answer Assessment systems (Ziai and Meurers, 2014). Building on the research that established detailed annotation guidelines for manual annotation of information structural concepts for written (Dipper et al., 2007; Ziai and Meurers, 2014) and spoken language data (Calhoun et al., 2010), this paper presents the first approach automating the analysis of focus in authentic written data. Our classification approach combines a range of lexical, syntactic, and semantic features to achieve an accuracy of 78.1% for identifying focus.

label: naacl
text: The interest in analyzing language in context from both theoretical and computational perspectives has increased in recent years. Research in linguistics on discourse and information structure has been complemented by computational linguistics, which has demonstrated that identifying discourse concepts can improve the performance of applications such as Short Answer Assessment systems (Ziai and Meurers, 2014). This paper presents the first approach to automate the analysis of focus in authentic written data, building upon previous research that established detailed annotation guidelines for manual annotation of information structural concepts in both written (Dipper et al., 2007; Ziai and Meurers, 2014) and spoken language data (Calhoun et al., 2010). Our classification approach, which combines lexical, syntactic, and semantic features, achieves an accuracy rate of 78.1% in identifying focus.

label: naacl
text: Automatic text summarization systems commonly involve humans for preparing data or evaluating model performance, yet, there lacks a systematic understanding of humans' roles, experience, and needs when interacting with or being assisted by AI. From a human-centered perspective, we map the design opportunities and considerations for human-AI interaction in text summarization and broader text generation tasks. We first conducted a systematic literature review of 70 papers, developing a taxonomy of five interactions in AI-assisted text generation and relevant design dimensions. We designed text summarization prototypes for each interaction. We then interviewed 16 users, aided by the prototypes, to understand their expectations, experience, and needs regarding efficiency, control, and trust with AI in text summarization and propose design considerations accordingly.

label: naacl
text: Automatic text summarization systems often require human involvement in the preparation of data or evaluation of the model's performance. However, there is a lack of understanding about the roles, experiences, and needs of humans when interacting with or being assisted by AI. From a human-centered perspective, we aim to identify design opportunities and considerations for human-AI interaction in text summarization and other text generation tasks. To do this, we conducted a systematic literature review of 70 papers and developed a taxonomy of five different interactions in AI-assisted text generation, along with relevant design dimensions. We then created text summarization prototypes for each interaction and interviewed 16 users to understand their expectations, experiences, and needs with regards to efficiency, control, and trust with AI in text summarization. Based on these findings, we propose design considerations for improving the human-AI interaction in this field.

label: acl
text: A knowledge base is a large repository of facts that are mainly represented as RDF triples, each of which consists of a subject, a predicate (relationship), and an object. The RDF triple representation offers a simple interface for applications to access the facts. However, this representation is not in a natural language form, which is difficult for humans to understand. We address this problem by proposing a system to translate a set of RDF triples into natural sentences based on an encoder-decoder framework. To preserve as much information from RDF triples as possible, we propose a novel graph-based triple encoder. The proposed encoder encodes not only the elements of the triples but also the relationships both within a triple and between the triples. Experimental results show that the proposed encoder achieves a consistent improvement over the baseline models by up to 17.6%, 6.0%, and 16.4% in three common metrics BLEU, METEOR, and TER, respectively.

label: acl
text: A knowledge base is a vast collection of facts that are primarily stored as RDF triples. Each RDF triple is comprised of a subject, a predicate (relationship), and an object. Although the RDF triple representation offers a straightforward interface for applications to access the facts, it is not in a natural language form, making it challenging for humans to understand. To overcome this issue, we propose a system that translates a set of RDF triples into natural sentences using an encoder-decoder framework. Our proposed system includes a novel graph-based triple encoder that encodes not only the elements of the triples but also the relationships between the triples and within a triple. Our experiments show that the proposed encoder outperforms baseline models by up to 17.6%, 6.0%, and 16.4% in BLEU, METEOR, and TER metrics, respectively.

label: naacl
text: Generic unstructured neural networks have been shown to struggle on out-of-distribution compositional generalization. Compositional data augmentation via example recombination has transferred some prior knowledge about compositionality to such black-box neural models for several semantic parsing tasks, but this often required task-specific engineering or provided limited gains. We present a more powerful data recombination method using a model called Compositional Structure Learner (CSL). CSL is a generative model with a quasi-synchronous context-free grammar backbone, which we induce from the training data. We sample recombined examples from CSL and add them to the fine-tuning data of a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model (T5). This procedure effectively transfers most of CSL's compositional bias to T5 for diagnostic tasks, and results in a model even stronger than a T5-CSL ensemble on two real world compositional generalization tasks. This results in new state-of-the-art performance for these challenging semantic parsing tasks requiring generalization to both natural language variation and novel compositions of elements.

label: naacl
text: Generic unstructured neural networks have been found to be inadequate in handling out-of-distribution compositional generalization. Previously, compositional data augmentation via example recombination has been used to transfer some knowledge about compositionality to these black-box neural models for semantic parsing tasks, but this approach often requires task-specific engineering and provides limited gains. We introduce a more effective data recombination method using the Compositional Structure Learner (CSL), a generative model with a quasi-synchronous context-free grammar backbone, which is induced from the training data. By adding recombined examples generated by CSL to the fine-tuning data of a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model (T5), we effectively transfer CSL's compositional bias to T5 for diagnostic tasks, resulting in a model that outperforms a T5-CSL ensemble in two real-world compositional generalization tasks. This leads to new state-of-the-art performance in these challenging semantic parsing tasks that require generalization to both natural language variation and novel compositions of elements.

label: coling
text: Diversity can be decomposed into three distinct concepts, namely: variety, balance and disparity. This paper borrows from the extensive formalization and measures of diversity developed in ecology in order to evaluate the variety and balance of multiword expression annotation produced by automatic annotation systems. The measures of richness, normalized richness, and two variations of Hill's evenness are considered in this paper. We observe how these measures behave against increasingly smaller samples of gold annotations of multiword expressions and use their comportment to validate or invalidate their pertinence for multiword expressions in annotated texts. We apply the validated measures to annotations in 14 languages produced by systems during the PARSEME shared task on automatic identification of multiword expressions and on the gold versions of the corpora. We also explore the limits of such evaluation by studying the impact of lemmatization errors in the Turkish corpus used in the shared task.
