text: Understanding privacy policies is essential for users as it gives them the ability to learn about the information that is relevant to them. The sentences in a privacy policy document explain the privacy practices and the text spans within the document provide more specific information about those practices. We refer to the task of predicting the privacy practice explained in a sentence as "intent classification" and identifying the text spans that share specific information as "slot filling." In this work, we introduce PolicyIE, an English corpus consisting of 5,250 intent annotations and 11,788 slot annotations from 31 privacy policies of websites and mobile applications. PolicyIE is a challenging, real-world benchmark with limited labeled examples, reflecting the cost of obtaining large-scale annotations from domain experts. We present two neural approaches as baselines: (1) joint sequence tagging for intent classification and slot filling, and (2) modeling them as a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) learning task. The experimental results show that both approaches perform similarly in intent classification, while the Seq2Seq method outperforms the sequence tagging approach in slot filling by a significant margin. We conduct a thorough error analysis to highlight the challenges of the proposed corpus.

label: coling
text: The most approaches to Knowledge Base Question Answering are based on semantic parsing. In this paper, we address the problem of learning vector representations for complex semantic parses that consist of multiple entities and relations. Previous work largely focused on selecting the correct semantic relations for a question and disregarded the structure of the semantic parse: the connections between entities and the directions of the relations. We propose to use Gated Graph Neural Networks to encode the graph structure of the semantic parse. We show on two data sets that the graph networks outperform all baseline models that do not explicitly model the structure. The error analysis confirms that our approach can successfully process complex semantic parses.

label: coling
text: In this paper, we tackle the challenge of learning vector representations for complex semantic parses that involve multiple entities and relations. Most existing approaches to Knowledge Base Question Answering are based on semantic parsing, but previous work has primarily focused on selecting the correct semantic relations for a question and ignored the structure of the semantic parse. To address this issue, we propose the use of Gated Graph Neural Networks to encode the graph structure of the semantic parse. Our experiments on two datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms all baseline models that do not consider the graph structure. Our error analysis confirms that our Gated Graph Neural Network approach can effectively process complex semantic parses.

label: acl
text: Although neural models have achieved competitive results in dialogue systems, they have shown limited ability in representing core semantics, such as ignoring important entities. To this end, we exploit Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) to help dialogue modeling. Compared with the textual input, AMR explicitly provides core semantic knowledge and reduces data sparsity. We develop an algorithm to construct dialogue-level AMR graphs from sentence-level AMRs and explore two ways to incorporate AMRs into dialogue systems. Experimental results on both dialogue understanding and response generation tasks show the superiority of our model. To our knowledge, we are the first to leverage a formal semantic representation into neural dialogue modeling.

label: acl
text: Although neural models have produced competitive results in dialogue systems, they have demonstrated a limited ability to represent core semantics, often ignoring important entities. To address this limitation, we utilize Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) to enhance dialogue modeling. AMR explicitly provides core semantic knowledge, reducing data sparsity, and is more effective than textual input alone. Our algorithm constructs dialogue-level AMR graphs from sentence-level AMRs, and we explore two ways to incorporate AMRs into dialogue systems. Our experiments on both dialogue understanding and response generation tasks demonstrate the superiority of our model. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to incorporate a formal semantic representation into neural dialogue modeling.

label: acl
text: Fine-grained Entity Typing (FET) has made great progress based on distant supervision but still suffers from label noise. Existing FET noise learning methods rely on prediction distributions in an instance-independent manner, which causes the problem of confirmation bias. In this work, we propose a clustering-based loss correction framework named Feature Cluster Loss Correction (FCLC), to address these two problems. FCLC first train a coarse backbone model as a feature extractor and noise estimator. Loss correction is then applied to each feature cluster, learning directly from the noisy labels. Experimental results on three public datasets show that FCLC achieves the best performance over existing competitive systems. Auxiliary experiments further demonstrate that FCLC is stable to hyperparameters and it does help mitigate confirmation bias. We also find that in the extreme case of no clean data, the FCLC framework still achieves competitive performance.

label: acl
text: Fine-grained Entity Typing (FET) has advanced significantly, thanks to distant supervision, however, it still faces the challenge of label noise. Existing methods for addressing noise in FET rely on instance-independent prediction distributions, leading to the issue of confirmation bias. To tackle these problems, we propose a Feature Cluster Loss Correction (FCLC) framework that leverages clustering. FCLC trains a coarse backbone model as a feature extractor and noise estimator, and then applies loss correction to each feature cluster, learning directly from the noisy labels. Our experiments on three public datasets show that FCLC outperforms existing systems and is robust to hyperparameters. Additionally, even in the absence of clean data, FCLC still performs competitively.

label: acl
text: Entity linking (EL) is the task of disambiguating mentions appearing in text by linking them to entities in a knowledge graph, a crucial task for text understanding, question answering or conversational systems. In the special case of short-text EL, which poses additional challenges due to limited context, prior approaches have reached good performance by employing heuristics-based methods or purely neural approaches. Here, we take a different, neuro-symbolic approach that combines the advantages of using interpretable rules based on first-order logic with the performance of neural learning. Even though constrained to use rules, we show that we reach competitive or better performance with SoTA black-box neural approaches. Furthermore, our framework has the benefits of extensibility and transferability. We show that we can easily blend existing rule templates given by a human expert, with multiple types of features (priors, BERT encodings, box embeddings, etc), and even with scores resulting from previous EL methods, thus improving on such methods. As an example of improvement, on the LC-QuAD-1.0 dataset, we show more than 3% increase in F1 score relative to previous SoTA. Finally, we show that the inductive bias offered by using logic results in a set of learned rules that transfers from one dataset to another, sometimes without finetuning, while still having high accuracy.

text: The task of Entity Linking (EL) involves disambiguating mentions in text by linking them to entities in a knowledge graph, which is crucial for text understanding, question answering, and conversational systems. In the case of short-text EL, which presents additional challenges due to limited context, prior approaches have achieved good performance using heuristics-based methods or purely neural methods. However, in this work, we take a neuro-symbolic approach that combines the interpretable rules based on first-order logic with the performance of neural learning. Although our approach is limited to using rules, we demonstrate that it can achieve competitive or better performance compared to state-of-the-art black-box neural approaches. Our framework also offers benefits such as extensibility and transferability. We show that we can easily blend existing rule templates provided by a human expert with multiple types of features, including priors, BERT encodings, box embeddings, and scores from previous EL methods, resulting in improved performance. As an example, on the LC-QuAD-1.0 dataset, we demonstrate a more than 3% increase in F1 score compared to the previous state-of-the-art. Finally, we show that the inductive bias offered by using logic results in a set of learned rules that can transfer from one dataset to another without fine-tuning, while still maintaining high accuracy.

label: acl
text: Recent years have brought about an interest in the challenging task of summarizing conversation threads (meetings, online discussions, etc.). Such summaries help analysis of the long text to quickly catch up with the decisions made and thus improve our work or communication efficiency. To spur research in thread summarization, we have developed an abstractive Email Thread Summarization (EmailSum) dataset, which contains human-annotated short (30 words) and long (100 words) summaries of 2,549 email threads (each containing 3 to 10 emails) over a wide variety of topics. We perform a comprehensive empirical study to explore different summarization techniques (including extractive and abstractive methods, single-document and hierarchical models, as well as transfer and semisupervised learning) and conduct human evaluations on both short and long summary generation tasks. Our results reveal the key challenges of current abstractive summarization models in this task, such as understanding the sender's intent and identifying the roles of sender and receiver. Furthermore, we find that widely used automatic evaluation metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) are weakly correlated with human judgments on this email thread summarization task. Hence, we emphasize the importance of human evaluation and the development of better metrics by the community.

label: acl
text: In recent years, there has been growing interest in the challenging task of summarizing conversation threads, such as meetings and online discussions. These summaries help to quickly understand the decisions made within a long text, thereby improving work or communication efficiency. To further research in this area, we have created the Email Thread Summarization (EmailSum) dataset. This dataset contains human-annotated short (30 words) and long (100 words) summaries of 2,549 email threads, each containing 3 to 10 emails, on a wide range of topics. We conducted a comprehensive study to evaluate different summarization techniques, including extractive and abstractive methods, single-document and hierarchical models, transfer and semi-supervised learning. Our results highlight the challenges faced by current abstractive summarization models, such as understanding the sender's intent and identifying the roles of sender and receiver. Additionally, we found that commonly used automatic evaluation metrics, such as ROUGE and BERTScore, are weakly correlated with human judgments on this email thread summarization task. Therefore, we emphasize the importance of human evaluation and the development of better metrics by the research community.

label: naacl
text: We present deep communicating agents in an encoder-decoder architecture to address the challenges of representing a long document for abstractive summarization. With deep communicating agents, the task of encoding a long text is divided across multiple collaborating agents, each in charge of a subsection of the input text. These encoders are connected to a single decoder, trained end-to-end using reinforcement learning to generate a focused and coherent summary. Empirical results demonstrate that multiple communicating encoders lead to a higher quality summary compared to several strong baselines, including those based on a single encoder or multiple non-communicating encoders.

label: naacl
text: We propose utilizing deep communicating agents in an encoder-decoder architecture to tackle the difficulties of representing lengthy documents for abstractive summarization. By using these agents, the task of encoding a long text is divided among multiple collaborating agents, each responsible for a specific segment of the input text. These encoders are linked to a single decoder, trained end-to-end through reinforcement learning, to produce a concise and informative summary. Our empirical results show that implementing multiple communicating encoders leads to a higher-quality summary compared to several strong baselines, including single-encoder and non-communicating encoder-based methods.

label: acl
text: While the use of character models has been popular in NLP applications, it has not been explored much in the context of psycholinguistic modeling. This paper presents a character model that can be applied to a structural parser-based processing model to calculate word generation probabilities. Experimental results show that surprisal estimates from a structural processing model using this character model deliver substantially better fits to self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and fMRI data than those from large-scale language models trained on much more data. This may suggest that the proposed processing model provides a more humanlike account of sentence processing, which assumes a larger role of morphology, phonotactics, and orthographic complexity than was previously thought.

label: acl
text: The popularity of character models in NLP applications has been well-established, but their use in psycholinguistic modeling has not been thoroughly explored. This paper introduces a character model that can be integrated into a structural parser-based processing model to calculate word generation probabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that the structural processing model with this character model produces much better fits to self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and fMRI data than large-scale language models trained on extensive data. This implies that the proposed processing model offers a more human-like account of sentence processing, which places greater emphasis on morphology, phonotactics, and orthographic complexity than previously believed.

label: acl
text: Previous work on review summarization focused on measuring the sentiment toward the main aspects of the reviewed product or business, or on creating a textual summary. These approaches provide only a partial view of the data: aspect-based sentiment summaries lack sufficient explanation or justification for the aspect rating, while textual summaries do not quantify the significance of each element, and are not well-suited for representing conflicting views. Recently, Key Point Analysis (KPA) has been proposed as a summarization framework that provides both textual and quantitative summary of the main points in the data. We adapt KPA to review data by introducing Collective Key Point Mining for better key point extraction; integrating sentiment analysis into KPA; identifying good key point candidates for review summaries; and leveraging the massive amount of available reviews and their metadata. We show empirically that these novel extensions of KPA substantially improve its performance. We demonstrate that promising results can be achieved without any domain-specific annotation, while human supervision can lead to further improvement.

label: acl
text: Previous work in review summarization has mainly focused on measuring the sentiment towards the main aspects of the reviewed product or business and creating a textual summary. However, these methods only provide a limited view of the data. Aspect-based sentiment summaries do not explain or justify the aspect ratings, and textual summaries do not quantify the significance of each element and are not suitable for representing conflicting views. To address these limitations, Key Point Analysis (KPA) has been proposed as a summarization framework that provides both a textual and quantitative summary of the main points in the data. Our work extends KPA by introducing Collective Key Point Mining for improved key point extraction, integrating sentiment analysis, identifying good key point candidates for review summaries, and leveraging the vast amount of available reviews and their metadata. Our results show that these novel extensions of KPA significantly improve its performance, and that promising results can be achieved without domain-specific annotation, while human supervision can lead to further improvement.

label: acl
text: Neural models for question answering (QA) over documents have achieved significant performance improvements. Although effective, these models do not scale to large corpora due to their complex modeling of interactions between the document and the question. Moreover, recent work has shown that such models are sensitive to adversarial inputs. In this paper, we study the minimal context required to answer the question, and find that most questions in existing datasets can be answered with a small set of sentences. Inspired by this observation, we propose a simple sentence selector to select the minimal set of sentences to feed into the QA model. Our overall system achieves significant reductions in training (up to 15 times) and inference times (up to 13 times), with accuracy comparable to or better than the state-of-the-art on SQuAD, NewsQA, TriviaQA and SQuAD-Open. Furthermore, our experimental results and analyses show that our approach is more robust to adversarial inputs.

label: acl
text: Neural models for Question Answering (QA) have made remarkable progress in recent years. However, they are not suitable for large corpora due to their complex interactions between the document and the question. Additionally, these models are vulnerable to adversarial inputs. In this paper, we investigate the minimum context required to answer a question and find that most questions can be answered with a small set of sentences. Based on this discovery, we propose a simplified sentence selector to identify the essential sentences for the QA model. Our system demonstrates significant reductions in both training and inference times (up to 15 times and 13 times, respectively) while maintaining comparable or better accuracy on popular QA datasets such as SQuAD, NewsQA, TriviaQA, and SQuAD-Open. Furthermore, our results indicate that our approach is more resilient to adversarial inputs.

text: State-of-the-art entity linkers achieve high accuracy scores with probabilistic methods. However, these scores should be considered in relation to the properties of the datasets they are evaluated on. Until now, there has not been a systematic investigation of the properties of entity linking datasets and their impact on system performance. In this paper we report on a series of hypotheses regarding the long tail phenomena in entity linking datasets, their interaction, and their impact on system performance. Our systematic study of these hypotheses shows that evaluation datasets mainly capture head entities and only incidentally cover data from the tail, thus encouraging systems to overfit to popular/frequent and non-ambiguous cases. We find the most difficult cases of entity linking among the infrequent candidates of ambiguous forms. With our findings, we hope to inspire future designs of both entity linking systems and evaluation datasets. To support this goal, we provide a list of recommended actions for better inclusion of tail cases.

text: The latest entity linkers boast high accuracy scores achieved through probabilistic methods. However, these scores must be evaluated in context of the datasets used for evaluation. To date, there has been no comprehensive examination of the properties of entity linking datasets and their impact on system performance. In this paper, we explore a series of hypotheses related to the "long tail" phenomenon in entity linking datasets and its impact on system performance. Our systematic study supports the conclusion that evaluation datasets primarily capture head entities and only occasionally cover data from the tail, leading to systems that overfit to popular, frequent, and unambiguous cases. Our findings indicate that the most challenging cases of entity linking occur among the infrequent and ambiguous forms. Our hope is that this work will inspire future advancements in both entity linking systems and evaluation datasets. To further this goal, we have provided a list of recommended actions to better incorporate tail cases.

text: Pre-trained language models have been recently shown to benefit task-oriented dialogue (TOD) systems. Despite their success, existing methods often formulate this task as a cascaded generation problem which can lead to error accumulation across different sub-tasks and greater data annotation overhead. In this study, we present PPTOD, a unified plug-and-play model for task-oriented dialogue. In addition, we introduce a new dialogue multi-task pre-training strategy that allows the model to learn the primary TOD task completion skills from heterogeneous dialog corpora. We extensively test our model on three benchmark TOD tasks, including end-to-end dialogue modelling, dialogue state tracking, and intent classification. Experimental results show that PPTOD achieves new state of the art on all evaluated tasks in both high-resource and low-resource scenarios. Furthermore, comparisons against previous SOTA methods show that the responses generated by PPTOD are more factually correct and semantically coherent as judged by human annotators.

text: Recently, pre-trained language models have been found to enhance task-oriented dialogue (TOD) systems. However, current methods often approach this task as a cascaded generation problem, resulting in error accumulation and increased data annotation requirements. Our study presents PPTOD, a unified plug-and-play model for TOD, and introduces a novel dialogue multi-task pre-training strategy. This allows the model to learn primary TOD skills from diverse dialog corpora. We evaluate PPTOD on three benchmark TOD tasks: end-to-end dialogue modeling, dialogue state tracking, and intent classification. Our results show that PPTOD outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on all evaluated tasks, both in high- and low-resource scenarios. Furthermore, human annotators judged the responses generated by PPTOD to be more factually correct and semantically coherent compared to previous SOTA methods.

text: Split and rephrase is the task of breaking down a sentence into shorter ones that together convey the same meaning. We extract a rich new dataset for this task by mining Wikipedia's edit history: WikiSplit contains one million naturally occurring sentence rewrites, providing sixty times more distinct split examples and a ninety times larger vocabulary than the WebSplit corpus introduced by Narayan et al. (2017) as a benchmark for this task. Incorporating WikiSplit as training data produces a model with qualitatively better predictions that score 32 BLEU points above the prior best result on the WebSplit benchmark.

text: We study the problem of learning a named entity recognition (NER) tagger using noisy labels from multiple weak supervision sources. Though cheap to obtain, the labels from weak supervision sources are often incomplete, inaccurate, and contradictory, making it difficult to learn an accurate NER model. To address this challenge, we propose a conditional hidden Markov model (CHMM), which can effectively infer true labels from multi-source noisy labels in an unsupervised way. CHMM enhances the classic hidden Markov model with the contextual representation power of pre-trained language models. Specifically, CHMM learns token-wise transition and emission probabilities from the BERT embeddings of the input tokens to infer the latent true labels from noisy observations. We further refine CHMM with an alternate-training approach (CHMM-ALT). It fine-tunes a BERT-NER model with the labels inferred by CHMM, and this BERT-NER's output is regarded as an additional weak source to train the CHMM in return. Experiments on four NER benchmarks from various domains show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised NER models by wide margins.

text: We investigate the challenge of learning a Named Entity Recognition (NER) tagger using noisy labels from multiple weak supervision sources. These sources are cheap to obtain, but their labels are often incomplete, inaccurate, and contradictory, making it difficult to learn an accurate NER model. To overcome this challenge, we propose a Conditional Hidden Markov Model (CHMM) that can effectively infer the true labels from multi-source noisy labels in an unsupervised manner. CHMM leverages the contextual representation power of pre-trained language models, such as BERT, to learn token-wise transition and emission probabilities, which are then used to infer the latent true labels from the noisy observations. To further refine CHMM, we use an alternate-training approach (CHMM-ALT), which fine-tunes a BERT-NER model with the labels inferred by CHMM, and then uses the BERT-NER's output as an additional weak source to train CHMM. Our experiments on four NER benchmarks from various domains demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised NER models by a significant margin.

text: Most work in relation extraction forms a prediction by looking at a short span of text within a single sentence containing a single entity pair mention. This approach often does not consider interactions across mentions, requires redundant computation for each mention pair, and ignores relationships expressed across sentence boundaries. These problems are exacerbated by the document- (rather than sentence-) level annotation common in biological text. In response, we propose a model which simultaneously predicts relationships between all mention pairs in a document. We form pairwise predictions over entire paper abstracts using an efficient self-attention encoder. All-pairs mention scores allow us to perform multi-instance learning by aggregating over mentions to form entity pair representations. We further adapt to settings without mention-level annotation by jointly training to predict named entities and adding a corpus of weakly labeled data. In experiments on two Biocreative benchmark datasets, we achieve state of the art performance on the Biocreative V Chemical Disease Relation dataset for models without external KB resources. We also introduce a new dataset an order of magnitude larger than existing human-annotated biological information extraction datasets and more accurate than distantly supervised alternatives.

text: The existing work in relation extraction forms a prediction by examining a short span of text within a single sentence with a single entity pair mention. This approach has several limitations, such as ignoring interactions across mentions, repetitive computation for each mention pair, and neglecting relationships expressed across sentence boundaries. These issues are further complicated by the document-level annotation that is commonly used in biological text. To address these problems, we propose a model that predicts relationships between all mention pairs in a document simultaneously. Our model uses an efficient self-attention encoder to form pairwise predictions over entire paper abstracts. The all-pairs mention scores enable us to perform multi-instance learning by aggregating mention representations to form entity pair representations. Furthermore, we adapt to settings without mention-level annotation by jointly training to predict named entities and incorporating a corpus of weakly labeled data. In experiments on two benchmark datasets from Biocreative, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Biocreative V Chemical Disease Relation dataset for models without external KB resources. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset that is an order of magnitude larger than existing human-annotated biological information extraction datasets and more accurate than distantly supervised alternatives.

text: CommonsenseQA (CQA) (Talmor et al., 2019) dataset was recently released to advance the research on common-sense question answering (QA) task. Whereas the prior work has mostly focused on proposing QA models for this dataset, our aim is to retrieve as well as generate explanation for a given (question, correct answer choice, incorrect answer choices) tuple from this dataset. Our explanation definition is based on certain desiderata, and translates an explanation into a set of positive and negative common-sense properties (aka facts) which not only explain the correct answer choice but also refute the incorrect ones. We human-annotate a first-of-its-kind dataset (called ECQA) of positive and negative properties, as well as free-flow explanations, for C-C-C QA pairs taken from the CQA dataset. We propose a latent representation based property retrieval model as well as a GPT-2 based property generation model with a novel two step fine-tuning procedure. We also propose a free-flow explanation generation model. Extensive experiments show that our retrieval model beats BM25 baseline by a relative gain of 100% in D-D-D score, property generation model achieves a respectable E-E-E score of 36.4, and free-flow generation model achieves a similarity score of 61.9, where last two scores are based on a human correlated semantic similarity metric.

text: The recently released CommonsenseQA (CQA) dataset (Talmor et al., 2019) aims to advance research in common-sense question answering (QA). While previous work has primarily focused on developing QA models for this dataset, our goal is to retrieve and generate explanations for a given question, correct answer choice, and incorrect answer choices. Our explanation definition is based on specific requirements and translates into a set of positive and negative common-sense properties that not only explain the correct answer but also refute the incorrect ones. To achieve this, we have human-annotated a first-of-its-kind dataset, ECQA, of positive and negative properties, as well as free-flow explanations, for C-C-C QA pairs from the CQA dataset. We propose a latent representation-based property retrieval model, a GPT-2-based property generation model with a novel two-step fine-tuning procedure, and a free-flow explanation generation model. Our experiments show that the retrieval model outperforms the BM25 baseline by 100% in D-D-D score, the property generation model achieves an E-E-E score of 36.4, and the free-flow generation model achieves a similarity score of 61.9. These scores are based on a human-correlated semantic similarity metric.

text: Learning high-quality sentence representations benefits a wide range of natural language processing tasks. Though BERT-based pre-trained language models achieve high performance on many downstream tasks, the native derived sentence representations are proved to be collapsed and thus produce a poor performance on the semantic textual similarity (STS) tasks. In this paper, we present ConSERT, a Contrastive Framework for Self-Supervised SEntence Representation Transfer, that adopts contrastive learning to fine-tune BERT in an unsupervised and effective way. By making use of unlabeled texts, ConSERT solves the collapse issue of BERT-derived sentence representations and make them more applicable for downstream tasks. Experiments on STS datasets demonstrate that ConSERT achieves an 8% relative improvement over the previous state-of-the-art, even comparable to the supervised SBERT-NLI. And when further incorporating NLI supervision, we achieve new state-of-the-art performance on STS tasks. Moreover, ConSERT obtains comparable results with only 1000 samples available, showing its robustness in data scarcity scenarios.

text: The task of adopting a model with good performance to a target domain that is different from the source domain used for training has received considerable attention in sentiment analysis. Most existing approaches mainly focus on learning representations that are domain-invariant in both the source and target domains. Few of them pay attention to domain-specific information, which should also be informative. In this work, we propose a method to simultaneously extract domain specific and invariant representations and train a classifier on each of the representation, respectively. And we introduce a few target domain labeled data for learning domain-specific information. To effectively utilize the target domain labeled data, we train the domain invariant representation based classifier with both the source and target domain labeled data and train the domain-specific representation based classifier with only the target domain labeled data. These two classifiers then boost each other in a co-training style. Extensive sentiment analysis experiments demonstrated that the proposed method could achieve better performance than state-of-the-art methods.

text: The study of adapting a model with strong performance to a target domain that differs from the source domain used for training has received considerable attention in sentiment analysis. Most existing techniques concentrate on learning representations that are domain-invariant across both the source and target domains. However, few of them take into account domain-specific information, which can also be valuable. In this research, we propose a method that simultaneously extracts domain-specific and invariant representations and trains a classifier on each representation, respectively. We also incorporate a small amount of target domain labeled data to learn domain-specific information. To effectively use this data, we train the domain-invariant representation-based classifier using both source and target domain labeled data, and train the domain-specific representation-based classifier using only target domain labeled data. These two classifiers then boost each other in a co-training manner. Our extensive sentiment analysis experiments show that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques.

text: Recent years have witnessed the emergence of a variety of post-hoc interpretations that aim to uncover how natural language processing (NLP) models make predictions. Despite the surge of new interpretation methods, it remains an open problem how to define and quantitatively measure the faithfulness of interpretations, i.e., to what extent interpretations reflect the reasoning process by a model. We propose two new criteria, sensitivity and stability, that provide complementary notions of faithfulness to the existed removal-based criteria. Our results show that the conclusion for how faithful interpretations are could vary substantially based on different notions. Motivated by the desiderata of sensitivity and stability, we introduce a new class of interpretation methods that adopt techniques from adversarial robustness. Empirical results show that our proposed methods are effective under the new criteria and overcome limitations of gradient-based methods on removal-based criteria. Besides text classification, we also apply interpretation methods and metrics to dependency parsing. Our results shed light on understanding the diverse set of interpretations.

text: In recent years, various post-hoc interpretations have emerged to shed light on how natural language processing (NLP) models make predictions. Despite the growing number of methods, it remains uncertain how to accurately define and measure the faithfulness of these interpretations, i.e., how well they reflect the reasoning process of a model. To address this issue, we propose two new criteria, sensitivity and stability, which provide a more comprehensive understanding of faithfulness compared to existing removal-based criteria. Our findings indicate that the level of faithfulness can vary greatly depending on the criteria used. To enhance sensitivity and stability, we introduce a new class of interpretation methods that utilize techniques from adversarial robustness. Our empirical results demonstrate that these methods are effective and overcome the limitations of gradient-based methods on removal-based criteria. Additionally, we apply our interpretation methods and metrics to dependency parsing, providing further insight into the diverse set of interpretations.

text: Many NLP applications can be framed as a graph-to-sequence learning problem. Previous work proposing neural architectures on graph-to-sequence obtained promising results compared to grammar-based approaches but still rely on linearisation heuristics and/or standard recurrent networks to achieve the best performance. In this work propose a new model that encodes the full structural information contained in the graph. Our architecture couples the recently proposed Gated Graph Neural Networks with an input transformation that allows nodes and edges to have their own hidden representations, while tackling the parameter explosion problem present in previous work. Experimental results shows that our model outperforms strong baselines in generation from AMR graphs and syntax-based neural machine translation.

text: Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) has attracted increasing attention in the affective computing research field. Previous works have mainly focused on modeling the semantic interactions in the dialogue and implicitly inferring the evolution of the speakers' emotional states. Few works have considered the emotional interactions, which directly reflect the emotional evolution of speakers in the dialogue. According to psychological and behavioral studies, the emotional inertia and emotional stimulus are important factors that affect the speaker's emotional state in conversations. In this work, we propose a novel Dialogue Emotion Interaction Network, DialogueEIN, to explicitly model the intra-speaker, inter-speaker, global and local emotional interactions to respectively simulate the emotional inertia, emotional stimulus, global and local emotional evolution in dialogues. Extensive experiments on four ERC benchmark datasets, IEMOCAP, MELD, EmoryNLP and DailyDialog, show that our proposed DialogueEIN considering emotional interaction factors can achieve superior or competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our codes and models are released.

text: Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) is attracting growing interest in the field of affective computing research. Previous studies have primarily focused on modeling semantic interactions in dialogues and inferring the emotional states of speakers implicitly. However, few studies have taken into account emotional interactions, which directly reflect the emotional evolution of speakers in a dialogue. Psychological and behavioral studies indicate that emotional inertia and emotional stimulus play a crucial role in determining a speaker's emotional state during a conversation. To address this, we propose a novel Dialogue Emotion Interaction Network (DialogueEIN) that explicitly models intra-speaker, inter-speaker, global and local emotional interactions to simulate emotional inertia, emotional stimulus, global and local emotional evolution in dialogues. Our experiments on four benchmark datasets in ERC (IEMOCAP, MELD, EmoryNLP, and DailyDialog) show that our DialogueEIN, which considers emotional interaction factors, outperforms or is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and models are available for public use.

text: Parody is a figurative device used for mimicking entities for comedic or critical purposes. Parody is intentionally humorous and often involves sarcasm. This paper explores jointly modelling these figurative tropes with the goal of improving performance of political parody detection in tweets. To this end, we present a multi-encoder model that combines three parallel encoders to enrich parody-specific representations with humor and sarcasm information. Experiments on a publicly available data set of political parody tweets demonstrate that our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods.

text: Parody is a literary tool used to mock entities for comedic or critical purposes. It is intentionally humorous and often involves sarcasm. This study examines the joint modeling of these figurative elements with the aim of enhancing the accuracy of political parody detection in tweets. Our proposed multi-encoder model employs three parallel encoders to enhance the representation of parody-specific information with humor and sarcasm information. Our experiments on a publicly accessible dataset of political parody tweets show that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

text: We propose a simple modification to existing neural machine translation (NMT) models that enables using a single universal model to translate between multiple languages while allowing for language specific parameterization, and that can also be used for domain adaptation. Our approach requires no changes to the model architecture of a standard NMT system, but instead introduces a new component, the contextual parameter generator (CPG), that generates the parameters of the system (e.g., weights in a neural network). This parameter generator accepts source and target language embeddings as input, and generates the parameters for the encoder and the decoder, respectively. The rest of the model remains unchanged and is shared across all languages. We show how this simple modification enables the system to use monolingual data for training and also perform zero-shot translation. We further show it is able to surpass state-of-the-art performance for both the IWSLT-15 and IWSLT-17 datasets and that the learned language embeddings are able to uncover interesting relationships between languages.

text: We propose a modification to existing Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models that allows for the use of a single universal model to translate between multiple languages. This is achieved through language-specific parameterization and can also be used for domain adaptation. Our approach involves the introduction of a new component, the Contextual Parameter Generator (CPG), which generates the parameters for the NMT system. The CPG accepts source and target language embeddings as inputs and generates the parameters for the encoder and decoder, respectively. The rest of the NMT model remains unchanged and is shared across all languages. Our modification enables the system to use monolingual data for training and perform zero-shot translation. Our results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art performance on the IWSLT-15 and IWSLT-17 datasets, and the learned language embeddings reveal interesting relationships between languages.

text: Training with noisy labelled data is known to be detrimental to model performance, especially for high-capacity neural network models in low-resource domains. Our experiments suggest that standard regularisation strategies, such as weight decay and dropout, are ineffective in the face of noisy labels. We propose a simple noisy label detection method that prevents error propagation from the input layer. The approach is based on the observation that the projection of noisy labels is learned through memorisation at advanced stages of learning, and that the Pearson correlation is sensitive to outliers. Extensive experiments over real-world human-disagreement annotations as well as randomly-corrupted and data-augmented labels, across various tasks and domains, demonstrate that our method is effective, regularising noisy labels and improving generalisation performance.

text: Training with noisy labeled data can have a negative impact on the performance of high-capacity neural network models, especially in low-resource domains. Our experiments indicate that common regularization techniques, such as weight decay and dropout, are ineffective when dealing with noisy labels. To address this issue, we propose a simple method for detecting noisy labels that prevents error propagation from the input layer. This approach is based on the idea that noisy labels are learned through memorization at later stages of learning, and that the Pearson correlation is sensitive to outliers. Our extensive experiments, conducted on real-world human-disagreement annotations, as well as randomly-corrupted and data-augmented labels in various tasks and domains, demonstrate that our method is effective in regularizing noisy labels and improving generalization performance.

text: Creating effective visualization is an important part of data analytics. While there are many libraries for creating visualization, writing such code remains difficult given the myriad of parameters that users need to provide. In this paper, we propose the new task of synthesizing visualization programs from a combination of natural language utterances and code context. To tackle the learning problem, we introduce PlotCoder, a new hierarchical encoder-decoder architecture that models both the code context and the input utterance. We use PlotCoder to first determine the template of the visualization code, followed by predicting the data to be plotted. We use Jupyter notebooks containing visualization programs crawled from GitHub to train PlotCoder. On a comprehensive set of test samples from those notebooks, we show that PlotCoder correctly predicts the plot type of about 70% samples, and synthesizes the correct programs for 35% samples, performing 3-4.5% better than the baselines.

text: Creating an effective visualization is a crucial aspect of data analytics. In this paper, we present a new task of synthesizing visualization programs by combining natural language utterances with code context. To address this challenge, we introduce PlotCoder, a novel hierarchical encoder-decoder architecture that models both the code context and the input utterance. PlotCoder is used to first identify the template of the visualization code, followed by predicting the data to be plotted. label: acl
text: Despite inextricable ties between race and language, little work has considered race in NLP research and development. In this work, we survey 79 papers from the ACL anthology that mention race. These papers reveal various types of race-related bias in all stages of NLP model development, highlighting the need for proactive consideration of how NLP systems can uphold racial hierarchies. However, persistent gaps in research on race and NLP remain: race has been siloed as a niche topic and remains ignored in many NLP tasks; most work operationalizes race as a fixed single-dimensional variable with a ground-truth label, which risks reinforcing differences produced by historical racism; and the voices of historically marginalized people are nearly absent in NLP literature. By identifying where and how NLP literature has and has not considered race, especially in comparison to related fields, our work calls for inclusion and racial justice in NLP research practices.

text: Despite the close relationship between race and language, there has been little examination of race in the field of NLP research and development. This study reviews 79 papers from the ACL anthology that mention race. The results of this review reveal various forms of race-related biases present in all stages of NLP model development, emphasizing the need for proactive consideration of how NLP systems can perpetuate racial hierarchies. However, there are still significant gaps in research on race and NLP. Race is often treated as a niche topic and is frequently overlooked in many NLP tasks. Additionally, race is often viewed as a fixed, single-dimensional variable with a pre-determined label, which can reinforce historical racial differences. Furthermore, the perspectives of historically marginalized groups are largely absent in NLP literature. By identifying the areas where NLP literature has and has not addressed race, and comparing it to related fields, this study calls for greater inclusivity and racial justice in NLP research practices.

text: Evaluating on adversarial examples has become a standard procedure to measure robustness of deep learning models. Due to the difficulty of creating white-box adversarial examples for discrete text input, most analyses of the robustness of NLP models have been done through black-box adversarial examples. We investigate adversarial examples for character-level neural machine translation (NMT), and contrast black-box adversaries with a novel white-box adversary, which employs differentiable string-edit operations to rank adversarial changes. We propose two novel types of attacks which aim to remove or change a word in a translation, rather than simply break the NMT. We demonstrate that white-box adversarial examples are significantly stronger than their black-box counterparts in different attack scenarios, which show more serious vulnerabilities than previously known. In addition, after performing adversarial training, which takes only 3 times longer than regular training, we can improve the model's robustness significantly.

text: Evaluating the robustness of deep learning models through adversarial examples has become an established practice. However, creating white-box adversarial examples for discrete text input in NLP (natural language processing) models has proven to be difficult, leading most analyses to be done using black-box adversarial examples. Our research focuses on character-level neural machine translation (NMT) and compares black-box adversarial examples with a novel white-box adversary that uses differentiable string-edit operations to rank adversarial changes. We introduce two new types of attacks that target the removal or alteration of words in a translation, rather than simply breaking the NMT. Our results show that white-box adversarial examples are significantly stronger than black-box examples in various attack scenarios, revealing previously unknown vulnerabilities. Furthermore, by performing adversarial training, which takes only three times longer than regular training, the model's robustness can be significantly improved.

text: In this paper, we propose a neural model EPT-X (Expression-Pointer Transformer with Explanations), which utilizes natural language explanations to solve an algebraic word problem. To enhance the explainability of the encoding process of a neural model, EPT-X adopts the concepts of plausibility and faithfulness which are drawn from math word problem solving strategies by humans. A plausible explanation is one that includes contextual information for the numbers and variables that appear in a given math word problem. A faithful explanation is one that accurately represents the reasoning process behind the model's solution equation. The EPT-X model yields an average baseline performance of 69.59% on our PEN dataset and produces explanations with quality that is comparable to human output. The contribution of this work is two-fold. (1) EPT-X model: An explainable neural model that sets a baseline for algebraic word problem solving task, in terms of model's correctness, plausibility, and faithfulness. (2) New dataset: We release a novel dataset PEN (Problems with Explanations for Numbers), which expands the existing datasets by attaching explanations to each number/variable.

text: We propose a novel neural model, EPT-X (Expression-Pointer Transformer with Explanations), to solve algebraic word problems using natural language explanations. To improve the interpretability of the encoding process, EPT-X incorporates the concepts of plausibility and faithfulness, which are derived from human strategies for solving math word problems. A plausible explanation includes relevant contextual information for the numbers and variables in a problem, while a faithful explanation accurately reflects the reasoning behind the model's solution. Our EPT-X model achieves an average baseline performance of 69.59% on our newly created PEN (Problems with Explanations for Numbers) dataset, producing explanations that are comparable to human output. This work makes two significant contributions: (1) the EPT-X model, which sets a baseline for algebraic word problem solving in terms of its accuracy, plausibility, and faithfulness, and (2) the PEN dataset, which expands existing datasets by including explanations for each number and variable.

text: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) has received increasing attention recently. ABSA can be divided into multiple tasks according to the different extracted elements. Existing generative methods usually treat the output as a whole string rather than the combination of different elements and only focus on a single task at once. This paper proposes a unified generative multi-task framework that can solve multiple ABSA tasks by controlling the type of task prompts consisting of multiple element prompts. Further, the proposed approach can train on simple tasks and transfer to difficult tasks by assembling task prompts, like assembling Lego bricks. We conduct experiments on six ABSA tasks across multiple benchmarks. Our proposed multi-task approach achieves new state-of-the-art results in almost all tasks and competitive results in task transfer scenarios.

text: Recently, aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) has gained considerable attention. ABSA can be divided into various tasks based on the elements that are extracted. This paper presents a unified generative multi-task framework that can solve multiple ABSA tasks by controlling the type of task prompts, which are comprised of multiple element prompts. Moreover, the proposed approach can be trained on simple tasks and then transferred to more complex tasks by assembling task prompts, similar to assembling Lego bricks. We conducted experiments on six ABSA tasks using multiple benchmarks, and our multi-task approach achieved new state-of-the-art results in almost all tasks, and competitive results in task transfer scenarios.

text: This paper presents a task for machine listening comprehension in the argumentation domain and a corresponding dataset in English. We recorded 200 spontaneous speeches arguing for or against 50 controversial topics. For each speech, we formulated a question, aimed at confirming or rejecting the occurrence of potential arguments in the speech. Labels were collected by listening to the speech and marking which arguments were mentioned by the speaker. We applied baseline methods addressing the task, to be used as a benchmark for future work over this dataset. All data used in this work is freely available for research.

text: This paper presents a machine listening comprehension task in the argumentation domain, along with a corresponding English dataset. The dataset consists of 200 spontaneous speeches, where the speakers argue for or against 50 controversial topics. For each speech, a question was formulated to determine the presence of potential arguments in the speech. The arguments were identified by listening to the speech and annotating which arguments were mentioned by the speaker. Baseline methods have been applied to the task, serving as a benchmark for future research on this dataset. The data used in this study is freely accessible for research purposes.

label: acl
text: To help individuals express themselves better, quotation recommendation is receiving growing attention. Nevertheless, most prior efforts focus on modeling quotations and queries separately and ignore the relationship between the quotations and the queries. In this work, we introduce a transformation matrix that directly maps the query representations to quotation representations. To better learn the mapping relationship, we employ a mapping loss that minimizes the distance of two semantic spaces (one for quotation and another for mapped-query). Furthermore, we explore using the words in history queries to interpret the figurative language of quotations, where quotation-aware attention is applied on top of history queries to highlight the indicator words. Experiments on two datasets in English and Chinese show that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art models.

label: acl
text: To improve individuals' ability to express themselves, the focus on quotation recommendation is increasing. However, prior efforts have mainly focused on modeling quotations and queries separately, neglecting the relationship between the two. To address this, we introduce a transformation matrix that directly maps query representations to quotation representations. We utilize a mapping loss to effectively learn the mapping relationship between the two semantic spaces (one for quotations and another for mapped-queries). Additionally, we investigate the use of historical query words to interpret figurative language in quotations, applying quotation-aware attention to highlight relevant indicator words. Our model demonstrates superior performance compared to previous state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated in experiments on English and Chinese datasets.

label: coling
text: Knowledge graph embedding, which aims to learn representations of entities and relations in knowledge graphs, finds applications in various downstream tasks. The key to success of knowledge graph embedding models are the ability to model relation patterns including symmetry/antisymmetry, inversion, commutative composition and non-commutative composition. Although existing methods fail in modeling the non-commutative composition patterns, several approaches support this pattern by modeling beyond Euclidean space and complex space. Nevertheless, expanding to complicated spaces such as quaternion can easily lead to a substantial increase in the amount of parameters, which greatly reduces the computational efficiency. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge graph embedding method called RotateCT, which first transforms the coordinates of each entity, and then represents each relation as a rotation from head entity to tail entity in complex space. By design, RotateCT can infer the non-commutative composition patterns and improve the computational efficiency. Experiments on multiple datasets empirically show that RotateCT outperforms most state-of-the-art methods on link prediction and path query answering.

text: The purpose of knowledge graph embedding is to learn representations of entities and relations in knowledge graphs, and it has various applications in downstream tasks. The key to success of these models is their ability to model relation patterns, including symmetry/antisymmetry, inversion, commutative composition, and non-commutative composition. However, current methods struggle with modeling non-commutative composition patterns. Some approaches have attempted to overcome this by modeling beyond Euclidean space and into complex space, but this can lead to a significant increase in the number of parameters, reducing computational efficiency. To address this issue, we propose a new knowledge graph embedding method called RotateCT. This method transforms the coordinates of each entity and represents each relation as a rotation from the head entity to the tail entity in complex space. The result is a model that can infer non-commutative composition patterns while improving computational efficiency. Our experiments on multiple datasets show that RotateCT outperforms most state-of-the-art methods in link prediction and path query answering.

label: coling
text: This paper presents a novel multi-perspective document revision task. In conventional studies on document revision, tasks such as grammatical error correction, sentence reordering, and discourse relation classification have been performed individually; however, these tasks simultaneously should be revised to improve the readability and clarity of a whole document. Thus, our study defines multi-perspective document revision as a task that simultaneously revises multiple perspectives. To model the task, we design a novel Japanese multi-perspective document revision dataset that simultaneously handles seven perspectives to improve the readability and clarity of a document. Although a large amount of data that simultaneously handles multiple perspectives is needed to model multi-perspective document revision elaborately, it is difficult to prepare such a large amount of this data. Therefore, our study offers a multi-perspective document revision modeling method that can use a limited amount of matched data (i.e., data for the multi-perspective document revision task) and external partially-matched data (e.g., data for the grammatical error correction task). Experiments using our created dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of using multiple partially-matched datasets to model the multi-perspective document revision task.

label: coling
text: This paper introduces a new multi-perspective document revision task. Previously, document revision studies have focused on individual tasks such as grammatical error correction, sentence reordering, and discourse relation classification. However, to improve the readability and clarity of a document, these tasks must be revised simultaneously. Our study defines multi-perspective document revision as the simultaneous revision of multiple perspectives. To model this task, we have created a Japanese multi-perspective document revision dataset that addresses seven perspectives to improve readability and clarity. However, creating a large amount of data that covers multiple perspectives is challenging. Therefore, our study proposes a method for modeling multi-perspective document revision using a limited amount of matched data and external partially-matched data. Results from our experiments using this dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of using multiple partially-matched datasets in modeling multi-perspective document revision.
