We also propose a new benchmark split based on the Epic-kitchen dataset, which is significantly larger in terms of the number of classes and samples. Results show that DARK outperforms the baselines by a large margin, proving the effectiveness of our approach.

label: naacl
text: Article prediction is a task that has long defied accurate linguistic description. As such, this task is ideally suited to evaluate models on their ability to emulate native-speaker intuition. To this end, we compare the performance of native English speakers and pre-trained models on the task of article prediction set up as a three way choice (a/an, the, zero). Our experiments with BERT show that BERT outperforms humans on this task across all articles. In particular, BERT is far superior to humans at detecting the zero article, possibly because we insert them using rules that the deep neural model can easily pick up. More interestingly, we find that BERT tends to agree more with annotators than with the corpus when inter-annotator agreement is high but switches to agreeing more with the corpus as inter-annotator agreement drops. We contend that this alignment with annotators, despite being trained on the corpus, suggests that BERT is not memorising article use, but captures a high level generalisation of article use akin to human intuition.

label: naacl
text: Article prediction is a challenging task that has eluded accurate linguistic description. As a result, it is an ideal task to assess the ability of models to emulate native speaker intuition. To this end, we compared the performance of native English speakers and pre-trained models in a three-way article prediction task (a/an, the, zero). Our experiments using BERT showed that the model outperformed humans in all article categories, particularly in detecting the zero article, which may be due to its ability to easily pick up rules for inserting them. Interestingly, we found that BERT tended to agree more with annotators than with the corpus when inter-annotator agreement was high, but switched to agreeing more with the corpus as inter-annotator agreement decreased. This alignment with annotators, despite being trained on the corpus, suggests that BERT is not simply memorizing article use, but is capturing a high-level generalization of article use similar to human intuition.

label: emnlp
text: Cross-lingual Entity Linking (XEL) aims to ground entity mentions written in any language to an English Knowledge Base (KB), such as Wikipedia. XEL for most languages is challenging, owing to limited availability of resources as supervision. We address this challenge by developing the first XEL approach that combines supervision from multiple languages jointly. This enables our approach to: (a) augment the limited supervision in the target language with additional supervision from a high-resource language (like English), and (b) train a single entity linking model for multiple languages, improving upon individually trained models for each language. Extensive evaluation on three benchmark datasets across 8 languages shows that our approach significantly improves over the current state-of-the-art. We also provide analyses in two limited resource settings: (a) zero-shot setting, when no supervision in the target language is available, and in (b) low-resource setting, when some supervision in the target language is available. Our analysis provides insights into the limitations of zero-shot XEL approaches in realistic scenarios, and shows the value of joint supervision in low-resource settings.

label: emnlp
text: Cross-lingual Entity Linking (XEL) aims to associate entity mentions in any language with an English Knowledge Base (KB) such as Wikipedia. The task is challenging due to limited resources for supervision, particularly in most languages. To overcome this challenge, we present the first XEL approach that combines supervision from multiple languages. This approach enables us to: (a) enhance the limited supervision in the target language with additional supervision from a high-resource language such as English, and (b) train a single entity linking model for multiple languages, outperforming models trained individually for each language. Our extensive evaluation on three benchmark datasets across 8 languages demonstrates significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art. We also analyze the performance in two resource-constrained settings: (a) zero-shot, when no supervision in the target language is available, and (b) low-resource, when some supervision in the target language is available. Our analysis sheds light on the limitations of zero-shot XEL in realistic scenarios and highlights the benefits of joint supervision in low-resource settings.

label: acl
text: While hyper-parameters (HPs) are important for knowledge graph (KG) learning, existing methods fail to search them efficiently. To solve this problem, we first analyze the properties of different HPs and measure the transfer ability from small subgraph to the full graph. Based on the analysis, we propose an efficient two-stage search algorithm KGTuner, which efficiently explores HP configurations on small subgraph at the first stage and transfers the top-performed configurations for fine-tuning on the large full graph at the second stage. Experiments show that our method can consistently find better HPs than the baseline algorithms within the same time budget, which achieves 9.1% average relative improvement for four embedding models on the large-scale KGs in open graph benchmark. Our code is released in https://github. com/AutoML-Research/KGTuner.

label: acl
text: The efficiency of hyper-parameter (HP) searching is crucial for knowledge graph (KG) learning, but current methods are inadequate. To address this issue, we analyze the properties of different HPs and evaluate their ability to transfer from small subgraphs to the full graph. Based on these findings, we present an efficient two-stage algorithm, KGTuner, that explores HP configurations on small subgraphs in the first stage and transfers the best-performing configurations for fine-tuning on the full graph in the second stage. Our experiments demonstrate that KGTuner consistently outperforms baseline algorithms, achieving a 9.1% average relative improvement for four embedding models on large-scale KGs in the open graph benchmark. The code for KGTuner is available at https://github.com/AutoML-Research/KGTuner.

label: naacl
text: As the use of interactive machines grow, the task of Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) became more important. If the machine-generated sentences reflect emotion, more human-like sympathetic conversations are possible. Since emotion recognition in conversation is inaccurate if the previous utterances are not taken into account, many studies reflect the dialogue context to improve the performances. Many recent approaches show performance improvement by combining knowledge into modules learned from external structured data. However, structured data is difficult to access in non-English languages, making it difficult to extend to other languages. Therefore, we extract the pre-trained memory using the pre-trained language model as an extractor of external knowledge. We introduce CoMPM, which combines the speaker's pre-trained memory with the context model, and find that the pre-trained memory significantly improves the performance of the context model. CoMPM achieves the first or second performance on all data and is state-of-the-art among systems that do not leverage structured data. In addition, our method shows that it can be extended to other languages because structured knowledge is not required, unlike previous methods. Our code is available on github .

label: naacl
text: As the use of interactive machines increases, the importance of Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) becomes more apparent. If these machines can reflect emotions in their generated sentences, more human-like and empathetic conversations can be achieved. However, accurate ERC is only possible if the machine takes into account the previous utterances in the conversation. To improve performance, many studies have incorporated the dialogue context into their ERC models. Despite these advances, many recent approaches still struggle to extend their methods to non-English languages due to the difficulty of accessing structured data. To overcome this challenge, we present CoMPM, which combines a speaker's pre-trained memory with a context model. Our results show that the pre-trained memory significantly improves the performance of the context model, making CoMPM state-of-the-art among systems that do not leverage structured data. Additionally, our approach does not require structured knowledge, making it easily extendable to other languages. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

label: acl
text: Despite the well-developed cut-edge representation learning for language, most language representation models usually focus on specific levels of linguistic units. This work introduces universal language representation learning, i.e., embeddings of different levels of linguistic units or text with quite diverse lengths in a uniform vector space. We propose the training objective MiSAD that utilizes meaningful n-grams extracted from large unlabeled corpus by a simple but effective algorithm for pre-trained language models. Then we empirically verify that well designed pre-training scheme may effectively yield universal language representation, which will bring great convenience when handling multiple layers of linguistic objects in a unified way. Especially, our model achieves the highest accuracy on analogy tasks in different language levels and significantly improves the performance on downstream tasks in the GLUE benchmark and a question answering dataset.

label: acl
text: Despite the advanced cut-edge representation learning for language, most language representation models tend to focus on specific levels of linguistic units. This work introduces the concept of universal language representation learning, which embeds different levels of linguistic units or texts of diverse lengths in a uniform vector space. We propose the MiSAD training objective, which utilizes meaningful n-grams extracted from a large unlabeled corpus using a simple but effective algorithm for pre-trained language models. Our results show that a well-designed pre-training scheme can effectively yield universal language representation, making it easier to handle multiple layers of linguistic objects in a unified manner. Our model achieved the highest accuracy on analogy tasks across different language levels and significantly improved performance on downstream tasks in the GLUE benchmark and a question answering dataset.

label: acl
text: Most state-of-the-art open-domain question answering systems use a neural retrieval model to encode passages into continuous vectors and extract them from a knowledge source. However, such retrieval models often require large memory to run because of the massive size of their passage index. In this paper, we introduce Binary Passage Retriever (BPR), a memory-efficient neural retrieval model that integrates a learning-to-hash technique into the state-of-the-art Dense Passage Retriever (DPR) to represent the passage index using compact binary codes rather than continuous vectors. BPR is trained with a multi-task objective over two tasks: efficient candidate generation based on binary codes and accurate reranking based on continuous vectors. Compared with DPR, BPR substantially reduces the memory cost from 65GB to 2GB without a loss of accuracy on two standard open-domain question answering benchmarks: Natural Questions and TriviaQA. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/studio-ousia/bpr.

label: acl
text: The state-of-the-art open-domain question answering systems use neural retrieval models to encode passages into continuous vectors, which are then extracted from a knowledge source. However, these retrieval models are memory-intensive due to the large size of their passage index. To address this issue, we present Binary Passage Retriever (BPR), a memory-efficient neural retrieval model that integrates a learning-to-hash technique into the Dense Passage Retriever (DPR). BPR represents the passage index using compact binary codes instead of continuous vectors, and is trained with a multi-task objective over two tasks - efficient candidate generation based on binary codes and accurate re-ranking based on continuous vectors. Our results show that BPR reduces the memory cost significantly from 65GB to 2GB without sacrificing accuracy on two open-domain question answering benchmarks - Natural Questions and TriviaQA. The code and trained models are available at https://github.com/studio-ousia/bpr.

label: naacl
text: In this paper, we propose a novel end-to-end neural architecture for ranking candidate answers, that adapts a hierarchical recurrent neural network and a latent topic clustering module. With our proposed model, a text is encoded to a vector representation from an word-level to a chunk-level to effectively capture the entire meaning. In particular, by adapting the hierarchical structure, our model shows very small performance degradations in longer text comprehension while other state-of-the-art recurrent neural network models suffer from it. Additionally, the latent topic clustering module extracts semantic information from target samples. This clustering module is useful for any text related tasks by allowing each data sample to find its nearest topic cluster, thus helping the neural network model analyze the entire data. We evaluate our models on the Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus and consumer electronic domain question answering dataset, which is related to Samsung products. The proposed model shows state-of-the-art results for ranking question-answer pairs.

label: naacl
text: This paper presents a novel end-to-end neural architecture for ranking candidate answers. The architecture consists of a hierarchical recurrent neural network and a latent topic clustering module. The text is encoded into a vector representation at the word-level and chunk-level to capture its entire meaning effectively. The hierarchical structure of the model results in minimal performance degradation in longer text comprehension, which is a common issue in other state-of-the-art recurrent neural network models. The latent topic clustering module extracts semantic information from target samples and allows each data sample to find its nearest topic cluster, thereby improving the analysis of the entire data. The proposed model was evaluated on the Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus and a consumer electronic domain question-answering dataset related to Samsung products and showed state-of-the-art results for ranking question-answer pairs.

label: naacl
text: Recently, a boom of papers has shown extraordinary progress in zero-shot and few-shot learning with various prompt-based models. It is commonly argued that prompts help models to learn faster in the same way that humans learn faster when provided with task instructions expressed in natural language. In this study, we experiment with over 30 prompts manually written for natural language inference (NLI). We find that models can learn just as fast with many prompts that are intentionally irrelevant or even pathologically misleading as they do with instructively “good” prompts. Further, such patterns hold even for models as large as 175 billion parameters (Brown et al., 2020) as well as the recently proposed instruction-tuned models which are trained on hundreds of prompts (Sanh et al., 2021). That is, instruction-tuned models often produce good predictions with irrelevant and misleading prompts even at zero shots. In sum, notwithstanding prompt-based models' impressive improvement, we find evidence of serious limitations that question the degree to which such improvement is derived from models understanding task instructions in ways analogous to humans' use of task instructions.

label: naacl
text: Recently, there has been a surge in papers documenting significant progress in zero-shot and few-shot learning using various prompt-based models. These models are said to learn faster because they are provided with task instructions expressed in natural language, in the same way that humans learn faster with task instructions. In this study, we conducted experiments using over 30 prompts written manually for natural language inference (NLI). Our results showed that models can learn just as quickly with irrelevant or even misleading prompts as they do with "good" prompts. This was true even for models with 175 billion parameters and instruction-tuned models trained on hundreds of prompts. Despite the impressive improvement seen in prompt-based models, our findings suggest that there are limitations to their understanding of task instructions, casting doubt on the extent to which their improvement is derived from human-like understanding.

label: acl
text: The huge cost of creating labeled training data is a common problem for supervised learning tasks such as sentiment classification. Recent studies showed that pretraining with unlabeled data via a language model can improve the performance of classification models. In this paper, we take the concept a step further by using a conditional language model, instead of a language model. Specifically, we address a sentiment classification task for a tweet analysis service as a case study and propose a pretraining strategy with unlabeled dialog data (tweet-reply pairs) via an encoder-decoder model. Experimental results show that our strategy can improve the performance of sentiment classifiers and outperform several state-of-the-art strategies including language model pretraining.

label: acl
text: The cost of creating labeled training data is a major challenge for supervised learning tasks, such as sentiment classification. Recent studies have demonstrated that pretraining with unlabeled data using a language model can enhance the performance of classification models. In this paper, we take this idea a step further by proposing a pretraining strategy with unlabeled dialog data (tweet-reply pairs) using a conditional language model (encoder-decoder model). We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study of sentiment classification for a tweet analysis service. Our results show that our strategy outperforms several state-of-the-art methods, including language model pretraining, and leads to improved performance in sentiment classification.

label: naacl
text: As NLP models achieved state-of-the-art performances over benchmarks and gained wide applications, it has been increasingly important to ensure the safe deployment of these models in the real world, e.g., making sure the models are robust against unseen or challenging scenarios. Despite robustness being an increasingly studied topic, it has been separately explored in applications like vision and NLP, with various definitions, evaluation and mitigation strategies in multiple lines of research. In this paper, we aim to provide a unifying survey of how to define, measure and improve robustness in NLP. We first connect multiple definitions of robustness, then unify various lines of work on identifying robustness failures and evaluating models' robustness. Correspondingly, we present mitigation strategies that are data-driven, model-driven, and inductive-prior-based, with a more systematic view of how to effectively improve robustness in NLP models. Finally, we conclude by outlining open challenges and future directions to motivate further research in this area.

label: naacl
text: As NLP models have achieved state-of-the-art performance and gained widespread applications, it is becoming increasingly important to ensure their safe deployment in the real world. This requires ensuring that the models are robust against unseen or challenging scenarios. Despite the growing interest in robustness, the topic has been explored separately in applications such as vision and NLP, with different definitions, evaluation methods, and mitigation strategies. In this paper, we aim to provide a comprehensive survey of robustness in NLP. We begin by connecting multiple definitions of robustness, then unifying various lines of work on identifying robustness failures and evaluating model robustness. We present data-driven, model-driven, and inductive-prior-based mitigation strategies to effectively improve robustness in NLP models. Finally, we conclude by outlining open challenges and future directions for further research in this area.

text: MixUp is a data augmentation strategy where additional samples are generated during training by combining random pairs of training samples and their labels. However, selecting random pairs is not potentially an optimal choice. In this work, we propose TDMixUp, a novel MixUp strategy that leverages Training Dynamics and allows more informative samples to be combined for generating new data samples. Our proposed TDMixUp first measures confidence, variability, (Swayamdipta et al., 2020), and Area Under the Margin (AUM) (Pleiss et al., 2020) to identify the characteristics of training samples (e.g., as easy-to-learn or ambiguous samples), and then interpolates these characterized samples. We empirically validate that our method not only achieves competitive performance using a smaller subset of the training data compared with strong baselines, but also yields lower expected calibration error on the pre-trained language model, BERT, on both in-domain and out-of-domain settings in a wide range of NLP tasks. We publicly release our code.

label: naacl
text: MixUp is a data augmentation strategy that generates additional samples during training by combining random pairs of training samples and their labels. However, a random selection of pairs may not be the optimal choice. In this work, we present TDMixUp, a novel MixUp strategy that leverages training dynamics to combine more informative samples. TDMixUp measures the confidence, variability, and Area Under the Margin of training samples to identify their characteristics (e.g. easy-to-learn or ambiguous), and then interpolates these characterized samples. Our results show that TDMixUp not only outperforms strong baselines with a smaller subset of training data, but also has a lower expected calibration error on the pre-trained language model, BERT, in a wide range of NLP tasks, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Our code is publicly available.

label: emnlp
text: Background research is an essential part of document writing. Search engines are great for retrieving information once we know what to look for. However, the bigger challenge is often identifying topics for further research. Automated tools could help significantly in this discovery process and increase the productivity of the writer. In this paper, we formulate the problem of recommending topics to a writer. We consider this as a supervised learning problem and run a user study to validate this approach. We propose an evaluation metric and perform an empirical comparison of state-of-the-art models for extreme multi-label classification on a large data set. We demonstrate how a simple modification of the cross-entropy loss function leads to improved results of the deep learning models.

label: emnlp
text: Background research is an integral aspect of document writing and plays a crucial role in ensuring the quality and reliability of the final product. Search engines are an indispensable tool for retrieving information, but the real challenge lies in identifying relevant topics for further investigation. Automated tools have the potential to significantly streamline this discovery process and enhance the efficiency of the writer. In this study, we address the problem of topic recommendation for writers and approach it as a supervised learning problem. To validate this approach, we conduct a user study and propose a new evaluation metric. We then perform an empirical comparison of state-of-the-art models for extreme multi-label classification on a large dataset and demonstrate the effectiveness of a simple modification of the cross-entropy loss function in improving the results of deep learning models.

label: acl
text: For evaluating generation systems, automatic metrics such as BLEU cost nothing to run but have been shown to correlate poorly with human judgment, leading to systematic bias against certain model improvements. On the other hand, averaging human judgments, the unbiased gold standard, is often too expensive. In this paper, we use control variates to combine automatic metrics with human evaluation to obtain an unbiased estimator with lower cost than human evaluation alone. In practice, however, we obtain only a 7-13% cost reduction on evaluating summarization and open-response question answering systems. We then prove that our estimator is optimal: there is no unbiased estimator with lower cost. Our theory further highlights the two fundamental bottlenecks—the automatic metric and the prompt shown to human evaluators—both of which need to be improved to obtain greater cost savings.

label: acl
text: To evaluate generation systems, automatic metrics, such as BLEU, are cost-effective as they require no expenses to run. On the other hand, using human judgment as the unbiased gold standard is expensive. This paper proposes using control variates to combine automatic metrics with human evaluation to obtain an unbiased estimator with a lower cost than human evaluation alone. In practice, this results in a cost reduction of 7-13% when evaluating summarization and open-response question answering systems. Our findings prove that this estimator is optimal, meaning there is no other unbiased estimator with a lower cost. Our theory also highlights the two critical bottlenecks in the evaluation process - the automatic metric and the prompt shown to human evaluators - that need to be improved to achieve greater cost savings.

label: naacl
text: Counterfactually Augmented Data (CAD) aims to improve out-of-domain generalizability, an indicator of model robustness. The improvement is credited to promoting core features of the construct over spurious artifacts that happen to correlate with it. Yet, over-relying on core features may lead to unintended model bias. Especially, construct-driven CAD—perturbations of core features—may induce models to ignore the context in which core features are used. Here, we test models for sexism and hate speech detection on challenging data: non-hate and non-sexist usage of identity and gendered terms. On these hard cases, models trained on CAD, especially construct-driven CAD, show higher false positive rates than models trained on the original, unperturbed data. Using a diverse set of CAD—construct-driven and construct-agnostic—reduces such unintended bias.

label: naacl
text: Counterfactually Augmented Data (CAD) aims to improve the generalizability of models when they are used outside of their training domain. This is accomplished by promoting the core features of the constructs being modeled, rather than relying on spurious artifacts that may happen to be correlated with the construct. However, over-reliance on core features can lead to unintended bias in the model. In particular, construct-driven CAD, which involves perturbing core features, may cause the model to ignore the context in which these core features are used. To test this, we evaluated models for detecting sexism and hate speech on challenging data, consisting of non-hate and non-sexist usage of identity and gendered terms. Our results showed that models trained on CAD, particularly construct-driven CAD, had higher false positive rates compared to models trained on unperturbed data. However, using a diverse set of CAD, both construct-driven and construct-agnostic, reduced this unintended bias.

label: emnlp
text: The 20 Questions (Q20) game is a well known game which encourages deductive reasoning and creativity. In the game, the answerer first thinks of an object such as a famous person or a kind of animal. Then the questioner tries to guess the object by asking 20 questions. In a Q20 game system, the user is considered as the answerer while the system itself acts as the questioner which requires a good strategy of question selection to figure out the correct object and win the game. However, the optimal policy of question selection is hard to be derived due to the complexity and volatility of the game environment. In this paper, we propose a novel policy-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) method, which enables the questioner agent to learn the optimal policy of question selection through continuous interactions with users. To facilitate training, we also propose to use a reward network to estimate the more informative reward. Compared to previous methods, our RL method is robust to noisy answers and does not rely on the Knowledge Base of objects. Experimental results show that our RL method clearly outperforms an entropy-based engineering system and has competitive performance in a noisy-free simulation environment.

label: emnlp
text: The 20 Questions (Q20) game is a well-known game that promotes deductive reasoning and creativity. In this game, the answerer initially thinks of an object, such as a famous person or animal, and the questioner tries to guess the object by asking 20 questions. In a Q20 game system, the user is considered the answerer, while the system acts as the questioner, requiring an effective strategy to select questions to correctly identify the object and win the game. However, determining the optimal policy for question selection is challenging due to the complexity and volatility of the game environment. To address this, we propose a novel policy-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) method that enables the questioner agent to learn the optimal question selection policy through continuous interaction with users. We also introduce a reward network to estimate the most informative reward for training purposes. Our RL method is robust to noisy answers and does not rely on a knowledge base of objects, making it superior to prior methods. Our experiments demonstrate that our RL method outperforms an entropy-based engineering system, and it has competitive performance in a noise-free simulation environment.

label: emnlp
text: Capabilities to categorize a clause based on the type of situation entity (e.g., events, states and generic statements) the clause introduces to the discourse can benefit many NLP applications. Observing that the situation entity type of a clause depends on discourse functions the clause plays in a paragraph and the interpretation of discourse functions depends heavily on paragraph-wide contexts, we propose to build context-aware clause representations for predicting situation entity types of clauses. Specifically, we propose a hierarchical recurrent neural network model to read a whole paragraph at a time and jointly learn representations for all the clauses in the paragraph by extensively modeling context influences and inter-dependencies of clauses. Experimental results show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance for clause-level situation entity classification on the genre-rich MASC+Wiki corpus, which approaches human-level performance.

label: emnlp
text: The ability to categorize clauses based on the type of situation entity they introduce (such as events, states, and generic statements) can greatly benefit numerous NLP applications. We propose a context-aware clause representation model to predict the situation entity type of clauses, considering that the type of situation entity depends on the discourse functions played by the clause within a paragraph and that these functions are heavily influenced by paragraph-wide context. Our proposed hierarchical recurrent neural network model reads the entire paragraph and jointly learns representations for all clauses, taking into account context influences and inter-dependencies between clauses. Our experiments show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art for clause-level situation entity classification on the genre-rich MASC+Wiki corpus, approaching human-level performance.

label: naacl
text: The application of supervised methods to automatic summarization requires the availability of adequate corpora consisting of a set of document-summary pairs. As in most Natural Language Processing tasks, the great majority of available datasets for summarization are in English, making it difficult to develop automatic summarization models for other languages. Although Spanish is gradually forming part of some recent summarization corpora, it is not the same for minority languages such as Catalan.In this work, we describe the construction of a corpus of Catalan and Spanish newspapers, the Dataset for Automatic summarization of Catalan and Spanish newspaper Articles (DACSA) corpus. It is a high-quality large-scale corpus that can be used to train summarization models for Catalan and Spanish.We have carried out an analysis of the corpus, both in terms of the style of the summaries and the difficulty of the summarization task. In particular, we have used a set of well-known metrics in the summarization field in order to characterize the corpus. Additionally, for benchmarking purposes, we have evaluated the performances of some extractive and abstractive summarization systems on the DACSA corpus.

label: naacl
text: The use of supervised methods for automatic summarization requires access to adequate corpora that consist of document-summary pairs. Unfortunately, most available datasets for summarization are in English, making it challenging to develop models for other languages. Although Spanish is increasingly being included in some recent summarization corpora, this is not the case for minority languages such as Catalan. In this study, we present the construction of the Dataset for Automatic Summarization of Catalan and Spanish Newspaper Articles (DACSA) corpus, a high-quality, large-scale corpus that can be used to train summarization models for Catalan and Spanish. We analyzed the corpus in terms of the style of the summaries and the difficulty of the summarization task, using well-known metrics in the summarization field. Furthermore, we evaluated the performance of extractive and abstractive summarization systems on the DACSA corpus for benchmarking purposes.

label: emnlp
text: Learning a matching function between two text sequences is a long standing problem in NLP research. This task enables many potential applications such as question answering and paraphrase identification. This paper proposes Co-Stack Residual Affinity Networks (CSRAN), a new and universal neural architecture for this problem. CSRAN is a deep architecture, involving stacked (multi-layered) recurrent encoders. Stacked/Deep architectures are traditionally difficult to train, due to the inherent weaknesses such as difficulty with feature propagation and vanishing gradients. CSRAN incorporates two novel components to take advantage of the stacked architecture. Firstly, it introduces a new bidirectional alignment mechanism that learns affinity weights by fusing sequence pairs across stacked hierarchies. Secondly, it leverages a multi-level attention refinement component between stacked recurrent layers. The key intuition is that, by leveraging information across all network hierarchies, we can not only improve gradient flow but also improve overall performance. We conduct extensive experiments on six well-studied text sequence matching datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on all.

text: The problem of learning a matching function between two text sequences is a long-standing issue in NLP research. This task has numerous potential applications, including question answering and paraphrase identification. To address this challenge, this paper introduces Co-Stack Residual Affinity Networks (CSRAN), a novel and universal neural architecture. CSRAN is a deep architecture that employs stacked recurrent encoders, which are traditionally difficult to train due to issues such as feature propagation difficulties and vanishing gradients. To overcome these limitations, CSRAN incorporates two innovative components. Secondly, it leverages a multi-level attention refinement component between stacked recurrent layers. The goal is to improve gradient flow and overall performance by leveraging information across all network hierarchies. The effectiveness of CSRAN is demonstrated through extensive experiments on six well-studied text sequence matching datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on all.

label: acl
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsing aims to translate sentences to semantic representation with a hierarchical structure, and is recently empowered by pretrained sequence-to-sequence models. However, there exists a gap between their flat training objective (i.e., equally treats all output tokens) and the hierarchical AMR structure, which limits the model generalization. To bridge this gap, we propose a Hierarchical Curriculum Learning (HCL) framework with Structure-level (SC) and Instance-level Curricula (IC). SC switches progressively from core to detail AMR semantic elements while IC transits from structure-simple to -complex AMR instances during training. Through these two warming-up processes, HCL reduces the difficulty of learning complex structures, thus the flat model can better adapt to the AMR hierarchy. Extensive experiments on AMR2.0, AMR3.0, structure-complex and out-of-distribution situations verify the effectiveness of HCL.

label: acl
text: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsing aims to translate sentences into a semantic representation with a hierarchical structure. This task has been improved by the use of pretrained sequence-to-sequence models. However, there is a gap between the flat training objective of these models (which treats all output tokens equally) and the hierarchical AMR structure, hindering the model's ability to generalize. To address this issue, we propose a Hierarchical Curriculum Learning (HCL) framework that includes both Structure-level and Instance-level Curricula. The Structure-level Curriculum gradually shifts from core to detailed AMR semantic elements, while the Instance-level Curriculum moves from simple to complex AMR instances during training. By reducing the complexity of learning complex structures through these two warming-up processes, the HCL framework helps the flat model better adapt to the AMR hierarchy. Our experiments on AMR2.0, AMR3.0, structure-complex, and out-of-distribution situations demonstrate the effectiveness of the HCL framework.

label: emnlp
text: Adversarial training (AT) is a regularization method that can be used to improve the robustness of neural network methods by adding small perturbations in the training data. We show how to use AT for the tasks of entity recognition and relation extraction. In particular, we demonstrate that applying AT to a general purpose baseline model for jointly extracting entities and relations, allows improving the state-of-the-art effectiveness on several datasets in different contexts (i.e., news, biomedical, and real estate data) and for different languages (English and Dutch).

label: emnlp
text: Adversarial training (AT) is a regularization technique that enhances the robustness of neural network models by incorporating slight variations in the training data. This paper demonstrates the application of AT in entity recognition and relation extraction tasks. By applying AT to a general-purpose baseline model for joint entity and relation extraction, we improve the state-of-the-art performance on various datasets across different contexts, such as news, biomedical, and real estate data, and in both English and Dutch languages.

label: naacl
text: Word vector specialisation (also known as retrofitting) is a portable, light-weight approach to fine-tuning arbitrary distributional word vector spaces by injecting external knowledge from rich lexical resources such as WordNet. By design, these post-processing methods only update the vectors of words occurring in external lexicons, leaving the representations of all unseen words intact. In this paper, we show that constraint-driven vector space specialisation can be extended to unseen words. We propose a novel post-specialisation method that: a) preserves the useful linguistic knowledge for seen words; while b) propagating this external signal to unseen words in order to improve their vector representations as well. Our post-specialisation approach explicits a non-linear specialisation function in the form of a deep neural network by learning to predict specialised vectors from their original distributional counterparts. The learned function is then used to specialise vectors of unseen words. This approach, applicable to any post-processing model, yields considerable gains over the initial specialisation models both in intrinsic word similarity tasks, and in two downstream tasks: dialogue state tracking and lexical text simplification. The positive effects persist across three languages, demonstrating the importance of specialising the full vocabulary of distributional word vector spaces.

label: naacl
text: Word vector specialisation, also known as retrofitting, is a lightweight and portable approach for fine-tuning arbitrary distributional word vector spaces. This method injects external knowledge from rich lexical resources like WordNet into the vector spaces. However, traditional post-processing methods only update the vectors of words that occur in external lexicons, leaving the representations of unseen words unchanged. In this paper, we demonstrate that constraint-driven vector space specialisation can be extended to unseen words. Our novel post-specialisation method preserves the linguistic knowledge of seen words while also improving the vector representations of unseen words. This is achieved by using a deep neural network to predict specialised vectors from original distributional counterparts. The learned function is then applied to specialise the vectors of unseen words. Our approach, which can be applied to any post-processing model, outperforms initial specialisation models in intrinsic word similarity tasks and in two downstream tasks: dialogue state tracking and lexical text simplification. The positive results persist across three languages, highlighting the importance of specialising the full vocabulary of distributional word vector spaces.

label: acl
text: Beam search is a go-to strategy for decoding neural sequence models. The algorithm can naturally be viewed as a subset optimization problem, albeit one where the corresponding set function does not reflect interactions between candidates. Empirically, this leads to sets often exhibiting high overlap, e.g., strings may differ by only a single word. Yet in use-cases that call for multiple solutions, a diverse or representative set is often desired. To address this issue, we propose a reformulation of beam search, which we call determinantal beam search. Determinantal beam search has a natural relationship to determinantal point processes (DPPs), models over sets that inherently encode intra-set interactions. By posing iterations in beam search as a series of subdeterminant maximization problems, we can turn the algorithm into a diverse subset selection process. In a case study, we use the string subsequence kernel to explicitly encourage n-gram coverage in text generated from a sequence model. We observe that our algorithm offers competitive performance against other diverse set generation strategies in the context of language generation, while providing a more general approach to optimizing for diversity.

label: acl
text: Beam search is a widely used strategy for decoding neural sequence models. However, the algorithm can lead to high overlap in the sets of candidates, as it views the problem as a subset optimization problem where the set function does not reflect interactions between candidates. In use-cases that require multiple solutions, a diverse or representative set is often desired. To address this issue, we introduce determinantal beam search, which is based on determinantal point processes (DPPs). This reformulation allows us to turn beam search into a diverse subset selection process by posing each iteration as a subdeterminant maximization problem. In a case study, we use the string subsequence kernel to encourage n-gram coverage in text generated from a sequence model. Our results show that determinantal beam search offers competitive performance compared to other diverse set generation strategies in the context of language generation, while providing a more general approach to optimizing for diversity.

label: emnlp
text: To approximately parse an unfamiliar language, it helps to have a treebank of a similar language. But what if the closest available treebank still has the wrong word order? We show how to (stochastically) permute the constituents of an existing dependency treebank so that its surface part-of-speech statistics approximately match those of the target language. The parameters of the permutation model can be evaluated for quality by dynamic programming and tuned by gradient descent (up to a local optimum). This optimization procedure yields trees for a new artificial language that resembles the target language. We show that delexicalized parsers for the target language can be successfully trained using such “made to order” artificial languages.

label: emnlp
text: To effectively analyze an unknown language, it is beneficial to have a treebank of a similar language. However, if the closest available treebank has an incorrect word order, we present a method for transforming the constituents of the existing dependency treebank. This transformation is achieved through stochastic permutation and aims to match the surface part-of-speech statistics of the target language. The quality of the permutation model can be evaluated and improved through dynamic programming and gradient descent optimization. The end result is an artificial language that closely resembles the target language, and we demonstrate that parsers for the target language can be trained using this "custom-made" artificial language.

label: acl
text: With the popularity of smartphones, we have witnessed the rapid proliferation of multimodal posts on various social media platforms. We observe that the multimodal sentiment expression has specific global characteristics, such as the interdependencies of objects or scenes within the image. However, most previous studies only considered the representation of a single image-text post and failed to capture the global co-occurrence characteristics of the dataset. In this paper, we propose Multi-channel Graph Neural Networks with Sentiment-awareness (MGNNS) for image-text sentiment detection. Specifically, we first encode different modalities to capture hidden representations. Then, we introduce multi-channel graph neural networks to learn multimodal representations based on the global characteristics of the dataset. Finally, we implement multimodal in-depth fusion with the multi-head attention mechanism to predict the sentiment of image-text pairs. Extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for multimodal sentiment detection.

text: With the widespread use of smartphones, we have seen a rapid increase in the number of multimodal posts on various social media platforms. Our observations reveal that multimodal sentiment expressions have specific global characteristics, such as the interdependence of objects or scenes within the image. However, previous studies have only focused on the representation of single image-text posts, neglecting the global co-occurrence characteristics of the dataset. In this paper, we present Multi-channel Graph Neural Networks with Sentiment-awareness (MGNNS) for image-text sentiment detection. Our approach first encodes different modalities to uncover hidden representations, then employs multi-channel graph neural networks to learn multimodal representations based on the global characteristics of the dataset, and finally implements multimodal fusion with a multi-head attention mechanism to predict the sentiment of image-text pairs. Our extensive experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach for multimodal sentiment detection.
