Our findings are significant for the development of POS tagging models for endangered languages.

Most research on part-of-speech (POS) tagging has been focused on high-resource languages or simulated low-resource and active learning settings. We evaluate the effectiveness of POS tagging techniques on the endangered language, Griko, using a resource of 114 narratives with sentence-level translations in Italian and gold annotations for the test set. By comparing traditional methods and those that leverage monolingual data or cross-lingual POS tags, we demonstrate that a combination of a semi-supervised approach and cross-lingual transfer is best suited for this challenging scenario, with an accuracy of 72.9%. By incorporating an active learning scheme to collect sentence-level annotations, we observe improvements of over 21 percentage points. Our results have important implications for the development of POS tagging models for endangered languages.

label: acl
text: In this paper, we focus on the problem of citing sentence generation, which entails generating a short text to capture the salient information in a cited paper and the connection between the citing and cited paper. We present BACO, a BAckground knowledge- and COntent-based framework for citing sentence generation, which considers two types of information: (1) background knowledge by leveraging structural information from a citation network; and (2) content, which represents in-depth information about what to cite and why to cite. First, a citation network is encoded to provide background knowledge. Second, we apply salience estimation to identify what to cite by estimating the importance of sentences in the cited paper. During the decoding stage, both types of information are combined to facilitate the text generation, and then we conduct a joint training for the generator and citation function classification to make the model aware of why to cite. Our experimental results show that our framework outperforms comparative baselines.

label: acl
text: The focus of this paper is on the challenge of generating a concise text that summarizes the key information from a cited paper and the relationship between the citing and cited paper. We introduce BACO, a framework for citing sentence generation that takes into account two sources of information: (1) background knowledge, obtained by analyzing the structure of a citation network; and (2) content, which provides detailed information about what to cite and why to cite. To begin, a citation network is analyzed to provide background knowledge. Next, we use salience estimation to determine what to cite by evaluating the significance of sentences in the cited paper. During the text generation process, both types of information are combined to ensure the output is accurate. Finally, we conduct a joint training of the generator and citation function classifier to ensure the model understands why to cite. Our results demonstrate that our framework outperforms comparable baselines.

label: acl
text: Understanding the multi-scale visual information in a video is essential for Video Question Answering (VideoQA). Therefore, we propose a novel Multi-Scale Progressive Attention Network (MSPAN) to achieve relational reasoning between cross-scale video information. We construct clips of different lengths to represent different scales of the video. Then, the clip-level features are aggregated into node features by using max-pool, and a graph is generated for each scale of clips. For cross-scale feature interaction, we design a message passing strategy between adjacent scale graphs, i.e., top-down scale interaction and bottom-up scale interaction. Under the question's guidance of progressive attention, we realize the fusion of all-scale video features. Experimental evaluations on three benchmarks: TGIF-QA, MSVD-QA and MSRVTT-QA show our method has achieved state-of-the-art performance.

label: acl
text: To improve Video Question Answering (VideoQA), we introduce a Multi-Scale Progressive Attention Network (MSPAN) that can effectively handle multi-scale visual information in videos. Our approach involves constructing clips of varying lengths to represent different scales of the video, aggregating clip-level features into node features, and generating graphs for each scale of clips. We then employ a message passing strategy between adjacent scale graphs for cross-scale feature interaction, with progressive attention guided by the question. This allows us to achieve the fusion of all-scale video features. Our method has been evaluated on three benchmark datasets (TGIF-QA, MSVD-QA, and MSRVTT-QA) and has achieved state-of-the-art performance.

label: naacl
text: Avoiding to rely on dataset artifacts to predict hate speech is at the cornerstone of robust and fair hate speech detection. In this paper we critically analyze lexical biases in hate speech detection via a cross-platform study, disentangling various types of spurious and authentic artifacts and analyzing their impact on out-of-distribution fairness and robustness. We experiment with existing approaches and propose simple yet surprisingly effective data-centric baselines. Our results on English data across four platforms show that distinct spurious artifacts require different treatments to ultimately attain both robustness and fairness in hate speech detection. To encourage research in this direction, we release all baseline models and the code to compute artifacts, pointing it out as a complementary and necessary addition to the data statements practice.

label: naacl
text: To ensure robust and fair hate speech detection, it is essential to avoid relying on dataset artifacts. In this paper, we conduct a cross-platform study to critically analyze lexical biases in hate speech detection. We examine various types of spurious and authentic artifacts, and analyze their impact on fairness and robustness when applied to out-of-distribution data. We experiment with existing approaches and propose simple yet effective data-centric baselines. Our results, based on English data across four platforms, demonstrate that different spurious artifacts require different treatments to achieve both robustness and fairness in hate speech detection. To further advance research in this area, we release all baseline models and the code to compute artifacts, highlighting the importance of complementary and necessary data statements practices.

label: coling
text: We present a corpus of spoken Dutch image descriptions, paired with two sets of eye-tracking data: Free viewing, where participants look at images without any particular purpose, and Description viewing, where we track eye movements while participants produce spoken descriptions of the images they are viewing. This paper describes the data collection procedure and the corpus itself, and provides an initial analysis of self-corrections in image descriptions. We also present two studies showing the potential of this data. Though these studies mainly serve as an example, we do find two interesting results: (1) the eye-tracking data for the description viewing task is more coherent than for the free-viewing task; (2) variation in image descriptions (also called `image specificity'; Jas and Parikh, 2015) is only moderately correlated across different languages. Our corpus can be used to gain a deeper understanding of the image description task, particularly how visual attention is correlated with the image description process.

label: coling
text: We present a corpus of spoken Dutch image descriptions, paired with two sets of eye-tracking data: (1) Free viewing, where participants are simply observing images without any specific goal, and (2) Description viewing, where we track their eye movements as they verbally describe the images they are viewing. This paper provides an overview of the data collection method and the corpus, and conducts an initial analysis of self-corrections in the image descriptions. Two studies are also presented to demonstrate the potential of this data. Although these studies are primarily intended to serve as examples, two interesting findings emerged: (1) the eye-tracking data for the Description viewing task is more coherent than for the Free viewing task, and (2) the variation in image descriptions (known as "image specificity"; Jas and Parikh, 2015) is only moderately correlated across different languages. Our corpus offers valuable insights into the image description task, particularly the relationship between visual attention and the image description process.

label: coling
text: Cohesion devices, e.g., reiteration, coreference, are crucial for building cohesion links across sentences. In this paper, we propose a document-level neural machine translation framework, CoDoNMT, which models cohesion devices from two perspectives: Cohesion Device Masking (CoDM) and Cohesion Attention Focusing (CoAF). In CoDM, we mask cohesion devices in the current sentence and force NMT to predict them with inter-sentential context information. A prediction task is also introduced to be jointly trained with NMT. In CoAF, we attempt to guide the model to pay exclusive attention to relevant cohesion devices in the context when translating cohesion devices in the current sentence. Such a cohesion attention focusing strategy is softly applied to the self-attention layer. Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art document-level neural machine translation baselines. Further linguistic evaluation validates the effectiveness of the proposed model in producing cohesive translations.

label: coling
text: Cohesion devices, such as reiteration and coreference, are essential for establishing links between sentences in a text. In this study, we introduce a document-level neural machine translation framework, called CoDoNMT, which models these devices from two angles: Cohesion Device Masking (CoDM) and Cohesion Attention Focusing (CoAF). CoDM involves masking the cohesion devices in a sentence and requiring the NMT to predict them using inter-sentential context information. The prediction task is integrated into the NMT training process. CoAF, on the other hand, guides the model to focus exclusively on relevant cohesion devices in the context when translating the cohesion devices in the current sentence. This is achieved by softly applying the cohesion attention focusing strategy to the self-attention layer. Our experiments on three benchmark datasets show that CoDoNMT outperforms existing document-level neural machine translation models. Additionally, the results of our linguistic evaluation demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in producing coherent translations.

label: acl
text: The wanton spread of hate speech on the internet brings great harm to society and families. It is urgent to establish and improve automatic detection and active avoidance mechanisms for hate speech. While there exist methods for hate speech detection, they stereotype words and hence suffer from inherently biased training. In other words, getting more affective features from other affective resources will significantly affect the performance of hate speech detection. In this paper, we propose a hate speech detection framework based on sentiment knowledge sharing. While extracting the affective features of the target sentence itself, we make better use of the sentiment features from external resources, and finally fuse features from different feature extraction units to detect hate speech. Experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

label: acl
text: The rampant spread of hate speech on the internet is causing significant harm to society and families. It is imperative to establish and enhance automatic detection and active avoidance mechanisms for hate speech. Currently, existing methods for detecting hate speech are limited by their reliance on stereotyped words, which results in a biased training process. To improve the performance of hate speech detection, it is necessary to incorporate affective features from external resources. In this study, we propose a hate speech detection framework that leverages sentiment knowledge sharing. Our framework extracts affective features from the target sentence, while also utilizing sentiment features from external sources. The features are then fused from different feature extraction units to accurately detect hate speech. Our experiments on two public datasets show the effectiveness of our model.

label: emnlp
text: Despite the tremendous empirical success of neural models in natural language processing, many of them lack the strong intuitions that accompany classical machine learning approaches. Recently, connections have been shown between convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and weighted finite state automata (WFSAs), leading to new interpretations and insights. In this work, we show that some recurrent neural networks also share this connection to WFSAs. We characterize this connection formally, defining rational recurrences to be recurrent hidden state update functions that can be written as the Forward calculation of a finite set of WFSAs. We show that several recent neural models use rational recurrences. Our analysis provides a fresh view of these models and facilitates devising new neural architectures that draw inspiration from WFSAs. We present one such model, which performs better than two recent baselines on language modeling and text classification. Our results demonstrate that transferring intuitions from classical models like WFSAs can be an effective approach to designing and understanding neural models.

label: emnlp
text: Despite the great empirical success of neural models in natural language processing, many still lack the strong intuition that comes with classical machine learning approaches. Recent studies have revealed a connection between convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and weighted finite state automata (WFSAs), leading to new interpretations and insights. In this work, we extend this connection to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and formally characterize the connection as "rational recurrences." This is defined as recurrent hidden state update functions that can be calculated using Forward methods with a finite set of WFSAs. Our analysis shows that several recent neural models use rational recurrences and provides a new perspective on these models. We also present a new neural architecture that draws inspiration from WFSAs and outperforms two recent baselines in language modeling and text classification. Our results demonstrate that transferring intuition from classical models like WFSAs can be an effective way to design and understand neural models.

label: acl
text: Current event-centric knowledge graphs highly rely on explicit connectives to mine relations between events. Unfortunately, due to the sparsity of connectives, these methods severely undermine the coverage of EventKGs. The lack of high-quality labelled corpora further exacerbates that problem. In this paper, we propose a knowledge projection paradigm for event relation extraction: projecting discourse knowledge to narratives by exploiting the commonalities between them. Specifically, we propose Multi-tier Knowledge Projection Network (MKPNet), which can leverage multi-tier discourse knowledge effectively for event relation extraction. In this way, the labelled data requirement is significantly reduced, and implicit event relations can be effectively extracted. Intrinsic experimental results show that MKPNet achieves the new state-of-the-art performance and extrinsic experimental results verify the value of the extracted event relations.

label: acl
text: Current event-centric knowledge graphs heavily rely on explicit connectives to extract relationships between events. However, this method is limited by the scarcity of connectives, resulting in a low coverage of EventKGs. The lack of high-quality labeled corpora exacerbates this issue. To address this, we propose a knowledge projection paradigm for event relation extraction, which projects discourse knowledge onto narratives by utilizing their similarities. Our Multi-tier Knowledge Projection Network (MKPNet) leverages multi-level discourse knowledge to extract event relations, reducing the need for labeled data and effectively extracting implicit event relations. Our experiments show that MKPNet outperforms previous methods and the extracted event relations have been verified to be valuable.

label: coling
text: Automatic evaluation of open-domain dialogs remains an unsolved problem. Existing methods do not correlate strongly with human annotations. In this paper, we present a new automated evaluation method based on the use of follow-ups. We measure the probability that a language model will continue the conversation with a fixed set of follow-ups (e.g. not really relevant here, what are you trying to say?). When compared against twelve existing methods, our new evaluation achieves the highest correlation with human evaluations.

label: coling
text: The evaluation of open-domain dialogs remains a challenge, with existing methods failing to demonstrate strong correlation with human annotations. In this study, we introduce a novel automated evaluation approach that utilizes follow-up responses. Our method evaluates the likelihood of a language model to continue a conversation with a predefined set of follow-up responses (e.g. "not relevant here," "what are you trying to say?"). Our results show that our new evaluation method outperforms twelve existing methods, achieving the highest correlation with human evaluations.

label: emnlp
text: LSTMs are powerful tools for modeling contextual information, as evidenced by their success at the task of language modeling. However, modeling contexts in very high dimensional space can lead to poor generalizability. We introduce the Pyramidal Recurrent Unit (PRU), which enables learning representations in high dimensional space with more generalization power and fewer parameters. PRUs replace the linear transformation in LSTMs with more sophisticated interactions such as pyramidal or grouped linear transformations. This architecture gives strong results on word-level language modeling while reducing parameters significantly. In particular, PRU improves the perplexity of a recent state-of-the-art language model by up to 1.3 points while learning 15-20% fewer parameters. For similar number of model parameters, PRU outperforms all previous RNN models that exploit different gating mechanisms and transformations. We provide a detailed examination of the PRU and its behavior on the language modeling tasks. Our code is open-source and available at https://sacmehta.github.io/PRU/.

label: emnlp
text: LSTMs are highly effective in modeling contextual information, as demonstrated by their success in language modeling. However, modeling contexts in high-dimensional space can result in poor generalizability. To address this issue, we introduce the Pyramidal Recurrent Unit (PRU) that enables learning representations in high-dimensional space with improved generalization power and fewer parameters. The PRU replaces the linear transformation in LSTMs with more advanced interactions such as pyramidal or grouped linear transformations. This architecture delivers outstanding results in word-level language modeling while significantly reducing the number of parameters. Specifically, PRU improves the perplexity of a state-of-the-art language model by up to 1.3 points while using 15-20% fewer parameters. Despite having a similar number of model parameters, PRU outperforms all previous RNN models that employ different gating mechanisms and transformations. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the PRU and its performance on language modeling tasks. Our code is open-source and can be accessed at https://sacmehta.github.io/PRU/.

label: emnlp
text: Referring to entities in situated dialog is a collaborative process, whereby interlocutors often expand, repair and/or replace referring expressions in an iterative process, converging on conceptual pacts of referring language use in doing so. Nevertheless, much work on exophoric reference resolution (i.e. resolution of references to entities outside of a given text) follows a literary model, whereby individual referring expressions are interpreted as unique identifiers of their referents given the state of the dialog the referring expression is initiated. In this paper, we address this collaborative nature to improve dialogic reference resolution in two ways: First, we trained a words-as-classifiers logistic regression model of word semantics and incrementally adapt the model to idiosyncratic language between dyad partners during evaluation of the dialog. We then used these semantic models to learn the general referring ability of each word, which is independent of referent features. These methods facilitate accurate automatic reference resolution in situated dialog without annotation of referring expressions, even with little background data.

label: emnlp
text: The process of referring to entities in a situated dialogue is collaborative, where interlocutors often adjust, repair, and/or replace their referring expressions in an iterative manner, ultimately reaching a shared understanding of the language used for referring. However, much of the research on exophoric reference resolution (i.e. resolving references to entities outside of the text) relies on a literary model, which assumes that each referring expression is a unique identifier of its referent, based on the state of the dialogue when the expression was used. In this paper, we aim to improve reference resolution in dialogues by addressing this collaborative nature in two ways. Firstly, we trained a logistic regression model using words as classifiers, and adapted the model to the idiosyncratic language of the dyad partners during the evaluation of the dialogue. Secondly, we used these semantic models to determine the general referring ability of each word, which is independent of the features of the referent. These methods allow for accurate automatic reference resolution in situated dialogues, without the need for annotating referring expressions, even with limited background data.

label: coling
text: As manually labelling data can be costly, some recent studies tend to augment the training data for improving the generalization power of machine learning models, known as data augmentation (DA). With the arise of pre-trained language models (PLMs), some recent works on DA try to synthesize new samples benefiting from the knowledge learned from PLM's pre-training. Along the same direction, we in this paper propose to integrate text-to-text language models and construct a new two-phase framework for augmentation: 1) a fine-tuning phase where PLMs are well adapted to downstream classification with the help of two novel schemes, and 2) a generation phase where the fine-tuned models are leveraged to create new samples for performance lifting. This paradigm opens up a new way of designing fine-tuning scheme to better serve DA in an easy-to-implement manner, and can be easily extended to other desired tasks. We evaluate our proposal on two public classification datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness with remarkable gains.

label: coling
text: As manual labeling of data can be expensive, recent studies are exploring data augmentation (DA) to improve the generalization power of machine learning models. With the emergence of pre-trained language models (PLMs), some studies are using these models to synthesize new samples that benefit from the knowledge learned during pre-training. This paper proposes a new two-phase framework for augmentation that integrates text-to-text language models. The framework consists of a fine-tuning phase, where PLMs are adapted to downstream classification through two novel schemes, and a generation phase, where the fine-tuned models are used to create new samples for improved performance. This paradigm provides a new approach to designing fine-tuning schemes for DA and can be easily extended to other tasks. The effectiveness of the proposal is demonstrated through evaluations on two public classification datasets, showing remarkable gains.

label: coling
text: Recent evaluations on bilingual lexicon extraction from specialized comparable corpora have shown contrasted performance while using word embedding models. This can be partially explained by the lack of large specialized comparable corpora to build efficient representations. Within this context, we try to answer the following questions: First, (i) among the state-of-the-art embedding models, whether trained on specialized corpora or pre-trained on large general data sets, which one is the most appropriate model for bilingual terminology extraction? Second (ii) is it worth it to combine multiple embeddings trained on different data sets? For that purpose, we propose the first systematic evaluation of different word embedding models for bilingual terminology extraction from specialized comparable corpora. We emphasize how the character-based embedding model outperforms other models on the quality of the extracted bilingual lexicons. Further more, we propose a new efficient way to combine different embedding models learned from specialized and general-domain data sets. Our approach leads to higher performance than the best individual embedding model.

label: coling
text: Recent evaluations of bilingual lexicon extraction from specialized comparable corpora have produced mixed results when using word embedding models. This can be attributed, in part, to the scarcity of large specialized comparable corpora for building effective representations. In an effort to address this issue, we aim to answer two key questions: (i) Which among the state-of-the-art embedding models, whether trained on specialized corpora or pre-trained on large general data sets, is the most appropriate for bilingual terminology extraction? (ii) Is it beneficial to combine multiple embeddings trained on different data sets? To this end, we present the first systematic evaluation of different word embedding models for bilingual terminology extraction from specialized comparable corpora. Our results highlight the superiority of the character-based embedding model in terms of the quality of extracted bilingual lexicons. Additionally, we propose a novel and efficient approach to combining different embedding models learned from specialized and general-domain data sets, which leads to higher performance than the best individual embedding model.

label: emnlp
text: This paper introduces a document grounded dataset for conversations. We define “Document Grounded Conversations” as conversations that are about the contents of a specified document. In this dataset the specified documents were Wikipedia articles about popular movies. The dataset contains 4112 conversations with an average of 21.43 turns per conversation. This positions this dataset to not only provide a relevant chat history while generating responses but also provide a source of information that the models could use. We describe two neural architectures that provide benchmark performance on the task of generating the next response. We also evaluate our models for engagement and fluency, and find that the information from the document helps in generating more engaging and fluent responses.

label: emnlp
text: This paper presents a novel dataset of document-grounded conversations. We define these conversations as those that revolve around the contents of a specified document, in this case, Wikipedia articles about popular movies. The dataset comprises 4112 conversations, with an average of 21.43 turns per conversation. This makes it an ideal resource for both providing a relevant chat history and serving as a source of information for machine learning models. We also describe two neural architectures that demonstrate benchmark performance in generating the next response. Our evaluation of the models for engagement and fluency shows that incorporating the information from the document leads to more engaging and fluent responses.

label: acl
text: Adapter-based tuning has recently arisen as an alternative to fine-tuning. It works by adding light-weight adapter modules to a pretrained language model (PrLM) and only updating the parameters of adapter modules when learning on a downstream task. As such, it adds only a few trainable parameters per new task, allowing a high degree of parameter sharing. Prior studies have shown that adapter-based tuning often achieves comparable results to fine-tuning. However, existing work only focuses on the parameter-efficient aspect of adapter-based tuning while lacking further investigation on its effectiveness. In this paper, we study the latter. We first show that adapter-based tuning better mitigates forgetting issues than fine-tuning since it yields representations with less deviation from those generated by the initial PrLM. We then empirically compare the two tuning methods on several downstream NLP tasks and settings. We demonstrate that 1) adapter-based tuning outperforms fine-tuning on low-resource and cross-lingual tasks; 2) it is more robust to overfitting and less sensitive to changes in learning rates.

label: acl
text:
Our results suggest that adapter-based tuning is a promising alternative to fine-tuning for NLP tasks.

Recently, adapter-based tuning has emerged as a viable alternative to fine-tuning in NLP. It works by adding lightweight adapter modules to a pre-trained language model (PrLM) and only updating the parameters of these modules during learning for a downstream task. This approach results in a high degree of parameter sharing, with only a few trainable parameters added per new task. Previous studies have demonstrated that adapter-based tuning can achieve comparable results to fine-tuning, but have only focused on its parameter-efficiency aspect. This paper aims to further investigate the effectiveness of adapter-based tuning. We show that it is better at mitigating forgetting issues than fine-tuning and that it yields representations with less deviation from those generated by the initial PrLM. We also compare the two tuning methods on several NLP tasks and settings, demonstrating that adapter-based tuning outperforms fine-tuning on low-resource and cross-lingual tasks and is more robust to overfitting and less sensitive to changes in learning rates. Our results suggest that adapter-based tuning is a promising alternative to fine-tuning for NLP tasks.

label: acl
text: Text in many domains involves a significant amount of named entities. Predicting the entity names is often challenging for a language model as they appear less frequent on the training corpus. In this paper, we propose a novel and effective approach to building a language model which can learn the entity names by leveraging their entity type information. We also introduce two benchmark datasets based on recipes and Java programming codes, on which we evaluate the proposed model. Experimental results show that our model achieves 52.2% better perplexity in recipe generation and 22.06% on code generation than state-of-the-art language models.

label: acl
text: Many texts in various domains contain a considerable number of named entities, which can prove difficult for language models to predict as they tend to appear less frequently in the training corpus. In this paper, we present a new and effective approach for building a language model that can learn entity names by utilizing their entity type information. Additionally, we establish two benchmark datasets, one based on recipes and the other on Java programming codes, to evaluate our proposed model. Our experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art language models with a 52.2% improvement in perplexity for recipe generation and a 22.06% improvement for code generation.

label: coling
text: Cloze-style reading comprehension has been a popular task for measuring the progress of natural language understanding in recent years. In this paper, we design a novel multi-perspective framework, which can be seen as the joint training of heterogeneous experts and aggregate context information from different perspectives. Each perspective is modeled by a simple aggregation module. The outputs of multiple aggregation modules are fed into a one-timestep pointer network to get the final answer. At the same time, to tackle the problem of insufficient labeled data, we propose an efficient sampling mechanism to automatically generate more training examples by matching the distribution of candidates between labeled and unlabeled data. We conduct our experiments on a recently released cloze-test dataset CLOTH (Xie et al., 2017), which consists of nearly 100k questions designed by professional teachers. Results show that our method achieves new state-of-the-art performance over previous strong baselines.

label: coling
text: Cloze-style reading comprehension has become a popular method for evaluating progress in natural language understanding in recent years. In this paper, we present a novel multi-perspective framework that trains heterogeneous experts and aggregates context information from multiple perspectives. The framework is comprised of simple aggregation modules, each modeling a different perspective, which feed into a one-timestep pointer network to produce the final answer. To address the challenge of limited labeled data, we introduce an efficient sampling mechanism that generates additional training examples by aligning the distribution of candidates between labeled and unlabeled data. Our experiments are conducted on the CLOTH dataset (Xie et al., 2017), which contains nearly 100k questions created by professional teachers, and our results demonstrate that our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods.

label: acl
text: Fact-checking is an essential tool to mitigate the spread of misinformation and disinformation. We introduce the task of fact-checking in dialogue, which is a relatively unexplored area. We construct DialFact, a testing benchmark dataset of 22,245 annotated conversational claims, paired with pieces of evidence from Wikipedia. There are three sub-tasks in DialFact: 1) Verifiable claim detection task distinguishes whether a response carries verifiable factual information; 2) Evidence retrieval task retrieves the most relevant Wikipedia snippets as evidence; 3) Claim verification task predicts a dialogue response to be supported, refuted, or not enough information. We found that existing fact-checking models trained on non-dialogue data like FEVER fail to perform well on our task, and thus, we propose a simple yet data-efficient solution to effectively improve fact-checking performance in dialogue. We point out unique challenges in DialFact such as handling the colloquialisms, coreferences, and retrieval ambiguities in the error analysis to shed light on future research in this direction.

label: acl
text: Fact-checking is a crucial tool for reducing the spread of misinformation and disinformation. We present a new area of research: fact-checking in dialogue. To support this research, we have created DialFact, a benchmark dataset of 22,245 annotated conversational claims, paired with evidence from Wikipedia. DialFact includes three sub-tasks: 1) Verifiable claim detection, which determines if a response contains verifiable factual information; 2) Evidence retrieval, which identifies the most relevant Wikipedia snippets as evidence; and 3) Claim verification, which predicts if a dialogue response is supported, refuted, or if there is not enough information to make a determination. Our findings indicate that existing fact-checking models trained on non-dialogue data, such as FEVER, are not effective in our task. As a result, we propose a simple, data-efficient solution to improve fact-checking performance in dialogue. We also identify unique challenges in DialFact, such as handling colloquialisms, coreferences, and retrieval ambiguities, and highlight these challenges to guide future research in this area.

label: emnlp
text: We address fine-grained multilingual language identification: providing a language code for every token in a sentence, including codemixed text containing multiple languages. Such text is prevalent online, in documents, social media, and message boards. We show that a feed-forward network with a simple globally constrained decoder can accurately and rapidly label both codemixed and monolingual text in 100 languages and 100 language pairs. This model outperforms previously published multilingual approaches in terms of both accuracy and speed, yielding an 800x speed-up and a 19.5% averaged absolute gain on three codemixed datasets. It furthermore outperforms several benchmark systems on monolingual language identification.

label: emnlp
text: We tackle the challenge of fine-grained multilingual language identification by offering a language code for every token in a sentence, including codemixed text that contains multiple languages. This type of text is commonly found in various forms, such as online documents, social media posts, and message board conversations. Our results demonstrate that a feed-forward network with a globally constrained decoder can accurately and quickly label both codemixed and monolingual text in 100 languages and 100 language pairs. This model outperforms previous multilingual approaches in terms of accuracy and speed, resulting in an 800x speed increase and a 19.5% average absolute improvement on three codemixed datasets. Additionally, it surpasses several benchmark systems in monolingual language identification.

label: coling
text: Successful Machine Learning based Named Entity Recognition models could fail on texts from some special domains, for instance, Chinese addresses and e-commerce titles, where requires adequate background knowledge. Such texts are also difficult for human annotators. In fact, we can obtain some potentially helpful information from correlated texts, which have some common entities, to help the text understanding. Then, one can easily reason out the correct answer by referencing correlated samples. In this paper, we suggest enhancing NER models with correlated samples. We draw correlated samples by the sparse BM25 retriever from large-scale in-domain unlabeled data. To explicitly simulate the human reasoning process, we perform a training-free entity type calibrating by majority voting. To capture correlation features in the training stage, we suggest to model correlated samples by the transformer-based multi-instance cross-encoder. Empirical results on datasets of the above two domains show the efficacy of our methods.

label: coling
text: Successful Named Entity Recognition (NER) models based on Machine Learning may struggle with texts from specific domains, such as Chinese addresses and e-commerce titles, which require specialized knowledge. These texts are also challenging for human annotators. However, we can leverage information from related texts, which share common entities, to improve text understanding. By referencing these correlated samples, one can deduce the correct answer. In this paper, we propose a method to enhance NER models by incorporating correlated samples. We extract these samples using the sparse BM25 retriever from a large-scale in-domain unlabeled data set. To simulate the human reasoning process, we perform a training-free entity type calibration using majority voting. To capture correlation features during the training phase, we suggest using a transformer-based multi-instance cross-encoder. Our results on datasets from the aforementioned domains demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

label: naacl
text: Target-dependent classification tasks, such as aspect-level sentiment analysis, perform fine-grained classifications towards specific targets. Semantic compositions over tree structures are promising for such tasks, as they can potentially capture long-distance interactions between targets and their contexts. However, previous work that operates on tree structures resorts to syntactic parsers or Treebank annotations, which are either subject to noise in informal texts or highly expensive to obtain. To address above issues, we propose a reinforcement learning based approach, which automatically induces target-specific sentence representations over tree structures. The underlying model is a RNN encoder-decoder that explores possible binary tree structures and a reward mechanism that encourages structures that improve performances on downstream tasks. We evaluate our approach on two benchmark tasks: firm-specific cumulative abnormal return prediction (based on formal news texts) and aspect-level sentiment analysis (based on informal social media texts). Experimental results show that our model gives superior performances compared to previous work that operates on parsed trees. Moreover, our approach gives some intuitions on how target-specific sentence representations can be achieved from its word constituents.

text: Target-dependent classification tasks, such as aspect-level sentiment analysis, perform fine-grained classifications on specific targets. Semantic compositions over tree structures have shown promise for these tasks as they can capture long-distance interactions between targets and their contexts. However, previous work that uses tree structures requires either a syntactic parser or Treebank annotations, which can be noisy in informal texts or expensive to obtain. To overcome these challenges, we propose a reinforcement learning-based approach that automatically induces target-specific sentence representations over tree structures. Our model is a RNN encoder-decoder that explores binary tree structures and is guided by a reward mechanism that improves performance on downstream tasks. We evaluate our approach on two benchmark tasks: predicting firm-specific cumulative abnormal returns (using formal news texts) and aspect-level sentiment analysis (using informal social media texts). Our results show that our model outperforms previous approaches that use parsed trees and provide insights into how target-specific sentence representations can be derived from word constituents.

label: naacl
text: Hate speech is plaguing the cyberspace along with user-generated content. Adding counter speech has become an effective way to combat hate speech online. Existing datasets and models target either (a) hate speech or (b) hate and counter speech but disregard the context. This paper investigates the role of context in the annotation and detection of online hate and counter speech, where context is defined as the preceding comment in a conversation thread. We created a context-aware dataset for a 3-way classification task on Reddit comments: hate speech, counter speech, or neutral. Our analyses indicate that context is critical to identify hate and counter speech: human judgments change for most comments depending on whether we show annotators the context. A linguistic analysis draws insights into the language people use to express hate and counter speech. Experimental results show that neural networks obtain significantly better results if context is taken into account. We also present qualitative error analyses shedding light into (a) when and why context is beneficial and (b) the remaining errors made by our best model when context is taken into account.

label: naacl
text: Hate speech is becoming a growing problem in cyberspace, especially with the rise of user-generated content. To combat this issue, adding counter speech has proven to be an effective solution. However, existing datasets and models either focus on identifying hate speech or hate and counter speech, but ignore the importance of context. This paper explores the significance of context in the annotation and detection of online hate and counter speech. Context is defined as the preceding comment in a conversation thread. To better understand the role of context, we created a context-aware dataset for a 3-way classification task on Reddit comments: hate speech, counter speech, or neutral. Our analysis shows that context plays a critical role in identifying hate and counter speech, as human judgments can change based on the context. Additionally, a linguistic analysis provides insights into the language used to express hate and counter speech. The results of our experiments show that neural networks perform significantly better when context is taken into account. Finally, we conduct qualitative error analyses to understand when and why context is beneficial and to identify the remaining errors made by our best model when context is considered.

label: coling
text: Stance detection aims to identify the attitude from an opinion towards a certain target. Despite the significant progress on this task, it is extremely time-consuming and budget-unfriendly to collect sufficient high-quality labeled data for every new target under fully-supervised learning, whereas unlabeled data can be collected easier. Therefore, this paper is devoted to few-shot stance detection and investigating how to achieve satisfactory results in semi-supervised settings. As a target-oriented task, the core idea of semi-supervised few-shot stance detection is to make better use of target-relevant information from labeled and unlabeled data. Therefore, we develop a novel target-aware semi-supervised framework. Specifically, we propose a target-aware contrastive learning objective to learn more distinguishable representations for different targets. Such an objective can be easily applied with or without unlabeled data. Furthermore, to thoroughly exploit the unlabeled data and facilitate the model to learn target-relevant stance features in the opinion content, we explore a simple but effective target-aware consistency regularization combined with a self-training strategy. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach can achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark datasets in the few-shot setting.

label: coling
text: Stance detection aims to identify the attitude expressed in an opinion towards a specific target. Despite significant advancements in this field, collecting sufficient high-quality labeled data for every new target under fully-supervised learning is extremely time-consuming and cost-prohibitive. On the other hand, collecting unlabeled data is relatively easier. This paper focuses on few-shot stance detection and examines how to obtain satisfactory results in semi-supervised settings. As a target-oriented task, the core idea of semi-supervised few-shot stance detection is to utilize target-related information from both labeled and unlabeled data. To achieve this, we present a novel target-aware semi-supervised framework. Our framework includes a target-aware contrastive learning objective that helps to learn distinguishable representations for different targets. This objective can be easily implemented with or without unlabeled data. Additionally, to maximize the use of unlabeled data and encourage the model to learn target-related stance features in the opinion content, we employ a simple but effective target-aware consistency regularization and self-training strategy. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmark datasets in the few-shot setting, as demonstrated by our experimental results.

label: acl
text: Knowledge distillation has been proven to be effective in model acceleration and compression. It transfers knowledge from a large neural network to a small one by using the large neural network predictions as targets of the small neural network. But this way ignores the knowledge inside the large neural networks, e.g., parameters. Our preliminary study as well as the recent success in pre-training suggests that transferring parameters are more effective in distilling knowledge. In this paper, we propose Weight Distillation to transfer the knowledge in parameters of a large neural network to a small neural network through a parameter generator. On the WMT16 En-Ro, NIST12 Zh-En, and WMT14 En-De machine translation tasks, our experiments show that weight distillation learns a small network that is 1.88 2.94x faster than the large network but with competitive BLEU performance. When fixing the size of small networks, weight distillation outperforms knowledge distillation by 0.51 1.82 BLEU points.

label: acl
text:
The proposed weight distillation method is effective in transferring knowledge from large neural networks to small ones, leading to improved acceleration and compression.

 Knowledge distillation has been shown to effectively accelerate and compress models by transferring knowledge from a large neural network to a smaller one using the large network's predictions as targets for the small network. However, this approach ignores the valuable knowledge contained within the large network's parameters. Our preliminary study and recent advancements in pre-training suggest that transferring parameters is more effective in distilling knowledge. In this paper, we introduce Weight Distillation, a method for transferring the knowledge in a large network's parameters to a small network through a parameter generator. Our experiments on the WMT16 En-Ro, NIST12 Zh-En, and WMT14 En-De machine translation tasks demonstrate that weight distillation learns a small network that is 1.88 to 2.94 times faster than the large network while maintaining competitive BLEU performance. When the size of the small network is fixed, weight distillation outperforms knowledge distillation by 0.51 to 1.82 BLEU points. This demonstrates the effectiveness of weight distillation in transferring knowledge from large neural networks to small ones, resulting in improved acceleration and compression.

label: acl
text: We investigate the problem of Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) and present a new framework named Tail-to-Tail (TtT) non-autoregressive sequence prediction to address the deep issues hidden in CGEC. Considering that most tokens are correct and can be conveyed directly from source to target, and the error positions can be estimated and corrected based on the bidirectional context information, thus we employ a BERT-initialized Transformer Encoder as the backbone model to conduct information modeling and conveying. Considering that only relying on the same position substitution cannot handle the variable-length correction cases, various operations such substitution, deletion, insertion, and local paraphrasing are required jointly. Therefore, a Conditional Random Fields (CRF) layer is stacked on the up tail to conduct non-autoregressive sequence prediction by modeling the token dependencies. Since most tokens are correct and easily to be predicted/conveyed to the target, then the models may suffer from a severe class imbalance issue. To alleviate this problem, focal loss penalty strategies are integrated into the loss functions. Moreover, besides the typical fix-length error correction datasets, we also construct a variable-length corpus to conduct experiments. Experimental results on standard datasets, especially on the variable-length datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of TtT in terms of sentence-level Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Measure on tasks of error Detection and Correction.

label: acl
text: We investigate the problem of Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) and propose a new framework called Tail-to-Tail (TtT) non-autoregressive sequence prediction to address the deep challenges in CGEC. We utilize a BERT-initialized Transformer Encoder as the backbone model to model and convey information, considering that most tokens are correct and can be directly conveyed from source to target, and the error positions can be estimated and corrected based on bidirectional context information. To handle the variable-length correction cases, we stack a Conditional Random Fields (CRF) layer on the up tail to model token dependencies and conduct non-autoregressive sequence prediction through various operations such as substitution, deletion, insertion, and local paraphrasing. To mitigate the severe class imbalance issue, we integrate focal loss penalty strategies into the loss functions. We also construct a variable-length corpus to conduct experiments, in addition to using typical fixed-length error correction datasets. Our experimental results on standard datasets, particularly on the variable-length datasets, show that TtT is effective in terms of sentence-level Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Measure for both error Detection and Correction tasks.

label: coling
text: This paper describes a personalized text retrieval algorithm that helps language learners select the most suitable reading material in terms of vocabulary complexity. The user first rates their knowledge of a small set of words, chosen by a graph-based active learning model. The system trains a complex word identification model on this set, and then applies the model to find texts that contain the desired proportion of new, challenging, and familiar vocabulary. In an evaluation on learners of Chinese as a foreign language, we show that this algorithm is effective in identifying simpler texts for low-proficiency learners, and more challenging ones for high-proficiency learners.

label: coling
text: The present study outlines a personalized text retrieval algorithm that assists language learners in selecting the most appropriate reading material based on vocabulary complexity. The algorithm begins by having the user rate their knowledge of a carefully selected set of words, chosen through a graph-based active learning model. The system then trains a sophisticated word identification model using this set and applies it to find texts that contain the desired balance of new, challenging, and familiar vocabulary. Through an evaluation with learners of Chinese as a foreign language, it was demonstrated that the algorithm is effective in identifying simpler texts for low-proficiency learners and more challenging texts for high-proficiency learners.

label: naacl
text: Dialogue summarization is receiving increasing attention from researchers due to its extraordinary difficulty and unique application value. We observe that current dialogue summarization models have flaws that may not be well exposed by frequently used metrics such as ROUGE. In our paper, we re-evaluate 18 categories of metrics in terms of four dimensions: coherence, consistency, fluency and relevance, as well as a unified human evaluation of various models for the first time. Some noteworthy trends which are different from the conventional summarization tasks are identified. We will release DialSummEval, a multi-faceted dataset of human judgments containing the outputs of 14 models on SAMSum.

label: naacl
text: Researchers in the field of dialogue summarization are becoming increasingly interested in this area due to its exceptional difficulty and its unique value for application. We have found that current models for dialogue summarization have flaws that are not well exposed by commonly used metrics such as ROUGE. In our paper, we re-evaluate 18 categories of metrics across four dimensions: coherence, consistency, fluency, and relevance. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive human evaluation of various models for the first time. Our findings highlight some noteworthy trends that differ from conventional summarization tasks. We will also be releasing DialSummEval, a multi-faceted dataset of human judgments that includes the outputs of 14 models on the SAMSum dataset.

label: emnlp
text: There have been several recent attempts to improve the accuracy of grammar induction systems by bounding the recursive complexity of the induction model. Modern depth-bounded grammar inducers have been shown to be more accurate than early unbounded PCFG inducers, but this technique has never been compared against unbounded induction within the same system, in part because most previous depth-bounding models are built around sequence models, the complexity of which grows exponentially with the maximum allowed depth. The present work instead applies depth bounds within a chart-based Bayesian PCFG inducer, where bounding can be switched on and off, and then samples trees with or without bounding. Results show that depth-bounding is indeed significantly effective in limiting the search space of the inducer and thereby increasing accuracy of resulting parsing model, independent of the contribution of modern Bayesian induction techniques. Moreover, parsing results on English, Chinese and German show that this bounded model is able to produce parse trees more accurately than or competitively with state-of-the-art constituency grammar induction models.

text: There have been recent efforts to enhance the accuracy of grammar induction systems by limiting the recursive complexity of the induction model. Modern depth-bounded grammar inducers have been proven to be more accurate than early unbounded PCFG inducers. However, this technique has not been compared to unbounded induction within the same system. This is partly because previous depth-bounded models were built around sequence models, which become more complex as the maximum allowed depth increases. In this study, depth bounds are applied within a chart-based Bayesian PCFG inducer, where the bounds can be turned on and off, and trees are sampled with or without bounds. Results indicate that depth-bounding effectively reduces the search space of the inducer and increases the accuracy of the resulting parsing model, regardless of the contribution of modern Bayesian induction techniques. Additionally, parsing results on English, Chinese, and German reveal that this bounded model outperforms or is competitive with the state-of-the-art constituency grammar induction models.

label: emnlp
text: Existing question answering (QA) datasets fail to train QA systems to perform complex reasoning and provide explanations for answers. We introduce HotpotQA, a new dataset with 113k Wikipedia-based question-answer pairs with four key features: (1) the questions require finding and reasoning over multiple supporting documents to answer; (2) the questions are diverse and not constrained to any pre-existing knowledge bases or knowledge schemas; (3) we provide sentence-level supporting facts required for reasoning, allowing QA systems to reason with strong supervision and explain the predictions; (4) we offer a new type of factoid comparison questions to test QA systems' ability to extract relevant facts and perform necessary comparison. We show that HotpotQA is challenging for the latest QA systems, and the supporting facts enable models to improve performance and make explainable predictions.

label: emnlp
text: Existing question answering datasets are inadequate in training QA systems to perform complex reasoning and provide explanations for their answers. To address this issue, we present HotpotQA, a new dataset that features 113k Wikipedia-based question-answer pairs. HotpotQA has four key characteristics: (1) it requires finding and reasoning over multiple supporting documents to answer the questions; (2) the questions are diverse and not limited to any pre-existing knowledge bases or knowledge schemas; (3) it provides sentence-level supporting facts for reasoning, allowing QA systems to make explainable predictions with strong supervision; and (4) it includes a new type of factoid comparison questions to test the ability of QA systems to extract relevant facts and perform necessary comparisons. Our results demonstrate that HotpotQA presents a challenging task for the latest QA systems, and the supporting facts enable models to improve their performance and make more transparent predictions.

label: coling
text: As a fundamental natural language processing task and one of core knowledge extraction techniques, named entity recognition (NER) is widely used to extract information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER in which the named entities (NEs) are nested with each other. However, most of the previous studies on nested NER usually apply linear structure to model the nested NEs which are actually accommodated in a hierarchical structure. Thus in order to address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a sentence as a holistic structure, then we propose a holistic structure parsing algorithm to disclose the entire NEs once for all. Besides, there is no research on applying corpus-level information to NER currently. To make up for the loss of this information, we introduce Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics for even better performance by holistic modeling from sentence-level to corpus-level. Experiments show that our model yields promising results on widely-used benchmarks which approach or even achieve state-of-the-art. Further empirical studies show that our proposed corpus-aware features can substantially improve NER domain adaptation, which demonstrates the surprising advantage of our proposed corpus-level holistic structure modeling.

label: coling
text: Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental natural language processing task and a core knowledge extraction technique that is widely used to extract information from texts for downstream tasks. Nested NER is a branch of NER that involves the extraction of named entities (NEs) that are nested within each other. However, most previous studies on nested NER have applied linear structures to model the nested NEs, despite the fact that these entities are actually hierarchical in nature. To address this mismatch, this work models the full nested NEs in a sentence as a holistic structure and proposes a holistic structure parsing algorithm to extract all NEs in a single pass. Additionally, there has been no research on the application of corpus-level information to NER. To overcome this, the work introduces Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other frequency features from corpus-aware statistics to enhance performance by modeling the sentence-level and corpus-level holistically. Experiments show promising results on widely-used benchmarks, approaching or even achieving state-of-the-art performance. Further empirical studies demonstrate the surprising advantage of our proposed corpus-level holistic structure modeling, as it substantially improves NER domain adaptation.

label: acl
text: Splitting and rephrasing a complex sentence into several shorter sentences that convey the same meaning is a challenging problem in NLP. We show that while vanilla seq2seq models can reach high scores on the proposed benchmark (Narayan et al., 2017), they suffer from memorization of the training set which contains more than 89% of the unique simple sentences from the validation and test sets. To aid this, we present a new train-development-test data split and neural models augmented with a copy-mechanism, outperforming the best reported baseline by 8.68 BLEU and fostering further progress on the task.

label: acl
text: Splitting a complex sentence into several shorter sentences that convey the same meaning is a challenging problem in NLP. Vanilla seq2seq models can achieve high scores on the proposed benchmark (Narayan et al., 2017), but they have a tendency to memorize the training set. This training set contains over 89% of the unique simple sentences from the validation and test sets. To address this issue, we propose a new train-development-test data split and augment neural models with a copy-mechanism. This results in an improvement of 8.68 BLEU over the best reported baseline and opens the door for further progress on this task.

label: coling
text: The task of obfuscating writing style using sequence models has previously been investigated under the framework of obfuscation-by-transfer, where the input text is explicitly rewritten in another style. A side effect of this framework are the frequent major alterations to the semantic content of the input. In this work, we propose obfuscation-by-invariance, and investigate to what extent models trained to be explicitly style-invariant preserve semantics. We evaluate our architectures in parallel and non-parallel settings, and compare automatic and human evaluations on the obfuscated sentences. Our experiments show that the performance of a style classifier can be reduced to chance level, while the output is evaluated to be of equal quality to models applying style-transfer. Additionally, human evaluation indicates a trade-off between the level of obfuscation and the observed quality of the output in terms of meaning preservation and grammaticality.

label: coling
text: The task of obscuring writing style using sequence models has been explored in the past within the framework of obfuscation-by-transfer, where the input text is reworded in a different style. However, this framework often results in significant changes to the semantic content of the input. In this study, we introduce obfuscation-by-invariance and examine the extent to which models trained to be explicitly style-invariant preserve semantic content. We evaluate our models using both parallel and non-parallel settings and compare the results of automatic and human evaluations of the obfuscated sentences. Our experiments demonstrate that the performance of a style classifier can be reduced to chance level while maintaining equal quality to models using style-transfer. Furthermore, human evaluation reveals a trade-off between the level of obfuscation and the quality of the output in terms of meaning preservation and grammaticality.

label: naacl
text: Automatic summarization methods are efficient but can suffer from low quality. In comparison, manual summarization is expensive but produces higher quality. Can humans and AI collaborate to improve summarization performance? In similar text generation tasks (e.g., machine translation), human-AI collaboration in the form of “post-editing” AI-generated text reduces human workload and improves the quality of AI output. Therefore, we explored whether post-editing offers advantages in text summarization. Specifically, we conducted an experiment with 72 participants, comparing post-editing provided summaries with manual summarization for summary quality, human efficiency, and user experience on formal (XSum news) and informal (Reddit posts) text. This study sheds valuable insights on when post-editing is useful for text summarization: it helped in some cases (e.g., when participants lacked domain knowledge) but not in others (e.g., when provided summaries include inaccurate information). Participants' different editing strategies and needs for assistance offer implications for future human-AI summarization systems.

label: naacl
text: Automatic summarization methods are efficient but can result in low-quality output. On the other hand, manual summarization is more expensive but produces higher-quality results. This raises the question of whether humans and AI can collaborate to improve summarization performance. In other text generation tasks, such as machine translation, human-AI collaboration in the form of post-editing has been shown to reduce human workload and improve the quality of AI output. To investigate the potential benefits of post-editing in text summarization, we conducted an experiment with 72 participants, comparing post-edited summaries to manual summarization in terms of quality, human efficiency, and user experience for both formal (XSum news) and informal (Reddit posts) text. Our study provides valuable insights into the usefulness of post-editing in text summarization, revealing that it can be beneficial in some cases (e.g., when participants lack domain knowledge), but not in others (e.g., when provided summaries contain inaccurate information). Our findings regarding participants' different editing strategies and needs for assistance have implications for the design of future human-AI summarization systems.

label: acl
text: Existed pre-training methods either focus on single-modal tasks or multi-modal tasks, and cannot effectively adapt to each other. They can only utilize single-modal data (i.e., text or image) or limited multi-modal data (i.e., image-text pairs). In this work, we propose a UNIfied-MOdal pre-training architecture, namely UNIMO, which can effectively adapt to both single-modal and multi-modal understanding and generation tasks. Large scale of free text corpus and image collections are utilized to improve the capability of visual and textual understanding, and cross-modal contrastive learning (CMCL) is leveraged to align the textual and visual information into a unified semantic space, over a corpus of image-text pairs augmented with related images and texts. With the help of rich non-paired single-modal data, our model is able to learn more generalizable representations, by allowing textual knowledge and visual knowledge to enhance each other in the unified semantic space. The experimental results show that UNIMO greatly improves the performance of several single-modal and multi-modal downstream tasks. Our code and pre-trained models are public at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/Research/tree/master/NLP/UNIMO.

label: acl
text: Existing pre-training techniques either concentrate on single-modal or multi-modal tasks, but cannot effectively adapt to both. They can only utilize single-modal data (text or image) or limited multi-modal data (image-text pairs). In this work, we present a UNIfied-MOdal pre-training architecture, UNIMO, which can effectively adapt to both single-modal and multi-modal understanding and generation tasks. This is achieved by leveraging large-scale free text corpus and image collections to improve visual and textual understanding and using cross-modal contrastive learning (CMCL) to align the textual and visual information into a unified semantic space, using a corpus of image-text pairs augmented with related images and texts. With the help of rich non-paired single-modal data, our model is able to learn more generalizable representations by allowing textual and visual knowledge to enhance each other in the unified semantic space. The results of our experiments demonstrate that UNIMO significantly improves the performance of various single-modal and multi-modal downstream tasks. Our code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/Research/tree/master/NLP/UNIMO.

label: coling
text: Elastic weight consolidation (EWC, Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) is a promising approach to addressing catastrophic forgetting in sequential training. We find that the effect of EWC can diminish when fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained language models on different datasets. We present two simple objective functions to mitigate this problem by rescaling the components of EWC. Experiments on natural language inference and fact-checking tasks indicate that our methods require much smaller values for the trade-off parameters to achieve results comparable to EWC.

label: coling
text: Elastic weight consolidation (EWC, Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) is a promising solution to mitigating catastrophic forgetting during sequential training. Our findings suggest that the efficacy of EWC may be reduced when fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained language models on different datasets. To address this issue, we propose two simple objective functions that rescale the components of EWC. Our experiments on natural language inference and fact-checking tasks demonstrate that our methods require much smaller values for the trade-off parameters to achieve comparable results to EWC.

label: coling
text: Semantic role labeling (SRL) is to recognize the predicate-argument structure of a sentence, including subtasks of predicate disambiguation and argument labeling. Previous studies usually formulate the entire SRL problem into two or more subtasks. For the first time, this paper introduces an end-to-end neural model which unifiedly tackles the predicate disambiguation and the argument labeling in one shot. Using a biaffine scorer, our model directly predicts all semantic role labels for all given word pairs in the sentence without relying on any syntactic parse information. Specifically, we augment the BiLSTM encoder with a non-linear transformation to further distinguish the predicate and the argument in a given sentence, and model the semantic role labeling process as a word pair classification task by employing the biaffine attentional mechanism. Though the proposed model is syntax-agnostic with local decoder, it outperforms the state-of-the-art syntax-aware SRL systems on the CoNLL-2008, 2009 benchmarks for both English and Chinese. To our best knowledge, we report the first syntax-agnostic SRL model that surpasses all known syntax-aware models.

label: coling
text: The paper presents a novel end-to-end neural model that unifies the tasks of predicate disambiguation and argument labeling in semantic role labeling (SRL). Unlike previous studies, which have approached SRL as multiple subtasks, this model directly predicts all semantic role labels for all word pairs in a sentence without relying on any syntactic parse information. The model uses a biaffine scorer and is augmented with a non-linear transformation to distinguish between predicates and arguments. The results show that, despite being syntax-agnostic, the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art syntax-aware SRL systems on the CoNLL-2008 and 2009 benchmarks for both English and Chinese. This is the first syntax-agnostic SRL model to surpass all known syntax-aware models.

label: emnlp
text: Event detection (ED) and word sense disambiguation (WSD) are two similar tasks in that they both involve identifying the classes (i.e. event types or word senses) of some word in a given sentence. It is thus possible to extract the knowledge hidden in the data for WSD, and utilize it to improve the performance on ED. In this work, we propose a method to transfer the knowledge learned on WSD to ED by matching the neural representations learned for the two tasks. Our experiments on two widely used datasets for ED demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

label: emnlp
text: Event detection and word sense disambiguation are similar in nature as they both involve identifying the class or type of a specific word in a sentence. By extracting the knowledge from the data for WSD, we can improve the performance of ED. Our proposed method transfers the knowledge learned from WSD to ED by matching the neural representations of the two tasks. Our experiments on two commonly used datasets for ED show the effectiveness of our proposed method.

label: naacl
text: In empathetic conversations, humans express their empathy to others with empathetic intents. However, most existing empathetic conversational methods suffer from a lack of empathetic intents, which leads to monotonous empathy. To address the bias of the empathetic intents distribution between empathetic dialogue models and humans, we propose a novel model to generate empathetic responses with human-consistent empathetic intents, EmpHi for short. Precisely, EmpHi learns the distribution of potential empathetic intents with a discrete latent variable, then combines both implicit and explicit intent representation to generate responses with various empathetic intents. Experiments show that EmpHi outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of empathy, relevance, and diversity on both automatic and human evaluation. Moreover, the case studies demonstrate the high interpretability and outstanding performance of our model.

label: naacl
text: In empathetic conversations, humans express empathy towards others with empathetic intentions. However, many existing empathetic conversational methods struggle with a lack of empathetic intentions, resulting in monotonous empathy. To overcome this bias in the distribution of empathetic intentions between empathetic dialogue models and humans, we introduce a novel model, EmpHi, that generates empathetic responses with human-consistent empathetic intentions. EmpHi learns the distribution of potential empathetic intentions through a discrete latent variable and combines both implicit and explicit intent representation to generate responses with diverse empathetic intentions. Our experiments demonstrate that EmpHi outperforms current state-of-the-art models in terms of empathy, relevance, and diversity, as evaluated both automatically and by humans. Additionally, case studies highlight the high interpretability and exceptional performance of our model.

label: emnlp
text: A hallmark of variational autoencoders (VAEs) for text processing is their combination of powerful encoder-decoder models, such as LSTMs, with simple latent distributions, typically multivariate Gaussians. These models pose a difficult optimization problem: there is an especially bad local optimum where the variational posterior always equals the prior and the model does not use the latent variable at all, a kind of “collapse” which is encouraged by the KL divergence term of the objective. In this work, we experiment with another choice of latent distribution, namely the von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, which places mass on the surface of the unit hypersphere. With this choice of prior and posterior, the KL divergence term now only depends on the variance of the vMF distribution, giving us the ability to treat it as a fixed hyperparameter. We show that doing so not only averts the KL collapse, but consistently gives better likelihoods than Gaussians across a range of modeling conditions, including recurrent language modeling and bag-of-words document modeling. An analysis of the properties of our vMF representations shows that they learn richer and more nuanced structures in their latent representations than their Gaussian counterparts.

label: emnlp
text: The hallmark of VAEs for text processing is the combination of powerful encoder-decoder models, such as LSTMs, with simple latent distributions, typically multivariate Gaussians. However, these models pose a difficult optimization problem, leading to a "collapse" where the variational posterior always equals the prior and the model does not use the latent variable. In this study, we experiment with using the von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, which places mass on the surface of the unit hypersphere, as a latent distribution. This choice of prior and posterior enables us to treat the KL divergence term as a fixed hyperparameter, only depending on the variance of the vMF distribution. The results show that this approach not only prevents the KL collapse but also consistently leads to better likelihoods compared to Gaussians in various modeling conditions, including recurrent language modeling and bag-of-words document modeling. Additionally, the analysis of our vMF representations demonstrates that they learn more nuanced and rich structures in their latent representations than Gaussian counterparts.

label: coling
text: The variational encoder-decoder (VED) encodes source information as a set of random variables using a neural network, which in turn is decoded into target data using another neural network.
